When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. Lucy and her father were living at the Amberson Hotel, while Morgan got his small machine-shops built in a western outskirt of the town; and George grumbled about the shabbiness and the old-fashioned look of the hotel, though it was “still the best in the place, of course.” He remonstrated with his grandfather, declaring that the whole Amberson Estate would be getting “run-down and out-at-heel, if things weren’t taken in hand pretty soon.” He urged the general need of rebuilding, renovating, varnishing, and lawsuits. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

I will have to rise and fill it, then once more in the fragrance of My Lady Nicotine, I will sit and dream the old dreams over, and think, too, of the true friend at home awaiting my return in June for the summer vacation. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. Lucy and her father were living at the Amberson Hotel, while Morgan got his small machine-shops built in a western outskirt of the town; and George grumbled about the shabbiness and the old-fashioned look of the hotel, though it was “still the best in the place, of course.” He remonstrated with his grandfather, declaring that the whole Amberson Estate would be getting “run-down and out-at-heel, if things weren’t taken in hand pretty soon.” He urged the general need of rebuilding, renovating, varnishing, and lawsuits. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

Ellery Vane came home in the first week of October, after an absence of three years and some months, and he came home with a mustache. It was not a large mustache, nor a dark one; in certain lights it was not visible at all, and in others it gave to his upper lip merely the effect of having been insufficiently attended to. But he was conscious of it at every moment, as a man newly knighted is conscious of his title, and he touched it frequently, with the side of his forefinger, in a manner he had acquired from a Hungarian gentleman upon the Boulevard Saint-Michel.

He had been in Paris "studying architecture," as his family put it to callers, though Ellery himself preferred to say that he had been "living." His letters home had borne this out. They had been long letters, written upon thin foreign paper in a hand that grew larger and more sloping as the months went by, and they had dealt principally with cafés, with the opinions of persons named Achille and Bertrand upon the subject of art, and with Ellery's own opinions upon the subject of nearly everything. His mother had read them aloud at Sunday dinners, and his Aunt Lavinia Gilmore, who lived three squares farther out upon Fennimore Street, had borrowed them and read them aloud at Sunday dinners of her own. Thus it happened that the Gilmore family knew a great deal about Achille and Bertrand, and somewhat more than Ellery suspected about Ellery.

On the afternoon of his second day at home he walked out Fennimore Street to call upon his aunt and her family. It was a walk he had taken, as a boy, perhaps two thousand times, generally at a run and often pursued; but he took it now at the deliberate gait of a man who has seen the Seine by moonlight and does not expect to be much astonished by anything in his native town. He carried a stick. Nobody in the town carried a stick except old Judge Brattle, who was lame, and Ellery was aware that he attracted notice. He was not displeased to attract it. A grocer's boy upon a bicycle wobbled perilously in turning to look at him, and Ellery bore the incident with composure.

He was thinking, as he walked, of his cousin Hattie.

He remembered her perfectly. She had been thirteen when he went away, a long, thin, freckled creature with two braids of hair the colour of wet straw, and knees that were usually skinned. She had followed him about from the time she could walk. She had fetched and carried for him, kept his secrets, lied for him to her mother and his, and been permitted, in return, to hold the rope while he climbed things. On the day he left for New York and the steamer she had wept so violently on the station platform that the conductor had asked whether the young lady was ill. Ellery had been touched by this, though embarrassed; and on the voyage over, gazing upon the Atlantic, he had more than once thought of her with a melancholy that he found not unpleasant.

He was prepared, therefore, to be very kind to Hattie. He would not crush her. He would let her see, gently, how far apart the years had carried them; he would tell her a little of the world, as much as was suitable for a young girl; and he would perhaps bring her, on some later occasion, one of the small engravings he had in his trunk, and explain it to her. He composed, as he went, the first thing he would say to her. It was to be, "Well, Tadpole!" said with a sort of weary fondness, and accompanied by a pat upon the head.

The Gilmore house had not changed, except that it seemed to have grown smaller, as such houses do, and there was a new iron fence along the front, with spikes. Ellery opened the gate, which squealed exactly as it always had, and was proceeding up the walk when a small boy in a sailor blouse rose from behind the hydrangea bush and regarded him with deep suspicion.

"Who you?" said the small boy.

"I," said Ellery, "am your cousin. You must be Wilfred."

"I'm Buster," said the small boy. "What's that on your lip?"

Ellery did not answer. He went up the steps and rang the bell, while Buster, at a distance of several feet behind him, made a careful study of the stick, the gloves, the coat, and the mustache, and appeared to arrive at an unfavourable verdict upon all four.

The door was opened by a young lady.

She was a tall young lady, in a dress of some soft grey stuff with a great deal of white at the throat. Her hair, which was neither the colour of wet straw nor of dry, but of something warmer than either, was done high upon her head in the manner of the drawings in the illustrated weeklies, and her face beneath it was of a kind that Ellery, had he encountered it in the Luxembourg Gardens, would have described in a letter home as "a type." There was not a freckle in it anywhere. She looked at him for a moment with polite inquiry, and then her eyes widened and she laughed.

"Why, Ellery!" she said. "It's Ellery! Mother! Mother, it's Ellery, and he's got a cane!"

Ellery's hand, which had been rising toward the level at which he had intended to pat her head, changed its course in some confusion and went to his hat. He removed the hat. He bowed—the bow was from the Boulevard Saint-Michel also—and said, "Ah—how do you do?" which was not at all what he had meant to say.

"How do I do?" cried Hattie. "Oh, my! Come in, come in! Don't stand there being foreign on the porch; the Pettibones are looking. Buster, go get your father out of the cellar. Tell him Cousin Ellery's here."

"I don't think he's Cousin Ellery," said Buster darkly. "I think he's a man."

"Go along!"

Buster went along, though not swiftly, and Ellery found himself in the front hall, where the same hat-rack held out the same antlers, and where there was the same smell, compounded of furnace and furniture polish and something baking, that had been the smell of his Aunt Lavinia's house for as long as he could remember. It affected him unexpectedly. He had been prepared to find it provincial; he found it, instead, so precisely and overwhelmingly familiar that for an instant he forgot his mustache altogether, and stood with his hat in his hand looking about him like a boy who has come home late for supper.

Then his aunt was upon him, a stout, flushed, voluble lady with flour on her forearms, who embraced him without regard for his coat and declared that he was thin, that he was pale, that he was the image of his poor grandfather, and that he must stay to supper because there was a chicken. Behind her, by degrees, came his Uncle Henry Gilmore, a large, slow, bald man in his shirt-sleeves, who had been attending to the furnace and who now shook hands with his nephew and looked at him over his spectacles with an expression that Ellery could not quite read.

"Well, well," said Uncle Henry. "Back from Paris, France."

"Yes, sir."

"How'd you leave it?"

"Leave it, sir?"

"Paris. Was it about where it ought to be when you came away?"

Ellery said, with a slight smile, that he believed Paris was much as usual; and Uncle Henry said, "That's good," and nodded several times, as though a weight had been lifted from his mind. Hattie made a small sound and turned it into a cough.

They put him in the front parlour, in the best chair, which was a mahogany rocker with a crocheted thing upon its back, and his aunt went away to the kitchen, calling over her shoulder that she would be back in two minutes and that nobody was to say anything interesting until she came. Uncle Henry, after standing a moment, observed that he would just go wash up, and went. Ellery was left alone with his cousin.

She sat down upon the sofa opposite him, folded her hands in her lap, and looked at him with an air of the frankest enjoyment. It was not an air he had anticipated. He had been ready for awe; he had been ready even for a little shyness, which he would have known how to dispel. He was not ready to be enjoyed. He touched his mustache.

"You've grown up, Hattie," he said, with what he hoped was an indulgent kindliness.

"So have you," she returned. "At least, you've grown something."

Ellery chose not to notice this. He leaned back in the rocker, crossed his knees, and allowed his gaze to travel about the room, slowly, as though appraising it. "It's curious," he said, "coming back. Everything seems so—so small. One gets used, over there, to a different scale of things. The proportions are different. I remember Bertrand saying to me once—"

"Bertrand's the one with the red beard," said Hattie, "that lives on a barge."

Ellery paused. "Why—yes. How did you—"

"And Achille's the one that painted the picture of the onion and the Salon wouldn't take it, and he said the jury were all bourgeois pigs, and you agreed with him. And there was a Hungarian count, only you weren't sure he was a count, and he borrowed forty francs from you and went to Vienna." She ticked them off upon her fingers. "Aunt Mattie used to bring your letters over every Sunday afternoon, and Mother read them out loud after supper. Father liked the one about the onion best. He made her read it twice."

Ellery felt himself growing warm about the ears. It occurred to him for the first time—and it was a novel and disagreeable idea—that his letters, which he had written in solitude and in a mood of some exaltation, had been received not in solitude at all, but by a circle of relatives sitting about a lamp after a heavy supper; and that some of those relatives had perhaps not been exalted.

"Your father," he said stiffly, "is hardly in a position to judge of painting."

"Oh, he didn't judge it," said Hattie. "He just liked it. He said he'd always thought there ought to be more pictures of onions, and he was glad somebody'd finally got round to it. He used to say it at the store." She laughed again, and then, seeing his face, she leaned forward quickly and put her hand upon his sleeve. "Oh, Ellery, don't! I didn't mean to make fun. We loved the letters, truly. You can't think how dull it is here in the winter, and every Sunday there'd be something new from you—it was like a serial in a magazine. I used to wonder what was going to happen to you next. Honestly I did."

The hand upon his sleeve was a very different hand from the grubby one that used to hold the rope. Ellery looked at it, and then at her, and for the space of a breath he was not altogether sure what he felt. It was not displeasure. It resembled, in some respects, the sensation of a man who has stepped confidently down a stair in the dark and found one step fewer than he expected.

"Did you?" he said.

"Of course I did. I used to think about you sitting at those little tables on the sidewalk, with everybody talking French, and wish I could see it. Is it really like that? With the little tables?"

"Yes," said Ellery. "It's really like that." And then, because she was looking at him with such straightforward interest, he forgot for a moment to be a man of the world, and began to tell her about the little tables—not as he had told it in his letters, with Achille's opinions and Bertrand's, but about the way the waiters swept the sawdust in the mornings, and the old woman who sold violets at the corner of the Rue Soufflot and called everybody "mon petit," and how cold his room had been in February, so that he had worn his overcoat to bed and once, for three days, his hat. Hattie laughed at the hat, and he found that he did not mind her laughing at it; he laughed himself, and the mustache, for the time being, was forgotten.

"You never wrote about the hat," she said.

"No," said Ellery. "I don't suppose I did."

"Why not? It's the best part."

He considered this, and was unable to answer it, and therefore changed the subject. "But you haven't told me anything about yourself," he said. "What have you been doing all this while?"

"Oh, me!" said Hattie. "Nothing. Growing up, Mother says. I finished at Miss Parkhurst's in June, and I've been to a good many parties, and I'm in a Browning club, only I don't understand Browning, and neither does anybody else in it except Mrs. Tolliver, and I'm not sure about her. And I've learned to ride a bicycle. Do you remember the old tree-house in the Pettibones' maple?"

"Remember it!" said Ellery. "I built it."

"You did not," said Hattie promptly. "I built it. You sat on the fence and told me where to put the boards."

"I supervised it," said Ellery, with dignity. "That is the function of an architect."

"Well, the architect fell out of it," said Hattie, "the very first day, and broke his collar-bone, and I had to run for Doctor Spence, and you made me promise to say you'd been pushed by the Kittredge boy."

"I was pushed," said Ellery.

"You were not! You were showing off. You stood up on the edge to show me how a man on a ship looks for whales, and the board went." She was laughing so that she had to put her handkerchief to her eyes. "And I told the whole neighbourhood the Kittredge boy did it, and Mr. Kittredge whipped him, and I've felt wicked about it ever since. I saw him at the Pettibones' dance last spring—he's a great tall thing now, with a moustache too—and I very nearly told him."

"I hope you didn't."

"No. I thought I'd better wait and ask you first. You always did decide those things."

Ellery looked at her sharply, but she was quite grave. He found, in that moment, a strong desire to hear more about the Kittredge boy—particularly about his moustache, and whether it was larger than his own, and why he had been at the Pettibones' dance, and with whom he had danced there—but he did not see how the inquiry could be decently made, and while he was considering the matter, there came a tremendous double knock at the front door, of the sort that announces either a telegraph messenger or a young man who has been there often before.

Hattie rose with a slight change of colour that Ellery did not fail to observe. "That'll be—excuse me just a minute," she said, and went out into the hall.

Ellery heard the door open, and a man's voice, cheerful and loud, inquiring whether it was too early; and Hattie's voice, lower, saying something he could not make out; and then the man's voice again, inquiring, with what seemed to Ellery an unnecessary heartiness, "The cousin from Paris? No! Well, bring him on—I want to see him!" And before Ellery had altogether composed himself in the rocker, the doorway was filled by a large, pink, extremely healthy young man in a brown suit, with a straw hat in one hand and a box of candy in the other.

"Ellery, this is Mr. Kittredge," said Hattie. "Lew, this is my cousin, Mr. Vane."

Ellery rose. He did not bow, this time; he found that he had no desire at all to bow. He shook hands. Mr. Kittredge's grip was of the sort that is described in the advertisements of physical culture establishments, and when it released him, Ellery stood for a moment flexing his fingers covertly behind his back.

"Mighty glad to know you," said Mr. Kittredge. "Heard a lot about you. Hattie used to read me your letters." He grinned broadly. "That fellow with the onion—say, I'd give a dollar to see that onion!"

Ellery said, in a voice which he endeavoured to make quite pleasant, that he believed the onion had been painted over.

"No! What with?"

"With—I believe it was a portrait of his landlady."

Mr. Kittredge appeared to find this the finest thing he had ever heard. He threw back his head and laughed so that the prisms on the parlour lamp shivered; and from the dining-room, where he had evidently been listening, there came an answering rumble that Ellery recognized as his Uncle Henry. Hattie looked from one young man to the other with an expression which, had Ellery been in a condition to read it, he would have seen to be compounded in nearly equal parts of anxiety and delight.

Mr. Kittredge sat down upon the sofa, which received him with a groan, and Hattie sat down beside him—not very near beside him, Ellery noted, but nearer than she had been sitting before. The box of candy lay between them. Ellery resumed the rocker.

"You'll find the old town changed some," said Mr. Kittredge genially.

"It seems to me," said Ellery, "not very much changed."

"Oh, it's changed! Why, we've got the electric cars clear out to the Fair Grounds now, and they're talking about paving Fennimore Street with brick, all the way. And there's three new buildings downtown over five stories. You'll have to go see the new Commerce Block—you being an architect. It's a corker."

"I shall make a point of it," said Ellery.

"Six stories and a basement," said Mr. Kittredge, "and an elevator that'll take you right up to the roof. And the whole front's pressed brick, with stone trimmings, and the name cut right in over the door in letters this high. I've got an office on the fourth floor." He paused modestly. "Insurance."

"Indeed," said Ellery.

It was at this point, and while Ellery was searching for some remark about pressed brick that would be at once courteous and annihilating, that he chanced to glance at his cousin, and found her looking at him. She was not laughing now. Her eyes, which he remembered as having been of no particular colour, were grey, and quite steady, and they held in them something that was at the same time an appeal and a challenge—as if she were asking him, without words, whether he was going to be decent; and as if she rather thought he was, but was not entirely sure.

Ellery looked at her for a moment. Then he turned to Mr. Kittredge.

"I'm told," he said, "that I owe you an apology."

Mr. Kittredge stared. "Me? What for?"

"About eleven years ago," said Ellery, "I fell out of a tree-house, and it was given out that you had pushed me. You hadn't. I was showing off, and the board went. I believe you suffered for it."

Mr. Kittredge's mouth opened slowly. He looked at Ellery, and then at Hattie, who had turned a deep and becoming pink, and then back at Ellery; and then a great light broke over his large, honest face, and he smote his knee with a blow that made the candy box leap.

"Well, I'll be—!" he cried. "Well, I'll be—! I always said I never did it! I always said so! The old man licked me in the woodshed and I told him all the way through I never did it, and he said that made it worse!" He turned upon Hattie. "And you knew it all the time!"

"I was only eight," said Hattie faintly.

"Eight! You were going on nine if you were a day!" But he was laughing, and he reached across and shook Ellery's hand again, with no diminution of pressure. "Mr. Vane, you're all right. I don't care what anybody says—you're all right!"

Ellery, nursing his fingers, did not inquire what anybody said. He had a general notion, and he found that he no longer cared to have it particularized.

Supper was a long affair and a loud one. There was the chicken, and there were hot biscuits, and three kinds of preserves, and a cake upon which his Aunt Lavinia had caused to be inscribed, in pink icing, the word WELCOME, the last two letters somewhat crowded against the edge. Buster, who was seated next to Ellery, ate steadily throughout and spoke only once, to inquire whether they had chicken in France, and on being told that they had, to observe that he did not believe it. Uncle Henry asked about the onion, and laughed until he had to be pounded upon the back. Mr. Kittredge stayed, as it appeared he usually did on Thursdays, and told a long story about a fire at the Commerce Block, in which nobody had been hurt and which seemed chiefly remarkable for the conduct of the elevator. And Ellery, to his own surprise, found himself telling about the hat he had worn to bed, and about the violet woman, and about the Hungarian count, whom he presented now not as an exotic acquaintance but as a man who had got away with forty francs of his money; and the table liked it better than anything in the letters.

It was late when he rose to go. Hattie came with him to the door, and out upon the porch, where the October night was sharp and still and the arc light at the corner made the maple leaves look as if they had been cut out of paper. Inside, Mr. Kittredge could be heard explaining something to Uncle Henry with great energy.

"Ellery," said Hattie, "that was nice of you. About the tree-house."

"It was true," said Ellery.

"I know. But you needn't have said it. I've always felt so mean."

He drew on his gloves slowly. "Is he—" he began, and stopped. "Is Mr. Kittredge a—a particular friend of yours?"

Hattie looked out at the arc light. "He's very kind," she said. "And he's coming along awfully well in the insurance business. Father thinks a great deal of him."

"Ah," said Ellery.

"But nothing's settled," she said quickly. "Nothing at all. I'm only nineteen."

"Of course," said Ellery. He did not know why this news should cheer him as it did, and he decided not to examine the matter. He took up his stick from where it leaned against the railing, looked at it for a moment as though he had never seen it before, and then, on an impulse, held it out to her.

"Would you give this to Buster?" he said. "I believe he'd like to have it. I don't think I'll need it."

Hattie took it, wondering. "Why, Ellery—"

"Good-night, Tadpole," said Ellery, and went down the steps and out through the gate, which squealed after him.

He walked home slowly. At the corner, under the arc light, he paused and drew the side of his forefinger once across his upper lip, thoughtfully, as a man might test the edge of a razor; and the next morning, to the profound relief of his mother and the open disappointment of the grocer's boy, it was gone.

Here is an excerpt of Booth Tarkington's writing, to show you their style:

We debate sometimes what is to be the future of this nation when we think that in a few years public affairs may be in the hands of the fin-de-siècle gilded youths we see about us during the Christmas holidays. Such foppery, such luxury, such insolence, was surely never practised by the scented, overbearing patricians of the Palatine, even in Rome’s most decadent epoch. In all the wild orgy of wastefulness and luxury with which the nineteenth century reaches its close, the gilded youth has been surely the worst symptom. With his airs of young milord, his fast horses, his gold and silver cigarette-cases, his clothes from a New York tailor, his recklessness of money showered upon him by indulgent mothers or doting grandfathers, he respects nothing and nobody. Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can. Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
There is a period in the life of every householder when he discovers that he has become, without any formal ceremony of investiture, an Authority; and the discovery is seldom agreeable. Up to that time he has thought of himself, if he has thought of the matter at all, as still more or less a boy who happens to pay the gas bill; but one evening his wife meets him in the front hall with a certain expression, and lowers her voice, and says, "Lucius, you'll have to speak to him," and the boy who happened to pay the gas bill perceives, with a sinking at the waistcoat, that he is expected to become majestic before supper.

Mr. Lucius Hobart, of the Hobart Hardware and Implement Company, reached home at a quarter to six on a Thursday in late April, and found this expression awaiting him. He had walked from the street-car with the comfortable sensation of a man who has sold eleven lawn-mowers in a single afternoon. He had even been humming. At the sight of his wife, however, standing at the foot of the stairs with one hand pressed flat upon the newel post, as though she were holding the house together by main strength, he stopped humming, and his heart, which had been light, took on the weight of approximately one of the lawn-mowers.

"What is it?" he asked. "Is anybody sick?"

"Nobody is sick," Mrs. Hobart said. "Nobody is sick, Lucius. I almost wish somebody were. It would be easier to understand." She took something from the hall table, where it had been lying concealed beneath a newspaper, and held it out to him without a word.

Mr. Hobart looked at it for some time before he consented to recognize it. It was, or it had been, a tall silk hat. Its crown had been pressed inward, as by a foot, and then outward again, as by a fist, so that it now bore a resemblance to a concertina which had met with misfortune. Its nap, once of so lustrous a black that Mr. Hobart had been able to see his own moustache in it, was matted and streaked with a yellowish substance which proved, upon closer examination, to be clay. A considerable portion of the brim was missing altogether. From within there came a faint odour of damp earth and of something else, less wholesome, which Mr. Hobart could not at once identify and did not care to.

"It's my hat," he said at last, in a hollow voice.

"It was your hat," said Mrs. Hobart.

This hat had a history. Mr. Hobart had bought it eleven years before, when he was elected Second Vice-President of the Commercial Club, and he had worn it upon perhaps thirty occasions since: to funerals of the more important sort, to the unveiling of the Soldiers' Monument, to the Governor's reception, and once, memorably, upon a platform with a United States Senator, who had spoken of the hat afterward as "a fine piece of goods." Between these occasions it reposed in a leather box upon the highest shelf of Mr. Hobart's closet, wrapped in tissue paper, and Mr. Hobart had sometimes taken it down merely to look at it, as other men take down a family Bible. It represented, in a way, the summit of his civic pretensions; and he had supposed, until this moment, that its shelf was beyond the reach of any member of the household under the height of five feet and seven inches.

"He stood on the wash-stand," said Mrs. Hobart, answering his look. "He stood on the wash-stand, Lucius, and then on the towel-rack, and then I don't know what. The towel-rack is broken too."

"Chester?"

"Who else?" she said. "Who else in this world?"

Mr. Hobart turned the hat over in his hands, and something rattled within it. He shook it gently, and a small, stiff, feathered object fell out upon the hall carpet. It lay there with its feet in the air.

"That," said Mrs. Hobart, with an effort at calmness that was more terrible than any outcry, "is a robin. It is a dead robin. It has been dead, I should say, since about Sunday. They found it in the alley behind the Spurgises' barn, he and that Elmer Spurgis, and they held a funeral for it. They held a funeral for it with your hat. Your hat was the hearse, Lucius. They pulled it around the block in Chester's express-wagon, with Elmer beating on a dish-pan, and then they buried it, hat and all, in the Kinseys' asparagus bed, because Elmer said asparagus was more like a cemetery than anything else. And then Mrs. Kinsey saw them from her window and came out, and they dug it up again and ran, and it rained in the middle of the afternoon, and they left it under the grape-arbour. I found it at five o'clock. Mrs. Kinsey had already telephoned. Mrs. Kinsey," she added, with a fine bitterness, "was very nice about it."

Mr. Hobart stood looking down at the robin. He was a man of forty-two, a deacon of the Second Presbyterian Church, a member of the Board of the Young Men's Christian Association, and he was conscious, at this moment, of an inward disturbance which he could not altogether account for and certainly did not mean to encourage. It was, to some degree, grief for the hat; it was, in another degree, indignation; but there was mixed with these a third ingredient, faint and treacherous, rising up from some forgotten cellar of his being, and he recognized it with alarm as a desire to ask whether the dish-pan had been loud.

"Where is he?" he said sternly, to put this feeling down.

"Upstairs. I've had him washed. I've told him you would see him in the library." She came closer and laid her hand upon his sleeve. "Lucius, you must be firm with him this time. You must really be firm. You always begin firm and then you get to talking with him, and the first thing anybody knows the two of you are discussing how high a robin can fly. He doesn't respect anything. He doesn't respect property. He doesn't respect his father's hat. If he doesn't learn now, when will he learn? I don't want you to whip him. You know I don't believe in it. But you must make him understand. You must make him feel it."

"I'll make him feel it," said Mr. Hobart, and he went into the library with the ruined hat in one hand and the robin, by way of evidence, wrapped in a sheet of the Evening News in the other. He placed both upon the centre-table, under the green-shaded lamp, where they presented a spectacle of such desolation that he was obliged to look away from them; and he arranged himself in his leather chair, crossed his legs, uncrossed them, and finally rose and stood with his back to the mantelpiece, which seemed to him the more judicial position. Then he cleared his throat and called, in a voice he had heard his own father use some thirty-five years before:

"Chester! Come down here, sir!"

There was a pause, of a quality well understood by all parents: the pause of a person upstairs who has heard perfectly and is collecting himself. Then came a slow descent of the stairs, each step taken separately and with a little silence after it, as though the person descending were reluctant to wear them out; then a further pause in the hall; and then the library door opened by degrees, and Chester Hobart, aged eight years and four months, came into the room.

He had been washed, as his mother had said; he had been washed with a thoroughness that amounted almost to persecution. His face shone. His hair, which was of a light, dry, rebellious sort, had been wetted and parted and plastered down, and it was already beginning, at the crown, to rise again, like grass after a cart has gone over it. He wore a clean blouse with a large collar, and his knees, though scrubbed, retained in their creases a faint memorial of the Kinseys' asparagus bed. His expression was that of a person attending a solemn function in which he has no personal concern; it was grave, polite, and abstracted, and his eyes, which were large and of a candid blue, went at once to the hat upon the table and then, with a slight flicker, away from it, and fixed themselves upon a point in the wallpaper about a foot above his father's left shoulder.

"Good evening, papa," he said.

Mr. Hobart had intended to begin with a long silence, during which the culprit should come to understand the enormity of his position; but this greeting, so courteous and so unexpected, disarranged his plans, and before he could stop himself he had answered, "Good evening, Chester." Then, realizing his error, he frowned heavily and said, "Come here."

Chester advanced to a point exactly midway between the door and his father, and stopped.

"Closer, sir."

Chester advanced six inches.

"Do you know," said Mr. Hobart, lifting one hand toward the table in a gesture which he had seen employed by an attorney for the prosecution, "do you know what that is?"

Chester considered the table attentively, as if to make sure he should not be guilty of any inaccuracy. "Yes, sir," he said. "It's Cock Robin."

Mr. Hobart had meant the hat. He was disconcerted to find that the robin had been christened, and he paused to recover himself; but he did not recover himself entirely, for there now appeared in his mind, unbidden, the old rhyme of the Sparrow and the Bow and Arrow, and with it the inquiry as to who should be the parson, and who should toll the bell, and he was obliged to fasten his gaze sharply upon the brass andirons until the rhyme had gone away.

"I mean the hat," he said. "I mean my hat, Chester. My silk hat. That hat cost eight dollars and a half."

Chester's eyes widened slightly, not with remorse, but with what appeared to be a sincere respect for the sum. "Gee!" he said softly.

"Don't say 'gee.' Do you know what that hat means to me? Do you know where I have worn that hat? I have worn that hat to the funeral of Judge Thurlow. I have worn that hat on the platform with Senator Pettibone. I have worn that hat," said Mr. Hobart, his voice rising, for he found that the catalogue moved him, "at the dedication of the new court-house, when there were five thousand people present, and I stood next the Governor of this State! And you—you, sir—you take that hat, without asking anybody, without a word to your mother or to me, and you climb up on the furniture and break the towel-rack, and you put a dead bird in it, and you drag it through the public streets in a wagon, and you bury it in Mrs. Kinsey's asparagus! What have you got to say for yourself?"

It was a good speech; Mr. Hobart felt that it was a good speech; and he waited, breathing a little hard, for its effect. Chester's lower lip moved, and for a moment his father believed, with a pang that was not altogether one of triumph, that he was going to cry. But Chester did not cry. He merely drew a long breath, of the kind that precedes a full and reasonable explanation, and said:

"Well, Elmer said."

"I don't care what Elmer said."

"Well, but papa, Elmer said you can't have a regular funeral without a black hat. He said it's the law. He said the undertaker has to have a black hat or they won't let him in the cemetery. He said his uncle saw one, and the undertaker had a tall black hat just exactly like yours, only it had a kind of a ribbon hanging down the back. We didn't have any ribbon." He looked at the hat regretfully. "We had to use your hat for the hearse, too, because there wasn't anything else that was black, only Elmer's mother's work-basket, and she was home."

"And you thought," said Mr. Hobart, "that because Elmer Spurgis told you it was the law, it was perfectly all right to take my property and destroy it?"

"I didn't destroy it," Chester said earnestly. "Not on purpose, I didn't. It got stepped on when I got down off the towel-rack, but that was just an accident; I fell on it. And then the wagon has a wheel that wobbles, and it fell out twice going around Mr. Pruitt's corner. And then when we buried it, we didn't know it was going to rain. And then Mrs. Kinsey came out." He paused, and added, with the air of one supplying a mitigating circumstance that could not fairly be overlooked: "We were going to dig it up again afterwards anyway, papa. We were only going to leave Cock Robin. We were going to bring the hat back."

"When?"

Chester appeared to calculate. "Before you needed it," he said.

Mr. Hobart turned abruptly to the mantelpiece and examined, with deep interest, a small bronze figure of a dog which had stood there for nine years and which he had never before looked at. His shoulders moved once, slightly. When he faced about again his countenance was grimmer than before, and Chester, who had been watching those shoulders with the alert and scientific attention of a man reading a barometer, became visibly less hopeful.

"Chester," said his father, "you are old enough to know better. You are eight years old. When I was eight years old—" He stopped; for there had come to him, without the least warning, a clear picture of a summer afternoon in the year 1871, and of a stovepipe hat belonging to his own father, and of a mud-turtle, and of a certain creek; and he recollected also, with peculiar distinctness, the conversation in the woodshed which had followed. He had not thought of that afternoon in thirty years. He found that he did not wish to pursue the comparison, and he went on with some haste: "At your age a boy ought to understand that other people's things are not to be taken without permission. Particularly his father's things. Particularly valuable things. You have caused your mother a great deal of distress. You have caused me a great deal of distress. You have made us both ashamed before the neighbours. Do you understand that?"

"Yes, sir," said Chester, in a small voice.

"Are you sorry?"

There was a pause. Chester looked at the hat, and then at the newspaper which contained the robin, and his face took on an expression of complicated honesty.

"I'm sorry about the hat," he said slowly. "I'm awful sorry about the hat, papa. And the towel-rack. And Mrs. Kinsey's asparagus, kind of. But I'm not sorry we had the funeral." He raised his eyes, for the first time, directly to his father's. "Somebody had to bury him, papa. He was just laying out there in the alley. Nobody else was going to do it. Elmer said if nobody buries them they don't go to heaven, and the cats get them."

It was here that Mr. Hobart's position, already precarious, gave way entirely beneath him; and he knew it, and knew that his wife would know it, too, the moment she looked at him. He had been prepared for defiance, which can be met with sternness, and for tears, which can be met with a kind of sorrowful sternness; but he had not been prepared for a theological argument concerning the salvation of robins, presented without guile by a person in a sailor collar whose hair was coming up at the crown. He sat down in the leather chair rather heavily, and for a little while he said nothing at all.

"Chester," he said finally, and his voice, to his own chagrin, had lost a good deal of its court-house quality, "it was right to want to bury the bird. That was a good thing to want to do. But it was wrong to take my hat. A thing can be good to want to do, and the way a person does it can be wrong. Do you see?"

"Yes, sir," said Chester. "You mean I ought to have asked."

"I mean you ought to have asked."

Chester thought this over. "Would you have let me have it if I'd asked?"

"Certainly not!"

"Well, then—" said Chester, and stopped, perceiving perhaps that the logic of his position, however sound, was not likely to be well received. His father perceived it too, and perceived also that the argument was drifting into waters where a deacon of the Second Presbyterian Church might very well be drowned. He rose once more, and resumed his station at the mantelpiece, and folded his arms.

"You will have no allowance," he said, "for five weeks. Your allowance will go toward a new towel-rack. You will go to Mrs. Kinsey to-morrow morning, before school, and you will tell her you are sorry about her asparagus, and you will offer to weed her garden on Saturday. And you will go to bed to-night without any dessert. Now go upstairs."

Chester received this sentence without protest, as a man receives the weather. "Yes, sir," he said; and he turned and went toward the door. At the door, however, he paused, with his hand upon the knob, and looked back—not at his father, but at the table under the green lamp.

"Papa?"

"Well?"

"What's going to happen to Cock Robin?"

Mr. Hobart looked at the newspaper on the table. He had, in truth, intended to have the bird thrown upon the ash-heap by the hired girl, and he had not given the matter another thought; but it now became plain to him that this disposition, which half an hour earlier would have seemed the most natural thing in the world, was no longer possible to a man of any decent feeling.

"I'll see to it," he said gruffly. "Go on upstairs."

The door closed. Mr. Hobart heard the slow ascent of the stairs, each step separate, and then a rapid scamper over the last three, which indicated that the culprit's spirits had begun, at a safe distance, to revive. A moment later his wife came in. She had been in the dining-room, which shared a thin partition with the library, and she had the look of a woman who has heard everything and intends to hear it again from the beginning.

"Well?" she said.

"I was firm with him," said Mr. Hobart.

"Were you?"

"I was extremely firm. No allowance for five weeks. No dessert to-night. He's to apologize to Mrs. Kinsey and weed her garden."

Mrs. Hobart looked at him searchingly. "And what are you going to do with that bird?"

Mr. Hobart did not answer immediately. He looked at the bird, and at the hat, and at the bronze dog upon the mantelpiece, and the third ingredient of his earlier emotion, which he had so carefully kept down throughout the interview, now rose to the surface without opposition and spread itself comfortably over his features.

"Mary," he said, "I think after supper I'll just step out and put it under the lilac bush. It'll only take a minute." And then, as his wife continued to regard him in silence: "Well, somebody's got to do it. The cats would get it."

Mrs. Hobart opened her mouth, and closed it, and went out of the room without a word; but her husband, gathering up the remnants of his eight-dollar-and-a-half hat with something like tenderness, observed that her shoulders, as she passed through the dining-room door, had moved once, slightly, in precisely the manner that his own had moved at the mantelpiece. And at nine o'clock that evening, when she went upstairs to see that Chester was asleep, she found upon the table beside his bed a saucer containing the crumbs of a slice of chocolate cake; and she knew perfectly well that the hired girl had not carried it up, for the hired girl had gone home at eight.

author: Booth Tarkington
content:
Here are three excerpts of Booth Tarkington's writing, to show you their style:

Excerpt 1: The ineligible young men of the town (they were all ineligible) were unable to content themselves with the view that had so charmed Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster: they spent their time struggling to keep Miss Amberson’s face turned toward them. She turned it most often, observers said, toward two: one excelling in the general struggle by his sparkle, and the other by that winning if not winsome old trait, persistence. The sparkling gentleman “led germans” with her, and sent sonnets to her with his bouquets—sonnets lacking neither music nor wit. He was generous, poor, well-dressed, and his amazing persuasiveness was one reason why he was always in debt. No one doubted that he would be able to persuade Isabel, but he unfortunately joined too merry a party one night, and, during a moonlight serenade upon the lawn before the Amberson Mansion, was easily identified from the windows as the person who stepped through the bass viol and had to be assisted to a waiting carriage. One of Miss Amberson’s brothers was among the serenaders, and, when the party had dispersed, remained propped against the front door in a state of helpless liveliness; the Major going down in a dressing-gown and slippers to bring him in, and scolding mildly, while imperfectly concealing strong impulses to laughter. Miss Amberson also laughed at this brother, the next day, but for the suitor it was a different matter: she refused to see him when he called to apologize. “You seem to care a great deal about bass viols!” he wrote her. “I promise never to break another.” She made no response to the note, unless it was an answer, two weeks later, when her engagement was announced. She took the persistent one, Wilbur Minafer, no breaker of bass viols or of hearts, no serenader at all. A few people, who always foresaw everything, claimed that they were not surprised, because though Wilbur Minafer “might not be an Apollo, as it were,” he was “a steady young business man, and a good church-goer,” and Isabel Amberson was “pretty sensible—for such a showy girl.” But the engagement astounded the young people, and most of their fathers and mothers, too; and as a topic it supplanted literature at the next meeting of the “Women’s Tennyson Club.”

“Wilbur Minafer!” a member cried, her inflection seeming to imply that Wilbur’s crime was explained by his surname. “Wilbur Minafer! It’s the queerest thing I ever heard! To think of her taking Wilbur Minafer, just because a man any woman would like a thousand times better was a little wild one night at a serenade!”

“No,” said Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “It isn’t that. It isn’t even because she’s afraid he’d be a dissipated husband and she wants to be safe. It isn’t because she’s religious or hates wildness; it isn’t even because she hates wildness in him.”

“Well, but look how she’s thrown him over for it.”

“No, that wasn’t her reason,” said the wise Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “If men only knew it—and it’s a good thing they don’t—a woman doesn’t really care much about whether a man’s wild or not, if it doesn’t affect herself, and Isabel Amberson doesn’t care a thing!”

“Mrs. Foster!”

“No, she doesn’t. What she minds is his making a clown of himself in her front yard! It made her think he didn’t care much about her. She’s probably mistaken, but that’s what she thinks, and it’s too late for her to think anything else now, because she’s going to be married right away—the invitations will be out next week. It’ll be a big Amberson-style thing, raw oysters floating in scooped-out blocks of ice and a band from out-of-town—champagne, showy presents; a colossal present from the Major. Then Wilbur will take Isabel on the carefulest little wedding trip he can manage, and she’ll be a good wife to him, but they’ll have the worst spoiled lot of children this town will ever see.”

“How on earth do you make that out, Mrs. Foster?”

“She couldn’t love Wilbur, could she?” Mrs. Foster demanded, with no challengers. “Well, it will all go to her children, and she’ll ruin ’em!” The prophetess proved to be mistaken in a single detail merely: except for that, her foresight was accurate. The wedding was of Ambersonian magnificence, even to the floating oysters; and the Major’s colossal present was a set of architect’s designs for a house almost as elaborate and impressive as the Mansion, the house to be built in Amberson Addition by the Major. The orchestra was certainly not that local one which had suffered the loss of a bass viol; the musicians came, according to the prophecy and next morning’s paper, from afar; and at midnight the bride was still being toasted in champagne, though she had departed upon her wedding journey at ten. Four days later the pair had returned to town, which promptness seemed fairly to demonstrate that Wilbur had indeed taken Isabel upon the carefulest little trip he could manage. According to every report, she was from the start “a good wife to him,” but here in a final detail the prophecy proved inaccurate. Wilbur and Isabel did not have children; they had only one.

“Only one,” Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster admitted. “But I’d like to know if he isn’t spoiled enough for a whole carload!” Again she found none to challenge her. At the age of nine, George Amberson Minafer, the Major’s one grandchild, was a princely terror, dreaded not only in Amberson Addition but in many other quarters through which he galloped on his white pony. “By golly, I guess you think you own this town!” an embittered labourer complained, one day, as Georgie rode the pony straight through a pile of sand the man was sieving. “I will when I grow up,” the undisturbed child replied. “I guess my grandpa owns it now, you bet!” And the baffled workman, having no means to controvert what seemed a mere exaggeration of the facts could only mutter “Oh, pull down your vest!”

“Don’t haf to! Doctor says it ain’t healthy!” the boy returned promptly. “But I’ll tell you what I’ll do: I’ll pull down my vest if you’ll wipe off your chin!” This was stock and stencil: the accustomed argot of street badinage of the period; and in such matters Georgie was an expert. He had no vest to pull down; the incongruous fact was that a fringed sash girdled the juncture of his velvet blouse and breeches, for the Fauntleroy period had set in, and Georgie’s mother had so poor an eye for appropriate things, where Georgie was concerned, that she dressed him according to the doctrine of that school in boy decoration. Not only did he wear a silk sash, and silk stockings, and a broad lace collar, with his little black velvet suit: he had long brown curls, and often came home with burrs in them. Except upon the surface (which was not his own work, but his mother’s) Georgie bore no vivid resemblance to the fabulous little Cedric. The storied boy’s famous “Lean on me, grandfather,” would have been difficult to imagine upon the lips of Georgie. A month after his ninth birthday anniversary, when the Major gave him his pony, he had already become acquainted with the toughest boys in various distant parts of the town, and had convinced them that the toughness of a rich little boy with long curls might be considered in many respects superior to their own. He fought them, learning how to go berserk at a certain point in a fight, bursting into tears of anger, reaching for rocks, uttering wailed threats of murder and attempting to fulfil them. Fights often led to intimacies, and he acquired the art of saying things more exciting than “Don’t haf to!” and “Doctor says it ain’t healthy!” Thus, on a summer afternoon, a strange boy, sitting bored upon the gate-post of the Reverend Malloch Smith, beheld George Amberson Minafer rapidly approaching on his white pony, and was impelled by bitterness to shout: “Shoot the ole jackass! Look at the girly curls! Say, bub, where’d you steal your mother’s ole sash!”

“Your sister stole it for me!” Georgie instantly replied, checking the pony. “She stole it off our clo’es-line an’ gave it to me.”

“You go get your hair cut!” said the stranger hotly. “Yah! I haven’t got any sister!”

“I know you haven’t at home,” Georgie responded. “I mean the one that’s in jail.”

“I dare you to get down off that pony!” Georgie jumped to the ground, and the other boy descended from the Reverend Mr. Smith’s gatepost—but he descended inside the gate. “I dare you outside that gate,” said Georgie.

“Yah! I dare you half way here. I dare you—” But these were luckless challenges, for Georgie immediately vaulted the fence—and four minutes later Mrs. Malloch Smith, hearing strange noises, looked forth from a window; then screamed, and dashed for the pastor’s study. Mr. Malloch Smith, that grim-bearded Methodist, came to the front yard and found his visiting nephew being rapidly prepared by Master Minafer to serve as a principal figure in a pageant of massacre. It was with great physical difficulty that Mr. Smith managed to give his nephew a chance to escape into the house, for Georgie was hard and quick, and, in such matters, remarkably intense; but the minister, after a grotesque tussle, got him separated from his opponent, and shook him.

“You stop that, you!” Georgie cried fiercely; and wrenched himself away. “I guess you don’t know who I am!”

“Yes, I do know!” the angered Mr. Smith retorted. “I know who you are, and you’re a disgrace to your mother! Your mother ought to be ashamed of herself to allow—” “Shut up about my mother bein’ ashamed of herself!” Mr. Smith, exasperated, was unable to close the dialogue with dignity. “She ought to be ashamed,” he repeated. “A woman that lets a bad boy like you—” But Georgie had reached his pony and mounted. Before setting off at his accustomed gallop, he paused to interrupt the Reverend Malloch Smith again. “You pull down your vest, you ole Billygoat, you!” he shouted, distinctly. “Pull down your vest, wipe off your chin—an’ go to hell!” Such precocity is less unusual, even in children of the Rich, than most grown people imagine. However, it was a new experience for the Reverend Malloch Smith, and left him in a state of excitement. He at once wrote a note to Georgie’s mother, describing the crime according to his nephew’s testimony; and the note reached Mrs. Minafer before Georgie did. When he got home she read it to him sorrowfully. Dear Madam:
Your son has caused a painful distress in my household. He made an unprovoked attack upon a little nephew of mine who is visiting in my household, insulted him by calling him vicious names and falsehoods, stating that ladies of his family were in jail. He then tried to make his pony kick him, and when the child, who is only eleven years old, while your son is much older and stronger, endeavoured to avoid his indignities and withdraw quietly, he pursued him into the enclosure of my property and brutally assaulted him. When I appeared upon this scene he deliberately called insulting words to me, concluding with profanity, such as “go to hell,” which was heard not only by myself but by my wife and the lady who lives next door. I trust such a state of undisciplined behaviour may be remedied for the sake of the reputation for propriety, if nothing higher, of the family to which this unruly child belongs. Georgie had muttered various interruptions, and as she concluded the reading he said: “He’s an ole liar!”

“Georgie, you mustn’t say ‘liar.’ Isn’t this letter the truth?”

“Well,” said Georgie, “how old am I?”

“Ten.”

“Well, look how he says I’m older than a boy eleven years old.”

“That’s true,” said Isabel. “He does. But isn’t some of it true, Georgie?” Georgie felt himself to be in a difficulty here, and he was silent.

“Georgie, did you say what he says you did?”

“Which one?”

“Did you tell him to—to—Did you say, ‘Go to hell?’” Georgie looked worried for a moment longer; then he brightened. “Listen here, mamma; grandpa wouldn’t wipe his shoe on that ole story-teller, would he?”

“Georgie, you mustn’t—” “I mean: none of the Ambersons wouldn’t have anything to do with him, would they? He doesn’t even know you, does he, mamma?”

“That hasn’t anything to do with it.”

“Yes, it has! I mean: none of the Amberson family go to see him, and they never have him come in their house; they wouldn’t ask him to, and they prob’ly wouldn’t even let him.”

“That isn’t what we’re talking about.”

“I bet,” said Georgie emphatically, “I bet if he wanted to see any of ’em, he’d haf to go around to the side door!”

“No, dear, they—” “Yes, they would, mamma! So what does it matter if I did say somep’m’ to him he didn’t like? That kind o’ people, I don’t see why you can’t say anything you want to, to ’em!”

“No, Georgie. And you haven’t answered me whether you said that dreadful thing he says you did.”

“Well—” said Georgie. “Anyway, he said somep’m’ to me that made me mad.” And upon this point he offered no further details; he would not explain to his mother that what had made him “mad” was Mr. Smith’s hasty condemnation of herself: “Your mother ought to be ashamed,” and, “A woman that lets a bad boy like you—” Georgie did not even consider excusing himself by quoting these insolences. Isabel stroked his head. “They were terrible words for you to use, dear. From his letter he doesn’t seem a very tactful person, but—” “He’s just riffraff,” said Georgie.

“You mustn’t say so,” his mother gently agreed “Where did you learn those bad words he speaks of? Where did you hear any one use them?”

“Well, I’ve heard ’em several places. I guess Uncle George Amberson was the first I ever heard say ’em. Uncle George Amberson said ’em to papa once. Papa didn’t like it, but Uncle George was just laughin’ at papa, an’ then he said ’em while he was laughin’.”

“That was wrong of him,” she said, but almost instinctively he detected the lack of conviction in her tone. It was Isabel’s great failing that whatever an Amberson did seemed right to her, especially if the Amberson was either her brother George, or her son George. She knew that she should be more severe with the latter now, but severity with him was beyond her power; and the Reverend Malloch Smith had succeeded only in rousing her resentment against himself. Georgie’s symmetrical face—altogether an Amberson face—had looked never more beautiful to her. It always looked unusually beautiful when she tried to be severe with him. “You must promise me,” she said feebly, “never to use those bad words again.”

“I promise not to,” he said promptly—and he whispered an immediate codicil under his breath: “Unless I get mad at somebody!” This satisfied a code according to which, in his own sincere belief, he never told lies.

“That’s a good boy,” she said, and he ran out to the yard, his punishment over. Some admiring friends were gathered there; they had heard of his adventure, knew of the note, and were waiting to see what was going to “happen” to him. They hoped for an account of things, and also that he would allow them to “take turns” riding his pony to the end of the alley and back. They were really his henchmen: Georgie was a lord among boys. In fact, he was a personage among certain sorts of grown people, and was often fawned upon; the alley negroes delighted in him, chuckled over him, flattered him slavishly. For that matter, he often heard well-dressed people speaking of him admiringly: a group of ladies once gathered about him on the pavement where he was spinning a top. “I know this is Georgie!” one exclaimed, and turned to the others with the impressiveness of a showman. “Major Amberson’s only grandchild!” The others said, “It is?” and made clicking sounds with their mouths; two of them loudly whispering, “So handsome!” Georgie, annoyed because they kept standing upon the circle he had chalked for his top, looked at them coldly and offered a suggestion: “Oh, go hire a hall!” As an Amberson, he was already a public character, and the story of his adventure in the Reverend Malloch Smith’s front yard became a town topic. Many people glanced at him with great distaste, thereafter, when they chanced to encounter him, which meant nothing to Georgie, because he innocently believed most grown people to be necessarily cross-looking as a normal phenomenon resulting from the adult state; and he failed to comprehend that the distasteful glances had any personal bearing upon himself. If he had perceived such a bearing, he would have been affected only so far, probably, as to mutter, “Riffraff!” Possibly he would have shouted it; and, certainly, most people believed a story that went round the town just after Mrs. Amberson’s funeral, when Georgie was eleven. Georgie was reported to have differed with the undertaker about the seating of the family; his indignant voice had become audible: “Well, who is the most important person at my own grandmother’s funeral?” And later he had projected his head from the window of the foremost mourners’ carriage, as the undertaker happened to pass.

“Riffraff!”

After this I’ll just keep out of his way.” Isabel looked up, searching his face with the fond puzzlement which her eyes sometimes showed when they rested upon him; then she glanced down the hall toward Fanny’s room, and, after another moment of hesitation, came quickly in, and closed the door.

“Dear,” she said, “I wish you’d tell me something: Why don’t you like Eugene?”

“Oh, I like him well enough,” George returned, with a short laugh, as he sat down and began to unlace his shoes. “I like him well enough—in his place.”

“No, dear,” she said hurriedly. “I’ve had a feeling from the very first that you didn’t really like him—that you really never liked him. Sometimes you’ve seemed to be friendly with him, and you’d laugh with him over something in a jolly, companionable way, and I’d think I was wrong, and that you really did like him, after all; but to-night I’m sure my other feeling was the right one: you don’t like him. “Well, it’s seemed—as if—as if—” Isabel began timidly. “It did seem—At least, you haven’t looked at any other girl, ever since they came here and—and certainly you’ve seemed very much interested in her. Certainly you’ve been very great friends?”

“Well, what of that?”

“It’s only that I’m like your grandfather: I can’t see how you could be so much interested in a girl and—and not feel very pleasantly toward her father.”

“Now, what do you mean by that?”

“Never mind!”

“All right, I don’t. But for heaven’s sake stare at somebody else awhile. Try it on the house-maid!”

Sunday evening was the time, he explained, for going over the week’s work with his factory managers. George took on colour, himself, as, he rose and nodded indifferently; and the hot suffusion to which he became subject extended its area to include his neck and ears. “How d’you do,” he said. “I trust that ah—I trust—I do trust—” He stopped, for it seemed to him that the word “trust” sounded idiotic. Then, to cover his awkwardness, he coughed, and even to his own rosy ears his cough was ostentatiously a false one. Whereupon, seeking to be plausible, he coughed again, and instantly hated himself: the sound he made was an atrocity. Meanwhile, Lucy sat silent, and the two Sharon girls leaned forward, staring at him with strained eyes, their lips tightly compressed; and both were but too easily diagnosed as subject to an agitation which threatened their self-control. He began again.

“I er—I hope you have had a—a pleasant time. I er—I hope you are well. I hope you are extremely—I hope extremely—extremely—” And again he stopped in the midst of his floundering, not knowing how to progress beyond “extremely,” and unable to understand why the infernal word kept getting into his mouth.

“I beg your pardon?” Lucy said. George was never more furious; he felt that he was “making a spectacle of himself”; and no young gentleman in the world was more loath than George Amberson Minafer to look a figure of fun. And while he stood there, undeniably such a figure, with Janie and Mary Sharon threatening to burst at any moment, if laughter were longer denied them, Lucy sat looking at him with her eyebrows delicately lifted in casual, polite inquiry. Her own complete composure was what most galled him.

“Nothing of the slightest importance!” he managed to say. “I was just leaving. Good afternoon!” And with long strides he reached the door and hastened through the hall; but before he closed the front door he heard from Janie and Mary Sharon the outburst of wild, irrepressible emotion which his performance had inspired. He drove home in a tumultuous mood, and almost ran down two ladies who were engaged in absorbing conversation at a crossing. They were his Aunt Fanny and the stout Mrs. Johnson; a jerk of the reins at the last instant saved them by a few inches; but their conversation was so interesting that they were unaware of their danger, and did not notice the runabout, nor how close it came to them. George was so furious with himself and with the girl whose unexpected coming into a room could make him look such a fool, that it might have soothed him a little if he had actually run over the two absorbed ladies without injuring them beyond repair. At least, he said to himself that he wished he had; it might have taken his mind off of himself for a few minutes. For, in truth, to be ridiculous (and know it) was one of several things that George was unable to endure. He was savage.
