Each night, after Sierra Vista had gone to bed, she rose and let in White Fang to sleep in the big hall. Now White Fang was not a house-dog, nor was he permitted to sleep in the house; so each morning, early, she slipped down and let him out before the family was awake. On one such night, while all the house slept, White Fang awoke and lay very quietly. And very quietly he smelled the air and read the message it bore of a strange god’s presence. And to his ears came sounds of the strange god’s movements. White Fang burst into no furious outcry. It was not his way. The strange god walked softly, but more softly walked White Fang, for he had no clothes to rub against the flesh of his body. He followed silently. In the Wild he had hunted live meat that was infinitely timid, and he knew the advantage of surprise. The strange god paused at the foot of the great staircase and listened, and White Fang was as dead, so without movement was he as he watched and waited. Up that staircase the way led to the love-master and to the love-master’s dearest possessions. White Fang bristled, but waited. The strange god’s foot lifted. He was beginning the ascent. Then it was that White Fang struck. He gave no warning, with no snarl anticipated his own action. Into the air he lifted his body in the spring that landed him on the strange god’s back. White Fang clung with his fore-paws to the man’s shoulders, at the same time burying his fangs into the back of the man’s neck. He clung on for a moment, long enough to drag the god over backward. Together they crashed to the floor. White Fang leaped clear, and, as the man struggled to rise, was in again with the slashing fangs. Sierra Vista awoke in alarm. The noise from downstairs was as that of a score of battling fiends. There were revolver shots. A man’s voice screamed once in horror and anguish. There was a great snarling and growling, and over all arose a smashing and crashing of furniture and glass. But almost as quickly as it had arisen, the commotion died away. The struggle had not lasted more than three minutes. The frightened household clustered at the top of the stairway. From below, as from out an abyss of blackness, came up a gurgling sound, as of air bubbling through water. Sometimes this gurgle became sibilant, almost a whistle. But this, too, quickly died down and ceased. Then naught came up out of the blackness save a heavy panting of some creature struggling sorely for air. Weedon Scott pressed a button, and the staircase and downstairs hall were flooded with light. Then he and Judge Scott, revolvers in hand, cautiously descended. There was no need for this caution. White Fang had done his work. In the midst of the wreckage of overthrown and smashed furniture, partly on his side, his face hidden by an arm, lay a man. Weedon Scott bent over, removed the arm and turned the man’s face upward. A gaping throat explained the manner of his death.

“Jim Hall,” said Judge Scott, and father and son looked significantly at each other. Then they turned to White Fang. He, too, was lying on his side. His eyes were closed, but the lids slightly lifted in an effort to look at them as they bent over him, and the tail was perceptibly agitated in a vain effort to wag. Weedon Scott patted him, and his throat rumbled an acknowledging growl. But it was a weak growl at best, and it quickly ceased. His eyelids drooped and went shut, and his whole body seemed to relax and flatten out upon the floor.

“He’s all in, poor devil,” muttered the master.

“We’ll see about that,” asserted the Judge, as he started for the telephone.

“Frankly, he has one chance in a thousand,” announced the surgeon, after he had worked an hour and a half on White Fang. Dawn was breaking through the windows and dimming the electric lights. With the exception of the children, the whole family was gathered about the surgeon to hear his verdict.

“One broken hind-leg,” he went on. “Three broken ribs, one at least of which has pierced the lungs. He has lost nearly all the blood in his body. There is a large likelihood of internal injuries. He must have been jumped upon. To say nothing of three bullet holes clear through him. One chance in a thousand is really optimistic. He hasn’t a chance in ten thousand.”

“But he mustn’t lose any chance that might be of help to him,” Judge Scott exclaimed. “Never mind expense. Put him under the X-ray—anything. Weedon, telegraph at once to San Francisco for Doctor Nichols. No reflection on you, doctor, you understand; but he must have the advantage of every chance.” The surgeon smiled indulgently. “Of course I understand. He deserves all that can be done for him. He must be nursed as you would nurse a human being, a sick child. And don’t forget what I told you about temperature. I’ll be back at ten o’clock again.” White Fang received the nursing. Judge Scott’s suggestion of a trained nurse was indignantly clamoured down by the girls, who themselves undertook the task. And White Fang won out on the one chance in ten thousand denied him by the surgeon. The latter was not to be censured for his misjudgment. All his life he had tended and operated on the soft humans of civilisation, who lived sheltered lives and had descended out of many sheltered generations. Compared with White Fang, they were frail and flabby, and clutched life without any strength in their grip. White Fang had come straight from the Wild, where the weak perish early and shelter is vouchsafed to none. In neither his father nor his mother was there any weakness, nor in the generations before them. A constitution of iron and the vitality of the Wild were White Fang’s inheritance, and he clung to life, the whole of him and every part of him, in spirit and in flesh, with the tenacity that of old belonged to all creatures. Bound down a prisoner, denied even movement by the plaster casts and bandages, White Fang lingered out the weeks. He slept long hours and dreamed much, and through his mind passed an unending pageant of Northland visions. All the ghosts of the past arose and were with him. Once again he lived in the lair with Kiche, crept trembling to the knees of Grey Beaver to tender his allegiance, ran for his life before Lip-lip and all the howling bedlam of the puppy-pack. He ran again through the silence, hunting his living food through the months of famine; and again he ran at the head of the team, the gut-whips of Mit-sah and Grey Beaver snapping behind, their voices crying “Ra! Raa!” when they came to a narrow passage and the team closed together like a fan to go through. He lived again all his days with Beauty Smith and the fights he had fought. At such times he whimpered and snarled in his sleep, and they that looked on said that his dreams were bad. But there was one particular nightmare from which he suffered—the clanking, clanging monsters of electric cars that were to him colossal screaming lynxes. He would lie in a screen of bushes, watching for a squirrel to venture far enough out on the ground from its tree-refuge. Then, when he sprang out upon it, it would transform itself into an electric car, menacing and terrible, towering over him like a mountain, screaming and clanging and spitting fire at him. It was the same when he challenged the hawk down out of the sky. Down out of the blue it would rush, as it dropped upon him changing itself into the ubiquitous electric car. Or again, he would be in the pen of Beauty Smith. Outside the pen, men would be gathering, and he knew that a fight was on. He watched the door for his antagonist to enter. The door would open, and thrust in upon him would come the awful electric car. A thousand times this occurred, and each time the terror it inspired was as vivid and great as ever. Then came the day when the last bandage and the last plaster cast were taken off. It was a gala day. All Sierra Vista was gathered around. The master rubbed his ears, and he crooned his love-growl. The master’s wife called him the “Blessed Wolf,” which name was taken up with acclaim and all the women called him the Blessed Wolf. He tried to rise to his feet, and after several attempts fell down from weakness. He had lain so long that his muscles had lost their cunning, and all the strength had gone out of them. He felt a little shame because of his weakness, as though, forsooth, he were failing the gods in the service he owed them. Because of this he made heroic efforts to arise and at last he stood on his four legs, tottering and swaying back and forth.

“The Blessed Wolf!” chorused the women. Judge Scott surveyed them triumphantly.

“Out of your own mouths be it,” he said. “Just as I contended right along. No mere dog could have done what he did. He’s a wolf.”

“A Blessed Wolf,” amended the Judge’s wife.

“Yes, Blessed Wolf,” agreed the Judge. “And henceforth that shall be my name for him.”

“He’ll have to learn to walk again,” said the surgeon; “so he might as well start in right now. It won’t hurt him. Take him outside.” And outside he went, like a king, with all Sierra Vista about him and tending on him. He was very weak, and when he reached the lawn he lay down and rested for a while. Then the procession started on, little spurts of strength coming into White Fang’s muscles as he used them and the blood began to surge through them. The stables were reached, and there in the doorway, lay Collie, a half-dozen pudgy puppies playing about her in the sun. White Fang looked on with a wondering eye. Collie snarled warningly at him, and he was careful to keep his distance. The master with his toe helped one sprawling puppy toward him. He bristled suspiciously, but the master warned him that all was well. Collie, clasped in the arms of one of the women, watched him jealously and with a snarl warned him that all was not well. The puppy sprawled in front of him. He cocked his ears and watched it curiously. Then their noses touched, and he felt the warm little tongue of the puppy on his jowl. White Fang’s tongue went out, he knew not why, and he licked the puppy’s face. Hand-clapping and pleased cries from the gods greeted the performance. He was surprised, and looked at them in a puzzled way. Then his weakness asserted itself, and he lay down, his ears cocked, his head on one side, as he watched the puppy. The other puppies came sprawling toward him, to Collie’s great disgust; and he gravely permitted them to clamber and tumble over him. At first, amid the applause of the gods, he betrayed a trifle of his old self-consciousness and awkwardness. This passed away as the puppies’ antics and mauling continued, and he lay with half-shut patient eyes, drowsing in the sun.

Excerpt 3: It was wanton slaughter, and all for woman’s sake. No man ate of the seal meat or the oil. After a good day’s killing I have seen our decks covered with hides and bodies, slippery with fat and blood, the scuppers running red; masts, ropes, and rails spattered with the sanguinary colour; and the men, like butchers plying their trade, naked and red of arm and hand, hard at work with ripping and flensing-knives, removing the skins from the pretty sea-creatures they had killed. It was my task to tally the pelts as they came aboard from the boats, to oversee the skinning and afterward the cleansing of the decks and bringing things ship-shape again. It was not pleasant work. My soul and my stomach revolted at it; and yet, in a way, this handling and directing of many men was good for me. It developed what little executive ability I possessed, and I was aware of a toughening or hardening which I was undergoing and which could not be anything but wholesome for “Sissy” Van Weyden. One thing I was beginning to feel, and that was that I could never again be quite the same man I had been. While my hope and faith in human life still survived Wolf Larsen’s destructive criticism, he had nevertheless been a cause of change in minor matters. He had opened up for me the world of the real, of which I had known practically nothing and from which I had always shrunk. I had learned to look more closely at life as it was lived, to recognize that there were such things as facts in the world, to emerge from the realm of mind and idea and to place certain values on the concrete and objective phases of existence. I saw more of Wolf Larsen than ever when we had gained the grounds. For when the weather was fair and we were in the midst of the herd, all hands were away in the boats, and left on board were only he and I, and Thomas Mugridge, who did not count. But there was no play about it. The six boats, spreading out fan-wise from the schooner until the first weather boat and the last lee boat were anywhere from ten to twenty miles apart, cruised along a straight course over the sea till nightfall or bad weather drove them in. It was our duty to sail the Ghost well to leeward of the last lee boat, so that all the boats should have fair wind to run for us in case of squalls or threatening weather. It is no slight matter for two men, particularly when a stiff wind has sprung up, to handle a vessel like the Ghost, steering, keeping look-out for the boats, and setting or taking in sail; so it devolved upon me to learn, and learn quickly. Steering I picked up easily, but running aloft to the crosstrees and swinging my whole weight by my arms when I left the ratlines and climbed still higher, was more difficult. This, too, I learned, and quickly, for I felt somehow a wild desire to vindicate myself in Wolf Larsen’s eyes, to prove my right to live in ways other than of the mind. Nay, the time came when I took joy in the run of the masthead and in the clinging on by my legs at that precarious height while I swept the sea with glasses in search of the boats. I remember one beautiful day, when the boats left early and the reports of the hunters’ guns grew dim and distant and died away as they scattered far and wide over the sea. There was just the faintest wind from the westward; but it breathed its last by the time we managed to get to leeward of the last lee boat. One by one—I was at the masthead and saw—the six boats disappeared over the bulge of the earth as they followed the seal into the west. We lay, scarcely rolling on the placid sea, unable to follow. Wolf Larsen was apprehensive. The barometer was down, and the sky to the east did not please him. He studied it with unceasing vigilance.

“If she comes out of there,” he said, “hard and snappy, putting us to windward of the boats, it’s likely there’ll be empty bunks in steerage and fo’c’sle.” By eleven o’clock the sea had become glass. By midday, though we were well up in the northerly latitudes, the heat was sickening. There was no freshness in the air. It was sultry and oppressive, reminding me of what the old Californians term “earthquake weather.” There was something ominous about it, and in intangible ways one was made to feel that the worst was about to come. Slowly the whole eastern sky filled with clouds that over-towered us like some black sierra of the infernal regions. So clearly could one see cañon, gorge, and precipice, and the shadows that lie therein, that one looked unconsciously for the white surf-line and bellowing caverns where the sea charges on the land. And still we rocked gently, and there was no wind.

“It’s no squall,” Wolf Larsen said. “Old Mother Nature’s going to get up on her hind legs and howl for all that’s in her, and it’ll keep us jumping, Hump, to pull through with half our boats. You’d better run up and loosen the topsails.”

“But if it is going to howl, and there are only two of us?” I asked, a note of protest in my voice.

“Why we’ve got to make the best of the first of it and run down to our boats before our canvas is ripped out of us. After that I don’t give a rap what happens. The sticks ’ll stand it, and you and I will have to, though we’ve plenty cut out for us.” Still the calm continued. We ate dinner, a hurried and anxious meal for me with eighteen men abroad on the sea and beyond the bulge of the earth, and with that heaven-rolling mountain range of clouds moving slowly down upon us. Wolf Larsen did not seem affected, however; though I noticed, when we returned to the deck, a slight twitching of the nostrils, a perceptible quickness of movement. His face was stern, the lines of it had grown hard, and yet in his eyes—blue, clear blue this day—there was a strange brilliancy, a bright scintillating light. It struck me that he was joyous, in a ferocious sort of way; that he was glad there was an impending struggle; that he was thrilled and upborne with knowledge that one of the great moments of living, when the tide of life surges up in flood, was upon him. Once, and unwitting that he did so or that I saw, he laughed aloud, mockingly and defiantly, at the advancing storm. I see him yet standing there like a pigmy out of the Arabian Nights before the huge front of some malignant genie. He was daring destiny, and he was unafraid. He walked to the galley. “Cooky, by the time you’ve finished pots and pans you’ll be wanted on deck. Stand ready for a call.”

“Hump,” he said, becoming cognizant of the fascinated gaze I bent upon him, “this beats whisky and is where your Omar misses. I think he only half lived after all.” The western half of the sky had by now grown murky. The sun had dimmed and faded out of sight. It was two in the afternoon, and a ghostly twilight, shot through by wandering purplish lights, had descended upon us. In this purplish light Wolf Larsen’s face glowed and glowed, and to my excited fancy he appeared encircled by a halo. We lay in the midst of an unearthly quiet, while all about us were signs and omens of oncoming sound and movement. The sultry heat had become unendurable. The sweat was standing on my forehead, and I could feel it trickling down my nose. I felt as though I should faint, and reached out to the rail for support. And then, just then, the faintest possible whisper of air passed by. It was from the east, and like a whisper it came and went. The drooping canvas was not stirred, and yet my face had felt the air and been cooled.

“Cooky,” Wolf Larsen called in a low voice. Thomas Mugridge turned a pitiable scared face. “Let go that foreboom tackle and pass it across, and when she’s willing let go the sheet and come in snug with the tackle. And if you make a mess of it, it will be the last you ever make. Understand?”

“Mr. Van Weyden, stand by to pass the head-sails over. Then jump for the topsails and spread them quick as God’ll let you—the quicker you do it the easier you’ll find it. As for Cooky, if he isn’t lively bat him between the eyes.” I was aware of the compliment and pleased, in that no threat had accompanied my instructions. We were lying head to north-west, and it was his intention to jibe over all with the first puff.

“We’ll have the breeze on our quarter,” he explained to me. “By the last guns the boats were bearing away slightly to the south’ard.” He turned and walked aft to the wheel. I went forward and took my station at the jibs. Another whisper of wind, and another, passed by. The canvas flapped lazily.

“Thank Gawd she’s not comin’ all of a bunch, Mr. Van Weyden,” was the Cockney’s fervent ejaculation. And I was indeed thankful, for I had by this time learned enough to know, with all our canvas spread, what disaster in such event awaited us. The whispers of wind became puffs, the sails filled, the Ghost moved. Wolf Larsen put the wheel hard up, to port, and we began to pay off. The wind was now dead astern, muttering and puffing stronger and stronger, and my head-sails were pounding lustily. I did not see what went on elsewhere, though I felt the sudden surge and heel of the schooner as the wind-pressures changed to the jibing of the fore- and main-sails. My hands were full with the flying-jib, jib, and staysail; and by the time this part of my task was accomplished the Ghost was leaping into the south-west, the wind on her quarter and all her sheets to starboard. Without pausing for breath, though my heart was beating like a trip-hammer from my exertions, I sprang to the topsails, and before the wind had become too strong we had them fairly set and were coiling down. Then I went aft for orders. Wolf Larsen nodded approval and relinquished the wheel to me. The wind was strengthening steadily and the sea rising. For an hour I steered, each moment becoming more difficult. I had not the experience to steer at the gait we were going on a quartering course.

“Now take a run up with the glasses and raise some of the boats. We’ve made at least ten knots, and we’re going twelve or thirteen now. The old girl knows how to walk.” I contested myself with the fore crosstrees, some seventy feet above the deck. As I searched the vacant stretch of water before me, I comprehended thoroughly the need for haste if we were to recover any of our men. Indeed, as I gazed at the heavy sea through which we were running, I doubted that there was a boat afloat. It did not seem possible that such frail craft could survive such stress of wind and water. I could not feel the full force of the wind, for we were running with it; but from my lofty perch I looked down as though outside the Ghost and apart from her, and saw the shape of her outlined sharply against the foaming sea as she tore along instinct with life. Sometimes she would lift and send across some great wave, burying her starboard-rail from view, and covering her deck to the hatches with the boiling ocean. At such moments, starting from a windward roll, I would go flying through the air with dizzying swiftness, as though I clung to the end of a huge, inverted pendulum, the arc of which, between the greater rolls, must have been seventy feet or more. Once, the terror of this giddy sweep overpowered me, and for a while I clung on, hand and foot, weak and trembling, unable to search the sea for the missing boats or to behold aught of the sea but that which roared beneath and strove to overwhelm the Ghost. But the thought of the men in the midst of it steadied me, and in my quest for them I forgot myself. For an hour I saw nothing but the naked, desolate sea. And then, where a vagrant shaft of sunlight struck the ocean and turned its surface to wrathful silver, I caught a small black speck thrust skyward for an instant and swallowed up. I waited patiently. Again the tiny point of black projected itself through the wrathful blaze a couple of points off our port-bow. I did not attempt to shout, but communicated the news to Wolf Larsen by waving my arm. He changed the course, and I signalled affirmation when the speck showed dead ahead. It grew larger, and so swiftly that for the first time I fully appreciated the speed of our flight. Wolf Larsen motioned for me to come down, and when I stood beside him at the wheel gave me instructions for heaving to.

“Expect all hell to break loose,” he cautioned me, “but don’t mind it. Yours is to do your own work and to have Cooky stand by the fore-sheet.” I managed to make my way forward, but there was little choice of sides, for the weather-rail seemed buried as often as the lee. Having instructed Thomas Mugridge as to what he was to do, I clambered into the fore-rigging a few feet. The boat was now very close, and I could make out plainly that it was lying head to wind and sea and dragging on its mast and sail, which had been thrown overboard and made to serve as a sea-anchor. The three men were bailing. Each rolling mountain whelmed them from view, and I would wait with sickening anxiety, fearing that they would never appear again. Then, and with black suddenness, the boat would shoot clear through the foaming crest, bow pointed to the sky, and the whole length of her bottom showing, wet and dark, till she seemed on end. There would be a fleeting glimpse of the three men flinging water in frantic haste, when she would topple over and fall into the yawning valley, bow down and showing her full inside length to the stern upreared almost directly above the bow. Each time that she reappeared was a miracle. The Ghost suddenly changed her course, keeping away, and it came to me with a shock that Wolf Larsen was giving up the rescue as impossible. Then I realized that he was preparing to heave to, and dropped to the deck to be in readiness. We were now dead before the wind, the boat far away and abreast of us. I felt an abrupt easing of the schooner, a loss for the moment of all strain and pressure, coupled with a swift acceleration of speed. She was rushing around on her heel into the wind.

The cold had come down upon the land in the night, and by morning it lay upon the valley of the Stewart like a thing of weight and substance that might almost be handled. The spirit thermometer nailed beside the cabin door stood at fifty-two below zero. There was no wind. There was never wind in such cold. The spruce stood motionless on the white flanks of the hills, each bough bowed under its burden of snow, and the river, locked in ice from bank to bank, was a white road that ran nowhere and ended in silence. Over all brooded the grey half-light of the northern winter, a light that was not day and not night, but a sullen twilight in which the world seemed to hold its breath and wait.

In the cabin, a squat thing of logs chinked with moss and banked to the eaves with snow, John Thorne laced his moccasins by the light of the stove. He was a big man, heavy of shoulder and long of arm, and his face had been weathered by many winters until it was the colour and texture of old harness leather. He had come into the country in the rush of 'ninety-eight, and he had stayed when the rush went out again, because the country had got into him and he could not shake it off. He had taken a wife at Dawson, a woman of his own breed, strong and quiet, and she had borne him a son. The son was seven years old now, and he sat on the edge of the bunk with his chin on his knees and watched his father with grave eyes.

The woman lay in the other bunk. She had been sick three days with a fever that came and went, and her face on the caribou-skin pillow was flushed and thin. She slept, breathing quickly and lightly, as a bird breathes.

"Kit," said the father, when the second moccasin was laced, "come here."

The boy slid down from the bunk and came and stood before him. He was small for his years, but there was promise of bone in him, and his eyes were the eyes of his father, grey and steady.

"I'm goin' up the hill for wood," Thorne said. "There ain't enough dry stuff to last the day, an' I can't leave your ma with a cold stove. I'll be gone four hours, maybe five. You know what you got to do?"

"Keep the fire," said the boy.

"What else?"

"Give Ma water when she wants it."

"What else?"

The boy hesitated, and the father waited. He did not hurry the boy. He had learned in the North that a thing learned slowly is a thing learned well.

"Not go past the cache," the boy said at last.

"Not go past the cache," the father repeated. "Not a step. Not for nothin'. You hear me, Kit?"

"Yes, Pa."

Thorne put his hand on the boy's head for a moment, a big hand, scarred and knotted, that covered the small skull like a cap. Then he drew on his fur cap and his mittens, took up his axe, and went out. The cold leaped in at the door like a live thing and rolled in a white vapour across the floor, and then the door was shut and the boy was alone with his sleeping mother and the crackling of the stove.

It was a long morning for the boy. He fed the fire as he had been told, and he gave his mother water when she woke and asked for it, holding the tin cup to her lips while she drank. She smiled at him and called him her little man, and slept again. And then there was nothing to do but sit and listen to the fire and the silence. The silence was the worse of the two. It pressed in upon the cabin from every side, and it seemed to the boy that it pressed in upon him as well, filling his ears and his head until there was no room in him for anything else.

It was out of the silence that the thought came to him. He had snares set below the bend of the river, three of them, made of brass wire his father had given him at Christmas. He had not visited them in four days, for his father had forbidden him to go so far in the deep cold. But there might be rabbits in them. There might be a fat rabbit, frozen stiff and waiting. And his mother was sick, and had eaten nothing but beans and bacon and sour-dough bread, and a sick woman needed fresh meat. His father had said so himself, only the night before, sitting by the stove with his pipe and frowning at the floor.

The boy thought about it for a long time. He was a good boy, as boys go, and he knew the law his father had laid down. But he was seven years old, and at seven years the law of the father is a thing of words, while a fat rabbit in a snare is a thing of flesh and blood. Nor did he know the cold. He had been born in it and had lived in it all his life, but always there had been the cabin and the stove and the big shape of his father between him and it. He did not know what the cold could do. He thought of it as a thing that made the fingers ache and the nose run, a thing to be stamped and slapped away. He did not know that it was a hunter, patient and without pity, that it had killed strong men, and that it would kill a small boy as readily as it would freeze a drop of water.

So he filled the stove with wood until it roared, and he drew on his parka and his moccasins and his mittens, and he went out softly so as not to wake his mother. He passed the cache, a little log house on stilts, and he did not look at it. He went down the bank to the river and turned downstream toward the bend.

The cold took him by the face at once. It was like the touch of hot iron, and it made him gasp, and the gasp drew the cold down into his lungs so that they burned. He pulled his parka hood close and went on. His breath froze as it left his lips and gathered in frost upon the fur about his face. His eyelashes frosted and stuck together when he blinked, and he had to pull them apart with his mittened fingers. But he went on, for the bend was not so very far, and the snares were just beyond.

It was farther than he remembered. In the summer, when he had come down with his father to fish, it had been a short walk. Now each step was labour, for the snow on the river was soft beneath its crust, and he broke through to the knee and must drag his feet out again. He grew warm with the work, and then he grew cold again, a deeper cold that began at his feet and crept upward. But he was near the bend now, and he would not turn back. To turn back with nothing would be to confess that he had been foolish. And he wanted very much to come back with a rabbit and lay it on the table and see his mother's face.

He rounded the bend at last. The first snare was empty. The second had been sprung, and the loop of wire hung limp and bare. The third held a rabbit, frozen hard as a stick of wood, its white fur stiff with rime. The boy gave a little cry of triumph and knelt in the snow to free it.

The wire was tangled about the rabbit's neck and frozen fast. He could not loosen it with his mittens on. He pulled off his right mitten and worked at the wire with his bare fingers. The cold bit into them instantly, and in a moment they were aching, and in another moment they had ceased to ache. He did not notice when the ache stopped. He was intent upon the wire. When at last it came free, he found that he could not close his fingers on the rabbit. They would not obey him. They were white, and they would not bend.

He was frightened then, for the first time. He looked about him, and the white land looked back at him, vast and silent and indifferent. The spruce trees on the bank stood like grey ghosts. The river stretched away into the twilight. There was no sound anywhere, save the beating of his own heart. And then he saw the tracks.

They came down off the bank above the snares, and they were large tracks, larger than the tracks of any dog of his father's team. They circled the place where he knelt, at a little distance, and went away again up the bank into the trees. They were fresh. The snow was still crumbling at their edges.

The boy did not know how long he crouched there. He tried to pull his mitten on again, but his fingers would not do it, and the mitten fell into the snow. He tried to pick it up and could not. The cold was in him now, deep in him, and it was making him sleepy. That was the strange thing. He was frightened, and yet he wanted to sleep. He thought that if he rested a little, only a little, he would be strong enough to start back. He curled down in the snow beside the frozen rabbit and pulled his bare hand up into his sleeve.

It was so that John Thorne found him.

The man had come down off the hill an hour early, for a strange uneasiness had been upon him all the morning, and he had learned in the North not to disregard such things. He found the cabin hot, the stove red, his wife asleep, and the boy gone. He did not wake the woman. He read the story in the snow outside the door as plainly as though it had been printed in a book, and he followed it down the river at a run, his long legs eating up the distance that had cost the boy an hour. He did not call out. He saved his breath for running.

When he came around the bend and saw the small dark shape curled in the snow, something happened in his chest that he had not felt since the night the boy was born. But his hands did not tremble. He knelt and turned the boy over, and saw that he was alive, and saw the white fingers and the white patch upon one cheek. He rubbed the fingers with snow, hard, until the boy cried out with the pain of it, and then he rubbed the cheek. He found the mitten and thrust the boy's hand into it, and his own mitten over that. He took the boy up in his arms and turned toward home. And as he turned, he saw the tracks that circled the place, and he looked at them a long moment with narrowed eyes, and his face grew harder than it had been.

He did not speak all the way back. The boy, who had come awake with the pain in his fingers, lay against his father's chest and wept quietly, and the tears froze upon his cheeks. Thorne did not hush him. He walked steadily, carrying the boy and the frozen rabbit, and the cabin came in sight at last, with its thin plume of smoke rising straight up into the still air.

Inside, he set the boy down on a box by the stove and stripped off the parka and the mittens and the moccasins. He looked at the feet, and they were whole. He looked at the fingers again, and they were red now and swelling, and the boy whimpered when he touched them. The skin would peel, and there would be pain for many days, but the fingers would keep. The cheek, too, would heal, though it would be black for a week. He grunted, and went to the stove and set water to heat, and all the while he said nothing.

The woman had awakened. She lifted herself on her elbow and looked at the boy, and then at the man, and her face went white under the flush of the fever.

"John—"

"He's all right," said Thorne. "Lie down, Mary."

She lay down, but her eyes did not leave the boy.

Thorne poured the warm water into a basin and set the boy's hands in it, and held them there when the boy tried to pull away. Then, when the worst of it had passed, he drew another box across the floor and sat down upon it, facing the boy, so that their eyes were on a level. He sat for some time without speaking. He was a man who had never had much use for words, and he was searching now for the right ones, and they were slow in coming.

He was thinking, though the boy did not know it, of his own father. His own father had been a lumber-jack in the Michigan woods, a hard man in a hard trade, and he had known but one way of teaching a boy, and that was with a strap. John Thorne had learned many things under that strap, but the chief thing he had learned was to hate the hand that held it. He had run away from that hand when he was fourteen, and he had never gone back. And he had sworn, lying awake on the night his own son was born, that no son of his should learn the lesson of the strap. Fear was a poor schoolmaster. It taught a boy to hide, and to lie, and to wait for the day when he would be big enough to strike back. It did not teach him to see.

And it was seeing that the North demanded. The North did not care for a man's courage, nor for his strength, nor for the goodness of his heart. It cared only whether he saw truly. It cared whether he knew the thickness of the ice and the meaning of the sky and the number of the matches in his pocket. The man who saw truly might live. The man who did not, died. There was no appeal from that judgment and no mercy in it. It was the oldest law of the land, older than men, older than the wolves, and it was graven in the cold itself.

"Kit," the father said at last, "look at me."

The boy looked up. His eyes were red and wet, and his lip trembled.

"What did I tell you this mornin'?"

"Not to go past the cache," the boy whispered.

"An' what did you do?"

The boy's lip trembled harder. "I went past it."

"Why?"

"I wanted—" The boy's voice broke, and he swallowed and tried again. "I wanted to get a rabbit for Ma. You said she needed fresh meat. I heard you."

Thorne's face did not change, but something moved behind his eyes. He glanced at the rabbit, lying stiff upon the table, and then back at the boy.

"I know what you wanted," he said slowly. "It was a good thing to want. I ain't sayin' it wasn't. But listen to me now, Kit, an' listen hard, for I ain't goin' to say this twice. Wantin' ain't nothin' up here. Wantin' don't count. The cold don't care what you want. It don't care if you're a good boy or a bad boy. It don't care if you went out to get meat for your ma or to throw rocks at the ravens. It'll kill you just the same, an' it'll never know it done it, nor care."

The boy stared at him.

"You know what you done to your ma?" Thorne went on. "You left her alone, sick, with the stove crammed so full it like to've set the roof afire. If I hadn't come back early, the fire'd've burned down an' gone out by noon, an' she couldn't've got up to tend it. You know what happens in a cabin with no fire at fifty below? In a couple hours it's as cold inside as out. You'd've come back an' found her—" He stopped. He did not finish it. He did not need to.

The boy began to cry again, harder now, with great sobs that shook his small body. Thorne let him cry. He did not reach out to him. He sat with his big hands on his knees and waited, and his face was like a face carved out of wood.

In the bunk the woman stirred. "John," she said softly. "He's only a baby."

"He ain't a baby," said Thorne, without turning his head. "Not up here. There ain't no babies up here, Mary. There's them that lives an' them that don't."

He waited until the worst of the sobbing had passed. Then he spoke again, and his voice was lower.

"I knew a man once," he said, "a Swede called Larssen, down on the Sixtymile. Big man. Bigger'n me. He'd been in the country longer'n me, too, an' he knew it better. One winter, cold like this, he went out to look at his traps. Just a little ways. He'd done it a hundred times. An' he got his feet wet in an overflow, an' he went to build a fire, an' his hands was too cold to strike the matches. They found him in the spring, Kit. Two hundred yards from his own door. He could've seen the smoke from his chimney, if there'd been anybody to light it. Two hundred yards." He let the words hang in the air. "He was a strong man, an' a good man, an' he knew the cold. An' he figured, just that once, that he knew it better'n it knew him."

The boy had stopped crying. He was listening now, with his wet eyes fixed upon his father's face.

"Out there," Thorne said, and he jerked his head toward the door and the white world beyond it, "there's no second chance. You do a fool thing in the city, an' somebody comes an' picks you up an' dusts you off, an' you go on. Up here there ain't nobody to pick you up. There's only the cold, an' it's waitin'. It's always waitin'. It waits for you to get tired, or to get careless, or to think you know better. An' when you do—" He closed one big hand slowly into a fist. "That's all."

He leaned forward a little.

"You saw them tracks?"

The boy nodded, and his face went pale.

"Wolf," said Thorne. "A big one. He'd been round you twice. He was sittin' up there in the trees, waitin' for you to go to sleep. Another half hour, maybe less." He did not soften it. He wanted the boy to see it, to see it clearly and never to forget it. "He wasn't mad at you. He wasn't wicked. He was hungry, that's all, an' you was meat. That's all you are out there, Kit, if you ain't careful. Meat."

There was a long silence in the cabin. The stove ticked and muttered. Outside, far off, a raven croaked once, and the sound fell into the stillness like a stone into deep water.

"Now," said Thorne, "here's what's goin' to be. You don't go to your snares no more this winter. Not till I say. An' every stick of wood that comes into this cabin, you carry from the pile. Every stick. Your hands'll be sore, an' it'll hurt, an' I don't care. You'll carry it. An' every mornin', before you eat, you'll stand here an' tell me the rules. All of 'em. Till you know 'em better'n you know your own name."

"Yes, Pa," the boy whispered.

"Say 'em now."

The boy said them, haltingly, his voice catching. Not past the cache. Never out without telling. Never the bare hand in the cold. Never sit down to rest. Never sleep in the snow. Thorne made him say them three times, and the third time the voice was steadier.

Then, and only then, the father put out his hand and laid it on the boy's head, as he had done that morning. He did not say anything. He did not need to. The boy leaned against the big knee and closed his eyes, and his small shoulders shook once more and then were still.

That night, when the boy slept in the bunk beside his mother with his swollen hands wrapped in rags greased with bacon fat, John Thorne sat long by the stove with his pipe gone cold between his teeth. The woman watched him from the shadows.

"You were hard on him, John," she said.

"I was," he agreed.

"He meant well."

"I know he did." He took the pipe from his mouth and looked at it, turning it over in his fingers. "That's what scares me, Mary. Meanin' well don't help. I seen a lot of men die up here that meant well." He was silent a while. Then he said, so low that she barely heard, "I never laid a hand on him. Not once. You saw."

"I saw."

"My old man'd have skinned me." He laughed shortly, without mirth. "An' I'd have hated him for it, an' learned nothin'. I want the boy to learn, Mary. I want him to see. The strap don't make a boy see. It just makes him scared of the strap." He stared into the red slits of the stove door. "I want him scared of the right thing."

She did not answer. After a while her breathing grew slow and even, and he knew that she slept. But he sat on, hour after hour, feeding the fire, while the cold pressed close about the little cabin and the stars burned white and pitiless above the silent land. And once, toward morning, he rose and went to the bunk and stood looking down at the sleeping boy, at the black frost-mark on the small cheek and the bandaged hands curled upon the blanket. His face, in the dim glow of the stove, was not the face of wood it had been that afternoon. It was the face of a man who had looked into the white silence and seen the thing that waited there, and had snatched his own from its very jaws.

The whistle at the Bessemer mill had blown for the change of shift at six o'clock, and it was nearly half-past seven before Janos Halasz came up the hill to the row of company houses where he lived. He was not drunk, as his wife had half feared he might be, for it was a Saturday, and there were eleven saloons between the mill gate and the foot of Shanty Hill, each of them lit up and roaring like a furnace. But he walked with his head down and his hands thrust deep into the pockets of his coat, and when he came in at the door he did not look at her, nor at the baby who lay on the bed in the corner, but went and sat down upon the box by the stove and stared at the floor.

Erzsi had his supper waiting for him. It was a pot of cabbage soup with a piece of pork in it the size of a man's two fingers, and a loaf of the gray bread that came from the company store at six cents. She had been keeping it warm for an hour, and the cabbage had gone soft and stringy, and the smell of it filled the room. The room was perhaps ten feet by twelve, and it served them as kitchen and parlor and bedroom all at once. Behind a curtain made of two flour sacks sewn together there was another room, smaller still, and in this slept the two boarders, Ferenc and old Mihaly, who paid them three dollars a week apiece and without whom the family could not have lived at all. The boarders were not at home tonight, it being Saturday. They would come in at two or three in the morning, and one of them would be sick on the step, as he had been last Saturday and the Saturday before that; and Erzsi would lie awake listening to him and thinking about the rent.

The rent was eleven dollars a month. It was taken out of Janos's pay by the company, before ever he saw it, and so was the bill at the company store, and so was the dollar a month for the company doctor, who came when he pleased and who had not come at all when the baby was born. There were many people in the outside world who believed that the steel workers of the Monongahela valley were well paid—had not the newspapers said so, and had not the president of the corporation himself declared, at a banquet in New York where the terrapin had cost four dollars a plate, that the American workingman was the most prosperous in the world? Janos Halasz earned two dollars and ten cents for a turn of twelve hours, and he worked seven days in the week, and every second Sunday he worked the "long turn" of twenty-four hours, when the shifts were changed about. When everything had been deducted that the company chose to deduct, there was left to him in a good month perhaps thirty dollars, and with this he had to feed and clothe his wife and himself and his two children, and to send something back to his old mother in the village beyond Kassa, who had sold her cow to pay his passage to America.

Erzsi put the soup before him and he did not touch it. She stood waiting, with her hands wrapped in her apron, and the fear that had been in her all day rose up and caught her by the throat.

"Janos," she said, "what is it? You have been laid off?"

He shook his head.

"Then you are hurt? Something has happened at the mill?"

"Nothing has happened," he said. "Let me be."

But she could not let him be. She had been married to him for six years, and she knew every shade of his silences, and this one was new to her. It was not the silence of weariness, which was the one she knew best of all—that dull, stupefied silence of a man who has stood for twelve hours before the mouth of a converter, with the heat beating upon him till the sweat ran down into his shoes and the flame of the blow roaring in his ears like the end of the world. This was something else; there was a hardness in it, and a kind of shame. And so she pulled the other box up beside him and sat down and put her hand upon his knee.

"Tell me," she said.

He was a long time about it. He took the spoon and stirred the soup, and watched the bits of cabbage go round, and then he laid the spoon down again. At last he said, without looking up, "Kinney spoke to me today."

Kinney was the foreman of the blowing floor—a big, red-faced Irishman with a voice like a steam whistle, who had come up from the ranks himself and had forgotten everything about the ranks except how to drive them. Erzsi had seen him once, on the day of the accident to Gyula Toth, when he had stood over the body and cursed because the converter would be shut down for half an hour.

"What did he say?" she asked.

"He said that there is talk among the men. About the union."

Erzsi's hand tightened upon his knee. Everybody in Shanty Hill knew about the talk of the union; it was whispered over the back fences and in the corners of the saloons, and at the Greek Catholic church after mass, when the men stood about in their Sunday collars. There was an organizer who had come up from Pittsburgh, a thin young man with spectacles who spoke Hungarian very badly and Slovak rather better, and who held meetings in the back room of Novak's hall until the company had bought Novak's hall, and after that in the woods above the slag dump. Two men had been discharged already for going to these meetings; one of them had been beaten by the deputies and put on a train with a ticket to Cleveland, and his wife had gone after him with the children a week later, carrying everything they owned in a bedsheet.

"He asked if you went to the meetings?" Erzsi said, and her voice was a whisper.

"No. He did not ask me that." Janos laughed, a short ugly sound. "He knows who goes. He knows everything. He wanted something else."

"What then?"

Janos lifted his head and looked at her for the first time, and she saw that his eyes were red, and not from the heat of the converter.

"He wants me to tell him who goes," he said. "He wants me to go myself, and sit with them, and listen, and come back and tell him the names. He says he will put me on the ladle crane. That is three dollars and forty cents the turn, Erzsi. Three dollars and forty cents. And he says that there will be something besides, five dollars at the end of each month, from the office, that nobody needs to know about."

There was a long silence in the room. Outside, somewhere down the hill, a man was singing in a drunken voice, and a dog was barking, and over everything, so constant that one ceased to hear it, there came the pounding of the mill—the rumble of the blooming rolls, the clang of the cars, the deep, shuddering breath of the blast furnaces, which never stopped, by day or by night, from one year's end to the next. The sky over the river was red with the glare of them, and the light came in at the one small window and lay upon the floor in a dull smear, like blood that had been wiped up carelessly.

Erzsi did not speak at once. She was doing sums in her head; she could not help it, any more than she could help breathing. For six years she had been doing these sums, morning and night, until they had become a part of the very fabric of her mind. Three dollars and forty cents instead of two dollars and ten—that was one dollar and thirty cents more in each turn, and there were thirty turns in the month, and that was thirty-nine dollars; and the five dollars besides made forty-four. Forty-four dollars more in a month! It was more than they had now altogether. It meant the rent paid on the first, and no more slips of paper from the company store with the figures in red ink. It meant shoes for little Jozsi, who had been going barefoot since September, though there had been frost upon the slag heaps these two weeks. It meant—her eyes went in spite of herself to the bed in the corner, where the baby lay breathing with that small, harsh, rattling sound that had kept her awake for five nights now—it meant a real doctor, a doctor from Pittsburgh, and medicine that was not a bottle of colored water with a company label on it.

Janos saw where her eyes had gone, and his face twisted.

"Yes," he said, bitterly. "I know. Do you think I did not think of that? I thought of nothing else all the afternoon. I stood on the floor and watched the blow, and I said to myself, the little one is coughing, and Kinney is offering money, and what is a name? A name is nothing. They know the names already, most of them. What harm is it if I tell them what they know?"

"And what did you tell him?" Erzsi asked.

"I told him I would think."

She let out her breath. She had not known that she was holding it. And then, because she was a woman who had been hungry, and who had watched her children be hungry, and who had learned in a hard school that it is the poor who pay for every pride, she said the thing that she would afterwards have given her right hand not to have said.

"Janos," she said, "it is not as if you were a union man yourself. You have never signed anything. You have never even been to the woods. What do you owe to these people?"

He turned on her so suddenly that she shrank back.

"What do I owe them?" he cried. "What do I owe to Gyula Toth, who was burned in the face so that his own wife screamed when they brought him home? What do I owe to Pista Varga, who has worked on the floor for nine years and has not had one Sunday in all that time to go to church, and is coughing like the baby there, only it is the dust in his lungs and no doctor in the world can cure that? What do I owe to the men who stand next to me in the heat, and drink out of the same bucket, and carry each other out when they fall down? You ask me what I owe them!"

"Hush," she said, "you will wake the children."

But Jozsi was awake already; she could see the gleam of his eyes from the pallet on the floor where he slept, beneath the window. He was five years old, and he had learned already that when his father raised his voice it was best to lie very still and pretend to be asleep. There are children all over the world who learn this lesson, in the tenements of New York and in the back streets of Manchester and in the mill towns of the valley; and they learn it before they learn their letters, and they never forget it.

Janos lowered his voice, but it was no less fierce.

"Do you know what they do to a man who carries tales?" he said. "Do you know what they called Sandor Kis, who did it last year at the Edgar Thomson works? They called him the dog's son, and they spat when he went by, and in the end somebody dropped a pig of iron on his foot from the charging floor, and nobody saw who did it, and he is walking with a crutch now in Homestead, and the company will not give him even a job at the gate. That is what happens to a spotter. And that is the best that happens. The worst is that you have to live with yourself."

"And what happens to a man who will not be a spotter?" Erzsi said. Her voice was low and steady now, but her hands were shaking in her lap. "I will tell you. Kinney asked you, and you would not, and so Kinney knows you are not his man. Do you think he will forget it? He will find a reason. He will say you were slow on the blow, he will say you were drunk, he will say you spoke back to him. And then you will have no job at all, and we will have no house, because the house belongs to the company, and they will put our things in the road the same as they did to the Kovacs. And where will we go then, with the winter coming and the baby sick? Will the union feed us? The union has no money. The young man with the spectacles has no money. He has a room in Pittsburgh and a clean shirt, and when it is finished he will go away to another town and talk to other men, and we will be in the road!"

She had not meant to cry, but now the tears came, and she put her apron over her face. Janos sat and looked at her, and the anger went out of him, and left him gray and old. He was twenty-nine years old, and there were times, like this one, when he looked fifty.

"Erzsi," he said, after a while, "listen to me."

She did not take the apron from her face.

"You think I do not know all that? I know it better than you. I have known it since I came across the water. In the old country it was the count, and his stewards, and the gendarmes with feathers in their hats, and you took off your cap when they rode by, and you said, yes, your honor, and no, your honor, and you starved quietly. And then we heard about America. The agent came to the village with his pictures—do you remember? The houses with gardens, and the men in collars, and the wages written large, so that the old women crossed themselves. A free country, he said. A man is a man in America, he said. And we came. And what is it here? It is the count again, only now he lives in New York and nobody has ever seen his face, and his stewards are called superintendents, and his gendarmes are called the Coal and Iron Police, and instead of feathers they have clubs. And it is the same thing, only worse, because in the old country at least the count did not pretend he was our friend."

She took the apron down and looked at him. He had never talked to her like this before; she did not know that he had these thoughts in him. It was as if a stranger had come and sat down by her stove.

"Where did you learn to talk so?" she said.

"In the woods," he said simply. "Above the slag dump."

And then she understood, and the room seemed to turn about her.

"You have been going," she whispered. "All this time—the Sundays when you said you were sleeping at Mihaly's cousin's—"

"Three times," he said. "Only three. And I have not signed. But I have been listening, and I have been thinking. And when Kinney came to me today and put his hand on my shoulder, and smiled at me with his big teeth, and talked to me as if we were brothers, I knew that he had seen me there, or somebody had seen me and told him. And I knew that he was not asking me. He was telling me. Either I am his dog, or I am finished."

Erzsi sat very still. The baby coughed, a long racking cough that ended in a thin wail, and she got up and went to the bed and lifted it, and held it against her shoulder, and walked up and down the narrow space between the stove and the curtain, patting the small back with her worn hand. The child was hot to the touch, hotter than it had been in the morning; she could feel the heat of it through her dress. She thought of the doctor from Pittsburgh, and of the medicine, and of the forty-four dollars, and she thought of Sandor Kis walking on his crutch in Homestead, and of men spitting when Janos went by, and of Janos sitting on this box night after night, not looking at her, not looking at anyone, with that hard shame in his eyes growing harder every day until there was nothing left of him but the shame. And she understood, in that moment, a thing which the gentlemen who write about labor in the magazines have never understood, and never will—that the choice which the company had put before her husband was not a choice between riches and poverty, nor even between bread and hunger, but between two kinds of death; and that it was the same choice which it put before every man in the valley, every day of his life, so softly that most of them never knew they were choosing at all.

"What will you do?" she said at last.

Janos was a long time answering.

"I do not know," he said. "Tell me what to do, Erzsi. You have a better head than I have. You always had. Tell me, and I will do it."

It was the cruelest thing he could have said to her, and he did not know it. She stood with the sick child against her breast, and the light of the furnaces lay red upon the floor, and the mill pounded on and on beneath them like the heart of some great beast that fed upon the bodies of men. She looked at her husband's hands, lying open upon his knees, the palms seamed with old burns and the knuckles swollen; and she looked at the eyes of her son, gleaming at her silently from the pallet beneath the window; and she knew that whatever she said now, he would remember it, and she would remember it, for as long as either of them lived.

"Eat your soup," she said. "It is getting cold."

He looked at her, and then he picked up the spoon and began to eat, slowly, mechanically, as a man eats who does not taste anything. She walked up and down with the baby, and the baby coughed and quieted and coughed again, and the drunken man down the hill had stopped singing.

When he had finished she took the bowl from him and set it in the basin, and then she came and stood in front of him.

"Monday," she said, "you will go to Kinney, and you will tell him that you have thought, and that you cannot do it, because you are a slow man with words and you would make mistakes with the names. Tell him you are stupid. They believe that of us; let them believe it. Perhaps he will let it go, and perhaps he will not. If he does not—" her voice faltered, and then went on—"if he does not, there is my cousin Marika in Johnstown, at the car works. She has written that they are taking men. It is not much. It is nothing. But it is not this."

Janos bowed his head, and she saw his shoulders shake. She put her free hand upon his hair, which was stiff with the dust of the mill, and stood so for a long time.

"And the little one?" he said, very low.

"I will take him to the Sisters at the hospital in Braddock," she said. "They do not ask for money first. Mrs. Toth told me."

She did not tell him what else Mrs. Toth had told her—that the Sisters were kind, but that the ward was full of children from the valley with the same cough, and that half of them did not come home. There are some things a woman carries by herself.

Outside, the whistle blew for some change of shift in some other department; it was impossible, in Shanty Hill, to know which. The red light flickered upon the window as a furnace was tapped down by the river, and for a moment the whole room was lit up—the stove and the boxes and the flour-sack curtain, and the man with his head bowed, and the woman standing over him with the child in her arms—like a picture of the Holy Family that some mad painter had set down in the pit of hell. And then the glare died away, and the room was dark again, and the mill went on pounding, as it would pound tomorrow, and the day after, and the year after that, making steel for the bridges and the skyscrapers and the battleships of the richest nation in the world.
