Every member of the Bunch was expected to telephone to every other member at least once a week. “Why haven’t you called me up?” Babbitt was asked accusingly, not only by Tanis and Carrie but presently by new ancient friends, Jennie and Capitolina and Toots. If for a moment he had seen Tanis as withering and sentimental, he lost that impression at Carrie Nork’s dance. Mrs. Nork had a large house and a small husband. To her party came all of the Bunch, perhaps thirty-five of them when they were completely mobilized. Babbitt, under the name of “Old Georgie,” was now a pioneer of the Bunch, since each month it changed half its membership and he who could recall the prehistoric days of a fortnight ago, before Mrs. Absolom, the food-demonstrator, had gone to Indianapolis, and Mac had “got sore at” Minnie, was a venerable leader and able to condescend to new Petes and Minnies and Gladyses. At Carrie’s, Tanis did not have to work at being hostess. She was dignified and sure, a clear fine figure in the black chiffon frock he had always loved; and in the wider spaces of that ugly house Babbitt was able to sit quietly with her. He repented of his first revulsion, mooned at her feet, andhappily drove her home. Next day he bought a violent yellow tie, to make himself young for her. He knew, a little sadly, that he could not make himself beautiful; he beheld himself as heavy, hinting of fatness, but he danced, he dressed, he chattered, to be as young as she was... as young as she seemed to be. As all converts, whether to a religion, love, or gardening, find as by magic that though hitherto these hobbies have not seemed to exist, now the whole world is filled with their fury, so, once he was converted to dissipation, Babbitt discovered agreeable opportunities for it everywhere. He had a new view of his sporting neighbor, Sam Doppelbrau. The Doppelbraus were respectable people, industrious people, prosperous people, whose ideal of happiness was an eternal cabaret. Their life was dominated by suburban bacchanalia of alcohol, nicotine, gasoline, and kisses. They and their set worked capably all the week, and all week looked forward to Saturday night, when they would, as they expressed it, “throw a party;” and the thrown party grew noisier and noisier up to Sunday dawn, and usually included an extremely rapid motor expedition to nowhere in particular. One evening when Tanis was at the theater, Babbitt found himself being lively with the Doppelbraus, pledging friendship with men whom he had for years privily denounced to Mrs. Babbitt as a “rotten bunch of tin-horns that I wouldn’t go out with, not if they were the last people on earth.” That evening he had sulkily come home and poked about in front of the house, chipping off the walk the ice-clots, like fossil footprints, made by the steps of passers-by during the recent snow. Howard Littlefield came up snuffling.

“Still a widower, George?”

“Yump. Cold again to-night.”

“What do you hear from the wife?”

“She’s feeling fine, but her sister is still pretty sick.”

“Say, better come in and have dinner with us to-night, George.”

“Oh—oh, thanks. Have to go out.” Suddenly he could not endure Littlefield’s recitals of the more interesting statistics about totally uninteresting problems. He scraped at the walk and grunted. Sam Doppelbrau appeared.

“Evenin’, Babbitt. Working hard?”

“Yuh, lil exercise.”

“Cold enough for you to-night?”

“Well, just about.”

“Still a widower?”

“Uh-huh.”

Probably the poor guy is off his nut.” Babbitt drove, not at all carefully or fussily, sliding viciously past trucks, ignoring the truckmen’s curses, to the City Hall; he stopped with a grind of wheels against the curb, and ran up the marble steps to the office of the Hon. Mr. Lucas Prout, the mayor. He bribed the mayor’s doorman with a dollar; he was instantly inside, demanding, “You remember me, Mr. Prout? Babbitt—vice-president of the Boosters—campaigned for you? Say, have you heard about poor Riesling? Well, I want an order on the warden or whatever you call um of the City Prison to take me back and see him. Good. Thanks.” In fifteen minutes he was pounding down the prison corridor to a cage where Paul Riesling sat on a cot, twisted like an old beggar, legs crossed, arms in a knot, biting at his clenched fist. Paul looked up blankly as the keeper unlocked the cell, admitted Babbitt, and left them together. He spoke slowly: “Go on! Be moral!” Babbitt plumped on the couch beside him. “I’m not going to be moral! I don’t care what happened! I just want to do anything I can. I’m glad Zilla got what was coming to her.” Paul said argumentatively, “Now, don’t go jumping on Zilla. I’ve been thinking; maybe she hasn’t had any too easy a time. Just after I shot her— I didn’t hardly mean to, but she got to deviling me so I went crazy, just for a second, and pulled out that old revolver you and I used to shoot rabbits with, and took a crack at her. Didn’t hardly mean to— After that, when I was trying to stop the blood— It was terrible what it did to her shoulder, and she had beautiful skin— Maybe she won’t die. I hope it won’t leave her skin all scarred. But just afterward, when I was hunting through the bathroom for some cotton to stop the blood, I ran onto a little fuzzy yellow duck we hung on the tree one Christmas, and I remembered she and I’d been awfully happy then— Hell. I can’t hardly believe it’s me here.” As Babbitt’s arm tightened about his shoulder, Paul sighed, “I’m glad you came. But I thought maybe you’d lecture me, and when you’ve committed a murder, and been brought here and everything—there was a big crowd outside the apartment house, all staring, and the cops took me through it— Oh, I’m not going to talk about it any more.” But he went on, in a monotonous, terrified insane mumble. To divert him Babbitt said, “Why, you got a scar on your cheek.”

“Yes. That’s where the cop hit me. I suppose cops get a lot of fun out of lecturing murderers, too. He was a big fellow. And they wouldn’t let me help carry Zilla down to the ambulance.”

“Paul! Quit it! Listen: she won’t die, and when it’s all over you and I’ll go off to Maine again. And maybe we can get that May Arnold to go along. I’ll go up to Chicago and ask her. Good woman, by golly. And afterwards I’ll see that you get started in business out West somewhere, maybe Seattle—they say that’s a lovely city.” Paul was half smiling. It was Babbitt who rambled now. He could not tell whether Paul was heeding, but he droned on till the coming of Paul’s lawyer, P. J. Maxwell, a thin, busy, unfriendly man who nodded at Babbitt and hinted, “If Riesling and I could be alone for a moment—” Babbitt wrung Paul’s hands, and waited in the office till Maxwell came pattering out. “Look, old man, what can I do?” he begged.

“Nothing. Not a thing. Not just now,” said Maxwell. “Sorry. Got to hurry. And don’t try to see him. I’ve had the doctor give him a shot of morphine, so he’ll sleep.” It seemed somehow wicked to return to the office. Babbitt felt as though he had just come from a funeral. He drifted out to the City Hospital to inquire about Zilla. She was not likely to die, he learned. The bullet from Paul’s huge old .44 army revolver had smashed her shoulder and torn upward and out. He wandered home and found his wife radiant with the horrified interest we have in the tragedies of our friends. “Of course Paul isn’t altogether to blame, but this is what comes of his chasing after other women instead of bearing his cross in a Christian way,” she exulted. He was too languid to respond as he desired. He said what was to be said about the Christian bearing of crosses, and went out to clean the car. Dully, patiently, he scraped linty grease from the drip-pan, gouged at the mud caked on the wheels. He used up many minutes in washing his hands; scoured them with gritty kitchen soap; rejoiced in hurting his plump knuckles. “Damn soft hands—like a woman’s. Aah!” At dinner, when his wife began the inevitable, he bellowed, “I forbid any of you to say a word about Paul! I’ll ’tend to all the talking about this that’s necessary, hear me? There’s going to be one house in this scandal-mongering town to-night that isn’t going to spring the holier-than-thou. And throw those filthy evening papers out of the house!” But he himself read the papers, after dinner. Before nine he set out for the house of Lawyer Maxwell. He was received without cordiality. “Well?” said Maxwell.

“I want to offer my services in the trial. I’ve got an idea. Why couldn’t I go on the stand and swear I was there, and she pulled the gun first and he wrestled with her and the gun went off accidentally?”

“And perjure yourself?”

“Huh? Yes, I suppose it would be perjury. Oh— Would it help?”

“But, my dear fellow! Perjury!”

“Oh, don’t be a fool! Excuse me, Maxwell; I didn’t mean to get your goat. I just mean: I’ve known and you’ve known many and many a case of perjury, just to annex some rotten little piece of real estate, and here where it’s a case of saving Paul from going to prison, I’d perjure myself black in the face.”

“No. Aside from the ethics of the matter, I’m afraid it isn’t practicable. The prosecutor would tear your testimony to pieces. It’s known that only Riesling and his wife were there at the time.”

“Then, look here! Let me go on the stand and swear—and this would be the God’s truth—that she pestered him till he kind of went crazy.”

“No. Sorry. Riesling absolutely refuses to have any testimony reflecting on his wife. He insists on pleading guilty.”

“Then let me get up and testify something—whatever you say. Let me do something!”

“I’m sorry, Babbitt, but the best thing you can do— I hate to say it, but you could help us most by keeping strictly out of it.” Babbitt, revolving his hat like a defaulting poor tenant, winced so visibly that Maxwell condescended: “I don’t like to hurt your feelings, but you see we both want to do our best for Riesling, and we mustn’t consider any other factor. The trouble with you, Babbitt, is that you’re one of these fellows who talk too readily. You like to hear your own voice. If there were anything for which I could put you in the witness-box, you’d get going and give the whole show away. Sorry. Now I must look over some papers— So sorry.”

He spent most of the next morning nerving himself to face the garrulous world of the Athletic Club. They would talk about Paul; they would be lip-licking and rotten. But at the Roughnecks’ Table they did not mention Paul. They spoke with zeal of the coming baseball season. He loved them as he never had before.

He had, doubtless from some story-book, pictured Paul’s trial as a long struggle, with bitter arguments, a taut crowd, and sudden and overwhelming new testimony. Actually, the trial occupied less than fifteen minutes, largely filled with the evidence of doctors that Zilla would recover and that Paul must have been temporarily insane. Next day Paul was sentenced to three years in the State Penitentiary and taken off—quite undramatically, not handcuffed, merely plodding in a tired way beside a cheerful deputy sheriff—and after saying good-by to him at the station Babbitt returned to his office to realize that he faced a world which, without Paul, was meaningless.

He was busy, from March to June. He kept himself from the bewilderment of thinking. His wife and the neighbors were generous. Every evening he played bridge or attended the movies, and the days were blank of face and silent. In June, Mrs. Babbitt and Tinka went East, to stay with relatives, and Babbitt was free to do—he was not quite sure what. All day long after their departure he thought of the emancipated house in which he could, if he desired, go mad and curse the gods without having to keep up a husbandly front. He considered, “I could have a reg’lar party to-night; stay out till two and not do any explaining afterwards. Cheers!” He telephoned to Vergil Gunch, to Eddie Swanson. Both of them were engaged for the evening, and suddenly he was bored by having to take so much trouble to be riotous. He was silent at dinner, unusually kindly to Ted and Verona, hesitating but not disapproving when Verona stated her opinion of Kenneth Escott’s opinion of Dr. John Jennison Drew’s opinion of the opinions of the evolutionists. Ted was working in a garage through the summer vacation, and he related his daily triumphs: how he had found a cracked ball-race, what he had said to the Old Grouch, what he had said to the foreman about the future of wireless telephony. Ted and Verona went to a dance after dinner. Even the maid was out. Rarely had Babbitt been alone in the house for an entire evening. He was restless. He vaguely wanted something more diverting than the newspaper comic strips to read. He ambled up to Verona’s room, sat on her maidenly blue and white bed, humming and grunting in a solid-citizen manner as he examined her books: Conrad’s “Rescue,” a volume strangely named “Figures of Earth,” poetry (quite irregular poetry, Babbitt thought) by Vachel Lindsay, and essays by H. L. Mencken—highly improper essays, making fun of the church and all the decencies. He liked none of the books. In them he felt a spirit of rebellion against niceness and solid-citizenship. These authors—and he supposed they were famous ones, too—did not seem to care about telling a good story which would enable a fellow to forget his troubles. He sighed. He noted a book, “The Three Black Pennies,” by Joseph Hergesheimer. Ah, that was something like it! It would be an adventure story, maybe about counterfeiting—detectives sneaking up on the old house at night. He tucked the book under his arm, he clumped down-stairs and solemnly began to read, under the piano-lamp: “A twilight like blue dust sifted into the shallow fold of the thickly wooded hills. It was early October, but a crisping frost had already stamped the maple trees with gold, the Spanish oaks were hung with patches of wine red, the sumach was brilliant in the darkening underbrush. A pattern of wild geese, flying low and unconcerned above the hills, wavered against the serene ashen evening. Howat Penny, standing in the comparative clearing of a road, decided that the shifting regular flight would not come close enough for a shot.... He had no intention of hunting the geese. With the drooping of day his keenness had evaporated; an habitual indifference strengthened, permeating him....” There it was again: discontent with the good common ways. Babbitt laid down the book and listened to the stillness. The inner doors of the house were open. He heard from the kitchen the steady drip of the refrigerator, a rhythm demanding and disquieting. He roamed to the window. The summer evening was foggy and, seen through the wire screen, the street lamps were crosses of pale fire. The whole world was abnormal.

While he brooded, Verona and Ted came in and went up to bed. Silence thickened in the sleeping house. He put on his hat, his respectable derby, lighted a cigar, and walked up and down before the house, a portly, worthy, unimaginative figure, humming “Silver Threads among the Gold.” He casually considered, “Might call up Paul.” Then he remembered. He saw Paul in a jailbird’s uniform, but while he agonized he didn’t believe the tale. It was part of the unreality of this fog-enchanted evening. If she were here Myra would be hinting, “Isn’t it late, Georgie?” He tramped in forlorn and unwanted freedom. Fog hid the house now. The world was uncreated, a chaos without turmoil or desire. Through the mist came a man at so feverish a pace that he seemed to dance with fury as he entered the orb of glow from a street-lamp. At each step he brandished his stick and brought it down with a crash. His glasses on their broad pretentious ribbon banged against his stomach. Babbitt incredulously saw that it was Chum Frink. Frink stopped, focused his vision, and spoke with gravity:
“There’s another fool. George Babbitt. Lives for renting howshes—houses. Know who I am? I’m traitor to poetry. I’m drunk. I’m talking too much. I don’t care. Know what I could’ve been? I could’ve been a Gene Field or a James Whitcomb Riley. Maybe a Stevenson. I could’ve. Whimsies. ’Magination. Lissen. Lissen to this. Just made it up: Glittering summery meadowy noise Of beetles and bums and respectable boys. Hear that? Whimzh—whimsy. I made that up. I don’t know what it means! Beginning good verse. Chile’s Garden Verses. And whadi write? Tripe! Cheer-up poems. All tripe! Could have written— Too late!” He darted on with an alarming plunge, seeming always to pitch forward yet never quite falling. Babbitt would have been no more astonished and no less had a ghost skipped out of the fog carrying his head. He accepted Frink with vast apathy; he grunted, “Poor boob!” and straightway forgot him. He plodded into the house, deliberately went to the refrigerator and rifled it. When Mrs. Babbitt was at home, this was one of the major household crimes. He stood before the covered laundry tubs, eating a chicken leg and half a saucer of raspberry jelly, and grumbling over a clammy cold boiled potato. He was thinking. It was coming to him that perhaps all life as he knew it and vigorously practised it was futile; that heaven as portrayed by the Reverend Dr. John Jennison Drew was neither probable nor very interesting; that he hadn’t much pleasure out of making money; that it was of doubtful worth to rear children merely that they might rear children who would rear children. What was it all about? What did he want? He blundered into the living-room, lay on the davenport, hands behind his head. What did he want? Wealth? Social position? Travel? Servants? Yes, but only incidentally.

“I give it up,” he sighed. But he did know that he wanted the presence of Paul Riesling; and from that he stumbled into the admission that he wanted the fairy girl—in the flesh. If there had been a woman whom he loved, he would have fled to her, humbled his forehead on her knees. He thought of his stenographer, Miss McGoun. He thought of the prettiest of the manicure girls at the Hotel Thornleigh barber shop. As he fell asleep on the davenport he felt that he had found something in life, and that he had made a terrifying, thrilling break with everything that was decent and normal. He had forgotten, next morning, that he was a conscious rebel, but he was irritable in the office and at the eleven o’clock drive of telephone calls and visitors he did something he had often desired and never dared: he left the office without excuses to those slave-drivers his employees, and went to the movies. He enjoyed the right to be alone. He came out with a vicious determination to do what he pleased. As he approached the Roughnecks’ Table at the club, everybody laughed.

“Well, here’s the millionaire!” said Sidney Finkelstein.

“Yes, I saw him in his Locomobile!” said Professor Pumphrey.

“Gosh, it must be great to be a smart guy like Georgie!” moaned Vergil Gunch. “He’s probably stolen all of Dorchester. I’d hate to leave a poor little defenseless piece of property lying around where he could get his hooks on it!” They had, Babbitt perceived, “something on him.” Also, they “had their kidding clothes on.” Ordinarily he would have been delighted at the honor implied in being chaffed, but he was suddenly touchy. He grunted, “Yuh, sure; maybe I’ll take you guys on as office boys!” He was impatient as the jest elaborately rolled on to its dénouement.

“Of course he may have been meeting a girl,” they said, and “No, I think he was waiting for his old roommate, Sir Jerusalem Doak.” He exploded, “Oh, spring it, spring it, you boneheads! What’s the great joke?”

“Hurray! George is peeved!” snickered Sidney Finkelstein, while a grin went round the table. Gunch revealed the shocking truth: He had seen Babbitt coming out of a motion-picture theater—at noon! They kept it up. With a hundred variations, a hundred {275}

guffaws, they said that he had gone to the movies during business-hours. He didn’t so much mind Gunch, but he was annoyed by Sidney Finkelstein, that brisk, lean, red-headed explainer of jokes. He was bothered, too, by the lump of ice in his glass of water. It was too large; it spun round and burned his nose when he tried to drink. He raged that Finkelstein was like that lump of ice. But he won through; he kept up his banter till they grew tired of the superlative jest and turned to the great problems of the day. He reflected, “What’s the matter with me to-day? Seems like I’ve got an awful grouch. Only they talk so darn much. But I better steer careful and keep my mouth shut.” As they lighted their cigars he mumbled, “Got to get back,” and on a chorus of “If you will go spending your mornings with lady ushers at the movies!” he escaped. He heard them giggling. He was embarrassed. While he was most bombastically agreeing with the coat-man that the weather was warm, he was conscious that he was longing to run childishly with his troubles to the comfort of the fairy child.

Excerpt 2: The great events of Babbitt’s spring were the secret buying of real-estate options in Linton for certain street-traction officials, before the public announcement that the Linton Avenue Car Line would be extended, and a dinner which was, as he rejoiced to his wife, not only “a regular society spread but a real sure-enough highbrow affair, with some of the keenest intellects and the brightest bunch of little women in town.” It was so absorbing an occasion that he almost forgot his desire to run off to Maine with Paul Riesling. Though he had been born in the village of Catawba, Babbitt had risen to that metropolitan social plane on which hosts have as many as four people at dinner without planning it for more than an evening or two. But a dinner of twelve, with flowers from the florist’s and all the cut-glass out, staggered even the Babbitts. For two weeks they studied, debated, and arbitrated the list of guests. Babbitt marveled, “Of course we’re up-to-date ourselves, but still, think of us entertaining a famous poet like Chum Frink, a fellow that on nothing but a poem or so every day and just writing a few advertisements pulls down fifteen thousand berries a year!”

“Yes, and Howard Littlefield. Do you know, the other evening Eunice told me her papa speaks three languages!” said Mrs. Babbitt.

“Huh! That’s nothing! So do I—American, baseball, and poker!”

“I don’t think it’s nice to be funny about a matter like that.

Think how wonderful it must be to speak three languages, and so useful and— And with people like that, I don’t see why we invite the Orville Joneses.”

“Well now, Orville is a mighty up-and-coming fellow!”

“Yes, I know, but— A laundry!”

“I’ll admit a laundry hasn’t got the class of poetry or real estate, but just the same, Orvy is mighty deep. Ever start him spieling about gardening? Say, that fellow can tell you the name of every kind of tree, and some of their Greek and Latin names too! Besides, we owe the Joneses a dinner. Besides, gosh, we got to have some boob for audience, when a bunch of hot-air artists like Frink and Littlefield get going.”

“Well, dear—I meant to speak of this—I do think that as host you ought to sit back and listen, and let your guests have a chance to talk once in a while!”

“Oh, you do, do you! Sure! I talk all the time! And I’m just a business man—oh sure!—I’m no Ph.D. like Littlefield, and no poet, and I haven’t anything to spring! Well, let me tell you, just the other day your darn Chum Frink comes up to me at the club begging to know what I thought about the Springfield school-bond issue. And who told him? I did! You bet your life I told him! Little me! I certainly did! He came up and asked me, and I told him all about it! You bet! And he was darn glad to listen to me and— Duty as a host! I guess I know my duty as a host and let me tell you—” In fact, the Orville Joneses were invited. On the morning of the dinner, Mrs. Babbitt was restive.

“Now, George, I want you to be sure and be home early to-night. Remember, you have to dress.”

“Uh-huh. I see by the Advocate that the Presbyterian General Assembly has voted to quit the Interchurch World Movement. That—” “George! Did you hear what I said? You must be home in time to dress to-night.”

“Dress? Hell! I’m dressed now! Think I’m going down to the office in my B.V.D.’s?”

“I will not have you talking indecently before the children! And you do have to put on your dinner-jacket!”

“I guess you mean my Tux. I tell you, of all the doggone nonsensical nuisances that was ever invented—” Three minutes later, after Babbitt had wailed, “Well, I don’t know whether I’m going to dress or not” in a manner which showed that he was going to dress, the discussion moved on.

“Now, George, you mustn’t forget to call in at Vecchia’s on the way home and get the ice cream. Their delivery-wagon is broken down, and I don’t want to trust them to send it by—” “All right! You told me that before breakfast!”

“Well, I don’t want you to forget. I’ll be working my head off all day long, training the girl that’s to help with the dinner—” “All nonsense, anyway, hiring an extra girl for the feed. Matilda could perfectly well—” “—and I have to go out and buy the flowers, and fix them, and set the table, and order the salted almonds, and look at the chickens, and arrange for the children to have their supper up-stairs and— And I simply must depend on you to go to Vecchia’s for the ice cream.”

“All riiiiiight! Gosh, I’m going to get it!”

“All you have to do is to go in and say you want the ice cream that Mrs. Babbitt ordered yesterday by ’phone, and it will be all ready for you.” At ten-thirty she telephoned to him not to forget the ice cream from Vecchia’s. He was surprised and blasted then by a thought. He wondered whether Floral Heights dinners were worth the hideous toil involved. But he repented the sacrilege in the excitement of buying the materials for cocktails. Now this was the manner of obtaining alcohol under the reign of righteousness and prohibition:
He drove from the severe rectangular streets of the modern business center into the tangled byways of Old Town—jagged blocks filled with sooty warehouses and lofts; on into The Arbor, once a pleasant orchard but now a morass of lodging-houses, tenements, and brothels. Exquisite shivers chilled his spine and stomach, and he looked at every policeman with intense innocence, as one who loved the law, and admired the Force, and longed to stop and play with them. He parked his car a block from Healey Hanson’s saloon, worrying, “Well, rats, if anybody did see me, they’d think I was here on business.” He entered a place curiously like the saloons of ante-prohibition days, with a long greasy bar with sawdust in front and streaky mirror behind, a pine table at which a dirty old man dreamed over a glass of something which resembled whisky, and with two men at the bar, drinking something which resembled beer, and giving that impression of forming a large crowd which two men always give in a saloon. The bartender, a tall pale Swede with a diamond in his lilac scarf, stared at Babbitt as he stalked plumply up to the bar and whispered, “I’d, uh— Friend of Hanson’s sent me here. Like to get some gin.” The bartender gazed down on him in the manner of an outraged bishop. “I guess you got the wrong place, my friend. We sell nothing but soft drinks here.” He cleaned the bar with a rag which would itself have done with a little cleaning, and glared across his mechanically moving elbow. The old dreamer at the table petitioned the bartender, “Say, Oscar, listen.” Oscar did not listen.

“Aw, say, Oscar, listen, will yuh? Say, lis-sen!” The decayed and drowsy voice of the loafer, the agreeable stink of beer-dregs, threw a spell of inanition over Babbitt. The bartender moved grimly toward the crowd of two men. Babbitt followed him as delicately as a cat, and wheedled, “Say, Oscar, I want to speak to Mr. Hanson.”

“Whajuh wanta see him for?”

“I just want to talk to him. Here’s my card.” It was a beautiful card, an engraved card, a card in the blackest black and the sharpest red, announcing that Mr. George F. Babbitt was Estates, Insurance, Rents. The bartender held it as though it weighed ten pounds, and read it as though it were a hundred words long. He did not bend from his episcopal dignity, but he growled, “I’ll see if he’s around.” From the back room he brought an immensely old young man, a quiet sharp-eyed man, in tan silk shirt, checked vest hanging open, and burning brown trousers—Mr. Healey Hanson. Mr. Hanson said only “Yuh?” but his implacable and contemptuous eyes queried Babbitt’s soul, and he seemed not at all impressed by the new dark-gray suit for which (as he had admitted to every acquaintance at the Athletic Club) Babbitt had paid a hundred and twenty-five dollars.

“Glad meet you, Mr. Hanson. Say, uh— I’m George Babbitt of the Babbitt-Thompson Realty Company. I’m a great friend of Jake Offutt’s.”

“Well, what of it?”

“Say, uh, I’m going to have a party, and Jake told me you’d be able to fix me up with a little gin.” In alarm, in obsequiousness, as Hanson’s eyes grew more bored, “You telephone to Jake about me, if you want to.” Hanson answered by jerking his head to indicate the entrance to the back room, and strolled away. Babbitt melodramatically crept into an apartment containing four round tables, eleven chairs, a brewery calendar, and a smell. He waited. Thrice he saw Healey Hanson saunter through, humming, hands in pockets, ignoring him. By this time Babbitt had modified his valiant morning vow, “I won’t pay one cent over seven dollars a quart” to “I might pay ten.” On Hanson’s next weary entrance he besought, “Could you fix that up?” Hanson scowled, and grated, “Just a minute—Pete’s sake—just a min-ute!” In growing meekness Babbitt went on waiting till Hanson casually reappeared with a quart of gin—what is euphemistically known as a quart—in his disdainful long white hands.

“Twelve bucks,” he snapped.

“Say, uh, but say, cap’n, Jake thought you’d be able to fix me up for eight or nine a bottle.”

“Nup. Twelve. This is the real stuff, smuggled from Canada. This is none o’ your neutral spirits with a drop of juniper extract,” the honest merchant said virtuously. “Twelve bones—if you want it. Course y’ understand I’m just doing this anyway as a friend of Jake’s.”

“Sure! Sure! I understand!” Babbitt gratefully held out twelve dollars. He felt honored by contact with greatness as Hanson yawned, stuffed the bills, uncounted, into his radiant vest, and swaggered away. He had a number of titillations out of concealing the gin-bottle under his coat and out of hiding it in his desk. All afternoon he snorted and chuckled and gurgled over his ability to “give the Boys a real shot in the arm to-night.” He was, in fact, so exhilarated that he was within a block of his house before he remembered that there was a certain matter, mentioned by his wife, of fetching ice cream from Vecchia’s. He explained, “Well, darn it—” and drove back. Vecchia was not a caterer, he was The Caterer of Zenith. Most coming-out parties were held in the white and gold ballroom of the Maison Vecchia; at all nice teas the guests recognized the five kinds of Vecchia sandwiches and the seven kinds of Vecchia cakes; and all really smart dinners ended, as on a resolving chord, in Vecchia Neapolitan ice cream in one of the three reliable molds—the melon mold, the round mold like a layer cake, and the long brick. Vecchia’s shop had pale blue woodwork, tracery of plaster roses, attendants in frilled aprons, and glass shelves of “kisses” with all the refinement that inheres in whites of eggs. Babbitt felt heavy and thick amid this professional daintiness, and as he waited for the ice cream he decided, with hot prickles at the back of his neck, that a girl customer was giggling at him. He went home in a touchy temper. The first thing he heard was his wife’s agitated: “George! Did you remember to go to Vecchia’s and get the ice cream?”

“Say! Look here! Do I ever forget to do things?”

“Yes! Often!”

“Well now, it’s darn seldom I do, and it certainly makes me tired, after going into a pink-tea joint like Vecchia’s and having to stand around looking at a lot of half-naked young girls, all rouged up like they were sixty and eating a lot of stuff that simply ruins their stomachs—” “Oh, it’s too bad about you! I’ve noticed how you hate to look at pretty girls!” With a jar Babbitt realized that his wife was too busy to be impressed by that moral indignation with which males rule the world, and he went humbly up-stairs to dress. He had an impression of a glorified dining-room, of cut-glass, candles, polished wood, lace, silver, roses. With the awed swelling of the heart suitable to so grave a business as giving a dinner, he slew the temptation to wear his plaited dress-shirt for a fourth time, took out an entirely fresh one, tightened his black bow, and rubbed his patent-leather pumps with a handkerchief. He glanced with pleasure at his garnet and silver studs. He smoothed and patted his ankles, transformed by silk socks from the sturdy shanks of George Babbitt to the elegant limbs of what is called a Clubman. He stood before the pier-glass, viewing his trim dinner-coat, his beautiful triple-braided trousers; and murmured in lyric beatitude, “By golly, I don’t look so bad. I certainly don’t look like Catawba. If the hicks back home could see me in this rig, they’d have a fit!” He moved majestically down to mix the cocktails. As he chipped ice, as he squeezed oranges, as he collected vast stores of bottles, glasses, and spoons at the sink in the pantry, he felt as authoritative as the bartender at Healey Hanson’s saloon. True, Mrs. Babbitt said he was under foot, and Matilda and the maid hired for the evening brushed by him, elbowed him, shrieked “Pleasopn door,” as they tottered through with trays, but in this high moment he ignored them. Besides the new bottle of gin, his cellar consisted of one half-bottle of Bourbon whisky, a quarter of a bottle of Italian vermouth, and approximately one hundred drops of orange bitters. He did not possess a cocktail-shaker. A shaker was proof of dissipation, the symbol of a Drinker, and Babbitt disliked being known as a Drinker even more than he liked a Drink. He tasted the sacred essence. “Now, by golly, if that isn’t pretty near one fine old cocktail! Kind of a Bronx, and yet like a Manhattan. Ummmmmm! Hey, Myra, want a little nip before the folks come?” Bustling into the dining-room, moving each glass a quarter of an inch, rushing back with resolution implacable on her face, her gray and silver-lace party frock protected by a denim towel, Mrs. Babbitt glared at him, and rebuked him, “Certainly not!”

“Yeh.”

“Well, be sure now. Don’t go putting anything on this top shelf.”

“Yeh.”

To her party came all of the Bunch, perhaps thirty-five of them when they were completely mobilized. Babbitt, under the name of “Old Georgie,” was now a pioneer of the Bunch, since each month it changed half its membership and he who could recall the prehistoric days of a fortnight ago, before Mrs. Absolom, the food-demonstrator, had gone to Indianapolis, and Mac had “got sore at” Minnie, was a venerable leader and able to condescend to new Petes and Minnies and Gladyses. She was dignified and sure, a clear fine figure in the black chiffon frock he had always loved; and in the wider spaces of that ugly house Babbitt was able to sit quietly with her. He repented of his first revulsion, mooned at her feet, andhappily drove her home. Next day he bought a violent yellow tie, to make himself young for her. Their life was dominated by suburban bacchanalia of alcohol, nicotine, gasoline, and kisses. Howard Littlefield came up snuffling.

“Still a widower, George?”

“Yump. Cold again to-night.”

“What do you hear from the wife?”

“She’s feeling fine, but her sister is still pretty sick.”

“Say, better come in and have dinner with us to-night, George.”

“Oh—oh, thanks. Have to go out.” Suddenly he could not endure Littlefield’s recitals of the more interesting statistics about totally uninteresting problems. He scraped at the walk and grunted. Sam Doppelbrau appeared.

“Evenin’, Babbitt. Working hard?”

“Yuh, lil exercise.”

“Cold enough for you to-night?”

“Well, just about.”

“Still a widower?”

“Uh-huh.”

The calling of Mr. and Mrs. J. Ambrose Hockaday upon the Lowell T. Sprakers, on the second Sunday in October, was an event that had been arranged for in the Spraker household with a thoroughness elsewhere reserved for funerals, weddings, and the annual inspection of the Spraker Paint & Varnish Company by the agents of the fire-insurance underwriters. Mr. Hockaday was vice-president of the Second National Bank of Monarch. He was also, which was more important, the man who would decide whether the Spraker Paint & Varnish Company was to have its new drying-shed and its new mixing-vats and its new and wholly unnecessary office with the mahogany rail, or whether it was to go on as it had gone on for eleven years, honest, profitable, and invisible.

For three days Mrs. Spraker had polished. She had polished the brass andirons, which were never used, before the fireplace, which was never lighted. She had polished the cut-glass bowl on the library table and the photograph of Lowell in his Shriner's fez. She had had the girl beat the Wilton rug in the side yard until the neighbors came to their windows, and she had bought, at Fenwick's, two pounds of the little sugared almonds in pastel colors which were known in Elmhurst Terrace to be the correct thing for callers who were not quite friends and were rather more than acquaintances.

And Willis Spraker, aged seven, had been washed. He had been washed with a thoroughness which he regarded as malicious, put into the blue serge suit with the round white collar, and instructed, "Now you sit still and be a little gentleman, and don't you speak unless you're spoken to, and if Mr. Hockaday asks you anything you say 'Yes, sir' and 'No, sir,' and don't you dare go near those almonds."

He had sat still. He had been a little gentleman for forty-one minutes, through the weather, through the new paving on Chautauqua Boulevard, through Mrs. Hockaday's sister in Pasadena and the healthfulness of the climate there, through Mr. Hockaday's opinion that the country was sound, fundamentally sound, if the farmers would only quit their eternal belly-aching. And then, in a lull, while his father was leaning forward with the large and bloodless smile of a man about to mention a drying-shed, Willis had looked up at the banker with the candid blue eyes of the innocent and inquired:

"Mr. Hockaday, did you ever really skin a flea for its hide?"

Mr. Hockaday said, "What's that, son?"

"Papa says you would. He told Mama. He said you were an old skinflint that'd skin a flea for its hide and then sell the hide back to the flea. I don't see how you could, though. A flea's awful little."

There had followed a silence which Lowell Spraker was afterward to remember, at intervals and without warning, for the rest of his life: in his bath, at the Kiwanis luncheons, once in the middle of the Doxology. He remembered the ticking of the mission clock. He remembered the creak of Mrs. Hockaday's corsets as she drew herself up. He remembered his own voice, very high and very hearty, crying, "Ha, ha! Kids! The things they think up! Well, I declare! Ha, ha! Willis, where in the world did you get hold of a notion like—" and he remembered that Mr. Hockaday had not laughed at all, but had taken out his gold watch and looked at it as though it, too, had been insolent to him.

The Hockadays left eleven minutes later. Mr. Hockaday shook hands. He said, "Well, Spraker, you drop round to the bank some day and we'll talk over that little matter." He did not say which day. He did not say which little matter. He had the air of a man who would be at a directors' meeting on whatever day was chosen.

Now Lowell Spraker stood in the front hall with the door closed behind him, and heard the Hockaday sedan go purring down Elmhurst Terrace, and he did not turn around. His wife, behind him, said in a small voice, "Lowell—" and he did not answer her. He was a large man, pink and smooth, with the comfortable belly and the uncomfortable collar of the successful, and from the back his neck was redder than anyone had ever seen it.

He turned. He said, quite gently, "Willis, you come into the den."

Now the den of Lowell T. Spraker was the one room in the house which he regarded as his own, and to which he retired, in the manner of the head of a household, to read the sporting page, to smoke the cigars his wife would not permit in the living-room, and to sleep. It contained a leather Morris chair with a burn on the left arm; a rack of pipes which he had bought because a man ought to have a rack of pipes, and never smoked; a set of the "Little Journeys" of Elbert Hubbard, in limp leather, uncut after the second volume; a framed motto, "The Man Who Wins Is the Man Who Thinks He Can"; a mounted bass, caught at Lake Minnewaska in 1916 and weighed, on the occasion of every telling, at a slightly higher figure; and a desk, at which he did nothing whatever. It was, he had often said, the place where he did his thinking.

He did his thinking there now. He sat down in the Morris chair. He motioned Willis to stand before him on the hooked rug, and Willis stood there, his hands at his sides, his round white collar slightly askew, his face composed in the expression of a small person who has done something tremendous and is not yet sure whether it is to be punished or admired.

"Well, young man," said Lowell Spraker.

Willis said nothing. It seemed to him the safest thing.

"Well, young man, I suppose you know what you've done."

"Yes, Papa."

"No, you don't! You don't know the first thing about it! You haven't the faintest conception! Do you know who that man is? Do you know who Mr. J. Ambrose Hockaday is?"

"He's a banker."

"He's a banker! Yes, sir, he's a banker, and I'll tell you what kind of a banker. He's the kind of a banker that—that—" Mr. Spraker found that he could not readily explain, to a person of seven, what kind of a banker Mr. Hockaday was, and he shifted ground with the agility of a speaker at a Chamber of Commerce smoker who has lost his notes. "Never mind what kind of a banker he is. That's not the point. The point is, here we have callers in the house, important callers, a man and his wife who've got a position in this town, that are known from one end of the state to the other, and you get up and you insult them! In my own house! In front of your own mother! Of all the doggone—"

"Lowell!" came from the hall.

"Well, I will say doggone! I guess a man can say doggone in his own den!" He lowered his voice and glared. "Of all the fool things I ever heard a kid say in my life—and I've heard a few, believe me—"

"I didn't insult him, Papa."

"You did so insult him!"

"I only asked him about the flea."

There was a pause. Mr. Spraker breathed heavily through his nose. He had, he recalled, read in the American Magazine an article by a Distinguished Child Psychologist, illustrated with a photograph of the psychologist's own child (a boy of placid aspect with a hoop), which had advised that the modern parent should never reprimand in anger, but should reason with the young mind calmly, as one reasonable person to another, and so develop in it the habit of self-government. It had seemed to him at the time a sound and progressive idea, and he had read the passage aloud to his wife, who had said, "Well, I'd like to see that man try it on Willis." He determined now to try it on Willis.

"Now, see here, son," he said, in the voice he used on bookkeepers who wanted a raise. "Let's sit down and talk this over like a couple of men. Let's be reasonable about this. Here—you sit on the hassock. That's the boy." Willis sat on the hassock. "Now. You know that what you said to Mr. Hockaday wasn't nice, don't you?"

"No."

"Well, it wasn't."

"Why wasn't it?"

"Because it wasn't true, that's why! Because it was a—a fib, and you know it was a fib, and you know what happens to little boys that tell fibs!"

Willis considered this with the deep gravity of the young. "But you said it," he pointed out. "You said it to Mama Thursday night when you were taking your shoes off. You said, 'That old skinflint Hockaday would skin a flea for its hide and then—'"

"I know what I said!"

"—sell it back to the flea. I heard you. I was on the stairs."

"What were you doing on the stairs at that time of night? Hey? Answer me that! What business has a kid your age got hanging round on the stairs, listening to what his elders—" Mr. Spraker perceived, with the abrupt and uncomfortable clarity which sometimes visited him on the golf links after a bad slice, that he was not reasoning calmly, as one reasonable person to another, and he stopped. He took a cigar from the humidor on the desk, examined it, bit the end off with a savage click, and did not light it. He sat with it in his fingers like a pointer.

"Now, look here," he said. "I'll explain this to you. I'll make it so plain that a—that anybody can understand it. There's a difference, see, between what a man says in the privacy of his own home, to his own wife, when he's tired out and kind of joshing, and what he says right out in front of folks. You get that? That's a big difference. That's all the difference in the world."

"Why?"

"Because it is!"

"But if it's true in the bedroom, isn't it true in the parlor, too?"

Lowell Spraker opened his mouth and shut it again. It occurred to him, dimly, as a vagrant thought crosses the windshield of a speeding car and is gone, that this was a question to which he did not know the answer; that it was, in fact, a question which he had never asked himself in forty-four years of selling paint and attending the First Methodist Church and voting the straight Republican ticket; and that he did not care to ask it now. He felt, obscurely, that the child was being impudent in some way more alarming than any impudence he had ever been taught to deal with.

"Don't you get smart with me, young man!" he roared, and was relieved, for it was a familiar sound. "Don't you go trying to argue with your father! When I want any back-talk out of you, I'll ask for it! You hear me?"

"Yes, Papa."

"Well, then!"

He rose and walked to the window. Outside, Elmhurst Terrace lay in the thin October sunshine, its lawns trimmed, its maples turning, its two-car garages proclaiming the triumph of Progress over the horse. Across the street Dr. Whitcomb Pettibone was washing his Hupmobile with the solemn and loving care of a priest at the altar. The sight, ordinarily, would have soothed Mr. Spraker. Today it reminded him that Dr. Pettibone was on the board of the Second National, and that by Tuesday noon Dr. Pettibone would have heard the story of the flea, and that by Tuesday evening it would be told at the Monarch Athletic Club, with improvements, by men who would slap him on the back and call him "Skinflint" for a year.

He turned on the boy with renewed fury.

"Do you know what you've done? I'll tell you what you've done! You've maybe cost your father a drying-shed! You've maybe cost him two new vats and a twenty-thousand-dollar loan and Lord knows what all! You think that's funny? You think that's something to grin about?"

"I'm not grinning, Papa."

"Well, you were thinking about it! I can tell! Don't you contradict me!" He paced. The bass on the wall looked down on him with a glassy and sardonic eye. "Here I work my head off, day in and day out, down at that plant, from eight in the morning till all hours, to give you a good home and decent clothes and a good education, and send you to the best school in Monarch and buy you that velocipede, and I guess there's not many kids your age got a velocipede like that one, and this is the thanks I get! This is gratitude! You go and make a monkey of me in front of the biggest man in the Second National Bank!"

Willis's lower lip, which had hitherto held firm with a fine Spartan rigidity, began to tremble. It was not the drying-shed that moved him, for he did not know what a drying-shed was, and imagined it as a kind of large towel. It was the velocipede. He had a sudden and terrible vision of the velocipede being taken away; of the velocipede being given to the Pettibone boy, who already had a Flexible Flyer and a dog.

"I'm sorry, Papa," he said, with a quaver.

Now Lowell Spraker was not a cruel man. He was, in the opinion of everyone who knew him, including himself, a regular fellow, a good scout, a man who'd give you the shirt off his back. He liked children; he liked dogs; he liked to see his name on the list of donors to the Y.M.C.A. building fund, in type of a size proportionate to the gift. At the quaver in his son's voice something in him softened, and with the softening came a sharp desire to be done with the whole business, to have it settled and tied up and put away, so that he could go and get into his old sweater and listen to the band concert on the radio and forget that J. Ambrose Hockaday existed.

But he was a father, and he knew, from the Sunday-school papers, from the American Magazine, from the remarks of the Rev. Dr. Orrin Gatling on the fifth Sunday after Easter, that a father must on such occasions be firm. He was firm. He sat down again in the Morris chair and assumed the expression of a judge in a motion picture.

"Well, being sorry's all very well," he said. "Being sorry's a good start. But it isn't enough, see? When a fellow makes a mistake, he's got to make it right. That's what a real man does. That's the American way. Now, I'll tell you what you're going to do. Tomorrow, after school, your mother's going to take you down to the Second National Bank, and you're going to go in and ask to see Mr. Hockaday, and you're going to tell him you're sorry. You're going to tell him you made it all up. Understand? You're going to say, 'Mr. Hockaday, I'm sorry I said what I did yesterday, and I didn't mean it, and my Papa never said anything of the kind, I just made it up out of my own head because I'm a bad boy.' You got that?"

Willis looked at him.

"Say it after me," said Mr. Spraker. "'Mr. Hockaday, I'm sorry—'"

"But you did say it, Papa."

"Never mind whether I said it!"

"But you told me not to tell fibs. You said what happens to little boys that tell fibs. You said—"

"Willis!"

"—that God sees them, and the Bible says—"

"That'll do! That'll be about enough out of you!" Mr. Spraker struck the arm of the Morris chair, precisely upon the burn, which hurt. "Of all the—I never in my life—Myrtle! Myrtle, you come in here! You come in here and listen to this kid!"

Mrs. Spraker came in. She had been, it is to be feared, in the hall all along, near the hat-rack, rearranging a pair of gloves which required no rearrangement. She was a small, anxious, faded, pretty woman who had once played the mandolin, and she looked from her husband to her son with the expression of a referee who has been warned that both teams have friends in the stands.

"Now, Lowell," she said, "don't get yourself all worked up. Remember your blood-pressure. Dr. Pettibone said—"

"Never mind Pettibone! Listen to him! I tell him he's got to go down and apologize to Hockaday and tell him he made it up, and he stands there and tells me that's a fib! He tells me—his own father—about fibbing! Out of the Bible!"

"Well," said Mrs. Spraker, carefully, "well, dear, it would be a fib, wouldn't it? Kind of? I mean, you did say it. I heard you. And I said at the time, I said, 'Lowell, I wish you wouldn't talk that way about people, with the children in the house'—"

"Oh, you did, did you? Oh, that's fine! That's just dandy! Here I am trying to teach the kid a lesson, and you go siding with him!"

"I'm not siding with anybody. I only meant—"

"I know what you meant!"

What Mrs. Spraker had meant was never established, for at that moment Willis, who had been looking from one parent to the other with an absorption more scientific than filial, began, quite without warning, to cry. He did not cry well. He cried in the manner of the young male who has been told since infancy that big boys don't cry and is now discovering that this is untrue: with a loud gulp, a mighty wrinkling of the nose, and a long, wet, outraged howl, out of which emerged at last the words, "I don't—want—to give—the velocipede—to Harold Pettibone!"

"Who said anything about the velocipede?" demanded his father, startled.

"You did! You said you bought it! You said—you said—"

"I never said I'd take it away, did I?"

"You were going to!"

"I was not!" Mr. Spraker was wounded. He had, in fact, intended to take it away; he had been on the very point of it; but to be accused of it beforehand seemed to him a monstrous injustice. "Now, look here. Look here, old man. Quit that bawling. Nobody's going to take your velocipede. There! Hear me? Blow your nose. Here. Here's Papa's handkerchief. That's the boy. Blow."

Willis blew. Mrs. Spraker knelt and straightened his collar. Mr. Spraker stood over them both, cigar in hand, enormous, perplexed, and conscious that the interview had escaped him somewhere, the way the last nine holes on the Monarch Country Club course always escaped him, without his ever being quite able to say where it had happened.

"Well, now," he said at last, gruffly. "Well, now. We'll say no more about it. Only, I want you to remember this, see? I want you to remember that there's things a fellow says and there's things a fellow doesn't say, and when you're older you'll understand. Every successful man in this town understands it. You think Mr. Hockaday goes around telling everybody what he thinks of them? I'll say he doesn't! Not by a long shot! That's—that's diplomacy, see? That's tact. That's the way business is done, and that's the way the whole country's run, and I guess it's done pretty well for us, hey? Got the finest country in the world, haven't we? Got the highest standard of living? Well, then!" He felt better. He had arrived at a principle, and a principle, once arrived at, was a comfortable place to sit. "So you just remember that, and don't you go repeating things you hear on the stairs."

"Do I have to go to the bank?" asked Willis, damply.

Mr. Spraker hesitated. He thought of the round marble lobby of the Second National Bank, of its brass grilles and its silent tellers and its air of a cathedral built to a god who took six per cent; he thought of Willis standing in the middle of it in his blue serge suit, looking up at Mr. Hockaday with those terrible blue eyes, and beginning, "Mr. Hockaday, my Papa says I have to tell you I made it up, only I didn't—"

"No," he said. "No, I guess we'll let that ride. I'll—I'll fix it up with him myself. Man to man. Run along now. Go on out and play. Get out of that suit first, though!"

Willis went, with the velocity of the reprieved. They heard him on the stairs, and they heard him, a moment later, singing, in a voice of the purest and most untroubled joy, "Skin a flea, skin a flea, skin a flea for its hide!" until a door slammed upon it.

Mrs. Spraker looked at her husband. Mr. Spraker looked at the mounted bass.

"I suppose," she said, "you'll want me to send Mrs. Hockaday some of my chili sauce."

"Well—might not be a bad idea. Couple jars. Nothing too—you know."

"I know."

She went out. Lowell Spraker sat down again in the Morris chair. He lighted the cigar at last, and it was a good cigar, a twenty-five-center, and it drew well, and the smoke went up in a fine blue curl past the motto which asserted that The Man Who Wins Is the Man Who Thinks He Can. He thought he could. He would drop round to the bank Tuesday. He would take Hockaday to lunch at the Athletic Club, and order the planked whitefish, and tell him a couple of good ones he'd heard at the Kiwanis, and say, offhand, "Say, about that fool kid of mine—you know how kids are, get things all twisted round—" and Hockaday would laugh, because Hockaday had kids of his own, and it would be all right. It would be perfectly all right.

But he found that he was not thinking of Hockaday at all. He was thinking, with an irritation he could not account for, of a small boy on a dark staircase, listening; and of a question which had been asked him in his own den, on the hooked rug which Myrtle had bought at the church bazaar, and which he had not answered. If it was true in the bedroom, was it true in the parlor, too?

"Damn foolishness," said Lowell T. Spraker aloud, and reached for the sporting page.

The house in which the Gersbachs had their two rooms stood upon the north side of Washington Street, a little below the crest of the hill, where the cable cars of the Powell Street line, coming up out of the hollow of the town, swung around the curve with a prolonged clashing of iron upon iron, and went grinding and lurching onward toward the Bay. All day long, and far into the night, the cable hummed in its slot beneath the cobbles, a low, unceasing note, monotonous, interminable, like the drone of some vast insect buried in the earth. It was the first sound Delia Gersbach heard upon waking and the last sound she heard before she slept. After four years she had ceased to notice it at all, as one ceases to notice the beating of one's own heart. Only when it stopped, as it did sometimes in the small hours when the power-house shut down for repairs, would she start up in her bed, wide awake and vaguely frightened, as if something had died in the night.

Anton Gersbach was a gripman upon that line. He was a huge, slow, blond German of thirty-five, with enormous shoulders, a thick red neck, and great hands, square-ended, hard as the wooden handles of the grip lever, the palms ridged and yellow with callous. His hair was cropped close to his round skull, and his mustache, stiff and colorless as dry straw, hung down over a mouth that was heavy and good-natured and a trifle stupid. He was not quick. He thought with difficulty, laboriously, one idea at a time, turning it over and over as he would have turned a stone in his fingers. But he was strong, and he was steady, and for eleven years he had stood in the front of the dummy, his feet planted wide, his two fists upon the lever, and had driven his car up the terrific grade of Powell Street and down again, two hundred times a month, and never a mishap. The company knew him for a good man. He was proud of that. It was the one thing in the world of which he was proud.

Delia was little and dark and quick, Irish to the finger-tips, with a narrow, pale face, black eyebrows that nearly met above her nose, and a small, tight mouth that could shut like a purse. She was a good manager. She bought her meat at the shop on Stockton Street where it was a cent cheaper by the pound, and she carried it home herself rather than pay the boy to bring it. She had a passion for order. The two rooms were scrubbed and blacked and polished till they shone; the stove was a mirror; the oilcloth upon the kitchen table had been washed so often that the pattern of blue tiles was nearly gone from it. Every Saturday night, when Anton brought home his wages, she counted the money out upon that table, coin by coin, sorting the silver from the gold, and put away into the tin box behind the flour bin what could be spared. There were a hundred and forty dollars in the box now. She knew the sum to the very nickel. She thought of it often during the day, at odd moments, while she ironed, while she peeled potatoes, and the thought of it warmed her like a little fire.

It was a Thursday, toward the end of October, a day of high wind and blowing dust, when the trade-wind came booming in through the Golden Gate and swept the hill-tops of the city clean. At six o'clock Delia had the supper ready—a stew of mutton and onions, a loaf of bread, a pot of coffee black as ink. The lamp was lit. The window rattled in its frame. Below, in the street, the cable hummed in its slot.

At a quarter past six she heard Anton's heavy tread upon the stairs, slow, deliberate, each step jarring the flimsy house. He came in, filling the doorway with his bulk, and hung his cap upon its nail, and said, as he said every evening:

"Well, Dele."

"Well," she answered.

He went to the sink and washed his hands and face, blowing and snorting in the water like a horse, and dried himself upon the roller towel, and sat down at the table. She put the stew before him. He began to eat at once, bending over his plate, shovelling the food into his mouth with his knife, chewing enormously, his jaws working with the steady, mechanical regularity of some great machine. Delia did not eat. She sat opposite him, her hands folded upon the oilcloth, and watched him. He did not notice. He never noticed. When he was eating he was conscious of nothing but the food.

"Anton," she said at length.

"Huh?"

"How was the road to-day?"

"All right," he said, with his mouth full. "Pretty good. Wind's bad on the hill."

"Was it?"

"Yes. Blows the dust in the slot. She drags some."

"Who was your conductor to-day?"

He paused. It was only for an instant, the fraction of an instant, his knife suspended half-way to his mouth. Then he went on eating.

"Schultz," he said. "Same as always."

Delia drew a long breath. Her small mouth shut tight. Her hands upon the oilcloth gripped one another till the knuckles whitened.

"You're a liar, Anton Gersbach," she said.

He stopped eating then. He laid down his knife and looked up at her, slowly, his small blue eyes wide and puzzled under their pale lashes. For a long moment he did not speak. The lamp flared and smoked a little. The window rattled. Down in the street a car came grinding up the grade, and the cable sang beneath it, a long, shrill, rising note, and then fell again to its eternal hum.

"What's that?" he said at last.

"You heard me. You're a liar. You ain't been on the road to-day. You ain't been on the road this week. You ain't been on the road since the Tuesday before last. Don't you go telling me no, because I know."

He stared at her stupidly. His great red face grew slowly redder, the blood creeping up from his thick neck into his cheeks and over his forehead to the roots of his cropped hair. He moved in his chair, and the chair creaked under him.

"Who told you?" he said.

"Never you mind who told me. Mrs. Flaherty told me, if you want to know, that's who told me, and her husband's in the barn, and he told her, and she come up here this afternoon and sat right there where you're sitting, and told me, and asked me how I liked it. Me! That didn't know a thing about it. Me, that's been putting up your dinner-pail every morning this ten days, and you taking it and going off with it down the stairs as big as life, and saying, 'Good-by, Dele,' and all the time—all the time—" Her voice rose and broke. "Where've you been? Where've you been going all day long, every day, with that dinner-pail?"

Anton looked down at his plate. He did not answer at once. It was very hard for him to find words; it had always been hard. Words did not come to him; he had to go and seek them out, one by one, as one gropes for tools in the dark.

"I been looking for a job," he said.

"A job! And you with a job! What did you do? What did they let you go for? Eleven years you been with them. Eleven years! What did you do?"

He was silent again. His huge hands lay upon the table on either side of his plate, palm downward, and Delia saw the fingers of them curl slowly inward, as though they closed upon something, upon the handle of a lever, perhaps, gripping, gripping, with all the force of his enormous strength.

"There was a kid," he said.

Delia did not move.

"There was a kid," he said again, in his slow, thick voice. "Down by Jackson Street. Little girl. Coming out from behind a wagon. I didn't see her. I couldn't see her, Dele. The wagon was there, see, a brewery wagon, standing, and she come out from behind it with a hoop, running after the hoop. I put on the brake. I put her on hard. I put her on so hard I bent the shoe. But it's steep there, Dele. It's steep there by Jackson. You don't stop a car on that grade, not like you'd stop a horse."

"Did you—was she—"

"No. She ain't dead. She got her leg broke. They took her to the Receiving Hospital. She'll get well, the doctor says. But her father's a man that knows a lawyer, and he come to the company, and the company says somebody's got to go. So it was me. I was the man on the grip." He lifted his hands a little from the table and let them fall again. "It wasn't my fault, Dele. I put the brake on. I put her on hard."

For a moment—only for a moment—something softened in Delia's narrow face. Her lips parted. She looked at the great hands lying there upon the worn oilcloth, so strong, so helpless, and it seemed as if she would reach out and touch them. But the moment passed. A thought had come to her, a little, sharp, cold thought, and her mouth shut again.

"Ten days," she said. "Ten days, and you never told me."

"I was going to tell you."

"When? When was you going to tell me? When the rent come due? When there wasn't nothing in the house to eat? Ten days, and you going off every morning with your pail, making a fool of me, letting me think—letting me put by—" She stopped short. Her eyes narrowed. She leaned forward across the table. "Anton. Where's your wages? Saturday. You brought me your wages Saturday. Eleven dollars. You put it right there on the table, and I counted it. Where'd you get it?"

He did not answer.

"Where'd you get it?"

Still he said nothing. He sat there motionless, his head lowered, his eyes upon his plate, his great shoulders hunched, like an ox that waits for the goad. And Delia, watching him, felt a sudden fear take hold of her, a fear that made her heart beat thick and fast. She rose from the table so quickly that her chair went over behind her with a clatter, and ran to the corner where the flour bin stood, and dragged it out from the wall, and thrust her arm in behind it, groping. Her fingers found the tin box. She drew it out and pried off the lid with her nails and turned it out upon the drain-board of the sink. The coins rang upon the wood, rolled, spun, and lay still. She counted them, her lips moving, her fingers flying, pushing the gold to one side and the silver to the other.

There were a hundred and twenty-nine dollars.

She counted them again. A hundred and twenty-nine. She turned and faced him, the empty box in her hand.

"You took it," she said. Her voice was very low. "You took it out of the box. Eleven dollars. You took my money out of my box and brought it to me and put it on the table and let me count it and put it back. Like it was your wages. Like it was—" She choked. "My money!"

"It ain't your money," said Anton slowly. "It's our money."

"It's my money! Who saved it? Who went without? Who walked to Stockton Street for the meat, and wore her old jacket two winters, and turned her skirt, and never had a thing, not a ribbon, not a thing, so's there'd be something put by? It's my money, every cent of it, and you went and took it, sneaking, behind my back, like a thief—like a common thief—"

"Dele—"

"Like a thief!"

Then, all at once, Anton Gersbach rose to his feet.

He rose slowly, heavily, his chair scraping back upon the floor, and stood upright in the little kitchen, and the lamp-light, striking upward, threw his shadow enormous upon the wall and the ceiling, so that it seemed to fill the room, to crowd it, to loom over the small, dark woman by the sink. His face was crimson. His small eyes had grown suddenly bright and hard. His hands hung at his sides, and they were shut, and Delia saw the cords stand out upon the backs of them like ropes.

For a long moment neither spoke. And in that silence, from somewhere very deep down within the man, from beneath the slow stupidity, the patience, the good-nature, the eleven years of steady and faithful toil, something stirred—something blind and ancient and evil, that had lain there all his life, asleep, and was not asleep now. Delia felt it. She could not have said what it was, but she felt it, as one feels the first faint tremor of the earth before the great shock comes. She shrank back against the sink. The empty tin box slid from her fingers and fell clanging to the floor.

"Don't you call me that," said Anton.

His voice was not loud. It was thick and low, and it seemed to come from his chest rather than his throat, a sort of rumble, a growl.

"Don't you call me that, Dele. I ain't a thief. I worked. Eleven years I worked. Every day, rain or shine, fog, wind, every day, up that hill and down again. You know how many people I took up that hill? I don't know. Nobody knows. Thousands. Millions, maybe. And never a mishap. Never once. And then one kid comes out from behind a wagon, and they say, 'Gersbach, you go.' Like that. 'You go.' And I go. I go down to the barn every morning and stand there with my pail and ask Rafferty is there anything, and he says no. And I go down to the docks and ask is there anything, and they say no. And I go out to the gas-works, and they say no. And I walk. All day I walk. I eat my dinner out of the pail sitting on a pile of lumber by the water. And I think, I can't tell Dele. I can't go home and tell Dele. Because I knew what you'd say. I knew you'd say about the money. That's all you think about. The money. The money in the box."

He took a step toward her. The floor shook.

"Well, I took it," he said. "I took eleven dollars out of the box. So you wouldn't know. So you wouldn't look like that. You're looking like that now, Dele. You're looking at me like I was dirt."

Delia did not answer. She could not. She stood pressed against the sink, her hands behind her, gripping the edge of the drain-board, her face white as paper, her black eyes fixed upon him. She was afraid. For the first time in the four years of their marriage she was afraid of her husband. She had never thought of him as a thing to be feared. He had been to her only a great, slow, harmless creature, a kind of beast of burden, that went out in the morning and came back at night and brought her its wages and ate its supper and slept. And now, all at once, she saw that he was something else as well. She saw the size of him, the bulk of him, the terrible strength of those hands that had held back a loaded car upon the steepest grade in the city. And she saw that there was nothing—nothing at all—between that strength and herself but some thin, frail thing, some habit, some custom, that might snap at any moment like a rotten thread.

And Anton saw that she was afraid.

He stopped. He stood quite still in the middle of the floor, his head lowered, breathing hard through his nose. The red ebbed slowly out of his face. His hands opened. He looked down at them, at his great, yellow, callused hands, as though he had never seen them before, as though they belonged to some one else; and a puzzled, troubled expression came into his small eyes, the expression of a dog that has bitten and does not know why.

"Dele," he said, in a different voice. "Dele, I wouldn't—you know I wouldn't—"

She did not move.

He turned away from her. He went back to the table and stood beside it, looking down at his half-eaten supper, at the stew grown cold upon the plate, with a film of white fat creeping over it. He put out one hand and touched the back of his chair, aimlessly, and drew it back again.

"I'll get a job," he said. "I'll get one, Dele. Rafferty says maybe at the Market Street line, after the first of the month. They want gripmen there. He says he'll put in a word."

Delia drew a long, shuddering breath. The color began to come back into her face, a little at a time. She let go of the drain-board. She stooped, slowly, and picked up the tin box from the floor, and turned to the sink, and began to gather up the coins, one by one, the gold and the silver, and drop them into it. Her fingers were shaking so that she could hardly hold them. A dime slipped from her hand and rolled away under the stove, and she got down upon her knees and fished for it with a hairpin until she found it, and put it in the box with the rest.

Anton watched her do it. He said nothing.

When the coins were all in, she pressed down the lid, and pushed the box back into its place behind the flour bin, and dragged the bin back against the wall. Then she stood up and smoothed her apron with both hands, and came back to the table, and picked up her fallen chair, and set it upright, and sat down in it.

"Sit down and eat your supper," she said. "It's getting cold."

He sat down. He took up his knife again. But he did not eat. He sat there with the knife in his hand, staring at the plate.

"Dele," he said at last.

"Well?"

"You ain't going to tell nobody? About the eleven dollars?"

"Who'd I tell?"

"Mrs. Flaherty."

"I ain't going to tell Mrs. Flaherty nothing," said Delia, and her small mouth shut tight again. "It's none of Mrs. Flaherty's business."

That was all. They did not speak of it again that night. Anton ate a little of the cold stew, and drank his coffee, and then sat for a long time by the stove in his stocking feet, smoking his pipe and looking at nothing. Delia washed the dishes and dried them and put them away, and wiped the oilcloth, and blacked the stove, and set the bread to rise for the morning. At ten o'clock they went to bed.

But Delia did not sleep. She lay upon her back in the darkness, her eyes wide open, listening to the heavy breathing of the man beside her—the long, slow, even breathing of a great animal at rest. The wind had fallen. The window was still. Down below in the street the cable hummed in its slot, low, unceasing, monotonous, the voice of the vast, blind machine that ran beneath the city, that never stopped, that never rested, that did not care. She lay and listened to it, and thought about the little girl who had come out from behind the brewery wagon, running after her hoop; and about the hands that had put on the brake, put it on hard, so hard they bent the shoe, and could not stop the car; and about the look that had come into her husband's face when he rose up out of his chair and stood over her with the lamp-light throwing his shadow on the wall.

She had seen something to-night. She did not know what it was. She had not the words for it. But she knew that it was there now, and that it had always been there, and that it would never go away again. It was down there in him, deep, deep down, beneath the good-nature and the patience and the slow, plodding stupidity, as the cable was down there beneath the cobbles—hidden, buried, out of sight, but alive, and moving, and strong, stronger than he, stronger than she, stronger than either of them.

Toward morning, a little before four, the power-house shut down. The humming in the street ceased. And in the sudden, enormous silence Delia Gersbach started up in her bed, her heart pounding, her hands clutching at the blankets, wide awake and terribly afraid, as if something, somewhere in the dark, had died in the night.
