Carry’s vague presentment of Mrs. Norma Hatch (whose reversion to her Christian name was explained as the result of her latest divorce), left her under the implication of coming “from the West,” with the not unusual extenuation of having brought a great deal of money with her. She was, in short, rich, helpless, unplaced: the very subject for Lily’s hand. Mrs. Fisher had not specified the line her friend was to take; she owned herself unacquainted with Mrs. Hatch, whom she “knew about” through Melville Stancy, a lawyer in his leisure moments, and the Falstaff of a certain section of festive club life. Socially, Mr. Stancy might have been said to form a connecting link between the Gormer world and the more dimly-lit region on which Miss Bart now found herself entering. It was, however, only figuratively that the illumination of Mrs. Hatch’s world could be described as dim: in actual fact, Lily found her seated in a blaze of electric light, impartially projected from various ornamental excrescences on a vast concavity of pink damask and gilding, from which she rose like Venus from her shell. The analogy was justified by the appearance of the lady, whose large-eyed prettiness had the fixity of something impaled and shown under glass. This did not preclude the immediate discovery that she was some years younger than her visitor, and that under her showiness, her ease, the aggression of her dress and voice, there persisted that ineradicable innocence which, in ladies of her nationality, so curiously coexists with startling extremes of experience. The environment in which Lily found herself was as strange to her as its inhabitants. She was unacquainted with the world of the fashionable New York hotel—a world over-heated, over-upholstered, and over-fitted with mechanical appliances for the gratification of fantastic requirements, while the comforts of a civilized life were as unattainable as in a desert. Through this atmosphere of torrid splendour moved wan beings as richly upholstered as the furniture, beings without definite pursuits or permanent relations, who drifted on a languid tide of curiosity from restaurant to concert-hall, from palm-garden to music-room, from “art exhibit” to dress-maker’s opening. High-stepping horses or elaborately equipped motors waited to carry these ladies into vague metropolitan distances, whence they returned, still more wan from the weight of their sables, to be sucked back into the stifling inertia of the hotel routine. Somewhere behind them, in the background of their lives, there was doubtless a real past, peopled by real human activities: they themselves were probably the product of strong ambitions, persistent energies, diversified contacts with the wholesome roughness of life; yet they had no more real existence than the poet’s shades in limbo. Lily had not been long in this pallid world without discovering that Mrs. Hatch was its most substantial figure. That lady, though still floating in the void, showed faint symptoms of developing an outline; and in this endeavour she was actively seconded by Mr. Melville Stancy. It was Mr. Stancy, a man of large resounding presence, suggestive of convivial occasions and of a chivalry finding expression in “first-night” boxes and thousand dollar bonbonnieres, who had transplanted Mrs. Hatch from the scene of her first development to the higher stage of hotel life in the metropolis. It was he who had selected the horses with which she had taken the blue ribbon at the Show, had introduced her to the photographer whose portraits of her formed the recurring ornament of “Sunday Supplements,” and had got together the group which constituted her social world. It was a small group still, with heterogeneous figures suspended in large unpeopled spaces; but Lily did not take long to learn that its regulation was no longer in Mr. Stancy’s hands. As often happens, the pupil had outstripped the teacher, and Mrs. Hatch was already aware of heights of elegance as well as depths of luxury beyond the world of the Emporium. This discovery at once produced in her a craving for higher guidance, for the adroit feminine hand which should give the right turn to her correspondence, the right “look” to her hats, the right succession to the items of her MENUS. It was, in short, as the regulator of a germinating social life that Miss Bart’s guidance was required; her ostensible duties as secretary being restricted by the fact that Mrs. Hatch, as yet, knew hardly any one to write to. The daily details of Mrs. Hatch’s existence were as strange to Lily as its general tenor. The lady’s habits were marked by an Oriental indolence and disorder peculiarly trying to her companion. Mrs. Hatch and her friends seemed to float together outside the bounds of time and space. No definite hours were kept; no fixed obligations existed: night and day flowed into one another in a blur of confused and retarded engagements, so that one had the impression of lunching at the tea-hour, while dinner was often merged in the noisy after-theatre supper which prolonged Mrs. Hatch’s vigil till daylight. Through this jumble of futile activities came and went a strange throng of hangers-on—manicures, beauty-doctors, hair-dressers, teachers of bridge, of French, of “physical development”: figures sometimes indistinguishable, by their appearance, or by Mrs. Hatch’s relation to them, from the visitors constituting her recognized society. But strangest of all to Lily was the encounter, in this latter group, of several of her acquaintances. She had supposed, and not without relief, that she was passing, for the moment, completely out of her own circle; but she found that Mr. Stancy, one side of whose sprawling existence overlapped the edge of Mrs. Fisher’s world, had drawn several of its brightest ornaments into the circle of the Emporium. To find Ned Silverton among the habitual frequenters of Mrs. Hatch’s drawing-room was one of Lily’s first astonishments; but she soon discovered that he was not Mr. Stancy’s most important recruit. It was on little Freddy Van Osburgh, the small slim heir of the Van Osburgh millions, that the attention of Mrs. Hatch’s group was centred. Freddy, barely out of college, had risen above the horizon since Lily’s eclipse, and she now saw with surprise what an effulgence he shed on the outer twilight of Mrs. Hatch’s existence. This, then, was one of the things that young men “went in” for when released from the official social routine; this was the kind of “previous engagement” that so frequently caused them to disappoint the hopes of anxious hostesses. Lily had an odd sense of being behind the social tapestry, on the side where the threads were knotted and the loose ends hung. For a moment she found a certain amusement in the show, and in her own share of it: the situation had an ease and unconventionality distinctly refreshing after her experience of the irony of conventions. But these flashes of amusement were but brief reactions from the long disgust of her days. Compared with the vast gilded void of Mrs. Hatch’s existence, the life of Lily’s former friends seemed packed with ordered activities. Even the most irresponsible pretty woman of her acquaintance had her inherited obligations, her conventional benevolences, her share in the working of the great civic machine; and all hung together in the solidarity of these traditional functions. The performance of specific duties would have simplified Miss Bart’s position; but the vague attendance on Mrs. Hatch was not without its perplexities. It was not her employer who created these perplexities. Mrs. Hatch showed from the first an almost touching desire for Lily’s approval. Far from asserting the superiority of wealth, her beautiful eyes seemed to urge the plea of inexperience: she wanted to do what was “nice,” to be taught how to be “lovely.” The difficulty was to find any point of contact between her ideals and Lily’s. Mrs. Hatch swam in a haze of indeterminate enthusiasms, of aspirations culled from the stage, the newspapers, the fashion journals, and a gaudy world of sport still more completely beyond her companion’s ken. To separate from these confused conceptions those most likely to advance the lady on her way, was Lily’s obvious duty; but its performance was hampered by rapidly-growing doubts. Lily was in fact becoming more and more aware of a certain ambiguity in her situation. It was not that she had, in the conventional sense, any doubt of Mrs. Hatch’s irreproachableness. The lady’s offences were always against taste rather than conduct; her divorce record seemed due to geographical rather than ethical conditions; and her worst laxities were likely to proceed from a wandering and extravagant good-nature. But if Lily did not mind her detaining her manicure for luncheon, or offering the “Beauty-Doctor” a seat in Freddy Van Osburgh’s box at the play, she was not equally at ease in regard to some less apparent lapses from convention. Ned Silverton’s relation to Stancy seemed, for instance, closer and less clear than any natural affinities would warrant; and both appeared united in the effort to cultivate Freddy Van Osburgh’s growing taste for Mrs. Hatch. There was as yet nothing definable in the situation, which might well resolve itself into a huge joke on the part of the other two; but Lily had a vague sense that the subject of their experiment was too young, too rich and too credulous. Her embarrassment was increased by the fact that Freddy seemed to regard her as cooperating with himself in the social development of Mrs. Hatch: a view that suggested, on his part, a permanent interest in the lady’s future. There were moments when Lily found an ironic amusement in this aspect of the case. The thought of launching such a missile as Mrs. Hatch at the perfidious bosom of society was not without its charm: Miss Bart had even beguiled her leisure with visions of the fair Norma introduced for the first time to a family banquet at the Van Osburghs’. But the thought of being personally connected with the transaction was less agreeable; and her momentary flashes of amusement were followed by increasing periods of doubt. The sense of these doubts was uppermost when, late one afternoon, she was surprised by a visit from Lawrence Selden. He found her alone in the wilderness of pink damask, for in Mrs. Hatch’s world the tea-hour was not dedicated to social rites, and the lady was in the hands of her masseuse. Selden’s entrance had caused Lily an inward start of embarrassment; but his air of constraint had the effect of restoring her self-possession, and she took at once the tone of surprise and pleasure, wondering frankly that he should have traced her to so unlikely a place, and asking what had inspired him to make the search. Selden met this with an unusual seriousness: she had never seen him so little master of the situation, so plainly at the mercy of any obstructions she might put in his way. “I wanted to see you,” he said; and she could not resist observing in reply that he had kept his wishes under remarkable control. She had in truth felt his long absence as one of the chief bitternesses of the last months: his desertion had wounded sensibilities far below the surface of her pride. Selden met the challenge with directness. “Why should I have come, unless I thought I could be of use to you? It is my only excuse for imagining you could want me.” This struck her as a clumsy evasion, and the thought gave a flash of keenness to her answer. “Then you have come now because you think you can be of use to me?” He hesitated again. “Yes: in the modest capacity of a person to talk things over with.” For a clever man it was certainly a stupid beginning; and the idea that his awkwardness was due to the fear of her attaching a personal significance to his visit, chilled her pleasure in seeing him. Even under the most adverse conditions, that pleasure always made itself felt: she might hate him, but she had never been able to wish him out of the room. She was very near hating him now; yet the sound of his voice, the way the light fell on his thin dark hair, the way he sat and moved and wore his clothes—she was conscious that even these trivial things were inwoven with her deepest life. In his presence a sudden stillness came upon her, and the turmoil of her spirit ceased; but an impulse of resistance to this stealing influence now prompted her to say: “It’s very good of you to present yourself in that capacity; but what makes you think I have anything particular to talk about?” Though she kept the even tone of light intercourse, the question was framed in a way to remind him that his good offices were unsought; and for a moment Selden was checked by it. The situation between them was one which could have been cleared up only by a sudden explosion of feeling; and their whole training and habit of mind were against the chances of such an explosion. Selden’s calmness seemed rather to harden into resistance, and Miss Bart’s into a surface of glittering irony, as they faced each other from the opposite corners of one of Mrs. Hatch’s elephantine sofas. The sofa in question, and the apartment peopled by its monstrous mates, served at length to suggest the turn of Selden’s reply.

“Gerty told me that you were acting as Mrs. Hatch’s secretary; and I knew she was anxious to hear how you were getting on.” Miss Bart received this explanation without perceptible softening. “Why didn’t she look me up herself, then?” she asked.

“Because, as you didn’t send her your address, she was afraid of being importunate.” Selden continued with a smile: “You see no such scruples restrained me; but then I haven’t as much to risk if I incur your displeasure.” Lily answered his smile. “You haven’t incurred it as yet; but I have an idea that you are going to.”

“That rests with you, doesn’t it? You see my initiative doesn’t go beyond putting myself at your disposal.”

“But in what capacity? What am I to do with you?” she asked in the same light tone. Selden again glanced about Mrs. Hatch’s drawing-room; then he said, with a decision which he seemed to have gathered from this final inspection: “You are to let me take you away from here.” Lily flushed at the suddenness of the attack; then she stiffened under it and said coldly: “And may I ask where you mean me to go?”

“Back to Gerty in the first place, if you will; the essential thing is that it should be away from here.” The unusual harshness of his tone might have shown her how much the words cost him; but she was in no state to measure his feelings while her own were in a flame of revolt. To neglect her, perhaps even to avoid her, at a time when she had most need of her friends, and then suddenly and unwarrantably to break into her life with this strange assumption of authority, was to rouse in her every instinct of pride and self-defence.

“I am very much obliged to you,” she said, “for taking such an interest in my plans; but I am quite contented where I am, and have no intention of leaving.” Selden had risen, and was standing before her in an attitude of uncontrollable expectancy.

“That simply means that you don’t know where you are!” he exclaimed. Lily rose also, with a quick flash of anger. “If you have come here to say disagreeable things about Mrs. Hatch——” “It is only with your relation to Mrs. Hatch that I am concerned.”

“My relation to Mrs. Hatch is one I have no reason to be ashamed of. She has helped me to earn a living when my old friends were quite resigned to seeing me starve.”

“Nonsense! Starvation is not the only alternative. You know you can always find a home with Gerty till you are independent again.”

“You show such an intimate acquaintance with my affairs that I suppose you mean—till my aunt’s legacy is paid?”

“I do mean that; Gerty told me of it,” Selden acknowledged without embarrassment. He was too much in earnest now to feel any false constraint in speaking his mind.

“But Gerty does not happen to know,” Miss Bart rejoined, “that I owe every penny of that legacy.”

Excerpt 3: Meanwhile the holidays had gone by and the season was beginning. Fifth Avenue had become a nightly torrent of carriages surging upward to the fashionable quarters about the Park, where illuminated windows and outspread awnings betokened the usual routine of hospitality. Other tributary currents crossed the mainstream, bearing their freight to the theatres, restaurants or opera; and Mrs. Peniston, from the secluded watch-tower of her upper window, could tell to a nicety just when the chronic volume of sound was increased by the sudden influx setting toward a Van Osburgh ball, or when the multiplication of wheels meant merely that the opera was over, or that there was a big supper at Sherry’s. Mrs. Peniston followed the rise and culmination of the season as keenly as the most active sharer in its gaieties; and, as a looker-on, she enjoyed opportunities of comparison and generalization such as those who take part must proverbially forego. No one could have kept a more accurate record of social fluctuations, or have put a more unerring finger on the distinguishing features of each season: its dulness, its extravagance, its lack of balls or excess of divorces. She had a special memory for the vicissitudes of the “new people” who rose to the surface with each recurring tide, and were either submerged beneath its rush or landed triumphantly beyond the reach of envious breakers; and she was apt to display a remarkable retrospective insight into their ultimate fate, so that, when they had fulfilled their destiny, she was almost always able to say to Grace Stepney—the recipient of her prophecies—that she had known exactly what would happen. This particular season Mrs. Peniston would have characterized as that in which everybody “felt poor” except the Welly Brys and Mr. Simon Rosedale. It had been a bad autumn in Wall Street, where prices fell in accordance with that peculiar law which proves railway stocks and bales of cotton to be more sensitive to the allotment of executive power than many estimable citizens trained to all the advantages of self-government. Even fortunes supposed to be independent of the market either betrayed a secret dependence on it, or suffered from a sympathetic affection: fashion sulked in its country houses, or came to town incognito, general entertainments were discountenanced, and informality and short dinners became the fashion. But society, amused for a while at playing Cinderella, soon wearied of the hearthside role, and welcomed the Fairy Godmother in the shape of any magician powerful enough to turn the shrunken pumpkin back again into the golden coach. The mere fact of growing richer at a time when most people’s investments are shrinking, is calculated to attract envious attention; and according to Wall Street rumours, Welly Bry and Rosedale had found the secret of performing this miracle. Rosedale, in particular, was said to have doubled his fortune, and there was talk of his buying the newly-finished house of one of the victims of the crash, who, in the space of twelve short months, had made the same number of millions, built a house in Fifth Avenue, filled a picture gallery with old masters, entertained all New York in it, and been smuggled out of the country between a trained nurse and a doctor, while his creditors mounted guard over the old masters, and his guests explained to each other that they had dined with him only because they wanted to see the pictures. Mr. Rosedale meant to have a less meteoric career. He knew he should have to go slowly, and the instincts of his race fitted him to suffer rebuffs and put up with delays. But he was prompt to perceive that the general dulness of the season afforded him an unusual opportunity to shine, and he set about with patient industry to form a background for his growing glory. Mrs. Fisher was of immense service to him at this period. She had set off so many newcomers on the social stage that she was like one of those pieces of stock scenery which tell the experienced spectator exactly what is going to take place. But Mr. Rosedale wanted, in the long run, a more individual environment. He was sensitive to shades of difference which Miss Bart would never have credited him with perceiving, because he had no corresponding variations of manner; and it was becoming more and more clear to him that Miss Bart herself possessed precisely the complementary qualities needed to round off his social personality. Such details did not fall within the range of Mrs. Peniston’s vision. Like many minds of panoramic sweep, hers was apt to overlook the MINUTIAE of the foreground, and she was much more likely to know where Carry Fisher had found the Welly Brys’ CHEF for them, than what was happening to her own niece. She was not, however, without purveyors of information ready to supplement her deficiencies. Grace Stepney’s mind was like a kind of moral fly-paper, to which the buzzing items of gossip were drawn by a fatal attraction, and where they hung fast in the toils of an inexorable memory. Lily would have been surprised to know how many trivial facts concerning herself were lodged in Miss Stepney’s head. She was quite aware that she was of interest to dingy people, but she assumed that there is only one form of dinginess, and that admiration for brilliancy is the natural expression of its inferior state. She knew that Gerty Farish admired her blindly, and therefore supposed that she inspired the same sentiments in Grace Stepney, whom she classified as a Gerty Farish without the saving traits of youth and enthusiasm. In reality, the two differed from each other as much as they differed from the object of their mutual contemplation. Miss Farish’s heart was a fountain of tender illusions, Miss Stepney’s a precise register of facts as manifested in their relation to herself. She had sensibilities which, to Lily, would have seemed comic in a person with a freckled nose and red eyelids, who lived in a boarding-house and admired Mrs. Peniston’s drawing-room; but poor Grace’s limitations gave them a more concentrated inner life, as poor soil starves certain plants into intenser efflorescence. She had in truth no abstract propensity to malice: she did not dislike Lily because the latter was brilliant and predominant, but because she thought that Lily disliked her. It is less mortifying to believe one’s self unpopular than insignificant, and vanity prefers to assume that indifference is a latent form of unfriendliness. Even such scant civilities as Lily accorded to Mr. Rosedale would have made Miss Stepney her friend for life; but how could she foresee that such a friend was worth cultivating? How, moreover, can a young woman who has never been ignored measure the pang which this injury inflicts? And, lastly, how could Lily, accustomed to choose between a pressure of engagements, guess that she had mortally offended Miss Stepney by causing her to be excluded from one of Mrs. Peniston’s infrequent dinner-parties? Mrs. Peniston disliked giving dinners, but she had a high sense of family obligation, and on the Jack Stepneys’ return from their honeymoon she felt it incumbent upon her to light the drawing-room lamps and extract her best silver from the Safe Deposit vaults. Mrs. Peniston’s rare entertainments were preceded by days of heart-rending vacillation as to every detail of the feast, from the seating of the guests to the pattern of the table-cloth, and in the course of one of these preliminary discussions she had imprudently suggested to her cousin Grace that, as the dinner was a family affair, she might be included in it. For a week the prospect had lighted up Miss Stepney’s colourless existence; then she had been given to understand that it would be more convenient to have her another day. Miss Stepney knew exactly what had happened. Lily, to whom family reunions were occasions of unalloyed dulness, had persuaded her aunt that a dinner of “smart” people would be much more to the taste of the young couple, and Mrs. Peniston, who leaned helplessly on her niece in social matters, had been prevailed upon to pronounce Grace’s exile. After all, Grace could come any other day; why should she mind being put off? It was precisely because Miss Stepney could come any other day—and because she knew her relations were in the secret of her unoccupied evenings—that this incident loomed gigantically on her horizon. She was aware that she had Lily to thank for it; and dull resentment was turned to active animosity. Mrs. Peniston, on whom she had looked in a day or two after the dinner, laid down her crochet-work and turned abruptly from her oblique survey of Fifth Avenue.

“Gus Trenor?—Lily and Gus Trenor?” she said, growing so suddenly pale that her visitor was almost alarmed.

“Oh, cousin Julia . . . of course I don’t mean....”

“I don’t know what you DO mean,” said Mrs. Peniston, with a frightened quiver in her small fretful voice. “Such things were never heard of in my day. And my own niece! I’m not sure I understand you. Do people say he’s in love with her?” Mrs. Peniston’s horror was genuine. Though she boasted an unequalled familiarity with the secret chronicles of society, she had the innocence of the school-girl who regards wickedness as a part of “history,” and to whom it never occurs that the scandals she reads of in lesson-hours may be repeating themselves in the next street. Mrs. Peniston had kept her imagination shrouded, like the drawing-room furniture. She knew, of course, that society was “very much changed,” and that many women her mother would have thought “peculiar” were now in a position to be critical about their visiting-lists; she had discussed the perils of divorce with her rector, and had felt thankful at times that Lily was still unmarried; but the idea that any scandal could attach to a young girl’s name, above all that it could be lightly coupled with that of a married man, was so new to her that she was as much aghast as if she had been accused of leaving her carpets down all summer, or of violating any of the other cardinal laws of house-keeping. Miss Stepney, when her first fright had subsided, began to feel the superiority that greater breadth of mind confers. It was really pitiable to be as ignorant of the world as Mrs. Peniston! She smiled at the latter’s question. “People always say unpleasant things—and certainly they’re a great deal together. A friend of mine met them the other afternoon in the Park—quite late, after the lamps were lit. It’s a pity Lily makes herself so conspicuous.”

“CONSPICUOUS!” gasped Mrs. Peniston. She bent forward, lowering her voice to mitigate the horror. “What sort of things do they say? That he means to get a divorce and marry her?” Grace Stepney laughed outright. “Dear me, no! He would hardly do that. It—it’s a flirtation—nothing more.”

“A flirtation? Between my niece and a married man? Do you mean to tell me that, with Lily’s looks and advantages, she could find no better use for her time than to waste it on a fat stupid man almost old enough to be her father?” This argument had such a convincing ring that it gave Mrs. Peniston sufficient reassurance to pick up her work, while she waited for Grace Stepney to rally her scattered forces. But Miss Stepney was on the spot in an instant. “That’s the worst of it—people say she isn’t wasting her time! Every one knows, as you say, that Lily is too handsome and—and charming—to devote herself to a man like Gus Trenor unless—” “Unless?” echoed Mrs. Peniston. Her visitor drew breath nervously. It was agreeable to shock Mrs. Peniston, but not to shock her to the verge of anger. Miss Stepney was not sufficiently familiar with the classic drama to have recalled in advance how bearers of bad tidings are proverbially received, but she now had a rapid vision of forfeited dinners and a reduced wardrobe as the possible consequence of her disinterestedness. To the honour of her sex, however, hatred of Lily prevailed over more personal considerations. Mrs. Peniston had chosen the wrong moment to boast of her niece’s charms.

“Unless,” said Grace, leaning forward to speak with low-toned emphasis, “unless there are material advantages to be gained by making herself agreeable to him.” She felt that the moment was tremendous, and remembered suddenly that Mrs. Peniston’s black brocade, with the cut jet fringe, would have been hers at the end of the season. Mrs. Peniston put down her work again. Another aspect of the same idea had presented itself to her, and she felt that it was beneath her dignity to have her nerves racked by a dependent relative who wore her old clothes.

“If you take pleasure in annoying me by mysterious insinuations,” she said coldly, “you might at least have chosen a more suitable time than just as I am recovering from the strain of giving a large dinner.” The mention of the dinner dispelled Miss Stepney’s last scruples. “I don’t know why I should be accused of taking pleasure in telling you about Lily. I was sure I shouldn’t get any thanks for it,” she returned with a flare of temper. “But I have some family feeling left, and as you are the only person who has any authority over Lily, I thought you ought to know what is being said of her.”

“Well,” said Mrs. Peniston, “what I complain of is that you haven’t told me yet what IS being said.”

“I didn’t suppose I should have to put it so plainly. People say that Gus Trenor pays her bills.”

“Pays her bills—her bills?” Mrs. Peniston broke into a laugh. “I can’t imagine where you can have picked up such rubbish. Lily has her own income—and I provide for her very handsomely—” “Oh, we all know that,” interposed Miss Stepney drily. “But Lily wears a great many smart gowns—” “I like her to be well-dressed—it’s only suitable!”

“Certainly; but then there are her gambling debts besides.” Miss Stepney, in the beginning, had not meant to bring up this point; but Mrs. Peniston had only her own incredulity to blame. She was like the stiff-necked unbelievers of Scripture, who must be annihilated to be convinced.

“Gambling debts? Lily?” Mrs. Peniston’s voice shook with anger and bewilderment. She wondered whether Grace Stepney had gone out of her mind. “What do you mean by her gambling debts?”

“Simply that if one plays bridge for money in Lily’s set one is liable to lose a great deal—and I don’t suppose Lily always wins.”

“Who told you that my niece played cards for money?”

“Mercy, cousin Julia, don’t look at me as if I were trying to turn you against Lily! Everybody knows she is crazy about bridge. Mrs. Gryce told me herself that it was her gambling that frightened Percy Gryce—it seems he was really taken with her at first. But, of course, among Lily’s friends it’s quite the custom for girls to play for money. In fact, people are inclined to excuse her on that account——” “To excuse her for what?”

“For being hard up—and accepting attentions from men like Gus Trenor—and George Dorset——” Mrs. Peniston gave another cry. “George Dorset? Is there any one else? I should like to know the worst, if you please.”

“Don’t put it in that way, cousin Julia. Lately Lily has been a good deal with the Dorsets, and he seems to admire her—but of course that’s only natural. And I’m sure there is no truth in the horrid things people say; but she HAS been spending a great deal of money this winter. Evie Van Osburgh was at Celeste’s ordering her trousseau the other day—yes, the marriage takes place next month—and she told me that Celeste showed her the most exquisite things she was just sending home to Lily. And people say that Judy Trenor has quarrelled with her on account of Gus; but I’m sure I’m sorry I spoke, though I only meant it as a kindness.” Mrs. Peniston’s genuine incredulity enabled her to dismiss Miss Stepney with a disdain which boded ill for that lady’s prospect of succeeding to the black brocade; but minds impenetrable to reason have generally some crack through which suspicion filters, and her visitor’s insinuations did not glide off as easily as she had expected. Mrs. Peniston disliked scenes, and her determination to avoid them had always led her to hold herself aloof from the details of Lily’s life. In her youth, girls had not been supposed to require close supervision.

The door had no sooner closed upon Mrs. Rensselaer Tallant than Mrs. Gerard Lyle, who had accompanied her visitor to the threshold of the drawing-room with every outward sign of composure, turned back into the room and sat down abruptly on the nearest chair, as though the last half-hour had been a long ascent and she had only now reached a landing where she might take breath.

The room still bore the marks of the encounter. The tea-cups stood about in the attitudes in which they had been abandoned; the seed-cake, which Mrs. Tallant had declined with a slight movement of her gloved fingers, as if it were a proposal of doubtful propriety, lay untouched on its plate; and the sofa-cushion against which that lady had leaned showed a dent so precise that it seemed to Mrs. Lyle less the impression of a human form than the seal set upon a document. She looked at these objects with the fixed attention which the mind, unwilling to confront a large disaster, will bestow upon its smallest accessories; and it was some moments before she allowed herself to consider what had actually occurred.

Mrs. Tallant was one of those women whose importance is the more absolute for resting on no visible foundation. She was not rich, as riches were beginning to be reckoned in New York; she had never been handsome, and her conversation, which consisted chiefly of the names of persons she had known and the dates at which they had died, could not have been called brilliant even by those who most depended on her favour. But she had sat for forty years at the right end of the right tables, and had thereby acquired that mysterious authority which, in a society without a court, devolves upon whoever is most persistently present at its ceremonies. Her opinion was not so much sought as anticipated; people arranged their lives in the expectation of it, as farmers arrange their sowing by a calendar they have never troubled to verify. And among the institutions over which she presided with this unquestioned dominion was the Friday dancing-class held in the long front room of her house in Washington Square, to which, for three generations, the children of a certain New York had been conducted, in white kid slippers and sashes of a regulation width, to learn the polka and the art of not being surprised.

It was to secure for her daughter a place in this class that Mrs. Lyle had invited Mrs. Tallant to tea. The undertaking had required delicacy. Mrs. Lyle had been a Miss Ashbridge of Philadelphia, and though the Ashbridges were irreproachable on their own side of the Delaware, their excellence had a provincial flavour which did not wholly survive the journey; while Gerard Lyle, whose mother had been a Schermerhorn cousin, possessed precisely the claims that his wife lacked, and precisely the indifference to their exercise which would have made them useful. It had therefore fallen to Mrs. Lyle to manage the matter alone; and she had managed it, she believed, with a nice adjustment of deference and reserve, letting it appear that the request was a mere form, while conveying at the same time that its refusal would be felt as an injury. Mrs. Tallant had received these advances with the impassive benevolence of an idol accepting rice; and the business had been all but concluded when Mrs. Lyle, in an access of confidence which she now recognised as the fatal weakness of the successful negotiator, had rung for the nurse to bring Dora down.

Dora had come down very prettily. She had made her curtsey, and given her hand, and answered with propriety the questions which Mrs. Tallant, who had a fixed series of them for children, as she had for invalids and the recently bereaved, addressed to her in turn. She had said that she was eight; that she liked her French lessons; that her doll was called Augusta. And then Mrs. Tallant, bending upon her that faded and impartial gaze which had surveyed so many small faces in its time, had asked whether she would like to come and dance on Fridays with the other little girls; and Dora, with the grave candour of one supplying a piece of information she supposed to be generally useful, had replied:

"Mamma says it is dreadfully dull at your house, but that nobody counts who doesn't go."

There had followed a pause which Mrs. Lyle was persuaded she would hear, at intervals, for the remainder of her life. It was not long, as pauses are measured by clocks; but it had in it the whole length of a social career. Then Mrs. Tallant had set down her cup, with the deliberation of a judge laying aside his pen, and had said, in a voice of unaltered mildness: "Your mamma is quite right, my dear. It is very pleasant to know that one is counted." And she had stayed precisely seven minutes longer, and talked of the weather and the death of old Mr. Beekman, and gone away without once again alluding to the dancing-class.

Mrs. Lyle sat on in the darkening room and went over the scene as one turns over a letter that has brought bad news, in the irrational hope of finding in it some sentence that was overlooked. She was not, she told herself, a woman to exaggerate the importance of such things. She had always been able to smile at the solemnities of New York; it was, indeed, her private distinction to smile at them, and the faculty had been a solace to her in many a long evening spent among people who did not. But she had never supposed that her smiles would be repeated; and there is a great difference between holding an opinion and seeing it walk abroad in a white frock with a blue sash.

The worst of it, as she was obliged at last to acknowledge, was that the phrase had been her own. She remembered the occasion perfectly. It had been at breakfast, three days before, when Gerard, behind his newspaper, had asked with his habitual languor whether it was really necessary to "go through all that business with the Tallant woman"; and she had answered, with a little flourish which she had rather admired at the time, that it was dreadfully dull at Mrs. Tallant's, but that nobody counted who didn't go. Gerard had laughed, and she had been pleased with his laughing; and neither of them had observed that Dora, who was allowed down to breakfast on Sundays as a mark of advancing years, had been sitting all the while at the end of the table, cutting her toast into very small squares and listening with the inexhaustible attention of a child to whom nothing has yet been explained.

There is no witness so dangerous as one who does not know the value of what she has seen. Mrs. Lyle perceived this with a sharpness that made her rise and walk to the window, where the lamplighter was going his rounds in the street below, and where the brown-stone fronts opposite, each with its identical stoop and its identical curtained windows, seemed to look back at her with a uniform and silent disapproval. It occurred to her that every one of those houses contained a drawing-room in which, by to-morrow evening, Dora's remark would have been repeated; and that in none of them would it be attributed to Dora.

She turned from the window and rang the bell.

"Ask Bates to bring Miss Dora down again," she said to the parlour-maid; and while she waited she lit the lamp on the centre table herself, with hands that were not quite steady, because it seemed to her that the conversation which lay before her could not be conducted in the dark.

Dora came in alone. Bates, with the discretion of her kind, had delivered her at the door and withdrawn, and the child advanced across the carpet with a step whose slowness betrayed that she, too, had been considering the afternoon. She was a slight, fair little girl, with straight hair tied back from a forehead too wide for prettiness, and a pair of grey eyes which had not yet learned to wait upon the expression of the rest of her face. She stopped on the hearth-rug, at the precise distance from her mother which long custom had established as suitable to interviews of a serious nature, and folded her hands before her.

Mrs. Lyle had seated herself again, and for a moment she looked at her daughter without speaking. She had intended to begin with severity; but the sight of the small figure on the hearth-rug, so composed in its anticipation of judgment, disconcerted her, as the calm of a prisoner sometimes disconcerts the court.

"Dora," she said at length, "do you know why I have sent for you?"

"Yes, Mamma. Because of what I said to the old lady."

"To Mrs. Tallant. You will not speak of her as 'the old lady.'"

"No, Mamma." Dora considered. "Because of what I said to Mrs. Tallant."

"You were very rude to her. You were very rude, and you have made me exceedingly unhappy."

Dora received this in silence. Her eyes, which had been fixed on her mother's face, travelled slowly to the dent in the sofa-cushion, as though she too found there some record of the transaction; then they returned.

"I didn't mean to be rude," she said. "I only said what you said."

It was the reply Mrs. Lyle had foreseen; but there is a difference between foreseeing a blow and receiving it, and she felt the colour rise to her face.

"That," she said, "is exactly the point. You repeated something you had heard. Little girls who repeat what they hear are very troublesome and very ill-bred, and nobody likes to have them about."

"But it was true, wasn't it?" Dora persisted, not defiantly, but with the air of one anxious to get a difficult matter straight. "You said it was dull there. You told Papa."

"What I told Papa is no concern of yours."

"But was it true?"

Mrs. Lyle hesitated. She had always prided herself on never deceiving her child. It was one of the principles on which she had resolved, in the first exalted months of motherhood, to differ from the mothers of her acquaintance, who reared their daughters on a diet of agreeable fictions and then wondered at their indigestion when they came to taste the world. She had determined that Dora should be told the truth; and she now perceived, with a kind of dismay, that she had never considered how much of the truth a child might be expected to keep to herself.

"It was—it was a manner of speaking," she said. "When grown-up people talk among themselves, they say things which are not meant to be taken quite literally."

"Then it wasn't true?"

"I did not say that."

Dora looked down at her slippers, and up again.

"Then is it wicked to say things that are true?"

The question was put with perfect simplicity, and it seemed to Mrs. Lyle that the whole edifice of her moral instruction rocked upon its base. She had taught Dora that it was wicked to tell lies; she had taught her that it was vulgar to boast, unkind to tease, and unladylike to raise her voice; but she had never thought it necessary to teach her the most important article of the creed by which she herself lived, and which was to be learned in no catechism—that the truth is a currency which loses its value in circulation, and that the well-bred keep it, like their jewels, in a safe place, and wear it only on occasions when it is certain to be admired.

"It is not wicked," she said slowly, "to say what is true. But it is sometimes very unkind; and it is always unkind to say things which may hurt people's feelings, whether they are true or not."

"Did I hurt Mrs. Tallant's feelings?"

Mrs. Lyle recalled the impassive face, the deliberate setting-down of the cup, and the seven minutes of conversation about old Mr. Beekman's funeral.

"I am afraid you did," she said, though she was not at all sure that Mrs. Tallant possessed any feelings in the sense in which the word was used in the nursery. What Mrs. Tallant possessed, she reflected, was a memory; and that was a great deal more to be feared.

"Then were your feelings hurt too, Mamma?"

"Mine?"

"You said I had made you very unhappy."

Mrs. Lyle found herself unable for a moment to reply. It was impossible to explain to a child of eight that her unhappiness had nothing whatever to do with feeling, and everything to do with Friday afternoons in Washington Square; that she was grieved, not because Dora had wounded an old woman, but because the old woman was in a position to wound them both; and that the offence lay not in the sentiment itself, which half the mothers in New York shared with her, but in the indiscretion which had made it audible. She was aware, as she sat there in the lamplight, that she was being called upon to justify a system of conduct which she had never examined, because no one had ever before been so tactless as to ask her to; and she resented the necessity, as a traveller resents being asked at the frontier to declare what he has been carrying for years without remark.

"You have made me unhappy," she said, taking refuge in the authority which is the last resource of argument, "because you have behaved badly, and because I had hoped my little girl knew better. When people come to this house they are our guests, and it is our duty to make them comfortable. A lady never says anything to a guest which might make her uncomfortable. That is the first rule of good manners, and you must learn it."

"Even if she is dull?"

"Especially if she is dull," said Mrs. Lyle, and was startled to hear in her own voice an accent so like Gerard's at his most ironical that she glanced involuntarily toward the door, as though he might have come in unobserved.

But the room was empty save for themselves; and Dora, who had no ear for irony, accepted the statement with the same grave docility with which she received the facts of geography.

"I'm sorry, Mamma," she said. "I won't do it again."

"I hope not. But being sorry is not enough. When we have been rude to people we must tell them so. You will write a little letter to Mrs. Tallant this evening, and say that you beg her pardon."

Dora's face clouded for the first time.

"Must I say I'm sorry I said it, or sorry it was true?"

"You will say," said Mrs. Lyle, with great firmness, "that you are sorry you were rude. Sit down at my desk and I will tell you what to write."

The child obeyed. Mrs. Lyle's writing-desk, a slender rosewood affair inherited from a Philadelphia grandmother, stood between the windows, and Dora, perched on the edge of the chair with her feet not quite reaching the floor, drew toward her a sheet of the thick cream-laid paper with the small engraved address and dipped her pen with the anxious care of a person handling a dangerous instrument. Mrs. Lyle stood behind her and dictated; and the composition, which went through three drafts, ran finally as follows:

"Dear Mrs. Tallant, I am very sorry I was rude to you this afternoon. I did not mean to say anything unkind. I hope you will forgive me. Your affectionate little friend, Theodora Ashbridge Lyle."

Mrs. Lyle had hesitated over "affectionate," which seemed to her to claim more than the situation warranted, and over "little friend," which seemed to claim too little; but she let both stand, reflecting that the phrase, if it did nothing else, would remind Mrs. Tallant of the age of the offender, and that there is no plea in mitigation so effective as an infant's handwriting. The letters, indeed, sloped and wavered across the page with a pathos which would have softened any heart less seasoned than the one for which they were intended; and the word "forgive" had been spelt with a final "e" scratched out and restored, as though the writer had been uncertain whether the virtue it denoted required one.

When the envelope had been addressed and laid on the hall table for the morning post, Dora came back and stood again on the hearth-rug, as if awaiting the sentence that should complete the proceedings.

"You will have your supper in the nursery to-night," said her mother, "and you will not go to Aunt Lyle's on Saturday."

Dora bowed her head to this decree without protest. Then, as she turned to go, she paused and asked, with an inflection of genuine inquiry:

"Shall I still go to the dancing-class, Mamma?"

"I don't know," said Mrs. Lyle. "I should think it very unlikely."

The child stood a moment longer, her hand on the knob of the door. Then she said, in a tone so carefully neutral that her mother looked at her more closely:

"I didn't want to go, you know. Edith Beekman says you have to dance with the boys, and they pull your sash."

She went out, and Mrs. Lyle heard her small feet mounting the stairs, slowly at first, and then, as they reached the turn of the landing, with a lightness which might have been only the natural buoyancy of eight years, but which struck upon her mother's ear with a sudden and disquieting significance.

In the town of Pickerel, Ohio, which lies along the Wheeling and Lake Erie railroad not far from where the land begins to fall away toward the lake, there lived a man named Joe Hardesty and his wife Ellen. They lived in a frame house on Pearl Street, at the end where the sidewalk stopped and the road went on, dusty in summer and deep with mud in the spring, out past the cemetery and into the country. Joe Hardesty worked in the plow works by the tracks. He had worked there eleven years. He was a heavy man with a red neck and his hands were large and the backs of them were covered with fine yellow hairs that caught the light when he sat under the lamp in the evening, reading the Cleveland paper and turning the pages slowly as though the paper were a thing that might break.

Ellen Hardesty had been a schoolteacher before she married. She had taught for two years in a little brick schoolhouse out on the Turner Pike, and the children who had been in her school remembered her as a tall, thin woman with brown hair who sometimes stood for a long time by the window looking out at the fields and did not hear when they spoke to her. Then she would turn suddenly and her face would be red and she would be very kind to them for the rest of the day, as though she had done them some wrong.

It is a strange thing about people that live together for a long time in one house. They come to know each other's ways, the way a man clears his throat before he speaks, the sound of a woman's feet on the stairs, and they think they know everything there is to know. Then something happens, some little thing, and it is as though a door had opened in a wall where no door had been, and there is a dark room beyond and in the room something moving about.

This is the story of an evening in the fall of the year when Joe Hardesty came home from the plow works and found his wife sitting in the kitchen in the dark.

---

It was late in October. All day the wind had been blowing from the west and the leaves of the maple trees along Pearl Street had come down and lay in the gutters and against the fences, and when the wind blew they moved along the ground with a dry, whispering sound. Joe walked home from the works with his dinner pail in his hand. He walked as he always walked, with his head a little down and his shoulders hunched, and when he passed the house of Will Sommers, the drayman, Will called to him from the porch, and Joe lifted the hand that did not have the dinner pail in it but did not stop.

When he came into his own yard he saw that there was no light in the kitchen window. He stood for a moment by the gate. The thing was unusual. For eleven years there had been a light in the kitchen window when he came home, and the smell of supper cooking, and his wife's figure moving back and forth past the window. He thought she might be ill. Then he thought she might have gone to her sister's on Duane Street, and he felt a little anger rise in him because she had not told him. He went around to the back of the house and opened the kitchen door.

She was sitting at the table. In the gray light that came in at the window he could see her shape there, very straight in the chair, with her hands lying on the oilcloth before her. She did not move when he came in.

"Ellen," he said. "What's the matter? Are you sick?"

"No," she said. "I'm not sick."

He set the dinner pail down on the shelf by the door. He did not know what to do with his hands then, and he stood rubbing them together. The stove was cold. He could feel that it was cold. There was no fire in it at all.

"I'll light the lamp," he said.

"Don't," she said. "Not yet. Sit down a minute, Joe."

He sat down across the table from her. He was a man who did not like things to be out of their places and he felt uneasy. He thought of the supper that was not cooked and was ashamed that he should think of it. He looked at his wife's face, but in the dark it was only a pale shape, like a plate that has been set on a shelf in a dim room.

"I went down to the station today," she said.

"To the station? What for?"

"I don't know what for. I just went. I put on my hat and my good coat and I went down there and sat on the bench and waited for the two-forty to come in from Toledo. Then I watched it go out again."

Joe Hardesty said nothing. He put one of his big hands on the table and moved it slowly over the oilcloth as though he were smoothing out a wrinkle that was not there.

"Was there somebody on it you knew?" he asked.

"No. There wasn't anybody on it I knew. That's what I mean. There wasn't anybody."

---

It should be said here that Ellen Hardesty was the daughter of a man named Abner Pruett, who had kept a harness shop on Main Street in Pickerel for thirty years and who had died when Ellen was nineteen. He had been a small, silent man who wore a leather apron and smelled always of neat's-foot oil, and on Sunday afternoons he used to walk out alone along the railroad tracks for miles, stepping from tie to tie, and come back after dark with his shoes covered with cinders. No one ever knew where he went or why. Once, when Ellen was a child, he had taken her with him, and they had walked until the town was out of sight behind them and there was nothing but the shining rails going on and on between the cornfields. Her father had stopped then and stood looking along the tracks to where they came together at the edge of the sky. "There," he had said. "Do you see it?" She had looked and looked but she had seen nothing, only the rails and the fields and a crow flying. She had been afraid to tell him she saw nothing. "Yes," she had said, and he had taken her hand and they had walked back.

She had not thought of that day for years. But on this day, sitting on the bench at the station in her good coat, she had thought of it, and it had seemed to her that her whole life had been like that, like standing on the tracks beside her father and saying yes, yes, she saw it, when she saw nothing at all.

---

"I don't understand you, Ellen," Joe said. "What are you trying to say?"

"I'm not trying to say anything. I'm just telling you."

"You're telling me you went down to the station and watched a train."

"Yes."

"Well, what of it? A person can go down to the station. There's nothing wrong in that."

She laughed then, a short, sharp laugh, and the sound of it in the cold kitchen startled him so that he drew his hand back from the table. "No," she said. "There's nothing wrong in it. There's nothing wrong in anything. That's the trouble, Joe. You don't see. There's nothing wrong in anything and there's nothing right either. There's just the days."

He was silent. Outside the wind had risen again and a branch of the apple tree by the woodshed scraped against the side of the house. It made a sound like someone trying to get in. Joe Hardesty thought of the plow works, of the long shed where he worked, with the dust floating in the shafts of light that came down through the high windows and the noise of the machines that went on all day, so that a man could not hear himself think and did not want to. He thought that a man who worked all day had a right to come home and find a fire in the stove. Then he thought that it was not right of him to think that, not now. He did not know what was right to think.

"You've been sitting here all afternoon," he said. "In the cold."

"I came home and sat down and I didn't get up. I meant to. I kept saying to myself, now get up, Ellen, get up and make the fire, it's getting late, Joe will be coming. And I didn't get up."

"Why didn't you?"

"I don't know."

"You must know."

"I don't know, Joe. Can't you understand a person not knowing?"

He could not. That was the truth of it, and she could see that it was the truth of it, even in the dark. He was a man who had always known why he did a thing. He went to work because it was time to go to work. He came home because it was time to come home. He had married her because he had wanted her and she had been there, walking along Main Street on a Saturday evening in a white dress with a blue sash, and he had walked beside her and talked to her about the weather and the price of hogs and the new waterworks the town was building, and after a time she had let him take her arm. It had all been simple. Everything had been simple.

---

They sat for a long time. It grew darker in the kitchen until he could not see her at all, could only hear her breathing across the table. Once she moved her hand and it struck against the sugar bowl and the lid of the bowl rattled. Joe started at the sound.

"Joe," she said, "do you remember when we used to go walking out on the Turner Pike? Before we were married?"

"I remember."

"There was a place where the road went over a little bridge, by the Collier farm, and we used to stand on the bridge and look down at the creek. Do you remember that?"

"Yes."

"One night you asked me what I was thinking about. We were standing on the bridge and it was summer and there were frogs in the creek and you asked me what I was thinking about and I said nothing. Do you remember?"

"I don't remember that," he said.

"I wasn't thinking about nothing. I was thinking about something. I was thinking that if I could only say it to you, what I was thinking, then everything would be all right forever. And I couldn't say it. I tried and it wouldn't come. It was like my mouth was full of cotton. So I said nothing. And you said, well, I was thinking about you, and you kissed me, and I let you. And then it was too late."

"Too late for what?"

"For saying it."

He leaned forward in his chair. His big hands were clenched together on the table now and his knuckles hurt. "Well, say it now, then," he said, and his voice was louder than he had meant it to be. "Go on and say it. Whatever it is. I'm here. I'm sitting right here."

She did not answer. He could hear her breathing, quick and shallow, as though she had been running.

"I can't," she said at last. "It's gone. It's been gone a long time. I don't even know what it was anymore. That's what I found out today, sitting down there at the station. I found out I don't even know what it was."

---

There is a kind of loneliness that comes to people in small towns in the Middle West that is not like any other kind. It is not the loneliness of a man lost in a great city among strangers, nor of a man alone on a mountain or at sea. It is the loneliness of people who are known to everyone and to whom everyone is known, who have walked the same streets all their lives and said good morning to the same faces, and who wake suddenly in the night and lie in their beds and listen to the clock ticking in the hall and think, Who am I? What am I doing here? And there is no one to tell them. The wind goes through the bare trees and a dog barks somewhere far off and a train whistles out beyond the edge of town, going away, going toward Cleveland or Chicago or some place they have never seen, and that is all.

Ellen Hardesty had felt this loneliness for a long time without knowing what it was. She had felt it when she stood by the window of the little schoolhouse on the Turner Pike. She had felt it on her wedding night, lying awake beside Joe while he slept, listening to his heavy breathing and looking at the square of moonlight on the floor. She had felt it in the mornings, packing his dinner pail, putting in the bread and the cold meat and the piece of pie wrapped in a napkin, the same things every day, and snapping the lid shut. And on this day it had come up in her all at once, like water rising in a well, and she had put on her hat and her good coat and gone down to the station.

---

"Are you going to go away?" Joe asked.

He said it very quietly. She heard the fear in his voice and something in her went out to him, and she wanted to reach across the table and touch his hand. But she did not do it.

"No," she said. "Where would I go?"

"I don't know. Chicago. Your cousin is in Chicago."

"I'm not going to Chicago."

"Then what is it? What do you want, Ellen? You tell me what you want and I'll get it for you. If it's money, I've got some put by. More than you know. I've been saving. I was going to buy the lot next to the Weatherbys', to build on. We could build a better house. With a parlor, a real parlor. You could have a piano."

"I don't want a piano."

"Then what do you want?"

She stood up suddenly. He heard the chair scrape on the floor. She went to the window and stood there, and now he could see her again, a little, a dark shape against the lesser darkness of the window. Beyond her the yard was full of moving shadows where the wind shook the apple tree.

"I wanted you to come in," she said, "and see me sitting here in the dark, and not ask me if I was sick. I wanted you to come in and know. Without my saying anything. That's all. It's foolish. I know it's foolish."

Joe Hardesty sat at the table. He looked at the dark shape of his wife at the window and he felt something he had never felt before. It was as though there were a great weight on his chest. He thought that he ought to get up and go to her. He thought that if he went to her and put his arms around her, it might be all right. But his legs would not move. He sat there with his hands clenched on the oilcloth and he could not move.

"I'm not a smart man, Ellen," he said. "You knew that when you married me. I don't know about things like that. I work. I come home. I don't know what you want me to know."

"I know," she said. "It isn't your fault."

"Then whose fault is it?"

"Nobody's. It isn't anybody's fault. Don't you see, Joe? That's the worst of it. If it was somebody's fault, we could do something."

---

After a while he got up and lit the lamp. His hands shook as he struck the match, and the first match went out and he had to strike another. When the wick caught and the yellow light filled the kitchen they both looked at each other, blinking, like people who have come up out of a cellar. Her face was very white and there were marks under her eyes and she looked older than he had ever seen her look. He saw for the first time that there was gray in her hair, above the ears. He did not know when it had come there.

She looked at him too. She looked at his red neck and his heavy shoulders and his big hands with the yellow hairs on the backs of them, and at his face, which was frightened and puzzled, like the face of a boy who has been punished and does not know why. She thought, He is a good man. She thought it clearly, as though someone had spoken the words aloud in the kitchen. He is a good man, and I have lived with him eleven years, and I do not know him and he does not know me, and that is the way it is going to be.

"I'll make the fire," she said.

"No. Let me do it."

He went out to the woodshed. The wind caught at his coat as he crossed the yard and the branch of the apple tree whipped against the shed wall. He stood in the dark shed for a long time with his hands on the pile of split wood and did not gather any of it up. He thought of his own father, who had farmed a hundred and sixty acres south of town and who had never in his life said more than a dozen words at a time to Joe's mother, and of his mother, who had lived to be seventy and died in the front bedroom with her face to the wall. He had thought they were happy. It had never come into his mind to think anything else. Now he wondered. He stood in the woodshed and wondered about his father and his mother and about all the people in Pickerel, in all the houses along all the streets, sitting in their kitchens in the evening with the lamps lit. He wondered if they were all like this. He wondered if every one of them was sitting across a table from someone and could not say what they wanted to say.

It was a terrible thought and he did not want to have it. He gathered up an armload of wood and went back across the yard to the house.

---

When he came into the kitchen Ellen was standing by the stove. She had taken off her good coat at last and hung it on the hook behind the door and she was standing with her hands folded in front of her, waiting. He knelt down and opened the firebox and began laying in the kindling. He did it slowly and carefully, the way he did everything, and she stood above him and watched his big hands moving among the sticks of wood.

"Joe," she said.

"What?"

She did not say anything more. He looked up at her and waited, and she looked down at him, and for a moment it seemed to both of them that something was going to be said, something that would change everything. The lamp hissed on the table. The wind blew outside. Far off, out beyond the edge of town, a freight train was whistling for the crossing at Turner Pike, a long sound and then two short ones, going away.

"Nothing," she said. "I was just going to say the wood's damp. It won't draw well."

"It'll draw," he said. "Give it time."

He struck a match and held it to the paper under the kindling, and the flame caught and ran along the edge of the paper and climbed up into the sticks. They both watched it. When the fire was going he closed the firebox door and stood up, and his knees cracked, and he brushed the bits of bark from his trousers.

Ellen got the skillet down from its nail. She went to the pantry and came back with the potatoes and a knife and sat down at the table to peel them. Joe sat down across from her and picked up the Cleveland paper, which he had dropped on the chair when he came in, and opened it, and held it up before him. But he did not read it. He sat holding the paper and looking at it and over the top of it he could see the top of his wife's head, bent over the potatoes, and the gray in her hair above the ears, and her thin hands moving with the knife.

Neither of them spoke again. After a time the kitchen grew warm and the smell of frying potatoes filled the room, and the window grew black and gave back the image of the lamp and the table and the two people sitting there. Anyone passing along Pearl Street that night, going out toward the cemetery and the country, would have looked in and seen them and thought nothing of it. They would have seen only a man reading his paper and a woman cooking his supper in a lighted kitchen, the way it was in every house in Pickerel, the way it had always been.
