Now as he sat on the hillside he talked earnestly while he gesticulated with his hands. “I hate this town,” he said. “The men here think they are confoundedly funny. They don't care for anything but making foolish jokes and getting drunk. I want to go away.” His voice rose and hatred flamed up in him. “You wait,” he boasted. “I'll make men stop being fools. I'll make children of them. I'll——” Pausing he looked at his two companions. Beaut poked the ground with a stick. The boy sitting beside him laughed. He was a short well—dressed black—haired boy with rings on his fingers who worked in the town poolroom, racking the pool balls. “I'd like to go where there are women with blood in them,” he said. Three women came up the hill toward them, a tall pale brown-haired woman of twenty-seven and two fairer young girls. The black-haired boy straightened his tie and began thinking of a conversation he would start when the women reached him. Beaut and the other boy, a fat fellow, the son of a grocer, looked down the hill to the town over the heads of the newcomers and continued in their minds the thoughts that had made the conversation.

“Hello girls, come and sit here,” shouted the black-haired boy, laughing and looking boldly into the eyes of the tall pale woman. They stopped and the tall woman began stepping over the fallen logs, coming to them. The two young girls followed, laughing. They sat down on the log beside the boys, the tall pale woman at the end beside red-haired McGregor. An embarrassed silence fell over the party. Both Beaut and the fat boy were disconcerted by this turn to their afternoon's outing and wondered how it would turn out. The pale woman began to talk in a low tone. “I want to get away from here,” she said, “I wish I could hear birds sing and see green things grow.” Beaut McGregor had an idea. “You come with me,” he said. He got up and climbed over the logs and the pale woman followed. The fat boy shouted at them, relieving his own embarrassment by trying to embarrass them. “Where're you going—you two?” he shouted. Beaut said nothing. He stepped over the logs to the road and began climbing the hill. The tall woman walked beside him and held her skirts out of the deep dust of the road. Even on this her Sunday gown there was a faint black mark along the seams—the mark of Coal Creek. As McGregor walked his embarrassment left him. He thought it fine that he should be thus alone with a woman. When she had tired from the climb he sat with her on a log beside the road and talked of the black-haired boy. “He has your ring on his finger,” he said, looking at her and laughing. She held her hand pressed tightly against her side and closed her eyes. “The climbing hurts me,” she said. Tenderness took hold of Beaut. When they went on again he walked behind her, his hand upon her back pushing her up the hill. The desire to tease her about the black-haired boy had passed and he wished he had said nothing about the ring. He remembered the story the black-haired boy had told him of his conquest of the woman. “More than likely a mess of lies,” he thought. Over the crest of the hill they stopped and rested, leaning against a worn rail fence by the woods. Below them in a wagon a party of men went down the hill. The men sat upon boards laid across the box of a wagon and sang a song. One of them stood in the seat beside the driver and waved a bottle. He seemed to be making a speech. The others shouted and clapped their hands. The sounds came faint and sharp up the hill. In the woods beside the fence rank grass grew. Hawks floated in the sky over the valley below. A squirrel running along the fence stopped and chattered at them. McGregor thought he had never had so delightful a companion. He got a feeling of complete, good fellowship and friendliness with this woman. Without knowing how the thing had been done he felt a certain pride in it. “Don't mind what I said about the ring,” he urged, “I was only trying to tease you.” The woman beside McGregor was the daughter of an undertaker who lived upstairs over his shop near the bakery. He had seen her in the evening standing in the stairway by the shop door. After the story told him by the black-haired boy he had been embarrassed about her. When he passed her standing in the stairway he went hurriedly along and looked into the gutter. They went down the hill and sat on the log upon the hillside. A clump of elders had grown about the log since his visits there with Cracked McGregor so that the place was closed and shaded like a room. The woman took off her hat and laid it beside her on the log. A faint colour mounted to her pale cheeks and a flash of anger gleamed in her eyes. “He probably lied to you about me,” she said, “I didn't give him that ring to wear. I don't know why I gave it to him. He wanted it. He asked me for it time and again. He said he wanted to show it to his mother. And now he has shown it to you and I suppose told lies about me.” Beaut was annoyed and wished he had not mentioned the ring. He felt that an unnecessary fuss was being made about it. He did not believe that the black-haired boy had lied but he did not think it mattered. He began talking of his father, boasting of him. His hatred of the town blazed up. “They thought they knew him down there,” he said, “they laughed at him and called him 'Cracked.' They thought his running into the mine just a crazy notion like a horse that runs into a burning stable. He was the best man in town. He was braver than any of them. He went in there and died when he had almost enough money saved to buy a farm over here.” He pointed down the valley. Beaut began to tell her of the visits to the hillside with his father and described the effect of the scene on himself when he was a child. “I thought it was paradise,” he said. She put her hand on his arm and seemed to be soothing him like a careful groom quieting an excitable horse. “Don't mind them,” she said, “you will go away after a time and make a place for yourself out in the world.” He wondered how she knew. A profound respect for her came over him. “She is keen to guess that,” he thought. He began to talk of himself, boasting and throwing out his chest. “I'd like to have the chance to show what I can do,” he declared. A thought that had been in his mind on the winter day when Uncle Charlie Wheeler put the name of Beaut upon him came back and he walked up and down before the woman making grotesque motions with his hands as Cracked McGregor had walked up and down before him.

“I'll tell you what,” he began and his voice was harsh. He had forgotten the presence of the woman and half forgotten what had been in his mind. He sputtered and glared over his shoulder up the hillside as he struggled for words. “Oh to Hell with men!” he burst forth. “They are cattle, stupid cattle.” A fire blazed up in his eyes and a confident ring came into his voice. “I'd like to get them together, all of them,” he said, “I'd like to make them——” Words failed him and again he sat down on the log beside the woman. “Well I'd like to lead them to an old mine shaft and push them in,” he concluded resentfully.

On the eminence Beaut and the tall woman sat and looked down into the valley. “I wonder why we don't go there, mother and I,” he said. “When I see it I'm filled with the notion. I think I want to be a farmer and work in the fields. Instead of that mother and I sit and plan of the city. I'm going to be a lawyer. That's all we talk about. Then I come up here and it seems as though this is the place for me.” The tall woman laughed. “I can see you coming home at night from the fields,” she said. “It might be to that white house there with the windmill, You would be a big man and would have dust in your red hair and perhaps a red beard growing on your chin. And a woman with a baby in her arms would come out of the kitchen door to stand leaning on the fence waiting for you. When you came up she would put her arm around your neck and kiss you on the lips. The beard would tickle her cheek. You should have a beard when you grow older. Your mouth is so big.” A strange new feeling shot through Beaut. He wondered why she had said that and wanted to take hold of her hand and kiss her then and there. He got up and looked at the sun going down behind the hill far away at the other end of the valley. “We'd better be getting along back,” he said. The woman remained seated on the log. “Sit down,” she said, “I'll tell you something—something it's good for you to hear. You're so big and red you tempt a girl to bother you. First though you tell me why you go along the street looking into the gutter when I stand in the stairway in the evening.” Beaut sat down again upon the log, and thought of what the black-haired boy had told him of her. “Then it was true—what he said about you?” he asked.

“No! No!” she cried, jumping up in her turn and beginning to pin on her hat. “Let's be going.” Beaut sat stolidly on the log. “What's the use bothering each other,” he said. “Let's sit here until the sun goes down. We can get home before dark.” They sat down and she began talking, boasting of herself as he had boasted of his father.

“I'm too old for that boy,” she said; “I'm older than you by a good many years. I know what boys talk about and what they say about women. I do pretty well. I don't have any one to talk to except father and he sits all evening reading a paper and going to sleep in his chair. If I let boys come and sit with me in the evening or stand talking with me in the stairway it is because I'm lonesome. There isn't a man in town I'd marry—not one.” The speech sounded discordant and harsh to Beaut. He wished his father were there rubbing his hands together and muttering rather than this pale woman who stirred him up and then talked harshly like the women at the back doors in Coal Creek. He thought again as he had thought before that he preferred the black-faced miners drunk and silent to their pale talking wives. On an impulse he told her that, saying it crudely so that it hurt. Their companionship was spoiled. They got up and began to climb the hill, going toward home. Again she put her hand to her side and again he wished to put his hand at her back and push her up the hill. Instead he walked beside her in silence, again hating the town. Halfway down the hill the tall woman stopped by the road-side. Darkness was coming on and the glow of the coke ovens lighted the sky. “One living up here and never going down there might think it rather grand and big,” he said. Again the hatred came. “They might think the men who live down there knew something instead of being just a lot of cattle.” A smile came into the face of the tall woman and a gentler look stole into her eyes. “We get at one another,” she said, “we can't let one another alone. I wish we hadn't quarrelled. We might be friends if we tried. You have got something in you. You attract women. I've heard others say that. Your father was that way. Most of the women here would rather have been the wife of Cracked McGregor ugly as he was than to have stayed with their own husbands. I heard my mother say that to father when they lay quarrelling in bed at night and I lay listening.” The boy was overcome with the thought of a woman talking to him so frankly. He looked at her and said what was in his mind. “I don't like the women,” he said, “but I liked you, seeing you standing in the stairway and thinking you had been doing as you pleased. I thought maybe you amounted to something. I don't know why you should be bothered by what I think. I don't know why any woman should be bothered by what any man thinks. I should think you would go right on doing what you want to do like mother and me about my being a lawyer.” He sat on a log beside the road near where he had met her and watched her go down the hill. “I'm quite a fellow to have talked to her all afternoon like that,” he thought and pride in his growing manhood crept over him.

Excerpt 3: All through the early months of that year in Chicago, rumours of a new and not understandable movement among labourers ran about among men of affairs. In a way the labourers understood the undercurrent of terror their marching together had inspired and like the advertising man dancing on the sidewalk before the grocery were made happy by it. Grim satisfaction dwelt in their hearts. Remembering their boyhoods and the creeping terror that invaded their fathers' houses in times of depression they were glad to spread terror among the homes of the rich and the well-to-do. For years they had been going through life blindly, striving to forget age and poverty. Now they felt that life had a purpose, that they were marching toward some end. When in the past they had been told that power dwelt in them they had not believed. “He is not to be trusted,” thought the man at the machine looking at the man at work at the next machine. “I have heard him talk and at bottom he is a fool.” Now the man at the machine did not think of his brother at the next machine. In his dreams at night he was beginning to have a new vision. Power had breathed its message into his brain. Of a sudden he saw himself as a part of a giant walking in the world. “I am like a drop of blood running through the veins of labour,” he whispered to himself. “In my own way I am adding strength to the heart and the brain of labour. I have become a part of this thing that has begun to move. I will not talk but will wait. If this marching is the thing then I will march. Though I am weary at the end of the day that shall not stop me. Many times I have been weary and was alone. Now I am a part of something vast. This I know, that a consciousness of power has crept into my brain and although I be persecuted I shall not surrender what I have gained.” In the offices of the plough trust a meeting of men of affairs was called. The purpose of the meeting was to discuss the movement going on among the workers. At the plough works it had broken out. No more at evening did the men shuffle along, like a disorderly mob but marched in companies along the brick-paved street that ran by the factory door. At the meeting David Ormsby had been as always quiet and self-possessed. A halo of kindly intent hung over him and when a banker, one of the directors of the company, had finished a speech he arose and walked up and down, his hands thrust into his trousers pockets. The banker was a fat man with thin brown hair and delicate hands. As he talked he held a pair of yellow gloves and beat with them on a long table at the centre of the room. The soft thump of the gloves upon the table made a chorus to the things he had to say. David motioned for him to be seated. “I will myself go to see this McGregor,” he said, walking across the room and putting an arm about the shoulder of the banker. “Perhaps there is as you say a new and terrible danger here but I do not think so. For thousands, no doubt for millions of years, the world has gone on its way and I do not think it is to be stopped now.

“It has been my fortune to see and to know this McGregor,” added David smiling at the others in the room. “He is a man and not a Joshua to make the sun stand still.” In the office in Van Buren Street, David, the grey and confident, stood before the desk at which sat McGregor. “We will get out of here if you do not mind,” he said. “I want to talk to you and I would not like being interrupted. I have a fancy that we talk out of doors.” The two men went in a street car to Jackson Park and, forgetting to dine, walked for an hour along the paths under the trees. The wind from the lake had chilled the air and the park was deserted. They went to stand on a pier that ran out into the lake. On the pier David tried to begin the talk that was the object of their being together but felt that the wind and the water that beat against the piling of the pier made talk too difficult. Although he could not have told why, he was relieved by the necessity of delay. Into the park they went again and found a seat upon a bench facing a lagoon. In the presence of the silent McGregor David felt suddenly embarrassed and awkward. “By what right do I question him?” he asked himself and in his mind could find no answer. A half dozen times he started to say what he had come to say but stopped and his talk ran off into trivialities. “There are men in the world you have not taken into consideration,” he said finally, forcing himself to begin. With a laugh he went on, relieved that the silence had been broken. “You see the very inner secret of strong men has been missed by you and others.” David Ormsby looked sharply at McGregor. “I do not believe that you believe we are after money, we men of affairs. I trust you see beyond that. We have our purpose and we keep to our purpose quietly and doggedly.” Again David looked at the silent figure sitting in the dim light and again his mind ran out, striving to penetrate the silence. “I am not a fool and perhaps I know that the movement you have started among the workers is something new. There is power in it as in all great ideas. Perhaps I think there is power in you. Why else should I be here?” Again David laughed uncertainly. “In a way I am in sympathy with you,” he said. “Although all through my life I have served money I have not been owned by it. You are not to suppose that men like me have not something beyond money in mind.” The old plough maker looked away over McGregor's shoulder to where the leaves of the trees shook in the wind from the lake. “There have been men and great leaders who have understood the silent competent servants of wealth,” he said half petulantly. “I want you to understand these men. I should like to see you become such a one yourself—not for the wealth it would bring but because in the end you would thus serve all men. You would get at truth thus. The power that is in you would be conserved and used more intelligently.”

“To be sure, history has taken little or no account of the men of whom I speak. They have passed through life unnoticed, doing great work quietly.” The plough maker paused. Although McGregor had said nothing the older man felt that the interview was not going as it should. “I should like to know what you have in mind, what in the end you hope to gain for yourself or for these men,” he said somewhat sharply. “There is after all no point to our beating about the bush.” McGregor said nothing. Arising from the bench he began again to walk along the path with Ormsby at his side.

“The really strong men of the world have had no place in history,” declared Ormsby bitterly. “They have not asked that. They were in Rome and in Germany in the time of Martin Luther but nothing is said of them. Although they do not mind the silence of history they would like other strong men to understand. The march of the world is a greater thing than the dust raised by the heels of some few workers walking through the streets and these men are responsible for the march of the world. You are making a mistake. I invite you to become one of us. If you plan to upset things you may get yourself into history but you will not really count. What you are trying to do will not work. You will come to a bad end.” When the two men emerged from the park the older man had again the feeling that the interview had not been a success. He was sorry. The evening he felt had marked for him a failure and he was not accustomed to failures. “There is a wall here that I cannot penetrate,” he thought. Along the front of the park beneath a grove of trees they walked in silence. McGregor seemed not to have heard the words addressed to him. When they came to where a long row of vacant lots faced the park he stopped and stood leaning against a tree to look away into the park, lost in thought. David Ormsby also became silent. He thought of his youth in the little village plough factory, of his efforts to get on in the world, of the long evenings spent reading books and trying to understand the movements of men.

“Is there an element in nature and in youth that we do not understand or that we lose sight of?” he asked. “Are the efforts of the patient workers of the world always to be abortive? Can some new phase of life arise suddenly upsetting all of our plans? Do you, can you, think of men like me as but part of a vast whole? Do you deny to us individuality, the right to stand forth, the right to work things out and to control?” The ploughmaker looked at the huge figure standing beside the tree. Again he was irritated and kept lighting cigars which after two or three puffs he threw away. In the bushes at the back of the bench insects began to sing. The wind coming now in gentle gusts swayed slowly the branches of the trees overhead.

“Is there an eternal youth in the world, a state out of which men pass unknowingly, a youth that forever destroys, tearing down what has been built?” he asked. “Are the mature lives of strong men of so little account? Have you like the empty fields that bask in the sun in the summer the right to remain silent in the presence of men who have had thoughts and have tried to put their thoughts into deeds?” Still saying nothing McGregor pointed with his finger along the road that faced the park. From a side street a body of men swung about a corner, coming with long strides toward the two. As they passed beneath a street lamp that swung gently in the wind their faces flashing in and out of the light seemed to be mocking David Ormsby. For a moment anger burned in him and then something, perhaps the rhythm of the moving mass of men, brought a gentler mood. The men swinging past turned another corner and disappeared beneath the structure of an elevated railroad. The ploughmaker walked away from McGregor. Something in the interview, terminating thus with, the presence of the marching figures had he felt unmanned him. “After all there is youth and the hope of youth. What he has in mind may work,” he thought as he climbed aboard a street car. In the car David put his head out at the window and looked at the long line of apartment buildings that lined the streets. He thought again of his own youth and of the evenings in the Wisconsin village when, himself a youth, he went with other young men singing and marching in the moonlight. In a vacant lot he again saw a body of the Marching Men moving back and forth and responding quickly to the commands given by a slender young man who stood on the sidewalk beneath a street lamp and held a stick in his hand. In the car the grey-haired man of affairs put his head down upon the back of the seat in front. Half unconscious of his own thoughts his mind began to dwell upon the figure of his daughter. “Had I been Margaret I should not have let him go. No matter what the cost I should have clung to the man,” he muttered. It is difficult not to be of two minds about the manifestation now called, and perhaps rightly, “The Madness of the Marching Men.” In one mood it comes back to the mind as something unspeakably big and inspiring. We go each of us through the treadmill of our lives caught and caged like little animals in some vast menagerie. In turn we love, marry, breed children, have our moments of blind futile passion and then something happens. All unconsciously a change creeps over us. Youth passes. We become shrewd, careful, submerged in little things. Life, art, great passions, dreams, all of these pass. Under the night sky the suburbanite stands in the moonlight. He is hoeing his radishes and worrying because the laundry has torn one of his white collars. The railroad is to put on an extra morning train. He remembers that fact heard at the store. For him the night becomes more beautiful. For ten minutes longer he can stay with the radishes each morning. There is much of man's life in the figure of the suburbanite standing absorbed in his own thoughts in the midst of his radishes. And so about the business of our lives we go and then of a sudden there comes again the feeling that crept over us all in the year of the Marching Men. In a moment we are again a part of the moving mass. The old religious exaltation, strange emanation from the man McGregor, returns. In fancy we feel the earth tremble under the feet of the men—the marchers. With a conscious straining of the mind we strive to grasp the processes of the mind of the leader during that year when men sensed his meaning, when they saw as he saw the workers—saw them massed and moving through the world. My own mind, striving feebly to follow that greater and simpler mind, gropes about. I remember sharply the words of a writer who said that men make their own gods and realise that I myself saw something of the birth of such a god. For he was near to being a god then—our McGregor. The thing he did rumbles in the minds of men yet. His long shadow will fall across men's thoughts for ages. The tantalising effort to understand his meaning will tempt us always into endless speculation. Only last week I met a man—he was a steward in a club and lingered talking to me by a cigar case in an empty billiard-room—who suddenly turned away to conceal from me two large tears that had jumped into his eyes because of a kind of tenderness in my voice at the mention of the Marching Men. Another mood comes. It may be the right mood. I see sparrows jumping about in an ordinary roadway as I walk to my office. From the maple trees the little winged seeds come fluttering down before my eyes. A boy goes past sitting in a grocery wagon and over-driving a rather bony horse. As I walk I overtake two workmen shuffling along. They remind me of those other workers and I say to myself that thus men have always shuffled, that never did they swing forward into that world-wide rhythmical march of the workers.

“You were drunk with youth and a kind of world madness,” says my normal self as I go forward again, striving to think things out. Chicago is still here—Chicago after McGregor and the Marching Men. The elevated trains still clatter over the frogs at the turning into Wabash Avenue; the surface cars clang their bells; the crowds pour up in the morning from the runway leading to the Illinois Central trains; life goes on. And men in their offices sit in their chairs and say that the thing that happened was abortive, a brain storm, a wild outbreak of the rebellious the disorderly and the hunger in the minds of men. What begging of the question. The very soul of the Marching Men was a sense of order. That was the message of it, the thing that the world has not come up to yet. Men have not learned that we must come to understand the impulse toward order, have that burned into our consciousness, before we move on to other things. There is in us this madness for individual expression. For each of us the little moment of running forward and lifting our thin childish voices in the midst of the great silence. We have not learned that out of us all, walking shoulder to shoulder, there might arise a greater voice, something to make the waters of the very seas to tremble.

On an evening in late August Abner Rowe came home from the stave mill at Turner's Junction and found his wife standing at the gate waiting for him. It was a thing she did not often do. Usually when he came along the dusty road past the Means place and the vacant lot where the circus had once pitched its tent she was in the kitchen and he saw only the smoke from the chimney going straight up into the still air. Now she stood with her hands wrapped in her apron and her face was red, and Abner, who was a slow heavy man with sawdust in the hair of his arms and in the creases of his neck, stopped in the road and looked at her and then looked away at the fields beyond the house where the corn stood high and yellow at the tips. A little he knew before she spoke that something had gone wrong. In the twelve years of their married life he had learned to read her face as a farmer reads the sky in the west, and he did not want to hear what she had to say. "It's Dick," she said. "He's been at the tin box. There's eighty cents gone out of it and he's had it, I know he's had it. I want you to see to him." She turned and went quickly up the path to the house and Abner stood alone at the gate with his dinner pail in his hand.

He went around to the back and set the pail on the bench by the pump and began to work the handle. The water came up cold out of the ground and he bent and washed his face and arms, throwing the water over the back of his neck and blowing through his nose like a horse. He was in no hurry. As he washed he thought of the tin box that sat on the shelf beside the clock in the kitchen and of the money that was in it, the egg money and the money his wife got for the butter she took to Sloan's store on Saturdays. It was not much money. Some weeks there was a dollar and some weeks less, and out of it came the thread and the needles and the calico for the boy's shirts. "Eighty cents," he said aloud and the words sounded strange in the quiet yard. A hen walked past him with her head jerking and looked at him out of one round eye. In the barn the cow lowed, wanting to be milked.

Abner Rowe was not a man who thought much about things. All day at the mill he stood before a saw and fed the oak bolts into it and the scream of the saw got into his head and stayed there so that at night when he lay in bed beside his wife he sometimes heard it still, going on and on in the darkness. He did not talk to the men at the mill. When they gathered at the noon hour on the loading platform and told stories about women and about the doings of the town he sat a little apart and ate his bread and meat and looked at the railroad tracks running away east and west, shining in the sun. The men called him Dummy Rowe and he knew it and did not care. He had been silent as a boy and he had grown up silent and now that he was nearly forty it seemed to him there was nothing left that he might want to say. And yet there were times when something stirred in him, a kind of hunger, and he did not know what it was. He would stop with an oak bolt held in his two hands and stare at the wall of the mill and the foreman would shout at him and he would come to himself and go on with his work.

Standing by the pump with the water dripping from his chin Abner thought of his own father. Of a sudden the old man came back to him very sharply, a tall bent man with a grey beard stained brown at the corners of the mouth, who had kept a farm on the Pike north of town and who had beaten his son with a leather strap that hung on a nail inside the door of the horse barn. Abner remembered the strap and the nail. He remembered how the light came through the cracks in the barn wall and lay in stripes across the floor and how the horses moved in their stalls and stamped while the beating went on. His father had never said why he beat him. He had only taken the strap down from the nail and done the thing and then hung the strap back again and gone out of the barn, and the boy had stayed there alone lying in the straw with his face hot and his back burning, hating the old man and hating the horses that had seen. "I will never do that," Abner had said to himself on such occasions. "When I have a boy I will not do it." He had forgotten the words for a long time and now they came back to him and he was ashamed, as though he had been caught at something.

The boy Dick was seven years old that summer. He was a thin boy with large ears and pale hair that stood up at the back of his head and would not lie down no matter how his mother wet it and pressed it with her hand. He did not play much with the other boys of the road. The Means boys, who lived in the unpainted house beyond the vacant lot and of whom there were four, all big and loud, had a way of standing in the road and shouting at him when he went past to the store, and once they had held him down in the ditch and filled his mouth with dust. Abner knew about that. His wife had told him. He had not done anything about it. It had seemed to him a thing between boys and not a thing a man should meddle in, and besides he did not know what he would have said to the elder Means, who drove a dray in town and was a big laughing man who drank.

When he had dried himself on the towel that hung on a nail by the door Abner went into the kitchen. His wife was at the stove. She did not turn around. "He's out in the barn," she said. "He's been out there since noon. Mrs. Sloan told me he came in the store this morning and bought candy, a whole sack of it, the striped kind, and paid in pennies and a dime. Where would he get pennies and a dime? He went and gave the candy to the Means boys. She saw him do it out of the window. He stood there in the road and gave it to them and they took it and ran off and left him standing. Now you go and see to him. I won't have a thief in the house. I won't have it." Her voice rose and broke and Abner saw that her shoulders were shaking. He wanted to go to her and put his hand on her back but he did not. He stood in the middle of the kitchen with his big hands hanging at his sides and then he turned and went out of the door and across the yard toward the barn.

It was nearly sunset and the light lay long and yellow across the yard. The shadow of the barn reached out toward him over the grass. On the way across the yard he stopped by the willow tree that grew beside the watering trough and with his pocket knife cut a switch. He did it without thinking, as though his hand had a mind of its own. The switch was long and green and when he had stripped the leaves off it he swung it once through the air and it made a thin whistling sound. He looked at it in his hand and a little wondered at himself. "It is the thing that is done," he thought. "A man has a boy and the boy does wrong and the man takes a switch to him. That is how it is done everywhere." He went on toward the barn holding the switch down along his leg so that it trailed in the grass.

Inside the barn it was dim and close and smelled of hay and of the cow. The cow turned her head and looked at him and lowed again. At first Abner did not see the boy. Then he saw him sitting in the corner beyond the cow's stall on an overturned bucket, his knees drawn up and his arms around his knees. The boy did not move. He looked at his father and then he looked at the switch and his face went white and still and his eyes grew large. Abner stood in the doorway. The light from the door fell past him into the barn and lay across the floor in a long bar and he saw the dust floating in it. Something in the scene struck at him. It was like a thing he had seen before and he stood without speaking, his throat tight.

"Come here," he said at last. His voice was harsh and he heard it with surprise. The boy got up off the bucket and came slowly across the barn floor and stood before him. He did not cry. He stood with his hands at his sides like a little man, like a soldier, and looked up into his father's face, and Abner thought he had never seen him look so small. "Your mother says you took money out of the box," Abner said. "Is that so? Did you take it?" The boy nodded his head. "Eighty cents," Abner said. "You took eighty cents." Again the boy nodded. Abner did not know what to say next. He had thought the boy would lie and that he would have to drag the truth out of him, and now that the truth had come so easily it left him with nothing to do. He shifted the switch from one hand to the other. He looked over the boy's head at the wall of the barn where the harness hung and the old scythe with the rusted blade.

"Do you know what eighty cents is?" he said, and his voice grew louder. "Do you know how long a man stands at the saw for eighty cents?" He began to walk up and down before the boy, three steps one way and three steps back, and as he walked he made motions with his hands, lifting them and letting them fall, as though he were trying to take hold of something in the air. "All morning a man stands there," he said. "All morning with the saw going and the dust in his eyes and his nose and his mouth. And your mother, she gathers the eggs, she churns the butter, she carries it to town on her arm. Every week she does that. That's what it is. That's what eighty cents is." He stopped and stood glaring at the boy, and the boy looked back at him, and Abner saw that he did not understand. How could he understand? He was seven years old. The words had gone out of Abner's mouth and into the dim air of the barn and were lost there like the dust in the bar of light. "Oh, what's the use," he muttered. He felt foolish standing there with the switch in his hand and shouting at a child about the saw at the mill. It was as though he had been shouting at the cow.

He sat down on the edge of the feed box. The boy still stood before him and Abner looked at the boy's bare feet, which were dirty and had a scratch across the top of one of them, and at the patched knees of his overalls. "Why did you do it?" he asked, more quietly now. "What did you want with it? Your mother says you gave the candy to the Means boys. Is that so? Why would you give candy to them?"

For a long time the boy did not answer. He stood looking at the floor of the barn and moving one foot back and forth in the litter of straw. Then he began to talk. He talked rapidly and in a low voice, and the words came out jumbled together so that Abner had to lean forward to hear. He said that the Means boys had a cave they had dug in the bank down by the creek and that they went there and built fires and roasted potatoes in the coals. He said they had told him he could come into the cave if he brought them something. They had said that a long time ago, in the spring. He had thought about it all summer. At night when he was in bed he thought about the cave and the fire and the potatoes roasting and the Means boys sitting around in the firelight and himself sitting with them. He had thought that if he brought them the candy they would take him there. "They said they would," he said. "They said it. Then they took the sack and ran off. Ed Means hit me on the head with his fist and they ran off down the road and I stood there." He stopped talking and his lip began to tremble, and still he did not cry, and Abner, sitting on the feed box, felt something turn over inside him.

He sat very still. It seemed to him that he had of a sudden been made to see into the boy as one sees into a well when the sun stands straight overhead, down and down into the cool dark place where the water lies. He thought of the boy lying in his bed at night in the little room at the top of the stairs and thinking of the cave and of the fire. He thought of him standing in the road with the empty sack and the Means boys running away, and a lump came into his throat. And then he thought of himself. He remembered how as a boy on the farm north of town he had wanted something, he did not know what. He remembered lying in the straw in the barn after his father had beaten him and looking up through a crack in the roof at a bit of the sky and wanting to be away, to be somewhere among people who would understand him. He had never found such a place. He had gone to the mill and stood before the saw and he had married and had this boy, and the thing he wanted had stayed in him unsatisfied all the years. "It's in him too," he thought. "I've given it to him. It's in the blood like the colour of the hair."

He looked at the switch in his hand. It was a foolish thing, a green willow stick with the leaves stripped off. He took it in his two hands and bent it until it broke, and then he broke the pieces again, and threw them into the corner where the boy had been sitting on the bucket. The boy watched him do it. His eyes followed the pieces of the switch and then came back to his father's face and there was a puzzled look in them. "You must not take money," Abner said. He wanted to say more. He wanted to tell the boy that it was no good trying to buy your way in among people, that the Means boys would never let him into the cave, that there was a cave a man was always trying to get into and never did. But the words would not come. He opened his mouth and closed it again. He put out one big hand and laid it on the boy's head and felt the hair that would not lie down stand up stiffly against his palm. "You must not do it again," he said. "Do you hear? You must not ever do it." The boy said nothing. He stood under his father's hand and did not move.

They went out of the barn together. The sun had gone down behind the line of trees along the creek and the sky over the fields was red and then grey and a few early stars had come out. Across the vacant lot the windows of the Means house were lighted and Abner could hear the voice of the drayman shouting at someone inside and the voices of the boys answering. He did not look that way. He walked across the yard with the boy beside him, and at the kitchen door his wife stood waiting with the lamp in her hand and the light fell on her face and he saw that she had been crying. She looked at the boy and then at Abner. "Well," she said. "Did you see to him?"

"I saw to him," Abner said. He went past her into the kitchen and sat down at the table, and the boy went and sat in his place, and the woman set the lamp on the table and brought the supper from the stove. It was fried potatoes and side meat and bread, and they ate in silence. Once the woman looked at the boy's face and then at her husband's face and seemed about to speak, but she did not. She was a woman who had learned to wait. When the boy had finished eating she took him up the stairs to bed and Abner heard their feet on the bare boards over his head and then he heard nothing.

He went out and sat on the back step in the darkness. The air had grown cool and from the fields came the smell of the corn and of the dust settling after the long hot day. In the barn the cow lowed again and he remembered that he had not milked her and got up and took the pail from its nail and went across the yard. While he milked he leaned his head against the warm flank of the cow and closed his eyes. The milk rang in the pail. He thought of the saw at the mill and of how it would go on screaming in the morning and all the next day and the day after that. He thought of his father, long dead now and buried in the cemetery on the hill beyond the Pike, and he wondered whether the old man too had stood in the barn sometimes with the strap in his hand and wanted to say something and had not been able to say it. "Maybe it was that way with him," he thought. "Maybe he didn't know how either." The idea came to him that perhaps all men were like that, the drayman Means and the foreman at the mill and the men who sat on the loading platform at the noon hour telling their stories, that all of them had something shut up inside them that they could not get out, and that the beating and the shouting were only a way of trying.

When he had finished milking he carried the pail to the house and set it on the table in the kitchen, and then, not knowing why, he took off his shoes and went up the stairs in his stocking feet. The door of the boy's room stood open. A little moonlight came in at the window and lay on the floor and on the edge of the bed. The boy was asleep. He lay on his back with one arm flung out and his mouth a little open, and the hair at the back of his head stood up against the pillow. Abner stood in the doorway and looked at him. He stood a long time. He thought that he would like to go in and sit on the edge of the bed and wake the boy and tell him things, all the things he had never told anyone, about the barn on the farm and the bit of sky through the crack in the roof and the saw that screamed in his head at night. Then he thought that the boy would not understand and that perhaps it was better so. "He'll find out for himself," he whispered. "There's no way to tell it. He'll have to find it out."

It is a strange thing, this business of fathers and sons. One sees a man walking along a country road in the evening with a small boy beside him, the man silent and heavy, the boy skipping a little to keep pace, and one thinks that nothing is passing between them. And yet something is passing. It passes without words, as the warmth passes from the earth into the seed, and neither of them knows. Years afterward the boy, grown into a man and walking in the streets of some city, will of a sudden remember the barn and the broken switch and the big hand upon his head, and he will stop on the sidewalk among the hurrying crowds and stand there not knowing why his throat has grown tight. He will not remember the eighty cents. He will remember only that once his father looked at him and did not strike him, and that in the dimness of the barn something had for a moment come very near.

Abner went back down the stairs and out on the step again and sat there until the moon was high over the cornfield. In the house his wife moved about, putting away the dishes, and then the light went out and she called to him softly from the bedroom window. He did not answer at once. He sat with his big hands hanging between his knees and looked at the dark shape of the barn against the sky. "I'm quite a fellow," he said finally, half aloud, and he did not know whether he was laughing at himself or whether the thing he felt was a kind of pride. Then he got up and went into the house.

Henry Tolliver came home from the colored graded school at a quarter past five, which was his invariable hour. He was a man who believed that a regular life was the outward sign of a well-ordered mind, and he had preached that doctrine so long to the boys and girls under his charge that he had come in time to practise it himself. He was perhaps thirty-five years of age, of a complexion which the census-taker, after a moment's hesitation, had set down as "black," and which his friends more charitably described as a rich brown. He was tall, a little stooped from much bending over slates and copy-books, and his face, which was not handsome, had that look of patient intelligence which is sometimes found in men who have been compelled to win by merit what others receive by favor.

His house stood on the upper side of Front Street, in that quarter of the town of Clarendon where the better class of colored people had built their homes since the war. It was a neat cottage of five rooms, painted white, with green blinds and a little porch overgrown with a climbing rose, and it represented eight years of saving and self-denial. Henry was justly proud of it, and he never opened the gate without a certain quiet satisfaction, as a man might feel who has made a fortress of his own against a world not over-friendly.

On this particular afternoon, however, the satisfaction was absent. He had been aware for three days that something was amiss in his household, and he had borne the knowledge with the forbearance of a man who knows that women, like the weather, are not to be hurried. But forbearance has its limits, even in a schoolmaster; and as he hung his hat upon the rack in the narrow hall and heard no light step coming to meet him, he resolved that the matter should be brought to an issue before he slept.

He found his wife in the little parlor, seated by the window with a piece of needlework in her lap, at which she was not working. Marian Tolliver was some six years younger than her husband, and so fair that strangers in the town, seeing her upon the street, were frequently at a loss to account for her presence in that neighborhood. Her hair was brown and soft, her eyes gray, and her features of that regular cast which the novelists are fond of calling patrician, and which, in the South of that day, was more often the token of an irregular descent. It was known in Clarendon, though it was not much spoken of, that she was the daughter of Colonel Edmund Revel of Revel Hall, in the adjoining county, by a woman who had been his housekeeper; that the colonel had educated the girl at a Northern seminary, and had afterward, upon his marriage with a lady of his own station, settled a small sum upon the mother and dismissed both from his life with the decent completeness of a gentleman closing an account. The mother had died some years since. The colonel, as the newspapers had announced with suitable expressions of regret, had died a fortnight ago.

"You are home early, Henry," said Marian, looking up.

"I am home at my usual hour," he replied, seating himself opposite her. "It is you, I think, who have lost count of the time."

She made no answer, but bent over her work, and drew a thread through with unnecessary care. Henry watched her for a moment in silence. He was not a man of quick speech, and he was accustomed to arrange his thoughts before he uttered them, as he would have arranged a lesson in arithmetic.

"Marian," he said at length, "you received a letter on Monday. I saw it on the hall table before you took it up. It bore a Richmond postmark, and it was addressed in a lawyer's hand. You have not mentioned it to me, and you have not been yourself since it came. I do not ask to read your letters. But I think I have a right to know what it is that has come between us."

"Nothing has come between us," she said quickly.

"Then something is standing very near," he returned, "for I can feel the shadow of it."

She laid down her needlework, rose, and went to the little writing-desk in the corner, which had been his wedding gift to her. From one of the pigeon-holes she took a long envelope, and, after a moment's hesitation, placed it in his hands. Then she returned to the window and stood looking out into the street, where the long shadows of the elms were stretching across the dust.

Henry unfolded the letter and read it slowly, as he read everything. It was written upon heavy paper, and it was couched in that elaborate and careful phraseology by which the legal profession contrives to say disagreeable things without seeming to say anything at all. It informed Mrs. Marian Tolliver that the writer, Mr. Archibald Pettigrew, attorney-at-law, had the honor to act for the estate of the late Colonel Edmund Revel; that the said colonel, by a codicil executed some months before his death, had bequeathed to his natural daughter, Marian, the sum of eight thousand dollars, the same to be paid to her in four annual instalments; that the bequest was, however, subject to certain conditions, which the writer was instructed to communicate. These conditions were, in brief, that the legatee should remove, within six months, to some place north of the Ohio River, at a distance of not less than five hundred miles from the county of her birth; that she should there assume such name as she might choose, other than that of Revel; and that she should "sever, completely and permanently, every tie of association connecting her with the colored race, to which the testator, in his affection for her, did not wish her to be held to belong." In the event of her compliance, the writer would be happy to assist her in every way consistent with his duty. In the event of her refusal, the bequest would lapse, and the sum would be applied to the endowment of a chapel in the parish church at Revelton, in the testator's memory.

Henry read the letter through twice. Then he folded it and laid it on the table beside him, and sat for some time without speaking. When he looked up, his wife had turned from the window and was watching him.

"Well?" she said.

"It is a handsome sum," he answered quietly. "Your father was a generous man, after his fashion."

"His fashion!" she cried, with a little catch in her voice. "Is that all you have to say?"

"What would you have me say, Marian? The letter is addressed to you, not to me. I observe that I am not mentioned in it, except by implication. I am one of the ties of association."

She flushed scarlet, and then grew pale.

"You need not put it so," she said.

"How else should I put it? The colonel was a man of exact mind, and his lawyer is a man of exact words. 'Every tie of association connecting her with the colored race.' I am the closest of those ties, I take it, unless the law of the State of North Carolina has been changed without my knowledge."

There was a silence. Outside, a wagon rattled past, and the voice of old Aunt Peggy Lane, who did washing for half the street, was heard calling to her grandson.

"Jim! You Jim! Come 'long heah wid dat basket 'fo' I wears you out! Ain' got no mo' sense dan a June-bug, dat boy ain'!"

The interruption seemed to break the tension, and Marian came and sat down again in her chair, her hands clasped in her lap.

"Henry," she said, "I have not answered the letter. I have not decided anything. I only wished to think before I spoke to you, for I knew how you would take it."

"And how is that?"

"As you are taking it now—coldly, as if it were a question of right and wrong, and nothing else. You do not consider what it means."

"I consider that it means eight thousand dollars," he said, "and a new name, and a new life, among people who will never know that you were once the wife of a colored schoolmaster in a little Southern town. I consider that it means you would be free of all that you have borne since you married me—the slights in the shops, the Jim Crow car, the women who stare at you on the street and whisper behind their hands, wondering what such a lady can be doing among such people. I have considered all these things, Marian, for three days, while you were considering them in silence. I am not so cold as you suppose."

His voice had grown unsteady toward the end, and she looked at him with a sudden softening.

"You know that I have never complained," she said.

"No, you have never complained. That is what has made it the harder to bear."

She was silent for a moment, and when she spoke again it was in a lower tone.

"You do not know what it is, Henry. You cannot know. You were born to it; you have never been anything else. But I—I was brought up in a white school, among white girls, who thought I was one of themselves. I learned their ways and their thoughts; I read their books and dreamed their dreams. And then I came home, and found that the world had a place for me already marked out, and that it was not the place I had been taught to expect. Do you suppose I have forgotten what that was? When I married you, I chose my side, and I have never regretted it. But sometimes, when I see a white woman go into a door that is shut to me, and know that there is no difference between us but a word in a book that nobody can read—"

She stopped, and pressed her handkerchief to her lips.

Henry rose and walked twice across the little room. It was a habit he had when a pupil gave an answer that was both right and wrong, and he wished to find the point of error without wounding the scholar.

"Marian," he said, stopping before her, "I have never asked you to pretend that you are other than you are. I knew when I married you that you might have married otherwise, and I have always counted it the greatest honor of my life that you chose me. But I will not stand in your way now. If you wish to go, you shall go. I will not hold you by any claim of law or of sentiment. The law, indeed, would scarcely trouble itself on my behalf; and as for sentiment—" he smiled a little bitterly—"I have heard it said that sentiment is a luxury of the well-to-do."

"Do you mean," she said slowly, "that you would let me go—that you would consent?"

"I mean that I would not prevent you. Consent is another matter."

"And you would remain here?"

"Where else should I go? My work is here. My people are here. The colonel's lawyer has not offered me a new name, nor would it be of much service to me if he did. A man may change his name, Marian, but he cannot change his face, and mine has been very clearly labelled by Providence."

There was a touch of his old dry humor in the words, and she looked up at him with something between a smile and a sob.

"You are making it very hard for me," she said.

"I am trying to make it easy," he answered. "That is perhaps why it is hard."

She sat for a long time without answering, looking down at her clasped hands. Henry resumed his seat and waited. He had learned, in his profession, that the most important part of a lesson is often the silence which follows it, when the mind of the learner is left to work upon what it has received.

"I will tell you what I have been thinking," she said at last. "I have thought that it would be easy. I have pictured myself in some city of the North—in Cleveland, perhaps, or Philadelphia—with a little house of my own, and friends who would never ask me any questions, and nothing to remind me of all this. I have thought how pleasant it would be to go where I liked, and sit where I liked, and never feel that cold look upon me. I have even thought," she went on, with an effort, "that you would be better without me—that I have been a burden to you, and that people have said you married above yourself, and that it has hurt you among your own people."

"It has not hurt me," he said.

"It has, Henry. I have heard them. Mrs. Barrow said at the church supper that you were 'too high-toned to marry in your own color,' and I saw your face when it was repeated to you. Do not deny it."

He did not deny it.

"And then," she continued, "I thought of what it would really be. I thought of living always in fear—fear that someone from the South would come and know me, fear that some letter would be opened, some old acquaintance met in the street. I thought of making friends and never daring to tell them the truth; of hearing them talk about 'darkies' and 'niggers' at the dinner-table, and laughing with them, as I should have to laugh. I thought of my mother, who is buried in the colored cemetery out on the Wilmington road, and that I could never go to her grave again. And I thought of you, Henry—here, in this house, alone—going to school at eight o'clock and coming home at a quarter past five, and no one to meet you at the door."

Her voice broke, and she covered her face with her hands.

Henry sat very still. A man of more impulsive temper would have gone to her at once; but he had a certain fine reticence which made him unwilling to claim a victory until it had been freely yielded.

"And what conclusion have you reached?" he asked, gently.

She lowered her hands and looked at him with wet eyes.

"I have reached the conclusion that my father was a cruel man," she said. "He gave me his blood and his features, and he took away my birthright. He educated me to be a lady, and then he left me to be a servant's child. And now that he is dead, he would buy from me the only things I have that are truly my own—my husband, and my mother's memory, and my self-respect. He thought he was being kind. I suppose he even thought he was being generous. Eight thousand dollars! It is a great deal of money, Henry, and we have so little. But I think I should feel, every time I spent a dollar of it, that I was spending a piece of my own soul."

She rose, and taking the letter from the table, held it for a moment in her hand.

"Will you get me a match?" she said.

Henry went to the mantel and took one from the little china box that stood there. But instead of handing it to her, he paused, and drew from the inner pocket of his coat a folded sheet of paper.

"Before you burn that," he said, "you had better burn this also. I wrote it last night, when you were asleep."

She took it from him wonderingly and unfolded it. It was written in his own careful, schoolmaster's hand, and it was addressed to Mr. Archibald Pettigrew, attorney-at-law, of Richmond, Virginia. It stated, in language as formal as the lawyer's own, that the undersigned, Henry Clay Tolliver, being informed of the conditions attached to the bequest of the late Colonel Revel to his wife, desired to remove any obstacle which his existence might present to her compliance therewith; that he would interpose no objection to any proceedings she might institute for the dissolution of their marriage, upon whatever ground the law might allow; and that he would hold himself at Mr. Pettigrew's disposal for the execution of any papers that might be required.

Marian read it to the end, and then looked up at her husband with an expression which he never afterward forgot.

"You would have sent this?" she whispered.

"If you had wished it."

"Without a word to me?"

"I would have given it to you, and let you send it, or not, as you chose. I did not wish you to feel that you must stay for my sake. A woman who stays from pity is a heavier burden than a woman who goes from choice."

She stood for a moment looking at him; and then she struck the match herself, upon the rough edge of the mantel, and held the two papers together in the flame. They curled and blackened, and the lawyer's heavy paper burned more slowly than the schoolmaster's thin sheet, so that for a little while the words "every tie of association" stood out in brown letters upon the charred surface before they too crumbled into ash. She dropped the last fragment into the empty grate and watched it until it was quite consumed.

"There," she said, turning to him. "Now there is nothing standing near."

Henry took her hands in his, and for once in his life he did not stop to arrange his thoughts before he spoke; which was perhaps the reason that what he said has not been recorded.

It may be added, for the benefit of those who like to follow the fortunes of property, that the chapel at Revelton was duly built, of good red brick with a slate roof, and that a handsome tablet was placed in it to the memory of Colonel Edmund Revel, "a just man, a kind master, and a lover of his kind." The rector, in his dedicatory sermon, dwelt with much feeling upon the colonel's well-known benevolence toward the colored people of the county; and it is said that several of them, who sat in the gallery reserved for their use, were visibly affected. Among these, however, was not Mrs. Henry Tolliver, who had not been invited, and who was, in any case, engaged that afternoon in hearing a class of small boys recite the multiplication table, in the absence of her husband, who was ill with a cold.
