Opening the sheet the general read aloud an editorial article, to which Carteret listened intently, his indignation increasing in strength from the first word to the last, while McBane's face grew darkly purple with anger. The article was a frank and somewhat bold discussion of lynching and its causes. It denied that most lynchings were for the offense most generally charged as their justification, and declared that, even of those seemingly traced to this cause, many were not for crimes at all, but for voluntary acts which might naturally be expected to follow from the miscegenation laws by which it was sought, in all the Southern States, to destroy liberty of contract, and, for the purpose of maintaining a fanciful purity of race, to make crimes of marriages to which neither nature nor religion nor the laws of other states interposed any insurmountable barrier. Such an article in a Northern newspaper would have attracted no special attention, and might merely have furnished food to an occasional reader for serious thought upon a subject not exactly agreeable; but coming from a colored man, in a Southern city, it was an indictment of the laws and social system of the South that could not fail of creating a profound sensation.

"Infamous—infamous!" exclaimed Carteret, his voice trembling with emotion. "The paper should be suppressed immediately."

"The impudent nigger ought to be horsewhipped and run out of town," growled McBane.

"Gentlemen," said the general soothingly, after the first burst of indignation had subsided, "I believe we can find a more effective use for this article, which, by the way, will not bear too close analysis,—there's some truth in it, at least there's an argument." "That is not the point," interrupted Carteret.

"No," interjected McBane with an oath, "that ain't at all the point. Truth or not, no damn nigger has any right to say it."

"This article," said Carteret, "violates an unwritten law of the South. If we are to tolerate this race of weaklings among us, until they are eliminated by the stress of competition, it must be upon terms which we lay down. One of our conditions is violated by this article, in which our wisdom is assailed, and our women made the subject of offensive comment. We must make known our disapproval."

"I say lynch the nigger, break up the press, and burn down the newspaper office," McBane responded promptly.

"Gentlemen," interposed the general, "would you mind suspending the discussion for a moment, while I mind Jerry across the street? I think I can then suggest a better plan." Carteret rang the bell for Jerry, who answered promptly. He had been expecting such a call ever since the gentlemen had gone in.

"Jerry," said the general, "step across to Brown's and tell him to send me three Calhoun cocktails. Wait for them,—here's the money."

"Yas, suh," replied Jerry, taking the proffered coin.

"And make has'e, charcoal," added McBane, "for we're gettin' damn dry." A momentary cloud of annoyance darkened Carteret's brow. McBane had always grated upon his aristocratic susceptibilities. The captain was an upstart, a product of the democratic idea operating upon the poor white man, the descendant of the indentured bondservant and the socially unfit. He had wealth and energy, however, and it was necessary to make use of him; but the example of such men was a strong incentive to Carteret in his campaign against the negro. It was distasteful enough to rub elbows with an illiterate and vulgar white man of no ancestry,—the risk of similar contact with negroes was to be avoided at any cost. He could hardly expect McBane to be a gentleman, but when among men of that class he might at least try to imitate their manners. A gentleman did not order his own servants around offensively, to say nothing of another's. The general had observed Carteret's annoyance, and remarked pleasantly while they waited for the servant's return:— "Jerry, now, is a very good negro. He's not one of your new negroes, who think themselves as good as white men, and want to run the government. Jerry knows his place,—he is respectful, humble, obedient, and content with the face and place assigned to him by nature."

"Yes, he's one of the best of 'em," sneered McBane. "He'll call any man 'master' for a quarter, or 'God' for half a dollar; for a dollar he'll grovel at your feet, and for a cast-off coat you can buy an option on his immortal soul,—if he has one! I've handled niggers for ten years, and I know 'em from the ground up. They're all alike,—they're a scrub race, an affliction to the country, and the quicker we're rid of 'em all the better." Carteret had nothing to say by way of dissent. McBane's sentiments, in their last analysis, were much the same as his, though he would have expressed them less brutally. "The negro," observed the general, daintily flicking the ash from his cigar, "is all right in his place and very useful to the community. We lived on his labor for quite a long time, and lived very well. Nevertheless we are better off without slavery, for we can get more out of the free negro, and with less responsibility. I really do not see how we could get along without the negroes. If they were all like Jerry, we'd have no trouble with them." Having procured the drinks, Jerry, the momentary subject of the race discussion which goes on eternally in the South, was making his way back across the street, somewhat disturbed in mind.

"O Lawd!" he groaned, "I never troubles trouble till trouble troubles me; but w'en I got dem drinks befo', Gin'l Belmont gimme half a dollar an' tol' me ter keep de change. Dis time he didn' say nothin' 'bout de change. I s'pose he jes' fergot erbout it, but w'at is a po' nigger gwine ter do w'en he has ter conten' wid w'ite folks's fergitfulniss? I don' see no way but ter do some fergittin' myse'f. I'll jes' stan' outside de do' here till dey gits so wrop' up in deir talk dat dey won' 'member nothin' e'se, an' den at de right minute I'll ban' de glasses 'roun, an' moa' lackly de gin'l 'll fergit all 'bout de change." While Jerry stood outside, the conversation within was plainly audible, and some inkling of its purport filtered through his mind.

"Now, gentlemen," the general was saying, "here's my plan. That editorial in the negro newspaper is good campaign matter, but we should reserve it until it will be most effective. Suppose we just stick it in a pigeon-hole, and let the editor,—what's his name?"

"The nigger's name is Barber," replied McBane. "I'd like to have him under me for a month or two; he'd write no more editorials."

"Let Barber have all the rope he wants," resumed the general, "and he'll be sure to hang himself. In the mean time we will continue to work up public opinion,—we can use this letter privately for that purpose,—and when the state campaign opens we'll print the editorial, with suitable comment, scatter it broadcast throughout the state, fire the Southern heart, organize the white people on the color line, have a little demonstration with red shirts and shotguns, scare the negroes into fits, win the state for white supremacy, and teach our colored fellow citizens that we are tired of negro domination and have put an end to it forever. The Afro-American Banner will doubtless die about the same time."

"And so will the editor!" exclaimed McBane ferociously; "I'll see to that. But I wonder where that nigger is with them cocktails? I'm so thirsty I could swallow blue blazes."

"Here's yo' drinks, gin'l," announced Jerry, entering with the glasses on a tray. The gentlemen exchanged compliments and imbibed—McBane at a gulp, Carteret with more deliberation, leaving about half the contents of his glass. The general drank slowly, with every sign of appreciation. "If the illustrious statesman," he observed, "whose name this mixture bears, had done nothing more than invent it, his fame would still deserve to go thundering down the endless ages."

"It ain't bad liquor," assented McBane, smacking his lips. Jerry received the empty glasses on the tray and left the room. He had scarcely gained the hall when the general called him back.

"O Lawd!" groaned Jerry, "he's gwine ter ax me fer de change. Yas, suh, yas, suh; comin', gin'l, comin', suh!"

"You may keep the change, Jerry," said the general. Jerry's face grew radiant at this announcement. "Yas, suh, gin'l; thank y', suh; much obleedzed, suh. I wuz jus' gwine ter fetch it in, suh, w'en I had put de tray down. Thank y', suh, truly, suh!" Jerry backed and bowed himself out into the hall.

"Dat wuz a close shave," he muttered, as he swallowed the remaining contents of Major Carteret's glass. "I 'lowed dem twenty cents wuz gone dat time,—an' whar I wuz gwine ter git de money ter take my gal ter de chu'ch festibal ter-night, de Lawd only knows!—'less'n I borried it offn Mr. Ellis, an' I owes him sixty cents a'ready. But I wonduh w'at dem w'ite folks in dere is up ter? Dere's one thing sho',—dey're gwine ter git after de niggers some way er 'nuther, an' w'en dey does, whar is Jerry gwine ter be? Dat's de mos' impo'tantes' question. I'm gwine ter look at dat newspaper dey be'n talkin' 'bout, an' 'less'n my min' changes might'ly, I'm gwine ter keep my mouf shet an' stan' in wid de Angry-Saxon race,—ez dey calls deyse'ves nowadays,—an' keep on de right side er my bread an' meat. Wat nigger ever give me twenty cents in all my bawn days?"

"By the way, major," said the general, who lingered behind McBane as they were leaving, "is Miss Clara's marriage definitely settled upon?"

"Well, general, not exactly; but it's the understanding that they will marry when they are old enough."

"I was merely thinking," the general went on, "that if I were you I'd speak to Tom about cards and liquor. He gives more time to both than a young man can afford. I'm speaking in his interest and in Miss Clara's,—we of the old families ought to stand together."

"Thank you, general, for the hint. I'll act upon it." This political conference was fruitful in results. Acting upon the plans there laid out, McBane traveled extensively through the state, working up sentiment in favor of the new movement. He possessed a certain forceful eloquence; and white supremacy was so obviously the divine intention that he had merely to affirm the doctrine in order to secure adherents. General Belmont, whose business required him to spend much of the winter in Washington and New York, lost no opportunity to get the ear of lawmakers, editors, and other leaders of national opinion, and to impress upon them, with persuasive eloquence, the impossibility of maintaining existing conditions, and the tremendous blunder which had been made in conferring the franchise upon the emancipated race. Carteret conducted the press campaign, and held out to the Republicans of the North the glittering hope that, with the elimination of the negro vote, and a proper deference to Southern feeling, a strong white Republican party might be built up in the New South. How well the bait took is a matter of history,—but the promised result is still in the future. The disfranchisement of the negro has merely changed the form of the same old problem. The negro had no vote before the rebellion, and few other rights, and yet the negro question was, for a century, the pivot of American politics. It plunged the nation into a bloody war, and it will trouble the American government and the American conscience until a sustained attempt is made to settle it upon principles of justice and equity. The personal ambitions entertained by the leaders of this movement are but slightly involved in this story. McBane's aims have been touched upon elsewhere. The general would have accepted the nomination for governor of the state, with a vision of a senatorship in the future. Carteret hoped to vindicate the supremacy of his race, and make the state fit for his son to live in, and, incidentally, he would not refuse any office, worthy of his dignity, which a grateful people might thrust upon him. So powerful a combination of bigot, self-seeking demagogue, and astute politician was fraught with grave menace to the peace of the state and the liberties of the people,—by which is meant the whole people, and not any one class, sought to be built up at the expense of another.

Carteret did not forget what General Belmont had said in regard to Tom. The major himself had been young, not so very long ago, and was inclined toward indulgence for the foibles of youth. A young gentleman should have a certain knowledge of life,—but there were limits. Clara's future happiness must not be imperiled. The opportunity to carry out this purpose was not long delayed. Old Mr. Delamere wished to sell some timber which had been cut at Belleview, and sent Tom down to the Chronicle office to leave an advertisement. The major saw him at the desk, invited him into his sanctum, and delivered him a mild lecture. The major was kind, and talked in a fatherly way about the danger of extremes, the beauty of moderation, and the value of discretion as a rule of conduct. He mentioned collaterally the unblemished honor of a fine old family, its contemplated alliance with his own, and dwelt upon the sweet simplicity of Clara's character. The major was a man of feeling and of tact, and could not have put the subject in a way less calculated to wound the amour propre of a very young man.

Mrs. Harriet Lomax had long held the opinion, which she was at no pains to conceal, that a well-ordered household was the surest outward sign of an inward grace, and that the colored people of Groveland would rise in the world precisely in proportion as their parlors were swept, their children's faces washed, and their speech purged of the barbarisms which slavery had bequeathed them. In pursuit of this ideal she had furnished her own parlor with a horsehair sofa, a marble-topped table bearing a family Bible and a stereoscope, and a piano upon which no member of the family could play, but which was dusted every morning with a reverence that would not have been misplaced upon an altar. Her husband, Mr. Edward Lomax, kept the principal barber shop on Front Street, where he shaved the judges, the bankers, and the cotton factors of the town, and where, by a happy dispensation of local custom, no colored man had ever sat in his chairs. Whatever reflections this circumstance may have prompted in Mr. Lomax's mind he kept to himself, and he was accounted, by white and colored alike, a prudent and prosperous man.

The Lomaxes belonged to that small and somewhat anxious class which stood midway between the two races of the South, sharing the ambitions of the one and the disabilities of the other. They were, for the most part, of mixed blood, and in some instances so slightly tinged with the darker strain that only the vigilance of the community, which in such matters was unsleeping, could have detected it. Mrs. Lomax herself was of a clear olive complexion, with straight black hair which she wore in a heavy coil, and features that might have passed without remark in any drawing-room in Charleston, had their owner ever been admitted to one. She was a member of the Ladies' Literary Circle, which met fortnightly to read papers upon Browning and the Brontës, and whose membership, without any rule to that effect ever having been written down, was found by a curious coincidence to be confined to ladies of her own complexion or lighter.

Her daughter Lucinda, a child of seven, had inherited her mother's features and her father's gray eyes, and was, in the partial judgment of both, the prettiest little girl in Groveland. She had been reared with a care which left nothing to chance. She was taught to say "yes, ma'am" and "no, sir," to hold her fork properly, to speak without dropping her final consonants, and to walk upon the street with her eyes before her, neither looking to the right nor to the left. Some other things she had learned which no one had set out to teach her, for children are like the photographer's plate, which records not merely what is placed deliberately before it, but whatever else may chance to fall within the range of the lens.

On a warm afternoon in early June, Mrs. Lomax was seated upon her back piazza, engaged with a piece of fancy-work, when the sound of a child's voice, raised in shrill and unmistakable derision, came to her from the yard below. She laid aside her embroidery and went to the railing.

The Lomax yard was separated from the lane behind it by a whitewashed paling fence, and at the gate, holding a bundle of clean clothes wrapped in a blue checked cloth, stood a little black girl of about Lucinda's age, barefoot, in a faded calico frock that had been many times turned and mended. Mrs. Lomax recognized her as the granddaughter of Aunt Peggy Holt, the washerwoman who did the family's linen, and whose cabin stood at the foot of the lane, near the branch. On the inside of the gate, with her small hands upon the palings and her pretty face distorted into an expression of the most uncompromising contempt, stood Lucinda.

"You can't come in here," Lucinda was saying. "This is our yard. Mamma doesn't allow black children in our yard. You go round to the kitchen door, where you belong."

"I ain' tryin' ter come in yo' ole ya'd," returned the other child, with a spirit which did her credit. "My granny tol' me ter fetch dese clo'es ter yo' mammy, an' I's gwine ter fetch 'em, an' you can't stop me, needer."

"You're blacker than a tar-bucket," cried Lucinda, with the fine instinct of her age for the weapon that would cut deepest. "You're as black as a crow. If you touched me, the black would come off on my dress. Go away, you old black crow, you!"

The little black girl's lip trembled, and she drew back a step from the gate; but she did not cry. She stood holding her bundle against her thin breast, and looked at Lucinda with an expression which a more observant person than Lucinda would not soon have forgotten,—an expression less of anger than of a sort of dull and wondering hurt, such as a dumb creature might show at an unexpected blow.

"Lucinda!" called Mrs. Lomax sharply.

Lucinda turned, and the contempt vanished from her countenance as by magic, giving place to the bland and innocent look which children wear when they are conscious of having been overheard and are uncertain how much.

"Yes, mamma?"

"Open the gate this instant, and let Mandy in."

Lucinda opened the gate with visible reluctance, and the little washerwoman's grandchild came up the walk and mounted the back steps, where she delivered her bundle to Mrs. Lomax with a duck of the head that was meant for a curtsy.

"Granny say dey's all dere, ma'am, 'ceptin' Mr. Lomax's Sunday shirt, w'at she gwine ter fetch ter-morrer, kase de bosom ain' dry yit."

"Very well, Mandy. Tell your grandmother I am much obliged." Mrs. Lomax hesitated, and then, with an impulse which she did not pause to examine, went into the kitchen and returned with a slice of cake wrapped in a napkin. "Here is something for you. Run along home now, and mind you don't loiter by the branch."

The child took the cake, ducked her head again, and went down the steps and out at the gate, without so much as a glance toward Lucinda, who had retreated to the shelter of a crape-myrtle bush and was pulling the blossoms from it with an air of elaborate unconcern. Mrs. Lomax watched the little figure until it had disappeared down the lane, and then turned to her daughter with a countenance from which every trace of softness had departed.

"Lucinda, come here to me."

Lucinda came slowly, and stood at the foot of the steps, twisting a crumpled blossom in her fingers.

"Come up on the piazza. I wish to speak to you."

The child mounted the steps, one at a time, with a deliberation that was in itself a form of protest, and stood before her mother, who had resumed her chair, and who regarded her for a long moment in a silence more terrible to a child than any words.

"Lucinda," said Mrs. Lomax at length, "what did I hear you saying to that little girl?"

"Nothing, mamma."

"Do not add a falsehood to your other fault. I heard you distinctly. You called her a crow, and a tar-bucket, and told her she was not fit to come into our yard. Is that not so?"

Lucinda's eyes sought the floor. "She was impudent to me, mamma."

"She was not impudent to you. You were impudent to her,—you were worse than impudent, you were cruel; and cruelty, Lucinda, is the vice of low and common natures. I had hoped that a daughter of mine would know better."

"But she is black, mamma," said Lucinda, lifting her eyes with an air of injured reasonableness, as though she had stated an axiom which no sensible person could dispute. "She's ever so black. And she hasn't any shoes."

Mrs. Lomax felt a curious tightening at her heart, and for a moment she could not trust herself to speak. The words were a child's words, and the logic a child's logic; but she had heard them before, in other mouths, clothed in more decorous language,—and the uncomfortable suspicion stirred within her that she had heard them in her own.

"What has the color of her skin to do with it?" she demanded, with a severity that was directed in part at a target other than the child. "Did Mandy make herself? Did she choose to be born black, any more than you chose to be born as you are? God made her, Lucinda, as He made you; and when you mock the work, you mock the Workman."

"Mrs. Cuthbert says,"—began Lucinda, and stopped.

"What does Mrs. Cuthbert say?"

The child hesitated, perceiving dimly that she had wandered upon dangerous ground, but having no clear notion of the way back.

"She said, when the ladies were here for the Circle, that the black people were pulling the rest of us down, and that it was a pity they couldn't all be sent back to Africa, and then the white folks would see that we were different. And you said, mamma, that there was a great deal in what she said, and that you wouldn't for the world have me playing with Aunt Peggy's children."

It may be said, in justice to Mrs. Lomax, that her color rose. She remembered the occasion perfectly. Mrs. Cuthbert, whose late husband had been a member of the legislature during the brief period when such things were possible, and who was so fair that she had once been ejected from the colored car of a railway train by a conductor who refused to believe her testimony as to her own ancestry, had held forth upon the subject at some length, over the tea and sponge-cake, and the ladies of the Circle had listened with a complacency in which Mrs. Lomax had freely shared. It had not occurred to any of them that a small pitcher with large ears had been sitting upon a hassock in the corner of the parlor, turning over the pictures in a volume of Godey's Lady's Book, and laying up these sayings in her heart. The discourse had seemed, at the time, both sensible and refined; it did not sound so well when repeated in the shrill treble of a child of seven, and Mrs. Lomax was conscious of an emotion which, had it been felt by another, she would have called shame.

"Lucinda," she said, more slowly, "there are things which grown people say among themselves which little girls do not understand, and which they ought not to repeat. When I said that I did not wish you to play with Aunt Peggy's children, I did not mean that you were to insult them. There is a great difference between choosing one's associates, which every lady has the right to do, and wounding the feelings of those whom one does not choose. A lady may decline an acquaintance, but she never gives offense."

This distinction, which was in reality the whole code of a certain sort of gentility, and which would have satisfied any member of the Ladies' Literary Circle, did not appear to satisfy Lucinda, who wrinkled her small brow over it in evident perplexity.

"But if they're no good, mamma, why mayn't I say so?"

"I did not say they were no good."

"Then why mayn't I play with Mandy?"

Mrs. Lomax opened her lips to reply, and closed them again. The question was a simple one, and she had answered harder ones at the Circle; but she found, upon searching her mind, that the answers which had served very well among her friends did not lend themselves readily to the comprehension of a child, and that, stripped of their decent phrases and laid bare in the plain light of Lucinda's gray eyes, they had a look which she did not altogether like. She was saved from the necessity of a reply by the appearance of a third person upon the scene.

Old Mrs. Lomax, the barber's mother, who lived with her son, came out upon the piazza, leaning upon a stick of polished hickory. She was a small, spare woman of seventy or thereabouts, of a deep brown complexion, with a white handkerchief bound about her head and a pair of steel-rimmed spectacles pushed up upon her forehead. She had been born a slave upon a plantation in the low country, had borne her son to a master whom she never mentioned, and had bought her own freedom, a year before the war made the purchase unnecessary, with money saved, a few cents at a time, from the sale of eggs and garden-truck. Her daughter-in-law treated her with every outward mark of respect, and was careful that she should want for nothing; but it had been tacitly understood, ever since the Circle had begun to meet in the Lomax parlor, that the old lady preferred her own room upon those evenings, and the old lady, who understood a great many things that were never put into words, had not once failed to prefer it.

"W'at's de matter wid de chile, Ha'iet?" she asked, lowering herself into a rocking-chair. "I heared you-all talkin' f'm de kitchen. Is she be'n sassy?"

"She has been very naughty, mother," replied the younger woman, with some constraint. "She was rude to Aunt Peggy's little Mandy,—called her names, and would not let her in at the gate."

"W'at kinder names?"

Mrs. Lomax hesitated, and the old woman turned her spectacles upon the child.

"W'at you call dat chile, honey?"

Lucinda, who loved her grandmother, and was a little afraid of her, looked from one to the other, and found no help in either face.

"I called her a black crow," she said in a small voice.

The old woman did not answer immediately. She rocked slowly back and forth, her thin brown hands folded upon the head of her stick, and looked out across the yard, beyond the paling fence and the lane, toward the line of pines that marked the course of the branch, as though she saw something there which was hidden from the others.

"Come yere ter yo' granny, Lucindy," she said at length.

The child went to her, and the old woman took one of the small soft hands in her own, and laid it, palm downward, upon the back of her wrinkled brown one, so that the two lay side by side in the afternoon light.

"Look at dat, honey. Look at it good. W'at color is yo' granny's han'?"

Lucinda looked, and said nothing.

"It's black, ain't it? Black ez Mandy's, mos'. An' dis han' rocked yo' daddy in de cradle, an' wo'ked in de fiel' fer ter buy hisse'f an' me, an' sewed de clo'es on his back w'en he wuz a little boy, an' nussed him th'oo de measles, an' de scarlet fever, an' de lockjaw w'at he tuk w'en he stepped on a nail. Ef it hadn' be'n fer dis black han', honey, dey wouldn' be no Lucindy fer ter call nobody names. Is yo' granny a black crow, chile?"

The child's lip began to quiver, and her eyes filled with tears. "No, granny," she whispered.

"Den Mandy ain' one needer. De Lawd don' make no crows outen folks. Dat's de w'ite folks' business, an' dey been at it a long time, an' dey's mighty good at it. Dey don' need no he'p f'm us."

Mrs. Lomax, who had listened to this discourse with a heightened color and a countenance that betrayed a struggle between pride and some better feeling, rose abruptly from her chair.

"Lucinda," she said, in a voice which she endeavored to keep steady, "you will go to your room and remain there until supper. You will think over what your grandmother has said to you, and what I have said to you. And to-morrow morning, when Mandy brings your father's shirt, you will go down to the gate and open it for her, and tell her that you are sorry for having been unkind. Do you understand me?"

"Yes, mamma," sobbed Lucinda.

"And you will ask her," continued Mrs. Lomax, after a pause which cost her something, "whether she would like to come in and see your doll-house."

Lucinda raised a face upon which astonishment struggled with grief, and seemed for a moment about to ask a question; but something in her mother's expression forbade it, and she went into the house, sobbing quietly, and the two women heard her small feet ascending the stairs.

For some minutes neither of them spoke. The younger woman stood at the railing, looking down into the yard, where the scattered blossoms of the crape-myrtle lay like drops of blood upon the trodden earth. The old woman rocked slowly, and said nothing. She was too wise to press a point already gained, and too kind to triumph over one whom she had come, in the course of years, to regard with a certain tolerant affection, as one regards a member of the family whose faults are of the head rather than the heart.

"I suppose," said Mrs. Lomax at length, without turning around, "that you think I have been very foolish, mother."

"I don' think nothin' 'bout it, Ha'iet," returned the old woman placidly. "Chillun's chillun. Dey pick up w'at's lyin' roun', lak chickens in a ya'd. You can't blame de chicken, an' you can't rightly blame de ya'd, needer. But it's a good notion fer ter keep de ya'd clean."

Mrs. Lomax made no reply. Whether she resolved, in that moment, to sweep her own yard of the refuse that had collected there, or whether she merely resolved to be more careful thereafter of the ears that might be listening from the hassock in the corner, is a question which the narrator does not feel competent to answer. Human nature is not remade in an afternoon, and the prejudices which have been woven into the fabric of a life are not to be picked out with a needle in an hour. It is enough to record that the Ladies' Literary Circle, at its next meeting, found its hostess somewhat less receptive than usual to Mrs. Cuthbert's views upon the deportation of the darker element, and that Mrs. Cuthbert went home that evening with the impression, which she confided to more than one of her friends, that Harriet Lomax was getting queer notions in her head.

As for Lucinda, she opened the gate the next morning, with a red face and a great deal of stammering; and Mandy, who bore no malice, came in and saw the doll-house, which was a very fine one, with real glass in the windows, and pronounced it the finest thing she had ever seen. Before an hour had passed the two children were seated together upon the back steps, sharing a plate of gingerbread with entire impartiality, and disputing, with the gravity of judges, whether a doll that had lost one shoe could properly attend a party. The sun shone upon them both with fine indifference, as it shines upon the just and the unjust, the light and the dark; and if there was any difference between them which it was bound to respect, it gave no sign of having discovered it.

It is the peculiar mercy of childhood that its wounds heal quickly and its wrongs are soon forgiven; and it is the peculiar tragedy of the world that children grow up, and learn, from those who love them best, the lessons that the world would have them learn. Whether Lucinda Lomax would remember, in the years to come, the brown hand laid beside her own upon the piazza that June afternoon, or whether she would remember instead the conversation of the ladies over their tea and sponge-cake, was a question which only time could answer,—and time, in the South, has been a slow and uncertain schoolmaster.

response:
The rain had come in the afternoon, and by night it had settled upon the town with the air of a creditor who intends to remain until he is paid. It beat upon the shingles of the little house at the end of Mill Street. It ran in gray ropes from the eaves. The street outside was a river of brown paste, and the one lamp at the corner stood in it like a sentry who has forgotten the password and is afraid to go home.

Within, the kitchen was yellow. The lamp upon the table threw a round, complacent light that reached as far as the stove and stopped there, as if it had no business with the corners. The stove itself glowered. Its belly was red, and from time to time it made small explosive remarks, like an old man who disapproves of the conversation but will not leave the room.

The woman sat by the table with a basket of mending in her lap. She had the stocking of a man drawn over one hand, and she was pushing the needle in and out with a terrible regularity. Her face was thin. It had been pretty once, in the way that a new tin cup is pretty, and now it was merely useful. She did not look up when the door opened.

The man came in with the rain. He stamped upon the sill, and the water fled from his boots in a little gray army. He was large and young, with a red neck and a mustache which he had cultivated through two summers with the devotion of a priest. He hung his coat upon the peg. Then he stood in the middle of the floor and looked at the back of his wife's head, and his face wore the expression of a man who has come to tell a great thing and finds the audience inattentive.

"Well," he said.

She bit a thread. "Supper's in the oven. It's dried up some. You said six."

"I know what I said." He went to the stove and spread his hands before it. The steam rose from his trousers. He appeared to be smoking at the knees. "I was down at the hall."

The needle paused, and then went on. "What hall?"

"The armory. Over the feed store." He cleared his throat. It was a large sound, and it filled the kitchen, and when it had gone the rain came back into the silence and drummed there. "They was signin' men tonight. For the regiment."

The woman laid the stocking upon her knee. She looked at it for a time as if she had found a hole in it which she had not expected. Then she raised her eyes to her husband. They were pale eyes, the color of a winter creek, and there was no expression in them at all.

"Jim," she said, "did you put your name down?"

He had prepared for this moment during the whole of his walk home through the mud. He had composed a number of speeches. They had been very fine speeches. In them he had spoken of the flag, and of the Spaniards, and of the poor people of the island who were starving, and of his duty as a man; and in each of these speeches his wife had at length wept and clung to him and called him brave. He had seen it plainly, under the dripping trees. But now, in the yellow kitchen, with the stove muttering and the pale eyes upon him, the speeches went out of his head like birds from a barn when the door is opened, and he could not call one of them back.

"Yes," he said.

She looked at him. He looked at the stove.

"Every feller in the shop went," he added presently. "Pete Shaughnessy went. Both the Lindquist boys. Old Hammond's son went, and him with a bad foot. You'd 'a' thought I was a coward or somethin', standin' there."

"Who'd 'a' thought it?"

"Why, all of 'em. Everybody."

"Did anybody say so?"

"No, they never said it. But they'd 'a' thought it."

The woman took up the stocking again. She thrust in the needle. She drew it out. The thread came after it with a little hissing sound, like something that has been insulted.

"You might 'a' come home first," she said.

"I knowed what you'd say if I come home first."

"Then you knowed it was wrong."

"I never knowed no such thing!" He swung round from the stove, and his shadow leaped up the wall behind him and hung over the shelf of crockery like a great dark bird. "I knowed you'd make a fuss, that's all. Women always make a fuss. It's their nature. You can't help it no more'n a hen can."

She did not reply to this. The clock upon the shelf ticked. It was a cheap clock, which they had bought from a peddler in the first month of their marriage, and it had the voice of a small, important official. It seemed to be taking notes.

The man waited. He had expected tears. He was, in a way, prepared to be generous with them. He had decided that he would put his hand upon her shoulder, and that he would say, "There, now," in a deep voice. But she did not weep. She sewed. And her silence began to press upon him, as the air of a cellar presses upon a boy who has gone down for apples and cannot find the stair.

"Well, ain't you goin' to say nothin'?" he demanded.

"What would you have me say?"

"Why — anythin'. A man goes an' does a thing like this, his wife ought to say somethin'."

"I said you might 'a' come home first."

"Well, that ain't much!"

She laid down the mending once more, and this time she folded her hands upon it. Her knuckles were red, and the skin upon them was split in two places from the lye in the wash-water. He noticed this with a kind of surprise, as a man might notice for the first time that the fence in his own yard is leaning.

"Jim," she said, "who's to pay the rent on this house?"

"Why, the gover'ment pays a soldier. Thirteen dollars a month. An' I can send it home."

"Rent is eight dollars. Coal is three, when it's cheap. Flour —"

"Oh, I know what flour is!"

"Do you?" She said it quite softly. "I didn't know you did."

He took a turn about the kitchen. It was not a large kitchen, and the turn was brief. He arrived again before the stove, and the stove regarded him with its red eye and made a small contemptuous noise.

"You talk like money was everythin'," he said. "There's things bigger'n money. There's a whole country out there. There's folks bein' starved an' shot down by them Spaniards, women an' little children —"

"Where?"

"In Cuba! Ain't you read the paper?"

"I read it," she said. "I read it at the Hendersons' when I do their wash. It said a lot of things. It had pictures."

"Well, then!"

"Jim, you never been further'n Port Jervis."

He stared at her. A dull color came up out of his collar and mounted his face until it reached the roots of his hair. He felt that this was a low blow. He felt that it had nothing to do with the question. It was a woman's argument, cunning and sidelong, and it slid under a man's guard like a cat under a gate.

"What's that got to do with it?" he said loudly.

"Nothin', maybe."

"It ain't got nothin' to do with it. A man don't have to 've been places to know what's right."

She looked away from him then, toward the black window. The rain was streaming down the glass, and the lamp's reflection hung there in the wet, wavering and ghostly, as if another kitchen existed out in the night, where another couple sat and quarreled in silence. She seemed to be watching this phantom room with great attention.

The man felt that the battle had turned against him, though he could not tell at what point it had turned. He had come into the house a hero. He had walked up Mill Street in the rain with his chest thrown out, and the drops striking him had seemed to be a sort of applause. Now he stood in his steaming trousers before his own stove, and he was a large, red, foolish young man who had done a thing without asking. The universe had executed this change upon him in the space of perhaps four minutes. He resented it deeply, and since he could not see the universe he resented his wife.

"I guess you'd rather I was like Henry Mapes," he said bitterly. "Settin' home by the fire while better men go an' fight."

"Henry Mapes has got a bad chest."

"Henry Mapes has got a yellow streak, is what he's got."

"Maybe," she said. "His wife's warm, anyhow."

The clock ticked. The stove muttered. Out in the street a wagon went by, its wheels sucking at the mud with long, greedy sounds, and the driver was singing a song of which only one word could be heard, and the word was "darling." It passed. The rain closed over the place where it had been.

The man sat down suddenly upon the other chair. He sat heavily, with his knees apart and his big hands hanging between them. He looked at the floor. There was a crack in the boards near his boot, and he examined it with care, as though it might contain an answer.

"Mary," he said after a while, "you don't understand."

"No."

"It ain't just the — the fightin'. It's — a man's got to do somethin' sometime. I been in that shop since I was fourteen. Fourteen years old. Every day the same. Plane the board, saw the board, plane the board. Old Kessler hollerin'. You come home, you eat, you go to bed, you get up. It's like — like bein' a mule in a treadmill. An' now here's this thing come along, an' everybody's goin', an' there's flags, an' the band was playin' down at the hall —" He stopped. He was a little ashamed of the band. He had not meant to mention it. "I just thought," he said, "a man could be somethin' for once."

For the first time she looked at him with an expression. It was a strange expression. It was not anger, and it was not pity, but it had something of both in it, as dusk has something of both day and night. She looked at him for a long moment, and he felt himself examined to the bottom, the way she examined a shirt for a stain before it went into the tub.

"An' what was I to be?" she said.

He did not understand the question. He frowned at it.

"What?"

"While you was bein' somethin'. What was I to be?"

"Why — you'd be home. Same as now."

"Same as now," she repeated. She nodded slowly. "Yes. Same as now."

She rose and went to the stove. She opened the oven door, and a gust of heat came out, carrying the smell of meat that has waited too long. She took a cloth and drew out a plate. Upon it lay a piece of pork, shriveled and brown, and some potatoes that had fallen in upon themselves like old men. She set this before him upon the table, and she laid a fork beside it, and a knife. She did these things with great exactness. There was something in her precision that frightened him more than any outcry would have done.

"Eat your supper," she said.

He looked at the plate. He was not hungry. A soldier, it seemed to him, should not be expected to eat dried pork in a kitchen on the night of his enlistment. But he took up the fork, because she stood there, and he cut a piece of the meat and put it in his mouth, and it was like chewing the sole of a boot.

She sat down again and took up the stocking. The needle went in and out.

"When do you go?" she asked.

"Thursday week. They're to drill at Middletown first. Then I dunno. Tampa, they say. Then the island."

"Thursday week."

"Yes."

"That's eleven days."

He had not counted them. He was startled that she had counted them so quickly, as though the number had been waiting in her mind all along, like a coin kept in a drawer against a bad time.

"I s'pose it is," he said.

"I'll want to turn your gray shirt. The collar's gone. An' you'll need stockin's. Two pair, anyhow." She held up the one upon her hand and looked at the heel of it critically. "This one won't last to Middletown."

He put down his fork. Something had happened in his throat. He could not tell what it was. It was as though a small hard object had lodged there, an apple seed, or a button. He swallowed, but it stayed.

"Mary," he said thickly. "Mary, I —"

"Eat your supper, Jim."

"I don't want no supper."

"You'll want it in Cuba," she said.

He laughed at that, a short, astonished bark, and then stopped laughing because she had not laughed. She sewed. The lamp burned steadily. The rain went on and on upon the roof with its insane industry, as if it had been contracted to drown the whole valley by morning and was behind in the work.

He sat and watched her hands. He watched them for a long while. They went to and fro, to and fro, red and split and quick, and it came to him slowly, as a thing comes to a man who has been asleep, that these hands had been doing this every night for three years while he sat by the stove and read the paper and spat into the coal-scuttle and thought about the injustice of old Kessler. He had never particularly watched them before. He had supposed, if he had supposed anything, that they did it of their own accord, like the clock.

He wished to say something regarding this discovery. He felt that it was important. But when he searched for the words he found that they were very small words, and that they would sound foolish in the kitchen, and that she would perhaps look at him in that strange way again. So he said nothing. He pushed the plate a little way from him.

"They give you a uniform," he said at last. "Blue. With a hat."

"That's nice."

"An' a rifle. A Springfield."

"Yes."

"Pete says we'll be home by fall. Pete says them Spaniards'll run soon as they see us comin'."

"Does Pete know Spaniards?"

He opened his mouth and shut it again. Then, to his own amazement, he grinned. It was a sheepish grin, and it sat upon his large red face with an air of having wandered in by mistake.

"No," he said. "Pete don't know nothin'. Pete's a fool."

"He is," she agreed.

"He's the biggest fool in the shop."

"He is that."

"He signed first, too. Stood up on a chair an' hollered."

"I'd 'a' thought he would."

They were silent again, but it was a different silence. The stove seemed to feel the difference; it ceased its mutterings and settled into a low, contented roar. The clock went on taking its notes, but with less severity. Out in the window the phantom kitchen still hung in the rain, and in it the phantom couple sat no nearer together than before, but their heads were bent in the same direction.

The man looked at his wife. He saw that there was a gray hair upon her temple, a single one, standing out from the brown like a thread from the mending. He had not seen it before either. She was twenty-three years old.

"Mary," he said, "I can go down to the hall tomorrow. Mebbe — mebbe they'd let a man take his name off. If he had reasons."

The needle stopped.

She sat very still. The lamplight lay upon her face and showed nothing in it, nothing at all, as the light of a lantern shows nothing upon the surface of a deep well. He waited, and his heart beat in great, slow, clumsy strokes, like a man pounding upon a door who is not certain he wishes it to be opened.

At length she shook her head.

"No," she said. "No, Jim. You'd only hate me for it. Ever after. Every time the band played."

"I wouldn't."

"You would. You'd set by that stove an' hate me. I know you." She drew the thread through, and bit it, and smoothed the stocking flat upon her knee. "Better you go. Better you go an' find out what it is. Then you'll come home an' know."

"Know what?"

She did not answer. She rolled the stocking into a ball and dropped it into the basket and took out another. This one was his also. They were all his.

He sat back in his chair. He was conscious of a vast and bewildering defeat. He had won. He was to go. No one would stop him; no one would weep upon his neck and beg him to remain. He would march away on Thursday week in a blue uniform with a Springfield rifle, and the band would play, and Pete Shaughnessy would holler from a chair. All of this was precisely what he had wanted when he came in out of the rain. And yet he felt as a man feels who has run very hard to catch a train, and caught it, and found when he sat down that he did not know where it was going.

He looked at the dried pork upon the plate. He took up the fork again and began, slowly, to eat it. It was very bad. He ate all of it.

The woman sewed. The lamp burned. Outside, the rain continued to fall upon Mill Street, upon the armory over the feed store, upon the dark river and the dark hills beyond it, and very far away to the south upon an island which neither of them would have been able to find upon a map. It fell upon all these places impartially. It had no opinion concerning any of them.

prompt:
Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Stephen Crane, depicting the following scene: Cousins catching up after a long time apart.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
I

The train came down out of the hills with a long yell, as if it were angry at the country for having so many curves. It swept along the edge of the town of Ballard's Mills, and the little yellow station, which had the cowering air of a dog that expects to be kicked, received it with a shiver of all its windows. A cloud of black smoke went rolling over the roof of the freight-shed and broke upon the elms beyond, and the elms tossed their heads in a kind of outraged dignity.

Upon the platform stood Orrin Pike. He had put on his Sunday coat. It was a coat of a stern black, and it had been worn to the funerals of eleven persons, so that it carried itself with gloom and with a certain authority. Orrin was not easy in it. He had been standing there for forty minutes, and in that time he had twice gone to the end of the platform to look along the rails, and twice come back, as a man will who has nothing to do with his hands but cannot bear to let them be still.

Two loafers sat upon a truck near the baggage-room. They had observed the Sunday coat, and they had drawn their own conclusions. One of them now spat with deliberation upon the planks and said: "Orrin's waitin' fer somebody."

The other loafer considered this for a time. "I guess he is," he said at last.

The train halted with a great sigh of steam, and the passengers began to descend. There was a fat woman with a basket, who peered fearfully about her as if the town might presently attack her. There was a drummer in a gray suit, who whistled. And then, in the doorway of the second car, there appeared a figure that caused the two loafers to sit up straight upon their truck.

It was a man of perhaps thirty-five years, and he was dressed in a checked suit of a pattern so loud that it seemed to shout across the platform. Upon his head was a brown derby, and from his waistcoat there hung a chain of yellow metal which caught the late sun and flung it about. He carried a valise of new leather, and he stepped down from the car with the manner of one who conferred a favor upon the earth by touching it.

Orrin Pike went forward. His face had become suddenly red. He had prepared, during the forty minutes, a great many things to say, but now they had all fled from him, and he could think of nothing but that his cousin had grown a mustache.

"Well, Lafe," he said.

"Well, Orrin," said the other.

They shook hands. It was a long handshake and an awkward one, for each man was trying to read the other's face, and each was conscious of being read. Orrin saw a stranger of evident importance, a man who had been in the great city and had been touched and polished by it. Lafe Hollister saw a mild, stooped fellow with a little dust of meal in the creases of his knuckles, and he felt for him a sudden and agreeable pity.

"You ain't changed much," said Lafe generously.

"No," said Orrin. "I guess not." He looked at the checked suit. "You have," he added, and then was immediately afraid that this might be taken amiss.

But Lafe laughed. He laughed in a large, easy way, throwing back his head. "Well, a man can't stay in Chicago fourteen years and come out the same as he went in," he said. "It ain't possible. The town gets into him."

The two loafers had heard the word "Chicago," and they looked at each other with the eyes of men who have received an important communication.

II

They went up the main street of the town together. It was the hour when the sun, having finished with the day, was painting the upper windows of the brick block a furious crimson, and the dust of the road lay in long golden sheets. A wagon creaked by with a sleepy team. From the open door of the blacksmith shop came the clang of iron, steady and indifferent, like the beating of some slow heart.

Lafe walked with his chin up. He was looking at everything, and his glance had in it a kind of fond contempt. "There's old Dutcher's store," he said. "Lord, it's got smaller. I used to think that was a big store."

"It's the same size," said Orrin.

"Well, it looks smaller." Lafe flicked an ash from his cigar. "Everything does, after you been away. You ought to see Marshall Field's, Orrin. You could put this whole street into the front of it and have room left for a circus."

Orrin said that he would like to see it some time. He said this humbly. He was thinking of his own store, the feed store at the foot of Water Street, where the sacks of bran leaned against each other like weary old men and the rats held long conversations under the floor. He had been proud of the store that morning. He had swept it. But now it seemed to him a shabby thing, and he was glad that their road did not lead past it.

"What line are you in now, Lafe?" he asked.

"Hardware," said Lafe. "Wholesale. I got a position with Heilbronner and Strauss." He pronounced the names as if they were the names of kings. "Responsible position. I handle a whole territory practically by myself. They think a good deal of me there. Old Heilbronner, he says to me once, he says, 'Hollister, I don't know what we'd do without you.' That's what he said."

Orrin was silent. He was very much impressed. It seemed to him that his cousin had climbed a high mountain, and was now calling down to him from the peak, and that his own voice, if he raised it, would sound thin and foolish in such air.

At the bridge they paused. Below them the river went sliding over its stones with a low, continuous chuckling, as if it were telling itself an old joke. The willows along the bank hung their heads in the water. Beyond, the mill-race shot black and smooth under the wheel-house, and the great wheel itself stood still and dripping, a dark ruin against the burning sky.

Lafe leaned upon the rail. For a moment his face lost some of its confidence. "That's where we had the raft," he said.

"Yes," said Orrin.

"You remember the raft?"

"I remember it."

"We was going to float her clean down to St. Louis," said Lafe, and he laughed again, but this time the laugh was smaller. "Clean down to St. Louis. And then to New Orleans, and then I don't know where. China, I guess."

"You was going to China," said Orrin. "I was going to stop at St. Louis and be a pilot."

They looked down at the water. A little brown bird skipped from stone to stone, entirely occupied with its own affairs.

"She broke up on the dam," said Lafe.

"She broke up on the dam," Orrin agreed, "because you would steer."

Lafe turned his head. "Because I would steer? I never steered. You had the pole."

"I didn't have the pole. You took it away from me."

"I never took it away from you. You dropped it."

The two men regarded each other. It was suddenly apparent that a dispute twenty-two years old had come up out of the river and was standing between them, dripping, upon the bridge. Lafe's face had grown pink above his collar. Orrin's mouth had set itself in a line which his wife would have recognized.

Then Lafe laughed once more, and slapped his cousin upon the shoulder with a large hand. "Well, it don't matter now, does it?" he said. "It don't matter a continental."

"No," said Orrin. "It don't matter." But privately he was certain that Lafe had taken the pole.

III

Orrin's house stood upon a little rise at the edge of the town, a white house that had been white a long time ago. There was a picket fence in front of it, and several of the pickets were missing, so that the fence had the appearance of an old man grinning. In the yard a hen went about her business with an air of grievance.

Mrs. Pike met them at the door. She was a thin woman with a face that seemed to have been made for the purpose of expecting the worst, and she wore an apron which she had forgotten to take off. When she saw the checked suit she drew in her breath. Then she wiped her hands upon the apron and gave one of them to the visitor.

"Pleased to meet you, Mr. Hollister," she said.

"Call me Lafe, ma'am," said the cousin magnificently. "We're all one family here."

Behind her, in the dimness of the hall, there was a stirring and a whispering, and three children became visible, ranged in order of their heights like a set of jugs upon a shelf. They stared at the visitor with round and solemn eyes. They had been told that a cousin was coming from Chicago, and they had formed in their minds an image of something enormous and terrible, perhaps with feathers. They were now trying to make the man in the checked suit fit this image, and he was not fitting it very well, and they were disappointed, but also they were not sure.

"These are the young ones," said Orrin.

Lafe bent down. "Well, well," he said. "Well, well, well." He took a coin from his pocket and held it up so that it shone. The smallest child put her finger in her mouth. The largest, a boy of ten, regarded the coin with deep suspicion, as if he suspected that it would be the beginning of some obligation.

At supper Lafe talked. The lamp had been lit, and it threw a round yellow glow upon the table, upon the ham and the biscuits and the dish of preserved pears, and beyond this glow the room was full of brown shadows in which the faces of the children floated like little moons. Lafe talked of the city. He talked of buildings ten stories high, and of the cable cars that ran without horses, and of the lake that was like an ocean. He talked of a fire he had seen, and of a man who had been run over by a dray in front of his very eyes, and he described the incident with such care that Mrs. Pike put down her fork.

"Did you ever see any Indians?" asked the boy suddenly.

Lafe hesitated. It was an important moment. Six eyes were fixed upon him with a terrible hope. "Well," he said, "I seen a good many."

"Wild ones?"

"Some of 'em was pretty wild."

The boy breathed deeply. He looked at his father with something like pity. His father had never seen an Indian. His father sold bran.

Orrin sat at the head of his table and ate his supper. He ate it slowly. He was listening to his cousin and he was proud of him, for it is a fine thing to have a relative who has seen wild Indians and a man run over by a dray; and at the same time there was growing within him a dull and secret resentment, which he did not understand and of which he was ashamed. He observed that his children did not look at him at all.

Mrs. Pike, in the kitchen afterward, said to him in a low voice: "Orrin, that suit."

"What about it?"

"Nothing," she said. "Only it's a mighty loud suit."

"It's a city suit," said Orrin with some heat. "That's how they wear 'em in the city."

"I expect so," said Mrs. Pike, and she rattled the dishes in the pan in a way that conveyed a great deal.

IV

Later the two cousins sat upon the porch. The night had come down over the valley, soft and enormous, and the stars were out in such numbers that they seemed to crowd one another. From the marsh beyond the river the frogs had begun their chorus, a vast, shrill, unending argument in which every frog was certain he was right. Now and then a dog barked far off in the town, and another dog answered him, and then both were quiet, as if ashamed.

Lafe had offered a cigar, and Orrin had accepted it. It was a cigar with a gold band, but it did not draw well, and it had a taste which Orrin could not name. He smoked it doggedly. He would have smoked it if it had been made of hay.

For a time they did not speak. The great talk of the supper-table had worn itself out, and now there was only the dark and the frogs and the two red points of the cigars, which brightened and faded, brightened and faded, like the slow eyes of some watchful animal.

"Aunt Mattie's dead," said Orrin presently.

"I heard," said Lafe. "I got the letter." He was silent. "I meant to come," he said.

"It was in March," said Orrin. "The roads was bad."

"I meant to come," said Lafe again.

Orrin said nothing. He was thinking of the burying, of the gray rain that had come down all through it, and of the minister, who had a cold, and of the few people who had stood about the grave with their collars turned up. He remembered that he had looked once at the road, half believing that he would see a figure coming. He had not told anyone this.

"She used to give us them molasses cookies," said Lafe. His voice had changed. It had grown husky and low, and some of the city had gone out of it. "You remember? She kept 'em in the blue crock on the shelf. And you'd climb up and I'd hold the chair."

"I held the chair," said Orrin.

"Now, Orrin—"

"I held the chair. You was always the one to climb. You was lighter."

Lafe began to protest, and then he stopped. In the darkness he made a curious sound, and Orrin perceived that his cousin was laughing, not in the large, fine way of the afternoon, but quietly, with his shoulders shaking.

"Lord," said Lafe, "we never can agree on nothing, can we?"

"I guess not," said Orrin, and then he too began to laugh. They sat there laughing together on the dark porch, two men no longer young, while the frogs went on with their argument in the marsh. It was not a thing that could have been explained to anyone. Mrs. Pike, hearing it through the kitchen window, paused with a dish in her hand and frowned, for it seemed to her an unreasonable noise.

When they had done, there was another silence, and it was a different silence from the first. The air seemed to have loosened between them.

Lafe threw the end of his cigar out into the yard, where it lay glowing in the grass. "Orrin," he said.

"What?"

"About that position."

Orrin waited.

"It ain't—" Lafe began, and halted. "Well, old Heilbronner, he didn't exactly say what I told you. That is, he said something like it, but it was a man named Gersten he said it to. I was standing right there. I heard it." He cleared his throat. "I handle a territory all right. But it ain't such a big territory. It's mostly down around Joliet."

Orrin turned this over in his mind. He was conscious of a feeling that was not disappointment, and was not triumph, but was some third thing that warmed him oddly about the heart. He perceived that the mountain upon which his cousin had stood was not so high, after all, and that the voice calling down from it had been, perhaps, a little frightened of the height.

"And the suit," said Lafe. "I'm owing on the suit."

"It's a good suit," said Orrin.

"It's a fool suit," said Lafe bitterly. "I seen it in a window and I thought, I'll go home in that. I'll show 'em. And all the way on the cars I was proud of it, and then when I got down on the platform and seen them two loafers looking at me, I felt like a parrot in a cage."

Orrin considered. Then, slowly, as a man will lay down a card he has been holding a long while, he said: "The store's mortgaged."

Lafe turned his head.

"Since two years back," said Orrin. "When the river come up and spoiled the corn. Bank's got a paper on it. And on the house too, partly." He drew upon the evil cigar. "I didn't tell Ella how much. She'd fret."

"Well," said Lafe softly. "Well, I'll be darned."

They sat and looked out at the night. And it seemed to each of them, in that moment, that he had come into possession of something valuable, though he could not have said what it was. They had each laid down a burden of pretense, and found that the other did not think the less of him. It was a small thing. The stars, which had looked upon a great many porches, did not remark it. The frogs did not pause. But the two men felt it, and they were silent for a long time out of a kind of shyness, as if they had been caught in some act of tenderness that was not proper between grown men.

"That raft," said Lafe at last.

"What about it?"

"I guess maybe I did take the pole."

Orrin was a long while in answering. "No," he said finally. "I guess maybe I dropped it."

V

In the morning the sun came up clean and bright, and the hen in the yard resumed her grievance where she had left it. Lafe came down to breakfast in the checked suit, for he had no other, and the children looked at it again, and the boy asked him whether the Indians had tried to scalp him, and Lafe, after a glance at Orrin, said that they had not tried very hard.

The two cousins walked down to the station together. The street was full of wagons, and the blacksmith's iron rang out as before, steady and indifferent. At the bridge Lafe paused and looked down at the water, and Orrin paused beside him, and neither of them said anything.

On the platform the two loafers were again seated upon their truck. They might have been sitting there all night. They regarded the checked suit with undiminished interest.

The train came out of the east with the same long yell, as if it had learned nothing in a day. It stopped, gasping. Lafe picked up his yellow valise.

"Well, Orrin," he said.

"Well, Lafe."

They shook hands. It was as long a handshake as the first, and almost as awkward, for there were a great many things to be said and no fit words to say them in. Then Lafe climbed into the car, and the train shrieked and jerked and drew away, and the yellow station shivered in all its windows, and the black smoke rolled over the freight-shed and broke upon the elms.

Orrin stood watching until the last car had gone around the curve. Then he turned and walked back up the street toward the feed store at the foot of Water Street, where the sacks of bran were waiting for him like patient old men.

One of the loafers spat upon the planks. "That feller from Chicago," he said. "Must be pretty well fixed."

The other loafer considered this for a long time. "I guess he is," he said.
