There was a war in the vacant lot behind the Methodist church. It had been declared shortly after the noon meal, and by three o'clock it had become one of those vast and complicated struggles in which the original causes are lost and only the hatreds remain. Two armies of small boys faced each other across a stretch of burnt grass and broken bottles. Between them lay a ditch, and in this ditch the dead sometimes rested and argued with the living as to whether they had been properly killed.

Georgie Vane was a general. He had appointed himself to the post, and the appointment had been confirmed by the circumstance that he possessed ammunition. This ammunition he carried in a flour sack, which hung from his shoulder and swung against his knees in a manner both martial and inconvenient. It contained some threescore objects, brown and round and papery, which he had procured that morning from a certain bed of earth beside his mother's kitchen. He had not inquired into their nature. It had been sufficient that they were of a size to fit the hand and of a weight to carry well through the air. When they struck, they burst with a soft and satisfactory sound, and the enemy howled.

"Charge 'em!" he cried. "Charge 'em, fellers! They ain't got nothin' left but clods!"

His army consisted of three boys and a dog. The boys were named Pete Holloway, Arthur Fenn and a small cousin of Arthur's who had come visiting from Ohio and who had been pressed into service with the understanding that he was a private and would remain a private forever. The dog had no rank. He went where his heart directed him, and his heart directed him chiefly toward the enemy's lunch, which lay in a paper parcel behind a heap of bricks.

The enemy was commanded by a large, freckled youth named Sammie Dorr, who was in the fifth reader and who therefore carried with him the dignity of an older civilization. He fought from behind the bricks. His face appeared above them now and then like a red moon, and his voice issued forth in great bellows of contempt.

"Yah! Yah! Georgie Vane, you can't hit a barn!"

Georgie drew back his arm. He felt within himself a swelling, as if his chest had become too small for the thing that lived in it. The sky was very blue, and the grass was very yellow, and the bricks were the color of old blood. He threw. The missile sang across the field and broke upon the edge of the brick pile, and a spray of brown fragments went up like a puff of smoke from a cannon. Sammie Dorr's face vanished. There was a short silence, and then a wail of genuine anguish.

"It's in my eye! Aw, it's in my eye!"

The army of Georgie Vane set up a cheer. It was a thin and piping cheer, but to the general it sounded like the roar of multitudes. He stood upon the lip of the ditch and waved his sack, and in that moment he was conscious of the eyes of nations upon him. He was a figure of bronze. Somewhere, in a city he had never seen, men were already preparing his statue.

Then, from beyond the church, beyond the board fence and the row of currant bushes and the grape arbor with its sagging wires, there came a voice. It was a woman's voice. It rose in a long note, and broke, and rose again.

"Geor-gie! Geor-gie Vane!"

The effect upon the field of battle was singular. Both armies paused. Sammie Dorr, with one hand clapped to his eye, put his head up from behind the bricks and regarded his late adversary with a sudden and terrible interest. The cousin from Ohio sat down in the ditch. Pete Holloway began to walk away in a casual manner, whistling, as one who had merely been passing and had stopped to look at the weather.

"Your ma," said Arthur Fenn, in a hushed voice. "That's your ma."

Georgie said nothing. The bronze had gone out of him. He was again a small boy with a flour sack, and the flour sack had become very heavy. He looked down into it, and the brown round things looked back at him with a strange and accusing look, as if they had been waiting all afternoon for this moment.

"Geor-gie!"

The voice had in it a quality which he recognized. It was not the voice that called him to supper, nor the voice that called him to have his ears washed. It was another voice, and he had heard it perhaps three times in his life. Each time it had been followed by events which his mind now declined to remember.

"I got to go," he said hoarsely.

"Yeh," said Sammie Dorr from behind the bricks. "I guess you have." He spoke with deep satisfaction, and his uninjured eye glittered.

Georgie went. He did not run. To run would have been to admit that the summons had power over him, and he had a vague idea that a general, even a defeated general, should march. So he marched, very slowly, through the gap in the board fence and past the currant bushes, and his army watched him go as men watch a comrade led out to be shot. The dog followed him a little way, and then remembered the lunch behind the bricks, and turned back.

His mother stood in the side yard. She was a small woman, and ordinarily she had a soft and indefinite face, like a face seen through a window on a rainy day. But now it had become sharp. It had edges. She stood beside the bed of earth by the kitchen wall, and the bed of earth was full of holes. They were neat round holes, dug with a garden trowel, and there were a great many of them. They gaped at the sky. They resembled, to the guilty eye of Georgie, a little cemetery in which all the graves had been robbed.

"Georgie," said his mother, "what is in that sack?"

He looked at the sack as if he had never seen it before. He looked at it with honest wonder, as if some stranger had hung it upon his shoulder while he slept.

"It's—it's a sack," he said.

"I can see that it is a sack. What is in it?"

He opened his mouth. Several explanations presented themselves to his mind. He had found the sack. Pete Holloway had given it to him. It had been in the barn. A tramp had left it. Each of these explanations seemed, as it approached his tongue, to grow thin and transparent, so that he could see his mother's face through it. He closed his mouth.

His mother reached out and took the sack from him. She looked into it. She was silent for a long time. Then she said, in a low voice, "These came from Philadelphia. They came all the way from Philadelphia, in a box, with straw. Your father sent away for them in the winter. They were to be tulips. There were to be red ones and yellow ones and some that were striped."

Georgie stared at the ground. A small black beetle was walking across the path. It walked with great purpose, as if it had an appointment, and Georgie watched it with a kind of envy.

"They were to come up in the spring," said his mother. Her voice shook a little. "Mrs. Fitch was going to come and see them. I told her. I told the whole Missionary Society."

"I didn't know they was tulips," said Georgie. "I thought they was just—things."

"Things," repeated his mother.

"I thought they was onions," said Georgie, gaining a little courage. "Old onions. I thought you didn't want 'em."

"You thought I buried onions beside the kitchen door, in rows, with little sticks to mark them."

Georgie could find no answer to this. It seemed to him a very unfair thing to say. It was the kind of thing that grown persons said, and there was no answer to it, and they knew there was no answer, and they said it anyway.

His mother handed him back the sack. It was a curious gesture, and it frightened him more than anything she had yet done. "Go up to your room," she said. "Your father will be home at six o'clock. He will want to see you in the library."

The library. The word fell upon Georgie like a stone dropped into a well. He heard it go down and down.

He went into the house and up the stairs. The stairs were very long. He had never before noticed how long they were. At each step the house seemed to grow more silent, as if it, too, had learned of his crime and was holding its breath. In the hall above, the clock ticked with a dreadful deliberation. It said, "Six—o'clock. Six—o'clock." He went into his room and shut the door and sat upon the edge of his bed with his hands between his knees.

The window of his room looked out upon the side yard. By leaning a little he could see the bed of earth with its holes. He did not lean. He looked instead at the wallpaper, which was covered with small blue sailboats, all sailing in the same direction, toward the bureau. He had counted them many times. There were two hundred and eleven, not counting the half ones that went behind the door.

He began to construct the future.

In the first future, he ran away. He climbed down the lightning rod at midnight and went to the railroad yards and hid himself in a freight car full of cattle. He traveled to the West. He became a scout, and later a great Indian fighter, and his name appeared in the newspapers. Years afterward he came riding back into the town on a black horse, with a long mustache and silver spurs, and his father and mother stood on the porch, very old and bent, and his mother said, "Is it—can it be—Georgie?" And he said coldly, "Madam, I have brought you some tulips," and threw a great bag of them at her feet, and rode away forever.

This future pleased him a great deal for a time. Then it occurred to him that he did not know how to climb down a lightning rod, and that the railroad yards were a long way off, and that it would be dark, and he abandoned it.

In the second future, he died. He was not certain how he died, but it was a slow and beautiful death, and he lay upon this very bed, very white, and the whole town came to look at him. Sammie Dorr came, and wept, and said, "He was the best general there ever was." His mother came, and fell upon her knees, and cried, "Oh, my boy, my boy, what are tulips beside thee?" And his father stood at the foot of the bed with his head bowed, and was sorry, and was sorry, and was sorry.

This future made Georgie's eyes sting with pity for himself, and he enjoyed it extremely. He went over it a second time, adding a band.

Meanwhile the light in the room was changing. It had been yellow, and now it was turning to the color of brass, and the sailboats on the wall had begun to look gray and tired. Down in the street a wagon went by, and its wheels made a sound like distant artillery. A bell rang somewhere. Georgie listened, and his heart rose up into his throat and stayed there, for he knew that this was the hour at which the streetcar stopped at the corner.

Presently there was the sound of the front gate. It was a particular sound, a click and then a creak, and Georgie had heard it every evening of his life without paying it any attention. Now it seemed to him the most terrible sound in the world. After it came footsteps on the walk. They were steady footsteps. They did not hurry. Then the front door opened and closed, and there were voices below—his mother's voice, low and rapid, rising and falling like water running over stones, and then his father's voice, which said only a few words, and those very quietly.

There was a long silence.

Then his mother's voice came up the stairway. It had lost its edges. It sounded almost sorry. "Georgie. Your father wants you."

He went down. He went down the long stairs and through the hall and past the parlor, where the plush chairs sat in the dusk like a row of fat old ladies who knew all about it. The door of the library stood half open. Through it there came the yellow light of a lamp.

His father sat in the leather chair beside the table. He was a tall, thin man with a close gray beard, and he wore spectacles which he took off when he wished to look at anything carefully. He had them off now. He was holding the flour sack upon his knee. He had evidently been examining its contents, for one of the brown bulbs lay upon the table in the lamplight, and it looked very small and naked there, like a thing in a museum.

Georgie stopped just inside the door. The carpet was red, with a pattern of vines, and he fixed his eyes upon a particular vine and did not move them.

"Come in, Georgie," said his father. "Shut the door."

Georgie shut the door. It closed with a soft click, and the click went through him from head to heel.

"Come here."

He came. He came as far as the edge of the table and stopped there, as if the table were a kind of fortification behind which a man might still make a stand.

His father regarded him for some time without speaking. This silence was worse than anything that could have been said. Georgie felt that his whole interior was being looked into, as his mother looked into the oven to see if the bread was done. He felt that his father could see the battle, and the brick pile, and Sammie Dorr's eye, and the statue in the distant city, and the black horse and the silver spurs, and the band. He grew hot all over.

"Your mother tells me," said his father at last, "that you dug up her tulip bulbs."

Georgie said nothing.

"Did you?"

"Yes, sir," whispered Georgie.

"All of them?"

"I guess so. Yes, sir."

"What did you do with them?"

Georgie's throat worked. "We was having a war," he said. "Me and Pete and Arthur, against Sammie Dorr's gang. They had clods. We didn't have nothin'. So I—I got those."

"I see," said his father. "You used them for ammunition."

"Yes, sir."

"Did they answer the purpose?"

Georgie looked up quickly. His father's face was perfectly grave. There was no expression upon it whatever. It was like the face of a judge on a picture in a schoolbook.

"They—they busted," said Georgie.

"They burst," said his father. "Yes. I imagine they would." He picked up the single bulb from the table and turned it in his fingers, holding it close to the lamp. "Do you know what this is, Georgie?"

"Mother says it's a tulip."

"It is not a tulip. It is going to be a tulip. Or rather, it was going to be." His father put the bulb down again, very carefully, in the exact center of the table. "There is a difference. A tulip is a thing you can see. This is a thing you have to wait for. Your mother waited for these since January. She read about them in a catalogue and showed me the pictures of them in the evenings, here, under this lamp. She planted them in October, on her knees, in the cold. She has been waiting all the winter, Georgie, and in a few weeks she would have seen them. And now she is not going to see them. Do you understand that?"

Georgie did not answer. A strange thing was happening to him. The vine on the carpet had begun to swim. It wavered and grew large and then small, and the red of it ran into the edges of things. He fought this with all his strength. He told himself that generals did not do it, that scouts did not do it, that men with silver spurs did not do it. He set his teeth.

"You did not ask anyone," his father continued in the same level voice. "You did not ask your mother whether you might have them. You simply took them because they were there and because they were convenient. That is what a thief does, Georgie. A thief sees a thing and wants it and takes it. He doesn't think about the person who owns it. He doesn't think at all. I do not believe you are a thief. But this afternoon you behaved like one."

The word struck Georgie like a blow. He had been called many things. He had been called a liar by Sammie Dorr and a baby by his cousin and a bad, wicked boy by Miss Ferris at the Sunday school. But no one had ever called him a thief. Thieves were men with masks who went to prison. Thieves were hanged. He had a sudden vision of himself in a striped suit, breaking rocks in the hot sun, while his mother's tulips nodded their red heads beyond the wall.

The vine on the carpet broke into pieces. Georgie made a sound. It was not a large sound, but it was the beginning of a large sound, and once begun it could not be stopped. It came up out of him in great gulps, and his shoulders shook, and his face screwed itself into a shape over which he had no control whatever. He stood by the table and howled. He howled for the tulips, and for his mother on her knees in the cold, and for the striped suit, and for the dead general on the white bed, and for the injustice of all things, and for nothing in particular, simply because the howl was there and must come out.

His father let him howl. He sat in the leather chair with his hands folded and waited, as a man waits for a shower to pass before going out of doors. When at length the sounds had diminished to a series of wet hiccoughs, he took a handkerchief from his pocket and held it out.

Georgie took it and used it with great thoroughness.

"Now," said his father, "we shall have to settle this. How much money is in your bank?"

Georgie's bank was a cast-iron dog with a slot in its back. It sat upon his bureau, and he had been feeding it pennies since Christmas with the object of buying a certain air rifle which lay in the window of Hubbell's Hardware. He knew to the cent what was in it. He had lain awake at night computing it.

"A dollar and eighteen cents," he said, and his voice shook again, for he saw where this was leading.

"The bulbs cost two dollars and forty cents," said his father, "not counting the express. You will give your mother the dollar and eighteen cents tomorrow morning. The remainder you will earn, by filling the woodbox and carrying out the ashes every day without being told, at five cents a day, until it is paid. And on Saturday you will fill in those holes, every one of them, and rake the bed smooth. And when the new bulbs come next fall, you will plant them yourself, with your mother showing you how."

Georgie gazed at his father with the eyes of one who has been told that the world is to end on Thursday.

"Is that understood?"

"Yes, sir."

"Then you may go up to bed. You will have your supper there."

Georgie went to the door. He went with his head down and his feet dragging, and the handkerchief still clutched in his fist. At the door he turned. He had an obscure feeling that something more ought to be said, that a scene of such magnitude ought not to end merely with a woodbox. But his father had put his spectacles back upon his nose and taken up the evening paper, and there was nothing in his attitude to encourage further speech. So Georgie went out and closed the door behind him and climbed the long stairs to the room of the sailboats.

In a little while his mother brought up a tray. There was bread and milk upon it, and a piece of cold chicken, and, curiously, a slice of the chocolate cake which had been meant for the Missionary Society. She set it down without a word, and touched his hair once, very lightly, and went away.

Georgie ate everything. Then he went to the window and leaned upon the sill. It was nearly dark. The holes in the bed of earth below had become shadows, and the shadows had become one shadow, and the shadow was creeping out across the yard toward the barn. Over the roof of the church a single star had come out, small and cold and white.

Down by the board fence something moved. It was the face of Arthur Fenn, peering through the gap, round and pale in the gloom.

"Georgie!" it whispered hoarsely. "Hey, Georgie! Did you get licked?"

Georgie considered. He looked down at his friend, and at the star, and at the shadow on the grass, and something in him that had been crushed began very slowly to unfold itself and stand up again.

"Licked?" he said scornfully. "Huh! He 'most killed me. He 'most killed me dead. But I never hollered once."

Arthur's face was filled with awe. "Gee," it breathed.

Below, in the library, the lamp still burned. Georgie's father had laid down his paper. He was looking at the small brown bulb that sat in the center of the table, and presently he picked it up and weighed it in his palm, and drew back his arm a little way, as if measuring a distance.

His wife, coming in at that moment, stopped short in the doorway.

"Henry!"

"It would carry a fair way," said Mr. Vane thoughtfully. "A fair way, I should say. Better than a clod." He put the bulb down. "I was thinking of Bill Akers, who lived behind us when I was a boy. I hit him with a green apple once at forty paces. I have never been able to do anything so well since."

Mrs. Vane looked at him for a long moment. Then she turned and went out, and her back was very straight, and her silence was of the variety that is

Here is an excerpt of Stephen Crane's writing, to show you their style:

The youth felt, however, that his problem was in no wise lifted from him. There was, on the contrary, an irritating prolongation. The tale had created in him a great concern for himself. Now, with the newborn question in his mind, he was compelled to sink back into his old place as part of a blue demonstration. For days he made ceaseless calculations, but they were all wondrously unsatisfactory. He found that he could establish nothing. He finally concluded that the only way to prove himself was to go into the blaze, and then figuratively to watch his legs to discover their merits and faults. He reluctantly admitted that he could not sit still and with a mental slate and pencil derive an answer. To gain it, he must have blaze, blood, and danger, even as a chemist requires this, that, and the other. So he fretted for an opportunity. Meanwhile, he continually tried to measure himself by his comrades. The tall soldier, for one, gave him some assurance. This man’s serene unconcern dealt him a measure of confidence, for he had known him since childhood, and from his intimate knowledge he did not see how he could be capable of anything that was beyond him, the youth. Still, he thought that his comrade might be mistaken about himself. Or, on the other hand, he might be a man heretofore doomed to peace and obscurity, but, in reality, made to shine in war. The youth would have liked to have discovered another who suspected himself. A sympathetic comparison of mental notes would have been a joy to him. He occasionally tried to fathom a comrade with seductive sentences. He looked about to find men in the proper mood. All attempts failed to bring forth any statement which looked in any way like a confession to those doubts which he privately acknowledged in himself. He was afraid to make an open declaration of his concern, because he dreaded to place some unscrupulous confidant upon the high plane of the unconfessed from which elevation he could be derided. In regard to his companions his mind wavered between two opinions, according to his mood. Sometimes he inclined to believing them all heroes. In fact, he usually admired in secret the superior development of the higher qualities in others. He could conceive of men going very insignificantly about the world bearing a load of courage unseen, and although he had known many of his comrades through boyhood, he began to fear that his judgment of them had been blind. Then, in other moments, he flouted these theories, and assured him that his fellows were all privately wondering and quaking. His emotions made him feel strange in the presence of men who talked excitedly of a prospective battle as of a drama they were about to witness, with nothing but eagerness and curiosity apparent in their faces. It was often that he suspected them to be liars. He did not pass such thoughts without severe condemnation of himself. He dinned reproaches at times. He was convicted by himself of many shameful crimes against the gods of traditions. In his great anxiety his heart was continually clamoring at what he considered the intolerable slowness of the generals. They seemed content to perch tranquilly on the river bank, and leave him bowed down by the weight of a great problem. He wanted it settled forthwith. He could not long bear such a load, he said. Sometimes his anger at the commanders reached an acute stage, and he grumbled about the camp like a veteran. One morning, however, he found himself in the ranks of his prepared regiment. The men were whispering speculations and recounting the old rumors. In the gloom before the break of the day their uniforms glowed a deep purple hue. From across the river the red eyes were still peering. In the eastern sky there was a yellow patch like a rug laid for the feet of the coming sun; and against it, black and patternlike, loomed the gigantic figure of the colonel on a gigantic horse. From off in the darkness came the trampling of feet. The youth could occasionally see dark shadows that moved like monsters. The regiment stood at rest for what seemed a long time. The youth grew impatient. It was unendurable the way these affairs were managed. He wondered how long they were to be kept waiting. As he looked all about him and pondered upon the mystic gloom, he began to believe that at any moment the ominous distance might be aflare, and the rolling crashes of an engagement come to his ears. Staring once at the red eyes across the river, he conceived them to be growing larger, as the orbs of a row of dragons advancing. He turned toward the colonel and saw him lift his gigantic arm and calmly stroke his mustache. At last he heard from along the road at the foot of the hill the clatter of a horse’s galloping hoofs. It must be the coming of orders. He bent forward, scarce breathing. The exciting clickety-click, as it grew louder and louder, seemed to be beating upon his soul. Presently a horseman with jangling equipment drew rein before the colonel of the regiment. The two held a short, sharp-worded conversation. The men in the foremost ranks craned their necks. As the horseman wheeled his animal and galloped away he turned to shout over his shoulder, “Don’t forget that box of cigars!” The colonel mumbled in reply. The youth wondered what a box of cigars had to do with war. A moment later the regiment went swinging off into the darkness. It was now like one of those moving monsters wending with many feet. The air was heavy, and cold with dew. A mass of wet grass, marched upon, rustled like silk. There was an occasional flash and glimmer of steel from the backs of all these huge crawling reptiles. From the road came creakings and grumblings as some surly guns were dragged away. The men stumbled along still muttering speculations. There was a subdued debate. Once a man fell down, and as he reached for his rifle a comrade, unseeing, trod upon his hand. He of the injured fingers swore bitterly, and aloud. A low, tittering laugh went among his fellows. Presently they passed into a roadway and marched forward with easy strides. A dark regiment moved before them, and from behind also came the tinkle of equipments on the bodies of marching men. The rushing yellow of the developing day went on behind their backs. The man came up from the barn when the light was nearly gone. The snow in the lane had been trodden into a gray paste, and his boots made little sucking noises in it, as if the earth were reluctant to let him go. Over the hill the sky was a cold green, with a single bar of crimson laid across it like a welt. The house squatted before him. A window glowed. He paused at the gate and regarded this window for some time, as a man might regard the eye of a creature he had wronged.

He had resolved upon a speech. He had composed it in the barn, among the patient cattle, and it had seemed to him there a fine and manly speech, with a beginning that was firm and an end that was tender. He had recited portions of it to the gray mare. She had made no objection. But now, with the window staring at him, he found that the speech had grown thin and threadbare in his mind, and certain of its noblest phrases had fled away altogether.

He scraped his boots upon the step with great deliberation. It was a long scraping. He was aware that it was a long scraping, and that it was audible within, and he began to feel that the scraping was itself a kind of confession.

The kitchen was hot. The stove sat in its corner and glared at him with a red, eternal eye. The lamp upon the table made a little island of yellow, and beyond its shores the room went off into brown shadow, where the dresser loomed and the clock ticked with the dull insistence of a thing that had been wound for a purpose. The woman sat by the lamp. She was sewing. The needle went in and came out, went in and came out, and flashed at each emergence like a small fish leaping.

She did not look up.

He hung his coat upon the peg. He was very careful about the hanging of the coat. He straightened the shoulders of it. He then stood for a moment with his hands hanging, and he discovered that his hands were enormous, and that they had no business anywhere.

"Cold," he said.

"It's January," said the woman.

He sat down across from her and began to unlace his boots. The laces had frozen and would not give. He picked at them with his great fingers, and he bent so low over this labor that his face was hidden. He felt that his face was a thing to be hidden.

The needle went in and came out.

"Supper's on the back of the stove," she said presently. "It's been there some time."

"I ain't hungry."

"You'll eat it, though."

"I s'pose."

He got one boot off and set it upon the floor with a small, careful thud. Then he began upon the other. The clock ticked. The stove muttered. Somewhere above them, in the dark of the loft, the child turned over in her sleep, and the rope bed creaked, and both of them lifted their faces to the ceiling and listened, and then lowered them again, and neither had looked at the other.

"Mis' Hatcher was in to the store this afternoon," said the woman.

The man's fingers paused upon the lace. He felt the blood go up into his face in a hot tide. The speech, which had been waiting somewhere in the back of his skull, rose up all at once and fell over itself and lay in a confused heap.

"Was she?" he said.

"She was."

"Well, I s'pose she's got a right to go to the store."

The woman bit off her thread. She did it with a sharp, decisive motion, as one who severs a rope that has held a boat. She looked at him then for the first time. Her eyes in the lamplight were very dark, and there was in them something he could not name—a quality of waiting, like that of a hawk upon a dead limb.

"She said Hatcher told her you'd put your name down. With that man from Omaha. She said you was going in the spring."

He had his boot off now. He held it in his two hands and studied it. It was an old boot, cracked across the instep, and he regarded it with profound attention, as if within its leather lay some answer that had hitherto escaped him.

"I was going to tell you," he said.

"When?"

"Tonight. I was going to tell you tonight."

"Hatcher knew it Tuesday."

There was a silence. The clock seemed to grow louder in it. Each tick fell into the room like a pebble into a well, and he found himself waiting for the splash.

He had known, of course, that she would come to know. He had known it in the way a man knows that winter will come, which is to say that he had known it and had not believed it. He had told Hatcher because Hatcher had been there, leaning upon the rail of the feed lot with his pipe, and the man from Omaha had just driven off in his yellow buggy, and the thing had been so large and so new in his breast that it had forced itself out of his mouth. He had told Hatcher, and then he had driven home, and he had looked at his wife across the supper table, and the words had shrunk within him to the size of seeds, and he had swallowed them.

That had been Tuesday. Since Tuesday he had swallowed them three times a day.

"Well," he said heavily, "you know it now."

"Yes. I know it now."

She took up another piece of cloth. It was a small piece, blue, a child's garment. She held it up to the lamp and looked at it, turning it this way and that, and then she laid it in her lap and folded her hands upon it and did not sew.

"Tell me about it," she said.

He set the boot down. He felt that he must now make his speech or be forever a coward. He drew in his breath. He fixed his eyes upon a point somewhat above her head, where a calendar from the implement company hung upon a nail, displaying a picture of a red reaper in a field of impossible gold.

"There's silver out there," he began. "In the mountains. This man—Pruitt, his name is—he's got a claim staked, and he's took on four men already, and he needs two more, and he says a man that's willing to work can clear more in a summer than he'd clear here in five years. "A seal," said the woman.

"A gold seal. Stamped right into it." He made a little circle in the air with his forefinger. "I seen it."

"No," said the woman. "I don't s'pose it does."

"And who's going to plant?"

"Ed Sayre's boy. I'll get Ed Sayre's boy."

"Ed Sayre's boy is twelve years old."

"He's big for twelve."

"He's simple."

"He ain't simple. He's slow. There's a difference."

The woman smiled. It was not a good smile. It was thin and quick, like the crack that runs across a pond when a man steps too far out upon the ice, and he saw it and was afraid.

"You talked to Hatcher," she said, "and you talked to the man with the seal, and I s'pose you talked to Ed Sayre about his boy. Did you talk to Ed Sayre?"

He did not answer.

"You talked to everybody in the county," said the woman, "excepting me."

The stove ticked as its iron settled. A gust of wind came down off the hill and leaned against the house, and the window rattled in its frame, and a fine sifting of snow struck the glass with a sound like a whisper. The man listened to this whisper. It seemed to him that the whole night outside was listening also, crowding close to the panes, putting its great black ear against the walls.

He began to feel a deep and righteous anger. It came up in him slowly, out of some well of grievance he had not known he possessed. He had labored. He had broken his back upon this ground. He had stood in the burnt field in August with the dust rising about his knees, and he had not wept, though he had wished to. And now he was to be judged by this woman, who sat in the warm with her sewing, and who had never had to face Gilfillan across a desk with his hat in his hands. He considered that he had been very ill-used. He considered that there was no man in the township so ill-used as he.

"A man's got to do something," he said loudly. "A man can't set and wait for the sky. A man's got a right to try."

"I never said you hadn't a right."

"You're saying it now. You're setting there saying it."

"I'm setting here," said the woman, "and I ain't said nothing about rights at all."

This was true, and he knew it was true, and the knowledge enraged him further. He got up from his chair. He walked to the stove and lifted the lid of the pot that waited there, and looked into it, and saw a gray mass of potatoes and pork lying in congealed fat, and he set the lid down again with a clang. He walked to the window. He could see nothing in it but his own face, hung against the darkness, yellow and enormous, with the eyes sunk into it like two holes. He regarded this face with distaste. It seemed to him the face of a stranger, and not a stranger he would care to know.

"I thought you'd be glad," he said to the window.

Behind him the woman made a small sound. He did not know whether it was a laugh.

"Glad," she said.

"I thought—I thought you'd see it was for you. And for her." He jerked his head toward the ceiling. "I ain't going off to have a high time. It's work out there. It's hard work. Pruitt says men die of it sometimes. The cold, and the rock falls. He told me square. He didn't hide nothing."

"He told you men die of it."

"He told me square."

"And you told Hatcher, and you didn't tell me."

He turned from the window. She had risen. She stood by the table with the little blue garment crushed in one hand, and the lamplight came up under her chin and made her face strange, all hollows and high places, like a country seen from a hill at evening. He had known this face for nine years. He had seen it flushed at the dances at the Grange hall, and white upon the pillow when the child came, and brown and sweat-streaked under a sunbonnet in the hay. But he had never seen it as it was now. It seemed to him to be made of some hard pale substance, like the china dog upon the shelf in her mother's parlor, and he could not imagine that it had ever been soft.

"Why didn't you tell me?" she said.

He opened his mouth. The speech was gone. It had fled entirely, and in its place there was nothing but a great white silence, like a field after snowfall, without a track upon it anywhere.

"I don't know," he said.

And it was true. He did not know. He searched himself and found only a vague and shameful confusion, as of a boy discovered in the orchard with green apples in his shirt. He had been afraid. That was the whole of it. He had been afraid of this kitchen, and of this lamp, and of this woman with the needle that went in and came out. He had been less afraid of the mountains, and the rock falls, and the cold that killed men, than he had been of the moment when she would look up from her sewing. He perceived this now with a terrible clearness, and he was humiliated by it, and he hated her a little for having made him perceive it.

"I don't know," he said again.

The woman looked at him for a long moment. Then she sat down. She smoothed the blue garment upon her knee, pressing the wrinkles out of it with the flat of her hand, slowly, over and over, as one smooths the hair of a sick child.

"My father went to Californy," she said. "In 'forty-nine. Did I ever tell you?"

"No."

"He went. He had a paper too. I don't know if it had a seal on it." She smoothed the cloth. "Mother kept the place two years. She was smaller than me. She used to plow with a rope tied around her middle, so if the horse bolted it wouldn't run off with the plow. I used to watch her from the fence. I was six."

He waited.

"He come back," said the woman. "He come back the third spring. He walked in the door and set down at the table, just about where you're standing, and he didn't have nothing. Not a thing. He had a cough. And he set there and he looked at her, and she looked at him, and nobody said a word. And then she got up and give him his supper." She paused. "That's all. She give him his supper."

The wind leaned against the house again. The snow whispered at the glass.

"I ain't your father," said the man hoarsely.

"No," said the woman. "I know you ain't."

She did not say it unkindly. That was the worst of it. If she had flung it at him, he could have caught it and flung it back. But she laid it down very gently, like a cup set upon a table, and he did not know whether it was meant for an insult or for a mercy, and he stood there with his hands hanging and could not decide.

He came back to the table and sat down. The chair groaned under him. He put his elbows upon the oilcloth and looked at the lamp. A moth, wakened untimely by the heat, had come out of some crevice and was beating itself against the chimney with small, soft, tireless blows. He watched it. It seemed to him a very foolish creature. It seemed to him that there was no creature in all the earth so foolish as this moth, which could not see that the glass was there, and would batter itself to dust against it before it would turn away.

"I put my name down," he said at last. "I can't take it off. I give my word."

"I know."

"Pruitt's counting on me."

"I know."

"It wouldn't be honest."

"No," said the woman. "It wouldn't be honest."

They sat. The clock ticked. Above them the child murmured something in her sleep—a name, perhaps, or the fragment of a song—and was quiet.

"You'll want your heavy coat mended," said the woman. "The lining's gone at the shoulder."

He looked at her. Her head was bent. The needle had come up out of the blue cloth and was waiting in her fingers, catching the light.

"I'll do it in March," she said. "There ain't no hurry for it now."

He felt something rise in his throat, something enormous and formless, that might have been gratitude and might have been grief, and might have been merely the potatoes and pork, which he had not eaten. He swallowed it. He had grown expert in swallowing.

"All right," he said.

She went back to her sewing. The needle went in and came out, went in and came out. He sat and watched it. After a time he got up and went to the stove and took the pot from the back of it and spooned the gray mass into a bowl, and sat down again, and ate. It was cold. He ate all of it.

When he had finished, she rose and took the bowl from him without a word and carried it to the basin. He heard the dipper strike the bottom of the pail. He heard water poured. These were small sounds, homely sounds, and he had heard them every night for nine years, and he had never once listened to them before.

Outside, the crimson bar had long since gone from the sky over the hill. The night was black and very large. Far off, beyond the hill and beyond the next hill and beyond all the hills there were, the mountains stood up in the darkness, white and indifferent, with the silver locked in their hearts. They did not know his name. They did not know that he was coming. He thought of this as he sat in the hot kitchen with the lamp before him, and it seemed to him, for a moment, a very lonely thing.

Then the woman came back and wound the clock.

Here is an excerpt of Stephen Crane's writing, to show you their style:

The youth felt, however, that his problem was in no wise lifted from him. There was, on the contrary, an irritating prolongation. The tale had created in him a great concern for himself. Now, with the newborn question in his mind, he was compelled to sink back into his old place as part of a blue demonstration. For days he made ceaseless calculations, but they were all wondrously unsatisfactory. He found that he could establish nothing. He finally concluded that the only way to prove himself was to go into the blaze, and then figuratively to watch his legs to discover their merits and faults. He reluctantly admitted that he could not sit still and with a mental slate and pencil derive an answer. To gain it, he must have blaze, blood, and danger, even as a chemist requires this, that, and the other. So he fretted for an opportunity. Meanwhile, he continually tried to measure himself by his comrades. The tall soldier, for one, gave him some assurance. This man’s serene unconcern dealt him a measure of confidence, for he had known him since childhood, and from his intimate knowledge he did not see how he could be capable of anything that was beyond him, the youth. Still, he thought that his comrade might be mistaken about himself. Or, on the other hand, he might be a man heretofore doomed to peace and obscurity, but, in reality, made to shine in war. The youth would have liked to have discovered another who suspected himself. A sympathetic comparison of mental notes would have been a joy to him. He occasionally tried to fathom a comrade with seductive sentences. He looked about to find men in the proper mood. All attempts failed to bring forth any statement which looked in any way like a confession to those doubts which he privately acknowledged in himself. He was afraid to make an open declaration of his concern, because he dreaded to place some unscrupulous confidant upon the high plane of the unconfessed from which elevation he could be derided. In regard to his companions his mind wavered between two opinions, according to his mood. Sometimes he inclined to believing them all heroes. In fact, he usually admired in secret the superior development of the higher qualities in others. He could conceive of men going very insignificantly about the world bearing a load of courage unseen, and although he had known many of his comrades through boyhood, he began to fear that his judgment of them had been blind. Then, in other moments, he flouted these theories, and assured him that his fellows were all privately wondering and quaking. His emotions made him feel strange in the presence of men who talked excitedly of a prospective battle as of a drama they were about to witness, with nothing but eagerness and curiosity apparent in their faces. It was often that he suspected them to be liars. He did not pass such thoughts without severe condemnation of himself. He dinned reproaches at times. He was convicted by himself of many shameful crimes against the gods of traditions. In his great anxiety his heart was continually clamoring at what he considered the intolerable slowness of the generals. They seemed content to perch tranquilly on the river bank, and leave him bowed down by the weight of a great problem. He wanted it settled forthwith. He could not long bear such a load, he said. Sometimes his anger at the commanders reached an acute stage, and he grumbled about the camp like a veteran. One morning, however, he found himself in the ranks of his prepared regiment. The men were whispering speculations and recounting the old rumors. In the gloom before the break of the day their uniforms glowed a deep purple hue. From across the river the red eyes were still peering. In the eastern sky there was a yellow patch like a rug laid for the feet of the coming sun; and against it, black and patternlike, loomed the gigantic figure of the colonel on a gigantic horse. From off in the darkness came the trampling of feet. The youth could occasionally see dark shadows that moved like monsters. The regiment stood at rest for what seemed a long time. The youth grew impatient. It was unendurable the way these affairs were managed. He wondered how long they were to be kept waiting. As he looked all about him and pondered upon the mystic gloom, he began to believe that at any moment the ominous distance might be aflare, and the rolling crashes of an engagement come to his ears. Staring once at the red eyes across the river, he conceived them to be growing larger, as the orbs of a row of dragons advancing. He turned toward the colonel and saw him lift his gigantic arm and calmly stroke his mustache. At last he heard from along the road at the foot of the hill the clatter of a horse’s galloping hoofs. It must be the coming of orders. He bent forward, scarce breathing. The exciting clickety-click, as it grew louder and louder, seemed to be beating upon his soul. Presently a horseman with jangling equipment drew rein before the colonel of the regiment. The two held a short, sharp-worded conversation. The men in the foremost ranks craned their necks. As the horseman wheeled his animal and galloped away he turned to shout over his shoulder, “Don’t forget that box of cigars!” The colonel mumbled in reply. The youth wondered what a box of cigars had to do with war. A moment later the regiment went swinging off into the darkness. It was now like one of those moving monsters wending with many feet. The air was heavy, and cold with dew. A mass of wet grass, marched upon, rustled like silk. There was an occasional flash and glimmer of steel from the backs of all these huge crawling reptiles. From the road came creakings and grumblings as some surly guns were dragged away. The men stumbled along still muttering speculations. There was a subdued debate. Once a man fell down, and as he reached for his rifle a comrade, unseeing, trod upon his hand. He of the injured fingers swore bitterly, and aloud. A low, tittering laugh went among his fellows. Presently they passed into a roadway and marched forward with easy strides. A dark regiment moved before them, and from behind also came the tinkle of equipments on the bodies of marching men. The rushing yellow of the developing day went on behind their backs. When the sunrays at last struck full and mellowingly upon the earth, the youth saw that the landscape was streaked with two long, thin, black columns which disappeared on the brow of a hill in front and rearward vanished in a wood. They were like two serpents crawling from the cavern of the night. The river was not in view. The tall soldier burst into praises of what he thought to be his powers of perception. Some of the tall one’s companions cried with emphasis that they, too, had evolved the same thing, and they congratulated themselves upon it. But there were others who said that the tall one’s plan was not the true one at all. They persisted with other theories. There was a vigorous discussion. The youth took no part in them. As he walked along in careless line he was engaged with his own eternal debate. He could not hinder himself from dwelling upon it. He was despondent and sullen, and threw shifting glances about him. He looked ahead, often expecting to hear from the advance the rattle of firing. But the long serpents crawled slowly from hill to hill without bluster of smoke. A dun-colored cloud of dust floated away to the right. The sky overhead was of a fairy blue. The youth studied the faces of his companions, ever on the watch to detect kindred emotions. He suffered disappointment. Some ardor of the air which was causing the veteran commands to move with glee—almost with song—had infected the new regiment. The men began to speak of victory as of a thing they knew. Also, the tall soldier received his vindication. They were certainly going to come around in behind the enemy. They expressed commiseration for that part of the army which had been left upon the river bank, felicitating themselves upon being a part of a blasting host. The youth, considering himself as separated from the others, was saddened by the blithe and merry speeches that went from rank to rank. The company wags all made their best endeavors. The regiment tramped to the tune of laughter. The blatant soldier often convulsed whole files by his biting sarcasms aimed at the tall one. And it was not long before all the men seemed to forget their mission. Whole brigades grinned in unison, and regiments laughed. A rather fat soldier attempted to pilfer a horse from a dooryard. He planned to load his knapsack upon it. He was escaping with his prize when a young girl rushed from the house and grabbed the animal’s mane. There followed a wrangle. The young girl, with pink cheeks and shining eyes, stood like a dauntless statue. The observant regiment, standing at rest in the roadway, whooped at once, and entered whole-souled upon the side of the maiden. The men became so engrossed in this affair that they entirely ceased to remember their own large war. They jeered the piratical private, and called attention to various defects in his personal appearance; and they were wildly enthusiastic in support of the young girl. To her, from some distance, came bold advice. “Hit him with a stick.” There were crows and catcalls showered upon him when he retreated without the horse. The regiment rejoiced at his downfall. Loud and vociferous congratulations were showered upon the maiden, who stood panting and regarding the troops with defiance. At nightfall the column broke into regimental pieces, and the fragments went into the fields to camp. Tents sprang up like strange plants. Camp fires, like red, peculiar blossoms, dotted the night. The youth kept from intercourse with his companions as much as circumstances would allow him. In the evening he wandered a few paces into the gloom. From this little distance the many fires, with the black forms of men passing to and fro before the crimson rays, made weird and satanic effects. He lay down in the grass. The blades pressed tenderly against his cheek. The moon had been lighted and was hung in a treetop. The liquid stillness of the night enveloping him made him feel vast pity for himself. There was a caress in the soft winds; and the whole mood of the darkness, he thought, was one of sympathy for himself in his distress. He wished, without reserve, that he was at home again making the endless rounds from the house to the barn, from the barn to the fields, from the fields to the barn, from the barn to the house. He remembered he had so often cursed the brindle cow and her mates, and had sometimes flung milking stools. But, from his present point of view, there was a halo of happiness about each of their heads, and he would have sacrificed all the brass buttons on the continent to have been enabled to return to them. He told himself that he was not formed for a soldier. And he mused seriously upon the radical differences between himself and those men who were dodging implike around the fires. As he mused thus he heard the rustle of grass, and, upon turning his head, discovered the loud soldier. He called out, “Oh, Wilson!” The latter approached and looked down. “Why, hello, Henry; is it you? What are you doing here?”

“Oh, thinking,” said the youth. The other sat down and carefully lighted his pipe. “You’re getting blue my boy. You’re looking thundering peek-ed. What the dickens is wrong with you?”

“Oh, nothing,” said the youth. The loud soldier launched then into the subject of the anticipated fight. “Oh, we’ve got ’em now!” As he spoke his boyish face was wreathed in a gleeful smile, and his voice had an exultant ring. “We’ve got ’em now. At last, by the eternal thunders, we’ll lick ’em good!”

“If the truth was known,” he added, more soberly, “they’ve licked us about every clip up to now; but this time—this time—we’ll lick ’em good!”

“I thought you was objecting to this march a little while ago,” said the youth coldly.

“Oh, it wasn’t that,” explained the other. “I don’t mind marching, if there’s going to be fighting at the end of it. What I hate is this getting moved here and moved there, with no good coming of it, as far as I can see, excepting sore feet and damned short rations.”

“Well, Jim Conklin says we’ll get plenty of fighting this time.”

“He’s right for once, I guess, though I can’t see how it come. This time we’re in for a big battle, and we’ve got the best end of it, certain sure. Gee rod! how we will thump ’em!” He arose and began to pace to and fro excitedly. The thrill of his enthusiasm made him walk with an elastic step. He was sprightly, vigorous, fiery in his belief in success. He looked into the future with clear proud eye, and he swore with the air of an old soldier. The youth watched him for a moment in silence. When he finally spoke his voice was as bitter as dregs. “Oh, you’re going to do great things, I s’pose!” The loud soldier blew a thoughtful cloud of smoke from his pipe. “Oh, I don’t know,” he remarked with dignity; “I don’t know. I s’pose I’ll do as well as the rest. I’m going to try like thunder.” He evidently complimented himself upon the modesty of this statement.

“How do you know you won’t run when the time comes?” asked the youth.

“Run?” said the loud one; “run?—of course not!” He laughed.

“Well,” continued the youth, “lots of good-a-’nough men have thought they was going to do great things before the fight, but when the time come they skedaddled.”

“Oh, that’s all true, I s’pose,” replied the other; “but I’m not going to skedaddle. The man that bets on my running will lose his money, that’s all.” He nodded confidently.

“Oh, shucks!” said the youth. “You ain’t the bravest man in the world, are you?”

“No, I ain’t,” exclaimed the loud soldier indignantly; “and I didn’t say I was the bravest man in the world, neither. I said I was going to do my share of fighting—that’s what I said. And I am, too. Who are you, anyhow? You talk as if you thought you was Napoleon Bonaparte.” He glared at the youth for a moment, and then strode away. The youth called in a savage voice after his comrade: “Well, you needn’t git mad about it!” But the other continued on his way and made no reply. He felt alone in space when his injured comrade had disappeared. His failure to discover any mite of resemblance in their viewpoints made him more miserable than before. No one seemed to be wrestling with such a terrific personal problem. He was a mental outcast. He went slowly to his tent and stretched himself on a blanket by the side of the snoring tall soldier. In the darkness he saw visions of a thousand-tongued fear that would babble at his back and cause him to flee, while others were going coolly about their country’s business. He admitted that he would not be able to cope with this monster. He felt that every nerve in his body would be an ear to hear the voices, while other men would remain stolid and deaf. And as he sweated with the pain of these thoughts, he could hear low, serene sentences. “I’ll bid five.” “Make it six.” “Seven.” “Seven goes.” He stared at the red, shivering reflection of a fire on the white wall of his tent until, exhausted and ill from the monotony of his suffering, he fell asleep.

The observant regiment, standing at rest in the roadway, whooped at once, and entered whole-souled upon the side of the maiden. The men became so engrossed in this affair that they entirely ceased to remember their own large war. They jeered the piratical private, and called attention to various defects in his personal appearance; and they were wildly enthusiastic in support of the young girl. To her, from some distance, came bold advice. “Hit him with a stick.” There were crows and catcalls showered upon him when he retreated without the horse. The regiment rejoiced at his downfall. Loud and vociferous congratulations were showered upon the maiden, who stood panting and regarding the troops with defiance. At nightfall the column broke into regimental pieces, and the fragments went into the fields to camp. Tents sprang up like strange plants. Camp fires, like red, peculiar blossoms, dotted the night. The youth kept from intercourse with his companions as much as circumstances would allow him. In the evening he wandered a few paces into the gloom. From this little distance the many fires, with the black forms of men passing to and fro before the crimson rays, made weird and satanic effects. He lay down in the grass. The blades pressed tenderly against his cheek. The moon had been lighted and was hung in a treetop. The liquid stillness of the night enveloping him made him feel vast pity for himself. There was a caress in the soft winds; and the whole mood of the darkness, he thought, was one of sympathy for himself in his distress. He wished, without reserve, that he was at home again making the endless rounds from the house to the barn, from the barn to the fields, from the fields to the barn, from the barn to the house. He remembered he had so often cursed the brindle cow and her mates, and had sometimes flung milking stools. But, from his present point of view, there was a halo of happiness about each of their heads, and he would have sacrificed all the brass buttons on the continent to have been enabled to return to them. He told himself that he was not formed for a soldier. And he mused seriously upon the radical differences between himself and those men who were dodging implike around the fires. As he mused thus he heard the rustle of grass, and, upon turning his head, discovered the loud soldier. He called out, “Oh, Wilson!” The latter approached and looked down. “Why, hello, Henry; is it you? What are you doing here?”

“Oh, thinking,” said the youth. The other sat down and carefully lighted his pipe. “You’re getting blue my boy. You’re looking thundering peek-ed. What the dickens is wrong with you?”

“Oh, nothing,” said the youth. The loud soldier launched then into the subject of the anticipated fight. “Oh, we’ve got ’em now!” As he spoke his boyish face was wreathed in a gleeful smile, and his voice had an exultant ring. “We’ve got ’em now. At last, by the eternal thunders, we’ll lick ’em good!”

“If the truth was known,” he added, more soberly, “they’ve licked us about every clip up to now; but this time—this time—we’ll lick ’em good!”

“I thought you was objecting to this march a little while ago,” said the youth coldly.

“Oh, it wasn’t that,” explained the other. “I don’t mind marching, if there’s going to be fighting at the end of it. What I hate is this getting moved here and moved there, with no good coming of it, as far as I can see, excepting sore feet and damned short rations.”

“Well, Jim Conklin says we’ll get plenty of fighting this time.”

“He’s right for once, I guess, though I can’t see how it come. This time we’re in for a big battle, and we’ve got the best end of it, certain sure. Gee rod! how we will thump ’em!” He arose and began to pace to and fro excitedly. The thrill of his enthusiasm made him walk with an elastic step. He was sprightly, vigorous, fiery in his belief in success. He looked into the future with clear proud eye, and he swore with the air of an old soldier. The youth watched him for a moment in silence. When he finally spoke his voice was as bitter as dregs. “Oh, you’re going to do great things, I s’pose!” The loud soldier blew a thoughtful cloud of smoke from his pipe. “Oh, I don’t know,” he remarked with dignity; “I don’t know. I s’pose I’ll do as well as the rest. I’m going to try like thunder.” He evidently complimented himself upon the modesty of this statement.

“How do you know you won’t run when the time comes?” asked the youth.

“Run?” said the loud one; “run?—of course not!” He laughed.

“Well,” continued the youth, “lots of good-a-’nough men have thought they was going to do great things before the fight, but when the time come they skedaddled.”

“Oh, that’s all true, I s’pose,” replied the other; “but I’m not going to skedaddle. The man that bets on my running will lose his money, that’s all.” He nodded confidently.

“Oh, shucks!” said the youth. “You ain’t the bravest man in the world, are you?”

“No, I ain’t,” exclaimed the loud soldier indignantly; “and I didn’t say I was the bravest man in the world, neither. I said I was going to do my share of fighting—that’s what I said. And I am, too. Who are you, anyhow? You talk as if you thought you was Napoleon Bonaparte.” He glared at the youth for a moment, and then strode away. The youth called in a savage voice after his comrade: “Well, you needn’t git mad about it!” But the other continued on his way and made no reply. He felt alone in space when his injured comrade had disappeared. His failure to discover any mite of resemblance in their viewpoints made him more miserable than before. No one seemed to be wrestling with such a terrific personal problem. He was a mental outcast. He went slowly to his tent and stretched himself on a blanket by the side of the snoring tall soldier. In the darkness he saw visions of a thousand-tongued fear that would babble at his back and cause him to flee, while others were going coolly about their country’s business. He admitted that he would not be able to cope with this monster. He felt that every nerve in his body would be an ear to hear the voices, while other men would remain stolid and deaf. And as he sweated with the pain of these thoughts, he could hear low, serene sentences. “I’ll bid five.” “Make it six.” “Seven.” “Seven goes.” He stared at the red, shivering reflection of a fire on the white wall of his tent until, exhausted and ill from the monotony of his suffering, he fell asleep.
