"Sit down, and call your lady-friend over," she said cordially to Pete. At his beckoning Maggie came and sat between Pete and the mere boy.

"I thought yeh were gone away fer good," began Pete, at once. "When did yeh git back? How did dat Buff'lo bus'ness turn out?" The woman shrugged her shoulders. "Well, he didn't have as many stamps as he tried to make out, so I shook him, that's all."

"Well, I'm glad teh see yehs back in deh city," said Pete, with awkward gallantry. He and the woman entered into a long conversation, exchanging reminiscences of days together. Maggie sat still, unable to formulate an intelligent sentence upon the conversation and painfully aware of it. She saw Pete's eyes sparkle as he gazed upon the handsome stranger. He listened smilingly to all she said. The woman was familiar with all his affairs, asked him about mutual friends, and knew the amount of his salary. She paid no attention to Maggie, looking toward her once or twice and apparently seeing the wall beyond. The mere boy was sulky. In the beginning he had welcomed with acclamations the additions.

"Let's all have a drink! What'll you take, Nell? And you, Miss what's-your-name. Have a drink, Mr. ——-, you, I mean." He had shown a sprightly desire to do the talking for the company and tell all about his family. In a loud voice he declaimed on various topics. He assumed a patronizing air toward Pete. As Maggie was silent, he paid no attention to her. He made a great show of lavishing wealth upon the woman of brilliance and audacity.

"Do keep still, Freddie! You gibber like an ape, dear," said the woman to him. She turned away and devoted her attention to Pete.

"We'll have many a good time together again, eh?"

"Sure, Mike," said Pete, enthusiastic at once.

"Say," whispered she, leaning forward, "let's go over to Billie's and have a heluva time."

"Well, it's dis way! See?" said Pete. "I got dis lady frien' here."

"Oh, t'hell with her," argued the woman. Pete appeared disturbed.

"All right," said she, nodding her head at him. "All right for you! We'll see the next time you ask me to go anywheres with you." Pete squirmed.

Excerpt 3: Pete did not consider that he had ruined Maggie. If he had thought that her soul could never smile again, he would have believed the mother and brother, who were pyrotechnic over the affair, to be responsible for it. Besides, in his world, souls did not insist upon being able to smile. "What deh hell?" He felt a trifle entangled. It distressed him. Revelations and scenes might bring upon him the wrath of the owner of the saloon, who insisted upon respectability of an advanced type.

"What deh hell do dey wanna raise such a smoke about it fer?" demanded he of himself, disgusted with the attitude of the family. He saw no necessity for anyone's losing their equilibrium merely because their sister or their daughter had stayed away from home. Searching about in his mind for possible reasons for their conduct, he came upon the conclusion that Maggie's motives were correct, but that the two others wished to snare him. He felt pursued. The woman of brilliance and audacity whom he had met in the hilarious hall showed a disposition to ridicule him.

"A little pale thing with no spirit," she said. "Did you note the expression of her eyes? There was something in them about pumpkin pie and virtue. That is a peculiar way the left corner of her mouth has of twitching, isn't it? Dear, dear, my cloud-compelling Pete, what are you coming to?" Pete asserted at once that he never was very much interested in the girl. The woman interrupted him, laughing.

"Oh, it's not of the slightest consequence to me, my dear young man. You needn't draw maps for my benefit. Why should I be concerned about it?" But Pete continued with his explanations. If he was laughed at for his tastes in women, he felt obliged to say that they were only temporary or indifferent ones. The morning after Maggie had departed from home, Pete stood behind the bar. He was immaculate in white jacket and apron and his hair was plastered over his brow with infinite correctness. No customers were in the place. Pete was twisting his napkined fist slowly in a beer glass, softly whistling to himself and occasionally holding the object of his attention between his eyes and a few weak beams of sunlight that had found their way over the thick screens and into the shaded room. With lingering thoughts of the woman of brilliance and audacity, the bartender raised his head and stared through the varying cracks between the swaying bamboo doors. Suddenly the whistling pucker faded from his lips. He saw Maggie walking slowly past. He gave a great start, fearing for the previously-mentioned eminent respectability of the place. He threw a swift, nervous glance about him, all at once feeling guilty. No one was in the room. He went hastily over to the side door. Opening it and looking out, he perceived Maggie standing, as if undecided, on the corner. She was searching the place with her eyes. As she turned her face toward him Pete beckoned to her hurriedly, intent upon returning with speed to a position behind the bar and to the atmosphere of respectability upon which the proprietor insisted. Maggie came to him, the anxious look disappearing from her face and a smile wreathing her lips.

"Oh, Pete—," she began brightly. The bartender made a violent gesture of impatience.

"Oh, my Gawd," cried he, vehemently. "What deh hell do yeh wanna hang aroun' here fer? Do yeh wanna git me inteh trouble?" he demanded with an air of injury. Astonishment swept over the girl's features. "Why, Pete! yehs tol' me—" Pete glanced profound irritation. His countenance reddened with the anger of a man whose respectability is being threatened.

"Say, yehs makes me tired. See? What deh hell deh yeh wanna tag aroun' atter me fer? Yeh'll git me inteh trouble wid deh ol' man an' dey'll be hell teh pay! If he sees a woman roun' here he'll go crazy an' I'll lose me job! See? Yer brudder come in here an' raised hell an' deh ol' man hada put up fer it! An' now I'm done! See? I'm done." The girl's eyes stared into his face. "Pete, don't yeh remem—" "Oh, hell," interrupted Pete, anticipating. The girl seemed to have a struggle with herself. She was apparently bewildered and could not find speech. Finally she asked in a low voice: "But where kin I go?" The question exasperated Pete beyond the powers of endurance. It was a direct attempt to give him some responsibility in a matter that did not concern him. In his indignation he volunteered information.

"Oh, go teh hell," cried he. He slammed the door furiously and returned, with an air of relief, to his respectability. Maggie went away. She wandered aimlessly for several blocks. She stopped once and asked aloud a question of herself: "Who?" A man who was passing near her shoulder, humorously took the questioning word as intended for him.

"Eh? What? Who? Nobody! I didn't say anything," he laughingly said, and continued his way. Soon the girl discovered that if she walked with such apparent aimlessness, some men looked at her with calculating eyes. She quickened her step, frightened. As a protection, she adopted a demeanor of intentness as if going somewhere. After a time she left rattling avenues and passed between rows of houses with sternness and stolidity stamped upon their features. She hung her head for she felt their eyes grimly upon her. Suddenly she came upon a stout gentleman in a silk hat and a chaste black coat, whose decorous row of buttons reached from his chin to his knees. The girl had heard of the Grace of God and she decided to approach this man. His beaming, chubby face was a picture of benevolence and kind-heartedness. His eyes shone good-will. But as the girl timidly accosted him, he gave a convulsive movement and saved his respectability by a vigorous side-step. He did not risk it to save a soul. For how was he to know that there was a soul before him that needed saving?

Upon a wet evening, several months after the last chapter, two interminable rows of cars, pulled by slipping horses, jangled along a prominent side-street. A dozen cabs, with coat-enshrouded drivers, clattered to and fro. Electric lights, whirring softly, shed a blurred radiance. A flower dealer, his feet tapping impatiently, his nose and his wares glistening with rain-drops, stood behind an array of roses and chrysanthemums. Two or three theatres emptied a crowd upon the storm-swept pavements. Men pulled their hats over their eyebrows and raised their collars to their ears. Women shrugged impatient shoulders in their warm cloaks and stopped to arrange their skirts for a walk through the storm. People having been comparatively silent for two hours burst into a roar of conversation, their hearts still kindling from the glowings of the stage. The pavements became tossing seas of umbrellas. Men stepped forth to hail cabs or cars, raising their fingers in varied forms of polite request or imperative demand. An endless procession wended toward elevated stations. An atmosphere of pleasure and prosperity seemed to hang over the throng, born, perhaps, of good clothes and of having just emerged from a place of forgetfulness. In the mingled light and gloom of an adjacent park, a handful of wet wanderers, in attitudes of chronic dejection, was scattered among the benches. A girl of the painted cohorts of the city went along the street. She threw changing glances at men who passed her, giving smiling invitations to men of rural or untaught pattern and usually seeming sedately unconscious of the men with a metropolitan seal upon their faces. Crossing glittering avenues, she went into the throng emerging from the places of forgetfulness. She hurried forward through the crowd as if intent upon reaching a distant home, bending forward in her handsome cloak, daintily lifting her skirts and picking for her well-shod feet the dryer spots upon the pavements. The restless doors of saloons, clashing to and fro, disclosed animated rows of men before bars and hurrying barkeepers. A concert hall gave to the street faint sounds of swift, machine-like music, as if a group of phantom musicians were hastening. A tall young man, smoking a cigarette with a sublime air, strolled near the girl. He had on evening dress, a moustache, a chrysanthemum, and a look of ennui, all of which he kept carefully under his eye. Seeing the girl walk on as if such a young man as he was not in existence, he looked back transfixed with interest. He stared glassily for a moment, but gave a slight convulsive start when he discerned that she was neither new, Parisian, nor theatrical. He wheeled about hastily and turned his stare into the air, like a sailor with a search-light. A stout gentleman, with pompous and philanthropic whiskers, went stolidly by, the broad of his back sneering at the girl. A belated man in business clothes, and in haste to catch a car, bounced against her shoulder. "Hi, there, Mary, I beg your pardon! Brace up, old girl." He grasped her arm to steady her, and then was away running down the middle of the street. The girl walked on out of the realm of restaurants and saloons. She passed more glittering avenues and went into darker blocks than those where the crowd travelled. A young man in light overcoat and derby hat received a glance shot keenly from the eyes of the girl. He stopped and looked at her, thrusting his hands in his pockets and making a mocking smile curl his lips. "Come, now, old lady," he said, "you don't mean to tel me that you sized me up for a farmer?" A labouring man marched along; with bundles under his arms. To her remarks, he replied, "It's a fine evenin', ain't it?" She smiled squarely into the face of a boy who was hurrying by with his hands buried in his overcoat pockets, his blonde locks bobbing on his youthful temples, and a cheery smile of unconcern upon his lips. He turned his head and smiled back at her, waving his hands.

"Not this eve—some other eve!" A drunken man, reeling in her pathway, began to roar at her. "I ain' ga no money!" he shouted, in a dismal voice. He lurched on up the street, wailing to himself: "I ain' ga no money. Ba' luck. Ain' ga no more money." The girl went into gloomy districts near the river, where the tall black factories shut in the street and only occasional broad beams of light fell across the pavements from saloons. In front of one of these places, whence came the sound of a violin vigorously scraped, the patter of feet on boards and the ring of loud laughter, there stood a man with blotched features. Further on in the darkness she met a ragged being with shifting, bloodshot eyes and grimy hands. She went into the blackness of the final block. The shutters of the tall buildings were closed like grim lips. The structures seemed to have eyes that looked over them, beyond them, at other things. Afar off the lights of the avenues glittered as if from an impossible distance. Street-car bells jingled with a sound of merriment. At the feet of the tall buildings appeared the deathly black hue of the river. Some hidden factory sent up a yellow glare, that lit for a moment the waters lapping oilily against timbers. The varied sounds of life, made joyous by distance and seeming unapproachableness, came faintly and died away to a silence.

In a partitioned-off section of a saloon sat a man with a half dozen women, gleefully laughing, hovering about him. The man had arrived at that stage of drunkenness where affection is felt for the universe.

"I'm good f'ler, girls," he said, convincingly. "I'm damn good f'ler. An'body treats me right, I allus trea's zem right! See?" The women nodded their heads approvingly. "To be sure," they cried out in hearty chorus. "You're the kind of a man we like, Pete. You're outa sight! What yeh goin' to buy this time, dear?"

"An't'ing yehs wants, damn it," said the man in an abandonment of good will. His countenance shone with the true spirit of benevolence. He was in the proper mode of missionaries. He would have fraternized with obscure Hottentots. And above all, he was overwhelmed in tenderness for his friends, who were all illustrious.

"An't'ing yehs wants, damn it," repeated he, waving his hands with beneficent recklessness. "I'm good f'ler, girls, an' if an'body treats me right I—here," called he through an open door to a waiter, "bring girls drinks, damn it. What 'ill yehs have, girls? An't'ing yehs wants, damn it!" The waiter glanced in with the disgusted look of the man who serves intoxicants for the man who takes too much of them. He nodded his head shortly at the order from each individual, and went.

"Damn it," said the man, "we're havin' heluva time. I like you girls! Damn'd if I don't! Yer right sort! See?" He spoke at length and with feeling, concerning the excellencies of his assembled friends.

"Don' try pull man's leg, but have a heluva time! Das right! Das way teh do! Now, if I sawght yehs tryin' work me fer drinks, wouldn' buy damn t'ing! But yer right sort, damn it! Yehs know how ter treat a f'ler, an' I stays by yehs 'til spen' las' cent! Das right! I'm good f'ler an' I knows when an'body treats me right!" Between the times of the arrival and departure of the waiter, the man discoursed to the women on the tender regard he felt for all living things. He laid stress upon the purity of his motives in all dealings with men in the world and spoke of the fervor of his friendship for those who were amiable. Tears welled slowly from his eyes. His voice quavered when he spoke to them. Once when the waiter was about to depart with an empty tray, the man drew a coin from his pocket and held it forth.

"Here," said he, quite magnificently, "here's quar'." The waiter kept his hands on his tray.

"I don' want yer money," he said. The other put forth the coin with tearful insistence.

"Here, damn it," cried he, "tak't! Yer damn goo' f'ler an' I wan' yehs tak't!"

"Come, come, now," said the waiter, with the sullen air of a man who is forced into giving advice. "Put yer mon in yer pocket! Yer loaded an' yehs on'y makes a damn fool of yerself." As the latter passed out of the door the man turned pathetically to the women.

"He don' know I'm damn goo' f'ler," cried he, dismally.

"Never you mind, Pete, dear," said a woman of brilliance and audacity, laying her hand with great affection upon his arm. "Never you mind, old boy! We'll stay by you, dear!"

"Das ri'," cried the man, his face lighting up at the soothing tones of the woman's voice. "Das ri', I'm damn goo' f'ler an' w'en anyone trea's me ri', I treats zem ri'! Shee!"

"Sure!" cried the women. "And we're not goin' back on you, old man." The man turned appealing eyes to the woman of brilliance and audacity. He felt that if he could be convicted of a contemptible action he would die.

"Shay, Nell, damn it, I allus trea's yehs shquare, didn' I? I allus been goo' f'ler wi' yehs, ain't I, Nell?"

"Sure you have, Pete," assented the woman. She delivered an oration to her companions. "Yessir, that's a fact. Pete's a square fellah, he is. He never goes back on a friend. He's the right kind an' we stay by him, don't we, girls?"

"Sure," they exclaimed. Looking lovingly at him they raised their glasses and drank his health.

"Girlsh," said the man, beseechingly, "I allus trea's yehs ri', didn' I? I'm goo' f'ler, ain' I, girlsh?"

"Sure," again they chorused.

"Well," said he finally, "le's have nozzer drink, zen."

"That's right," hailed a woman, "that's right. Yer no bloomin' jay! Yer spends yer money like a man. Dat's right." The man pounded the table with his quivering fists.

"Yessir," he cried, with deep earnestness, as if someone disputed him. "I'm damn goo' f'ler, an' w'en anyone trea's me ri', I allus trea's—le's have nozzer drink." He began to beat the wood with his glass.

"Shay," howled he, growing suddenly impatient. As the waiter did not then come, the man swelled with wrath.

"Shay," howled he again. The waiter appeared at the door.

"Bringsh drinksh," said the man. The waiter disappeared with the orders.

"Zat f'ler damn fool," cried the man. "He insul' me! I'm ge'man! Can' stan' be insul'! I'm goin' lickim when comes!"

"No, no," cried the women, crowding about and trying to subdue him. "He's all right! He didn't mean anything! Let it go! He's a good fellah!"

"Din' he insul' me?" asked the man earnestly.

"No," said they. "Of course he didn't! He's all right!"

"Sure he didn' insul' me?" demanded the man, with deep anxiety in his voice.

"No, no! We know him! He's a good fellah. He didn't mean anything."

"Well, zen," said the man, resolutely, "I'm go' 'pol'gize!" When the waiter came, the man struggled to the middle of the floor.

"Girlsh shed you insul' me! I shay damn lie! I 'pol'gize!"

"All right," said the waiter.

The court lay between two tenements like a crack in a dropped plate. Into it the sun, at a certain hour of the afternoon, poured a yellow heat that made the ash barrels exhale. Washing hung across from window to window in lines of grey flags, as if a dingy army had surrendered there and been forgotten by its conquerors. From the doorways came the odors of boiled cabbage and of babies. Women leaned upon the sills with their elbows planted in a strength of habit, and regarded the court below as generals regard a field upon which nothing of consequence has happened for some time.

Upon the flags of the court a horde of children waged an endless campaign. They had no particular enemy. They fought with the readiness of creatures who had found that the world was composed of knees and elbows, and that a man must use his own lest the other fellow use his first. Their cries arose shrilly to the windows, where the women heard them with the indifference of persons long accustomed to the sound of the sea.

Among these warriors was Patsy Kerrigan, aged six. He was a small, square boy with a face that seemed to have been modelled hastily out of dough and left in the weather. His hair stood up in a defiant brush. His trousers, which had been his brother's and before that had been the property of some unknown man of considerable girth, were folded about his waist and held by a cord. He carried himself with the swagger of one who has been told that he is too little, and who intends to prove the statement a lie.

At the mouth of the court, where it opened upon the avenue, stood the cart of a fruit vendor. It was heaped with apples, red and yellow and of a glistening that seemed wicked. The vendor was a lean man from a far country, with mournful eyes and a moustache that drooped as if it had been wept upon. He used the English tongue as a man uses a strange weapon, clumsily and with great noise. He sat upon an overturned box and fanned himself with his hat, regarding his apples with the tender expression of a father.

Three boys of greater years leaned against the wall near the cart. They were members of an organization that met upon the corner by Hennessy's, and they were of an age when a lad begins to spit with judgment. They had observed Patsy. They called to him.

"Say, kid, c'mere."

Patsy went. He went with a heart that leaped. It was a thing of glory to be summoned by such men.

"Yeh see dem apples?" said the eldest, a youth with a cap pulled over one eye and an air of having already exhausted the world. "Yeh ain't got deh nerve teh swipe one. Yer a baby."

Patsy surveyed the cart. It loomed before him like a fortress. The vendor's mournful eyes seemed to him the eyes of a dragon that slept with one lid open. He thought of the disgrace of being a baby. It was an intolerable thing. He thought also, dimly, of his mother; but she was far up in the sky, at a window on the fourth floor, and the youth with the cap was here, at his very elbow, sneering.

"I ain't no baby," said Patsy.

"Den git one."

He went forward. He walked with a bravado that his legs did not altogether share. The vendor had turned his head to bargain with a woman in a shawl. Patsy's hand went out. It closed upon an apple that was very red and very smooth and cool, and it seemed to him that all the bells of the city had begun to ring.

Then the vendor turned. He beheld his apple departing in the fist of a child, and he rose from his box with a cry of anguish that was heard in the remote windows. He waved both arms. He called upon a saint whose name nobody in the court had ever heard.

Patsy fled. He did not run toward the three youths, for when he looked for them they had already become merely three backs disappearing round the corner by Hennessy's, with the dignified haste of men who remember an engagement. He ran into the court, scattering the lesser warriors, and dived into the black mouth of his own doorway. Behind him came the vendor, shouting, his feet slapping upon the stones.

The stairs of the tenement were dark and smelled of many dinners. Patsy went up them like a squirrel. The vendor followed, panting, and his cries rang hollowly in the well of the building. Doors opened upon each landing. Heads were thrust forth. The sages of the second floor, who were three old women with nothing to do, came out and stood together in a grim row, prepared to judge.

Upon the fourth landing a door was flung open with a violence that shook the plaster. In it there appeared Mrs. Kerrigan.

She was a woman of vast proportions and a voice that had been trained upon the court for eleven years. Her arms were red to the elbows from the washtub. Her face, also, was red, and it glistened with steam and with an indignation that seemed always to lie waiting in her, like coals banked in a stove. Her hair had escaped its pins and stood about her head in a grey disorder. She held in one hand a wooden spoon, which she grasped as a sergeant grasps his sabre.

Patsy passed under her arm and was swallowed by the room behind her. The vendor arrived upon the landing. He paused, confronted by this mountain of a woman, and his courage visibly drooped like his moustache. Nevertheless, he was a man of great grievance, and grievance makes heroes.

"Your boy!" he cried, pointing. "Your boy, he steal! He take apple! I see! I see wit' my eye!"

Mrs. Kerrigan drew herself up. She seemed to fill the doorway from jamb to jamb.

"What's dat?" she demanded. "What's dat yer sayin'?"

"Your boy, he take apple. One apple. Is two cent. He steal."

"My boy!" said Mrs. Kerrigan. Her voice rose until it struck the ceiling and rebounded upon the heads of the sages below. "My boy steal! Listen at him! Listen at deh likes of him comin' up here an' callin' a decent woman's child a t'ief! My boy never took nottin' from nobody in his life! He's been brung up right, he has! He's been brung up in deh fear of Gawd!"

"I see," insisted the vendor, desperately. "I see wit' my eye."

"Yer eye!" said Mrs. Kerrigan, with infinite scorn. "Yer eye! An' what kinda eye is dat? Comin' up here, a man like you, wid yer rotten apples dat's half worms, an' tellin' me—me!—dat me child is a t'ief! Git out! Git down deh stairs before I t'row yeh down! Git out, I say!"

She advanced a step, brandishing the spoon. The vendor retreated a step. The sages of the second floor nodded their heads with approval, for they perceived that justice was being done, though they could not have said to whom. The vendor looked up at the woman, and then down the dark stairs, and his face assumed the expression of a man who contemplates the futility of the universe. He threw up his hands. He spoke rapidly in his own tongue, and it was evident from his tone that he was saying things concerning the women of this country which would not have been creditable to them. Then he descended, muttering, and his footsteps went down and down and faded, and presently the door at the bottom banged.

Mrs. Kerrigan remained for a moment upon the landing, surveying the faces at the various doors with the eye of a victor. The faces withdrew. She turned and went into her room and shut the door.

The room was a kitchen and also it was a parlor and also it was a place where four persons slept. A stove squatted in one corner like a black toad, breathing out heat. Upon it a boiler of clothes bubbled sullenly. Steam had fogged the single window and ran down the panes in grey tears. A table, with one leg shorter than its fellows, stood in the middle of the floor and rocked whenever anyone came near it. Upon the wall there hung a lithograph of a saint with an expression of mild reproach, and beside it a calendar advertising a brand of soap that no one in the house had ever bought. Upon a shelf, behind a cracked cup, stood a brass lamp of an elegance quite foreign to its surroundings. Mrs. Kerrigan had found this lamp one evening upon the doorstep of a house in a better street, where, she maintained, it had obviously been thrown away.

Patsy was crouched behind the stove. He still held the apple. It had become a hot and terrible thing in his hand, like a coal. He wished to drop it, but he could not think where.

His mother stood in the middle of the room and regarded the stove. Her bosom heaved. The glory of the landing had departed from her face, and in its place had come a look of dreadful purpose.

"Come out o' dere," she said.

Patsy did not come out. He made himself smaller. He thought that if he were small enough he might cease altogether to be.

"Come out o' dere, I tell yeh! Come out before I drag yeh out by deh ear!"

He came out. He came slowly, edging around the corner of the stove, with his eyes fixed upon the spoon. The apple was behind his back. His mother saw it. Her eyes, which had been merely furious, became luminous with wrath.

"Give it here."

He gave it. She took it and held it up between her thumb and finger, regarding it as a judge might regard a bloody knife. It was very red. It shone. It seemed to have no shame.

"So!" said she. "So! Dis is what I raised! Dis is deh t'anks I git! I slaves over deh tub from mornin' teh night, an' I cooks fer yeh an' I washes fer yeh an' I puts deh clo'es on yer back, an' yeh goes out on deh street an' steals like a reg'lar crook! Like a reg'lar crook outa deh Tombs! An' deh whole house hearin' it! Deh whole house standin' at deh doors an' hearin' it! Ol' lady Dolan an' deh Murphys an' all of 'em! What'll dey say? What'll dey say about me?"

Patsy looked at the floor. There was a crack in the boards in the shape of a river, and he followed it with his eyes, and it seemed to him that he would like to be very small and walk along it to some far place.

"Look at me when I'm talkin' teh yeh!"

He looked at her. Her face was enormous and red and it filled the world. Behind it the saint upon the wall regarded him with mild reproach.

"Didn't I tell yeh?" she cried. "Didn't I tell yeh a t'ousand times? Didn't I learn yeh right from wrong? Didn't I take yeh teh deh church an' make yeh say yer prayers? An' what did deh Father say? What did he say about stealin'? Hah? What did he say?"

Patsy did not remember what the Father had said. He remembered that the Father had a great purple face and a voice like a drum, and that the church was cold and smelled of candles, and that a boy named Mulcahy had pinched him during the Mass. He said nothing. Silence seemed to him a fortress.

"Answer me!"

"I dunno," said Patsy.

"Yeh dunno!" She lifted her eyes to the ceiling, as if calling upon the heavens to witness this depravity. "He dunno! Wid all deh learnin' I give him, he dunno! Yer gonna end up in deh jail, dat's where yer gonna end up! Yer gonna end up on deh Island wid deh rest of deh bums, an' yer poor mudder'll be visitin' yeh t'rough deh bars! Is dat what yeh want? Is it?"

The picture she drew affected her deeply. Her voice broke. Tears gathered in her eyes, and she wiped them with the back of a red wrist. Patsy, seeing the tears, was afraid, for he knew from experience that his mother's tears were the prelude to an exercise of great vigor.

"Who put yeh up teh it?" she demanded suddenly. "Somebody put yeh up teh it. It was dem Hennessy's corner loafers, wasn't it? Wasn't it?"

Patsy considered. Somewhere in the depths of him there stirred a dim sense of honor, a feeling that a man does not tell upon his comrades, even though his comrades have shown him their backs. It was a large and noble feeling, and it filled him with a strange warmth. He set his jaw.

"Nobody," he said.

"Nobody!" His mother advanced upon him. "Yeh lie teh me, too! Yeh steal an' den yeh lie teh yer own mudder! Oh, yer a fine one! Yer a fine, grand one!"

The spoon descended. It descended upon that portion of Patsy which nature seems to have designed for the purpose, and the sound of it rang through the room. Patsy howled. He howled not so much from pain as from a conviction that howling was expected of him and that a failure to perform would be regarded as defiance and would prolong the ceremony. The spoon descended again. With each stroke his mother delivered a sentence, so that the punishment had something of the character of a sermon with illustrations.

"Dat's—fer—stealin'! An' dat's—fer—lyin'! An' dat's—fer—disgracin' yer mudder—before—deh whole house!"

Below, upon the second landing, the sages listened at their doors with expressions of grave satisfaction. They agreed among themselves that Mrs. Kerrigan was a hard woman but a just one, and that children nowadays were not what they had been in the old country, where a boy that stole an apple would have been the scandal of three parishes.

At last the spoon was lowered. Mrs. Kerrigan sank into a chair, which protested, and fanned herself with her apron. She was breathing heavily. Her face had in it the exhausted nobility of one who has performed a painful duty.

"Now git in dat corner," she said, "an' don' let me hear a peep outa yeh."

Patsy went into the corner. He stood with his face toward the wall, where the paper hung in a long brown tongue, and he sniffled with diligence. After a time he ceased to sniffle, because nobody seemed to be paying attention, and he began to pick at the brown tongue of paper with his fingernail. He had now a feeling of great injury. He thought of the youth with the cap, and of the three backs disappearing round the corner. He thought of the apple, so red, so cool, so nearly his. He decided that the world was a place of treachery and that he would some day grow very large and go away into it and beat everybody.

His mother rose and went to the stove and stirred the clothes in the boiler with the spoon. She had laid the apple upon the table. After a time she took it up, regarded it, polished it absently upon her apron, and put it upon the shelf beside the brass lamp. It looked very well there. It gave a touch of color to the room.

At half past six there was a heavy tread upon the stairs and Kerrigan came home.

He was a coal heaver, and the day's labor had ground itself into every crease of him, so that he looked like a man drawn in charcoal by an artist who had pressed too hard. His shoulders were vast and sloping. He came in and sat down at the rocking table without a word and began to unlace his boots, which were of an immense size and seemed to have been made for the purpose of kicking things. He had stopped for a time upon the way home at a place where men stood before a long bar, and he brought with him an odor and a kind of heavy benevolence.

"Well," he said, "what's deh news?"

Mrs. Kerrigan told him the news. She told it at length and with feeling. She described the vendor and his insolence, and the deplorable conduct of the child, and the shame that had been brought upon the family before the eyes of the Dolans and the Murphys. She described her own conduct upon the landing with considerable relish. She described the punishment.

Kerrigan listened, working at a knot in his bootlace. When she had finished he turned his head and looked at the small figure in the corner.

"C'mere," he said.

Patsy came. He stood before his father with his hands at his sides. The coal heaver looked down at him from a great height, and it seemed to the boy that his father's face was a dark mountain upon which the weather was uncertain.

"Yeh swiped an apple off'n deh dago?" said Kerrigan.

Patsy nodded.

"An' he chased yeh?"

Patsy nodded again.

Kerrigan's brows came down. He was silent for a time, contemplating his son with a stern eye. Mrs. Kerrigan waited, the spoon poised, prepared for further justice.

"An' he follered yeh clean up teh deh fourt' floor?" said the father, at last.

"Yes."

Kerrigan struck the table with his fist, so that it rocked violently upon its short leg.

"Den yeh're a damn fool," he said. "A kid what can't outrun a dago wid a cart oughta stay home wid his mudder. Yeh hear me? Next time yeh run up deh alley an' t'rough Casey's cellar an' out deh back. Don' yeh never lead nobody teh yer own door! Never! Dat's deh first t'ing a man learns."

"Kerrigan!" cried his wife.

"Well, ain't it so?" said Kerrigan, aggrieved. "I'm learnin' him, ain't I? Yeh want him growin' up a fool?" He turned again to his son and shook a black forefinger at him. "An' don' let me hear of yeh stealin' no more," he added, as a man adds a postscript of no great importance. "It ain't right. Now git outa me sight."

Patsy got out of his sight. He returned to the corner without having been told, for it seemed to him the only place in the room that was entirely his own.

Supper was put upon the table. It consisted of bread and of potatoes and of a fragment of fish that had been purchased at the end of the day for a sum that reflected its condition. Patsy was not permitted to share it. He stood in his corner and smelled it and was very hungry, and his hunger seemed to him a part of the injustice of things. His father ate with the deliberate thoroughness of a laborer. His mother ate standing at the stove, and between mouthfuls she delivered to her husband a commentary on the moral decay of the neighborhood, of which she gave many examples, chiefly the Murphys.

Afterward Kerrigan lit his pipe and leaned back against the wall with his eyes closed, and the smoke went up from him in a slow blue column, as from the chimney of a factory that has ceased work for the night. Mrs. Kerrigan washed the dishes in the water from the boiler. The steam dwindled from the window. Outside, the court darkened, and the voices of the warriors below grew fewer and farther, and the women withdrew from the sills.

Patsy was sent to bed. His bed was a pallet in the corner of the inner room, a black closet without a window, where he slept with his little sister, who was three and had no opinions. She was already asleep, with her thumb in her mouth and her face screwed into an expression of fierce concentration, as if she were dreaming of battles.

He lay upon his back and looked at the darkness. Through the door came the murmur of his mother's voice and the occasional grunt of his father, and once the clink of a bottle against a glass. He thought of the apple upon the shelf beside the lamp. He thought of the youth with the cap. He thought of the fruit vendor's eyes, which had been sad, and he felt for a moment a strange discomfort, as if he had been told something he did not understand. He put it aside. It was too large for him.

Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
The rain had come in the night and gone again before morning and now the harbor was gray and flat and the boats lay against the stone of the mole with their sails furled. Out past the mouth of the harbor the sea was still running and you could see it break white on the rocks below the lighthouse. The fishermen had not gone out. They sat on overturned baskets along the wall and mended nets and did not talk much, and when the wind came they turned their backs to it and went on mending.

The café was at the end of the street where the street met the harbor. It had a long zinc bar and four tables inside and three tables outside under a canvas awning that the proprietor rolled up at night. In the summer all the tables had been full. Now it was October and the hotel up the hill had closed its dining room and there were only two of them at the outside tables, the man and the woman, and the canvas over them was dark with the rain and dripped at the edges.

"Do you want another?" the man said.

"I don't know."

"Have another. It's early."

"All right."

He raised his hand and the waiter came out from the dark of the café. He was an old man with a white jacket that had been washed too many times, and he walked slowly because his feet were bad.

"Two more," the man said in Spanish.

"Vermouth?"

"Yes. The same."

The waiter went in. They could hear him behind the bar and the sound of the bottle on the glass.

"You didn't fish today," the woman said.

"No. It was too rough on the mole."

"I thought you would go anyway."

"I thought so too. Then I didn't."

"You always go anyway."

"Not today."

The waiter came with the two glasses and set them down and took away the old ones and put a small dish of olives between them. The olives were green and good and the man ate one and put the pit in the saucer.

"They're good olives," he said.

"Yes."

"They're better here than in Madrid."

"Everything is better here than in Madrid. You've said that."

"Well, it's true."

"I know it's true, Walter."

He drank some of the vermouth. It was cold and sweet and bitter underneath and there was a piece of lemon peel in it. Out on the mole one of the fishermen stood up and stretched and then sat down again.

"Did you go to the post office?" he said.

"Yes."

"Was there anything?"

"There was a letter."

"From your sister?"

"No. Not from my sister."

He did not say anything. He looked at the harbor. A gull came down and walked along the edge of the wall and then went up again into the wind and hung there and then slid off toward the lighthouse.

"Aren't you going to ask who it was from?" she said.

"No."

"Why not?"

"Because I know who it was from."

"You don't know."

"All right. I don't know."

"You don't have to be like that."

"I'm not being like anything. I'm sitting here drinking a vermouth."

"You're being like that."

"Anne," he said. "Let's not."

"Let's not what?"

"Let's not do this. It's a nice evening."

"It isn't a nice evening. It's been raining all day."

"It stopped."

"It's going to start again."

He looked at the sky over the water. It was low and gray and moving fast and out to the west it was darker. She was right. It would rain again before dark.

"It's going to rain again," he said.

"I told you."

"You were right."

"I'm always right about the weather."

"You are," he said. "You're very good about the weather."

She picked up her glass and drank from it and put it down. Her hands were brown from the summer and she had a ring on the one hand and nothing on the other. She turned the ring on her finger. She had done that as long as he had known her when she was thinking about something.

"He wants me to come to Biarritz," she said.

"I thought he would."

"He says there's a house there. His mother's house. She doesn't use it after September."

"That's nice for him."

"He says I can stay as long as I like."

"That's very generous."

"Don't."

"I mean it. It's very generous. It's a big house?"

"I don't know. I suppose it is."

"It would be. His mother would have a big house."

"Walter."

"I'm only saying it would be a big house. That's all I'm saying."

The wind came in from the harbor and the canvas over them snapped and a little water came off the edge and fell on the table. He wiped it with his hand and then wiped his hand on his trousers.

"Do you want to go inside?" he said.

"No. I like it out here."

"You'll get cold."

"I'm not cold."

"You'll get cold later."

"Then I'll go inside later."

"All right."

They sat. Down the street a woman in black came out of a doorway with a basket and went along the wet stones close to the wall and turned up the hill toward the church. The bell in the church had rung for six o'clock a little while ago and it would not ring again for an hour.

"I haven't said I would go," she said.

"No."

"I haven't written him anything."

"You'll write him tonight."

"I don't know that."

"You'll write him tonight and you'll take it to the post in the morning and then you'll come down here and have a coffee and tell me you mailed it."

"You don't know that."

"No," he said. "I don't know anything. I'm a fool. I sit on the mole all day and catch nothing and come back and eat olives."

"You caught fish yesterday."

"I caught three small ones. The cook gave them to the cat."

"The cat liked them."

"The cat's not particular."

She laughed then, a little, and he looked at her and she stopped laughing.

"It isn't funny," she said.

"No. It isn't funny."

"I don't know why I laughed."

"It was a little funny. About the cat."

"It wasn't funny at all."

He finished his vermouth and looked at the empty glass and turned it on the table so that the lemon peel slid around in the bottom.

"Do you want something else?" he said. "Do you want to eat?"

"I'm not hungry."

"You didn't eat lunch."

"I wasn't hungry at lunch either."

"You have to eat something."

"I'll eat something later."

"Everything's later with you today."

"Yes," she said. "Everything's later."

He called the waiter and asked for a brandy. The waiter asked if the señora wanted a brandy too and she said no, and then she said yes, all right, a small one, and the waiter went in.

"I thought you didn't want one," he said.

"I changed my mind."

"That's all right. It's good to change your mind."

"Is it?"

"Sometimes."

"You never change yours."

"I change it."

"When? Tell me one time."

He thought about it. He looked at the boats. One of the boats was blue with a white line along the gunwale and a name painted on the bow that he could not read from here. He had watched that boat come in every evening in August, loaded down to the water with sardines, and the women had come down to the mole with baskets and the sardines had been silver in the baskets and the women had carried them up the hill on their heads. That was in August. It seemed like a long time ago.

"I can't think of one," he said.

"No. You can't."

"I changed my mind about coming here."

"You didn't. You wanted to come here from the beginning. I was the one who wanted to go to the mountains."

"That's right. You wanted the mountains."

"And we came here."

"You liked it here."

"I did like it here," she said. "In the summer I liked it."

The waiter brought the two brandies in small glasses with thick bottoms and set them down. The brandy was dark and smelled of wood. The man drank half of his and it was warm all the way down and he felt it in his chest and then in his hands.

"It's good brandy," he said.

"It's the same brandy."

"It's always good. That's why it's good."

"That doesn't make any sense."

"It makes sense to me."

She held the glass in both hands and did not drink from it. She looked out at the water.

"You could come too," she said.

"To Biarritz?"

"No. Not to Biarritz. I mean you could leave here. You could go to Paris. You said you wanted to go back to Paris."

"I said that in the spring."

"You could go now."

"There's nothing in Paris now."

"There's everything in Paris. There's everyone you know."

"That's what I mean."

"You can't stay here all winter. The hotel's closing in November. The señora told me."

"I know. She told me too."

"Then what will you do?"

"I'll get a room in the town. There are rooms."

"And do what?"

"Fish."

"In the winter?"

"They fish in the winter. Look at them. They're not going anywhere."

"They live here, Walter. They were born here."

"So?"

"So it's different."

"Everything's different. That's what you'll say about Biarritz. That it's different."

She put the glass down without drinking.

"I wasn't going to say anything about Biarritz."

"You were going to."

"No. You keep saying it. You keep saying Biarritz, Biarritz. I haven't said it once since I told you about the letter."

"All right."

"I haven't."

"I said all right."

"You always say all right when you don't mean it."

"What do you want me to say?"

She did not answer. She picked up the brandy and drank it all at once and put the glass down hard and it rang a little on the metal of the table.

"I want you to say something true," she said.

"I don't know anything true."

"You know lots of true things. You used to tell me true things all the time."

"That was a long time ago."

"It was this spring."

"That's a long time."

"It's six months."

"Six months is a long time."

The wind came again and harder and the canvas made a sound like a sail filling and the fishermen along the mole began to gather their nets. They folded them carefully and put them in the baskets and one of them, a boy, ran along the wall toward the street with a basket on his shoulder. The light was going. Out at the lighthouse the lamp had come on and it went around and came back and went around again.

"I'll tell you something true," he said.

"All right."

"I don't want you to go."

She looked at him. She did not say anything for a while.

"That's not enough," she said.

"I know it."

"It used to be enough."

"I know that too."

"Why isn't it enough anymore?"

"I don't know. You tell me. You're the one who knows."

"I don't know. I don't know anything either."

"Then we're even."

"We're not even. We're not anything."

"Don't say that."

"Why not? It's true. You wanted something true."

"I didn't want that."

"You don't get to pick."

He finished his brandy. His hand was steady and he was glad that it was steady. He put the glass down very gently in the wet ring it had made before.

"Do you love him?" he said.

"Don't ask me that."

"I'm asking."

"I don't want to talk about him."

"Then why did you tell me about the letter?"

"Because you asked. You asked if there was anything at the post office."

"You could have said no."

"I don't lie to you, Walter."

"No," he said. "You don't lie. That's one thing."

"I've never lied to you."

"I know it."

"Not once."

"I said I know it."

It began to rain then. It came first as a few large drops on the street and on the stones of the mole and then it came all at once and hard and the harbor went white with it and the boats disappeared behind it and they could not see the lighthouse anymore, only the lamp turning in the gray. The rain beat on the canvas over them and ran off the edges in a sheet and splashed up from the street onto their shoes.

"We should go in," he said.

"Yes."

But neither of them moved.

"Do you remember the first week," she said. "When we came here."

"Yes."

"We swam every morning off the rocks past the lighthouse. And it was so cold the first time I couldn't breathe."

"You came out blue."

"I wasn't blue."

"You were a little blue. Around the mouth."

"And then we came here and had coffee and those bread rolls and you said it was the best place in the world."

"It was."

"You said we'd stay forever."

"I said a lot of things."

"You meant it then."

"I meant it."

"Do you still mean it?"

He looked at the rain. He watched it on the water where the harbor had been.

"I don't know," he said. "I mean I'll stay."

"That's not the same thing."

"No. It isn't."

The waiter came out to the doorway and stood there with a towel over his arm and looked at the rain and then looked at them. He said something about the weather, that it would rain all night now, that the boats would not go out tomorrow either. The man said yes, it looked that way. The waiter asked if they wanted to come inside where it was dry and the man said in a minute. The waiter nodded and went back in. They could see him behind the bar in the yellow light, wiping glasses and holding them up to the light and wiping them again.

"He's a nice old man," she said.

"He's a good old man."

"I'll miss him."

He did not say anything to that. After a while he said, "You'll be all right in Biarritz. It's a good town."

"I haven't decided."

"You've decided."

"Walter, I haven't. I swear to you I haven't."

"All right. You haven't decided. But you'll decide tonight and in the morning you'll take it to the post."

"Stop saying that."

"I'm only saying what's going to happen."

"You don't know what's going to happen."

"No," he said. "That's right. Nobody does."

She stood up. She stood with one hand on the back of the chair and looked down at him and he looked up at her. Her hair was wet a little at the front from where the wind had blown the rain in under the canvas.

"I'm going up," she said.

"All right."

"Are you coming?"

"In a while. I'll have one more."

"You've had enough."

"I'll have one more and then I'll come up."

"Walter."

"I'll come up. Go on. You'll get wet."

"I'm already wet."

"You'll get wetter."

She stood there a moment longer. Then she bent down and kissed him on the side of the head, quickly, above the ear, and straightened up.

"Don't stay too long," she said.

"I won't."

"The señora locks the door at ten."

"I know when she locks the door."

"I'll leave the window."

"Thank you."

She went out from under the canvas into the rain and he watched her go up the street with her shoulders hunched and her hand holding her collar closed at the throat. She walked fast and close to the wall the way the old woman in black had walked and at the corner she did not look back and then she turned up the hill and he could not see her anymore.

He sat for a while and then he picked up his glass and saw that it was empty and he went inside. It was warm inside and smelled of wine and wet wood and the floor had sawdust on it. He stood at the bar and the waiter put down the towel and came over.

"Brandy," the man said.

The waiter poured it. He poured it full to the top of the glass, more than a measure, and pushed it across the zinc.

"The señora went up," the waiter said.

"Yes."

"It's bad weather for walking."

"It's bad weather for everything."

"For the fish it's good," the waiter said. "When it's like this the fish go deep and rest. And then after, when it clears, they come up hungry. After a storm is the best fishing."

"Is that true?"

"My father said it. He was a fisherman. Forty years."

"Then it must be true."

"Who knows," the waiter said. "He said many things."

The man drank some of the brandy. Through the window he could see the lamp of the lighthouse going around in the rain. It went around and came back and went around. It did not change. It would go on like that all night whether there were boats out or not, and in the morning it would go off, and tomorrow night it would come on again.

"How long until it clears?" he said.

The waiter shrugged and picked up the towel and a glass.

"Two days," he said. "Three. It's October. In October nobody knows."

"No," the man said. "Nobody knows."

He drank the brandy slowly and did not order another. When it was gone he put some coins on the zinc and said good night and the waiter said good night and told him to go with God. He went out into the rain. It was coming down hard and steady and the street was running with it and he did not hurry. He walked up the hill in the dark past the closed doors and the church and when he came to the hotel he looked up and the window was open, as she had said it would be, and there was no light in it.

The train came in at four o'clock in the afternoon and Joe was standing on the platform with his hat pushed back. The sun was low over the hills to the west and the shadows of the grain elevators lay long across the tracks. There were not many people getting off. A woman with two children got off and then a man carrying a sample case and then Lewis got off. He had one bag and he carried it in his left hand.

"Hello, Joe," he said.

"Hello, Lew."

They shook hands. Joe took the bag from him and Lewis let him take it.

"It's not heavy," Lewis said.

"I know it."

They walked down the platform to where the truck was parked in the dust beside the depot. It was a Ford and it had been red once. Joe put the bag in the back and they got in and he started the motor. It took two tries.

"Same truck," Lewis said.

"Same truck."

"I thought it would be gone by now."

"It runs," Joe said. "It runs fine if you know it."

They drove out of town on the gravel road. The fields on both sides had been cut and the stubble was yellow in the late light and there were magpies walking in the stubble. Beyond the fields the land rose into the hills and the hills were brown and then above them were the mountains and there was snow already on the mountains.

"There's snow," Lewis said.

"It came early. Two weeks ago it came."

"It looks good."

"It looks good from here."

Lewis rolled down the window and put his arm out. The air was cold and it smelled of dust and cut hay and something burning a long way off. He breathed it in. He had not smelled it in a long time.

"How's Helen?" he said.

"She's fine. She's cooking. She's been cooking since noon."

"She didn't have to do that."

"You tell her," Joe said. "I'm not going to tell her."

They drove on. The road went down to the creek and crossed it on a plank bridge and the planks rattled under the wheels. Lewis looked down at the water. It was low and clear and he could see the stones on the bottom.

"How's the fishing?"

"It's good. It's been good all fall. There are some big ones in the hole below the beaver dam."

"Still the beaver dam?"

"They rebuilt it. The water took it out in the spring and they built it back."

"They would."

"They built it back better," Joe said. "We can go up in the morning if you want."

"I'd like that."

"We'll go early."

"All right."

---

The house stood at the top of a rise with cottonwoods around it and the leaves of the cottonwoods had turned yellow and some of them had fallen and lay in the yard. There was smoke coming from the chimney. Helen came out on the porch when she heard the truck. She was wiping her hands on her apron.

"Lewis," she said. She came down the steps and kissed him on the cheek. "You're thin."

"I've been thin."

"You're thinner. Come in. Come in out of the cold."

The kitchen was warm and it smelled of roasting meat and bread. There was a fire in the stove and a lamp lit on the table though it was not yet dark. Joe brought the bag in and set it by the door.

"Sit down," Helen said. "Joe, get him a drink."

"I'm getting it."

Joe took a bottle down from the shelf above the stove. It was whiskey and it was about half full. He poured two glasses and then looked at Helen and she shook her head. He put water in the glasses from the pitcher and gave one to Lewis.

"Here's luck," Joe said.

"Luck."

They drank. The whiskey was good. It was warm going down and Lewis felt it in his stomach and then he felt it spreading out.

"That's good whiskey," he said.

"It's the old man's," Joe said. "There were two cases in the cellar. We found them after."

Lewis looked at the glass.

"He always had good whiskey," he said.

"He did."

Helen opened the oven and looked at the roast and closed it again. "Another half hour," she said. "You boys go sit in the front room. You're in my way."

"We're not in your way," Joe said.

"You will be."

They took the bottle and the glasses and went into the front room. It was cold in there and Joe knelt and lit the fire that was already laid in the fireplace. The kindling caught and then the split pine caught and the fire began to make a noise. Lewis sat down in the leather chair. It was the old man's chair and he knew it when he sat in it and he did not get up.

"Sit there," Joe said. "That's fine. Somebody ought to sit there."

"It's a good chair."

"It's the best chair in the house. Helen won't sit in it. I won't either."

"I'll get up."

"No," Joe said. "Sit."

Lewis sat. The fire was going well now and the room was getting warm. On the wall over the fireplace there was the head of an elk and the antlers threw a shadow on the ceiling. Lewis looked at it.

"That's the one from Sheep Creek," he said.

"That's the one."

"I was there. I was twelve."

"You were eleven," Joe said. "I was thirteen and you were eleven."

"I thought I was twelve."

"You were eleven. You cried when he shot it."

"I didn't cry."

"You cried. It's all right. I would have cried too only I'd already been once."

Lewis drank some of the whiskey.

"I remember he let me hold the rifle afterward," he said. "It was still warm."

"He let you carry it down too. All the way down to the horses."

"That's right. He did."

"He never let me carry it."

"You carried the liver."

Joe laughed. "I carried the damned liver," he said. "In a flour sack. It leaked all over my pants."

They sat and drank and looked at the fire. Outside it was getting dark and the window was blue and then it was black and Lewis could see the room in the glass with the fire in it.

"I got your letter," Joe said.

"I wanted to come."

"I know it."

"I couldn't come. I was in the hospital then."

"You said in the letter."

"I wanted to come anyway. I asked them. They wouldn't let me."

"It's all right," Joe said. "There wasn't anything to do. It was a small thing. The minister came out from town and said some words and we put him up on the hill by Mother. There were maybe twenty people."

"Twenty people."

"Maybe twenty-five. The Hansens came. Old man Becker came. He can't hardly walk now but he came."

"That was good of him."

"It was. He stood the whole time. I told him to sit down and he wouldn't."

Lewis turned the glass in his hand. The fire was reflected in it.

"Did he say anything?" he said. "At the end?"

Joe looked at the fire.

"He asked was the hay in," he said. "I told him it was."

"Was it?"

"No. It wasn't. We had about a third of it left."

"But you told him it was."

"I told him it was."

Lewis nodded. He did not say anything. After a while Joe reached over and poured more whiskey in both glasses.

"He asked about you," Joe said. "Before that. A week before. He asked had I heard."

"What did you tell him?"

"I told him you were fine. I told him you were coming home soon."

"I wasn't fine."

"I didn't know that then. I told him what I knew."

"It's all right," Lewis said. "It was a good thing to tell him."

"It was what I had."

---

Helen called them and they went in to supper. The roast was good and there were potatoes and carrots that had been cooked with the meat and there was fresh bread and butter. Lewis ate a great deal. He had not thought he was hungry and then he was very hungry.

"You eat," Helen said. "You eat it all."

"It's very good."

"Of course it's good."

"I mean it. I haven't eaten anything like this in a long time."

"Well, what did they feed you?"

"I don't know," Lewis said. "I don't remember. It all tasted the same."

Helen looked at him and then she looked at Joe and Joe was looking at his plate.

"There's pie," she said. "Apple. From the tree out back."

"The old tree?"

"It still bears. Not as much. But it bears."

After supper she would not let them help with the dishes and they went back into the front room and Joe put more wood on the fire. They did not drink any more whiskey. They sat and Joe smoked a pipe and Lewis watched the fire.

"How's the arm?" Joe said.

"It's all right."

"Can you use it?"

"Some. I can use it some. It gets better. They say it gets better."

"Can you cast?"

"I don't know. I haven't tried."

"Well," Joe said. "We'll find out."

"We'll find out."

"If you can't you can watch me."

"I'd rather fish."

"Sure. Everybody would rather fish."

Joe knocked his pipe out on the stone of the fireplace.

"I'm going to bed," he said. "You go when you want. Your room is the same room. Helen put the extra blankets on."

"Thanks."

"I'll wake you at five."

"I'll be up."

"I'll wake you anyway."

Joe went out and Lewis heard him on the stairs and then he heard the door close. He sat for a long time by the fire. When it burned down he did not put any more wood on. He sat and watched it go to coals and then he got up and went upstairs.

The room was the same room. It was the room he had slept in every summer from the time he was seven until he was seventeen. The bed was the same bed and the window looked out over the cottonwoods and down to the creek and the creek was silver now under the moon. He undressed in the dark and got into bed. The sheets were cold and then they warmed. He lay on his back and listened. He could hear the creek. He had forgotten that you could hear the creek from here. He lay and listened to it and after a while he slept and he did not dream.

---

Joe woke him at five but he was already awake. It was dark and cold in the room and he dressed quickly. Downstairs Joe had coffee on the stove and they drank it standing up. Then they took the rods from where they hung on the back porch and went out.

It was cold outside and their breath smoked and there was frost on the grass. They walked down through the pasture to the creek. The sky was getting light in the east over the hills and the stars were going out. By the time they reached the creek it was light enough to see the water.

They walked up along the bank. The grass was wet and soaked through their trousers below the knee. There were willows along the creek and the willows were bare and red and they had to push through them in places. A deer went crashing away through the brush ahead of them and they stopped and listened to it go.

"Doe," Joe said.

"I didn't see it."

"It was a doe. I saw the tail."

They came to the beaver dam. It was built of sticks and mud and it ran across the creek in a long low curve and the water came over the top of it in a smooth sheet and fell into the pool below. The pool was deep and green and the current moved slowly in it and turned back on itself at the edges.

"There," Joe said. "Under the far bank. Where the roots are."

"I see it."

"You take it. I'll go up above."

"No. You take it."

"I've fished it all fall," Joe said. "You take it."

Joe went on up around the dam. Lewis sat down on a log and took a fly from the box and tied it on. His right hand was slow with the knot and he had to do it twice. Then he stood up and walked down to the edge of the water.

He stripped line off the reel and let it lie in loops at his feet. He brought the rod back. His arm hurt when he brought it back but it was not a bad hurt. He brought it forward and the line went out and fell on the water too short and too heavy. He took it up and tried again. It was better. The third time the fly lit on the water just below the roots on the far bank and rode the current down and turned in the eddy.

Nothing came. He took it up and cast again. His arm hurt more now. He made himself be slow. The fly went out and lit and floated and then there was a swirl in the water under it and he lifted the rod and felt the trout.

It was a good trout. It went down and he could feel it shaking its head down there and then it ran upstream toward the dam and the line cut through the water and the reel made a noise. He held the rod up. His arm was shaking. The trout turned and came back down and he took in line with his left hand and then it jumped. It came all the way out of the water and he saw it in the light, heavy and spotted and bright, and it fell back with a splash.

"Keep him up," Joe called. He was standing on the dam. "Keep him out of the roots."

"I know."

"Keep him up."

The trout went for the roots and Lewis turned it. He did not know how he turned it. His arm was very bad now but he held the rod up and the trout came out from the bank and into the open water of the pool. It was tiring. He brought it in slowly. When it was close he could see it in the clear water, lying on its side and then righting itself and then lying on its side again.

Joe came down off the dam with the net. He waded into the shallow water at the tail of the pool and Lewis led the trout to him and Joe put the net under it and lifted it out.

"That's a fish," Joe said.

"It's a good one."

"It's the best one out of here all year."

"You're lying."

"I'm not lying. Look at him."

They looked at him. The trout lay in the net and its gills worked. It was dark on the back and silver on the sides and there were red spots along the sides with blue around them. Joe took it out and killed it with a blow against a rock and laid it in the grass.

Lewis sat down on the log. He held his right arm with his left hand. It was shaking and he could not make it stop.

"You all right?" Joe said.

"I'm fine."

"You're not fine."

"It's just the arm. It's just tired."

Joe sat down beside him on the log. He took out his pipe and filled it and lit it and they sat there. The sun had come up over the hills now and it was on the water and on the frost in the grass and the frost was beginning to melt.

"You can stay," Joe said. "If you want."

Lewis did not say anything.

"I mean it. There's work if you want it. There's the room. Helen would like it. I'd like it."

"I don't know what I'm going to do."

"You don't have to know. That's what I'm saying."

"I can't do much. With the arm."

"You did all right just now."

"That was a fish."

"It was a fish," Joe said. "It's a start."

Lewis looked at the water. A leaf came down the creek and went over the dam and into the pool and turned in the eddy where the trout had been and then went on.

"I used to think about this," he said. "In the hospital. I used to lie there and think about this creek. Every hole in it. I'd start at the bridge and go up. I'd fish every hole. Some nights I got all the way to the forks."

"Did you catch anything?"

"Every time. Every hole."

"Well," Joe said. "That's better than we ever did."

"That's what I'd think. I'd think, it was never this good."

"It's pretty good now."

"It's pretty good."

Joe stood up. "I'm going to go up above," he said. "You rest. Fish this again when he's settled. There's another one in there. I saw it."

"All right."

"You'll be all right?"

"I'll be fine."

Joe picked up his rod and went up along the bank and around the dam. Lewis watched him go. Then he sat on the log in the sun and looked at the trout lying in the wet grass. The color was going out of it already. He reached down and picked it up and wet it in the creek and laid it in the shade under the willows where it would keep.

His arm had stopped shaking. He flexed his hand and opened it and closed it. Then he sat a while longer in the sun. It was getting warm. He could hear Joe's reel up above the dam and he could hear the water coming over the dam and falling into the pool. After a while he got up and picked up his rod and stripped the line off the reel and let it lie in loops at his feet, and he looked across the water to the place under the roots where the other trout would be.

Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Ernest Hemingway, depicting the following scene: A parent reprimanding a young child.
