response:
The wind came up in the night and in the morning it was still blowing. The man woke early and lay in the bed and listened to it in the pines behind the cabin. He could hear the water working against the rocks below the point. It was a steady sound and he knew it would blow all day. He lay there and did not think about anything and then he got up and put on his trousers and his shirt and went out to the kitchen.

The stove was cold. He put in paper and kindling and some of the split birch and lit it and stood there with his hands over it until the birch caught. Then he filled the coffee pot from the pail and put it on. The boy's door was open. He did not look in because he thought the boy was sleeping and he did not want to wake him. The boy was seven and he slept hard in the mornings.

When the coffee was boiling he took it off and let the grounds settle and poured a cup and went out onto the porch with it. The lake was dark and rough and the waves were white on top all the way across to the far shore. The sky was clear and very blue and the wind came down out of the northwest cold and clean. He drank the coffee and looked at the lake. He looked at the dock. The rowboat was not there.

He set the cup down on the rail. He looked along the shore toward Halvorsen's place and then out at the water. He did not see anything at first. Then he saw the boat. It was a long way out, past the point and well toward the middle, and it was riding broadside to the waves. There was someone in it. It was small in the boat and it was not doing anything.

He went down the path to the dock. He did not run on the path because the roots were bad and he knew if he fell it would be worse. At the dock he stood and looked out again. The boat was drifting southeast with the wind. He could see now that the boy was sitting in the bottom of it and holding onto the gunwales. There was only one oar in the boat. He could not see the other oar anywhere.

Halvorsen's canoe was pulled up on the beach a hundred yards down. He went along the shore to it, over the rocks, and turned it over and found the paddle under it. He dragged the canoe down into the water and the wind took the bow around and he had to wade out to his knees to hold it. The water was very cold. He got in and knelt in the middle and began to paddle.

It was hard going out past the point. The waves came at the canoe on the quarter and he had to keep the bow into them and paddle hard on the one side. Water came over the bow and he could feel it cold on his knees in the bottom. He did not look at the boat for a while. He looked at the waves coming and kept the bow into them and paddled. When he was past the point and out in the open it was rougher and he had to quarter more. Then he looked up and saw the boat and it was closer. The boy had seen him. The boy was not waving. He was just sitting and holding on.

The man paddled. His shoulders began to hurt and then they stopped hurting and he did not think about them. He thought about the waves and about keeping the canoe straight. He thought that if the canoe went over he would hold onto it and kick toward the boat. He thought that the water was too cold to be in for long. Then he did not think about that anymore and only paddled.

When he came up alongside the boat the boy looked at him. The boy's face was very white and his lips were blue and his hair was wet from the spray. He had on his sweater and his short pants and his shoes were off. The man did not know why his shoes were off.

"Hold the gunwale," the man said. "Hold it tight."

The boy did not say anything. He held on.

The man brought the canoe in against the side of the boat and caught the oarlock and held it. The two boats knocked together in the waves. He took the painter of the canoe and made it fast to the stern ring of the rowboat with two half hitches. Then he got over into the rowboat, careful, low, his weight in the middle, and the canoe swung off behind on the line.

"Are you hurt?" he said.

"No."

"Get in the bow. Sit down in the bottom. Hold on."

The boy went forward on his hands and knees and sat down in the bottom of the bow with his back against the seat. The man took the one oar and looked at the shore. They had drifted a long way. He put the oar over the stern and began to scull. It was slow. The wind was against them and the canoe dragged behind. He sculled and kept the stern into the wind and watched the point and after a long while the point began to come nearer. The boy sat in the bow and did not look at him. The boy looked at the bottom of the boat where there was some water and an old sinker and a piece of line.

When they came in behind the point the water was smoother and the man sculled easier. He brought the boat in to the dock and the boy got out first and stood on the dock. The man made the boat fast and then he pulled the canoe in and untied it and carried it down the beach to Halvorsen's and turned it over where it had been and put the paddle under it. Then he walked back to the dock. The boy was still standing there. He had not moved. The man's trousers were wet to the thighs and his hands were stiff and his arms felt light, as though there were nothing in them.

"Come up to the house," he said.

They went up the path. The boy went ahead. At the porch the man said, "Sit down there," and the boy sat on the bench against the wall of the cabin. The man went inside and got the blanket off the boy's bed and came out and put it around him. Then he sat down on the step below the boy and took out a cigarette and tried to light it. The wind blew the match out. He lit another one with his hands cupped and got the cigarette going. His hands were shaking a little. He looked at them and then he put them on his knees.

"All right," he said. "Tell me."

The boy did not say anything.

"Tell me what happened."

"I took the boat."

"I know you took the boat."

"I wanted to go to the island."

The man looked out at the lake. The island was a long way down, beyond the bay, a little island with three pines on it and a rock beach on the south side. You could not see it from the porch.

"Why did you want to go to the island?"

"I just wanted to."

"That isn't any reason."

The boy pulled the blanket around himself. "There were the big perch there. Off the rocks. Where we caught them before."

"That was a long time ago."

"It was last summer."

"All right. It was last summer." The man smoked the cigarette. "What happened to the oar?"

"It came out of the lock. I was pulling hard and it came out and then it went away."

"Why didn't you sit down and wait?"

"I did. I sat down."

"Why were your shoes off?"

The boy looked at his feet. They were red and wet. "I thought I might have to swim."

The man did not say anything for a while. He looked at the boy's feet. They were very small. He threw the cigarette off the porch into the needles and then he got up and stepped on it and came back and sat down again.

"Listen to me," he said. "Are you listening?"

"Yes."

"Look at me."

The boy looked at him. His eyes were very dark and they were wet now but he was not crying.

"You don't take the boat," the man said. "You don't ever take the boat alone. Not to the island and not to the point and not to anywhere. Do you understand that?"

"Yes."

"Say it."

"I don't take the boat alone."

"Not ever."

"Not ever."

"You could have died out there," the man said. "Do you know that? You don't know that. You think you know it but you don't. That water is cold. If the boat went over you would have been in that water and you would have been all right for a little while and then you would not have been all right. Your arms would stop working. Then you would go down. You would go down and nobody would find you. Do you understand?"

The boy was crying now. He was not making any sound but the tears were coming down and he did not wipe them.

"Do you understand?" the man said.

"Yes."

"I didn't know where you were. I came out and the boat was gone. Do you know what that is like?"

"No."

"No," the man said. "You don't."

They sat there. The wind blew in the pines and the needles came down on the porch roof with a small sound. Down below the water broke on the rocks and drew back and broke again.

"Mother let me take it," the boy said.

The man did not look at him.

"She let me take it to the end of the dock and back. On the rope. She let me."

"That was on the rope."

"She said I could go farther when I was bigger."

"Your mother isn't here," the man said.

He said it and then it was said and he could not do anything about it. The boy looked at him. Then the boy looked away, out at the lake, and pulled the blanket up over his mouth.

The man stood up. He went inside and stood in the kitchen. The stove was going well and the kitchen was warm. He poured another cup of coffee. It was strong now from sitting and he drank it standing up by the stove. He looked at the window. There was a fly on the inside of the glass walking up and falling down and walking up again. He watched it for a while. Then he went to the cupboard and took down the bottle and poured some of the whiskey into the coffee and drank it. It was good. It went down hot and he felt it in his chest and then in his stomach. He did not pour any more.

He went back out onto the porch. The boy was still sitting there in the blanket.

"Go in and get your dry things on," the man said. "Then come out to the kitchen."

The boy got up and went in. The man stood on the porch and looked at the lake. The wind was still strong. It would blow all day and maybe tomorrow. He thought about the oar. It was out there somewhere going southeast, and it would come up on the far shore in a day or two, or it would not. It was a good oar. He had bought the pair in the town at the beginning of the summer. It did not matter about the oar.

In the kitchen he cut bacon and put it in the big pan. When it was cooking he cut bread and laid the slices out on the board. The boy came in. He had on his other trousers and a dry shirt and his wool socks and he stood in the doorway.

"Sit down," the man said.

The boy sat at the table. The man turned the bacon. When it was done he took it out and laid it on a paper and put the bread in the fat and fried it brown on both sides. He put the bread and the bacon on two plates and brought them to the table and sat down. He poured milk into a cup for the boy.

"Eat," he said.

The boy ate. He ate slowly at first and then he ate faster. The man watched him and then he ate too. The bread was good fried in the bacon fat and the bacon was crisp. They did not say anything while they ate.

When they were done the man took the plates to the basin. He stood with his back to the boy.

"For a week you don't go to the dock," he said. "Not without me. You don't go down the path. You stay up here at the house and you split the kindling and you carry the water. You do that every day."

"Yes."

"And after a week we will see."

"Yes."

The man washed the plates in the basin and dried them and put them in the cupboard. Then he turned around. The boy was sitting at the table looking at the oilcloth. There was a burn on it from a pan once and the boy was running his finger around the edge of the burn.

"You did one thing right," the man said.

The boy looked up.

"You sat down in the boat. You didn't stand up. That was right. And you held on. That was right too."

"I wanted to stand up. To see better."

"But you didn't."

"No."

"That was right," the man said.

The boy looked at the burn on the oilcloth again. "Would you have come if I didn't have the shoes off?"

"I would have come."

"Even if I went in?"

"Even then."

"But you said my arms would stop."

"I would have come anyway," the man said.

The boy nodded. He seemed to be thinking about it. Then he said, "Is the oar gone?"

"I guess it's gone."

"I'm sorry about the oar."

"It doesn't matter about the oar."

"Was it expensive?"

"It doesn't matter," the man said. "We will get another oar."

In the afternoon the boy split kindling on the block behind the cabin. He was not strong enough to split anything big and the man gave him the small hatchet and set up the pieces of dry cedar for him and showed him again how to hold it, short, with his other hand well back. The boy split the cedar into long thin pieces and stacked them in the box by the back door. The man sat on the back step and cleaned the shotgun, which did not need cleaning, and watched him. The wind came over the ridge and moved the tops of the pines but it was quiet behind the cabin and the sun was warm there. The boy worked carefully. When he had split all the cedar he came and stood by the step.

"I'm done."

"Good. Now the water."

The boy took the pail and went down the other path to the spring. It was not the lake path. The man watched him go down through the trees and then he could not see him and he listened. He heard the pail knock against a rock and then he heard it filling and then he heard the boy coming back up. The boy carried it with both hands and some of it slopped over and he came around the corner of the cabin with the front of his trousers wet.

"You spilled some."

"It's heavy."

"Carry it on one side. Change hands when you're tired."

"All right."

"Put it on the bench."

The boy put it on the bench and stood there. The man put the gun down across his knees.

"Come here," he said.

The boy came. The man put his hand on the back of the boy's neck. It was a very small neck and it was warm from the work.

"You did good with the kindling."

"Did I do it right?"

"You did it fine."

In the evening the wind began to go down. They sat on the porch after supper and watched the lake. The whitecaps were gone and the waves were long and slow now, and the light went yellow on the far shore and then red and then it was gone and the water was gray. The boy sat on the bench next to the man. He had the blanket again because it was cold. The man smoked.

"Tomorrow will it be calm?" the boy said.

"Maybe. I think it will be calm."

"Can we go to the island?"

The man looked at him.

"Both of us," the boy said. "In the boat. You row."

"With one oar?"

"Oh," the boy said.

"I can make one, I guess," the man said. "There's that ash board in the shed. I can make one out of that."

"Can I help?"

"You can hold the board."

"And then can we go?"

"Not tomorrow. You have a week."

"A week," the boy said. He did not argue. He pulled the blanket up. "After a week, can we go?"

"After a week we will see."

"The perch will still be there."

"They'll be there."

"Off the rocks."

"Off the rocks on the south side," the man said. "Where the deep water comes in."

"That's where Mother caught the big one."

"That's right," the man said. "That's where."

The boy did not say anything else. The man sat and smoked and after a while he felt the boy lean against him and then the boy's head was against his arm and he was asleep. The man did not move. It was dark now and the lake was flat and black and he could hear a loon out past the point. It called once and then it was quiet and then it called again farther off. The man sat and listened to it. His arms ached now, both of them, from the shoulders all the way down, and his back ached, and he did not mind it. He finished the cigarette and dropped it and put it out with his shoe. Then he sat there in the dark with the boy against him and did not get up for a long time.

Here is an excerpt of Ernest Hemingway's writing, to show you their style:

I was away for two days at the posts. When I got home it was too late and I did not see Miss Barkley until the next evening. She was not in the garden and I had to wait in the office of the hospital until she came down. There were many marble busts on painted wooden pillars along the walls of the room they used for an office. The hall too, that the office opened on, was lined with them. They had the complete marble quality of all looking alike. Sculpture had always seemed a dull business—still, bronzes looked like something. But marble busts all looked like a cemetery. There was one fine cemetery though—the one at Pisa. Genoa was the place to see the bad marbles. This had been the villa of a very wealthy German and the busts must have cost him plenty. I wondered who had done them and how much he got. I tried to make out whether they were members of the family or what; but they were all uniformly classical. You could not tell anything about them. I sat on a chair and held my cap. We were supposed to wear steel helmets even in Gorizia but they were uncomfortable and too bloody theatrical in a town where the civilian inhabitants had not been evacuated. I wore one when we went up to the posts and carried an English gas mask. We were just beginning to get some of them. They were a real mask. Also we were required to wear an automatic pistol; even doctors and sanitary officers. I felt it against the back of the chair. You were liable to arrest if you did not have one worn in plain sight. Rinaldi carried a holster stuffed with toilet paper. I wore a real one and felt like a gunman until I practised firing it. It was an Astra 7.65 caliber with a short barrel and it jumped so sharply when you let it off that there was no question of hitting anything. I practised with it, holding below the target and trying to master the jerk of the ridiculous short barrel until I could hit within a yard of where I aimed at twenty paces and then the ridiculousness of carrying a pistol at all came over me and I soon forgot it and carried it flopping against the small of my back with no feeling at all except a vague sort of shame when I met English-speaking people. I sat now in the chair and an orderly of some sort looked at me disapprovingly from behind a desk while I looked at the marble floor, the pillars with the marble busts, and the frescoes on the wall and waited for Miss Barkley. The frescoes were not bad. Any frescoes were good when they started to peel and flake off. I saw Catherine Barkley coming down the hall, and stood up. She did not seem tall walking toward me but she looked very lovely.

“Good-evening, Mr. Henry,” she said.

“How do you do?” I said. The orderly was listening behind the desk.

“Shall we sit here or go out in the garden?”

“Let’s go out. It’s much cooler.” I walked behind her out into the garden, the orderly looking after us. When we were out on the gravel drive she said, “Where have you been?”

“I’ve been out on post.”

“You couldn’t have sent me a note?”

“No,” I said. “Not very well. I thought I was coming back.”

"No," he said. "I guess it doesn't matter."

"You don't have to look like that."

"I'm not looking like anything."

"You are, though."

"I'm sorry," he said. "I didn't know I was."

The proprietor's wife came in with more bread and asked if they wanted anything and the woman smiled at her and said no, thank you, it was very good, and the proprietor's wife went out again. The woman's smile went away as soon as the door shut. He had seen it go like that before and it did not mean anything. It was only that she was tired of smiling.

"I thought we'd go down into Spain," he said. "When this was over. I thought we'd go to Burgos and then down to Madrid and see the pictures. You said you wanted to see the pictures."

"I know I did."

"It would be fine in Madrid now. It's still warm there. We could stay at that place on the Plaza Santa Ana."

"George."

"And the fights will go on until the end of the month. There's a good bull ring at Aranjuez. It's a nice small town and there are big trees by the river and you can get strawberries."

"George, please."

"What?"

"You know I don't want to go to Spain."

"You said you wanted to."

"That was in June."

"It's the same Spain," he said.

"It isn't the same anything."

He picked up the paper from Pau and looked at it and put it down again. He did not know why he had picked it up.

"Do you want a drink?" he said.

"It's ten o'clock in the morning."

"I know what time it is. I asked did you want a drink."

"No."

"I'm going to have one."

"Have one then."

He went to the door and called and the proprietor came this time and he asked for a marc. The proprietor brought it in a small heavy glass and set it down and looked out the window at the rain and said it was a bad year for rain, it was the worst he remembered, and the man said yes, it was very bad, and the proprietor went out. The man drank half the marc. It was raw and hot and it went down and spread out warm in his stomach and he felt better.

"Do you feel better?" she said.

"Yes."

"I'm glad. I'm glad something makes you feel better."

"Don't," he said.

"Don't what?"

"Don't start that."

"I'm not starting anything. I'm just sitting here. I'm just sitting here in this cold room in this hotel with the rain and you're drinking marc at ten o'clock and I'm glad it makes you feel better. That's all I said."

"All right."

"It's not all right, though. Is it?"

He finished the marc and set the glass down. He looked at her. Her face was very white and her eyes were very steady and he thought she was going to cry and then he saw that she was not going to cry. She had gotten past that somewhere. He did not know when.

"What do you want me to say?" he said.

"I don't want you to say anything. I want you to tell me the truth."

"About what?"

"About anything. Pick something."

"I don't know what you want."

"Yes, you do," she said. "You've always known. That's the thing about you, George. You always know and you always pretend you don't know and then everybody has to go along pretending. I'm tired of it. I'm awfully tired of it."

"I'm sorry you're tired."

"Don't be sorry. Just don't pretend."

The rain had gotten harder. You could hear it on the roof now and in the gutter at the corner of the building where it came down in a stream onto the stones. He thought about the river and the place below the bridge where the big trout had been lying in the slow water under the bank. The trout would be all right. The trout did not care about the rain. They would go down to the bottom in the deep places and wait and when the water cleared they would come up again and feed and it would be the same as before. He thought about that.

"Where are you?" she said.

"I'm right here."

"You're not. You're down at the river. You're thinking about your trout."

"How did you know that?"

"Because I know you. I know what you look like when you go away like that. You've been going away like that since August."

"I haven't been going anywhere."

"You've been going away every day. You get up in the morning and you take your rod and your bag and you go down to the river and you stand in it all day and you come back at night and you eat and you drink the wine and you go to sleep. And I'm here. I'm here the whole time, George. I sit on the bank and I read and I watch you and you never once turn around to see if I'm still there."

"I knew you were there."

"How did you know?"

"I just knew it."

"You didn't look, though."

"I didn't have to look."

"That's it," she said. "That's exactly it. You didn't have to look."

He wanted another marc but he did not call for it. He sat and turned the empty glass on the table and looked at the way the light from the window came through it and made a small round shape on the cloth.

"I'm not trying to be cruel," she said. Her voice was softer now. "You know I'm not."

"I know."

"I only want to go home. I want to see my mother. I want to sleep in a room where I know where everything is. I want to stop moving for a while. Can you understand that?"

"Sure."

"Can you really?"

"I said sure."

"You could come too."

He looked at her.

"You could," she said. "You could come back with me. We could take a place somewhere. In the country maybe. You could write there. You always said you could write if you had a place."

"I've got a place. I've got all of France."

"That isn't a place. That's just somewhere to be."

"It's the same thing."

"It isn't the same thing at all and you know it isn't."

"I can't go back there," he said.

"Why not?"

"I just can't."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the only one I've got."

She drank the rest of her coffee. It must have been cold by then. She put the cup down and folded her hands on the table and looked at them. They were good hands, long and brown from the summer, and she had taken off the ring sometime and he had not noticed. He noticed now. There was a pale mark on the finger where it had been.

"When did you take that off?" he said.

She looked at her hand.

"Last week."

"Why?"

"It was loose. I've lost weight. I was afraid I'd lose it in the river."

"You never go in the river."

"No," she said. "I never do."

"Where is it?"

"It's in my bag. Upstairs. It's quite safe."

"All right," he said.

"You don't have to worry about it."

"I wasn't worried about it."

"No," she said. "I don't suppose you were."

The proprietor's wife came in and lit the stove after all. She knelt down in front of it and put in paper and kindling and struck a match and the paper caught and then the kindling and she shut the little iron door and opened the draft and the fire began to roar in the pipe. She stood up and wiped her hands on her apron and said it would be warm soon, and went out. The stove ticked as it heated. The woman turned her chair a little toward it and held out her hands.

"There," he said. "That's better."

"Yes. That's better."

"You were cold."

"I told you I was."

"I should have asked her before."

"It doesn't matter now."

They sat there. The fire made its noise and the rain made its noise and the river made its noise under everything. He thought it was strange how many noises there were in a quiet room.

"There's a bus to Pau in the morning," she said. "At seven. It connects with the train for Bordeaux. There's a boat from Bordeaux on Thursday."

"You've looked it all up."

"Yes."

"When did you look it up?"

"Yesterday. While you were on the river."

"You asked the proprietor?"

"I asked his wife. She was very kind about it. She thought I'd had bad news from home."

"Did you tell her you had?"

"I didn't tell her anything. I let her think it."

"That was smart."

"I'm not smart, George. I'm just tired."

He stood up and went over to the window. The rain was coming straight down now and there was no wind and the poplars across the river stood very still with the water running off them. The man with the dog had gone. There was nobody on the bridge. He could see the river coming fast and thick under the arches and a whole branch went by turning over and over in the brown water and went under the bridge and was gone.

"Would you want me to come to Pau with you?" he said without turning around.

"No."

"I could see you onto the train."

"I'd rather you didn't."

"All right."

"It would only be worse."

"I said all right."

He heard her chair move. He heard her stand up. He did not turn around. He heard her come across the room and then she was standing beside him at the window and they both looked out at the rain.

"It's a beautiful river," she said.

"Yes."

"I always thought so. Even when I hated it, I thought it was beautiful."

"Did you hate it?"

"Sometimes. Not the river. Only you standing in it."

He did not say anything.

"You'll stay here?" she said.

"For a while. Until it clears."

"And then Spain."

"Maybe. I don't know."

"You'll go to Spain," she said. "You'll go to Madrid and stay in the place on the Plaza Santa Ana and see the fights at Aranjuez and eat the strawberries. You'll like it. You'll like it fine."

"I guess I will."

"You'll write to me?"

"Sure."

"You won't, though."

"I said I would."

"You'll mean to," she said. "That's not the same."

She put her hand on his arm. He could feel it through the sweater. She did not hold on. She only rested it there and then took it away.

"I'm going upstairs to pack," she said.

"Do you want help?"

"No. There isn't much."

"I'll come up later."

"Come up whenever you like."

She went to the door and stopped there with her hand on the frame.

"George."

"What?"

"You could tell me to stay."

He looked at her then. She was standing in the doorway with the light from the hall behind her and he could not see her face very well.

"Would you stay?" he said.

She did not answer for a long time.

"No," she said finally. "I don't think so. But you could tell me."

"What good would it do?"

"None," she said. "None at all. I just thought you might want to."

Then she went out and he heard her on the stairs and then he heard the door of their room close above him. He stood at the window. After a while he went to the door of the dining room and called and the proprietor came and he asked for another marc. The proprietor brought it and set it on the table by the stove and looked out at the rain and shook his head.

"Madame is not well?" the proprietor said.

"Madame is fine."

"She has had news?"

"Yes," the man said. "She's had news."

"It is a pity. With the weather also."

"Yes. It is a pity."

The proprietor went out. The man sat down by the stove and drank the marc slowly. It was warm now by the stove and he was warm inside and the rain went on outside and he could hear her moving around upstairs, opening the drawers of the bureau and shutting them, and the sound of the closet door, and her shoes on the bare boards. He listened to it. Then he stopped listening and thought about the river. In three days the water would go down. In four days it would be clear. He would go down early in the morning when there was still mist on the water and walk out on the gravel bar below the bridge and wade in where it was shallow and make his cast up under the far bank where the big trout lay. The water would be cold and very clear and he would be able to see the stones on the bottom. It would be fine. It would be a fine thing to do.

He finished the marc and sat there with the empty glass in his hand. Upstairs it had gotten quiet. He did not know if she was finished or only sitting on the bed. He thought he would go up in a little while. He sat by the stove and the fire ticked and the rain came down and he did not go up.

content:
Here is an excerpt of Ernest Hemingway's writing, to show you their style:

I was away for two days at the posts. When I got home it was too late and I did not see Miss Barkley until the next evening. She was not in the garden and I had to wait in the office of the hospital until she came down. There were many marble busts on painted wooden pillars along the walls of the room they used for an office. The hall too, that the office opened on, was lined with them. They had the complete marble quality of all looking alike. Sculpture had always seemed a dull business—still, bronzes looked like something. But marble busts all looked like a cemetery. There was one fine cemetery though—the one at Pisa. Genoa was the place to see the bad marbles. This had been the villa of a very wealthy German and the busts must have cost him plenty. I wondered who had done them and how much he got. I tried to make out whether they were members of the family or what; but they were all uniformly classical. You could not tell anything about them. I sat on a chair and held my cap. We were supposed to wear steel helmets even in Gorizia but they were uncomfortable and too bloody theatrical in a town where the civilian inhabitants had not been evacuated. I wore one when we went up to the posts and carried an English gas mask. We were just beginning to get some of them. They were a real mask. Also we were required to wear an automatic pistol; even doctors and sanitary officers. I felt it against the back of the chair. You were liable to arrest if you did not have one worn in plain sight. Rinaldi carried a holster stuffed with toilet paper. I wore a real one and felt like a gunman until I practised firing it. It was an Astra 7.65 caliber with a short barrel and it jumped so sharply when you let it off that there was no question of hitting anything. I practised with it, holding below the target and trying to master the jerk of the ridiculous short barrel until I could hit within a yard of where I aimed at twenty paces and then the ridiculousness of carrying a pistol at all came over me and I soon forgot it and carried it flopping against the small of my back with no feeling at all except a vague sort of shame when I met English-speaking people. I sat now in the chair and an orderly of some sort looked at me disapprovingly from behind a desk while I looked at the marble floor, the pillars with the marble busts, and the frescoes on the wall and waited for Miss Barkley. The frescoes were not bad. Any frescoes were good when they started to peel and flake off. I saw Catherine Barkley coming down the hall, and stood up. She did not seem tall walking toward me but she looked very lovely.

“Good-evening, Mr. Henry,” she said.

“How do you do?” I said. The orderly was listening behind the desk.

“Shall we sit here or go out in the garden?”

“Let’s go out. It’s much cooler.” I walked behind her out into the garden, the orderly looking after us. When we were out on the gravel drive she said, “Where have you been?”

“I’ve been out on post.”

“You couldn’t have sent me a note?”

“No,” I said. “Not very well. I thought I was coming back.”

“You ought to have let me know, darling.” We were off the driveway, walking under the trees. I took her hands, then stopped and kissed her.

“Isn’t there anywhere we can go?”

“No,” she said. “We have to just walk here. You’ve been away a long time.”

“This is the third day. But I’m back now.” She looked at me, “And you do love me?”

“Yes.”

“You did say you loved me, didn’t you?”

“Yes,” I lied. “I love you.” I had not said it before.

“And you call me Catherine?”

“Catherine.” We walked on a way and were stopped under a tree.

“Say, ‘I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.’ ” “I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.”

“Oh, darling, you have come back, haven’t you?”

“Yes.”

“I love you so and it’s been awful. You won’t go away?”

“No. I’ll always come back.”

“Oh, I love you so. Please put your hand there again.”

“It’s not been away.” I turned her so I could see her face when I kissed her and I saw that her eyes were shut. I kissed both her shut eyes. I thought she was probably a little crazy. It was all right if she was. I did not care what I was getting into. This was better than going every evening to the house for officers where the girls climbed all over you and put your cap on backward as a sign of affection between their trips upstairs with brother officers. I knew I did not love Catherine Barkley nor had any idea of loving her. This was a game, like bridge, in which you said things instead of playing cards. Like bridge you had to pretend you were playing for money or playing for some stakes. Nobody had mentioned what the stakes were. It was all right with me.

“I wish there was some place we could go,” I said. I was experiencing the masculine difficulty of making love very long standing up.

“There isn’t any place,” she said. She came back from wherever she had been.

“We might sit there just for a little while.” We sat on the flat stone bench and I held Catherine Barkley’s hand. She would not let me put my arm around her.

“Are you very tired?” she asked.

“No.” She looked down at the grass.

“This is a rotten game we play, isn’t it?”

“What game?”

“Don’t be dull.”

“I’m not, on purpose.”

“You’re a nice boy,” she said. “And you play it as well as you know how. But it’s a rotten game.”

“Do you always know what people think?”

“Not always. But I do with you. You don’t have to pretend you love me. That’s over for the evening. Is there anything you’d like to talk about?”

“But I do love you.”

“Please let’s not lie when we don’t have to. I had a very fine little show and I’m all right now. You see I’m not mad and I’m not gone off. It’s only a little sometimes.” I pressed her hand, “Dear Catherine.”

“It sounds very funny now—Catherine. You don’t pronounce it very much alike. But you’re very nice. You’re a very good boy.”

“That’s what the priest said.”

“Yes, you’re very good. And you will come and see me?”

“Of course.”

“And you don’t have to say you love me. That’s all over for a while.” She stood up and put out her hand. “Good-night.” I wanted to kiss her.

“No,” she said. “I’m awfully tired.”

“Kiss me, though,” I said.

“I’m awfully tired, darling.”

“Kiss me.”

“Do you want to very much?”

“Yes.” We kissed and she broke away suddenly. “No. Good-night, please, darling.” We walked to the door and I saw her go in and down the hall. I liked to watch her move. She went on down the hall. I went on home. It was a hot night and there was a good deal going on up in the mountains. I watched the flashes on San Gabriele. I stopped in front of the Villa Rossa. The shutters were up but it was still going on inside. Somebody was singing. I went on home. Rinaldi came in while I was undressing.

“Ah, ha!” he said. “It does not go so well. Baby is puzzled.”

“Where have you been?”

“At the Villa Rossa. It was very edifying, baby. We all sang. Where have you been?”

“Calling on the British.”

“Thank God I did not become involved with the British.” I came back the next afternoon from our first mountain post and stopped the car at the smistimento where the wounded and sick were sorted by their papers and the papers marked for the different hospitals. I had been driving and I sat in the car and the driver took the papers in. It was a hot day and the sky was very bright and blue and the road was white and dusty. I sat in the high seat of the Fiat and thought about nothing. A regiment went by in the road and I watched them pass. The men were hot and sweating. Some wore their steel helmets but most of them carried them slung from their packs. Most of the helmets were too big and came down almost over the ears of the men who wore them. The officers all wore helmets; better-fitting helmets. It was half of the brigata Basilicata. I identified them by their red and white striped collar mark. There were stragglers going by long after the regiment had passed—men who could not keep up with their platoons. They were sweaty, dusty and tired. Some looked pretty bad. A soldier came along after the last of the stragglers. He was walking with a limp. He stopped and sat down beside the road. I got down and went over.

“What’s the matter?” He looked at me, then stood up.

“I’m going on.”

“What’s the trouble?”

“—— the war.”

“What’s wrong with your leg?”

“It’s not my leg. I got a rupture.”

“Why don’t you ride with the transport?” I asked. “Why don’t you go to the hospital?”

“They won’t let me. The lieutenant said I slipped the truss on purpose.”

“Let me feel it.”

“It’s way out.”

“Which side is it on?”

“Here.” I felt it.

“Cough,” I said.

“I’m afraid it will make it bigger. It’s twice as big as it was this morning.”

“Sit down,” I said. “As soon as I get the papers on these wounded I’ll take you along the road and drop you with your medical officers.”

“He’ll say I did it on purpose.”

“They can’t do anything,” I said. “It’s not a wound. You’ve had it before, haven’t you?”

“But I lost the truss.”

“They’ll send you to a hospital.”

“Can’t I stay here, Tenente?”

“No, I haven’t any papers for you.” The driver came out of the door with the papers for the wounded in the car.

“Four for 105. Two for 132,” he said. They were hospitals beyond the river.

“You drive,” I said. I helped the soldier with the rupture up on the seat with us.

“You speak English?” he asked.

“Sure.”

“How you like this goddam war?”

“Rotten.”

“I say it’s rotten. Jesus Christ, I say it’s rotten.”

“Were you in the States?”

“Sure. In Pittsburg. I knew you was an American.”

“Don’t I talk Italian good enough?”

“I knew you was an American all right.”

“Another American,” said the driver in Italian looking at the hernia man.

“Listen, lootenant. Do you have to take me to that regiment?”

“Yes.”

“Because the captain doctor knew I had this rupture. I threw away the goddam truss so it would get bad and I wouldn’t have to go to the line again.”

“I see.”

“Couldn’t you take me no place else?”

“If it was closer to the front I could take you to a first medical post. But back here you’ve got to have papers.”

“If I go back they’ll make me get operated on and then they’ll put me in the line all the time.” I thought it over.

“You wouldn’t want to go in the line all the time, would you?” he asked.

“No.”

“Jesus Christ, ain’t this a goddam war?”

“Listen,” I said. “You get out and fall down by the road and get a bump on your head and I’ll pick you up on our way back and take you to a hospital. We’ll stop by the road here, Aldo.” We stopped at the side of the road. I helped him down.

“I’ll be right here, lieutenant,” he said.

“So long,” I said. We went on and passed the regiment about a mile ahead, then crossed the river, cloudy with snow-water and running fast through the spiles of the bridge, to ride along the road across the plain and deliver the wounded at the two hospitals. I drove coming back and went fast with the empty car to find the man from Pittsburg. First we passed the regiment, hotter and slower than ever: then the stragglers. Then we saw a horse ambulance stopped by the road. Two men were lifting the hernia man to put him in. They had come back for him. He shook his head at me. His helmet was off and his forehead was bleeding below the hair line. His nose was skinned and there was dust on the bloody patch and dust in his hair.

“Look at the bump, lieutenant!” he shouted. “Nothing to do. They come back for me.” When I got back to the villa it was five o’clock and I went out where we washed the cars, to take a shower. Then I made out my report in my room, sitting in my trousers and an undershirt in front of the open window. In two days the offensive was to start and I would go with the cars to Plava. It was a long time since I had written to the States and I knew I should write but I had let it go so long that it was almost impossible to write now. There was nothing to write about. I sent a couple of army Zona di Guerra post-cards, crossing out everything except, I am well. That should handle them. Those post-cards would be very fine in America; strange and mysterious. This was a strange and mysterious war zone but I supposed it was quite well run and grim compared to other wars with the Austrians. The Austrian army was created to give Napoleon victories; any Napoleon. I wished we had a Napoleon, but instead we had Il Generale Cadorna, fat and prosperous, and Vittorio Emmanuele, the tiny man with the long thin neck and the goat beard. Over on the right they had the Duke of Aosta. Maybe he was too good-looking to be a great general but he looked like a man. Lots of them would have liked him to be king. He looked like a king. He was the King’s uncle and commanded the third army. We were in the second army. There were some British batteries up with the third army. I had met two gunners from that lot, in Milan. They were very nice and we had a big evening. They were big and shy and embarrassed and very appreciative together of anything that happened. I wish that I was with the British. It would have been much simpler. Still I would probably have been killed. Not in this ambulance business. Yes, even in the ambulance business. British ambulance drivers were killed sometimes. Well, I knew I would not be killed. Not in this war. It did not have anything to do with me. It seemed no more dangerous to me myself than war in the movies. I wished to God it was over though. Maybe it would finish this summer. Maybe the Austrians would crack. They had always cracked in other wars. What was the matter with this war? Everybody said the French were through. Rinaldi said that the French had mutinied and troops marched on Paris. I asked him what happened and he said, “Oh, they stopped them.” I wanted to go to Austria without war. I wanted to go to the Black Forest. I wanted to go to the Hartz Mountains. Where were the Hartz Mountains anyway? They were fighting in the Carpathians. I did not want to go there anyway. It might be good though. I could go to Spain if there was no war. The sun was going down and the day was cooling off. After supper I would go and see Catherine Barkley. I wished she were here now.

“Yes,” I lied. “I love you.” I had not said it before.

“And you call me Catherine?”

“Catherine.” We walked on a way and were stopped under a tree.

“Say, ‘I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.’ ” “I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.”

“Oh, darling, you have come back, haven’t you?”

“Yes.”

“I love you so and it’s been awful. You won’t go away?”

“No. I’ll always come back.”

“Oh, I love you so. Please put your hand there again.”

“It’s not been away.” I turned her so I could see her face when I kissed her and I saw that her eyes were shut. I kissed both her shut eyes. I thought she was probably a little crazy. It was all right if she was. I did not care what I was getting into. This was better than going every evening to the house for officers where the girls climbed all over you and put your cap on backward as a sign of affection between their trips upstairs with brother officers. I knew I did not love Catherine Barkley nor had any idea of loving her. This was a game, like bridge, in which you said things instead of playing cards. Like bridge you had to pretend you were playing for money or playing for some stakes. Nobody had mentioned what the stakes were. It was all right with me.

“I wish there was some place we could go,” I said. I was experiencing the masculine difficulty of making love very long standing up.

“There isn’t any place,” she said. She came back from wherever she had been.

“We might sit there just for a little while.” We sat on the flat stone bench and I held Catherine Barkley’s hand. She would not let me put my arm around her.

“Are you very tired?” she asked.

“No.” She looked down at the grass.

“This is a rotten game we play, isn’t it?”

“What game?”

“Don’t be dull.”

“I’m not, on purpose.”

“You’re a nice boy,” she said. “And you play it as well as you know how. But it’s a rotten game.”

“Do you always know what people think?”

“Not always. But I do with you. You don’t have to pretend you love me. That’s over for the evening. Is there anything you’d like to talk about?”

“But I do love you.”

“Please let’s not lie when we don’t have to. I had a very fine little show and I’m all right now. You see I’m not mad and I’m not gone off. It’s only a little sometimes.” I pressed her hand, “Dear Catherine.”

“It sounds very funny now—Catherine. You don’t pronounce it very much alike. But you’re very nice. You’re a very good boy.”

“That’s what the priest said.”

“Yes, you’re very good. And you will come and see me?”

“Of course.”

“And you don’t have to say you love me. That’s all over for a while.” She stood up and put out her hand. “Good-night.” I wanted to kiss her.

“No,” she said. “I’m awfully tired.”

“Kiss me, though,” I said.

“I’m awfully tired, darling.”

“Kiss me.”

“Do you want to very much?”

“Yes.” We kissed and she broke away suddenly. “No. Good-night, please, darling.” We walked to the door and I saw her go in and down the hall. I liked to watch her move. She went on down the hall. I went on home. It was a hot night and there was a good deal going on up in the mountains. I watched the flashes on San Gabriele. I stopped in front of the Villa Rossa. The shutters were up but it was still going on inside. Somebody was singing. I went on home. Rinaldi came in while I was undressing.

“Ah, ha!” he said. “It does not go so well. Baby is puzzled.”

“Where have you been?”

“At the Villa Rossa. It was very edifying, baby. We all sang. Where have you been?”

“Calling on the British.”

“Thank God I did not become involved with the British.” I came back the next afternoon from our first mountain post and stopped the car at the smistimento where the wounded and sick were sorted by their papers and the papers marked for the different hospitals. I had been driving and I sat in the car and the driver took the papers in. It was a hot day and the sky was very bright and blue and the road was white and dusty. I sat in the high seat of the Fiat and thought about nothing. A regiment went by in the road and I watched them pass. The men were hot and sweating. Some wore their steel helmets but most of them carried them slung from their packs. Most of the helmets were too big and came down almost over the ears of the men who wore them. The officers all wore helmets; better-fitting helmets. It was half of the brigata Basilicata. I identified them by their red and white striped collar mark. There were stragglers going by long after the regiment had passed—men who could not keep up with their platoons. They were sweaty, dusty and tired. Some looked pretty bad. A soldier came along after the last of the stragglers. He was walking with a limp. He stopped and sat down beside the road. I got down and went over.

“What’s the matter?” He looked at me, then stood up.

“I’m going on.”

“What’s the trouble?”

“—— the war.”

“What’s wrong with your leg?”

“It’s not my leg. I got a rupture.”

“Why don’t you ride with the transport?” I asked. “Why don’t you go to the hospital?”

“They won’t let me. The lieutenant said I slipped the truss on purpose.”

“Let me feel it.”

“It’s way out.”

“Which side is it on?”

“Here.” I felt it.

“Cough,” I said.

“I’m afraid it will make it bigger. It’s twice as big as it was this morning.”

“Sit down,” I said. “As soon as I get the papers on these wounded I’ll take you along the road and drop you with your medical officers.”

“He’ll say I did it on purpose.”

“They can’t do anything,” I said. “It’s not a wound. You’ve had it before, haven’t you?”

“But I lost the truss.”

“They’ll send you to a hospital.”

“Can’t I stay here, Tenente?”

“No, I haven’t any papers for you.” The driver came out of the door with the papers for the wounded in the car.

“Four for 105. Two for 132,” he said. They were hospitals beyond the river.

“You drive,” I said. I helped the soldier with the rupture up on the seat with us.

“You speak English?” he asked.

“Sure.”

“How you like this goddam war?”

“Rotten.”

“I say it’s rotten. Jesus Christ, I say it’s rotten.”

“Were you in the States?”

“Sure. In Pittsburg. I knew you was an American.”

“Don’t I talk Italian good enough?”

“I knew you was an American all right.”

“Another American,” said the driver in Italian looking at the hernia man.

“Listen, lootenant. Do you have to take me to that regiment?”

“Yes.”

“Because the captain doctor knew I had this rupture. I threw away the goddam truss so it would get bad and I wouldn’t have to go to the line again.”

“I see.”

“Couldn’t you take me no place else?”

“If it was closer to the front I could take you to a first medical post. But back here you’ve got to have papers.”

“If I go back they’ll make me get operated on and then they’ll put me in the line all the time.” I thought it over.

“You wouldn’t want to go in the line all the time, would you?” he asked.

“No.”

“Jesus Christ, ain’t this a goddam war?”

“Listen,” I said. “You get out and fall down by the road and get a bump on your head and I’ll pick you up on our way back and take you to a hospital. We’ll stop by the road here, Aldo.” We stopped at the side of the road. I helped him down.

“I’ll be right here, lieutenant,” he said.

“So long,” I said. We went on and passed the regiment about a mile ahead, then crossed the river, cloudy with snow-water and running fast through the spiles of the bridge, to ride along the road across the plain and deliver the wounded at the two hospitals. I drove coming back and went fast with the empty car to find the man from Pittsburg. First we passed the regiment, hotter and slower than ever: then the stragglers. Then we saw a horse ambulance stopped by the road. Two men were lifting the hernia man to put him in. They had come back for him. He shook his head at me. His helmet was off and his forehead was bleeding below the hair line. His nose was skinned and there was dust on the bloody patch and dust in his hair.

“Look at the bump, lieutenant!” he shouted. “Nothing to do. They come back for me.” When I got back to the villa it was five o’clock and I went out where we washed the cars, to take a shower. Then I made out my report in my room, sitting in my trousers and an undershirt in front of the open window. In two days the offensive was to start and I would go with the cars to Plava. It was a long time since I had written to the States and I knew I should write but I had let it go so long that it was almost impossible to write now. There was nothing to write about. I sent a couple of army Zona di Guerra post-cards, crossing out everything except, I am well. That should handle them. Those post-cards would be very fine in America; strange and mysterious. This was a strange and mysterious war zone but I supposed it was quite well run and grim compared to other wars with the Austrians. The Austrian army was created to give Napoleon victories; any Napoleon. I wished we had a Napoleon, but instead we had Il Generale Cadorna, fat and prosperous, and Vittorio Emmanuele, the tiny man with the long thin neck and the goat beard. Over on the right they had the Duke of Aosta. Maybe he was too good-looking to be a great general but he looked like a man. Lots of them would have liked him to be king. He looked like a king. He was the King’s uncle and commanded the third army. We were in the second army. There were some British batteries up with the third army. I had met two gunners from that lot, in Milan. They were very nice and we had a big evening. They were big and shy and embarrassed and very appreciative together of anything that happened. I wish that I was with the British. It would have been much simpler. Still I would probably have been killed. Not in this ambulance business. Yes, even in the ambulance business. British ambulance drivers were killed sometimes. Well, I knew I would not be killed. Not in this war. It did not have anything to do with me. It seemed no more dangerous to me myself than war in the movies. I wished to God it was over though. Maybe it would finish this summer. Maybe the Austrians would crack. They had always cracked in other wars. What was the matter with this war? Everybody said the French were through. Rinaldi said that the French had mutinied and troops marched on Paris. I asked him what happened and he said, “Oh, they stopped them.” I wanted to go to Austria without war. I wanted to go to the Black Forest. I wanted to go to the Hartz Mountains. Where were the Hartz Mountains anyway? They were fighting in the Carpathians. I did not want to go there anyway. It might be good though. I could go to Spain if there was no war. The sun was going down and the day was cooling off. After supper I would go and see Catherine Barkley. I wished she were here now.

The train came in late and Paul got down from the last car with his bag and stood on the platform. It was a small station with a water tank and a low red building and there was nobody on the platform but the agent. The agent took the mail sack off and went inside. Paul set his bag down. Beyond the station there was a road and beyond the road there were fields of cut hay and beyond the fields were the woods. The woods were dark and the sun was low over them. He had not seen the woods in nine years.

A truck came down the road with dust behind it. It was an old Ford truck with a flat bed and boards along the sides. It stopped by the platform and a man got out and came up the steps. He was big and wore a wool shirt with the sleeves rolled and his arms were brown.

"Hello, Ned," Paul said.

"Hello, kid." They shook hands. Ned's hand was hard and dry. He looked at Paul and Paul looked at him.

"You got old," Ned said.

"So did you."

"I got fat. You got old. That's different." He picked up the bag. "Is this all you brought?"

"That's all."

"You travel light."

"I learned to."

They went down the steps and Ned put the bag in the bed of the truck and they got in. The seat was torn and there was a coil of rope on the floor and a box of shells. Ned started the truck and they went out along the road. The dust came up behind them and hung in the air and the sun was in it.

"How was the trip?"

"Long."

"I bet it was long. Where'd you come from?"

"New York. Before that Paris."

"Paris," Ned said. "Well."

"It's just a town."

"Sure. Just a town." He drove with one hand on the wheel and his elbow out the window. "Ma wanted to come. She couldn't come. Her legs are bad."

"I'm sorry."

"She's all right. She's seventy-one. Her legs are bad, is all. She's going to cook you a chicken tomorrow."

"That's fine."

"She said she'd cook you a chicken and I said he's been in Paris, Ma, he's not going to want a chicken, and she said he'll want a chicken."

"I want a chicken," Paul said.

"I'll tell her."

They drove on. The road went down a hill and crossed a creek on a plank bridge and the truck rattled on the planks. The creek was low and clear and there were stones in it. Then the road went up through the woods. It was cooler in the woods. The trees were hemlock and birch and there were ferns along the road.

"I remember this," Paul said.

"It hasn't changed."

"No. I can see it hasn't."

"They cut up on the ridge two years ago. But they didn't cut down here. It's the same down here."

"I remember the creek."

"We used to take trout out of there. You remember the big one?"

"I remember."

"You lost him."

"I didn't lose him. You stepped on the line."

"The hell I did."

"You stepped on the line and he broke off."

Ned laughed. "Maybe I did. It was a long time ago. He was a good fish though."

"He was a fine fish."

"He was the best fish either of us ever had on."

"I've had bigger since."

"Not in a creek like that you haven't."

"No," Paul said. "Not in a creek like that."

They came out of the woods and there was the lake. It was long and flat and the color of the sky and the sun was going down at the far end of it. The house stood back from the water on a rise and there was a dock below it and a boat tied to the dock. The house was white and needed paint. Ned stopped the truck in the yard and turned off the motor and they sat there. It was very quiet. A dog came around the side of the house and stood looking at the truck.

"That's Jack," Ned said. "He's no good. He won't hunt."

"He looks all right."

"He looks all right. He won't hunt though. Come on."

They got out and the dog came and smelled Paul's hand and went away. Ned took the bag and they went up on the porch. There was a swing on the porch and two chairs and a washtub with a block of ice in it and bottles of beer in the water around the ice.

"I got beer," Ned said. "I figured you'd want a beer."

"I want a beer."

Ned opened two bottles on the edge of the porch rail and gave one to Paul. The beer was very cold. They sat in the chairs and looked at the lake.

"It's good beer," Paul said.

"It's from Marquette. It's not bad."

"It's good."

"I guess you've had better."

"Not as cold."

"That's the ice. I cut it in January. There's sawdust in the shed and it keeps all summer."

"I remember when we cut it with your father."

"He's been dead six years."

"I know. I got the letter."

"You didn't come back."

"No."

"That's all right," Ned said. "I'm not saying anything. It was winter anyway. You couldn't have got here."

"I couldn't have got here."

They drank the beer. The sun went down behind the trees at the far end of the lake and the water turned dark at that end and stayed light at their end. A loon called somewhere out on the water. Paul finished his beer and Ned opened two more.

"Where's Margaret?" Paul asked.

"She's gone to her sister's."

"Is she coming back?"

"She's coming back Thursday. Her sister's in Escanaba. Her sister's going to have a baby."

"That's fine."

"It's her fourth. They have them like rabbits over there."

"And you?"

Ned did not say anything. He drank the beer. The loon called again.

"We had one," he said. "It didn't live. That was two years ago."

"I didn't know."

"I didn't write it. I don't write much."

"I'm sorry, Ned."

"It was a boy. He lived four days." He set the bottle down on the boards of the porch. "Margaret's all right now. She was bad for a while but she's all right now."

"I didn't know," Paul said again.

"There's no reason you'd know. Do you want to go out in the boat? There's still light. We could go out and try for some bass along the weeds."

"I'd like that."

"I'll get the rods."

He went into the house and Paul sat on the porch. He could hear Ned moving inside the house and then a door closing. He looked at the lake. The light was going and the water was very flat and there were small rings on it where fish were coming up. He thought about Paris and the café on the corner of the rue Cardinal Lemoine and the rain on the window and the woman who had sat there with him in the afternoons. He did not want to think about that. He looked at the lake and the rings on the water and the dark line of the trees and he made himself not think about it.

Ned came out with two rods and a tackle box and they went down to the dock. The boat was a flat-bottomed rowboat painted green and there was water in the bottom of it. Ned bailed it with a coffee can and they got in. Ned rowed. He rowed slowly and well and the oars made small sounds in the locks and dripped when he brought them back. They went along the shore where the weeds were. The weeds came up to the surface and lay flat on it and there were lily pads.

"Throw in by the pads," Ned said.

Paul cast. The plug went out and landed near the pads and he reeled it back slowly. Nothing hit. He cast again.

"Do you still fish over there?"

"Sometimes. There's a river in Spain. In the mountains. I went there twice."

"Good fishing?"

"Very good. Trout. The water is very cold. It comes down out of the snow."

"Like here."

"Colder. And the country's different. It's bare. There aren't trees like this."

"I don't think I'd like a country without trees."

"It's a fine country. The people are fine."

"I guess you've been everywhere."

"Not everywhere."

"More places than me."

"That isn't hard," Paul said, and Ned laughed.

"No. That isn't hard."

Something hit the plug and the rod bent and Paul struck. The fish came out of the water. It was a bass and it shook its head in the air and fell back. Paul held the rod up and the fish went down into the weeds and he worked it out and it came out of the water again.

"He's a good one," Ned said. "Keep him out of the weeds."

"I'm keeping him out."

"Don't horse him."

"I'm not horsing him."

The fish came in close to the boat and Ned reached down and took it by the lower jaw and lifted it in. It was a smallmouth bass, bronze and dark along the back, and it lay in the bottom of the boat in the water and flapped.

"That's a good fish," Ned said. "That's two pounds."

"It's a nice fish."

"We'll eat him."

"Your mother's going to cook a chicken."

"That's tomorrow. We'll eat him tonight." Ned killed the fish with the handle of his knife and put it under the seat. "You still know how to fish anyway."

"I didn't forget."

"I thought maybe you forgot."

"You don't forget it."

"No," Ned said. "I guess you don't."

They fished along the shore until it was too dark to see the plugs land. Ned caught two and Paul caught one more. Then Ned rowed them back across the dark water. There were stars coming out and the lake was very still and the oars made the only sound. There was a light on in the house up on the rise. Paul sat in the stern and watched Ned row. Ned's face was dark and he could not see it.

"You staying long?" Ned asked.

"I don't know."

"You can stay as long as you want."

"I know."

"I mean it. There's room. Margaret likes you. She's always liked you."

"I haven't seen her since the wedding."

"She likes you though. She said, he's the one who brought the French wine to the wedding. She remembers that."

"It was bad wine."

"Everybody said it was fine wine."

"It was bad wine. I bought it in Chicago. It wasn't French at all."

Ned stopped rowing and laughed and the boat drifted. "The hell it wasn't."

"It was from California. I changed the labels."

"Well, I'll be damned," Ned said. "Don't tell Margaret."

"I won't tell her."

"She talked about that wine for a year."

He started rowing again. They came in to the dock and Ned shipped the oars and the boat bumped against the pilings. Paul tied it and they got out and went up to the house with the fish and the rods.

In the kitchen Ned cleaned the fish in the sink and Paul sat at the table. The kitchen was the same. There was the same stove and the same oilcloth on the table and the same calendar from the feed store on the wall, only the year was different. Ned rolled the fish in cornmeal and fried them in a black pan with bacon grease and the kitchen smelled of it. He got two more beers out of the icebox.

"It's a fine kitchen," Paul said.

"It's the same kitchen."

"That's what's fine about it."

Ned put the fish on two plates with bread and they ate. The fish was very good. It was hot and the cornmeal was crisp and the meat came off the bones white and clean. They ate without talking. Outside the frogs had started down by the lake.

"That's good fish," Paul said.

"It's better than Paris."

"It's different."

"Is it better?"

"It's very good," Paul said. "Leave it at that."

When they had eaten Ned took a bottle of whiskey down from the shelf over the stove and they took it out on the porch with two glasses and sat in the dark. Ned poured the whiskey and they drank it without water. It was rough whiskey and it was warm going down.

"Where'd you get this?"

"A man in town."

"It's not bad."

"It's terrible. But it's what there is."

They drank. The stars were very thick over the lake now and there was no moon. The frogs were loud. Somewhere up the shore a dog was barking and Jack lifted his head on the porch and then put it down again.

"You were in the war," Ned said.

"Not really. I was with the ambulances. Then I was with a newspaper."

"Ma said you got hurt."

"A little. In the shoulder. It was nothing."

"She worried."

"I wrote her it was nothing."

"She worried anyway. She had your letter in the Bible. She took it out and read it to people. Everybody in town knows about your shoulder."

"That's a hell of a thing."

"That's how she is."

"I know how she is."

Ned poured more whiskey. He held the bottle up against the stars to see how much was left and then set it down.

"I tried to go," he said. "In the war. They wouldn't take me. They said somebody had to work the farm. Pa was already sick then. So I stayed."

"Somebody had to."

"That's what they said."

"It was true."

"I know it was true," Ned said. "I'm not complaining. I just wanted to go. I wanted to see something. You know how it is. Everybody was going. Johnny Larsen went. Fred Coyle went."

"Fred Coyle didn't come back."

"No. Fred didn't come back. Johnny came back with one hand." He drank. "I guess I was lucky."

"You were lucky."

"I know. But I wanted to go anyway."

"It wasn't anything to see," Paul said. "It was mud and it was noise and then it was over. That's all it was."

"Sure."

"There wasn't anything to it."

"Sure," Ned said. "I guess there wasn't."

They sat. Paul held the glass in both hands. He thought about the road at night and the trucks with no lights and the smell of the place. He did not want to think about that either. There were a lot of things he did not want to think about and he had found that whiskey was good for not thinking about them, but tonight it was not working well. He drank anyway.

"Is there a girl?" Ned asked.

"There was."

"What happened?"

"Nothing happened. She went back to England."

"Were you going to marry her?"

"I don't know. I don't think so. She was married already."

"Oh," Ned said.

"Her husband was in India. He was a major."

"I see."

"It wasn't anything. It was just a thing that happened."

"Sure."

"She was a fine girl, though."

"I bet she was."

"She was a very fine girl," Paul said. He drank the rest of the whiskey in his glass and Ned poured him more. The frogs went on.

"You don't have to talk about it," Ned said.

"I'm not talking about it."

"All right."

"There isn't anything to talk about."

"All right, kid."

They did not say anything for a long time. A breeze came up off the lake and moved the leaves of the birch tree by the porch and then it went away again and the water was still. Paul could see the white shape of the dock below them and the dark shape of the boat.

"Do you remember the summer we built the raft?" Ned said.

"I remember."

"We built it out of those old ties from the railroad and it sank."

"It didn't sink. It floated six inches under the water."

"That's sinking."

"It's not the same as sinking. We stood on it."

"We stood on it and we were up to our knees."

"We were up to our knees but we were standing on it."

Ned laughed. "Pa laughed so hard he fell off the dock."

"I remember. He fell in with his pipe."

"He kept the pipe in his teeth. He came up and the pipe was still in his teeth."

"It was out though."

"It was out," Ned said. "God, that was a summer."

"That was a fine summer."

"We were what? Eleven?"

"I was ten. You were twelve."

"That's right. You were the little one."

"I was always the little one."

"You're not now."

"No," Paul said. "I'm not now."

Ned stood up and went to the edge of the porch and looked out at the lake. He stood there with his glass in his hand. He was a big dark shape against the stars.

"It's good you came," he said.

"It's good to be here."

"I mean it. It's good you came. I didn't think you'd come."

"I said I would."

"You said a lot of times you would."

"I know."

"This time you did, though."

"This time I did."

Ned finished his whiskey and came back and sat down. He put the glass on the boards. "We'll go up to the creek tomorrow," he said. "Early. Before it gets hot. Then we'll come back and Ma will cook the chicken."

"That's fine."

"We'll see if that fish has any grandchildren."

"He'll have grandchildren."

"He'll have a lot of them. And I won't step on the line."

"You stepped on it."

"Maybe I did," Ned said. "I'll stay off it tomorrow."

They sat a while longer and then Ned said he was going to bed. He showed Paul the room at the top of the stairs. It was the room Paul had slept in when he was a boy. There was the same iron bed and a window that looked out on the lake. Ned stood in the doorway.

"Good-night, kid."

"Good-night, Ned."

Ned went down the hall. Paul heard his door close. He undressed and lay on the bed in the dark with the window open. The frogs were very loud and he could smell the lake and the hemlocks. He lay there and listened. He thought he would not sleep but he did not mind. It was all right to lie awake here. It was not like lying awake in the other places. He thought about the creek and the cold water over the stones and how it would be in the morning with the sun just coming into the trees. He thought about that for a long time. Then after a while he did not think about anything and then he slept.

Here is an excerpt of Ernest Hemingway's writing, to show you their style:

I was away for two days at the posts. When I got home it was too late and I did not see Miss Barkley until the next evening. She was not in the garden and I had to wait in the office of the hospital until she came down. There were many marble busts on painted wooden pillars along the walls of the room they used for an office. The hall too, that the office opened on, was lined with them. They had the complete marble quality of all looking alike. Sculpture had always seemed a dull business—still, bronzes looked like something. But marble busts all looked like a cemetery. There was one fine cemetery though—the one at Pisa. Genoa was the place to see the bad marbles. This had been the villa of a very wealthy German and the busts must have cost him plenty. I wondered who had done them and how much he got. I tried to make out whether they were members of the family or what; but they were all uniformly classical. You could not tell anything about them. I sat on a chair and held my cap. We were supposed to wear steel helmets even in Gorizia but they were uncomfortable and too bloody theatrical in a town where the civilian inhabitants had not been evacuated. I wore one when we went up to the posts and carried an English gas mask. We were just beginning to get some of them. They were a real mask. Also we were required to wear an automatic pistol; even doctors and sanitary officers. I felt it against the back of the chair. You were liable to arrest if you did not have one worn in plain sight.
