Mrs. Henry Croft had a way of removing her gloves, after an evening abroad, which her husband had long ago learned to read as a sailor reads the sky. When she drew them off briskly, finger by finger, and tossed them upon the hall table with a little laugh, the weather was fair. When she drew them off slowly, with her lips pressed together, and laid them down side by side as if she meant to have them identified later by the police, a storm was making up somewhere beyond the horizon. To-night she drew them off very slowly indeed, and Henry, hanging his overcoat upon the walnut rack that had been her mother's, perceived that he would do well to look to his rigging.

"It was a pleasant dinner," he ventured, which was a mistake, as he knew the moment he had said it.

"Was it?" said Mrs. Croft. "I'm glad you thought so. I'm sure you seemed to enjoy yourself."

"Well, the Bannings always do things handsomely."

"Handsomely!" She turned from the table and went into the parlour, where the gas had been left burning low, and turned it up with a decisive hand. "Yes, I should say they did things handsomely. I should say they could afford to. I should say, too, that some people might take a lesson from them, if some people weren't too stubborn to learn anything from anybody."

Henry followed her, but not too closely. He was a mild, broad, greyish man of fifty, with a moustache that drooped at the ends as if it, too, had been worn down by years of domestic weather, and he had been for twenty-two years the proprietor of Croft's Hardware and Implement Store on Washington Street, which was the most respectable hardware store in the town and, as Mrs. Croft had lately begun to observe, also the most old-fashioned. He sat down in his own chair by the base-burner, and, there being nothing else to do with his hands, he took up the evening paper, which he had already read.

"Henry, will you put that down?"

He put it down.

"I want to talk to you," said Mrs. Croft, "and I don't intend to talk to a newspaper. I've talked to newspapers long enough. I've talked to the back of one every evening since we were married, and I'm tired of it."

"Why, Addie, I only—"

"Never mind what you only. Did you see Mrs. Banning's face to-night, when Mrs. Fenwick asked us whether we'd decided on our lot in the Elmhurst Addition?"

Henry said he had not noticed Mrs. Banning's face particularly.

"No, you wouldn't. You never notice anything that a person with ordinary perceptions would see in a minute. Well, I noticed it. She looked at Mrs. Fenwick, and Mrs. Fenwick looked at her, and then they both looked at their plates. And I sat there and smiled, Henry Croft, and said we hadn't quite made up our minds between the corner lot on Linden Avenue and the one facing the little park—and I had to say it with every one of them knowing perfectly well that you've been putting me off about it since last March!"

There is a kind of husband who, being accused, defends himself, and there is another kind who, being accused, examines the pattern of the carpet. Henry Croft belonged to the second kind; and it may be said for the carpet, which was a Brussels of large red roses upon a ground of a green no longer to be found in nature, that it rewarded examination. He examined it now.

"I don't see that it's anybody's business but ours," he said at last.

"Oh, you don't! Then I'll tell you whose business it is. It's Edith's business. Edith is nineteen years old, and every girl she knows is either living out in Elmhurst already or going to be living there by next fall. The Fenwicks are building. The Bannings have built. Even the Pruitts—the Pruitts, Henry!—have bought a lot, and everybody knows Sam Pruitt never had a dollar he didn't owe to somebody. And here we sit in this house on Mercer Street with the smoke from the round-house coming in at every window, and the boarding-houses creeping up from the other end of the block, and a saloon—a saloon, Henry—not three doors from where your daughter has to walk to get the street-car!"

"It isn't a saloon, exactly," Henry said. "Schaefer calls it a sample-room."

"I don't care what he calls it! I know what it is, and so does every young man who comes to call on Edith, and so does every young man who doesn't come because of it!"

This was a new consideration, and Henry looked up from the roses. "Why, Addie, I didn't know any young man had stopped coming."

"Of course you didn't. You don't know anything that goes on in this house. You come home, and you eat your supper, and you read your paper, and you go to bed; and you'd think the whole world was a hardware store with a family attached to it for the convenience of the proprietor." Mrs. Croft's voice trembled slightly upon this, for it was a phrase she had been composing, at intervals, for several weeks, and she was moved by it herself. "Harvey Fenwick hasn't been here since Easter."

"Well, I never thought much of Harvey Fenwick."

"That's not the point! The point is that he doesn't come, and the reason he doesn't come is that his mother says Mercer Street isn't what it used to be—and she said it, Henry, she said it in my hearing at the Woman's Club, and pretended she didn't know I was standing right behind her!"

Henry was silent. He was thinking, not of Harvey Fenwick, whom he considered a young man of inferior character because he parted his hair in the middle and had once asked Henry, in a tone of light raillery, whether he still kept horseshoe nails, but of something else—something which had been lying at the bottom of his mind, like a stone at the bottom of a well, for the better part of a year. He had grown used to its being there. He had even, at times, contrived to forget it for an hour together. But it was there now, very large and cold, and his wife's voice seemed to be drawing a bucket down toward it.

"Addie," he said, "there's no use getting excited."

"Excited!" said Mrs. Croft. "Excited! I've never been calmer in my life."

It is a curious law of the domestic universe that no woman ever announces her calmness except at the precise moment when it has departed from her; and Henry, who had been married long enough to know this law, though he had never thought to formulate it, rose and went to the window, where he stood looking out at the dark shapes of the maples along Mercer Street and the yellow lamp of Schaefer's sample-room glimmering beyond them.

"I'm only asking you," his wife went on, "for a plain answer. Are we going to build in Elmhurst, or are we not?"

"I haven't said we weren't."

"You haven't said we were. You've said 'we'll see' and 'there's plenty of time' and 'let's wait till the spring trade's over' and 'let's wait till the fall trade's started,' and now it's November and the Linden Avenue lot is the only good one left, and Mr. Ormsby told me himself, on the street, that he had an offer for it from a man in Chicago. A man in Chicago, Henry!"

"Ormsby always has an offer from a man in Chicago," said Henry. "It's his way of doing business."

"I don't care whether it is or not. I want that lot." She came and stood beside him, and for a moment her voice softened, and she put her hand upon his sleeve—a hand that was still small and still pretty, though it had kept house for twenty-two years with one hired girl and sometimes none. "Henry, I've never asked for much. You know I haven't. When the Bannings had their carriage, I didn't say a word. When everybody put in electric light, I said gas was good enough for me, because you said it was cheaper. I've made over Edith's dresses and my own, and I've done it gladly, because I knew you were saving—and I've always thought, all these years, that when the time came, when Edith was grown and it really mattered, we'd have something to show for it. And now the time's come. It's come, Henry. And I don't understand why you won't—"

She stopped, for her husband had turned from the window, and something in his face, under the full light of the gas, arrested her.

"Henry," she said in a different voice, "what is it?"

"Nothing," said Henry.

"It isn't nothing. You look sick."

"I'm not sick." He went back to his chair and sat down heavily, and the springs of the chair, which had known his weight for a dozen years and were well acquainted with its customary manner of descent, complained at this one as at a stranger. "Sit down, Addie."

She did not sit down. She stood where he had left her, by the window, with her hands clasped before her, and the little ornamental clock upon the mantel, a wedding present from an aunt who had long since gone to her reward, ticked into the silence with an air of tactless cheerfulness.

"Henry, you'd better tell me."

"I've been meaning to tell you," he said. "I've been meaning to, for a long time. I—it's the Midland Traction stock."

"The what?"

"The Midland Traction Company. The interurban line they were going to build out to Bentonville and Meade's Crossing. You remember. Everybody was going into it, a year ago last summer. Banning was in it. Fenwick was in it. Judge Hollister was one of the directors."

"I remember there was talk about it," she said slowly. "I remember you said it was a speculation, and you didn't believe in speculations. You said it at this very table."

"Yes," said Henry. "I did say that." He looked at the base-burner, through whose little isinglass windows the fire glowed redly, as if he hoped to find some counsel there. "I said it in June. In August I put eleven thousand dollars into it."

Mrs. Croft did not cry out. For a moment, indeed, she did not say anything whatever, and when at last she spoke it was in a tone so quiet that Henry would almost have preferred the other.

"Eleven thousand dollars," she said. "That's—Henry, that's nearly all of it."

"It's all but about eighteen hundred," he said. "And the store, of course. The store's clear."

"And the Midland Traction Company—"

"There isn't any Midland Traction Company," said Henry. "Not any more. There was a receiver appointed in February. They'd laid about four miles of track out past the fair-grounds, and then the money gave out, and it turned out some of the money had given out before it ever got to the track. Judge Hollister's resigned. There's talk of an indictment, but there's always talk. The stockholders might get eight or nine cents on the dollar, some day, if the court ever gets through with it. I don't count on it."

"In February," Mrs. Croft repeated. "In February. And this is November."

"Yes."

"And all through the spring, and all through the summer, when I was talking about the lot, and the plans, and showing you the pictures out of the magazines, and asking you whether you liked the house with the round tower or the one with the porch all the way across—all that time you knew."

"Yes," said Henry. "I knew."

She sat down then, not in her own chair, but upon the end of the horsehair sofa nearest the window, as if she had been walking a long way and had come upon it by chance. Henry did not look at her. He had made his confession to the base-burner, and he went on addressing himself to that unresponsive object, because it was easier.

"I don't know why I did it," he said. "That's the truth, Addie. I've been in business twenty-two years and I never did a foolish thing with money in my life—not one. I used to laugh at men who did. And then everybody was talking about it, at the Commercial Club, and on the street, and Banning came into the store one day and said, 'Well, Henry, I suppose you're too old-fashioned for anything like this,' and laughed, and I—well, I didn't like it. I didn't like being old-fashioned. I'd been hearing it a good deal." He paused. "I'd been hearing it at home, too, some."

Mrs. Croft made a slight movement, but did not speak.

"I thought," Henry went on, "that if it went the way they all said it would, we'd have enough to build in Elmhurst and not touch the savings at all. I thought I'd surprise you. I used to think about how I'd tell you—how I'd come home some evening and say, 'Addie, you go and pick out any lot you want.' I used to think about it on the way home from the store. That's the fool part of it." He laughed, without much success. "And then when it went the other way, I couldn't tell you. I kept thinking something would turn up. I kept thinking the receiver might find something. And every time you'd bring out those magazine pictures—"

He stopped, because his voice had become unreliable, and Henry Croft was of a generation and a place which held that a man's voice should under no circumstances become unreliable in the presence of his wife.

There followed a silence of some length, during which the clock upon the mantel continued its tactless observations, and a street-car went clanging by at the end of the block, and somewhere beyond the maples a voice, presumably issuing from Schaefer's sample-room, lifted itself in fragmentary and uncertain song. Mrs. Croft sat looking at her husband. She was seeing, it may be, a number of things at once: the house with the round tower, and the house with the porch all the way across, and Mrs. Banning's face, and Mrs. Fenwick's; but she was also seeing a broad greyish man, a little stooped now, walking home from Washington Street in the summer dusk and composing, with laborious happiness, a speech that would never be delivered. It was this last picture, perhaps, that lingered.

"Henry," she said at length, "does anybody know?"

"Banning knows I was in it. I don't know whether he knows how much."

"Does Edith know?"

"No."

"Then nobody's to know," said Mrs. Croft, and her voice had in it something which Henry had not heard there for a long time—something brisk and capable and very nearly cheerful, such as it had held twenty years ago, when they had moved into the house on Mercer Street with a borrowed dray and four dollars and sixty cents between them. "Nobody's to know anything about it, do you hear? Not Edith, and not the Bannings, and certainly not Cora Fenwick."

"But the lot—what'll you tell them about the lot?"

"I'll tell them," said Mrs. Croft, rising and smoothing her skirt with a gesture that was almost martial, "that we've decided Elmhurst is too far out. I'll tell them the Addition's going to be overbuilt, and that the drainage is bad, and that anybody with any judgment can see the town's going to grow the other way, toward the river. I'll tell them we think it's very sensible of them to have built there, and that we hope they'll be comfortable, and that we've decided to keep this house and put in electric light and a new furnace and have the front porch widened. And I'll say it so that every one of them will go home wondering if they haven't made a mistake."

Henry stared at her. "Addie, can we afford—"

"We can afford the electric light," said Mrs. Croft. "The porch can wait. They won't know whether it's waiting or not." She came over to his chair and stood looking down at him, and her mouth, which had been pressed so firmly together when she laid down her gloves, now relaxed into an expression which he could not altogether interpret, though it was not unkind. "And as for Harvey Fenwick," she added, "if a sample-room three doors away is enough to keep him from calling on Edith, then I think Edith is well rid of him. I never did like the way he parts his hair."

"Why, that's just what I always—" Henry began, and then stopped, overcome by the singularity of the coincidence.

"I know it is," said his wife. "You've said it at least fifty times." She touched his shoulder lightly, as one might touch a child who has been brought home late and unexpectedly unpunished. "Now I'm going up to bed. You turn down the gas when you come, and see that the base-burner's shut. And Henry—"

"Yes, Addie?"

She hesitated in the doorway, and for a moment it seemed that she might say something tender, or something reproachful, or possibly both. But she was a woman of her time and place, as he was a man of his; and in the end she merely said:

"You might have told me in February. I'd have liked to have known in February."

Then she went upstairs, and Henry sat for a long while by the base-burner, watching the red glow behind the little isinglass windows and listening to the clock. Once he picked up the evening paper, and once he laid it down again. He felt that something had happened to him which he did not wholly understand; that he had expected to be struck, and had been struck, but not where he had braced himself, nor in the manner he had feared. He had dreaded her anger, and her anger had been brief. What he had not foreseen, and what remained with him now, was the quiet sentence in the doorway, which had in it neither anger nor forgiveness but only a kind of grave surprise, as if, after twenty-two years, she had found a door in the house that she had not known was there.

He was still turning it over when he rose at last, and shut the damper of the base-burner, and turned down the gas, and went up the dark stairs, treading carefully upon the third step, which creaked, so as not to wake his daughter.

Here is an excerpt of Booth Tarkington's writing, to show you their style:

We debate sometimes what is to be the future of this nation when we think that in a few years public affairs may be in the hands of the fin-de-siècle gilded youths we see about us during the Christmas holidays. He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

response:
Mrs. Croft had made the announcement at breakfast, between the oatmeal and the eggs, in the manner of a woman who has long held a piece of news in reserve and believes its effect will be heightened by a casual delivery.

"Your Aunt Lavinia is coming on the Thursday train," she said, "and she's bringing Harriet."

Lindley Croft, aged seventeen and some months, laid down his spoon with deliberation. He had lately adopted deliberation as a principle, having observed it in a travelling elocutionist who recited "The Wreck of the Hesperus" at the Second Presbyterian Church and who had seemed to him, in the pauses before his more striking lines, to carry the weight of a whole world's experience.

"Harriet?" he said. "Oh, yes. Harriet."

"Your cousin Harriet," said his mother, as if there might be some confusion with other Harriets in his life. "You haven't seen her since she was eleven. You were ten. She pushed you into Shaler's Creek the summer before they went East. You surely remember that."

Lindley did remember it, and he remembered as well that the push had been unprovoked, that the creek had been colder than anyone would have supposed in August, and that he had afterwards been made to apologize for losing his temper, while Harriet, who began it, was given a peach. Of Harriet herself he retained a picture both distinct and unflattering: a lean, brown, peremptory creature, all knees and elbows and pigtails, with a nose that peeled in summer and a voice that carried to the next block. That this person should now be coming back, presumably to be fussed over and introduced and taken to the band concerts in the park, seemed to him an imposition upon his time.

"I shall be pretty busy Thursday," he said.

"Busy with what?" his father asked, looking up from the Daily Courier.

Lindley found that he had not decided. "Things," he answered, with dignity; and Mr. Croft, who had been seventeen himself at a period so remote that he no longer believed it, returned to his newspaper with a short sound through the nose which his son preferred not to interpret.

It is one of the mercies of youth that its resolutions, however firmly taken at breakfast, are seldom binding by afternoon, and it is one of its torments that it never perceives this mercy at the time. By Thursday noon Lindley had arrived at a fixed plan for the reception of his cousin. He would be present, since his mother required it; but he would be present in the manner of a man who has outgrown family occasions and attends them out of courtesy. He would be civil, even kind. He would make it plain, without unpleasantness, that the boy who had been pushed into Shaler's Creek no longer existed, and that in his place stood one who had read a good deal of Bulwer-Lytton, had smoked four cigarettes (only one of them disagreeably), and had danced twice with Miss Mabel Rennick, who was nineteen.

With this in view he spent a considerable part of the afternoon before his mirror. He put on his new waistcoat, which was of a pale fawn shade and had been chosen in defiance of his mother's opinion that it made him look "like a bookmaker." He put on the highest of his collars, which held his chin at an angle of perpetual mild surprise, and he arranged his hair in the style then favoured by the more advanced young men of the town: parted precisely in the middle and drawn down on either side in two wings, with an effect, as his father once remarked, "of a gentleman peering out between a pair of curtains." Then, having found a book of essays by Mr. Emerson upon the parlour table, he carried it out to the porch and opened it at random, so that he might be discovered reading when the carriage arrived.

The carriage was late. Lindley read the same paragraph about Self-Reliance eleven times without learning what it said, and was beginning to feel that Mr. Emerson must have been a tiresome man to sit next to at dinner, when he heard wheels at the corner and his mother's voice calling from the hall. He did not look up. He turned a page, and frowned at it thoughtfully, and permitted himself to become aware of the visitors only when the gate clicked and his aunt's voice, which he recognized at once, exclaimed upon the size of the maples.

"My land, Ellen, how those trees have grown! And the Hollisters have painted their house yellow. Whatever possessed them?"

Lindley rose, closing his book upon one finger to keep the place, and descended the steps with what he intended to be the unhurried courtesy of a host. He shook hands with Aunt Lavinia, who was stouter than he remembered and who kissed him in spite of the collar, and then he turned, with his speech of welcome ready, toward the cousin.

The speech did not come.

There was nobody in front of him whom he could identify as Harriet. There was a tall young lady in a grey travelling dress and a hat with a curving plume, who was paying the driver from a small purse and laughing at something he had said. When she turned, he saw a face that was pale where he had expected brown, composed where he had expected peremptory, and possessed of a pair of grey eyes which regarded him for a moment with frank inquiry and then filled, slowly and unmistakably, with amusement.

"Why, it's Lindy!" she said. "Mamma, look—it's Lindy, and he's grown a moustache!"

He had not grown a moustache. He had grown something on his upper lip, and had been cultivating it with secret care for upward of six weeks, but he had not supposed it was yet visible to the public; and the discovery that it was visible, and that its first public notice should take the form of this announcement in the front yard, before the driver and very probably before Mrs. Hollister in her yellow house across the way, struck him dumb. He shook the hand she offered him and said, "How do you do, Harriet," in a voice that began in one register and ended in another, and then he followed the party into the house, carrying a hatbox and Mr. Emerson together, and not knowing what to do with either.

There followed that interval, familiar to every household that has ever received relatives, in which nobody listens to anybody and everybody talks at once. Aunt Lavinia had to be shown her room and had to say it was exactly the same, and then had to say it was not the same at all, because the wallpaper was new; Mrs. Croft had to apologize for the wallpaper; the hired girl had to be introduced and had to be told that Miss Harriet took no sugar in her tea; and through it all Lindley stood in the hall with the hatbox, until his mother took it from him with an absent-minded "Thank you, dear," and he found himself with nothing in his hands but Emerson, who did not help.

It was Harriet who rescued him, though he would not have described it so. She came down the stairs alone, presently, having taken off her hat, and he saw that her hair, which he remembered as two tight ropes of an indeterminate colour, was in reality a soft brown, done up in a manner that he did not understand but felt to be very becoming.

"Mamma and Aunt Ellen have begun on the Pruitt family," she said, "and they'll be at it till supper. Let's go out on the porch where it's cool. Unless you're too busy reading," she added, glancing at the book. "What is it?"

"Emerson," said Lindley.

"Oh dear," said Harriet. "Do you like him?"

He had meant to say that he found Emerson a profound thinker, but there was something in her tone that suggested she would not be impressed by this, and he heard himself saying instead, "Well, parts of him."

"Which parts?"

"The—the parts about self-reliance."

"I never could get through those," she said cheerfully. "I always wanted to tell him he'd been self-reliant long enough and might let somebody else talk." And she went out to the porch and settled herself in the wicker rocker, which had been his grandfather's, and looked out over the lawn and the street with an expression he could not read.

Lindley took the porch swing, which he had not intended; it was a seat for children and couples, and a man of the world would have chosen the steps. But he found the steps too far away, for some reason, and so he sat in the swing, and it moved under him with a faint creak of chains, and he was obliged to brace one foot against the floor to keep from drifting.

"It's queer," Harriet said, after a while. "Everything is smaller."

"Smaller?"

"The houses. The street. Even the trees, though Mamma says they're bigger. I suppose it's because I was smaller. When we left I thought the Hollister house was a palace. I used to make up stories that a princess lived in it." She laughed. "And now it's yellow."

"They only painted it last spring," Lindley said, feeling vaguely that the town ought to be defended. "Lots of things are new. They've got the trolley line clear out to the fairgrounds now, and there's a new opera house on Main Street that seats nine hundred. And they've cut up the Harbaugh orchard into lots."

"Not the Harbaugh orchard!"

"Yes. There's going to be a street through it. They're going to call it Fairview Avenue."

Harriet was silent for a moment. "We used to steal apples there," she said. "Don't you remember? You and I and Tommy Pruitt, and old Mr. Harbaugh came out with a buggy whip and you fell out of the tree and he was so frightened he gave us each a whole basket to take home."

Lindley did remember; he remembered it with a sudden and complete vividness that took him by surprise—the smell of the grass under the trees, and the bark scraping his knees, and the old man's face going from purple to white when he saw that the boy on the ground was not moving. He had not been badly hurt; he had only had the wind knocked out of him; but he had lain there with his eyes shut a little longer than was strictly necessary, because it was interesting to hear what people said about him while they thought him unconscious.

"I wasn't really hurt," he said now, a little stiffly.

"I know you weren't," said Harriet. "I saw you peeking. I didn't tell."

He looked at her. She was rocking gently, with her eyes on the street, and there was nothing in her face but a kind of peaceful reminiscence; and yet he had an uncomfortable conviction that she was laughing at him somewhere underneath. It was a conviction that would come to him a good many times in the course of the summer, and he never learned whether it was justified, which is perhaps the chief thing that a cousin a year older can do for a cousin a year younger.

"Well," he said, adjusting his collar, "a person grows out of that sort of thing."

"Out of stealing apples?"

"Out of—oh, the whole business. Children's games." He leaned back in the swing, which unfortunately carried him backward farther than he had intended, so that he had to recover with a jerk. "I suppose you've found the same thing, back East. I suppose you've seen a good deal of society."

"Some," said Harriet.

"I've been going out a good deal myself, lately," he went on, with an air of reluctant confession. "Dances and so on. Of course this isn't Philadelphia, but there's a pretty lively set here, among the older crowd. I don't care for most of it, though. I find most people pretty shallow, when you get to know them."

"Do you?" said Harriet. "I find most people pretty deep, when I get to know them. That's what makes them so hard to talk to at dances."

He did not know how to answer this, and so he let it pass, as one lets pass a remark in a foreign language that one has not quite caught; and he was relieved when she turned the conversation herself.

"Tell me about everybody," she said. "Tell me about Tommy Pruitt. Is he still horrid?"

"He's at the State University," said Lindley. "He's on the football team. He weighs a hundred and eighty pounds."

"Tommy Pruitt! He was the littlest boy in the Sunday school. He used to cry when they made him say the Golden Text."

"Well, he doesn't cry now," Lindley said, with some feeling; for Tommy Pruitt, in the season just past, had developed a habit of greeting him on Main Street by lifting him clear of the sidewalk, which was not a thing a man of the world could easily forgive. "And Bessie Lamb is married. She married a dentist from Terre Haute. And old Dr. Ruggles died, and they put up a drinking fountain for him in the courthouse square, only the water doesn't work."

"And Grandfather?" Harriet said.

The swing stopped. Lindley had known, of course, that she would ask; Aunt Lavinia had come back for the reading of the papers and the dividing of the house on Locust Street, and that was the real reason for the visit, though nobody had said so at breakfast. But he had somehow supposed that she would ask it of his mother, in the parlour, with lowered voices, and not of him, out here.

"It was in March," he said. "He wasn't sick long. He sat right there, mostly—in that chair you're in—up till about two weeks before. He used to tell me to sit up straight."

Harriet stopped rocking. She did not look at the chair, but he saw her hands, which had been lying in her lap, close upon each other.

"He used to tell me that, too," she said. "He used to say, 'Hattie, a lady may slump in her own bedroom, but nowhere else in the Republic.' And then he would give me a peppermint, because he thought he'd been too stern." She was quiet for a little. "He wrote to me every month, all the time we were away. Did you know that? Long letters, about everything—about the weather, and the price of wheat, and how the Hollisters' cow got into the Methodist church. I have all of them. Mamma thinks I'm silly to keep them."

"He wrote to you?" said Lindley. It was not jealousy that he felt; it was something stranger, a sense that he had been living for six years beside a man who had a whole correspondence he knew nothing about, and that the old gentleman in the wicker chair, who had seemed to him chiefly a source of admonitions about posture, had been a person of more resources than he had suspected.

"Every month," Harriet said. "He said he wanted me to know what was going on at home, so I wouldn't come back a stranger." She smiled, though not very steadily. "And here I am, and everything's smaller, and the Harbaugh orchard is Fairview Avenue, and Tommy Pruitt weighs a hundred and eighty pounds. I'm a stranger anyhow."

Lindley was aware that something was required of him, and that it was not anything he had learned from Bulwer-Lytton. He sat in the swing with his foot braced against the floor and his chin held up by his collar, and he searched his mind for the right thing to say, and found nothing in it but a recollection of the creek.

"You pushed me in Shaler's Creek," he said.

Harriet turned and looked at him.

"I mean," said Lindley, reddening, "I mean you can't be a stranger. Strangers don't push people in creeks. I remember it perfectly. It was the eleventh of August. You said I was a baby because I wouldn't wade out to the big rock, and then you pushed me, and I got a peach and you didn't—no, wait—you got a peach and I didn't. That's how it was. It was the most unjust thing that ever happened to me."

For a moment Harriet only looked at him, and then she began to laugh—not the amused, superior laugh he had been bracing against all afternoon, but a laugh of a different kind, helpless and warm, which made her put her hand over her eyes.

"Oh, Lindy," she said. "Oh, Lindy, you're exactly the same."

He was not sure this was a compliment, and he was quite sure it was not true; but he found, somewhat to his own surprise, that he did not mind. He let the swing move a little, and the chains creaked, and down the street the lamplighter came by on his bicycle, touching the posts with his long pole one after another, so that a row of small flames bloomed along the dusk.

"I'm not the same," he said, after a time, but without much conviction. "I've changed a good deal."

"I know," said Harriet, wiping her eyes. "You've got a moustache."

"It's not a moustache," he said. "Not yet."

"It's a very nice beginning of one."

He considered this. "Mabel Rennick says it makes me look older."

"Who is Mabel Rennick?"

"Oh, just a girl," said Lindley carelessly; and then, because the dusk was kind and the swing was moving and his cousin seemed to be listening with a real and friendly interest, he told her all about Mabel Rennick—her age, her accomplishments upon the mandolin, the two dances, and the deplorable fact that she had afterwards been seen at the Elks' picnic in the company of a druggist's clerk from Indianapolis who wore yellow shoes. It was a long recital and not altogether coherent, but Harriet heard it through without once laughing, and at the end of it she said, very gravely, that she thought Miss Rennick had shown poor judgment, and that it was probably the yellow shoes, which some girls could not resist.

They were still sitting there, talking about the druggist's clerk and Tommy Pruitt and the drinking fountain that would not work, when Mrs. Croft came to the screen door to call them in to supper. She stood a moment looking out at them, unseen—her son in the porch swing, with his collar wilted at last and one wing of his hair fallen down over his forehead as it used to fall when he was ten, and her niece in the old wicker chair, leaning forward, with her chin on her hand.

"Well," said Aunt Lavinia, coming up behind her, "they seem to be getting on."

"Yes," said Mrs. Croft; and something in her voice made her sister glance at her. "It's the chair, I think. Father always liked company on the porch in the evening."

Supper was a long affair, as such suppers are, and the talk at it was all of the house on Locust Street and the Pruitt family and the price of lots on Fairview Avenue. Lindley ate a great deal and said very little. Once, when his father asked him whether he had got much good out of Mr. Emerson that afternoon, he replied that Emerson was all right in parts, but that a man could be too self-reliant; and Mr. Croft, who had been about to make the short sound through his nose, looked at his son over his spectacles instead and said nothing at all.

Later, in his own room, with the high collar thrown across the back of a chair, Lindley sat for some time at the window, looking down at the porch roof and the dark lawn and the row of lamps along the street. He had kept a diary since January, in a leather book with a lock, and in it he had recorded, at intervals, his views on life, on society, and on the general shallowness of the feminine character. He opened it now and wet his pencil and considered.

"My cousin Harriet arrived to-day from Philadelphia," he wrote at last. "She is much changed in appearance. She is fairly intelligent for a girl." He looked at this for a while and frowned at it, as he had frowned at Emerson, and then he crossed out the last sentence with three heavy lines and wrote beneath it: "She remembered about the creek."

And that, though he could not have told you why, seemed to him to say everything.

content:
Here is an excerpt of Booth Tarkington's writing, to show you their style:

We debate sometimes what is to be the future of this nation when we think that in a few years public affairs may be in the hands of the fin-de-siècle gilded youths we see about us during the Christmas holidays. Such foppery, such luxury, such insolence, was surely never practised by the scented, overbearing patricians of the Palatine, even in Rome’s most decadent epoch. In all the wild orgy of wastefulness and luxury with which the nineteenth century reaches its close, the gilded youth has been surely the worst symptom. With his airs of young milord, his fast horses, his gold and silver cigarette-cases, his clothes from a New York tailor, his recklessness of money showered upon him by indulgent mothers or doting grandfathers, he respects nothing and nobody. He is blase if you please. Watch him at a social function, how condescendingly he deigns to select a partner for the popular waltz or two step, how carelessly he shoulders older people out of his way, with what a blank stare he returns the salutation of some old acquaintance whom he may choose in his royal whim to forget! The unpleasant part of all this is that the young women he so condescendingly selects as partners for the dance greet him with seeming rapture, though in their hearts they must feel humiliated by his languid hauteur, and many older people beam upon him almost fawningly if he unbends so far as to throw them a careless, disdainful word! One wonders what has come over the new generation. Of such as these the Republic was not made. Let us pray that the future of our country is not in the hands of these fin-de-siècle gilded youths, but rather in the calloused palms of young men yet unknown, labouring upon the farms of the land. When we compare the young manhood of Abraham Lincoln with the specimens we are now producing, we see too well that it bodes ill for the twentieth century— George yawned, and tossed the clipping into his waste-basket, wondering why his aunt thought such dull nonsense worth the sending. As for her insinuation, pencilled upon the border, he supposed she meant to joke—a supposition which neither surprised him nor altered his lifelong opinion of her wit. He read her letter with more interest:
... The dinner your mother gave for the Morgans was a lovely affair. It was last Monday evening, just ten days after you left. It was peculiarly appropriate that your mother should give this dinner, because her brother George, your uncle, was Mr. Morgan’s most intimate friend before he left here a number of years ago, and it was a pleasant occasion for the formal announcement of some news which you heard from Lucy Morgan before you returned to college. At least she told me she had told you the night before you left that her father had decided to return here to live. It was appropriate that your mother, herself an old friend, should assemble a representative selection of Mr. Morgan’s old friends around him at such a time. He was in great spirits and most entertaining. As your time was so charmingly taken up during your visit home with a younger member of his family, you probably overlooked opportunities of hearing him talk, and do not know what an interesting man he can be. He will soon begin to build his factory here for the manufacture of automobiles, which he says is a term he prefers to “horseless carriages.” Your Uncle George told me he would like to invest in this factory, as George thinks there is a future for automobiles; perhaps not for general use, but as an interesting novelty, which people with sufficient means would like to own for their amusement and the sake of variety. However, he said Mr. Morgan laughingly declined his offer, as Mr. M. was fully able to finance this venture, though not starting in a very large way. Your uncle said other people are manufacturing automobiles in different parts of the country with success. Your father is not very well, though he is not actually ill, and the doctor tells him he ought not to be so much at his office, as the long years of application indoors with no exercise are beginning to affect him unfavourably, but I believe your father would die if he had to give up his work, which is all that has ever interested him outside of his family. I never could understand it. Mr. Morgan took your mother and me with Lucy to see Modjeska in “Twelfth Night” yesterday evening, and Lucy said she thought the Duke looked rather like you, only much more democratic in his manner. I suppose you will think I have written a great deal about the Morgans in this letter, but thought you would be interested because of your interest in a younger member of his family. Hoping that you are finding college still as attractive as ever, Affectionately, Aunt Fanny. George read one sentence in this letter several times. Then he dropped the missive in his wastebasket to join the clipping, and strolled down the corridor of his dormitory to borrow a copy of “Twelfth Night.” Having secured one, he returned to his study and refreshed his memory of the play—but received no enlightenment that enabled him to comprehend Lucy’s strange remark. However, he found himself impelled in the direction of correspondence, and presently wrote a letter—not a reply to his Aunt Fanny. Dear Lucy: No doubt you will be surprised at hearing from me so soon again, especially as this makes two in answer to the one received from you since getting back to the old place. I hear you have been making comments about me at the theatre, that some actor was more democratic in his manners than I am, which I do not understand. You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. Well, here I sit smoking my faithful briar pipe, indulging in the fragrance of my tobacco as I look out on the campus from my many-paned window, and things are different with me from the way they were way back in Freshman year. I can see now how boyish in many ways I was then. I believe what has changed me as much as anything was my visit home at the time I met you. So I sit here with my faithful briar and dream the old dreams over as it were, dreaming of the waltzes we waltzed together and of that last night before we parted, and you told me the good news you were going to live there, and I would find my friend waiting for me, when I get home next summer. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. I am not capable of friendship except for the very few, and, looking back over my life, I remember there were times when I doubted if I could feel a great friendship for anybody—especially girls. I do not take a great interest in many people, as you know, for I find most of them shallow. Here in the old place I do not believe in being hail-fellow-well-met with every Tom, Dick, and Harry just because he happens to be a classmate, any more than I do at home, where I have always been careful who I was seen with, largely on account of the family, but also because my disposition ever since my boyhood has been to encourage real intimacy from but the few. What are you reading now? I have finished both “Henry Esmond” and “The Virginians.” I like Thackeray because he is not trashy, and because he writes principally of nice people. My theory of literature is an author who does not indulge in trashiness—writes about people you could introduce into your own home. I agree with my Uncle Sydney, as I once heard him say he did not care to read a book or go to a play about people he would not care to meet at his own dinner table. I believe we should live by certain standards and ideals, as you know from my telling you my theory of life. Well, a letter is no place for deep discussions, so I will not go into the subject. From several letters from my mother, and one from Aunt Fanny, I hear you are seeing a good deal of the family since I left. I hope sometimes you think of the member who is absent. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. It is the only girl’s photograph I ever took the trouble to have framed, though, as I told you frankly, I have had any number of other girls’ photographs, yet all were only passing fancies, and oftentimes I have questioned in years past if I was capable of much friendship toward the feminine sex, which I usually found shallow until our own friendship began. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. I will have to rise and fill it, then once more in the fragrance of My Lady Nicotine, I will sit and dream the old dreams over, and think, too, of the true friend at home awaiting my return in June for the summer vacation. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. Lucy and her father were living at the Amberson Hotel, while Morgan got his small machine-shops built in a western outskirt of the town; and George grumbled about the shabbiness and the old-fashioned look of the hotel, though it was “still the best in the place, of course.” He remonstrated with his grandfather, declaring that the whole Amberson Estate would be getting “run-down and out-at-heel, if things weren’t taken in hand pretty soon.” He urged the general need of rebuilding, renovating, varnishing, and lawsuits. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

Mr. Albert Crane came home that Thursday evening at a quarter past six, which was his hour, and set his umbrella in the rack, which was its place, and hung his hat upon the third peg of the hall-tree, which was its peg; for he was a man who believed that a household, like a bank, should be conducted upon principles, and he had been cashier of the Second National for eleven years without once permitting a principle to be overdrawn. He was of a moderate size, with a moderate moustache, and he wore the expression of patient rectitude which comes upon men who are obliged to say no to their neighbours across a brass grille six days in the week. It was an expression he had not intended to bring home with him; but, as Mrs. Crane had once observed to her sister, it was a little like his rubbers: he forgot to take it off at the door.

On this particular evening he found his wife waiting for him at the foot of the stairs, and there was that in her attitude which warned him. She was a small, pretty woman, inclined to plumpness and to laughter, and she was not laughing now. She had, instead, the look of one who carries a parcel that may go off.

"Albert," she said, "I want you to come into the sitting-room a moment before supper. Don't go upstairs."

"Why not?"

"Because he's up there."

Mr. Crane did not need to ask who was meant. In that house there was only one person who was ever referred to by the pronoun alone, and in a tone that implied capital letters. He was seven years old, he was named Wendell after his maternal grandfather, and he had been sent to his room at half-past three that afternoon, where, according to report, he had since been engaged in making a noise like a steam-calliope at intervals of about four minutes.

"What has he done now?" asked Mr. Crane, and followed his wife into the sitting-room, where she closed the door with a care that seemed excessive for so domestic an occasion.

Mrs. Crane did not answer at once. She went to the centre-table and took up from it, with both hands and a certain reverence, an object which she held out to her husband in silence. He looked at it for some moments before he recognized it, and when he did so his countenance underwent a change.

It was, or it had been, his silk hat. It was the hat he had bought in Chicago at the time of his brother-in-law's wedding; the hat he wore to funerals of directors and to the annual dinner of the Bankers' Association of the Fourth District; a hat of such lustre that Mrs. Crane had once said she could do her hair in it. It was now of a shape not readily described. The crown had been pushed down into the brim and then, apparently, hauled out again by main force, so that it rose in a series of terraces, like a pagoda; there was a long rent in the silk upon one side; and around the band, secured by what seemed to be several yards of the pink ribbon from Mrs. Crane's work-basket, there had been fastened a quantity of feathers which Mr. Crane, being a man of some experience, identified without difficulty as having come from the Wyandotte rooster belonging to Mrs. Purcell next door.

"Good heavens!" said Mr. Crane.

"That isn't all," said his wife.

"Isn't all!"

"He gave a circus," Mrs. Crane explained, in a voice that wavered a little, though whether toward tears or toward the other thing her husband could not be sure. "In the carriage-house. He charged two pins admission, and five pins for the reserved seats, which were the oat-bin. All the children on the street came. Albert, they say there were twenty-two. And he was the ringmaster, and he wore that, and he had your—your riding-crop——"

"I haven't ridden in nine years."

"Well, he had it. And the Purcell rooster was the Great Bird of Paradise from the Jungles of Borneo, only it got away, and they chased it through the Purcells' grape-arbour, and that's how the feathers—and then little Ethel Purcell's kitten was the Blue Tiger of India."

"The *blue* tiger?"

"He dipped it in the bluing," said Mrs. Crane faintly. "Bridget's tub was standing right there. It isn't hurt, Albert. It's only blue. Mrs. Purcell brought it over to show me. "There, there, Laura. Don't cry. I'll attend to it."

"I'm not crying," said Mrs. Crane in a muffled tone; and went on not crying, so far as he could tell, with considerable vehemence.

Now, it may be said at once that Mr. Albert Crane had very definite views upon the rearing of children, and that these views, like most views upon that subject, had been formed largely in the years before he had any children to rear. He believed in firmness. He believed that a boy should be reasoned with, but reasoned with from a height; that justice should be swift and quiet and adapted to the offence; and that the great error of the age—he had read an article about it in a magazine—was the modern parent's weakness, his habit of laughing at what should be punished, and of punishing, afterward and inconsistently, what he had laughed at before. Mr. Crane did not intend to be a modern parent. He had told his wife so, upon several occasions; and she had agreed with him, upon several occasions, with an air of being entertained by something not visible to him.

"Wendell! Come down here, please. I wish to see you in the library."

The steam-calliope, which had been in the midst of an ambitious passage, stopped abruptly. "Eight dollars!" he said. "*Gee!*"

"Don't say 'gee.' Yes, eight dollars. That is more money than you will have in your bank until you are a great deal older than you are now. And you took it without asking anybody, out of my closet, where you know perfectly well you are not allowed to go, and you wore it in a—a circus, and you allowed it to be ruined. "Yes, sir," said Wendell.

His father had expected a denial, or an evasion, or at least the beginning of tears; for each of these he had prepared a suitable rejoinder. Against a simple affirmative he had no defences ready. He was obliged to fall back upon the obvious.

"You did? Then why did you take it?"

Wendell drew a long breath, as a man does who is about to present a case he believes to be unanswerable.

"Well, a ringmaster has *got* to have a tall hat. Everybody knows that.
