response:
There is a kind of silence known only to people who have been married a long while. It is not the silence of strangers, which is merely empty, nor that of lovers, which is full. It is a furnished silence, crowded with old grievances and older habits, and either party may walk about in it at will, bumping into things. Mr. and Mrs. Lamar Dorsey had been married nineteen years, and they had furnished their silence handsomely.

They sat in it now, upon a warm evening in early September, in the front sitting-room of the frame house on Pennington Street which Mr. Dorsey had bought, "on very reasonable terms," the year their daughter Florence was born. He was reading the *Evening News*, or appeared to be; and she was rocking. The rocker had a squeak in it which Mr. Dorsey had promised to oil some time during the second Cleveland administration. Mrs. Dorsey had never reminded him of the promise. She preferred to rock.

Neighbours who passed the lighted window, and glanced in as neighbours will, would have seen nothing more than a pleasant domestic picture: a stoutish, sandy, middle-aged man in his shirt-sleeves, a newspaper held well up before his face, and a handsome woman of forty-odd in a lilac house-gown, her hands folded in her lap, gazing at the gas-log. They might have envied the Dorseys their peace. They would have been mistaken about it. Mrs. Dorsey had come home at half-past five from Mrs. J. Hartley Teague's card party, and she had not yet said one word about it. In nineteen years she had never before returned from a card party without saying a great many words about it, so Mr. Dorsey's newspaper was not so much a newspaper as a fortification.

"Lamar," she said at last.

"Mm?"

"Is there anything in the paper?"

"Nothing much. They're going to pave Hazel Avenue again."

"Again?" said Mrs. Dorsey. "I didn't know they'd ever paved it once."

"Well, they did. That was the trouble." He turned a page, rattling it with what he hoped was an air of absorption. "This fellow says the asphalt was half sawdust. I guess there's been considerable graft in it somewhere."

"I shouldn't wonder," said Mrs. Dorsey. "People are so deceitful nowadays."

The paper did not lower, but it ceased, for an instant, to rattle; and Mr. Dorsey, behind it, cleared his throat with elaborate unconcern. He was a man who had never in his life been able to clear his throat with any unconcern whatever. His wife knew this, and the knowledge was in her voice when she spoke again.

"Mrs. Teague's rooms looked lovely. She had them all done in yellow chrysanthemums. They came from Pfaffinger's, and I suppose they cost a fortune; but then the Teagues can afford it, I suppose. At least they can afford it *now*."

"Well, Hartley's always done pretty well," Mr. Dorsey said, from his entrenchment.

"Yes. And he's going to do better, Mrs. Teague says. A great deal better." She rocked twice; the chair squeaked twice. "She told me all about it, Lamar. She thought I knew. She took it for granted I knew. She said, 'Of course you and Mr. Dorsey must be so relieved it's all settled at last,' and then she said, 'I do think Lamar has been perfectly splendid about it.' Those were her words. 'Perfectly splendid.' And I sat there with my cards in my hand and said, 'Oh, yes, indeed!' like a parrot—like a perfect *parrot*—because I didn't have the faintest idea in the world what the woman was talking about!"

Mr. Dorsey slowly lowered his newspaper and folded it across his knee, smoothing it with a care that might have been bestowed upon a valuable document. He did not look at his wife; he looked at the gas-log. It was as if both of them expected the gas-log to say something.

"I was going to tell you, Addie," he said.

"When?"

"Why, pretty soon. I was just waiting till things got more—more settled."

"Mrs. Teague seems to think they're settled. Mrs. Teague seems to think they've been settled for two weeks. Mrs. Teague knew all about it, and Mrs. Teague's sister-in-law knew all about it, and I shouldn't be surprised if Mrs. Teague's hired girl knew all about it! Everybody in this town knew about it except me!"

"Now, Addie—"

"Don't 'now, Addie' me, Lamar Dorsey! I want to know what it is. I want to hear it from you. I think I have that much right, at least—to hear it from my own husband, instead of having it handed to me over a card table between the third and fourth rubbers, by a woman who used to be glad enough to borrow my egg-beater!"

The egg-beater, though it had been returned these twelve years, evidently still rankled; and Mr. Dorsey, who knew something of the long memory of women for kitchen utensils lent in times of adversity, perceived that the situation was even graver than he had feared. He drew a breath.

"Well," he said, "it's this way. You know old Mr. Pruett died in March."

"Of course I know. We sent flowers."

"Well, his heirs didn't want to keep in the woodenware business. They wanted to sell out his interest, and Hartley and I couldn't buy it—not without mortgaging everything we had, and then some. So this Chicago concern, the Consolidated Kitchen Supply Company, they made an offer for the whole business. They're buying up houses all over the Middle West."

"I know that, too," Mrs. Dorsey said. "You told me that much in June. You said it was 'only a rumour.'"

"Well, it was a rumour then. It got to be more than a rumour along about August." Mr. Dorsey shifted in his chair. "They bought it, Addie. They bought the whole thing—Pruett's share and Hartley's share and mine. It's not Dorsey & Teague any more. It's going to be 'The Consolidated Kitchen Supply Company, Southern Indiana Branch.' They're going to have the sign painted next week."

Mrs. Dorsey stopped rocking.

"Then you've sold out," she said. "Then we've got the money?"

"We've got some money. Not as much as you might think. Pruett's estate got the biggest share, and there were some notes to take up." He cleared his throat again, and this time it was clearly a bad sign. "And they're keeping me on."

"Keeping you on? What do you mean, keeping you on?"

"They want me to stay with the business. They need somebody that knows the trade in this territory, and I guess I know it about as well as anybody. They're giving me a salary. It's a pretty fair salary, too, Addie. It's more than some men in this town get, I can tell you."

"And Hartley Teague?" said Mrs. Dorsey, and her voice had grown very quiet, which was the most ominous thing about it. "Are they 'keeping Hartley on,' too?"

Mr. Dorsey looked at the gas-log with great earnestness.

"No," he said. "Hartley's going to Chicago. They've made him one of the vice-presidents."

The silence that followed was no longer furnished; it was bare as a barn. Mrs. Dorsey sat perfectly still, her hands now gripped together rather than folded, and her handsome face, which had a fine high colour at all times, became of a colour much finer and higher.

"A vice-president!" she said. "Hartley Teague! And you—*you*—you're to be a clerk!"

"I am not to be a clerk! I'm to be branch manager."

"Branch manager! For a company in Chicago! Taking orders from Hartley Teague! Lamar, I never in my life—when I think how that man used to come to *you* for every last thing—when I think how it was always 'I'll have to ask Dorsey' and 'Dorsey'll know about that'—and his wife sitting there this afternoon in a gown that she must have got from Indianapolis if she got it anywhere, telling me how 'perfectly splendid' you'd been! *Splendid!* No wonder she thought you'd been splendid! I should think she would! She meant you'd been splendid about letting her husband walk right over you!"

"Hartley didn't walk over anybody," said Mr. Dorsey, with some heat of his own. "He's got a brother-in-law in the Consolidated, that's all. That's how it goes, in these big concerns. It's who you know."

"Then why didn't you know somebody?"

This was unanswerable, and Mr. Dorsey did not attempt it. He took up the folded newspaper again, looked at it as though he had never before seen such an object, and put it down.

"There's no use your getting all worked up," he said. "I'm getting a good salary and I've got a sure thing. Lots of men my age would be glad of it. I'm not going to have to worry about bad debts any more, nor take inventory with my own two hands, nor lie awake nights wondering whether that Evansville bunch is going to pay up. I'm going to draw my money every month, regular, and the company takes all the risk. I don't see what's so terrible about that."

"You don't see!" cried Mrs. Dorsey. "No, you don't, Lamar! That's just it—you never have! You never *see*! You'd go along for the rest of your life drawing your money every month, regular, and never once think what people were saying!"

"What are people saying?"

"They're saying," said Mrs. Dorsey, rising from the rocker in her agitation, so that it continued to rock and squeak without her, as if in sympathy, "they're saying that Hartley Teague is a big man and Lamar Dorsey is a little one! That's what they're saying! Or they will be, by to-morrow noon. And I'll have to go to the Fortnightly Club on Thursday and sit there and listen to Mrs. Teague read her paper on 'The Women of Shakespeare,' and have every woman in the room looking sideways at me to see how I'm taking it!"

"Well, I don't see that it matters much how a lot of women look at you sideways."

"You wouldn't. It's not you they'll be looking at."

Mr. Dorsey rose, also. He was a mild man, as a rule, but there are limits even to mildness, and he had come upon one of them.

"See here, Addie," he said. "I'd like to know something. I'd like to know just one thing. What were you really mad about when you came in that front door to-night? Were you mad because I'm not going to be a vice-president, or were you mad because I didn't tell you?"

Mrs. Dorsey opened her lips to reply, and then closed them again. She was an honest woman, at bottom; and the question, as is the way with such questions, had gone to the bottom. She turned and walked to the window, where she stood with her back to him, gazing out at the dim street and the maple-leaves stirring under the arc-light at the corner.

"Both," she said finally, in a muffled voice.

"Well, which most?"

She was silent so long that he thought she did not mean to answer. Then she said, without turning round:

"Why didn't you tell me, Lamar?"

He did not answer at once. He walked over to the mantelpiece, picked up a china shepherdess that had stood there since their wedding, examined it with deep attention, and set it down again an inch to the left of its accustomed place, where it looked uneasy for the rest of the evening.

"I guess," he said slowly, "I guess I didn't want to see you look the way you're looking right now."

"How am I looking?"

"Why—disappointed," said Mr. Dorsey. "In me, I mean."

Something in this simple statement produced a change in the back of Mrs. Dorsey's head, though it would have been difficult to say just what the change was. Her shoulders, which had been held very high and straight, lowered a little; and she lifted one hand and touched the lace curtain, absently, as women do when they wish to be doing something with their hands.

"I'm not disappointed in you," she said.

"Yes, you are, Addie."

"I'm not! I'm disappointed in—in *things*. That's different."

"I don't know that it's so very different," said Mr. Dorsey. "Things are mostly people, when you come down to it." He paused, and then added, with an awkwardness that made the words sound as though they were being pried out of him: "You always did think I'd amount to more than I have."

"Lamar!"

"Well, you did. I knew it right from the start. When you married me you thought I'd be like your father, or better. I knew you did. I guess every girl thinks that." He picked up the shepherdess again, found it offered no help, and put it back. "I tried, Addie. I tried pretty hard. But I never was the kind that pushes. Hartley pushes. He always did. Even when we were boys in school, Hartley used to push. I'm not built that way."

Mrs. Dorsey turned from the window. Her eyes were bright, and she was biting her lower lip, which was a thing she had not done since she was a girl, and which her daughter Florence had been told, many times, was a vulgar habit.

"I never asked you to push," she said. "I never asked you for a thing!"

"No," Mr. Dorsey agreed. "You never asked."

This was perhaps the cruellest thing he had ever said to her, and he had no idea that it was cruel at all, which made it the more effective. She stood looking at him for a moment, and then, with a sudden motion, sat down in the rocking-chair again, and put her face in her hands.

Now, a man who has been married nineteen years knows that there are tears and tears; that some are a weapon and some a white flag, and that the experienced husband must distinguish between them at a glance, as an old soldier distinguishes the uniforms of the enemy. Mr. Dorsey, however, had never been an experienced husband in this respect. Mrs. Dorsey wept so seldom that he had never had sufficient practice. He stood helplessly beside the mantelpiece, then went to her and patted her shoulder in the same manner he would have used upon a restive horse.

"There, there," he said. "There, there, Addie. It isn't so bad as all that."

"It's not that," she said, behind her hands.

"Well, what is it, then?"

"It's—it's your never telling me! Two whole weeks! Coming home every night and eating your supper and reading your paper and saying 'Nothing much,' and all the time—all the time—" She lifted a tear-streaked face. "Lamar, did you think I'd *scold* you?"

"Well," said Mr. Dorsey candidly, "you're scolding me now, aren't you?"

She stared at him; and then, to his immense astonishment, she began to laugh. It was not a very steady laugh, and there was a good deal of the late weeping still in it, but it was unmistakably laughter; and Mr. Dorsey, who had expected anything rather than this, looked so bewildered that she laughed the harder.

"I suppose I am," she said, wiping her eyes with the back of her wrist, since her handkerchief was in a pocket she could not, for the moment, locate. "I suppose I am, at that! Oh, Lamar, you're the most—the most *exasperating* man!"

"I don't see what I've done that's so funny."

"Nothing. You haven't done anything. That's what's funny." She found the handkerchief at last, and used it with vigour. "Sit down. Sit down, for goodness' sake, and stop fidgeting with that shepherdess. You'll break it, and it was my Aunt Lulu's."

He sat down obediently, and she rocked for a while in a silence that was beginning, gradually, to refurnish itself.

"How much is it?" she said presently. "The salary?"

He told her.

"A month?"

"Yes."

"Why, Lamar, that's—" She stopped. It was a good deal more than she had expected; it was, indeed, a good deal more than the firm of Dorsey & Teague had ever enabled Mr. Dorsey to bring home in its most prosperous season, and she was a woman who could add. "That's very good," she said in a different tone.

"I told you it was a pretty fair salary."

"Yes, you did." She rocked again. "And there wouldn't be any more of those bad years? Like the year of the panic, when we had to let Bertha go and I did all the washing myself?"

"Not unless the whole Consolidated goes busted, and it won't. It's capitalized at four million."

"Four million," said Mrs. Dorsey thoughtfully; and those familiar with the processes of the feminine mind will understand that she was already, without being in the least aware of it, beginning to arrange the conversation she would hold at the Fortnightly Club on Thursday afternoon. "That's a very large company, isn't it, Lamar?"

"One of the biggest in the country."

"And they *asked* you to stay? Particularly?"

"Well, yes. They said they couldn't run this branch without somebody that knew the territory."

"They said they couldn't run it without you," Mrs. Dorsey corrected him, with gentle firmness. "That's what it amounts to. Hartley Teague can go to Chicago and sit in an office—anybody can sit in an office—but they couldn't run this whole branch without you." She rocked with increasing satisfaction. "I don't believe I'd care to live in Chicago, anyhow. The smoke's terrible, and they say the flats are so small you can't turn around in them, and there's no society at all unless you're born into it. Poor Mrs. Teague! I wonder if she's thought about that. She'll be just *nobody* up there."

Mr. Dorsey looked at his wife with the expression of a man who has watched a magician produce a rabbit from an empty hat and is not quite certain whether to applaud or to call the police.

"Why, Addie," he said, "half an hour ago you—"

"Half an hour ago I didn't understand it," said Mrs. Dorsey serenely. "You didn't explain it properly, Lamar. You never do explain things properly. If you'd just told me in the first place that they couldn't get along without you—"

"I never said they couldn't get along without me!"

"Well, it's what you meant." She rose, and crossed to him, and stooped and kissed the top of his head, where the sandy hair was growing thin. "And next time, you tell me *first*. Do you hear? Not Mrs. Teague. Me."

"All right," said Mr. Dorsey meekly.

"Promise."

"I promise."

She went out to the kitchen to see whether the hired girl had remembered to put the milk-bottles on the back step, and Mr. Dorsey sat alone, staring at the gas-log. After a time he took up the *Evening News* again and resumed his study of the Hazel Avenue paving scandal, though it may be doubted whether he absorbed much of it. He was conscious of having been, in some obscure manner, both defeated and victorious, and he could not for the life of him make out which.

On Thursday afternoon, at the Fortnightly Club, Mrs. Teague read her paper on "The Women of Shakespeare," and it was generally considered very instructive, particularly the portion upon Lady Macbeth. Afterward, over the chicken salad, several ladies were observed glancing sideways at Mrs. Lamar Dorsey, but they found nothing whatever to reward their attention. Mrs. Dorsey was in excellent spirits. She remarked to the lady upon her left, in a voice that carried agreeably to the lady upon her right, that she did hope dear Mrs. Teague would not find Chicago too lonely, and that she, for her part, would never dream of leaving a town where one *knew* people; and that the Consolidated had been "perfectly frantic" to keep Lamar, since, as everyone in the trade understood, the branch simply could not be run without him.

The lady upon her left, who was the wise Mrs. Ellery Bunce, and who had known Mrs. Dorsey since they were both in short dresses, said, "Of course, Adelaide," and helped herself to another olive. But on the way home she told her daughter that she had always liked Addie Dorsey, and always would, and that a woman who could take a thing like that and turn it inside out over a plate of chicken salad, so that the lining looked better than the goods, was a woman who would never, under any circumstances, need a vice-president.

"Nor a husband either, I'd think," said the daughter, who was nineteen and knew everything.

"There you're wrong," said Mrs. Bunce. "That's exactly what she does need one for."

content:
Here are three excerpts of Booth Tarkington's writing, to show you their style:

Excerpt 1: The ineligible young men of the town (they were all ineligible) were unable to content themselves with the view that had so charmed Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster: they spent their time struggling to keep Miss Amberson’s face turned toward them. She turned it most often, observers said, toward two: one excelling in the general struggle by his sparkle, and the other by that winning if not winsome old trait, persistence. The sparkling gentleman “led germans” with her, and sent sonnets to her with his bouquets—sonnets lacking neither music nor wit. He was generous, poor, well-dressed, and his amazing persuasiveness was one reason why he was always in debt. No one doubted that he would be able to persuade Isabel, but he unfortunately joined too merry a party one night, and, during a moonlight serenade upon the lawn before the Amberson Mansion, was easily identified from the windows as the person who stepped through the bass viol and had to be assisted to a waiting carriage. One of Miss Amberson’s brothers was among the serenaders, and, when the party had dispersed, remained propped against the front door in a state of helpless liveliness; the Major going down in a dressing-gown and slippers to bring him in, and scolding mildly, while imperfectly concealing strong impulses to laughter. Miss Amberson also laughed at this brother, the next day, but for the suitor it was a different matter: she refused to see him when he called to apologize. “You seem to care a great deal about bass viols!” he wrote her. “I promise never to break another.” She made no response to the note, unless it was an answer, two weeks later, when her engagement was announced. She took the persistent one, Wilbur Minafer, no breaker of bass viols or of hearts, no serenader at all. A few people, who always foresaw everything, claimed that they were not surprised, because though Wilbur Minafer “might not be an Apollo, as it were,” he was “a steady young business man, and a good church-goer,” and Isabel Amberson was “pretty sensible—for such a showy girl.” But the engagement astounded the young people, and most of their fathers and mothers, too; and as a topic it supplanted literature at the next meeting of the “Women’s Tennyson Club.”

“Wilbur Minafer!” a member cried, her inflection seeming to imply that Wilbur’s crime was explained by his surname. “Wilbur Minafer! It’s the queerest thing I ever heard! To think of her taking Wilbur Minafer, just because a man any woman would like a thousand times better was a little wild one night at a serenade!”

“No,” said Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “It isn’t that. It isn’t even because she’s afraid he’d be a dissipated husband and she wants to be safe. It isn’t because she’s religious or hates wildness; it isn’t even because she hates wildness in him.”

“Well, but look how she’s thrown him over for it.”

“No, that wasn’t her reason,” said the wise Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “If men only knew it—and it’s a good thing they don’t—a woman doesn’t really care much about whether a man’s wild or not, if it doesn’t affect herself, and Isabel Amberson doesn’t care a thing!”

“Mrs. Foster!”

“No, she doesn’t. What she minds is his making a clown of himself in her front yard! It made her think he didn’t care much about her. She’s probably mistaken, but that’s what she thinks, and it’s too late for her to think anything else now, because she’s going to be married right away—the invitations will be out next week. It’ll be a big Amberson-style thing, raw oysters floating in scooped-out blocks of ice and a band from out-of-town—champagne, showy presents; a colossal present from the Major. Then Wilbur will take Isabel on the carefulest little wedding trip he can manage, and she’ll be a good wife to him, but they’ll have the worst spoiled lot of children this town will ever see.”

“How on earth do you make that out, Mrs. Foster?”

“She couldn’t love Wilbur, could she?” Mrs. Foster demanded, with no challengers. “Well, it will all go to her children, and she’ll ruin ’em!” The prophetess proved to be mistaken in a single detail merely: except for that, her foresight was accurate. The wedding was of Ambersonian magnificence, even to the floating oysters; and the Major’s colossal present was a set of architect’s designs for a house almost as elaborate and impressive as the Mansion, the house to be built in Amberson Addition by the Major. The orchestra was certainly not that local one which had suffered the loss of a bass viol; the musicians came, according to the prophecy and next morning’s paper, from afar; and at midnight the bride was still being toasted in champagne, though she had departed upon her wedding journey at ten. Four days later the pair had returned to town, which promptness seemed fairly to demonstrate that Wilbur had indeed taken Isabel upon the carefulest little trip he could manage. According to every report, she was from the start “a good wife to him,” but here in a final detail the prophecy proved inaccurate. Wilbur and Isabel did not have children; they had only one.

“Only one,” Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster admitted. “But I’d like to know if he isn’t spoiled enough for a whole carload!” Again she found none to challenge her. At the age of nine, George Amberson Minafer, the Major’s one grandchild, was a princely terror, dreaded not only in Amberson Addition but in many other quarters through which he galloped on his white pony. “By golly, I guess you think you own this town!” an embittered labourer complained, one day, as Georgie rode the pony straight through a pile of sand the man was sieving. “I will when I grow up,” the undisturbed child replied. “I guess my grandpa owns it now, you bet!” And the baffled workman, having no means to controvert what seemed a mere exaggeration of the facts could only mutter “Oh, pull down your vest!”

“Don’t haf to! Doctor says it ain’t healthy!” the boy returned promptly. “But I’ll tell you what I’ll do: I’ll pull down my vest if you’ll wipe off your chin!” This was stock and stencil: the accustomed argot of street badinage of the period; and in such matters Georgie was an expert. He had no vest to pull down; the incongruous fact was that a fringed sash girdled the juncture of his velvet blouse and breeches, for the Fauntleroy period had set in, and Georgie’s mother had so poor an eye for appropriate things, where Georgie was concerned, that she dressed him according to the doctrine of that school in boy decoration. Not only did he wear a silk sash, and silk stockings, and a broad lace collar, with his little black velvet suit: he had long brown curls, and often came home with burrs in them. Except upon the surface (which was not his own work, but his mother’s) Georgie bore no vivid resemblance to the fabulous little Cedric. The storied boy’s famous “Lean on me, grandfather,” would have been difficult to imagine upon the lips of Georgie. A month after his ninth birthday anniversary, when the Major gave him his pony, he had already become acquainted with the toughest boys in various distant parts of the town, and had convinced them that the toughness of a rich little boy with long curls might be considered in many respects superior to their own. He fought them, learning how to go berserk at a certain point in a fight, bursting into tears of anger, reaching for rocks, uttering wailed threats of murder and attempting to fulfil them. Fights often led to intimacies, and he acquired the art of saying things more exciting than “Don’t haf to!” and “Doctor says it ain’t healthy!” Thus, on a summer afternoon, a strange boy, sitting bored upon the gate-post of the Reverend Malloch Smith, beheld George Amberson Minafer rapidly approaching on his white pony, and was impelled by bitterness to shout: “Shoot the ole jackass! Look at the girly curls! Say, bub, where’d you steal your mother’s ole sash!”

“Your sister stole it for me!” Georgie instantly replied, checking the pony. “She stole it off our clo’es-line an’ gave it to me.”

“You go get your hair cut!” said the stranger hotly. “Yah! I haven’t got any sister!”

“I know you haven’t at home,” Georgie responded. “I mean the one that’s in jail.”

“I dare you to get down off that pony!” Georgie jumped to the ground, and the other boy descended from the Reverend Mr. Smith’s gatepost—but he descended inside the gate. “I dare you outside that gate,” said Georgie.

“Yah! I dare you half way here. I dare you—” But these were luckless challenges, for Georgie immediately vaulted the fence—and four minutes later Mrs. Malloch Smith, hearing strange noises, looked forth from a window; then screamed, and dashed for the pastor’s study. Mr. Malloch Smith, that grim-bearded Methodist, came to the front yard and found his visiting nephew being rapidly prepared by Master Minafer to serve as a principal figure in a pageant of massacre. It was with great physical difficulty that Mr. Smith managed to give his nephew a chance to escape into the house, for Georgie was hard and quick, and, in such matters, remarkably intense; but the minister, after a grotesque tussle, got him separated from his opponent, and shook him.

“You stop that, you!” Georgie cried fiercely; and wrenched himself away. “I guess you don’t know who I am!”

“Yes, I do know!” the angered Mr. Smith retorted. “I know who you are, and you’re a disgrace to your mother! Your mother ought to be ashamed of herself to allow—” “Shut up about my mother bein’ ashamed of herself!” Mr. Smith, exasperated, was unable to close the dialogue with dignity. “She ought to be ashamed,” he repeated. “A woman that lets a bad boy like you—” But Georgie had reached his pony and mounted. Before setting off at his accustomed gallop, he paused to interrupt the Reverend Malloch Smith again. “You pull down your vest, you ole Billygoat, you!” he shouted, distinctly. “Pull down your vest, wipe off your chin—an’ go to hell!” Such precocity is less unusual, even in children of the Rich, than most grown people imagine. However, it was a new experience for the Reverend Malloch Smith, and left him in a state of excitement. He at once wrote a note to Georgie’s mother, describing the crime according to his nephew’s testimony; and the note reached Mrs. Minafer before Georgie did. When he got home she read it to him sorrowfully. Dear Madam:
Your son has caused a painful distress in my household. He made an unprovoked attack upon a little nephew of mine who is visiting in my household, insulted him by calling him vicious names and falsehoods, stating that ladies of his family were in jail. He then tried to make his pony kick him, and when the child, who is only eleven years old, while your son is much older and stronger, endeavoured to avoid his indignities and withdraw quietly, he pursued him into the enclosure of my property and brutally assaulted him. When I appeared upon this scene he deliberately called insulting words to me, concluding with profanity, such as “go to hell,” which was heard not only by myself but by my wife and the lady who lives next door. I trust such a state of undisciplined behaviour may be remedied for the sake of the reputation for propriety, if nothing higher, of the family to which this unruly child belongs. Georgie had muttered various interruptions, and as she concluded the reading he said: “He’s an ole liar!”

“Georgie, you mustn’t say ‘liar.’ Isn’t this letter the truth?”

“Well,” said Georgie, “how old am I?”

“Ten.”

“Well, look how he says I’m older than a boy eleven years old.”

“That’s true,” said Isabel. “He does. But isn’t some of it true, Georgie?” Georgie felt himself to be in a difficulty here, and he was silent.

“Georgie, did you say what he says you did?”

“Which one?”

“Did you tell him to—to—Did you say, ‘Go to hell?’” Georgie looked worried for a moment longer; then he brightened. “Listen here, mamma; grandpa wouldn’t wipe his shoe on that ole story-teller, would he?”

“Georgie, you mustn’t—” “I mean: none of the Ambersons wouldn’t have anything to do with him, would they? He doesn’t even know you, does he, mamma?”

“That hasn’t anything to do with it.”

“Yes, it has! I mean: none of the Amberson family go to see him, and they never have him come in their house; they wouldn’t ask him to, and they prob’ly wouldn’t even let him.”

“That isn’t what we’re talking about.”

“I bet,” said Georgie emphatically, “I bet if he wanted to see any of ’em, he’d haf to go around to the side door!”

“No, dear, they—” “Yes, they would, mamma! So what does it matter if I did say somep’m’ to him he didn’t like? That kind o’ people, I don’t see why you can’t say anything you want to, to ’em!”

“No, Georgie. And you haven’t answered me whether you said that dreadful thing he says you did.”

“Well—” said Georgie. “Anyway, he said somep’m’ to me that made me mad.” And upon this point he offered no further details; he would not explain to his mother that what had made him “mad” was Mr. Smith’s hasty condemnation of herself: “Your mother ought to be ashamed,” and, “A woman that lets a bad boy like you—” Georgie did not even consider excusing himself by quoting these insolences. Isabel stroked his head. “They were terrible words for you to use, dear. From his letter he doesn’t seem a very tactful person, but—” “He’s just riffraff,” said Georgie.

“You mustn’t say so,” his mother gently agreed “Where did you learn those bad words he speaks of? Where did you hear any one use them?”

“Well, I’ve heard ’em several places. I guess Uncle George Amberson was the first I ever heard say ’em. Uncle George Amberson said ’em to papa once. Papa didn’t like it, but Uncle George was just laughin’ at papa, an’ then he said ’em while he was laughin’.”

“That was wrong of him,” she said, but almost instinctively he detected the lack of conviction in her tone. It was Isabel’s great failing that whatever an Amberson did seemed right to her, especially if the Amberson was either her brother George, or her son George. She knew that she should be more severe with the latter now, but severity with him was beyond her power; and the Reverend Malloch Smith had succeeded only in rousing her resentment against himself. Georgie’s symmetrical face—altogether an Amberson face—had looked never more beautiful to her. It always looked unusually beautiful when she tried to be severe with him. “You must promise me,” she said feebly, “never to use those bad words again.”

“I promise not to,” he said promptly—and he whispered an immediate codicil under his breath: “Unless I get mad at somebody!” This satisfied a code according to which, in his own sincere belief, he never told lies.

“That’s a good boy,” she said, and he ran out to the yard, his punishment over. Some admiring friends were gathered there; they had heard of his adventure, knew of the note, and were waiting to see what was going to “happen” to him. They hoped for an account of things, and also that he would allow them to “take turns” riding his pony to the end of the alley and back. They were really his henchmen: Georgie was a lord among boys. In fact, he was a personage among certain sorts of grown people, and was often fawned upon; the alley negroes delighted in him, chuckled over him, flattered him slavishly. For that matter, he often heard well-dressed people speaking of him admiringly: a group of ladies once gathered about him on the pavement where he was spinning a top. “I know this is Georgie!” one exclaimed, and turned to the others with the impressiveness of a showman. “Major Amberson’s only grandchild!” The others said, “It is?” and made clicking sounds with their mouths; two of them loudly whispering, “So handsome!” Georgie, annoyed because they kept standing upon the circle he had chalked for his top, looked at them coldly and offered a suggestion: “Oh, go hire a hall!” As an Amberson, he was already a public character, and the story of his adventure in the Reverend Malloch Smith’s front yard became a town topic. Many people glanced at him with great distaste, thereafter, when they chanced to encounter him, which meant nothing to Georgie, because he innocently believed most grown people to be necessarily cross-looking as a normal phenomenon resulting from the adult state; and he failed to comprehend that the distasteful glances had any personal bearing upon himself. If he had perceived such a bearing, he would have been affected only so far, probably, as to mutter, “Riffraff!” Possibly he would have shouted it; and, certainly, most people believed a story that went round the town just after Mrs. Amberson’s funeral, when Georgie was eleven. Georgie was reported to have differed with the undertaker about the seating of the family; his indignant voice had become audible: “Well, who is the most important person at my own grandmother’s funeral?” And later he had projected his head from the window of the foremost mourners’ carriage, as the undertaker happened to pass.

“Riffraff!”

She was bareheaded, and Eugene held his hat and stick in his hand; evidently he had been calling upon her, and she had come from the house with him, continuing their conversation and delaying their parting. They had paused in their slow walk from the front door to the gate, yet still stood side by side, their shoulders almost touching, as though neither Isabel nor Eugene quite realized that their feet had ceased to bear them forward; and they were not looking at each other, but at some indefinite point before them, as people do who consider together thoughtfully and in harmony. The conversation was evidently serious; his head was bent, and Isabel’s lifted left hand rested against her cheek; but all the significances of their thoughtful attitude denoted companionableness and a shared understanding. Yet, a stranger, passing, would not have thought them married: somewhere about Eugene, not quite to be located, there was a romantic gravity; and Isabel, tall and graceful, with high colour and absorbed eyes, was visibly no wife walking down to the gate with her husband. George stared at them. A hot dislike struck him at the sight of Eugene; and a vague revulsion, like a strange, unpleasant taste in his mouth, came over him as he looked at his mother: her manner was eloquent of so much thought about her companion and of such reliance upon him. And the picture the two thus made was a vivid one indeed, to George, whose angry eyes, for some reason, fixed themselves most intently upon Isabel’s lifted hand, upon the white ruffle at her wrist, bordering the graceful black sleeve, and upon the little indentations in her cheek where the tips of her fingers rested. She should not have worn white at her wrist, or at the throat either, George felt; and then, strangely, his resentment concentrated upon those tiny indentations at the tips of her fingers—actual changes, however slight and fleeting, in his mother’s face, made because of Mr. Eugene Morgan. For the moment, it seemed to George that Morgan might have claimed the ownership of a face that changed for him. It was as if he owned Isabel. Instantly she smiled and waved her hand to him; while Eugene turned and nodded; but George, standing as in some rigid trance, and staring straight at them, gave these signals of greeting no sign of recognition whatever. Upon this, Isabel called to him, waving her hand again.

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

In fact, he was a personage among certain sorts of grown people, and was often fawned upon; the alley negroes delighted in him, chuckled over him, flattered him slavishly. For that matter, he often heard well-dressed people speaking of him admiringly: a group of ladies once gathered about him on the pavement where he was spinning a top. “I know this is Georgie!” one exclaimed, and turned to the others with the impressiveness of a showman. “Major Amberson’s only grandchild!” The others said, “It is?” and made clicking sounds with their mouths; two of them loudly whispering, “So handsome!” Georgie, annoyed because they kept standing upon the circle he had chalked for his top, looked at them coldly and offered a suggestion: “Oh, go hire a hall!” As an Amberson, he was already a public character, and the story of his adventure in the Reverend Malloch Smith’s front yard became a town topic. Many people glanced at him with great distaste, thereafter, when they chanced to encounter him, which meant nothing to Georgie, because he innocently believed most grown people to be necessarily cross-looking as a normal phenomenon resulting from the adult state; and he failed to comprehend that the distasteful glances had any personal bearing upon himself. If he had perceived such a bearing, he would have been affected only so far, probably, as to mutter, “Riffraff!” Possibly he would have shouted it; and, certainly, most people believed a story that went round the town just after Mrs. Amberson’s funeral, when Georgie was eleven. Georgie was reported to have differed with the undertaker about the seating of the family; his indignant voice had become audible: “Well, who is the most important person at my own grandmother’s funeral?” And later he had projected his head from the window of the foremost mourners’ carriage, as the undertaker happened to pass.

“Riffraff!”

“Never mind!”

Sunday evening was the time, he explained, for going over the week’s work with his factory managers. “How d’you do,” he said. “I trust that ah—I trust—I do trust—” He stopped, for it seemed to him that the word “trust” sounded idiotic. Whereupon, seeking to be plausible, he coughed again, and instantly hated himself: the sound he made was an atrocity. He began again.

“I beg your pardon?” Lucy said. “Nothing of the slightest importance!” he managed to say. “I was just leaving. He drove home in a tumultuous mood, and almost ran down two ladies who were engaged in absorbing conversation at a crossing. They were his Aunt Fanny and the stout Mrs. Johnson; a jerk of the reins at the last instant saved them by a few inches; but their conversation was so interesting that they were unaware of their danger, and did not notice the runabout, nor how close it came to them. George was so furious with himself and with the girl whose unexpected coming into a room could make him look such a fool, that it might have soothed him a little if he had actually run over the two absorbed ladies without injuring them beyond repair. At least, he said to himself that he wished he had; it might have taken his mind off of himself for a few minutes. “Hoopee!” said old Tom. “Mus’ been some white lady use Mist’ Jawge mighty bad! White lady say, ‘No, suh, I ain’ go’n out ridin’ ’ith Mist’ Jawge no mo’!’ Mist’ Jawge drive in. ‘Dam de dam worl’! Dam de dam hoss! Dam de dam nigga’! Dam de dam dam!’ Hoopee!”

“That’ll do!” George said sternly.

“Yessuh!” George strode from the stable, crossed the Major’s back yard, then passed behind the new houses, on his way home. These structures were now approaching completion, but still in a state of rawness hideous to George—though, for that matter, they were never to be anything except hideous to him. Behind them, stray planks, bricks, refuse of plaster and lath, shingles, straw, empty barrels, strips of twisted tin and broken tiles were strewn everywhere over the dried and pitted gray mud where once the suave lawn had lain like a green lake around those stately islands, the two Amberson houses. And George’s state of mind was not improved by his present view of this repulsive area, nor by his sensations when he kicked an uptilted shingle only to discover that what uptilted it was a brickbat on the other side of it. After that, the whole world seemed to be one solid conspiracy of malevolence. In this temper he emerged from behind the house nearest to his own, and, glancing toward the street, saw his mother standing with Eugene Morgan upon the cement path that led to the front gate. She was bareheaded, and Eugene held his hat and stick in his hand; evidently he had been calling upon her, and she had come from the house with him, continuing their conversation and delaying their parting. They had paused in their slow walk from the front door to the gate, yet still stood side by side, their shoulders almost touching, as though neither Isabel nor Eugene quite realized that their feet had ceased to bear them forward; and they were not looking at each other, but at some indefinite point before them, as people do who consider together thoughtfully and in harmony. The conversation was evidently serious; his head was bent, and Isabel’s lifted left hand rested against her cheek; but all the significances of their thoughtful attitude denoted companionableness and a shared understanding. Yet, a stranger, passing, would not have thought them married: somewhere about Eugene, not quite to be located, there was a romantic gravity; and Isabel, tall and graceful, with high colour and absorbed eyes, was visibly no wife walking down to the gate with her husband. George stared at them. A hot dislike struck him at the sight of Eugene; and a vague revulsion, like a strange, unpleasant taste in his mouth, came over him as he looked at his mother: her manner was eloquent of so much thought about her companion and of such reliance upon him. And the picture the two thus made was a vivid one indeed, to George, whose angry eyes, for some reason, fixed themselves most intently upon Isabel’s lifted hand, upon the white ruffle at her wrist, bordering the graceful black sleeve, and upon the little indentations in her cheek where the tips of her fingers rested. She should not have worn white at her wrist, or at the throat either, George felt; and then, strangely, his resentment concentrated upon those tiny indentations at the tips of her fingers—actual changes, however slight and fleeting, in his mother’s face, made because of Mr. Eugene Morgan. For the moment, it seemed to George that Morgan might have claimed the ownership of a face that changed for him. It was as if he owned Isabel. The two began to walk on toward the gate, where they stopped again, turning to face each other, and Isabel’s glance, passing Eugene, fell upon George. Instantly she smiled and waved her hand to him; while Eugene turned and nodded; but George, standing as in some rigid trance, and staring straight at them, gave these signals of greeting no sign of recognition whatever. Upon this, Isabel called to him, waving her hand again.

“Georgie!” she called, laughing. “Wake up, dear! Georgie, hello!” George turned away as if he had neither seen nor heard, and stalked into the house by the side door.

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

The return of Mr. Thomas Ridgely Carmody to the town of his boyhood was not, in the strict sense, an event; yet it was treated as one by a number of ladies whose windows commanded a view of Linden Street, and by at least one gentleman, old Judge Henley, who had sat behind young Thomas in church for nine years and still recalled, with no softening, the boy's habit of dropping hymnals. Eleven years had passed since the Carmodys removed to the East. The town had grown in that time, as towns of the Middle West were then growing, rapidly and somewhat carelessly, like a boy who outgrows his trousers before anyone has noticed the trousers were getting short. A trolley line now ran where the mule-car had dawdled. The old Bream place on Harrison Street had been "cut up into lots," and a row of narrow frame houses stood upon what had once been the finest strawberry bed in the county. These were matters of no great consequence to anybody except the people who had eaten the strawberries.

Mr. Carmody arrived upon the noon train. He descended with a walking-stick, a pair of pearl-gray spats, and an expression intended to convey that he had seen a great many railway stations and found this one, upon the whole, about what he had expected. The hackman who drove him to Linden Street reported afterward that the young man had addressed him as "my good fellow," and had asked whether the town "still had that rather jolly little park by the courthouse," as though the park were something a town might mislay. The hackman, a literal person, replied that it did, so far as he knew, unless somebody had took it in the night.

His cousin, who had been Adelaide Bream and was now Mrs. Lucius Pruett, was waiting for him on her front porch. She had been waiting there for some time; she had, in fact, put on and taken off two different shirtwaists before settling upon the third, which she considered the least likely to look as though she had thought about it. Her two children, Lucius Junior, aged seven, and a smaller person called Bunny, were stationed beside her under strict instructions to be good, and were already showing the strain. When the hack stopped at the gate, Lucius Junior was heard to inquire, in a voice that carried with great clarity to the Kessler house next door, "Is that him? What's he got on his feet?"

"Hush!" said his mother. "Those are spats."

"What are spats for?"

"Hush, I say! Go and shake hands with your Cousin Thomas."

But Lucius Junior did not go; he remained rooted, regarding the visitor's ankles with the profound and unwinking attention which children reserve for very large dogs and very small funerals. Mrs. Pruett, therefore, went down the walk herself; and the two cousins met halfway between the gate and the steps, under the maple tree, where, for an instant, neither appeared to know quite what to do. Then Adelaide laughed, and put both hands on his shoulders, and kissed him upon the cheek, a proceeding which Mr. Carmody received with an air of slightly alarmed gallantry.

"Why, Tod!" she cried. "Why, Toddles Carmody! I'd never have known you, never in this world!"

"My dear Adelaide," he said, and bowed a little over her hand, though she had already withdrawn it. "Charmed—really charmed. You're looking remarkably well. Remarkably."

"Remarkably!" she repeated, and laughed again. "Listen to him! 'Remarkably!' Well, I suppose I ought to be, at my age. Come up on the porch and be introduced. Lucius isn't home yet; he never gets away from the store before half-past five, and if there's a farmer in town wanting a pump he doesn't get away then. Children, this is your Cousin Thomas, that I've told you about."

Bunny, who was four, immediately put her thumb into her mouth and went behind her mother's skirt. Lucius Junior, however, advanced one step, and offered a remark which he had evidently been preparing.

"Mamma says you fell in the rain barrel."

"Lucius!"

"Well, you did say it. You said he fell in the rain barrel at Grandpa Bream's, and you had to pull him out by the legs, and he hollered."

Mr. Carmody's colour rose perceptibly above the line of his very high collar. "I'm afraid," he said, with a laugh that he intended to be easy, "that your mother's memory is—ah—somewhat more vivid than accurate."

"It is not!" said Adelaide. "You did fall in, and I did pull you out, and you did holler. You hollered so that Mrs. Gilpin came running all the way from across the alley with her apron full of clothespins. Don't you remember?"

"I can't say that I do," said Mr. Carmody. "It's so very long ago, you know. One forgets these—these rustic episodes."

"Rustic!" said Adelaide. "Oh, Tod!"

It was perhaps unfortunate for the young man that his cousin possessed a sense of humour, for nothing is so trying to a person of elegance as a relative who remembers him without it. Adelaide had been, in childhood, the elder by a year and the larger by several inches; she had been the leader of every expedition, the arbiter of every dispute, and the inventor of most of the punishments; and it was plain, even in this first moment, that she had never quite ceased to regard him as a small boy in short trousers who would get into difficulties if not watched. Mr. Carmody, on the other hand, had spent eleven years in becoming a person of whom nothing of the kind could be suspected, and he had brought these eleven years with him, together with his spats, as evidence.

They sat upon the porch, in two wicker rockers, and Adelaide sent Lucius Junior to the kitchen with instructions to tell Hilda to bring the lemonade. The order was received without enthusiasm, but obeyed, because Lucius Junior hoped to be present when the visitor took off his spats, and feared that he might do it while unobserved.

"Well," said Adelaide, folding her hands and looking at her cousin with frank delight, "tell me everything. Tell me all about yourself. Aunt Margaret writes to Mother, of course, but Aunt Margaret never tells anything except who's been sick. What have you been doing all these years?"

Mr. Carmody crossed his knees, laid his walking-stick across them, and contemplated the maple tree.

"Oh, one keeps busy," he said. "Business, you know—and a certain amount of the other thing. One has one's obligations. I'm associated with a rather large concern in New York—bonds and that sort of thing. Rather a responsible position, in its way. One can't always get off when one likes; I had the greatest difficulty in arranging this little trip."

"Bonds!" said Adelaide respectfully. "My! Lucius will be interested. He bought a bond once—a waterworks bond, from a man that came through here. It was the waterworks at some town in Kansas, and it turned out there wasn't any waterworks. Lucius always said afterward there wasn't any town either, but I think there was a town; I think it was just the waterworks that wasn't."

"Ah," said Mr. Carmody, with a slight compression of the lips. "Our concern doesn't deal in that class of security, I assure you."

"Oh, I'm sure it doesn't," she said hastily. "I didn't mean—Do you go out a great deal? Aunt Margaret said once you'd been to Newport."

"I have been to Newport," Mr. Carmody admitted, as a man admits to having been knighted. "Several times. Last August I was there for very nearly a week. One meets a great many people. Delightful, some of them; not all, of course. It's rather a strain, the life there—one dines out every evening, and there's the Casino, and the yachts, and so on. I confess I find it rather tiresome after a while."

"I should think you would," said Adelaide sympathetically. "Every single evening! I couldn't stand it. When Lucius and I go to Mrs. Harmon's for supper on a Thursday, I'm so tired by Friday I can hardly see." She paused, and then added, with a candour which he found disconcerting: "But I don't suppose it's the same thing, exactly."

"Not exactly," said Mr. Carmody.

The lemonade arrived, borne by Hilda, a large, flaxen, and serious young woman who set the tray down with an air of discharging a solemn trust, and then lingered in the doorway to stare at the spats. Lucius Junior, who had returned with her, stood beside her and stared also; and Bunny, emerging partially from behind her mother, took her thumb out of her mouth long enough to direct a comment toward the same objects.

"Shoes got coats on," she said.

Mr. Carmody drew his feet somewhat under his chair.

"That will do, Hilda," said Adelaide. "Bunny, that isn't polite. Lucius, take your sister and go play in the side yard. Go on! Go on, both of you!" And when, after some negotiation, the children had been dislodged, she turned back to her cousin with a laugh. "You mustn't mind them. They've never seen anybody dressed up before—not on a weekday."

"It's nothing," said Mr. Carmody graciously. "Children are—ah—children."

"They certainly are," said Adelaide. "You were."

He chose to let this pass. For a time they spoke of relatives, a subject upon which cousins may always fall back as upon a feather bed; and here Mr. Carmody became somewhat more natural, for it is difficult to be elegant about an uncle with gout, or an aunt who has joined the Christian Scientists over the protest of her entire family. Adelaide told him that Uncle Henry Bream had at last sold the livery stable and gone into the automobile business, and was regarded by the whole town as having lost his mind; and that Cousin Ella had married a dentist from Terre Haute, a man with a beautiful baritone voice and no chin to speak of. Mr. Carmody, in his turn, reported upon his mother's health and his father's opinions on the tariff, both of which, he said, were about as usual. And then, as the afternoon wore on and the shadows of the maple lengthened across the porch floor, he became aware that he was laughing—actually laughing, without first deciding to—at Adelaide's account of how old Judge Henley had fallen asleep during the Fourth of July oration and awakened in the middle of it to shout "Objection sustained!" at the speaker.

He checked himself, and brought out his cigarette-case, which was of silver and bore a monogram of considerable intricacy. He offered it, with a flourish, to the empty air, and then, recollecting himself, took a cigarette and asked whether she objected.

"Not a bit," said Adelaide. "Lucius smokes cigars, but only on the back porch, because Mother says it gets into the curtains. My, what a pretty case! Is that real silver?"

"It was a gift," said Mr. Carmody, with a touch of mystery.

"From a lady?" she asked at once, leaning forward.

"From—a friend," he said, and smiled faintly, as one who has known much and tells little.

Adelaide regarded him for a moment with an expression which he could not read; then she sat back and rocked, and looked out at the street. A trolley car went jangling by at the corner, and the Kessler girl came out of the house next door, with an elaborately casual air, to examine a rosebush that had not required examination for several years.

"Tod," said Adelaide suddenly, "would you like to walk over and see the old place?"

He hesitated. "The old place?"

"Grandpa Bream's. On Harrison Street. It's only four blocks. It isn't the same, of course; I suppose you'd heard they cut up the lots. But the house is still there—it's a boarding-house now, Mrs. Tolliver keeps it—and the barn's still standing, part of it. I go by sometimes. I don't know why I do; it always makes me feel silly afterward. Would you like to?"

"Why, yes," said Mr. Carmody, rising. "Yes, I believe I should."

They walked in the late sunshine, beneath the long arch of the elms, past lawns where men in shirtsleeves were watering the grass with that peculiar air of absorbed melancholy which the watering of grass induces in the American householder toward evening. Several of these gentlemen paused, hose in hand, to look after the young man with the walking-stick; and one of them, a Mr. Purdy, was so far distracted as to water his own front steps, upon which his wife happened at that moment to be sitting. Mr. Carmody was not aware of the sensation he created. He had fallen silent, and he walked more slowly than was his custom on Broad Street; for here and there a thing caught at him—a particular fence, an iron hitching-post in the shape of a horse's head, a hollow in a sidewalk where the brick had sunk—and each of these, though he would not have confessed it, delivered to him a small and curious shock, as though someone had laid a hand on his arm in the dark.

"That's where the Bixby dog bit you," said Adelaide, pointing with her parasol.

"Was it? I don't—" He stopped. "Yes," he said. "Yes, it was. Right on the shin. And you threw a brick at it."

"I hit it, too," said Adelaide with satisfaction. "And Mr. Bixby came out and said I was a little hellcat, and Grandpa went over and they didn't speak for a year. Do you remember that?"

"I do now," he said, and laughed; and this time he did not check himself.

The old house, when they reached it, was smaller than either of them had supposed, as old houses invariably are; it seemed to have shrunk inward upon itself, as if from embarrassment at the narrow new houses that crowded against it on either side. A sign in the front window said "Rooms—Table Board," and a young man in a celluloid collar was sitting on the steps, picking his teeth with an air of permanent residence. They did not go in. They went instead along the side, by the alley, to where a fragment of the old barn still stood, now used, evidently, for the storage of coal; and beside it, at the corner where the downspout came off the roof, there was a barrel.

It was not the same barrel. It could not have been the same barrel, after eleven years; it was a newer, meaner barrel, and it stood on a slant upon two loose bricks, and there was a dead leaf floating in it. Yet the two cousins stood and regarded it for some moments in silence, as though it were a monument erected by public subscription.

"It came up to here on me," said Mr. Carmody at last, and held his hand at about the level of his waistcoat pocket. "I was standing on the chopping-block, trying to sail a shingle in it. And you said I couldn't reach the middle, and I said I could."

"And you couldn't," said Adelaide.

"And I couldn't." He was silent a moment. "I thought I was drowning. I really did. I remember thinking I'd never get to go to the circus."

"You said so," said Adelaide softly. "When I got you out. You were all over mud, and crying, and you said, 'Now I won't ever see the elephant.' And I told you you would, and I gave you my circus money so you could, because you'd spent yours on a mouth-organ."

He turned and looked at her. "Did you? I'd forgotten that."

"You never knew it," she said. "I told you I'd found a quarter."

There was another silence. The young man in the celluloid collar, having finished his toothpick, rose and went indoors, and somewhere in the boarding-house a piano began to play "In the Good Old Summer Time," with a great many wrong notes and an evident determination to get through it regardless. Mr. Carmody poked at the dead leaf in the barrel with the ferrule of his stick.

"Adelaide," he said, not looking at her, "I suppose I ought to tell you that I'm not—that the position I mentioned isn't—" He stopped, and began again, with the recklessness of a man who leaps into cold water because he cannot bear to wade. "I'm a clerk. In the bond department. There are forty of us. I sit on a stool and add up columns, and the case was given me by the fellows in the office when I'd been there five years, and it isn't silver; it's plated. And I went to Newport once, last August, for four days, because one of the junior partners wanted somebody to help carry things for his mother. There! I don't know why I'm telling you. I suppose you think I'm a fearful ass."

Adelaide did not answer immediately. She was looking at the barrel too; and when at last she spoke, her voice had in it that quality, maddening to all men and to small boys particularly, of a person who has known a thing all along and is being kind about it.

"Aunt Margaret writes to Mother every two weeks, Tod," she said. "She tells who's been sick. But she tells everything else too."

He stared at her. "You knew? All the time you knew?"

"Of course I knew."

"Then why on earth," he demanded, with mounting indignation, "did you let me go on? About Newport, and the—and dining out every evening, and all of it? Why didn't you say something?"

"Because you were having such a good time," said Adelaide simply. "And because—oh, I don't know. Because you'd come all this way, and you looked so nice, and I didn't want to be the one to pull you out of the barrel this time. I thought maybe you'd climb out by yourself." She laughed, and put her hand through his arm. "And you did, didn't you?"

Mr. Carmody opened his mouth to reply, and found that he had nothing ready; and so, for the first time in a number of years, he said nothing at all, but merely stood there beside his cousin, a young man of twenty-nine in pearl-gray spats, feeling remarkably like a boy of eight who has been fished out of something and is not yet certain whether to be grateful or furious. It is an uncomfortable sensation; and it is, perhaps, the nearest approach to wisdom that most of us are permitted.

"Come home to supper," said Adelaide. "Lucius will be back, and Hilda's made a chicken pie, and you can tell him about bonds. He won't know whether you're a clerk or a partner; he only wants to know whether they're any good."

"They're not, most of them," said Mr. Carmody, and laughed.

They walked back under the elms, arm in arm, and it was observed by Mrs. Kessler, who happened to be examining her own rosebush when they returned, that the visitor had his hat pushed back upon his head and was swinging his walking-stick like a boy with a switch. "He's not so stuck-up as he looked," she reported that evening to Mrs. Purdy, whose husband had watered her. "I guess it was just the spats."

Mrs. Purdy, whose views upon the human race had been somewhat dampened, said that in her experience it was never just the spats.

Both ladies were partly right, as both ladies usually were. Mr. Carmody stayed three days, ate four of Hilda's chicken pies in succession, mended a kite for Lucius Junior, and permitted Bunny to unbutton his spats and wear them upon her arms as cuffs, a privilege she exercised with great solemnity throughout an entire afternoon. He departed upon the Thursday morning train with a shoebox of fried chicken under his arm and a promise to come again at Christmas. And it must be recorded, in the interest of truth, that when the porter on the eastbound sleeper asked whether he would require anything further, Mr. Carmody leaned back against the plush, drew out his plated cigarette-case, and replied, in an accent acquired upon a four-day visit to Newport, "Nothing just now, my good fellow—nothing just now."

But he looked out of the window, after that, for a long while, as the town and its elms slid away behind him; and once, unaccountably, he laughed aloud.

content:
Here are three excerpts of Booth Tarkington's writing, to show you their style:

Excerpt 1: The ineligible young men of the town (they were all ineligible) were unable to content themselves with the view that had so charmed Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster: they spent their time struggling to keep Miss Amberson’s face turned toward them. She turned it most often, observers said, toward two: one excelling in the general struggle by his sparkle, and the other by that winning if not winsome old trait, persistence. The sparkling gentleman “led germans” with her, and sent sonnets to her with his bouquets—sonnets lacking neither music nor wit. He was generous, poor, well-dressed, and his amazing persuasiveness was one reason why he was always in debt. No one doubted that he would be able to persuade Isabel, but he unfortunately joined too merry a party one night, and, during a moonlight serenade upon the lawn before the Amberson Mansion, was easily identified from the windows as the person who stepped through the bass viol and had to be assisted to a waiting carriage. One of Miss Amberson’s brothers was among the serenaders, and, when the party had dispersed, remained propped against the front door in a state of helpless liveliness; the Major going down in a dressing-gown and slippers to bring him in, and scolding mildly, while imperfectly concealing strong impulses to laughter. Miss Amberson also laughed at this brother, the next day, but for the suitor it was a different matter: she refused to see him when he called to apologize. “You seem to care a great deal about bass viols!” he wrote her. “I promise never to break another.” She made no response to the note, unless it was an answer, two weeks later, when her engagement was announced. She took the persistent one, Wilbur Minafer, no breaker of bass viols or of hearts, no serenader at all. A few people, who always foresaw everything, claimed that they were not surprised, because though Wilbur Minafer “might not be an Apollo, as it were,” he was “a steady young business man, and a good church-goer,” and Isabel Amberson was “pretty sensible—for such a showy girl.” But the engagement astounded the young people, and most of their fathers and mothers, too; and as a topic it supplanted literature at the next meeting of the “Women’s Tennyson Club.”

“Wilbur Minafer!” a member cried, her inflection seeming to imply that Wilbur’s crime was explained by his surname. “Wilbur Minafer! It’s the queerest thing I ever heard! To think of her taking Wilbur Minafer, just because a man any woman would like a thousand times better was a little wild one night at a serenade!”

“No,” said Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “It isn’t that. It isn’t even because she’s afraid he’d be a dissipated husband and she wants to be safe. It isn’t because she’s religious or hates wildness; it isn’t even because she hates wildness in him.”

“Well, but look how she’s thrown him over for it.”

“No, that wasn’t her reason,” said the wise Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “If men only knew it—and it’s a good thing they don’t—a woman doesn’t really care much about whether a man’s wild or not, if it doesn’t affect herself, and Isabel Amberson doesn’t care a thing!”

“Mrs. Foster!”

“No, she doesn’t. What she minds is his making a clown of himself in her front yard! It made her think he didn’t care much about her. She’s probably mistaken, but that’s what she thinks, and it’s too late for her to think anything else now, because she’s going to be married right away—the invitations will be out next week. It’ll be a big Amberson-style thing, raw oysters floating in scooped-out blocks of ice and a band from out-of-town—champagne, showy presents; a colossal present from the Major. Then Wilbur will take Isabel on the carefulest little wedding trip he can manage, and she’ll be a good wife to him, but they’ll have the worst spoiled lot of children this town will ever see.”

“How on earth do you make that out, Mrs. Foster?”

“She couldn’t love Wilbur, could she?” Mrs. Foster demanded, with no challengers. “Well, it will all go to her children, and she’ll ruin ’em!” The prophetess proved to be mistaken in a single detail merely: except for that, her foresight was accurate. The wedding was of Ambersonian magnificence, even to the floating oysters; and the Major’s colossal present was a set of architect’s designs for a house almost as elaborate and impressive as the Mansion, the house to be built in Amberson Addition by the Major. The orchestra was certainly not that local one which had suffered the loss of a bass viol; the musicians came, according to the prophecy and next morning’s paper, from afar; and at midnight the bride was still being toasted in champagne, though she had departed upon her wedding journey at ten. Four days later the pair had returned to town, which promptness seemed fairly to demonstrate that Wilbur had indeed taken Isabel upon the carefulest little trip he could manage. According to every report, she was from the start “a good wife to him,” but here in a final detail the prophecy proved inaccurate. Wilbur and Isabel did not have children; they had only one.

“Only one,” Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster admitted. “But I’d like to know if he isn’t spoiled enough for a whole carload!” Again she found none to challenge her. At the age of nine, George Amberson Minafer, the Major’s one grandchild, was a princely terror, dreaded not only in Amberson Addition but in many other quarters through which he galloped on his white pony. “By golly, I guess you think you own this town!” an embittered labourer complained, one day, as Georgie rode the pony straight through a pile of sand the man was sieving. “I will when I grow up,” the undisturbed child replied. “I guess my grandpa owns it now, you bet!” And the baffled workman, having no means to controvert what seemed a mere exaggeration of the facts could only mutter “Oh, pull down your vest!”

“Don’t haf to! Doctor says it ain’t healthy!” the boy returned promptly. “But I’ll tell you what I’ll do: I’ll pull down my vest if you’ll wipe off your chin!” This was stock and stencil: the accustomed argot of street badinage of the period; and in such matters Georgie was an expert. He had no vest to pull down; the incongruous fact was that a fringed sash girdled the juncture of his velvet blouse and breeches, for the Fauntleroy period had set in, and Georgie’s mother had so poor an eye for appropriate things, where Georgie was concerned, that she dressed him according to the doctrine of that school in boy decoration. Not only did he wear a silk sash, and silk stockings, and a broad lace collar, with his little black velvet suit: he had long brown curls, and often came home with burrs in them. Except upon the surface (which was not his own work, but his mother’s) Georgie bore no vivid resemblance to the fabulous little Cedric. The storied boy’s famous “Lean on me, grandfather,” would have been difficult to imagine upon the lips of Georgie. A month after his ninth birthday anniversary, when the Major gave him his pony, he had already become acquainted with the toughest boys in various distant parts of the town, and had convinced them that the toughness of a rich little boy with long curls might be considered in many respects superior to their own. He fought them, learning how to go berserk at a certain point in a fight, bursting into tears of anger, reaching for rocks, uttering wailed threats of murder and attempting to fulfil them. Fights often led to intimacies, and he acquired the art of saying things more exciting than “Don’t haf to!” and “Doctor says it ain’t healthy!” Thus, on a summer afternoon, a strange boy, sitting bored upon the gate-post of the Reverend Malloch Smith, beheld George Amberson Minafer rapidly approaching on his white pony, and was impelled by bitterness to shout: “Shoot the ole jackass! Look at the girly curls! Say, bub, where’d you steal your mother’s ole sash!”

“Your sister stole it for me!” Georgie instantly replied, checking the pony. “She stole it off our clo’es-line an’ gave it to me.”

“You go get your hair cut!” said the stranger hotly. “Yah! I haven’t got any sister!”

“I know you haven’t at home,” Georgie responded. “I mean the one that’s in jail.”

“I dare you to get down off that pony!” Georgie jumped to the ground, and the other boy descended from the Reverend Mr. Smith’s gatepost—but he descended inside the gate. “I dare you outside that gate,” said Georgie.

“Yah! I dare you half way here. I dare you—” But these were luckless challenges, for Georgie immediately vaulted the fence—and four minutes later Mrs. Malloch Smith, hearing strange noises, looked forth from a window; then screamed, and dashed for the pastor’s study. Mr. Malloch Smith, that grim-bearded Methodist, came to the front yard and found his visiting nephew being rapidly prepared by Master Minafer to serve as a principal figure in a pageant of massacre. It was with great physical difficulty that Mr. Smith managed to give his nephew a chance to escape into the house, for Georgie was hard and quick, and, in such matters, remarkably intense; but the minister, after a grotesque tussle, got him separated from his opponent, and shook him.

“You stop that, you!” Georgie cried fiercely; and wrenched himself away. “I guess you don’t know who I am!”

“Yes, I do know!” the angered Mr. Smith retorted. “I know who you are, and you’re a disgrace to your mother! Your mother ought to be ashamed of herself to allow—” “Shut up about my mother bein’ ashamed of herself!” Mr. Smith, exasperated, was unable to close the dialogue with dignity. “She ought to be ashamed,” he repeated. “A woman that lets a bad boy like you—” But Georgie had reached his pony and mounted. Before setting off at his accustomed gallop, he paused to interrupt the Reverend Malloch Smith again. “You pull down your vest, you ole Billygoat, you!” he shouted, distinctly. “Pull down your vest, wipe off your chin—an’ go to hell!” Such precocity is less unusual, even in children of the Rich, than most grown people imagine. However, it was a new experience for the Reverend Malloch Smith, and left him in a state of excitement. He at once wrote a note to Georgie’s mother, describing the crime according to his nephew’s testimony; and the note reached Mrs. Minafer before Georgie did. When he got home she read it to him sorrowfully. Dear Madam:
Your son has caused a painful distress in my household. He made an unprovoked attack upon a little nephew of mine who is visiting in my household, insulted him by calling him vicious names and falsehoods, stating that ladies of his family were in jail. When I appeared upon this scene he deliberately called insulting words to me, concluding with profanity, such as “go to hell,” which was heard not only by myself but by my wife and the lady who lives next door. “Georgie, you mustn’t say ‘liar.’ Isn’t this letter the truth?”

“Well,” said Georgie, “how old am I?”

“Ten.”

“Well, look how he says I’m older than a boy eleven years old.”

“Georgie, did you say what he says you did?”

“Which one?”

“Did you tell him to—to—Did you say, ‘Go to hell?’” Georgie looked worried for a moment longer; then he brightened. “Listen here, mamma; grandpa wouldn’t wipe his shoe on that ole story-teller, would he?”
