Arthur Lyle had arrived first, and for a quarter of an hour he sat at the corner table of the chophouse with his hat upon his knee and his eyes upon the door, composing in his mind the several sentences with which he would greet his cousin. It was not that he lacked words. Words were his trade, after a fashion, for he was chief clerk in the law offices of Bradbury and Coyle, and there was scarcely a day in which he did not frame some careful paragraph upon the transfer of a lot or the settlement of an estate. But these were words of a particular kind, nicely measured and precisely fitted, and he felt, with a vague discomfort he could not have explained, that they would be of little service to him now. Seven years is a long time. It had been seven years since Jim Haskell walked down the Oakland mole with a blanket roll upon his shoulder and a grin upon his face, bound for Seattle and the Chilkoot and the gold that every newspaper in the land declared was lying in the creek-beds of the North for any man with the stomach to dig it out. Arthur had stood upon the mole and waved his hat. He remembered that it had been raining, and that his mother, who had come with him, had wept a little and called Jim a wild boy, and that Jim had kissed her and laughed and told her he would bring her back a nugget as big as a hen's egg. She was dead now, three years dead, and the nugget had never come.

The chophouse was a low-ceilinged place near the foot of Broadway, frequented by teamsters and longshoremen and the masters of bay scows, and Arthur, in his stiff collar and his grey business suit, was conscious of being out of his element. It had been Jim's choosing. "I don't want any of your swell joints," he had written in the scrawled note that came to the office. "I want a steak and I want it thick, and I want to sit where a man can put his elbows on the table." Arthur had smiled at that, and then, curiously, had not smiled; for he had suddenly realized that he could not remember the last time he had put his elbows on a table.

The door swung open, letting in a gust of wind off the estuary and the smell of tide-flats and tar, and a man came in and stood looking about him. Arthur half rose, then hesitated. He had been watching for a boy of twenty-two, lean and freckled and quick-moving, and this was not a boy. This was a man, broad through the shoulders and thick through the chest, with a face burned to the colour of old saddle-leather and creased about the eyes as though from long squinting into great distances. His hair was cropped close, and there was grey in it at the temples, though he could not have been thirty. He wore a pea-jacket buttoned to the throat, and his hands, which hung at his sides, were enormous and scarred and knotted at the knuckles. Yet it was the eyes that gave Arthur pause. They were the same blue eyes, but there was something in them now, a stillness, a watchfulness, as of an animal that has learned the trick of waiting.

Then the eyes found him, and the stillness broke, and the old grin split the leathery face from ear to ear.

"Art! Art, you son of a gun!" And the man was across the room in three strides, scattering a waiter from his path, and Arthur's hand was seized in a grip that ground the bones together and his shoulder was pounded until he staggered. "Look at you! Look at the collar on you! By the Lord, you look like a parson—like a bank president!"

"Jim," was all Arthur could say, and all the careful sentences he had composed went out of his head like water from a sieve. "Jim. Good Lord, Jim."

They sat down, and for a long moment neither spoke, but only looked at each other across the scarred table with that hungry, searching scrutiny which men bestow upon the faces of those they have known in boyhood, seeking the old lines beneath the new ones. Arthur saw that a white seam ran from Jim's left cheekbone into his hairline, and that the tip of one ear was gone, and that two fingers of the left hand ended at the second joint. Jim, for his part, was looking at Arthur's soft white hands lying upon the table, and at the slight thickening beneath his waistcoat, and at the spectacles which had not been there seven years before.

"You've got fat, Art," Jim said at last, and he said it without malice, in the tone of a man stating a fact about the weather.

"And you've got—" Arthur cast about for the word. "Hard," he finished lamely.

Jim laughed, a short bark of a laugh. "Hard? Well, I guess maybe. The North does that. It takes what's soft in a man and freezes it off him, the way it froze off them fingers. And what's left, why, what's left is hard, or else there ain't nothing left at all." He beckoned to the waiter. "Steak," he said. "Two of 'em. Thick as your fist, and don't burn the life out of 'em. And coffee, a big pot, black as the inside of a cow."

When the waiter had gone, Arthur leaned forward. "We heard so little, Jim. A letter from Dawson the first winter, and then nothing for nearly two years, and then that one from Nome. Mother—" he stopped.

"I know," Jim said, and his face changed. "I got your letter. It caught up with me in Unalaska, eight months after it was wrote. I was on a sealing schooner then, the *Mary Thomas*, and we'd put in for water. I read it standing on the beach with the fog coming in, and I'll tell you, Art, I sat down on a rock and bawled like a calf. Aunt Martha was the only mother I ever had, near enough." He turned his coffee cup slowly between his great scarred hands. "I never did bring her that nugget."

"She didn't care about the nugget."

"No. She'd have cared I came back, though. And I didn't come back. I was too busy getting hard." He said it bitterly, and then shook himself as a dog shakes off water. "Well, there's no use crying over it now. A man does what he does. Tell me about yourself. You married that Hendricks girl? The one with the yellow hair that used to sing in the choir?"

"Clara. Yes. Five years ago this June." Arthur felt a warmth of pride, and with it, oddly, a faint embarrassment, as though he were showing a small and ordinary coin to a man who had handled bullion. "We have a boy. Three years old. We named him James."

Jim stared at him. Then he set down the cup, very carefully, and looked away toward the window, where the masts of the scow schooners swayed against the grey sky. When he looked back, his eyes were wet, and he made no attempt to hide it.

"James," he said. "After me?"

"After you."

"Well, I'll be damned." He was silent a moment. "I'll be everlastingly damned. A kid with my name on him, and me freezing my feet off on the Stewart River and never knowing a thing about it." He reached across and gripped Arthur's arm. "I'll see him, Art. I'll see him before I go."

"Before you go?" Arthur's heart sank a little. "You've only just come."

But the steaks arrived then, great slabs of meat swimming in their own juices, and Jim fell upon his as a wolf falls upon a kill. He ate as Arthur had never seen a man eat, swiftly and silently and with an absolute concentration, his elbows upon the table and his head bent low over his plate, and Arthur, picking at his own portion with knife and fork, watched him with a fascination that was almost fear. Here was hunger, the real thing, not the polite appetite of the dining-room but the old, primordial hunger that had driven men since the first of them crawled up out of the slime—the hunger that knows meat is life and that no man can tell when he will eat again.

When the plate was clean, Jim sat back and wiped his mouth with the back of his hand and laughed at the expression on his cousin's face.

"You'll have to excuse me," he said. "I ain't been around white tablecloths. Up there you eat when you can and as much as you can, because tomorrow there mayn't be any. There was a winter, Art—the second winter—when me and my partner, a Swede named Olaf Lindquist, was holed up in a cabin on Henderson Creek with forty pounds of flour and a side of bacon gone green, and the thermometer at sixty-five below. Sixty-five below! You don't know what that means. Nobody down here knows what that means. You spit, and the spit crackles in the air before it hits the snow. You breathe, and your breath freezes in your beard till you've got a mask of ice over your face, and you've got to break it off with your fingers. We ate the bacon, green and all. We ate the flour, a cupful a day between the two of us, mixed with snow-water. Then we ate our moccasins, boiled. Then we ate the dogs."

He spoke flatly, without emphasis, and somehow this was more terrible to Arthur than any amount of passion would have been.

"And Olaf?" Arthur asked.

"Olaf died in February. Scurvy, mostly, and the cold, and something else besides—something I don't know the name of. He just quit. One morning he sat up in his bunk and looked at me and said, 'Yim, I tink I go now,' and lay down again and turned his face to the wall. I talked to him. I cussed him. I told him he was a yellow-bellied Swede and a quitter. It didn't do no good. He was dead by night." Jim was silent a moment. "I couldn't bury him. The ground was froze like iron. I put him up in a cache on poles, the way the Indians do, to keep him from the wolverines, and in the spring I came back and dug a hole. He was a good man, Olaf. Strong as a horse, and never a growl out of him. But he quit, and the North don't forgive a man that quits."

The waiter cleared the plates, and Jim poured himself a fresh cup of the black coffee and drank it scalding. Arthur found that his own hands were trembling, and he hid them beneath the table.

"I don't know how you stood it," he said.

"You stand it or you don't. That's all there is to it." Jim shrugged his great shoulders. "There ain't any secret. It's the law, Art—the law of the whole blamed universe, only up there it's laid bare, with all the frills stripped off it. Down here you've got your laws and your courts and your policemen, and you think that's what keeps a man alive. It ain't. It's just a kind of padding. Up there the padding's gone, and you see the thing itself. The strong live and the weak die, and the cold don't care which you are. It just waits."

Arthur was silent. He thought of his office, with its green-shaded lamp and its rows of calf-bound volumes; of the brass rail along which the clients passed; of the clock upon the wall that ticked away the hours between eight and six; of the streetcar that carried him home each evening to the little white house on Telegraph Avenue, with its mortgage held by the very bank whose papers he drew up. Padding. He had never thought of it that way. He had thought of it as civilization, as order, as the fruit of a thousand generations of human striving. And yet—and here was the strange thing—sitting across from this scarred and weathered man, he felt something stir in him that he had not felt since boyhood, a restlessness, a discontent, a kind of envy that shamed him even as he felt it.

"Do you remember the creek?" he said suddenly. "Back of Grandfather's place, in the valley?"

Jim's face lit up. "Alamo Creek! Lord, yes! The swimming hole under the big sycamore. And the time you jumped off the high branch on a dare and like to broke your neck."

"You dared me."

"Sure I did. And you did it, too, and come up spitting mud and blood with your nose all bent over to one side. I never was so proud of anybody in my life." Jim laughed, and the laugh rolled through the low room so that the longshoremen at the bar turned their heads. "And Grandfather came down with his razor-strop and lit into the both of us, and you never said a word about it being my dare. Took your licking like a man."

"I remember," Arthur said softly. He had not thought of it in years. He had not thought of himself, in years, as a boy who would leap from a high branch into a muddy pool on a dare. He had become, without ever quite deciding to become it, a careful man, a man who weighed consequences and drew up contracts against contingencies, a man who did not leap from anything.

"Maria."

"Maria. That's it. We went at it behind the hay barn for an hour, and neither of us would quit, and at the end of it we was both too tuckered to stand up and just lay there in the straw laughing like a pair of loons. And she married the blacksmith's boy anyhow." Jim shook his head, still smiling. "We was a couple of young wolves then, Art. Both of us. I used to think you had more sand in you than I did, only you kept it hid."

Arthur looked down at his soft hands. "I don't think I have much sand left," he said.

Jim regarded him for a long moment with those still, watchful eyes. Then he leaned forward and spoke in a low voice, almost gently.

"Don't you go thinking that, now. I know what you're thinking. You're thinking you sat down here in a soft chair while I was up there freezing and starving and fighting, and that makes me more of a man than you. Well, it don't. I've seen the soft fellows go North—the counter-jumpers and the bank clerks and the college boys—and I've seen some of 'em die, sure, and I've seen some of 'em turn out the hardest men in the country. It ain't what you've done, Art. It's what's in you. And I've seen what's in you. I seen it behind the hay barn and I seen it under the sycamore." He sat back. "Besides, you got a wife and a kid and a house. What've I got? A poke of dust that'll be gone in six months, and a pair of feet that ache every time the wind shifts, and nothing to come home to. Which of us has done better?"

"But you're going back," Arthur said.

Jim was silent. He turned his head and looked again out the window, where the light was fading over the estuary and the riding lights of the scows were beginning to wink on, one by one, along the water. When he spoke, it was more to himself than to his cousin.

"I got to," he said. "I don't know why. I can't make you understand it, because I don't understand it myself. I been down here two weeks now, and every night I lay in my bed at the hotel and listen to the streetcars and the people going by, and I can't sleep. It's too close. It's too soft. I feel like I'm smothering. And then I shut my eyes, and I see the big white silence stretching away for a thousand miles, and the Northern Lights a-dancing over it, and I hear the dogs howling at the moon, and something in me just aches to be there, like a man aches for drink. It nearly killed me, the North. It killed Olaf, and a dozen other men I knew. And I want to go back to it worse than I ever wanted anything." He laughed shortly. "That's a fool thing, ain't it?"

"No," Arthur said. "No, I don't think it's a fool thing at all."

And he did not. For in that moment he understood his cousin as he had never understood him before—understood that the hardness he had seen in Jim's face was not the whole of the man, that beneath it lay something restless and hungering and unappeasable, the same thing that had driven men out of caves and across oceans and over mountains since the beginning of time, the thing that would not let them rest. And he understood, too, with a pang that was half sorrow and half relief, that this thing was in himself also, buried deep beneath the stiff collars and the calf-bound volumes and the ticking clock, and that he would never let it out. He had chosen. He had made his peace with the padding. And he would go home tonight to Clara and the boy, and he would be glad to go.

Then Jim drew a buckskin pouch from inside his pea-jacket and loosened the drawstring and shook out upon the table a single nugget, rough and lumpish and dull yellow, about the size of a hazelnut.

"It ain't as big as a hen's egg," he said. "But I been carrying it for her for five years. I want the kid to have it. Little Jim."

Arthur picked it up. It was heavier than he expected, and warm from the body that had carried it.

"I'll give it to him," he said, and his voice was not quite steady. "And you'll come to supper Sunday. You'll see him yourself."

"I'll come," Jim said.

They went out together into the dusk, and the wind off the bay struck them full in the face, cold and wet and smelling of salt. At the corner they shook hands, and Jim's grip ground the bones of Arthur's hand together once more, and neither of them winced. Then Jim turned and walked away toward the waterfront, with that slow, rolling, deliberate stride of a man who has walked many miles on snowshoes, and Arthur turned toward the streetcar line. Here is an excerpt of Jack London's writing, to show you their style:

Not but that I was afloat in a safe craft, for the Martinez was a new ferry-steamer, making her fourth or fifth trip on the run between Sausalito and San Francisco. The danger lay in the heavy fog which blanketed the bay, and of which, as a landsman, I had little apprehension. In fact, I remember the placid exaltation with which I took up my position on the forward upper deck, directly beneath the pilot-house, and allowed the mystery of the fog to lay hold of my imagination. A fresh breeze was blowing, and for a time I was alone in the moist obscurity—yet not alone, for I was dimly conscious of the presence of the pilot, and of what I took to be the captain, in the glass house above my head. I remember thinking how comfortable it was, this division of labour which made it unnecessary for me to study fogs, winds, tides, and navigation, in order to visit my friend who lived across an arm of the sea. It was good that men should be specialists, I mused. The peculiar knowledge of the pilot and captain sufficed for many thousands of people who knew no more of the sea and navigation than I knew. On the other hand, instead of having to devote my energy to the learning of a multitude of things, I concentrated it upon a few particular things, such as, for instance, the analysis of Poe’s place in American literature—an essay of mine, by the way, in the current Atlantic. Coming aboard, as I passed through the cabin, I had noticed with greedy eyes a stout gentleman reading the Atlantic, which was open at my very essay. And there it was again, the division of labour, the special knowledge of the pilot and captain which permitted the stout gentleman to read my special knowledge on Poe while they carried him safely from Sausalito to San Francisco. A red-faced man, slamming the cabin door behind him and stumping out on the deck, interrupted my reflections, though I made a mental note of the topic for use in a projected essay which I had thought of calling “The Necessity for Freedom: A Plea for the Artist.” The red-faced man shot a glance up at the pilot-house, gazed around at the fog, stumped across the deck and back (he evidently had artificial legs), and stood still by my side, legs wide apart, and with an expression of keen enjoyment on his face. I was not wrong when I decided that his days had been spent on the sea.

“It’s nasty weather like this here that turns heads grey before their time,” he said, with a nod toward the pilot-house.

“I had not thought there was any particular strain,” I answered. “It seems as simple as A, B, C. They know the direction by compass, the distance, and the speed. I should not call it anything more than mathematical certainty.”

“Strain!” he snorted. “Simple as A, B, C! Mathematical certainty!” He seemed to brace himself up and lean backward against the air as he stared at me. “How about this here tide that’s rushin’ out through the Golden Gate?” he demanded, or bellowed, rather. “How fast is she ebbin’? What’s the drift, eh? Listen to that, will you? A bell-buoy, and we’re a-top of it! See ’em alterin’ the course!” From out of the fog came the mournful tolling of a bell, and I could see the pilot turning the wheel with great rapidity. The bell, which had seemed straight ahead, was now sounding from the side. Our own whistle was blowing hoarsely, and from time to time the sound of other whistles came to us from out of the fog.

“That’s a ferry-boat of some sort,” the new-comer said, indicating a whistle off to the right. “And there! D’ye hear that? Blown by mouth. Some scow schooner, most likely. Better watch out, Mr. Schooner-man. Ah, I thought so. Now hell’s a poppin’ for somebody!” The unseen ferry-boat was blowing blast after blast, and the mouth-blown horn was tooting in terror-stricken fashion.

“And now they’re payin’ their respects to each other and tryin’ to get clear,” the red-faced man went on, as the hurried whistling ceased. His face was shining, his eyes flashing with excitement as he translated into articulate language the speech of the horns and sirens. “That’s a steam-siren a-goin’ it over there to the left. And you hear that fellow with a frog in his throat—a steam schooner as near as I can judge, crawlin’ in from the Heads against the tide.” A shrill little whistle, piping as if gone mad, came from directly ahead and from very near at hand. Gongs sounded on the Martinez. Our paddle-wheels stopped, their pulsing beat died away, and then they started again. The shrill little whistle, like the chirping of a cricket amid the cries of great beasts, shot through the fog from more to the side and swiftly grew faint and fainter. I looked to my companion for enlightenment.

“One of them dare-devil launches,” he said. “I almost wish we’d sunk him, the little rip! They’re the cause of more trouble. And what good are they? Any jackass gets aboard one and runs it from hell to breakfast, blowin’ his whistle to beat the band and tellin’ the rest of the world to look out for him, because he’s comin’ and can’t look out for himself! Because he’s comin’! And you’ve got to look out, too! Right of way! Common decency! They don’t know the meanin’ of it!” I felt quite amused at his unwarranted choler, and while he stumped indignantly up and down I fell to dwelling upon the romance of the fog. And romantic it certainly was—the fog, like the grey shadow of infinite mystery, brooding over the whirling speck of earth; and men, mere motes of light and sparkle, cursed with an insane relish for work, riding their steeds of wood and steel through the heart of the mystery, groping their way blindly through the Unseen, and clamouring and clanging in confident speech the while their hearts are heavy with incertitude and fear. The voice of my companion brought me back to myself with a laugh. I too had been groping and floundering, the while I thought I rode clear-eyed through the mystery.

“Hello! somebody comin’ our way,” he was saying. “And d’ye hear that? He’s comin’ fast. Walking right along. Guess he don’t hear us yet. Wind’s in wrong direction.” The fresh breeze was blowing right down upon us, and I could hear the whistle plainly, off to one side and a little ahead.

“Ferry-boat?” I asked. He nodded, then added, “Or he wouldn’t be keepin’ up such a clip.” He gave a short chuckle. “They’re gettin’ anxious up there.” I glanced up. The captain had thrust his head and shoulders out of the pilot-house, and was staring intently into the fog as though by sheer force of will he could penetrate it. His face was anxious, as was the face of my companion, who had stumped over to the rail and was gazing with a like intentness in the direction of the invisible danger. Then everything happened, and with inconceivable rapidity. The fog seemed to break away as though split by a wedge, and the bow of a steamboat emerged, trailing fog-wreaths on either side like seaweed on the snout of Leviathan. I could see the pilot-house and a white-bearded man leaning partly out of it, on his elbows. He was clad in a blue uniform, and I remember noting how trim and quiet he was. His quietness, under the circumstances, was terrible. He accepted Destiny, marched hand in hand with it, and coolly measured the stroke. As he leaned there, he ran a calm and speculative eye over us, as though to determine the precise point of the collision, and took no notice whatever when our pilot, white with rage, shouted, “Now you’ve done it!” On looking back, I realize that the remark was too obvious to make rejoinder necessary.

“Grab hold of something and hang on,” the red-faced man said to me. All his bluster had gone, and he seemed to have caught the contagion of preternatural calm. “And listen to the women scream,” he said grimly—almost bitterly, I thought, as though he had been through the experience before. The vessels came together before I could follow his advice. We must have been struck squarely amidships, for I saw nothing, the strange steamboat having passed beyond my line of vision. The Martinez heeled over, sharply, and there was a crashing and rending of timber. I was thrown flat on the wet deck, and before I could scramble to my feet I heard the scream of the women. This it was, I am certain,—the most indescribable of blood-curdling sounds,—that threw me into a panic. What happened in the next few minutes I do not recollect, though I have a clear remembrance of pulling down life-preservers from the overhead racks, while the red-faced man fastened them about the bodies of an hysterical group of women. This memory is as distinct and sharp as that of any picture I have seen. It is a picture, and I can see it now,—the jagged edges of the hole in the side of the cabin, through which the grey fog swirled and eddied; the empty upholstered seats, littered with all the evidences of sudden flight, such as packages, hand satchels, umbrellas, and wraps; the stout gentleman who had been reading my essay, encased in cork and canvas, the magazine still in his hand, and asking me with monotonous insistence if I thought there was any danger; the red-faced man, stumping gallantly around on his artificial legs and buckling life-preservers on all comers; and finally, the screaming bedlam of women. This it was, the screaming of the women, that most tried my nerves. It must have tried, too, the nerves of the red-faced man, for I have another picture which will never fade from my mind. The stout gentleman is stuffing the magazine into his overcoat pocket and looking on curiously. A tangled mass of women, with drawn, white faces and open mouths, is shrieking like a chorus of lost souls; and the red-faced man, his face now purplish with wrath, and with arms extended overhead as in the act of hurling thunderbolts, is shouting, “Shut up! Oh, shut up!” I remember the scene impelled me to sudden laughter, and in the next instant I realized I was becoming hysterical myself; for these were women of my own kind, like my mother and sisters, with the fear of death upon them and unwilling to die. And I remember that the sounds they made reminded me of the squealing of pigs under the knife of the butcher, and I was struck with horror at the vividness of the analogy. These women, capable of the most sublime emotions, of the tenderest sympathies, were open-mouthed and screaming. They wanted to live, they were helpless, like rats in a trap, and they screamed. The horror of it drove me out on deck. I was feeling sick and squeamish, and sat down on a bench. In a hazy way I saw and heard men rushing and shouting as they strove to lower the boats. It was just as I had read descriptions of such scenes in books. The tackles jammed. Nothing worked. One boat lowered away with the plugs out, filled with women and children and then with water, and capsized. Another boat had been lowered by one end, and still hung in the tackle by the other end, where it had been abandoned. Nothing was to be seen of the strange steamboat which had caused the disaster, though I heard men saying that she would undoubtedly send boats to our assistance. I descended to the lower deck. The Martinez was sinking fast, for the water was very near. Numbers of the passengers were leaping overboard. Others, in the water, were clamouring to be taken aboard again. No one heeded them. A cry arose that we were sinking. I was seized by the consequent panic, and went over the side in a surge of bodies. How I went over I do not know, though I did know, and instantly, why those in the water were so desirous of getting back on the steamer. The water was cold—so cold that it was painful. The pang, as I plunged into it, was as quick and sharp as that of fire. It bit to the marrow. It was like the grip of death. I gasped with the anguish and shock of it, filling my lungs before the life-preserver popped me to the surface. The taste of the salt was strong in my mouth, and I was strangling with the acrid stuff in my throat and lungs. But it was the cold that was most distressing. I felt that I could survive but a few minutes. People were struggling and floundering in the water about me. I could hear them crying out to one another. And I heard, also, the sound of oars. Evidently the strange steamboat had lowered its boats. As the time went by I marvelled that I was still alive. I had no sensation whatever in my lower limbs, while a chilling numbness was wrapping about my heart and creeping into it. Small waves, with spiteful foaming crests, continually broke over me and into my mouth, sending me off into more strangling paroxysms. The noises grew indistinct, though I heard a final and despairing chorus of screams in the distance, and knew that the Martinez had gone down. Later,—how much later I have no knowledge,—I came to myself with a start of fear. I was alone. I could hear no calls or cries—only the sound of the waves, made weirdly hollow and reverberant by the fog. A panic in a crowd, which partakes of a sort of community of interest, is not so terrible as a panic when one is by oneself; and such a panic I now suffered. Whither was I drifting? The red-faced man had said that the tide was ebbing through the Golden Gate. Was I, then, being carried out to sea? And the life-preserver in which I floated? Was it not liable to go to pieces at any moment? I had heard of such things being made of paper and hollow rushes which quickly became saturated and lost all buoyancy. And I could not swim a stroke. And I was alone, floating, apparently, in the midst of a grey primordial vastness. I confess that a madness seized me, that I shrieked aloud as the women had shrieked, and beat the water with my numb hands. How long this lasted I have no conception, for a blankness intervened, of which I remember no more than one remembers of troubled and painful sleep. When I aroused, it was as after centuries of time; and I saw, almost above me and emerging from the fog, the bow of a vessel, and three triangular sails, each shrewdly lapping the other and filled with wind. Where the bow cut the water there was a great foaming and gurgling, and I seemed directly in its path. I tried to cry out, but was too exhausted. The bow plunged down, just missing me and sending a swash of water clear over my head. Then the long, black side of the vessel began slipping past, so near that I could have touched it with my hands. I tried to reach it, in a mad resolve to claw into the wood with my nails, but my arms were heavy and lifeless. Again I strove to call out, but made no sound. The stern of the vessel shot by, dropping, as it did so, into a hollow between the waves; and I caught a glimpse of a man standing at the wheel, and of another man who seemed to be doing little else than smoke a cigar. I saw the smoke issuing from his lips as he slowly turned his head and glanced out over the water in my direction. It was a careless, unpremeditated glance, one of those haphazard things men do when they have no immediate call to do anything in particular, but act because they are alive and must do something.

It was just as I had read descriptions of such scenes in books. The tackles jammed. Nothing worked. One boat lowered away with the plugs out, filled with women and children and then with water, and capsized. Another boat had been lowered by one end, and still hung in the tackle by the other end, where it had been abandoned. Nothing was to be seen of the strange steamboat which had caused the disaster, though I heard men saying that she would undoubtedly send boats to our assistance. I descended to the lower deck. The Martinez was sinking fast, for the water was very near. Numbers of the passengers were leaping overboard. Others, in the water, were clamouring to be taken aboard again. No one heeded them. A cry arose that we were sinking. I was seized by the consequent panic, and went over the side in a surge of bodies. How I went over I do not know, though I did know, and instantly, why those in the water were so desirous of getting back on the steamer. The water was cold—so cold that it was painful. The pang, as I plunged into it, was as quick and sharp as that of fire. It bit to the marrow. It was like the grip of death. I gasped with the anguish and shock of it, filling my lungs before the life-preserver popped me to the surface. The taste of the salt was strong in my mouth, and I was strangling with the acrid stuff in my throat and lungs. But it was the cold that was most distressing. I felt that I could survive but a few minutes. People were struggling and floundering in the water about me. I could hear them crying out to one another. And I heard, also, the sound of oars. Evidently the strange steamboat had lowered its boats. As the time went by I marvelled that I was still alive. I had no sensation whatever in my lower limbs, while a chilling numbness was wrapping about my heart and creeping into it. Small waves, with spiteful foaming crests, continually broke over me and into my mouth, sending me off into more strangling paroxysms. The noises grew indistinct, though I heard a final and despairing chorus of screams in the distance, and knew that the Martinez had gone down. Later,—how much later I have no knowledge,—I came to myself with a start of fear. I was alone. I could hear no calls or cries—only the sound of the waves, made weirdly hollow and reverberant by the fog. A panic in a crowd, which partakes of a sort of community of interest, is not so terrible as a panic when one is by oneself; and such a panic I now suffered. Whither was I drifting? The red-faced man had said that the tide was ebbing through the Golden Gate. Was I, then, being carried out to sea? And the life-preserver in which I floated? Was it not liable to go to pieces at any moment? I had heard of such things being made of paper and hollow rushes which quickly became saturated and lost all buoyancy. And I could not swim a stroke. And I was alone, floating, apparently, in the midst of a grey primordial vastness. I confess that a madness seized me, that I shrieked aloud as the women had shrieked, and beat the water with my numb hands. How long this lasted I have no conception, for a blankness intervened, of which I remember no more than one remembers of troubled and painful sleep. When I aroused, it was as after centuries of time; and I saw, almost above me and emerging from the fog, the bow of a vessel, and three triangular sails, each shrewdly lapping the other and filled with wind. Where the bow cut the water there was a great foaming and gurgling, and I seemed directly in its path. I tried to cry out, but was too exhausted. The bow plunged down, just missing me and sending a swash of water clear over my head. Then the long, black side of the vessel began slipping past, so near that I could have touched it with my hands. I tried to reach it, in a mad resolve to claw into the wood with my nails, but my arms were heavy and lifeless. Again I strove to call out, but made no sound. The stern of the vessel shot by, dropping, as it did so, into a hollow between the waves; and I caught a glimpse of a man standing at the wheel, and of another man who seemed to be doing little else than smoke a cigar. I saw the smoke issuing from his lips as he slowly turned his head and glanced out over the water in my direction. It was a careless, unpremeditated glance, one of those haphazard things men do when they have no immediate call to do anything in particular, but act because they are alive and must do something.

response:
The cabin stood on a bench of land above the Stewart, where the river, bending wide, had flung up a great bar of gravel in some forgotten summer and then gone off and forgotten it. It was a small cabin, of spruce logs chinked with moss, and its roof was of poles and earth, so that in the summer grass grew upon it. Now there was no grass, nor anything that grew, nor any sound save the occasional sharp report of a tree splitting its heart in the frost. The thermometer which hung by the door, a spirit thermometer, for mercury had long since frozen solid in its bulb, stood at fifty-two degrees below zero. It had stood so for a week. And in that week John Thorpe had learned what he had always known, though never so keenly: that the Northland is a hard mistress, and that she neither forgives nor forgets, and that she takes her toll of the careless with the indifference of a machine.

He had been at the woodpile when he missed the boy. It was a matter of habit with him to lift his head every few minutes and look toward the cabin, where the smoke went straight up from the stovepipe like a grey thread pulled taut from the roof to the sky. The boy had been playing by the door, building a fort of snow-blocks against an imagined army of Indians, and the dog Shag lay near him, curled nose to tail, and watching him with one eye. Now the fort stood unfinished, and the dog was gone, and the boy was gone. The man dropped his axe. He did not call out. A man does not waste his breath calling in such cold, for every breath is a knife in the lungs, and the air takes the voice and freezes it and lets it fall a few feet off as though it had never been. Instead he went straight to the place where the fort stood and read the tracks in the snow, as a scholar reads a page.

The small moccasin-prints led down the bank. Beside them went the prints of the dog. They led down the bank and out upon the river.

John Thorpe was not a man given to fear. He had come over the Chilcoot in the rush of 'ninety-seven with a hundred and twenty pounds on his back, and he had run the White Horse when better men had drowned in it, and he had starved one winter on the Koyukuk till he ate his moccasins and the thongs of his snowshoes. He had seen men die in many ways, and he had come near to dying himself, and he had grown to look upon death as one looks upon weather, as a thing to be reckoned with and guarded against, but not to be wept over. Yet now, as he went down the bank, there was a tightness in his throat and a coldness in his belly that had nothing to do with the frost. For he knew the Stewart. He knew that a quarter of a mile below the cabin the river ran swift over a shallow ledge, and that warm springs bubbled up there from the deep places of the earth, so that even at sixty below the ice was rotten and treacherous and the water lay hidden beneath a thin skin of snow. It was a trap, such as the Northland sets everywhere for the unwary, and it was baited with nothing more than an innocent stretch of white.

He ran. He ran heavily, his breath going out of him in great clouds that hung behind him in the windless air. And as he ran he thought of the boy's mother, who lay beneath the frozen gravel behind the cabin, where he had burned the ground for a week with fires to dig her grave, and he thought that it was a poor thing for a man to bring a child into such a country, and a poorer thing to keep him there. But he had kept him there, because there was nowhere else to take him, and because the boy was all that was left to him of the woman.

Halfway to the ledge he saw them coming back. The boy was walking slowly, very slowly, with a curious stiff-legged gait, and the dog walked beside him, whining. The boy's face was white, whiter than the snow, save for two spots of an angry red upon the cheekbones, and his lashes were matted with frost, and the fur of his parka-hood was furred again with the rime of his breath. He was six years old. He was crying, but the tears had frozen upon his face as fast as they fell, so that it seemed as though he wore a mask of glass.

John Thorpe did not speak. He looked down at the boy's feet. The moccasins were sheathed in ice to the ankles, and above the ankles the legs of his trousers were stiff as boards. The man understood in a glance. The boy had gone out upon the ledge, where the springs were, and had broken through to the knees, and had climbed out again. That he had climbed out at all was a matter of luck, and of the shallowness of the water at that place, and of nothing else. And now his feet were freezing. Even as the man looked, he knew that they were freezing, that the flesh was hardening and the blood retreating from it as the tide retreats from a beach, leaving it barren.

He caught the boy up in his arms, without a word, and ran with him back to the cabin.

Inside, he flung the boy down upon the bunk and tore at the frozen moccasins with his knife, for they would not come off otherwise. The socks beneath were frozen to the feet. He cut them away too, and the feet lay bare in the light of the candle, small and white and waxen, like the feet of a doll carved out of tallow. He seized a pan and ran out and filled it with snow and ran back, and he began to rub the feet with the snow, hard, harder than he had ever rubbed anything, as though he would scour the frost out of them by main strength. The boy screamed. The man did not stop. He rubbed, and the boy screamed and struggled, and the dog Shag crouched in the corner by the stove and whined and showed the whites of his eyes.

"Hold still," the man said. It was the first word he had spoken. His voice was thick and strange in his own ears. "Hold still, I tell you!"

"It hurts!" the boy wailed. "Daddy, it hurts!"

"It's meant to hurt. Hurtin's good. When it stops hurtin', then you've got somethin' to cry about."

He rubbed until his own hands were numb and he had to thrust them into his armpits to warm them, and then he rubbed again. And slowly, with infinite slowness, as the grey dawn comes up over a winter sea, the colour came back into the boy's feet. First a faint pink, and then a deeper red, and then an angry purplish flush, and with the colour came the pain in earnest, the pain of returning blood, which is a pain more terrible than the pain of freezing. The boy ceased to scream and lay sobbing, with his face to the logs, while his father sat on the edge of the bunk and held the small feet in his great calloused hands and looked at them as a miser looks at gold.

They would be well. There would be blisters, and the skin would peel, and for a week the boy would hobble and cry when he walked; but they would be well. There would be no black flesh, no rot, no hacking away of toes with a knife sterilized in the flame of the candle, as he had seen done on the Koyukuk to a man who had been careless one day at forty below and who carried his carelessness thereafter in a shortened foot. The boy had escaped. The trap had been sprung, and the boy had slipped out of it, and the Northland, for once, had been cheated of her toll.

And now that the danger was past, the man found that he was trembling, and that his trembling was not of fear but of anger. It came up in him like a flood, hot and red and bitter, so that his hands shook and his jaw worked and he had to grip the edge of the bunk to keep from striking out at something. It was a strange thing, this anger, and he did not understand it, and he did not try to understand it. He was not a man who looked into himself. He only knew that it was there, that it was enormous, and that it was directed at the small sobbing creature on the bunk, whom he loved more than anything else in the world.

"Kit," he said. "Turn around and look at me."

The boy did not turn.

"Turn around, I said."

Slowly the boy turned. His eyes were swollen and his nose was running, and the red spots on his cheekbones had spread until his whole face was red and blotched. He looked up at his father with the wary, beseeching look of a young animal that knows it has done wrong and does not know what punishment is coming.

"Where'd you go?"

"Down the river," the boy whispered.

"Where down the river?"

"To where the water smokes."

The man nodded slowly. He knew the place. On the coldest days the open water over the springs sent up a thin white vapour, like the breath of a sleeping beast, and from the cabin door it could be seen hanging above the ledge, a little wavering column against the black spruce of the farther bank. He had pointed it out to the boy himself, a dozen times, and told him what it meant.

"And what did I tell you about the place where the water smokes?"

The boy's lips quivered. "Not to go there."

"Why not?"

"'Cause the ice is bad."

"And what happens when you go through bad ice?"

"You get wet."

"And what happens when you get wet at fifty below?"

The boy did not answer. He looked down at his feet, which lay red and swollen on the blanket, and he began to cry again, quietly, with his mouth open and no sound coming out of it.

"I'll tell you what happens," the man said. His voice was low and hard, and he leaned forward so that his face was close to the boy's face. "You freeze. That's what happens. You freeze. Your feet freeze first, and then your legs, and then you can't walk no more, and you sit down in the snow because you're tired, and you think it's nice and warm, and you go to sleep. And you don't never wake up. And come spring, when the ice goes out, maybe somebody finds you on a bar fifty miles down the river, and maybe they don't. Maybe the wolves find you first." He paused, and his breath came hard. "Is that what you want? Is that it?"

"No," the boy sobbed. "No, Daddy."

"Then why'd you go?"

"I wanted to see. I wanted to see the water. Shag went, and I went after him."

The man glanced at the dog in the corner. The dog, meeting his eye, flattened its ears and thumped its tail feebly upon the floor in propitiation. It was a big dog, half wolf, with the wolf's broad skull and the wolf's slant eyes, and it had come to the man as a pup from an Indian village on the Pelly. It knew the ice. It knew the springs. It had gone out upon the ledge, no doubt, nosing after some scent of mink or otter, and it had picked its way surely across the rotten places, as the wild things do, by an instinct older than thought. And the boy had followed it, trusting where the dog trusted, and had not the dog's instinct, and had gone through.

It came to John Thorpe then, sitting there on the edge of the bunk, that this was the whole of the matter. The dog had what the boy had not. The dog was of the Wild, and the Wild had made it, through ten thousand generations of its ancestors who had lived and died upon the ice, and those that had not learned the ice had died young and left no pups behind them, and those that had learned it had lived and bred and passed the learning on in their blood. That was the law. It was a simple law and a merciless one, and it took no account of tears, nor of love, nor of the small white faces of children. It asked only: Are you fit? And if you were not fit, it put you out of the way, as a man brushes a fly from his sleeve.

But the boy was not of the Wild. The boy was soft, as all his kind were soft, the product of a race that had spent ten thousand years building walls and fires and houses to keep the Wild away, until it had forgotten what the Wild was. The boy did not have the learning in his blood. He would have to get it some other way. He would have to get it from his father. And if his father could not give it to him, then the Wild would give it to him in its own fashion, and the giving would kill him.

"Listen to me, Kit," the man said, and his voice was different now, though still hard. "You listen to me, and you remember what I'm tellin' you, because I ain't goin' to tell you again. This country don't care about you. You hear? It don't care if you're six or sixty, if you're a good boy or a bad boy, if you got a daddy that loves you or if you ain't got nobody at all. It don't care. It ain't mean, and it ain't kind. It just is. And it'll kill you quicker'n you can spit if you give it the chance."

The boy stared at him with wide wet eyes.

"Shag can go out on that ice because Shag knows the ice. He was born knowin' it. You wasn't. You don't know nothin' yet. You don't know a blessed thing. And till you do know, you do what I tell you, and you don't do what I tell you not to, and you don't go followin' no dog, nor nobody else, out where I said not to go. Because next time—" His voice caught, and he stopped, and went on. "Next time maybe the water's deeper. Next time maybe you don't climb out. And then what'll I do? You tell me that. What'll I do then?"

The boy did not know what his father would do. He had never seen his father like this. His father was a large man, and a quiet one, who laughed seldom and spoke little and moved through the days with a slow, heavy certainty, like the river itself in the summer. He had seen his father angry before, at the dogs, at the weather, at a sled that broke or a fire that would not catch. But he had never seen his father's face work as it worked now, nor heard his father's voice break as it had broken, nor seen in his father's eyes the thing that was there now, which was a thing the boy had no name for, because he was too young, and which was fear.

"I'm sorry," the boy whispered. "I'm sorry, Daddy. I won't never do it again."

"You won't," the man said. "You won't, because if you do I'll take a strap to you, and you won't sit down for a week. You understand me?"

"Yes."

"Say it."

"I won't go out where the water smokes."

"Nor nowhere else I tell you not to."

"Nor nowhere else."

The man looked at him for a long time. Then he got up from the bunk, heavily, like an old man, and went to the stove and put in more wood, though the stove was already red. He stood with his back to the boy and his hands spread over the heat, and he did not move. Outside, a tree split with a sound like a rifle-shot, and the dog in the corner lifted its head and listened and put it down again. The candle guttered. The frost on the inside of the single window, which was made of a flour-sack soaked in grease, thickened imperceptibly, crystal growing upon crystal in the slow and patient manner of all the work of the cold.

It was a curious thing, the man reflected, standing there, and a thing he would not have believed in his younger days, that a man could be made a coward by so small a creature. He had faced the White Horse without a tremor. He had faced the long starvation on the Koyukuk and laughed at it, or near enough. He had faced the grizzly on the Hootalinqua with an empty rifle and nothing but a knife and his two hands, and he carried the marks of it still upon his shoulder, and he had not been afraid, or not much. But this—this small thing on the bunk, with its running nose and its swollen eyes and its red feet—this had made a coward of him. He could feel the cowardice in him now, like a sickness in the bowels, and he knew that it would never quite go away, not so long as the boy lived, and not so long as the Northland stretched its white and indifferent arms about the cabin on the Stewart.

He had been hard with the boy. He knew it. He had meant to be hard, and he would be hard again, if need be, and harder. For that was the only way. The softness that was in the boy must be burned out of him, or hammered out, or frozen out, before the Wild found it and took advantage of it. The man had no learning in books, and he had never heard of the philosophers who wrote of such things; yet he knew, as surely as the dog knew the ice, that the world was a place of struggle, and that the weak went under and the strong survived, and that a father who spared his child the hard lessons only delivered him the more surely to the hardest lesson of all. He knew it. And knowing it did not make it easier.

Behind him he heard the boy stir upon the bunk, and then a small voice, very small, said: "Daddy?"

"What?"

"My feet hurt."

"I know they do."

"Will they stop hurtin'?"

"In a while."

There was a silence. Then: "Daddy? Are you still mad?"

The man did not turn around at once. He stood with his hands over the stove, and he looked at the red iron, and he thought of many things. He thought of the woman under the gravel behind the cabin. He thought of the place where the water smoked, and of the thin white vapour rising from it, like the breath of a sleeping beast. He thought of the bar fifty miles down the river, where the spring floods left the drowned things, and of the wolves. And he thought that he would take the boy outside in the spring, when the ice went out, and in the summer, when the river ran open, and show him the ledge and the springs and the way the water boiled over them, and tell him again, and make him see it, and make him remember it, so that it would get into his blood as it was in the dog's blood, and he would never need to be told again.

Then he turned around. He went to the bunk and sat down on it, and the boy looked up at him, and the man put out one great hand, cracked and scarred and black with the pitch of the spruce, and laid it on the boy's head, upon the fine pale hair that was like the hair of the woman.

"No," he said. "I ain't mad no more."

The boy crept to him then, as a young dog creeps to its master after a beating, with a kind of humble and wondering gladness, and laid his head against his father's side. And the man sat there and held him, the while the stove roared and the candle guttered and the frost thickened on the window, and outside, in the vast and windless night, the Northland waited, patient and unhurried, with the patience of that which has all of time before it, and has never yet failed to collect its due.
