He was a slow man, and words did not come easy to him; he felt things a long time before he could say them, and sometimes he could never say them at all. But he made a try now.

"It's this way, Nora. I been sittin' in that booth for six years. I see 'em come in every mornin', and I see 'em go out every night. I see the women that's been on the line all day, and their hands is all cracked and bleedin' from the fruit acid, and they ain't allowed to wear gloves because it slows 'em down. I see the kids that's sixteen, and says they're eighteen, because their folks needs the money. I punch their cards, and I dock 'em when they're late, and I don't say nothin'. That's my job. But this here is different. This is—" he hunted for the word—"this is like I was a stool-pigeon."

"Don't you say that word in this house!"

"Well, that's what it is. That's what they'd call me. And that's what I'd be."

"Who'd call you? Them Reds? What do you care what they call you? They'll all be gone in a month!"

"I'd call myself," said Ed, in a low voice.

There was a silence. Out on the street a car went by with its cut-out open, making a noise like a machine-gun, and some young people in it were laughing and singing a song from the movies. Nora sat down again, slowly, and the dish-towel lay in her lap, and she twisted it in her hands.

She was not a bad woman, you understand; she was a woman who had been taught, by every voice she had ever listened to, that the thing which mattered in life was to get ahead. The preacher at the First Methodist Church said it on Sundays, in a roundabout way, telling about the parable of the talents; the *Herald* said it every day, in the stories about the poor boy who had become a millionaire; the movies said it, with their pictures of shop-girls who married the boss's son and lived in marble palaces; the advertisements said it, on every bill-board along the highway. Nora had never heard anybody say anything else, except the Reds, and they were wicked people who wanted to take away everything you had. And now here was her own husband, talking like them! It was as if he had come home and told her he had taken to drink.

"Ed," she said, and her voice had changed; it was soft now, and pleading, and there were tears in it. "Ed, honey, you know I ain't hard-hearted. I'm sorry for those people, same as you. But it ain't our fault the world's made this way. We didn't make it. If you don't tell Mr. Durfee, somebody else will. You know that. There's plenty of men at that plant would jump at the chance. And then they'll get fired jist the same, and somebody else'll have the job, and we'll be right where we are—or worse."

"Worse how?"

She looked at him. "Do you think Mr. Durfee's goin' to forget? Do you think he'll keep you on, after you turned him down? He'll know you were holdin' out on him. He'll figger you're one of 'em."

Ed had thought of this. He had thought of it all the way home, walking the two miles because he had not wanted to get in the Ford and have the neighbors see his face. Mr. Durfee had not said anything about it; he had been very pleasant, and had given Ed a cigar, and had talked about loyalty, and the company being one big family, and how a man who stood by the company would find the company standing by him. But there had been a look in his eye at the end, when Ed had said he would like to think it over; a little narrowing, like a man sighting along a gun-barrel.

"He might," Ed admitted.

"Might! He will! And then where'll we be? With the payment on the house due the first of the month, and the piano, and Alice needin' shoes for school! You'll be out on the street, and black-listed yourself, and for what? For a bunch of foreigners that never did nothin' for you but sit up one night with a sick baby!"

"Nora—"

"No, you listen to me! I've listened to you!" She was crying now, openly, the tears running down and making little streaks in the powder on her cheeks. "I've done without, Ed. I've done without for nine years and never complained. When you wanted to leave the hardware store and come out here, I come. When you put the money in that oil stock and lost it, I never said a word. But I ain't goin' to see my child go hungry because you've took a notion to be noble! It's easy enough to be noble when it's your wife and kid that pays for it!"

Ed flinched as if she had struck him. It was the oil stock that did it; he had thought she had forgotten that. It had been a company called the Great Western Petroleum Syndicate, and a smooth young man with a diamond ring had sold the units at a church social, and everybody had bought them, and the young man had gone away to Mexico. Ed had put in four hundred dollars, which was all they had saved in two years; and he had never forgiven himself, and he knew now that Nora had never forgiven him either, but had only put the thing away in some secret drawer of her mind, to be taken out when it would cut the deepest. That was the way with married people, he was beginning to understand; you kept a sort of ledger, and you never knew how the accounts stood until there came a day of settlement.

He got up and went over to the window and stood looking out. The street lamps had come on, and the moths were swarming about them, and across the way old Mr. Bascomb was sitting on his porch in his shirt-sleeves, smoking his pipe. Mr. Bascomb had been a railroad engineer, and had been in the big strike of '94, and had been black-listed for eleven years after it, so that he had had to change his name and go to Mexico to get work. He had told Ed about it once, sitting on that same porch; and at the end he had said, "They'll tell you it don't pay, son, and they're right. It don't pay a nickel. But I'm seventy-two years old, and I can still look at myself in the glass when I shave." Ed thought about that now.

"Well?" said Nora, behind him. "Ain't you goin' to say anything?"

"I'm thinkin'."

"You've had all afternoon to think! What did you tell Mr. Durfee you'd do?"

"I told him I'd let him know in the mornin'."

"Then you'll let him know you'll take it." It was not a question; she said it the way you would tell a child to wash its hands before supper.

Ed turned around and looked at her. She was sitting at the table, very straight, with the dish-towel twisted into a rope in her hands, and her eyes red, and her mouth set in a line. He loved her; he had loved her since the night he had met her at the Odd Fellows' dance in Wichita, when she had worn a pink dress with a sash, and had laughed at everything he said. He wondered where that girl had gone. He supposed the payments had eaten her up, a little at a time, so that you could not say just when it happened; the way the fruit acid ate the hands of the women on the peeling line.

"Nora," he said, "if I do it, will you be satisfied?"

"Of course I'll be satisfied! What a question!"

"I mean—will you be happy? Will we be happy? When we're in that new house up on Alta Vista Heights, and I'm drivin' to work in the sedan, and I pass Joe Martinez on the road lookin' for a job? Will you be happy then?"

"I won't even know Joe Martinez is on the road! And neither will you, if you've got any sense!"

"I'll know," said Ed.

She got up, and threw the dish-towel on the table, and went to the bedroom door. There she turned, with her hand on the knob.

"You'll do what you please, I suppose; you always do. But I'll tell you one thing, Ed Haskell. If you throw away this chance, don't you ever come to me and say you're sorry. Because I won't be listening." And she went in and shut the door, not slamming it, because Alice was asleep in the next room; but she shut it in a way that was worse than slamming.

Ed stood alone in the little living-room, with the piano that was not paid for, and the overstuffed set that was not paid for, and the picture of a sunset over the Golden Gate that had come free with a year's subscription to the *Herald*. He thought about the hundred and thirty-five dollars, and the two hundred and twenty-five, and the difference, which was ninety dollars a month; and he thought how strange it was that a man's soul should come to have a price on it, like a can of peaches, and be marked up and down according to the market. Nobody had ever told him that this was the way the world was run. They had told him in Sunday-school that you should love your neighbor, and they had told him in the high-school civics class that this was a free country, where every man had the right to speak his mind; and he had believed them both. And now it turned out that you could love your neighbor at the price of ninety dollars a month, and speak your mind at the price of your job, and your house, and your wife's good opinion; and the people who had told him those things in Sunday-school and in the civics class had known it all along, and had never let on.

He turned out the light, and went out on the porch and sat down on the steps, where he had sat when he came home. Across the street Mr. Bascomb's pipe glowed red in the dark, and went dim, and glowed again. Somewhere down the block a radio was playing a dance tune. The night was very warm, and the smell of the orange groves came in on the wind from the east, sweet and heavy, the way it does in that country; and the tourists who came out on the Santa Fe in the winter-time would write home about it, and say what a paradise California was. Ed Haskell sat there a long time, smelling it, and thinking; and the clock in the living-room struck eleven, and then twelve, and still he had not made up his mind.

Here is an excerpt of Upton Sinclair's writing, to show you their style:

Soon after this it was time for Bunny to visit his mother. Bunny’s mother did not bear Dad’s name, as other boys’ mothers do; she was called Mrs. Lang, and lived in a bungalow on the outskirts of Angel City. There was an arrangement whereby she had a right to have Bunny with her one week in every six months; Bunny always knew when this time was approaching, and looked forward to it with mixed emotions. His mother was sweet, and gave him the petting which he missed at other times; “pretty little Mamma,” was her name for herself. But in other ways the visit was embarrassing, because there were matters supposed to be kept hidden from Bunny, but which he could not help guessing. Mamma would question him about Dad’s affairs, and Bunny knew that Dad did not wish his affairs talked about. Then too, Mamma complained that she never had enough money; Dad allowed her only two hundred dollars a month, and how could a young and charming grass-widow exist on such a sum? Her garage bill was always unpaid, and she would tell Bunny about it, and expect him to tell Dad—but Dad would evade hearing. And next time, Mamma would cry, and say that Jim was a tyrant and a miser. The situation was especially difficult just now, because Mamma had read about the new well in the papers, and knew just how much money Dad had; she unfolded to Bunny a plan, that he should try to persuade Dad to increase her allowance, but without having Dad suspect that she had suggested it. And this, right after Bunny had renounced the luxury of small lies! Also there was the mystery about Mamma’s friends. There were always gentlemen friends who came to see her while Bunny was there, and who might or might not be agreeable to Bunny. When he came home, Aunt Emma would ask him questions, from which it was evident that she wanted to know about these gentlemen friends, but didn’t want Bunny to know that she wanted to know. Bunny noticed that Dad never referred to such matters; he never asked any questions about Mamma, and Aunt Emma always did her asking out of Dad’s presence. All this had a peculiar effect upon Bunny. Just as Dad kept a safe deposit box at the bank, into which nobody ever looked but himself, so Bunny kept a secret place in his own mind. Outwardly, he was a cheerful and frank little fellow, if somewhat too mature for his years; but all the time he was leading a dual life—picking up ideas here and there, and carrying them off and hiding them, as a squirrel does nuts, so that he may come back at a later season and crack them open and nibble them. Some nuts were good and some were bad, and Bunny learned to judge them, and to throw away the bad ones. One thing was plain: there was something which men and women did, which they were all in a conspiracy to keep you from knowing that they did. It was a dark corner of life, mysterious and rather hateful. In the beginning, Bunny was loyal to his father, not trying to find out what his father didn’t want him to know. But this could not continue indefinitely, for the mind automatically seeks understanding. It was not merely that the birds and the chickens and the dogs in the street gave you hints; it was not merely that every street-boy knew, and was eager to explain; it was that the stupid grown-ups themselves persisted in saying things which you couldn’t help getting. It was Aunt Emma’s fixed conviction that every lady was after Dad; “setting her cap at him,” or “making sheep’s eyes at him”—she had many such phrases. And Dad always showed a queer embarrassment whenever he had been the least bit polite to any lady; he seemed to be concerned lest Bunny should share Aunt Emma’s suspicions. But the truth was, Bunny was irritated by his aunt, and learned to evade her questions, and not tell what Dad had said to the nice lady in the hotel at Lobos River, and whether or not the lady had had dinner with them. These worldly arts Bunny acquired, but all the time he was in secret revolt. Why couldn’t people talk plainly? Why did they have to be pretending, and whispering, and making you uncomfortable? Within a week after bringing in Ross-Bankside No. 1, Dad had a new derrick under way on the lease, and in another week he had it rigged up, and the old string of tools was on its way into the earth again. Also he had two new derricks under way, and two new strings in process of delivery. There would be four wells, standing on the four corners of a diamond-shaped figure, three hundred feet on the side. It was necessary to call house-movers, and take the Bankside homestead to another lot; but that didn’t trouble Mr. Bankside, who had already moved himself to an ocean-front palace near Dad, and bought himself a whole outfit of furniture, and a big new limousine, also a “sport-car,” in which to drive himself to the country club to play golf every afternoon. The Bankside family was accustoming itself to the presence of a butler, and Mrs. Bankside had been proposed at the most exclusive of the ladies’ clubs. Efficiency was the watch-word out here in the West, and when you decided to change your social status, you put the job right through. Dad and Bunny made another trip to Lobos River, and not without some difficulty they conquered the “jinx” in Number Two, and brought in a very good well. There were to be two more derricks here, and more tools to be bought and delivered. That was the way in the oil business, as fast as you got any money, you put it back into new drilling—and, of course, new responsibilities. You were driven to this by the forces inherent in the game. You were racing with other people, who were always threatening to get your oil. As soon as you had one well, you had to have “offset wells” to protect it from the people on every side who would otherwise get your oil. Also, you might have trouble in marketing your oil, and would begin to think, how nice to have your own refinery, and be entirely independent. But independence had its price, for then you would have to provide enough oil to keep the refinery going, and you would want a chain of filling-stations to get rid of your products. It was a hard game for the little fellow; and no matter how big you got, there was always somebody bigger! But Dad had no kick just now; everything was a-comin’ his way a-whoopin’. Right in the midst of his other triumphs it had occurred to him to take one of his old Antelope wells and go a little lower, and see what he found; he tried it—and lo and behold, at eight hundred feet farther down the darn thing went and blew its head off. They were in a new layer of oil-sands; and every one of these sixteen old wells, that had been on the pump for a couple of years, and were about played out, were ready to present Dad with a new fortune, at a cost of only a few thousand dollars each! But right away came a new problem; there was no pipe-line to this field, and there ought to be one. Dad wanted some of the other operators to go in with him, and he was going up there and make a deal. Then Bunny came to him, looking very serious. “Dad, have you forgotten, it’s close to the fifteenth of November.”

“What about it, son?”

“You promised we were going quail-shooting this year.”

“By gosh, that’s so! But I’m frightfully rushed jist now, son.”

“You’re working too hard, Dad; Aunt Emma says you’re putting a strain on your kidneys, the doctor has told you so.”

“Does he recommend a quail diet?” Bunny knew by Dad’s grin that he was going to make some concession. “Let’s take our camping things,” the boy pleaded, “and when you get through at Antelope, let’s come home by the San Elido valley.”

“The San Elido! But son, that’s fifty miles out of our way!”

“They say there’s no end of quail there, Dad.”

“Yes, but we can get quail a lot nearer home.”

“I know, Dad; but I’ve never been there, and I want to see it.”

“But what made you hit on that place?” Bunny was embarrassed, because he knew Dad was going to think he was “queer.” Nevertheless, he persisted. “That’s where the Watkins family live.”

“Watkins family—who are they?”

“Don’t you remember that boy, Paul, that I met one night when you were talking about the lease?”

“Gosh, son! You still a-frettin’ about that boy?”

“I met Mrs. Groarty on the street yesterday, and she told me about the family; they’re in dreadful trouble, they’re going to lose their ranch to the bank because they can’t meet the interest on the mortgage, and Mrs. Groarty says she can’t think what they’ll do. You know Mrs. Groarty didn’t get any money herself—at least, she spent her bonus money for units, and she isn’t getting anything out of them, and has to live on what her husband gets as a night watchman.”

“What you want to do about it?”

“I want you to buy that mortgage, Dad; or anything, so the Watkinses can stay in their home. It’s wicked that people should be turned out like that, when they’re doing the best they can.”

“There’s plenty o’ people bein’ turned out when they don’t meet their obligations, son.”

“But when it’s not their fault, Dad?”

“It would take a lot of bookkeeping to figger jist whose fault it is; and the banks don’t keep books that way.” Then seeing the protest in Bunny’s face, “You’ll find, son there’s a lot o’ harsh things in the world, that ain’t in your power to change. You’ll jist have to make up your mind to that, sooner or later.”

“But Dad, there’s four children there, and three of them are girls, and where are they to go? Paul is away, and they haven’t any way to let him know what’s happened. Mrs. Groarty showed me a picture of them, Dad; they’re good, kind people, you can see they’ve never done anything but work hard. Honest, Dad, I couldn’t be happy if I didn’t help them. You said you’d buy me a car some day, and I’d rather you took the money and bought that mortgage. It’s less than a couple of thousand dollars, and that’s nothing to you.”

“I know, son; but then you’ll get them on your hands—” “No, they’re not like that, they’re proud; Mrs. Groarty says they wouldn’t take money from you, any more than Paul would. But if you bought the mortgage from the bank, they couldn’t help that. Or you might buy the ranch, Dad, and rent it back to them. Paul says there’s oil on that ranch—at least his Uncle Eby had seen it on top of the ground.”

“There’s thousands of ranches jist like that in California, son. Oil on top of the ground don’t mean anything special.”

“Well, Dad, you’ve always said you wanted to try some wild-catting; and you know, that’s the only way you’ll ever get what you talk about—a whole big tract that belongs to you, with no royalties to pay, and nobody to butt in. So let’s take a chance on Paradise, and drive through there and camp out a few days and get some quail, and we’ll see what we think of it, and we’ll help those poor people, and give your kidneys a rest at the same time.” So Dad said all right; and he went away thinking to himself: “Gosh! Funny kid!” The San Elido valley lay on the edge of the desert, and you crossed a corner of the desert to get to it; a bare wilderness of sun-baked sand and rock, with nothing but grey, dusty desert plants. You sped along upon a fine paved road, but the land was haunted by the souls of old-time pioneers who had crossed it in covered wagons or with pack-mules, and had left their bones beside many a trail. Even now, you had to be careful when you went off into side-trails across these wastes; every now and then a car would get stuck with an empty radiator, and the people would be lucky to get out alive. You could get water if you sunk a deep well; and so there were fruit ranches and fields of alfalfa here and there. There came long stretches where the ground was white, like salt; that was alkali, Dad said, and it made this country a regular boob-trap. The stranger from the East would come in and inspect a nice fruit ranch, and would think he was making a good bargain to get the land next door for a hundred dollars an acre; he would set out his fruit-trees and patiently water them, and they wouldn’t grow; nothing would grow but a little alfalfa, and maybe there was too much alkali for that. The would-be rancher would have to pull up the trees, and obliterate the traces of them, and set a real-estater to hunting for another boob. Strapped to the running-board of Dad’s car, on the right hand side where Bunny sat, was a big bundle wrapped in a water-proof cover; they were camping out—which meant that the mind of a boy was back amid racial memories, the perils and excitements of ten thousand years ago. Tightly clutched in Bunny’s two hands were a couple of repeating shot-guns; he held these for hours, partly because he liked the feel of them, and partly because they had to be carried in the open—if you shut them up in the compartment they would be “concealed weapons,” and that was against the law. Near the head of the valley a dirt road went off, and a sign said: “Paradise, eight miles.” They wound up a little pass, with mountains that seemed to be tumbled heaps of rock, of every size and color. There were fruit ranches, the trees now bare of leaves, with trunks calcimined white, and young trees with wire netting about them, to keep away the rabbits. The first rains of the season had fallen, and new grass was showing—the California spring, which begins in the fall. The pass broadened out; there were ranch-houses scattered here and there, and the village of Paradise—one street, with a few scattered stores, sheltered under eucalyptus trees that made long shadows in the late afternoon light. Dad drew up at the filling station, which was also a feed-store. “Can you tell me where is the Watkins ranch?”

“There’s two Watkinses,” said the man. “There’s old Abel Watkins—” “That’s the one!” exclaimed Bunny.

“He’s got a goat-ranch, over by the slide. It ain’t so easy to find. Was you plannin’ to get there tonight?”

“We shan’t worry if we get lost,” said Dad; “we got a campin’ outfit.” So the man gave them complicated directions. You took the lane back of the school-house, and you made several jogs, and then there were about sixteen forks, and you must get the right one, and you followed the slide that took the water down to Roseville, and it was the fourth arroyo after you had passed old man Tucker’s sheep-ranch, with the little house up under the pepper trees. And so they started and followed a winding road that had apparently been laid out by sheep, and the sun set behind the dark hills, and the clouds turned pink, and they dodged rocks that were too high for the clearance of the car and crawled down into little gullies, and up again with a constant shifting of gears. There was no need to ask about the quail, for the hills echoed with the melodious double call of the flocks gathering for the night.

Also, you might have trouble in marketing your oil, and would begin to think, how nice to have your own refinery, and be entirely independent. But independence had its price, for then you would have to provide enough oil to keep the refinery going, and you would want a chain of filling-stations to get rid of your products. It was a hard game for the little fellow; and no matter how big you got, there was always somebody bigger! But Dad had no kick just now; everything was a-comin’ his way a-whoopin’. Right in the midst of his other triumphs it had occurred to him to take one of his old Antelope wells and go a little lower, and see what he found; he tried it—and lo and behold, at eight hundred feet farther down the darn thing went and blew its head off. They were in a new layer of oil-sands; and every one of these sixteen old wells, that had been on the pump for a couple of years, and were about played out, were ready to present Dad with a new fortune, at a cost of only a few thousand dollars each! But right away came a new problem; there was no pipe-line to this field, and there ought to be one. Dad wanted some of the other operators to go in with him, and he was going up there and make a deal. Then Bunny came to him, looking very serious. “Dad, have you forgotten, it’s close to the fifteenth of November.”

“What about it, son?”

“You promised we were going quail-shooting this year.”

“By gosh, that’s so! But I’m frightfully rushed jist now, son.”

“You’re working too hard, Dad; Aunt Emma says you’re putting a strain on your kidneys, the doctor has told you so.”

“Does he recommend a quail diet?” Bunny knew by Dad’s grin that he was going to make some concession. “Let’s take our camping things,” the boy pleaded, “and when you get through at Antelope, let’s come home by the San Elido valley.”

“The San Elido! But son, that’s fifty miles out of our way!”

“They say there’s no end of quail there, Dad.”

“Yes, but we can get quail a lot nearer home.”

“I know, Dad; but I’ve never been there, and I want to see it.”

“But what made you hit on that place?” Bunny was embarrassed, because he knew Dad was going to think he was “queer.” Nevertheless, he persisted. “That’s where the Watkins family live.”

“Watkins family—who are they?”

“Don’t you remember that boy, Paul, that I met one night when you were talking about the lease?”

“Gosh, son! You still a-frettin’ about that boy?”

“I met Mrs. Groarty on the street yesterday, and she told me about the family; they’re in dreadful trouble, they’re going to lose their ranch to the bank because they can’t meet the interest on the mortgage, and Mrs. Groarty says she can’t think what they’ll do. You know Mrs. Groarty didn’t get any money herself—at least, she spent her bonus money for units, and she isn’t getting anything out of them, and has to live on what her husband gets as a night watchman.”

“What you want to do about it?”

“I want you to buy that mortgage, Dad; or anything, so the Watkinses can stay in their home. It’s wicked that people should be turned out like that, when they’re doing the best they can.”

“There’s plenty o’ people bein’ turned out when they don’t meet their obligations, son.”

“But when it’s not their fault, Dad?”

“It would take a lot of bookkeeping to figger jist whose fault it is; and the banks don’t keep books that way.” Then seeing the protest in Bunny’s face, “You’ll find, son there’s a lot o’ harsh things in the world, that ain’t in your power to change. You’ll jist have to make up your mind to that, sooner or later.”

“But Dad, there’s four children there, and three of them are girls, and where are they to go? Paul is away, and they haven’t any way to let him know what’s happened. Mrs. Groarty showed me a picture of them, Dad; they’re good, kind people, you can see they’ve never done anything but work hard. Honest, Dad, I couldn’t be happy if I didn’t help them. You said you’d buy me a car some day, and I’d rather you took the money and bought that mortgage. It’s less than a couple of thousand dollars, and that’s nothing to you.”

“I know, son; but then you’ll get them on your hands—” “No, they’re not like that, they’re proud; Mrs. Groarty says they wouldn’t take money from you, any more than Paul would. But if you bought the mortgage from the bank, they couldn’t help that. Or you might buy the ranch, Dad, and rent it back to them. Paul says there’s oil on that ranch—at least his Uncle Eby had seen it on top of the ground.”

“There’s thousands of ranches jist like that in California, son. Oil on top of the ground don’t mean anything special.”

“Well, Dad, you’ve always said you wanted to try some wild-catting; and you know, that’s the only way you’ll ever get what you talk about—a whole big tract that belongs to you, with no royalties to pay, and nobody to butt in. So let’s take a chance on Paradise, and drive through there and camp out a few days and get some quail, and we’ll see what we think of it, and we’ll help those poor people, and give your kidneys a rest at the same time.” So Dad said all right; and he went away thinking to himself: “Gosh! Funny kid!” The San Elido valley lay on the edge of the desert, and you crossed a corner of the desert to get to it; a bare wilderness of sun-baked sand and rock, with nothing but grey, dusty desert plants. You sped along upon a fine paved road, but the land was haunted by the souls of old-time pioneers who had crossed it in covered wagons or with pack-mules, and had left their bones beside many a trail. Even now, you had to be careful when you went off into side-trails across these wastes; every now and then a car would get stuck with an empty radiator, and the people would be lucky to get out alive. You could get water if you sunk a deep well; and so there were fruit ranches and fields of alfalfa here and there. There came long stretches where the ground was white, like salt; that was alkali, Dad said, and it made this country a regular boob-trap. The stranger from the East would come in and inspect a nice fruit ranch, and would think he was making a good bargain to get the land next door for a hundred dollars an acre; he would set out his fruit-trees and patiently water them, and they wouldn’t grow; nothing would grow but a little alfalfa, and maybe there was too much alkali for that. The would-be rancher would have to pull up the trees, and obliterate the traces of them, and set a real-estater to hunting for another boob. Strapped to the running-board of Dad’s car, on the right hand side where Bunny sat, was a big bundle wrapped in a water-proof cover; they were camping out—which meant that the mind of a boy was back amid racial memories, the perils and excitements of ten thousand years ago. Tightly clutched in Bunny’s two hands were a couple of repeating shot-guns; he held these for hours, partly because he liked the feel of them, and partly because they had to be carried in the open—if you shut them up in the compartment they would be “concealed weapons,” and that was against the law. Near the head of the valley a dirt road went off, and a sign said: “Paradise, eight miles.” They wound up a little pass, with mountains that seemed to be tumbled heaps of rock, of every size and color. There were fruit ranches, the trees now bare of leaves, with trunks calcimined white, and young trees with wire netting about them, to keep away the rabbits. The first rains of the season had fallen, and new grass was showing—the California spring, which begins in the fall. The pass broadened out; there were ranch-houses scattered here and there, and the village of Paradise—one street, with a few scattered stores, sheltered under eucalyptus trees that made long shadows in the late afternoon light. Dad drew up at the filling station, which was also a feed-store. “Can you tell me where is the Watkins ranch?”

“There’s two Watkinses,” said the man. “There’s old Abel Watkins—” “That’s the one!” exclaimed Bunny.

“He’s got a goat-ranch, over by the slide. It ain’t so easy to find. Was you plannin’ to get there tonight?”

“We shan’t worry if we get lost,” said Dad; “we got a campin’ outfit.” So the man gave them complicated directions. You took the lane back of the school-house, and you made several jogs, and then there were about sixteen forks, and you must get the right one, and you followed the slide that took the water down to Roseville, and it was the fourth arroyo after you had passed old man Tucker’s sheep-ranch, with the little house up under the pepper trees. And so they started and followed a winding road that had apparently been laid out by sheep, and the sun set behind the dark hills, and the clouds turned pink, and they dodged rocks that were too high for the clearance of the car and crawled down into little gullies, and up again with a constant shifting of gears. There was no need to ask about the quail, for the hills echoed with the melodious double call of the flocks gathering for the night.

It was eight years since Philip Ashby had seen his cousin Ruth, and he had grown so accustomed to not seeing her that the matter had ceased to trouble him. There had been a quarrel in the family; it had to do with Grandfather Mercer's will, and with a strip of land along the Arroyo Seco which Grandfather had left to his son, Philip's father, and which Aunt Margaret had claimed was promised to her. Philip had been eleven at the time, and had understood nothing about it, except that there were no more Sunday dinners at Aunt Margaret's cottage in Highland Park, and that when her name came up at table, his mother would look at his father, and his father would look at his plate. Afterward the strip of land had been cut up into building lots, and a company had been formed, and the lots had been sold to people from Iowa and Kansas at prices which made Philip's father a man of consequence in Pasadena. And so the quarrel had paid for itself, you might say; that was the way it went with quarrels among the well-to-do. The ones who won could afford to forget, and generally did.

But now Philip was twenty, and home from the university for the summer, and he had a roadster of his own, and a great deal of time on his hands. One day he was driving down Spring Street, in the heart of the city, and he saw a young woman waiting for a street-car at the corner of Fifth, and something about the set of her head made him turn and look again. She was slender and straight, in a plain blue dress, with a straw hat pulled down over brown hair, and she was holding a bundle of papers under her arm. Philip pulled over to the curb, and the motorist behind him blew his horn in a rage, but Philip didn't care. He leaned out and called, "Ruth! Ruth Mercer!" And the young woman turned, and stared at him for a moment, and then her face broke into a smile which was the very same smile he remembered from the orange grove behind Grandfather's house, when they had been eight and nine years old and had hidden together from the Japanese gardener.

"Why, Phil!" she said. "Is it really you? You've grown up!"

"So have you," he said. "Get in, won't you? I'll take you wherever you're going."

She hesitated, and he saw her glance at the roadster, which was a bright yellow one, and very new, with nickel trimmings that flashed in the sun. Then she laughed, and said, "All right; but I'm only going to Boyle Heights, and you'll be sorry you asked."

"I won't be sorry," he said. "I've been wanting to see you for years." This was not quite true, but it seemed true while he said it; and Ruth climbed in beside him, and put her bundle of papers on her lap, and they were off.

---

It is a strange thing, meeting a relative after a long absence; for you have known each other in a way that no stranger can know you, and yet you are strangers. You remember a little girl with skinned knees who cried because a bee had stung her, and here is a grown woman who has lived a whole life you know nothing about. Philip found himself searching her face for the little girl, and every now and then he would catch a glimpse of her, in a gesture, or a turn of speech, and then she would be gone again, and there would be this capable, self-possessed young person, who seemed in some way older than himself, though she was really a year younger.

"Tell me about yourself," he said. "What are you doing? How is Aunt Margaret?"

"Mother is well enough," said Ruth. "She takes in sewing. Didn't you know?"

He hadn't known; and he felt a little shock of embarrassment, as if he had been caught at something. "And Uncle Dan?"

"Father was hurt," she said. "Three years ago. He was a brakeman on the Southern Pacific, you remember, and he was crushed between two cars in the yards at Colton. He can walk now, with a crutch, but he can't work. The company paid him four hundred dollars, and their lawyer made him sign a paper saying it was his own fault."

"Good Lord!" said Philip. "Was it his own fault?"

"They had cut down the crews," said Ruth, quite matter-of-factly. "There used to be three men to do the work, and they made it two. Father was working his fourteenth hour that day. So you can say it was his fault, if you like; he ought to have been more wide awake."

Philip did not know what to answer. He drove for a while in silence, dodging a wagon loaded with crates of cantaloupes, and a jitney bus, and a Mexican boy selling newspapers. He was thinking that nobody had ever told him about Uncle Dan; and then he was thinking that perhaps somebody had known, and had not told him. That was a disquieting idea, and he put it away, to be taken out and examined later.

"And you?" he asked. "What are you doing?"

"I work in a cannery," said Ruth. "At least, I did until last week. I was a forelady on the packing line. Now I'm doing something else."

"What?"

She looked at him with a kind of amused defiance, and tapped the bundle of papers on her lap. "I'm organizing," she said.

---

Philip had heard of organizing, of course; everybody had. In the city of Los Angeles there was a great association of business men, which had decided many years ago that this was to be an "open shop" town, and which spent a great deal of money every year to keep it so. Philip's father belonged to this association, and gave money to it, and talked about it at the dinner table; and from these conversations Philip had gathered that a labor organizer was a sort of foreign agitator, who stirred up contented workingmen with lies, and lived on their dues, and probably threw bombs on the side. There had been a newspaper building dynamited once, long ago, before Philip was born, and the business men of the city had never let anybody forget it.

So here was a strange thing: his own cousin, with whom he had made mud pies under the pepper tree, was a labor organizer! Philip glanced at her sidewise, half expecting her to look different, now that he knew; but she looked just the same, with the sun on her cheek and a little wisp of brown hair blowing loose from under her hat.

"Well, I'll be darned!" he said, at last.

Ruth laughed outright. "You needn't be so shocked, Phil. It's not as wicked as they've told you."

"I didn't say it was wicked."

"No, but you were thinking it. I could see you thinking it. You've got your father's face when you think—your eyebrows go up and stay there."

"Have I really?" said Philip; and he was so interested by this that he forgot to be embarrassed. Nobody had ever told him before that he had his father's face; at the university they told him he looked like a movie actor, which was pleasanter, though not so interesting.

---

They came out upon the bridge over the river, which in summer was nothing but a broad bed of sand and stones, with a trickle of water down the middle, and a few willows; and beyond it lay Boyle Heights, where the poorer people lived—Russians and Jews and Mexicans, and the families of railroad men. The houses were small and wooden, set close together, with little patches of garden in front, and geraniums growing as high as the windows, for geraniums will grow anywhere in California, and ask nothing of anybody. Ruth directed him up a steep street, and then along another, and they stopped in front of a cottage with a porch that sagged a little at one end, and a lemon tree in the yard.

"This is where we live," she said. "Will you come in and see Mother? She'd like it, I think. She doesn't hold anything against you, you know. You were only a child."

Philip noted the "you"; it was plain enough whom she did hold something against. But he said that he would be glad to come in; and he followed her up the path, past the lemon tree, and onto the porch, where an old wicker chair stood with a cushion on it that had been mended many times.

Aunt Margaret was in the front room, sitting at a sewing machine by the window, and she got up when they came in, and peered at Philip over her spectacles. She was a small, grey woman, much smaller than he remembered; and he realized with a start that it was he who had grown, and not she who had shrunk. When she understood who he was, she put her hand to her throat, and then she came and took both his hands and looked up into his face.

"Philip!" she said. "Little Philip! Why, you're a man!" And she kissed him on the cheek, and her eyes were wet, and Philip felt himself turning red to the roots of his hair.

Then there came a thumping from the back of the house, and Uncle Dan appeared in the doorway, leaning on a crutch. He had been a big man once, with a red face and a hearty voice, and he had swung Philip up on his shoulders and run with him through the orange grove, roaring like a lion. Now his face was thin and yellowish, and his voice was quiet, and one leg dragged when he moved. But he grinned at Philip, and the grin was the same.

"Well, well," he said. "If it ain't the young feller from Pasadena! You come slummin', son?"

"Dad!" said Ruth.

"I'm only joshin' him," said Uncle Dan. "Set down, boy, set down. Ma, ain't there some of that lemonade left?"

---

So they sat in the little front room, which was very clean, and very crowded, with a horsehair sofa and a table covered with an oilcloth, and a picture of Grandfather Mercer on the wall—the same picture which hung in Philip's father's library, only there it had a gilt frame and here it had a plain black one. Aunt Margaret brought lemonade from the lemon tree, and they talked; or rather, the older people asked questions, and Philip answered them. How was his mother? Was it true they had a swimming pool? What was he studying at the university? Did he play football?

Philip told them that he was studying economics, because his father wished him to go into the business; and that he did not play football, but he was on the tennis team; and that he belonged to a fraternity, which was a sort of club where the fellows lived together. He found himself making these things sound less grand than they were; he did not mention that the fraternity house had a Steinway grand piano, or that the fellows kept a colored man to wait on table. He did not quite know why he left these things out; it was some instinct, some sense of the fitness of things, which told him that a Steinway piano would not go well with the horsehair sofa and the mended cushion on the porch.

"Economics," said Uncle Dan, thoughtfully. "That's the science of money, ain't it? What do they teach you about it?"

"Well," said Philip, "they teach you about supply and demand, and how prices are fixed, and about wages—"

"Wages!" said Uncle Dan. "Now that's interestin'. What do they say about wages?"

Philip tried to remember; it had been in the second semester, and there had been a long chapter about it, with graphs. "They say," he said, "that wages are fixed by the law of supply and demand, the same as anything else. If there are a lot of workers and not many jobs, wages go down; and if there are a lot of jobs and not many workers, they go up. And the professor says that it's no use trying to interfere with it, because it's a natural law, like gravitation."

Uncle Dan nodded slowly, and looked at Ruth, and Ruth looked at the ceiling. "Like gravitation," said Uncle Dan. "Well, now, I'll tell you somethin', son. When the railroad cut our crews from three men to two, there wasn't no fewer men wantin' to work. There was jist as many as before. What there was, was a feller in an office in San Francisco who figgered he could save so many thousand dollars a year if he got two men to do the work of three. Now maybe that's gravitation, I don't know. I never went to college. But it come down on my leg mighty heavy, whatever it was."

---

Philip did not argue; he had no argument ready, and besides, it did not seem the place for one. He drank his lemonade, which was sour, because sugar cost money; and presently Ruth said she must go to a meeting, and he offered to drive her, and she accepted. Aunt Margaret kissed him again at the door, and made him promise to come back, and Uncle Dan shook his hand and said, "No hard feelin's, boy. You tell your pa I said howdy." And Philip promised that he would, though he knew very well that he would not; there were some messages you did not carry into a house in Pasadena.

In the car, Ruth was silent for a while, and then she said, "I'm sorry about Father. He gets bitter sometimes. You can't blame him."

"I don't blame him," said Philip. "I—I didn't know about any of it, Ruth. Honestly I didn't. Nobody ever told me."

"No," she said. "I suppose nobody did."

He drove on, and he was thinking hard. He was thinking about the strip of land along the Arroyo Seco, and the building lots, and the people from Iowa; and about the four hundred dollars, and the paper Uncle Dan had signed; and about his own roadster, which had cost two thousand. He was not a stupid young man, though nobody had ever asked him to use his mind for anything more than passing examinations; and now, all at once, his mind was working of its own accord, putting things together and taking them apart, the way you take apart a watch to see what makes it go. It was not a comfortable sensation.

"Ruth," he said, "what was it really about? The quarrel, I mean. Between your mother and my father."

She looked at him. "Do you want the truth?"

"Of course I do."

"Grandfather meant the land for Mother. He said so, many times; he said it before witnesses. But he never put it in writing, and when he was sick at the end, your father was the one who looked after his affairs, and the will that came out was the will your father's lawyer drew. Mother could have gone to court, but she hadn't any money for lawyers, and Father said it would only make bad blood. So she let it go." Ruth paused, and then she added, quite gently, "I don't say your father did anything that wasn't legal, Phil. I'm sure it was all legal. That's the way things are done."

Philip said nothing. He was remembering the way his mother looked at his father, and his father looked at his plate.

---

The meeting was in a hall over a bakery on First Street, and there were women going up the stairs—Mexican women with black shawls, and Italian women, and some American girls in cheap bright dresses, and they all spoke to Ruth, and some of them looked at Philip and his yellow roadster with frank curiosity. Ruth got out, and gathered up her papers, and then she stood on the curb and looked at him.

"Thank you for the ride, Phil," she said. "It was nice to see you. Truly it was."

"Ruth," he said, "is there anything—I mean, could I help somehow? I've got some money of my own, an allowance, and I don't need half of it—"

She shook her head, and the smile came again, the old smile from the orange grove. "That's sweet of you. But it isn't money we need, not that kind. Do you know what these women earn in the cannery? Twenty cents an hour, in the rush season, standing ten hours on a cement floor, with their hands in brine till the skin comes off. If you gave every one of them a hundred dollars, it would be gone in a few months, and they'd be right back where they were. What they need is to stand together, so they can ask for what they've earned. You can't give them that. Nobody can give it to them. They have to take it."

"Take it!" said Philip. "That sounds like—"

"Like a Red? Yes, I know. That's what they'll call me in the papers, if they ever bother to call me anything." She laughed. "But you come to a meeting some time, and see for yourself whether these women look like Reds. Most of them go to Mass every morning."

"I will," said Philip, and he meant it, though he did not know how he could possibly explain it at home.

She turned to go, and then turned back. "Phil, do you still remember the time we buried the dead bird under the pepper tree, and you said a prayer over it, and you'd forgotten the words, so you said the multiplication table instead?"

"I'd forgotten that," he said. "Did I really?"

"You got as far as seven times eight," said Ruth, "and then you couldn't remember that either, so you said 'Amen.' I've thought of it lots of times." And she ran up the stairs, and was gone.

---

Philip drove home to Pasadena slowly, through the long golden afternoon, past miles of orange groves, and miles of new bungalows with their little lawns and their palm trees, all exactly alike, and all with signs on them saying "For Sale" or "Sold." He passed the place along the Arroyo where the strip of land had been; there were houses on it now, and a filling station, and a sign with his father's name in letters two feet high. He had passed it a thousand times, and had always felt a little glow of pride at the sign; now he looked at it, and felt something which was not pride, and which he could not have named.

When he got home, his mother was on the terrace, in a white dress, having tea with two ladies from the Shakespeare Club; and she called to him, and asked him where he had been all day, and he said, "Oh, just driving around." He went up to his room, and lay on the bed with his hands behind his head, and looked at the ceiling for a long time.

It is a curious thing about the minds of young people: they are full of locked rooms, which the grown-ups have locked for them, with signs on the doors saying "Not Your Business" and "Don't Ask." And mostly the young people obey, because it is easier, and because there is always tennis to be played, and dances to go to, and examinations to pass. But every now and then something happens, and one of the doors swings open, just a crack; and after that, no matter how hard you push against it, you can never quite get it shut again. That was what had happened to Philip Ashby this afternoon, on a street corner in Los Angeles, with the motorists blowing their horns behind him. He did not know it yet; he only knew that he was restless and unhappy, and that he did not want to go down to dinner. But the door was open, and the wind was blowing through.

Soon after this it was time for Bunny to visit his mother. Bunny’s mother did not bear Dad’s name, as other boys’ mothers do; she was called Mrs. Lang, and lived in a bungalow on the outskirts of Angel City. There was an arrangement whereby she had a right to have Bunny with her one week in every six months; Bunny always knew when this time was approaching, and looked forward to it with mixed emotions. His mother was sweet, and gave him the petting which he missed at other times; “pretty little Mamma,” was her name for herself. But in other ways the visit was embarrassing, because there were matters supposed to be kept hidden from Bunny, but which he could not help guessing. Mamma would question him about Dad’s affairs, and Bunny knew that Dad did not wish his affairs talked about. Then too, Mamma complained that she never had enough money; Dad allowed her only two hundred dollars a month, and how could a young and charming grass-widow exist on such a sum? Her garage bill was always unpaid, and she would tell Bunny about it, and expect him to tell Dad—but Dad would evade hearing. And next time, Mamma would cry, and say that Jim was a tyrant and a miser. The situation was especially difficult just now, because Mamma had read about the new well in the papers, and knew just how much money Dad had; she unfolded to Bunny a plan, that he should try to persuade Dad to increase her allowance, but without having Dad suspect that she had suggested it. And this, right after Bunny had renounced the luxury of small lies! Also there was the mystery about Mamma’s friends. There were always gentlemen friends who came to see her while Bunny was there, and who might or might not be agreeable to Bunny. When he came home, Aunt Emma would ask him questions, from which it was evident that she wanted to know about these gentlemen friends, but didn’t want Bunny to know that she wanted to know. Bunny noticed that Dad never referred to such matters; he never asked any questions about Mamma, and Aunt Emma always did her asking out of Dad’s presence. All this had a peculiar effect upon Bunny. Just as Dad kept a safe deposit box at the bank, into which nobody ever looked but himself, so Bunny kept a secret place in his own mind. Outwardly, he was a cheerful and frank little fellow, if somewhat too mature for his years; but all the time he was leading a dual life—picking up ideas here and there, and carrying them off and hiding them, as a squirrel does nuts, so that he may come back at a later season and crack them open and nibble them. Some nuts were good and some were bad, and Bunny learned to judge them, and to throw away the bad ones. One thing was plain: there was something which men and women did, which they were all in a conspiracy to keep you from knowing that they did. It was a dark corner of life, mysterious and rather hateful. In the beginning, Bunny was loyal to his father, not trying to find out what his father didn’t want him to know. But this could not continue indefinitely, for the mind automatically seeks understanding. It was not merely that the birds and the chickens and the dogs in the street gave you hints; it was not merely that every street-boy knew, and was eager to explain; it was that the stupid grown-ups themselves persisted in saying things which you couldn’t help getting. It was Aunt Emma’s fixed conviction that every lady was after Dad; “setting her cap at him,” or “making sheep’s eyes at him”—she had many such phrases. And Dad always showed a queer embarrassment whenever he had been the least bit polite to any lady; he seemed to be concerned lest Bunny should share Aunt Emma’s suspicions. But the truth was, Bunny was irritated by his aunt, and learned to evade her questions, and not tell what Dad had said to the nice lady in the hotel at Lobos River, and whether or not the lady had had dinner with them. These worldly arts Bunny acquired, but all the time he was in secret revolt. Why couldn’t people talk plainly? Why did they have to be pretending, and whispering, and making you uncomfortable? Within a week after bringing in Ross-Bankside No. 1, Dad had a new derrick under way on the lease, and in another week he had it rigged up, and the old string of tools was on its way into the earth again. Also he had two new derricks under way, and two new strings in process of delivery. There would be four wells, standing on the four corners of a diamond-shaped figure, three hundred feet on the side. Ned Harlowe was eight years old when he learned that there are two kinds of wrong-doing in the world: the kind that grown-ups punish you for, and the kind that they do themselves and call business. He did not learn it all at once, of course; nobody does. It came to him the way the frost comes into the ground in the fall—a little at a time, so that you do not notice until one morning the earth is hard under your feet, and you cannot remember when it was soft.

His father was Mr. Walter Harlowe, who owned the Harlowe Box and Crate Company, down by the river at the lower end of Millbridge. Everybody in town knew the Harlowe mill; you could hear its whistle at six in the morning and again at six at night, and in between you could hear the scream of the big saws, which went on all day like some creature in pain that never got tired of complaining. The mill made boxes for the fruit-growers up the valley, and crates for the furniture factories in Grand Junction, and cheese-boxes for the creameries; and since everything in America had to be shipped somewhere in something, there was always plenty of work, and Mr. Harlowe had a big brick house on Elm Street, with a porch that went around three sides, and a cook named Hilda, and a Pierce-Arrow car with a man to drive it.

Ned loved his father; it would be well to say that at the outset, so that what follows may not be misunderstood. Mr. Harlowe was a large, ruddy man with a voice that filled up a room, and when he laughed you felt it in the floor. He had come up from nothing—he liked to tell about it; he had started as a tally-boy in a lumber yard at four dollars a week, and had saved his money and bought a second-hand saw, and so on, step by step, the way it is told in the books which they give to boys in Sunday school. He believed in hard work, and in thrift, and in the Republican party, and in the Methodist church, in about that order; and he believed that any man who would do what he had done could have what he had got. That was the whole of his philosophy, and it seemed to him so plain that he could not understand how anyone could think otherwise—except, of course, the agitators, who were a special kind of person, like snakes, and not to be argued with.

Now it happened that in the spring of that year there was an accident at the mill. A man named Stanislaus Wojcik, who worked at the cut-off saw, got his hand caught in the carriage, and lost three fingers and part of the palm. Ned heard about it at the supper-table; his father mentioned it the way he mentioned the price of spruce, or the trouble with the freight cars on the Northern line. "Fellow got careless down at the cut-off," he said. "Lost part of his hand. They will do it—you can tell 'em and tell 'em." And Ned's mother said, "Oh, how dreadful!" and then asked whether the Andersons were coming on Thursday, and the matter was closed.

But it was not closed for Ned, because Ned knew Joey Wojcik. Joey was in the third grade at the Lincoln School, where Ned went too—Mr. Harlowe believed in the public schools, and said a boy ought to rub elbows with all kinds; it would make a man of him. Joey was a thin, freckled boy with pale hair that stuck up in back, and he could throw a ball farther than anybody in the class, and he had shown Ned how to make a whistle out of a willow stick. Next day Joey was not in school, and the day after that he was not in school either; and on the third day Ned walked home by way of Front Street, which was a way he was not supposed to go, and found the Wojcik house.

It was one of a row of houses that the mill had put up years ago and rented to its hands; they were all alike, with tar-paper on the sides that had once been meant to look like brick, and little porches that sagged in the middle, as if they were tired. There was a smell of cabbage, and of the river, and of something sour that Ned did not know the name of. "Hello," said Joey.
