At a quarter to ten on a Thursday evening in October, in the living-room of the residence at 1419 Elmhurst Avenue, Ossawa Falls, Minnesota, Mr. Howard T. Duckworth sat in his Morris chair and read the editorial page of the *Ossawa Falls Clarion-Herald* with the air of a man who has earned his repose and intends that the universe shall know it.

He was forty-four. He was the proprietor of the Duckworth Motor & Implement Company, distributors of the Overland, the Willys-Knight, and the Superior Line of Cream Separators. He was a past Exalted Ruler of the Elks, a Deacon of the Wesley Methodist Church, a member in excellent standing of the Kiwanis, the Commercial Club, the Ossawa Falls Golf and Country Club (associate), and the Republican Party. He had a round, pink, freshly barbered face, rimless eyeglasses that pinched a red seam across his nose, and a waistcoat which had of late become a source of mild apprehension, like a creditor who is courteous but persistent. He believed in Service, in the Protective Tariff, in the Future of Ossawa Falls, and in the proposition that any man who would not boost was a knocker, a crab, and very probably a Socialist.

The room in which he sat was, by the measure of Elmhurst Avenue, a highly satisfactory room. It contained a davenport upholstered in a mulberry plush which had been advertised as Genuine Mohair-Effect; a Victrola in a cabinet of fumed oak; a library table bearing a bronze lamp, a copy of *The Saturday Evening Post*, a copy of *The Ladies' Home Journal*, a cut-glass bowl of wax fruit, and a set of the Works of Robert Louis Stevenson in maroon limp leather which no one had ever opened, because they had been purchased to fill the bookcase and they filled it. Over the mantel hung a steel engraving of a stag at bay, and beside the stag, in a gilt frame, Howard's certificate of membership in the Ossawa Falls Boosters' Booster Club, signed by the Mayor. The radiator knocked twice, in the manner of an embarrassed caller, and was silent.

Across from him, in the rocker, sat his wife Myrtle, and Myrtle was not reading.

She had in her lap an envelope. It was a long envelope, of the heavy cream stock favored by the First National Bank of Ossawa Falls, and it had been slit open with a hairpin. She had been holding it for eleven minutes. Howard had not noticed this, because Howard had been reading an editorial entitled "WHY NOT A GREATER OSSAWA?" which agreed with everything he thought, and which he was therefore finding singularly intelligent.

"Says here," he observed, with the generous impulse of a man sharing his wealth, "says here that if we get that new bridge over the Minnetonka River, Ossawa'll be a town of twenty thousand inside five years. Twenty thousand! Why, that'd put us right up ahead of Fergus Falls, and I'll tell the world it's high time somebody did. Those Fergus Falls birds have been blowing about their waterworks till you'd think—"

"Howard."

"—you'd think nobody else ever had a pump. Hm? What is it, Myrt?"

"Howard, what is this?"

She held up the envelope. She did not hold it up as a woman displays a recipe, nor as she displays a son's report card; she held it as a District Attorney holds up a revolver before a jury that has already been told whose fingerprints are on it.

Howard lowered the paper four inches. He peered over it. He peered, specifically, over the rims of his eyeglasses, which was a gesture he had learned from Mr. J. Wilbur Sloane, President of the First National, and which he employed when he wished to convey that he was a man of affairs and that the person addressing him was, however dear, not.

"Why, that's—where'd you get that?"

"It came in the afternoon mail. It's addressed to Mr. and Mrs. Howard T. Duckworth. I believe I am Mrs. Howard T. Duckworth. I've been told so, at any rate, for nineteen years."

"Now, Myrt, there's no call to get sarcastic."

"I'm not being sarcastic. I'm asking a question. It says"—she drew the folded sheet from the envelope and smoothed it upon her knee, with that terrible deliberation which is the weapon of women who have been taught never to raise their voices—"it says, 'Dear Mr. and Mrs. Duckworth, We beg to acknowledge receipt of the executed instruments in connection with the second mortgage upon the property at 1419 Elmhurst Avenue, in the amount of Six Thousand Five Hundred Dollars ($6,500.00), and to advise that the proceeds have been credited as directed to the account of the Hiawatha Heights Development Corporation.' And then it says, 'Assuring you of our continued interest in your welfare,' and it's signed by Mr. Sloane's secretary. Howard, I didn't execute any instruments. I don't even know what an instrument is, unless it's a piano."

Howard folded the *Clarion-Herald*. He folded it once lengthwise and once across, and laid it upon the arm of the Morris chair, and smoothed it, and in all these operations he consumed perhaps nine seconds, which is, as anyone who has been married can attest, an exceedingly long time.

"Well, now," he said. "Well, now, Myrt. I was going to tell you about that."

"When?"

"Why, just as soon as—soon as the thing was all set. I didn't want to worry you with a lot of business details. You know how you get about figures."

"I do not 'get' about figures. I kept the books for Papa's store for three years before I ever met you, and they balanced, which is more than you can say for the Kiwanis picnic fund."

This was a low blow, and Howard felt it to be a low blow. The deficit in the Kiwanis picnic fund, amounting to eleven dollars and forty cents, had been the result of a misunderstanding about the ice cream, and it had been explained, fully and manfully, at the August luncheon, and he had believed the matter closed. He took off his eyeglasses and polished them upon his handkerchief, which was a gesture he had learned from no one in particular, but which gave him time.

"Now listen, Myrtle. Just listen to me a minute, will you, before you go flying off the handle? You know Charley Gartside."

"I know Charley Gartside."

There was a quality in the way she said it. Mr. Charles M. Gartside was a realtor. He had come to Ossawa Falls two years before from somewhere in Iowa, a place which, in his accounts of it, sometimes appeared to be Des Moines and sometimes Sioux City and once, after the Elks' Christmas party, Omaha. He wore a pearl-gray fedora and spats, and he had a laugh like a slammed door, and he called every man "old-timer" and every woman "little lady," and he had in eighteen months sold more lots than any realtor in the history of the county, chiefly to persons who had never seen them.

"Well, Charley's got hold of the biggest proposition this town's ever seen. Biggest. Now I'm not exaggerating. You know that tract out past the fairgrounds, the old Lindquist farm, runs clear down to the river?"

"The swamp."

"It is *not* a swamp! That's just exactly the kind of knocking talk that's held this town back for forty years. It's low-lying, I'll grant you that, but Charley's got an engineer—fellow from St. Paul, mighty high-class man—and he says all it needs is some drainage and fill, and you've got the finest residential development between the Twin Cities and Fargo. Hiawatha Heights. Curving streets, see, none of this checkerboard stuff, everything modern, cement sidewalks, restrictions so you don't get any undesirable element. And when they put the new bridge through—and they *will* put it through, Myrt, Senator Hogaboom as good as told me so himself at the Commercial Club—when they put that bridge through, those lots'll go up three, four hundred percent. I've got in on the ground floor. Ground floor! There's men in this town'd give their eyeteeth to get the chance I got."

"Then why didn't they?"

"Why didn't who what?"

"Why didn't the men who'd give their eyeteeth put up their eyeteeth? Why did Charley Gartside come to you?"

Howard looked at her with an expression of patient injury, the expression of a man who has brought home a fine fat pheasant and been asked whether he remembered to wipe his feet.

"Because," he said, with dignity, "because Charley happens to know a live wire when he sees one. Because Charley happens to think that Howard Duckworth is a man of vision. That's why. And I may say that's a good deal more than some people around here seem to think."

He was, as he said it, genuinely moved. He believed it. At the moment when Charley Gartside, leaning across a table in the grill of the Hotel Thorwaldsen with a cigar in one hand and a blueprint in the other, had said, "Old-timer, I'll be frank with you, there's maybe three men in this burg I'd let in on this, and you're the first one I thought of," Howard had felt a warmth spread through his chest that was not entirely attributable to the Hotel Thorwaldsen's pot roast. He had felt chosen. He had felt as he imagined Mr. Henry Ford must feel every morning on rising.

Myrtle did not appear to share this emotion. She sat very straight in the rocker. She was forty-one, a slight woman with brown hair turning, in streaks she did not trouble to hide, the color of weathered pine; and she had a way of pressing her lips together, when she was thinking, that made her look like her own mother, a fact which Howard had observed but had never had the courage to mention.

"Howard," she said, "this is our house."

"Well, I know it's our house. What d'you think I—"

"No. Listen to me. This is our *house*. We paid it off in March. You came home the day you made the last payment and you brought me a box of Whitman's and you said, 'Well, Myrt, she's ours, free and clear, and nobody can ever take her away from us.' You said that. You stood right there by the Victrola and said it. And I thought—I thought, well, all right then. All right. Maybe it was worth it."

"Maybe *what* was worth it?"

She did not answer at once. Out on Elmhurst Avenue a motor car went by, its cutout open, the sound rising and dwindling like a long derisive cheer; that would be the Pedersen boy in his father's Buick, on his way to the Bijou or to somewhere less respectable. Across the street, in the bungalow of Dr. and Mrs. Otto Schwab, a light went out in the front room and another came on upstairs, as regular as the turning of a page. It occurred to Myrtle, not for the first time, that she could have told the hour on any night of the year by the lights in the Schwab house, and that the Schwabs, very probably, could tell it by theirs.

"Everything," she said at last. "All of it. Pinching. Not getting the new dining set. Not going to Minneapolis when Sister had her operation, because the payment was due. Wearing that brown serge three winters running, so that Mrs. J. Wilbur Sloane asked me at the Altar Guild whether it was the same dress or whether I just liked the color. *Liked* the color! I thought, well, at least when it's done, it's done. At least we'll own something. At least there's one thing in this world that isn't owed to somebody."

"Now, Myrt—"

"And you've gone and given it to Charley Gartside."

"I have not given it to anybody! It's an *investment*. Don't you understand the first thing about money? You don't let capital lie idle. That's the whole principle of modern business. Why, a house that's paid off is just—it's just dead money, that's all it is. Every economist in the country'll tell you that. I read an article just last month in *Prosperity Magazine*—fellow that wrote it's a professor out at Northwestern or one of those places—and he said the American who sits on his equity is a—is a—well, I forget just what he said he was, but it wasn't anything good. The modern man puts his dollars to *work*."

"Then let him put his own dollars to work. That was half my dollars."

Howard sat up. The Morris chair, which had a mechanism for reclining, chose that moment to recline, and he went backward with a lurch that destroyed whatever effect of injured majesty he had been preparing. He righted himself, red to the ears.

"*Your* dollars! Well, I like that! I'd like to know who earned 'em. I'd like to know who's been down at that salesroom six days a week since nineteen-eleven, rain or shine, taking guff off every hayseed farmer in Wabasso County that wants to trade in a spavined horse on a new Overland, so's you could sit home and—and—"

He stopped. He was aware, even in the generous heat of his indignation, that he had walked into a room from which there was no good exit. Myrtle had grown very quiet, and when Myrtle grew quiet it was in the manner of a prairie sky before a hailstorm, a stillness so complete that the meadowlarks give up singing.

"And what, Howard?" she said. "So I could sit home and what?"

"Well, I didn't mean—"

"So I could sit home and put up three hundred quarts of tomatoes every August, because you said store-bought were a waste of money? So I could sit home and entertain the Kiwanis wives every time you were trying to sell old Gruenwald a tractor? So I could sit home and listen to Charley Gartside call me 'little lady' at your Fourth of July party and pinch my arm when he thought you weren't looking?"

"He what?"

"Oh, never mind. It doesn't matter."

"It does too matter! If Charley Gartside ever laid a hand on—"

"Howard, he's your business partner now. You've given him the house. You can't very well knock him down too."

There was a silence. The radiator knocked again, as though it had been waiting its turn and had concluded that no one else was going to.

Howard rose and walked to the window. He stood there with his hands in his trouser pockets, jingling his keys, and looked out at Elmhurst Avenue: at the even row of elms, planted in 1902 by the Ladies' Civic Improvement League; at the cement sidewalk that he had personally petitioned the City Council to lay, at a cost of fourteen dollars and sixty cents per frontage foot; at the square houses with their square porches and their square lawns, each lawn with its own wooden sign in the corner reading *Keep Off*. It was a fine street. It was as fine a street as any in the State of Minnesota. He had told a great many people so. And yet, standing there, he was visited by an emotion he could not name and had no wish to: a little cold breath, as if somewhere, far off, a door had been left open in a house he had believed to be locked.

He did not like the feeling. He set about dispelling it in the manner of his kind, which was by making a speech.

"Myrtle," he said, turning, "I want you to look at this thing in a big way. A *big* way. Now you take a man like J. Wilbur Sloane. Where'd J. Wilbur be today if he'd sat on his equity? You take Henry Ford. You take Mr. Rockefeller. Every one of those men took a chance. Every one of 'em put it all on the line, one time or another, and the other fellows laughed at 'em, and who's laughing now? That's the spirit that built this country, Myrt. That's what made America the greatest nation on the face of God's green earth. Vision. Faith. Get-up-and-go. And I'll be doggoned if I'm going to be the kind of a man that sits back in his rocker and lets the parade go by. No sir. Not Howard T. Duckworth."

He was rather pleased with this. He had delivered substantially the same address, with the substitution of "Kiwanians" for "Myrt," at the June luncheon, and it had been well received; Doc Hapgood had pounded the table and called out "Atta boy, Howard!" and the minutes had recorded it as "a peppy talk." He waited now for something analogous.

Myrtle looked at him for a long moment. Then she looked down at the bank's letter in her lap.

"Do you know what I wanted to be?" she said. "Before?"

"Before what?"

"Before I married you. Do you know what I wanted to be?"

He did not know. It had not, in nineteen years, occurred to him that she had wanted to be anything; it would have seemed to him rather like asking what the furnace had wanted to be before it was installed. He said, cautiously, "Well, you were clerking for your dad."

"I wanted to teach elocution. At the Normal, in Mankato. Miss Ingersoll said I had a gift. She said I had the best speaking voice she'd heard in eleven years, and she'd heard Maude Adams in St. Paul. I had a scholarship. Did you know that? A real one. Fifty dollars a term."

"Well, why in thunder didn't you—"

"Because you came into Papa's store to sell him a cream separator, and you had on a straw hat and a striped blazer, and you said Ossawa Falls was going to be the Minneapolis of the Minnetonka Valley inside ten years and you were going to be the biggest man in it. And I believed you." She smiled; it was not, precisely, an unkind smile, which made it a great deal worse. "You were so *sure*, Howard. Nobody I'd ever known was sure of anything except the price of hogs. And I thought, well, I'd rather be married to that than recite 'The Wreck of the Hesperus' to a lot of farm girls in Mankato. I thought it'd be—bigger."

"Well, by golly, it *has* been big! Look at this house! Look at that Victrola! There isn't a woman on this street that's got a better—"

"I know. I know it has. I'm not complaining, Howard. Really I'm not." She folded the letter, and put it back in its envelope, and laid it on the library table beside the wax fruit. "I'm only saying that I gave up one thing to have this, and now you've gone and given *this* to Charley Gartside, and you didn't even ask me. You signed my name. That's what it is, isn't it? That's what 'executed instruments' means. You signed my name, or you got me to sign something I didn't read, one of those nights you brought papers home and said 'just a little insurance thing, Myrt, put your John Hancock right there.' And I did. Because I always do."

Howard opened his mouth. He found, to his considerable surprise, that he had nothing to put into it. The speeches were all there, ranked and ready—Vision and Faith and the Spirit of America and the Ground Floor—but they appeared, at that moment, to belong to someone else, someone in a striped blazer whom he had once known slightly and had lost track of.

"It'll come out all right," he said at last. His voice was smaller than he had intended. "Honest it will, Myrt. Charley says—"

"I know what Charley says."

"The bridge'll go through. Senator Hogaboom as good as promised."

"I'm sure he did."

"And when it does, why—why, I'll buy you that dining set. The walnut one, at Bjornstad's, with the sideboard. And we'll go to California. Pasadena. How'd you like that? Sit in the sun all winter like the Sloanes. I'll—I'll pay off the paper in a year, eighteen months at the outside, and we'll be sitting pretty. You'll see."

She stood up. She came over to him at the window, and for an instant he thought—he hoped, with a boy's sudden helpless hope—that she would put her arms around him. Instead she reached up and straightened his necktie, which had worked itself askew during the passage with the Morris chair, and patted it flat against his shirtfront, as she had done every morning for nineteen years before he went down to the salesroom.

"Yes, Howard," she said. "I expect I'll see."

She went upstairs. He heard her steps on the stair, and on the landing, and in the hall; he heard the bathroom door, and the water running, and the familiar small clatter of her hairpins dropping one by one into the china dish on the washstand.

He stood a while longer at the window. Then he went back to the Morris chair, and sat down, and took up the *Clarion-Herald*, and found his place in the editorial. "WHY NOT A GREATER OSSAWA?" it demanded, and went on to explain that the obstacles to greatness were three: lack of civic spirit, failure of nerve, and the corrosive influence of the Knocker. Howard read it through twice, moving his lips slightly. By the second reading he had begun to feel a good deal better. It was, he reflected, a mighty sound piece of writing; that fellow Bostwick down at the paper had a real head on his shoulders; and Myrtle—well, Myrtle was a fine little woman, the finest in the world, but women didn't understand these things, they couldn't be expected to, it wasn't their fault, it was just the way they were made. She'd come around. They always came around. When the bridge went through she'd be the first one to say, "Howard, I don't know how you ever had the vision."

At half-past ten he wound the clock on the mantel, put out the cat, examined the lock on the front door, examined it again, turned off the bronze lamp, and climbed the stairs, humming "Smile, Smile, Smile" in a baritone that he believed was not bad at all.

Myrtle was in bed, her face turned toward the wall. He said "'Night, Myrt," and she said "Good night, Howard," in her ordinary voice, and he was reassured. He was asleep inside of ten minutes, and he snored, as he always did, with the regularity and self-confidence of a well-tuned four-cylinder engine.

It was a Thursday in June, and the city of Prosper, Nebraska, which in the literature of its Chamber of Commerce was known as "The Prairie Pittsburgh" and also, somewhat inconsistently, as "The Garden Spot of the Platte," lay sweating under a sky of bleached denim. On the platform of the Union Depot, a structure of yellow brick and municipal ambition which had cost two hundred and eleven thousand dollars and was referred to by every citizen as "our two-hundred-thousand-dollar depot," stood Mr. Harlan T. Pettibone, waiting for his cousin.

Mr. Pettibone was forty-seven. He was pink, he was firm in the jowl and softer below it, and he was the exclusive dealer for the Monitor Six motor car in Prosper and the eleven counties adjacent. He wore a suit of gray worsted, a straw hat with a band in the colors of the Brotherly Order of Bison, a gold watch-chain from which depended a Bison's tooth set in gold, and an expression of hearty readiness, the expression of a man who expects at any moment to be called upon to say a few words. He was, at the moment, thinking about his cousin Everett Lunt, whom he had not seen in twenty-two years, and he was thinking about him with a mixture of affection, curiosity, and the faint apprehension which a man of business feels toward any relative who has gone East and done something artistic.

For Everett had been an artist. That is to say, Everett had, in the year nineteen-one, departed from the farm outside Wahoo with a carpet-bag, a box of water-colors, and the announced intention of becoming a great painter, and the family had heard of him since chiefly through Christmas cards, which grew smaller and more peculiar in design as the years went on, and through a magazine cover once — a girl in a canoe — which Aunt Lettie had cut out and framed and hung in the front parlor between the Rock of Ages and the enlarged crayon portrait of Grandpa Lunt in his G.A.R. uniform.

"Course, Ev was always kind of a dreamer," Harlan had explained that morning to his wife, Myrtle, over the waffles. "But he's done mighty well for himself, I guess. Illustrating and that. They pay big money for that stuff back East. Big money. Why, a fellow told me — fellow from Omaha, in the advertising game — told me some of those fellows that draw pictures for the magazines pull down fifteen, twenty thousand a year. Think of that! Just for drawing pictures!"

"Well, I hope he isn't one of those Bohemians," said Myrtle, who had read about Bohemians in a Sunday supplement and believed them to subsist on absinthe and divorces.

"Bohemian nothing! He's a Lunt, isn't he? He's my own cousin!"

But now, on the platform, watching the Overland Limited heave in from the east with its brass-and-soot dignity, Harlan felt the apprehension rise. He hoped Ev wouldn't have a beard. He hoped Ev wouldn't wear one of those floppy ties. He hoped, above all, that Ev wouldn't say anything to the boys at the Bison Club that would make them look at each other.

The train stopped. Porters descended with the little steps. A fat drummer in a checked suit got off, then a woman with three children and a canary, then two young men in the bell-bottomed trousers that were beginning to be seen even in Prosper, and then, last, an elderly-looking person in a suit of brown tweed, rather baggy at the knees, carrying a cracked leather valise and a walking stick, who stood for a moment blinking at the yellow brick as though he had never before beheld a depot.

Harlan's heart did a curious thing. It was Ev; it was unmistakably Ev, for there was the long Lunt nose and the jaw that Grandpa had in the crayon portrait; but Ev was gray. Ev was thin. Ev had a little gray mustache clipped close like an Englishman's, and the skin about his eyes was crinkled and brown, and he looked, Harlan thought with a shock that he concealed instantly beneath a roar, at least ten years older than a man of forty-five had any business looking.

"Well, well, WELL!" Harlan bellowed, plowing down the platform with his hand outstretched like a man boarding a streetcar. "If it isn't the old son-of-a-gun himself! Ev Lunt! Ev, you old horse-thief! Say, you're looking great! Great! How the dickens are you?"

"Hello, Harlan," said Everett, and he smiled, and there was something in the smile, something shy and boyish, which made the twenty-two years shrink briefly to nothing. Then his hand was seized and pumped, and his shoulder was slapped, and his valise was snatched away, and he was being propelled toward the street by a force as irresistible and well-meaning as a Rotary luncheon.

"Got the car right outside," Harlan was saying. "Brand-new Monitor Six, the Sport Phaeton model, just came in from the factory Tuesday. Hundred and sixteen-inch wheelbase. Balloon tires. Four-wheel brakes — say, there's a feature for you! The old Monitor people sure are on their toes. Well, sir, you'll see. You'll see a lot of changes in Prosper, Ev. A whale of a lot of changes. Why, the last time you were through here — when was that? Nineteen-three? — this town didn't have but nineteen thousand population. Know what we've got now? Eighty-one thousand, three hundred and forty, by the last census, and that was three years ago, and conservative estimates put us well over ninety thousand today. Conservative estimates! Think of that!"

"That's very — remarkable," said Everett.

"Remarkable? It's the fastest-growing city of its size between Chicago and Denver, that's what it is! And I'm not saying that because I live here. Those are facts. You can look 'em up."

The Monitor Six stood at the curb, scarlet and nickeled, its top folded back, gleaming in the sun like a fire engine in a Fourth of July parade. Harlan regarded it with the tender pride of a father at a christening. He put the valise in the tonneau, held open the door for his cousin, went around and climbed in, and pressed the self-starter with a little flourish, as though he were bestowing the motor upon the world.

They drove up Platte Avenue. Harlan pointed out, with the zeal of a guide in Rome, the new Farmers' and Mechanics' National Bank Building, eleven stories, "tallest in the state outside Omaha, and they're only ahead of us by two stories, and there's talk of us putting up a fourteen-story job on the corner of Fifth and Douglas"; the Orpheum Theatre, "seats sixteen hundred, and they get the very same acts as Kansas City"; the Hotel Cornhusker, "running water in every room, and a ballroom finished in genuine Circassian walnut"; the Bison Temple, "cost us better than three hundred thousand, and every cent raised by popular subscription"; and the plate-glass establishment of Pettibone Motor Sales Company, Inc., before which he slowed reverently to five miles an hour.

"There she is," he said. "Started with one little shed and a secondhand Ford in nineteen-ten. Now we got twenty-two employees and a service department second to none. I'm not bragging, Ev. I'm just giving you the facts. But I tell you, a fellow can't help feeling kind of proud."

Everett looked at the showroom, at the three scarlet Monitors poised on the polished floor like tigers in a zoo, at the sign which said in gold letters "PETTIBONE — WHERE YOUR DOLLAR DRIVES FARTHER," and something flickered across his face, which might have been amusement and might have been envy and might have been merely the glare.

"It's a fine place, Harlan," he said. "You've done well. I'm glad."

And Harlan, who had been prepared for condescension, who had braced himself against some Eastern smartness about Main Street and Babbittry and the Booboisie, which he had heard was the fashion among the high-brows, was so disarmed by the plain words that he could think of nothing to say for a whole block, which was for Harlan T. Pettibone a silence of almost geological duration.

The Pettibone residence stood in Maple Crest, Prosper's newest and most exclusive residential section, which had been a cornfield in nineteen-sixteen and was now laid out in curving streets named Fairview Drive and Bon Air Lane and Kenilworth Circle, after the manner of all newest and most exclusive residential sections from Bangor to San Diego. It was a Dutch Colonial house with green shutters and a sun-parlor, and it contained a living-room with a fireplace which had never had a fire in it, a mahogany Victrola, a radio cabinet with seven tubes on which Harlan had once received Havana, Cuba, at two in the morning, a set of the Book of Knowledge, a set of the World's Best Literature in half-morocco, uncut, a floor lamp with a parchment shade depicting a Spanish galleon, a davenport, two overstuffed chairs, and a framed motto above the telephone stand reading "Smile, Darn You, Smile!"

Myrtle Pettibone received the visitor in the hall. She was a plump, kindly, anxious woman with a permanent wave and a voice which went up at the ends of sentences, and she had spent the morning in preparing a dinner of fried chicken, mashed potatoes, creamed corn, hot biscuits, three kinds of jelly, a molded salad of lime gelatin containing walnuts, celery, and maraschino cherries, and an angel food cake, and in hiding the copy of True Romances from the living-room table.

"We're just so glad to have you, Mr. Lunt — Everett — I may call you Everett, mayn't I? — seeing as we're family?" she said. "Harlan's talked about nothing else all week? Have you had a nice trip? Isn't it dreadful, the heat?"

Everett said that he was very glad to be there, that the trip had been quite pleasant, that it was indeed dreadful, the heat, and that she must call him Ev, as everyone in the family always had. Myrtle went pink with pleasure and fled to the kitchen, from which there presently arose the sound of a percolator and of a hired girl named Hulda being exhorted.

And after dinner, when Ev had praised the chicken with a sincerity that made Myrtle glow for a week, and when the children — Harlan Junior, sixteen, who was mad about radio and spoke a dialect consisting chiefly of "kilocycles" and "the bunk," and Gladys, fourteen, who wanted to be a movie actress and regarded her Eastern cousin with frank disappointment because he did not resemble John Barrymore — had been excused, the two men went out to the screened porch with cigars.

The cigars were Harlan's. They were El Supremos, at fifteen cents straight, and he offered them with a gesture which implied that they were the very same cigars smoked by Calvin Coolidge, Henry Ford, and the Prince of Wales. They sat in wicker chairs, and the evening came down blue and tender over Maple Crest, and the sprinklers whispered on the lawns of Fairview Drive, and somewhere a phonograph was playing "Yes, Sir, That's My Baby," and Harlan, tilting back and putting his feet on the rail, felt the large and expansive contentment of a man who has eaten well in his own house.

"Well, Ev," he said, "tell me all about yourself. I want to hear the whole works. How's the art game?"

Everett looked at the end of his cigar. "Oh, it goes along," he said.

"Still doing those magazine covers? Aunt Lettie's still got that one with the girl in the canoe. Says it's the prettiest picture she ever saw. Hangs right next to Grandpa."

"Does she?" Everett laughed — a short laugh, without much breath behind it. "That was in nineteen-twelve, Harlan. I haven't done a cover in — oh, eight or nine years now."

"That so? Went into something bigger, I suppose? Portrait painting? I hear there's big money in portraits. Fellow in Omaha had his wife done in oil, cost him twelve hundred dollars."

"No. Not portraits." Everett was silent a moment. Then, as though he had decided something, he said, rather quickly, "I teach, Harlan. Drawing. At a sort of school — a commercial art school, in Brooklyn. Teaching young fellows how to draw corsets and tooth-paste for the advertisements. Tuesdays and Thursdays and Saturday mornings. And I paint, on the side. For myself."

"Oh," said Harlan. He was not quite sure what response was called for, and he fell back upon the universal formula of the Bison Club. "Well, say, that's fine! That's a fine profession, teaching. Molding the youth of the nation, and so on. Mighty fine."

"It pays forty-two dollars a week," said Everett.

There was a pause. In that pause Harlan T. Pettibone, who sold eleven hundred motor cars a year and who had once spoken for twelve minutes on "Service: the Keynote of Modern Business" before the state convention of the Brotherly Order of Bison, found that he had absolutely nothing to say. Forty-two dollars a week! Why, his own head mechanic, Gus Stoltenberg, a Swede who could hardly write his name, drew forty-five! And here was Ev, who had gone away with all that talent, with all the family's hopes, Ev who had been going to be a great painter and show 'em all —

"Why, Ev," he said at last, and his voice was oddly gentle, "why, gosh, old man, I didn't — Say, if you ever need — I mean, if things ever get kind of — you know you can always —"

"I know, Harlan. Thank you. It's quite all right. I manage. I have a room on Columbia Heights with a north light, and I can see the harbor from it, and the ships go out in the morning with the sun on them, and I paint them. I paint them very badly, mostly. But once in a long while I paint one that's not so bad, and then I'm happier than you'd believe." He smiled again, that shy smile. "I sold one last spring. To a dentist from Philadelphia. Sixty dollars."

Harlan stared at him in the dusk. He was trying to comprehend it. He was trying to comprehend a man who could be happy at forty-two dollars a week and a room with a north light, a man who did not own an automobile nor a radio nor a membership in anything, who was going gray in a boarding house in Brooklyn painting ships, and who said, apparently meaning it, that he was happier than you'd believe. It was as though Ev had confessed to being a Mohammedan. And yet, under the bewilderment, Harlan felt something else stir, something he could not have named, a faint ache like an old football knee before rain.

"Well," he said heartily, "everybody to his own taste, as the old lady said when she kissed the cow!" And he laughed very loudly, and Ev laughed politely, and the phonograph down the street began "Barney Google."

They talked then of the family, which was safe. Of Aunt Lettie, who was eighty-one and still put up forty quarts of piccalilli every fall. Of Cousin Fred, who had gone into the hardware business in Hastings and failed, and then into insurance and succeeded, and had become a Methodist and a Mason and a power in the Hastings Kiwanis. Of Uncle Wendell, who had been, it was whispered, a free-thinker and a Populist, and had died reading Ingersoll. Of the old farm outside Wahoo, which had been sold in nineteen-eighteen when wheat was two dollars and twenty cents, and which was now owned by a Bohemian family — "real Bohemians, Ev, I mean, from Bohemia, not your kind" — who had put up a silo.

"The willows," said Everett suddenly. "Are the willows still there? Down on Sand Creek, below the pasture?"

"Willows? Why, I don't know, Ev. I haven't been out there in — well, quite a spell. I guess so. Why?"

"Do you remember the swimming hole? Below the willows, where the creek bent around? You and I used to sneak off there in July, when we were supposed to be shocking oats. Do you remember the time you dared me to swing out on the grapevine and drop in, and the vine broke, and I came down in the mud on the far bank up to my waist, and you laughed so hard you fell in yourself?"

Harlan was silent. His cigar had gone out. And for a moment, sitting there on the screened porch of the Dutch Colonial house in Maple Crest, with the Monitor Six in the garage and the Bison tooth on his watch-chain, he was not Harlan T. Pettibone, Exclusive Dealer, at all. He was a skinny, freckled, barefoot boy of twelve named Harley, lying on his back in the warm grass under the willows, with the sun coming down through the leaves in coins of gold, and the creek talking to itself over the stones, and the cicadas going like little sawmills, and nobody in the whole world expecting him to say a few words or to make his quota or to put over the Community Chest drive; and beside him, chewing a grass stem, his cousin Ev, who was going to be a great painter some day, and who was saying, very seriously, "Harley, when I'm famous I'm going to come back and paint this. Just exactly this. So it'll never go away."

"Yes," said Harlan, rather hoarsely. "Yes, I remember, Ev."

"I never did paint it," said Everett. "I tried, a dozen times. It never came out right."

Neither of them spoke for a while. The sprinklers whispered. A Monitor Six — not Harlan's — went by on Fairview Drive with its cut-out open, and a girl in it shrieked with laughter. And Harlan felt the ache in him grow until it was nearly unbearable, and he wanted to say something, he did not know what — that he too had been going to do something once, though he could no longer remember what it was; that the eleven hundred cars a year and the Bison Temple and the ninety thousand by conservative estimate were all very fine, but that sometimes, lying awake at three in the morning beside Myrtle, he wondered what they were for; that he would have given a good deal, a very good deal, to lie under those willows again for one afternoon with nobody wanting anything.

He did not say it. He had not the words, and if he had had them he would have been ashamed. A man in his position. A man who had addressed the state convention.

Instead he relit his cigar, and cleared his throat, and swung his feet down off the rail.

"Say, Ev," he said, "tomorrow noon I want you to come down to the Bison Club with me. Luncheon. We got a speaker coming — fellow from the National Association of Credit Men, going to talk on 'Pep, Push, and Prosperity.' Darn good speaker, they say. And I want the boys to meet you. Want 'em to meet my cousin the artist, from New York. Why, they'll eat it up! And afterwards I'll run you out to the country club and show you the new eighteen holes. Cost us better than ninety thousand, but believe me, there's not a finer course in the Middle West."

"That would be very nice, Harlan," said Everett.

"And, say — you'll tell 'em you're an artist, of course. An illustrator. A New York illustrator." Harlan hesitated. "No need to go into the — the teaching business, and that. Not that there's anything wrong with it. But you know how folks are."

Everett looked at him in the dusk for a long moment. Then he smiled, and the smile was kind, and a little tired, and very old.

"I know how folks are, Harley," he said.

Harlan started at the name. Nobody had called him Harley in thirty years. Then he laughed, loudly, and slapped his cousin on the knee, and said, "Well, it's getting late, and I guess you're pretty well tuckered out after that trip. Myrtle's fixed up the guest room. Got a new Simmons mattress in there — genuine coil springs. You'll sleep like a top."

He stood, and held open the screen door, and the light from the living-room fell across the porch, across the wicker chairs and the floor lamp with its Spanish galleon and the motto that said "Smile, Darn You, Smile!"; and the two men went in, talking of the weather, and of the price of wheat, and of whether Coolidge would run again, and of the fine new course at the country club, which had cost better than ninety thousand dollars.

But that night, long after the house was dark, Harlan T. Pettibone lay awake on his own Simmons mattress beside his gently snoring wife, staring at the ceiling, and listening, through the open window, past the whisper of the sprinklers and the far hoot of a freight on the Burlington, for something that he could not hear — the sound, perhaps, of a creek talking to itself over the stones, a long way off, below the willows, where two boys lay in the grass and were going to be great men.

The house of Homer Q. Gaddis stood on Ridgemere Drive, in the section of Elkhorn Falls which the Elkhorn Falls Realty & Development Corporation had for six years been advertising as "Restful, Restricted, and Refined." It was a Dutch Colonial house, which is to say that it was neither Dutch nor Colonial but was painted a sober cream and had a gambrel roof, two green shutters for every window, and a brass knocker in the shape of a lion's head which no one ever used, since there was also an electric bell. It had a sun-parlor with wicker furniture and a canary, a breakfast nook with a built-in bench upon which no one could sit comfortably for more than eleven minutes, a cedar closet, a laundry chute, and a basement furnished with a Torrid Twin-Draft Furnace which Homer Gaddis regarded with something of the pride with which a medieval baron regarded his keep.

It was, in all its particulars, precisely like the houses on either side of it, and Homer Gaddis knew this, and was content, for he believed that a man who wished his house to be different from his neighbors' was probably a Socialist, or at the very least a fellow who wrote poetry and did not pay his bills.

At a quarter past six on a Saturday evening in October, Homer Gaddis drove his sedan into the two-car garage, shut off the motor with the finality of a judge pronouncing sentence, and sat for a moment with his hands upon the wheel. He was forty-four. He was the proprietor of the Gaddis Office Appliance Company, sole agents in four counties for the Ever-Ready Rotary Duplicator and the Phalanx Steel Filing Cabinet ("A Phalanx Never Falls Down on the Job!"). He was a Kiwanian, an Elk, a deacon of the Wesley Avenue Methodist Church, and a member of the Tamarack Country Club, where he had that afternoon shot a ninety-seven and had been informed, between the fourteenth and fifteenth holes, of the most mortifying thing that had happened to him since 1911.

He sat in the garage and breathed heavily through his nose.

The informant had been Chet Applegate, of Applegate's Quality Footwear, a man of large and cheerful malice, who had approached him with the expression of a dog that has found something dead and wishes to share it.

"Say, Homer, old socks," Chet had said, "I hear your kid's turning into a regular little orator. Regular William Jennings Bryan. Yes sir, they tell me he gave Mrs. T. Lucius Beane a speech at the Ladies' Aid bazaar yesterday she won't forget in a hurry."

Homer had laughed, the large, comfortable, manly laugh of a father who supposes that his son has said something cute about Santa Claus. He had not continued laughing. For it developed, as Chet Applegate unwound the tale with the loving deliberation of a man reeling in a pike, that Homer's son Clifford, aged seven years and four months, had approached Mrs. T. Lucius Beane at the fancy-work booth, had studied her for some time with the grave candor of the very young, and had then informed her, in a clear and carrying voice, that his papa said Mr. Beane was a tight-fisted old pickerel who would foreclose on his own grandmother and who only came to church to count the house.

Mr. T. Lucius Beane was president of the Second National Bank of Elkhorn Falls.

Mr. T. Lucius Beane was the man to whom Homer Gaddis had, nine days ago, applied for a loan of eighteen thousand dollars with which to open a branch office in the thriving city of Pawnee Center.

It is true that Homer had said it. He had said it at dinner, on the evening when the loan committee had asked him for a second statement of assets, and he had said it with relish, between bites of pot roast, while his wife Ione murmured, "Now Homer, not in front of the children." He had not supposed that the children were listening. In twelve years of fatherhood he had never quite grasped that children were always listening, and that they listened most carefully precisely when they appeared to be building a fort out of mashed potatoes.

He got out of the car. He slammed the door, which was not necessary, and went in through the kitchen, which was.

Ione was at the stove. She was a plump, pleasant woman with a permanent wave of terrible regularity, and she had learned in fifteen years of marriage to read her husband's moods by the manner in which he hung up his hat. He hung it up now as though he were hanging a horse thief.

"Well," she said brightly, "how was the golf?"

"Golf," said Homer, "was rotten. Where is that boy?"

"Clifford? Why, he's up in his room, I think, playing with his Meccano set. Homer, what on earth—"

"I'll tell you what on earth. I'll tell you what on earth, and then you can tell me how a youngster brought up in a decent Christian home, with every advantage, with a father that's worked his fingers to the bone to give him everything a kid could want, with an Indian suit and a velocipede and a set of the Boy's Own Encyclopedia in eight volumes, bound in genuine imitation leather—how a kid like that comes to go around town shooting off his mouth like a—like a common I.W.W."

He told her. She listened with her mixing spoon held aloft, and when he had finished she said, "Oh, dear," and then, after reflection, "Well, you did say it, Homer."

This was not the support he required. He looked at her with the injured dignity of a senator who has been asked, in public, what he did with the money.

"That," he said, "has nothing whatsoever to do with it. What a man says in the privacy of his own home, to his own wife, in confidence, is one thing. It's his privilege. It's practically in the Constitution. What a kid goes and blabs to the wife of the biggest banker in town, at a church function, mind you, at a church function, with Chet Applegate's wife standing right there with her ears flapping, is something else again. It's a question of—of loyalty. Of discretion. Of knowing what's what. And that boy has got to learn it, and he's got to learn it now, before he grows up and goes around telling the whole world his old man's business. I'm going up there."

"Homer, don't you be too hard on him. He's only seven."

"Seven! When I was seven I was carrying papers, by golly, and I knew enough to keep my trap shut. Seven! Why, Lindbergh probably—" He could not immediately recall what Lindbergh had done at the age of seven, and so he left the sentence in the air, where it hung impressively, and climbed the stairs.

He climbed them slowly, and as he climbed, his indignation began to arrange itself, as his indignations always did, into a speech. Homer Gaddis was a celebrated speaker. He had addressed the Kiwanis Club on "The Office of Tomorrow," the Chamber of Commerce on "Pep, Punch, and Profits," and the Wesley Avenue Men's Bible Class on "Was Jesus a Go-Getter?" (He had concluded, after an analysis of the parable of the talents, that He was.) He had never been at a loss for words in his life, and he did not intend to be at a loss now before an audience of one, three feet nine inches high.

The door of Clifford's room bore a sign, lettered in red crayon on a piece of shirt cardboard, which read, KEEP OUT THIS MEANS YOU PRIVIT. Homer regarded the misspelling with a fresh pang, as further evidence of a general collapse of standards, and opened the door without knocking.

Clifford was sitting on the floor in the midst of a construction of Meccano strips and brass bolts which was either a crane or a suspension bridge or a very nervous giraffe. He was a thin child, with his mother's round face and his father's large ears, and he had a smear of machine oil across his forehead like the mark of some obscure religious order. He looked up. He saw his father's face. He put down his screwdriver with the slow care of a man who senses that the next few minutes may be the last in which he will be permitted to hold a screwdriver.

"Hello, Papa."

"Don't you 'hello Papa' me, young man."

Clifford considered this. It seemed to leave him no further conversational avenue, so he said nothing at all.

Homer shut the door. He looked about the room for a place of judgment. There was the bed, covered with a counterpane on which a number of cowboys pursued a number of Indians around and around in eternal and inconclusive warfare. There was the little desk, with its inkwell that had never held ink. There was a chair, a small painted chair, designed for a child, and Homer, after a moment's hesitation, lowered himself onto it, so that he sat with his knees nearly at his chin and his stomach advanced before him like the prow of a ship. It was not a magisterial posture. He was aware of this and resented it, and the resentment went, unjustly, into his voice.

"Clifford," he said, "do you know what I heard today? At the club? From Mr. Applegate?"

Clifford's eyes grew large and round and wholly without guile. He did not know. He had, in the past twenty-four hours, committed several acts which might conceivably have reached the ears of Mr. Applegate: he had thrown a crab apple at the Wiggins' cat; he had told Dorothy Pruett that if she swallowed a watermelon seed a watermelon would grow out of her ears; he had, in a spirit of pure scientific inquiry, put a June bug in the mailbox of old Mrs. Fetterman. He weighed these possibilities and decided that the most prudent course was to await further particulars.

"No, Papa."

"I heard," said Homer, and his voice rose to the pitch with which he customarily announced the winners of the Kiwanis attendance contest, "that you went up to Mrs. T. Lucius Beane, at the bazaar, in front of everybody, and said—said certain things about Mr. Beane. Now, did you or did you not say those things?"

A great light dawned in Clifford's face. It was the light of relief. This was not about the June bug at all.

"Oh, that," he said. "I just told her what you said, Papa. About Mr. Beane being a pickerel. Is a pickerel a fish? I thought it was a fish, but Ronnie Pruett said it was a kind of a pickle, and I said it was a fish, and we had a fight about it, and—"

"Never mind about the pickerel!"

"But is it a fish, Papa?"

"Yes, it is a fish, and that's not the point! The point is, young man, that you said things—things about a gentleman—to his wife—things you had absolutely no business to say."

"But you said them," said Clifford reasonably. "At supper. You said he'd foreclose on his own grandmother. Does Mr. Beane have a grandmother? He's awful old. I didn't think people that old had grandmothers."

Homer Gaddis drew a deep breath. He had been prepared for defiance; he had been prepared for tears; he had a speech ready for either. He had not been prepared for logic, which he had always regarded as a weapon suitable only for lawyers and college professors, and he felt himself, for an instant, as a man feels who reaches for the next stair in the dark and finds that it is not there.

He recovered. He was, after all, a businessman, and a businessman who could not change his line of argument in mid-sentence would never have sold four hundred Phalanx Steel Filing Cabinets to the County of Muskrat in a single fiscal year.

"Now see here, Clifford. You listen to me. There's a difference—there's all the difference in the world—between what a man says in his own home, in confidence, among his own family, and what he says out in public. You understand? A man's home is his castle. Did you ever hear that? A man's home is his castle. And what's said in a man's castle stays in his castle. That's what you call discretion. That's what you call loyalty. Now, you wouldn't want to be disloyal to your own father, would you?"

"No, Papa." Clifford considered his father's castle, and the Wiggins' cat, and the nature of loyalty, and then he asked, with the terrible innocence of the age of seven, "But was it true?"

"Was what true?"

"About Mr. Beane. About him being a pickerel and counting the house. If it's true, then why can't I say it? Miss Hodgkins at Sunday school said we should always tell the truth and shame the devil. She said it was in the Bible. Is it in the Bible, Papa?"

Homer had been a deacon for nine years. He had passed the collection plate on some four hundred and sixty Sunday mornings, and on each of those mornings he had heard the truth commended in the warmest possible terms by the Reverend Dr. Ormsby Platt, who was himself a sound man and a member of the Rotary Club and who believed that truth was the foundation of all good business. Homer believed it too. He would have said so at any luncheon in the state. But he had never, until this moment, considered the possibility that the truth might be something a person actually went around telling.

"Now that," he said, "that is—well, it's different. It's a whole different proposition. The Bible—certainly the Bible says to tell the truth, and you should always tell the truth, Clifford, I don't want you ever to tell a lie, see? Never. A lie is the worst thing a fellow can do, practically. But there's such a thing as—as tact. There's such a thing as using your bean. A fellow doesn't have to go around blurting out every blessed thing that comes into his head. Suppose—now look here—suppose Mrs. Beane told Mr. Beane, and Mr. Beane got sore. Suppose Mr. Beane decided not to lend Papa some money that Papa needs for his business. Then where'd we be? Then maybe Papa couldn't buy you that electric train you've been hollering about for Christmas. You see? You see how it all ties in? Everything ties in, Clifford. That's the way the world is. You can't just go shooting off your mouth."

Clifford's lower lip, at the mention of the electric train, had begun almost imperceptibly to tremble. He was beginning to understand that he had done something enormous, though he could not have said precisely what. It seemed to him that he had been punished for telling the truth and would also be punished for telling a lie, and that the only safe course in this world was to say nothing at all to anybody, which was precisely the lesson his father was attempting, with great labor and sincerity, to teach him.

"I'm sorry, Papa," he said, very small.

Homer looked at his son. He saw the oil smear on the forehead, the big ears that were his own ears, the thin wrists sticking out of the sleeves of a sailor blouse that Ione had bought at Dorfman's Department Store during the August white sale. And for a moment—it was only a moment, and he would have been embarrassed to admit it afterward to anyone at the Elks—he felt something stir in him that was not indignation, nor anxiety about the eighteen thousand dollars, nor anything that could have been entered in a ledger. He remembered, without wishing to, a day long ago in the village of Hartsburg, Ohio, when he himself had been seven years old and had told the minister's wife that her new hat looked like a dead chicken, which it had; and he remembered his own father, a silent, rawboned harness-maker, taking him out to the woodshed, and the smell of the woodshed, and the sound of the strap, and how afterward he had lain in the hayloft and looked through a crack at the sky and resolved, with the fierce clarity of childhood, that when he grew up he would never, never tell anybody anything he really thought.

He had kept that resolution admirably. He had become, by keeping it, a success.

He cleared his throat. It was necessary, he felt, to conclude the proceedings in a manner suitable to the dignity of the occasion. He did not intend to use a strap. He was a modern father; he subscribed to the Ladies' Home Journal on Ione's account and had once skimmed an article by a prominent Chicago child psychologist which stated that corporal punishment was liable to produce complexes, which Homer understood vaguely to be something like adenoids. But some penalty there must be. A man could not run a family any more than he could run a business without some system of discipline. He thought of his own sales force, and of the means by which he kept it on its toes.

"All right," he said. "All right, Clifford. Now here's what's going to happen. First off, there won't be any movies for you next Saturday. No Hoot Gibson, nothing. Second, you're going to go to bed tonight right after supper, and no reading in bed with a flashlight, either; I know all about that flashlight. And third—" he paused, and the inspiration came to him like the idea for a new advertising slogan, "—third, tomorrow, after church, you're going to go up to Mrs. Beane, polite as you please, and you're going to tell her you're sorry, and you're going to tell her you made a mistake, and that your papa never said any such thing, and that you got him mixed up with—with somebody else. You understand?"

Clifford looked at him. The round, unguarded eyes were very steady.

"But Papa, that'd be a lie."

There was a silence in the room. Outside, on Ridgemere Drive, someone was starting a car, and the self-starter whined and caught and whined again. Down in the kitchen Ione was rattling the lid of the potato kettle. On the counterpane the cowboys pursued the Indians.

Homer Gaddis opened his mouth, and then he shut it, and then he opened it again.

"Never mind," he said at last, heavily. "You just tell her you're sorry. That's all. You just say you're sorry and let it go at that. And another thing. You don't ever—you hear me?—you don't ever repeat anything you hear at the supper table. Not to anybody. Not to Ronnie Pruett nor Mrs. Beane nor Miss Hodgkins nor anybody. Is that clear?"

"Yes, Papa."

"All right, then."

He rose, with difficulty, from the little painted chair. His knees cracked. He stood for a moment looking down at the nervous Meccano giraffe, and he wished, obscurely, that he could think of something more to say, something that would set it all straight; but nothing came, and he went to the door.

"Papa?"

"What is it?"

"Is a pickerel a good fish? To eat, I mean?"

Homer considered. "Pretty bony," he said. "Pretty bony, but some folks like 'em." And he went out and closed the door upon the sign that said PRIVIT.

He did not go downstairs at once. He went instead to the sleeping porch at the back of the house, which looked out over the identical back yards of Ridgemere Drive, each with its clothesline and its garbage can and its single, dutiful elm, and he stood there in the dusk and took from his vest pocket a cigar. He had sworn off cigars, on the advice of Dr. Pfluger, the previous Tuesday. He lit it anyway and smoked it in short, irritable puffs.

He felt that he had handled the situation pretty well, on the whole. He had been firm. He had been fair. He had laid down the law, and the boy had taken it like a little man. Tomorrow Clifford would apologize, and Mrs. Beane would be mollified, and very likely T. Lucius would laugh the whole thing off over a cigar of his own; for a banker, after all, was a regular fellow at bottom, and knew that kids said the darnedest things. Very likely the loan would go through on Wednesday. Very likely there would be a branch office in Pawnee Center, with GADDIS lettered in gold leaf upon the window, and a Phalanx Steel Filing Cabinet in every courthouse from here to the Dakota line.

And yet he stood a long while on the sleeping porch, until the cigar went out and the yards below were dark, troubled by something he could not name; something that had to do with a hayloft in Hartsburg, Ohio, and a crack through which one could see the sky, and a small boy with an oil-smeared forehead who had asked him, in perfect good faith, whether a thing was true.

Then Ione called up the stairs

Here is an excerpt of Sinclair Lewis's writing, to show you their style:

The assurance of Tanis Judique’s friendship fortified Babbitt’s self-approval. At the Athletic Club he became experimental. Though Vergil Gunch was silent, the others at the Roughnecks’ Table came to accept Babbitt as having, for no visible reason, “turned crank.” They argued windily with him, and he was cocky, and enjoyed the spectacle of his interesting martyrdom. He even praised Seneca Doane. Professor Pumphrey said that was carrying a joke too far; but Babbitt argued, “No! Fact! I tell you he’s got one of the keenest intellects in the country. Why, Lord Wycombe said that—” “Oh, who the hell is Lord Wycombe? What you always lugging him in for? You been touting him for the last six weeks!” protested Orville Jones.

“George ordered him from Sears-Roebuck. You can get those English high-muckamucks by mail for two bucks apiece,” suggested Sidney Finkelstein.

“That’s all right now! Lord Wycombe, he’s one of the biggest intellects in English political life. As I was saying: Of course I’m conservative myself, but I appreciate a guy like Senny Doane because—” Vergil Gunch interrupted harshly, “I wonder if you are so conservative? I find I can manage to run my own business without any skunks and reds like Doane in it!” The grimness of Gunch’s voice, the hardness of his jaw, disconcerted Babbitt, but he recovered and went on till they looked bored, then irritated, then as doubtful as Gunch. He thought of Tanis always. With a stir he remembered her every aspect. His arms yearned for her. “I’ve found her! I’ve dreamed of her all these years and now I’ve found her!” he exulted. He met her at the movies in the morning; he drove out to her flat in the late afternoon or on evenings when he was believed to be at the Elks. He knew her financial affairs and advised her about them, while she lamented her feminine ignorance, and praised his masterfulness, and proved to know much more about bonds than he did. They had remembrances, and laughter over old times. Once they quarreled, and he raged that she was as “bossy” as his wife and far more whining when he was inattentive. But that passed safely. Their high hour was a tramp on a ringing December afternoon, through snow-drifted meadows down to the icy Chaloosa River. She was exotic in an astrachan cap and a short beaver coat; she slid on the ice and shouted, and he panted after her, rotund with laughter.... Myra Babbitt never slid on the ice. He was afraid that they would be seen together. In Zenith it is impossible to lunch with a neighbor’s wife without the fact being known, before nightfall, in every house in your circle. But Tanis was beautifully discreet. However appealingly she might turn to him when they were alone, she was gravely detached when they were abroad, and he hoped that she would be taken for a client. Orville Jones once saw them emerging from a movie theater, and Babbitt bumbled, “Let me make you ’quainted with Mrs. Judique. Now here’s a lady who knows the right broker to come to, Orvy!” Mr. Jones, though he was a man censorious of morals and of laundry machinery, seemed satisfied. His predominant fear—not from any especial fondness for her but from the habit of propriety—was that his wife would learn of the affair. He was certain that she knew nothing specific about Tanis, but he was also certain that she suspected something indefinite. For years she had been bored by anything more affectionate than a farewell kiss, yet she was hurt by any slackening in his irritable periodic interest, and now he had no interest; rather, a revulsion. He was completely faithful—to Tanis. He was distressed by the sight of his wife’s slack plumpness, by her puffs and billows of flesh, by the tattered petticoat which she was always meaning and always forgetting to throw away. But he was aware that she, so long attuned to him, caught all his repulsions. He elaborately, heavily, jocularly tried to check them. He couldn’t. They had a tolerable Christmas. Kenneth Escott was there, admittedly engaged to Verona. Mrs. Babbitt was tearful and called Kenneth her new son. Babbitt was worried about Ted, because he had ceased complaining of the State University and become suspiciously acquiescent. He wondered what the boy was planning, and was too shy to ask. Himself, Babbitt slipped away on Christmas afternoon to take his present, a silver cigarette-box, to Tanis. When he returned Mrs. Babbitt asked, much too innocently, “Did you go out for a little fresh air?”

“Yes, just lil drive,” he mumbled. After New Year’s his wife proposed, “I heard from my sister to-day, George. She isn’t well. I think perhaps I ought to go stay with her for a few weeks.” Now, Mrs. Babbitt was not accustomed to leave home during the winter except on violently demanding occasions, and only the summer before, she had been gone for weeks. Nor was Babbitt one of the detachable husbands who take separations casually. He liked to have her there; she looked after his clothes; she knew how his steak ought to be cooked; and her clucking made him feel secure. But he could not drum up even a dutiful “Oh, she doesn’t really need you, does she?” While he tried to look regretful, while he felt that his wife was watching him, he was filled with exultant visions of Tanis.

“Do you think I’d better go?” she said sharply.

“You’ve got to decide, honey; I can’t.” She turned away, sighing, and his forehead was damp. Till she went, four days later, she was curiously still, he cumbrously affectionate. Her train left at noon. As he saw it grow small beyond the train-shed he longed to hurry to Tanis.

“No, by golly, I won’t do that!” he vowed. “I won’t go near her for a week!” But he was at her flat at four. He who had once controlled or seemed to control his life in a progress unimpassioned but diligent and sane was for that fortnight borne on a current of desire and very bad whisky and all the complications of new acquaintances, those furious new intimates who demand so much more attention than old friends. Each morning he gloomily recognized his idiocies of the evening before. With his head throbbing, his tongue and lips stinging from cigarettes, he incredulously counted the number of drinks he had taken, and groaned, “I got to quit!” He had ceased saying, “I will quit!” for however resolute he might be at dawn, he could not, for a single evening, check his drift. He had met Tanis’s friends; he had, with the ardent haste of the Midnight People, who drink and dance and rattle and are ever afraid to be silent, been adopted as a member of her group, which they called “The Bunch.” He first met them after a day when he had worked particularly hard and when he hoped to be quiet with Tanis and slowly sip her admiration. From down the hall he could hear shrieks and the grind of a phonograph. As Tanis opened the door he saw fantastic figures dancing in a haze of cigarette smoke. The tables and chairs were against the wall.

“Oh, isn’t this dandy!” she gabbled at him. “Carrie Nork had the loveliest idea. She decided it was time for a party, and she ’phoned the Bunch and told ’em to gather round.... George, this is Carrie.”

“Carrie” was, in the less desirable aspects of both, at once matronly and spinsterish. She was perhaps forty; her hair was an unconvincing ash-blond; and if her chest was flat, her hips were ponderous. She greeted Babbitt with a giggling “Welcome to our little midst! Tanis says you’re a real sport.” He was apparently expected to dance, to be boyish and gay with Carrie, and he did his unforgiving best. He towed her about the room, bumping into other couples, into the radiator, into chair-legs cunningly ambushed. As he danced he surveyed the rest of the Bunch: A thin young woman who looked capable, conceited, and sarcastic. Another woman whom he could never quite remember. Three overdressed and slightly effeminate young men—soda-fountain clerks, or at least born for that profession. A man of his own age, immovable, self-satisfied, resentful of Babbitt’s presence. When he had finished his dutiful dance Tanis took him aside and begged, “Dear, wouldn’t you like to do something for me? I’m all out of booze, and the Bunch want to celebrate. Couldn’t you just skip down to Healey Hanson’s and get some?”

“Sure,” he said, trying not to sound sullen.

It was eleven minutes past ten by the Tower-Tone mantel clock, which had a chime like a Methodist bell and a guarantee like a government bond, when Harvey Kittredge discovered that his wife was not going to bed.

He had been ready for bed since half-past nine. He had yawned, elaborately and with sound effects, three times. He had wound his watch. He had stood at the front window of the living-room of their Dutch Colonial house on Linnwood Terrace, in the Sunset Ridge district of Vernondale, and announced to the street-lamp that it looked like rain to-morrow, and that if it did rain the boys down at the Chamber would have to call off the Booster Golf Tourney, and it was a crime, a regular crime, the way the weather never consulted a fellow. These were the rituals of retirement in the Kittredge household, as fixed as the order of service at the First Congregational, and Lorena Kittredge had, for nineteen years, answered them with the proper responses: "Yes, dear," and "I'll be up in a minute," and "Did you put the milk-bottles out?"

To-night she said nothing. She sat in the wing chair by the floor-lamp with the parchment shade, the floor-lamp which had cost thirty-eight dollars at Hartigan's and which Harvey liked to describe to guests as "real artistic, kind of Italian in effect," and she held in her lap a long envelope of the kind that is never good news. She did not open it. She merely held it, as a woman might hold a small animal that had died.

Harvey had seen the envelope. He had seen it the moment he came in from the Optimists' Brotherhood supper, and something in his stomach, which was a well-cared-for stomach and accustomed to only the mildest of surprises, had turned over like a sleeper in a strange hotel. He decided that he had not seen it. He was a man of decision.

"Well!" he said. He rubbed his hands together. "Well, sir! Some supper to-night, I'll tell the world.
