"He wanted to know," said Lorena, "whether I understood that the house was security on a note for eleven thousand dollars."

The Tower-Tone clock ticked. Down the street a Ford sedan, driven by young Donald Haverstick, who was home from the State University and believed that a muffler was an instrument of tyranny, went exploding by; and Harvey listened to it with an absorption he had never before shown to the passage of a Ford.

"Oh, that," he said.

"Yes, Harvey. That."

"Why, honey, that isn't anything. That's just business. That's just a—a technicality. Bert hadn't any business coming around bothering you with it. I'll speak to him about it. I'll certainly speak to him. A bank's got no call to come scaring a man's wife about technicalities. I'll tell him—"

"Did you put a mortgage on this house?"

"Now, I wouldn't call it a mortgage exactly."

"What would you call it?"

He took the cigar out of his mouth and regarded it. It had gone out. He did not relight it. He sat down, at last, on the davenport, the davenport with the cut-velvet upholstery in a shade the salesman at Hartigan's had called "Mulberry Mist," and he leaned forward with his elbows on his knees in the attitude which he had learned at a Dale Carnegie-ish course called "Personality Plus in Salesmanship" was "frank, man-to-man, and confidence-inspiring."

"Lorry," he said, "I'm going to be absolutely frank with you."

She did not seem inspired with confidence. She waited.

"You know Clyde Ostrander."

"I know Clyde Ostrander."

"Well, now, there's no call to say it like that. Clyde's one of the most go-ahead young fellows in this town. He's on the Publicity Committee of the Chamber. He's going to put Vernondale on the map, that's what he's going to do. You know that tract of land out past the fairgrounds, out along the old Mill Road? The old Schiller farm?"

"Where the cows are."

"Where the cows *were*. Where the cows are going to *not* be, about a year from now. Lorry, that's going to be Ostrander Heights. Paved streets, ornamental lamp-posts, every lot restricted—no shacks, no foreigners, nothing under six thousand dollars. Bungalows and Colonials and these here English half-timber jobs. Clyde's got the plans drawn up by an architect from Chicago. From *Chicago*, Lorry! And the Interurban's going to run a spur line out there, practically guaranteed, Clyde's got a cousin on the board, and when it does—well, you just figure it. The lots are going for eight hundred now. The day that spur's announced, they'll go for two thousand. Twenty-five hundred. You know what this town's going to be, ten years from now? Fifty thousand population. Easy. The Chamber's got the figures. And the men who get in on the ground floor—"

"How much of the ground floor did you get in on, Harvey?"

He made a small, deprecating gesture with the dead cigar. "Well—I took twelve lots."

"Twelve."

"Corner lots, a lot of 'em. Clyde gave me first pick. Because I'm in on the organization. I'm what you call a—well, he calls it a 'founding associate.' There's only five of us. Me and Clyde and Doc Herrold and Walt Bissell from the Bissell Hardware and a fella from over at Jefferson City that's got a lot of capital. It's practically a closed corporation."

"And you paid for twelve lots with this house."

"I didn't *pay* with the house. Good Lord, Lorry, you talk like I'd gone and sold it out from under you! I just put it up as security. That's all. It's done every day. Every big man in this country, he started by borrowing. Look at Henry Ford. Look at—well, look at any of 'em. You can't make money without money. That's economics. Even old Pfaff said so to-night, in a way. He said the American businessman has got to have *vision*—"

"I don't care what Judge Pfaff said."

It was the first sentence in nineteen years in which Lorena Kittredge had expressed indifference to the views of a Circuit Judge, and Harvey looked at her as though she had removed her marcel wave and revealed beneath it the head of a stranger.

"Well," he said, injured, "I'm only telling you."

"You're not telling me anything. You're making a speech. You've been making speeches since you walked in that door. You made a speech about the weather, and a speech about the folding chairs, and now you're making a speech about Henry Ford." She smoothed the envelope on her knee. Her hands, he noticed, were not quite steady, and the noticing made him angry, because he did not know what to do about it. "Harvey, when did you sign this?"

"Oh—a while back."

"When?"

"October, I guess. Along in there."

"October. And it's April." She looked at him, and her eyes, which were a pale and pleasant blue and had for nineteen years regarded him chiefly with the mild, unseeing benevolence a woman feels for a reliable furnace, were neither mild nor unseeing. "You've known for six months. You sat at that table every night for six months. You carved the turkey at Thanksgiving with my mother right there, and you'd done this. You gave me that wrist-watch at Christmas—"

"Now, the wrist-watch hasn't got a thing to do with it—"

"—and you'd done this. Why didn't you tell me?"

He rose. He felt that a man explained himself better standing up; that the vertical posture was itself a kind of argument. He walked to the radio cabinet, which was walnut veneer and had a loud-speaker concealed behind a fretwork panel representing a Spanish galleon in full sail, and he put his hand upon it as though for support.

"Because," he said, "I didn't want to worry you."

"Harvey."

"That's the truth, Lorry, so help me. A man's got a right to protect his wife from worry, hasn't he? Business is a man's affair. I never asked you to bother your head about it. I never came to you and said, 'Lorry, the Goodrich people are cutting our discount,' or, 'Lorry, there's a new fella opening a filling station out on Route Nine.' I carried that. That's what a man's for. You run the house, and you run it fine, nobody better, and I run the business. That's the way it's always been, and that's the way it ought to be. You women go to your Literary Circle and talk about—about Ibsen and so on—and that's fine, I'm all for culture, I'm a hundred percent for it, but you don't want to go filling up your head with notes and interest rates and so on. It'd only get you all upset. Like you are now."

"I'm upset," said Lorena, "because I found out from Bert Voorhees."

"Well, he had no business—"

"I'm upset because I stood in my own front hall, with my apron on, and Bert Voorhees told me something about my own house that my own husband hadn't told me, and he looked at me—Harvey, he looked at me as if he were *sorry* for me." For the first time her voice wavered. "Bert Voorhees. Whose wife wears that awful fox scarf to church in July."

There was in this a logic which Harvey could not refute, because he could not, in fact, follow it; and like most men confronted with an argument they cannot follow, he concluded that it was not an argument at all but an emotion, and that emotions, like head colds, were best treated with patience and a few kind words.

"Now, honey," he said. He came toward her. He meant to put his hand on her shoulder. He had seen it done in a photoplay at the Bijou only the week before, by Mr. Lewis Stone, with great success. "Now, honey, you're just tired. You've been working too hard on that rummage sale. You're taking this all wrong. Ten years from now we'll laugh about this. Ten years from now you'll have a fur coat—a real sealskin, not any of your Hudson seal—and we'll have a place up on the lake, and you'll say, 'Harvey, I'll never doubt you again,' and—"

She moved her shoulder. It was a small movement, but his hand found nothing.

"Is the spur line going through?"

"Huh?"

"The Interurban. The spur line. Clyde's cousin. Is it going through?"

"Well—it's practically certain. It's all but signed."

"Bert Voorhees said the Interurban board voted in February not to build any more spurs this year. He said it was in the Courier."

"That," said Harvey with dignity, "is just the *Courier*. You know what the *Courier* is. Bunch of knockers. Always running down the town. If a fella wants to build anything in this town, the *Courier*'s against it. They were against the new viaduct, too. Clyde says—"

"What does Clyde say?"

He hesitated. In that hesitation, which lasted perhaps three ticks of the Tower-Tone clock, he saw, as clearly as though it were printed in the Courier in the twelve-point type reserved for local disasters, the twelve lots lying out past the fairgrounds, with the March mud on them and the Schiller cows standing in it, regarding with ruminative contempt the four surveyor's stakes which were all that existed of Ostrander Heights. He saw Clyde Ostrander at the last meeting of the founding associates, a month ago, talking very fast and laughing very much and saying that this was only a temporary setback, boys, only a temporary setback; and he saw the fellow from Jefferson City, the fellow with the capital, who had not been at that meeting, and who had not been at the meeting before that either.

"Clyde says," said Harvey, "it's only a temporary setback."

Lorena said nothing at all.

The silence of a wife is a thing for which the American husband has never been adequately equipped. He has been trained by the luncheon clubs to meet heckling with a joke, by the lodges to meet tragedy with a resolution of sympathy suitably engrossed, by the newspapers to meet doubt with a statistic. But for silence he has no slogan. Harvey Kittredge stood in the middle of his own living-room, with its Mulberry Mist davenport and its Spanish-galleon radio and its framed reproduction of "The Song of the Lark" over the mantel, and felt himself a stranger there, like a salesman who has rung the wrong bell.

"Darn it, Lorry," he burst out, "say something!"

"What do you want me to say?"

"Well—I don't know. Bawl me out. Go on. I'd feel better if you'd bawl me out."

"I know you would," said Lorena.

He had not expected that, and he did not like it. He took a turn to the window and back. "I suppose you think I'm a fool."

"No."

"Yes, you do. You think I'm a fool. You think I'm just a—a sucker. Well, let me tell you something. Let me just tell you something. Every man that ever amounted to anything in this country, people called him a fool. They called Edison a fool. They laughed at Columbus. If I'd listened to everybody that—what are you smiling at?"

"I wasn't smiling."

"You were too smiling."

"I was thinking," she said slowly, "that you'd say Columbus. I knew you'd say Columbus. You always say Columbus. You said it when you bought the radio stock, and you said it when you were going to sell those cement burial vaults with Elmer Platt, and you said it when you put that awful gold-fish pond in the back yard that froze and cracked." She looked down at the envelope. "Nineteen years, Harvey. I could say all your speeches for you. I could stand up at the Brotherhood and make every speech you'll ever make, and nobody would know the difference."

He stared at her, and his face, which was a large, pink, trustworthy face, a face which had sold a great many tires to a great many farmers on the strength of its trustworthiness, went slowly red from the collar up.

"That," he said, "is a heck of a thing to say to a man."

"Yes," said Lorena. "I suppose it is."

For a moment it seemed that something would happen—that she would weep, or that he would shout, or that one of them would say a thing that could not afterward be pretended away. The Tower-Tone clock drew in its breath and chimed the half-hour, sweetly, like a Methodist bell. Down the block the Havestick Ford came exploding home again.

Lorena stood up. She laid the envelope, very neatly, on the walnut veneer of the radio cabinet, squared with its edge, as she laid out his clean collars in the morning.

"What are you going to do?" he said. His voice was small. He was surprised at how small it was.

"I'm going to bed. I've got the Circle to-morrow. We're doing Bernard Shaw." She went to the foot of the stairs, and turned there, one hand on the newel post, which was of golden oak and had been a source of great pride when they built the house in 1916. "You'll go see Bert Voorhees in the morning. And you'll find out exactly how much we owe and when it's due, and you'll come home at noon and tell me. All of it. With figures. And then we'll decide what to do."

"*We'll* decide—"

"We'll decide," said Lorena.

He opened his mouth to explain that business was a man's affair, that a wife's place was—but the words, which had always come so readily, so roundly, like coins from a slot machine, did not come. He shut his mouth again.

She went up the stairs. He heard her steps cross the hall, heard the bathroom door, heard the water run in the basin, as it had run every night for nineteen years at precisely this hour.

Harvey Kittredge stood alone. He looked at the envelope. He did not touch it. He relit his cigar, and it tasted of ashes and of October, and he put it out in the mouth of the bronze Scotch terrier. Then, because he did not know what else to do, he went to the front door and set out the milk-bottles, two quarts and a half-pint of cream, which, he reflected, they would perhaps have to cut down to one quart and no cream; and he stood a while on the porch in the damp April dark, looking at the street-lamp, and he said aloud, to no one, in a voice that had lost its conviction:

"Looks like rain to-morrow."

From upstairs Lorena called, as she had called every night for nineteen years, "Harvey? Did you put the milk-bottles out?"

"Yes, dear," he said. And then, for the first time he could remember, he added nothing at all.

Here is an excerpt of Sinclair Lewis's writing, to show you their style:

The assurance of Tanis Judique’s friendship fortified Babbitt’s self-approval. At the Athletic Club he became experimental. Though Vergil Gunch was silent, the others at the Roughnecks’ Table came to accept Babbitt as having, for no visible reason, “turned crank.” They argued windily with him, and he was cocky, and enjoyed the spectacle of his interesting martyrdom. He even praised Seneca Doane. Professor Pumphrey said that was carrying a joke too far; but Babbitt argued, “No! Fact! I tell you he’s got one of the keenest intellects in the country. Why, Lord Wycombe said that—” “Oh, who the hell is Lord Wycombe? What you always lugging him in for? You been touting him for the last six weeks!” protested Orville Jones.

“George ordered him from Sears-Roebuck. You can get those English high-muckamucks by mail for two bucks apiece,” suggested Sidney Finkelstein.

“That’s all right now! Lord Wycombe, he’s one of the biggest intellects in English political life. As I was saying: Of course I’m conservative myself, but I appreciate a guy like Senny Doane because—” Vergil Gunch interrupted harshly, “I wonder if you are so conservative? I find I can manage to run my own business without any skunks and reds like Doane in it!” The grimness of Gunch’s voice, the hardness of his jaw, disconcerted Babbitt, but he recovered and went on till they looked bored, then irritated, then as doubtful as Gunch. He thought of Tanis always. With a stir he remembered her every aspect. His arms yearned for her. “I’ve found her! I’ve dreamed of her all these years and now I’ve found her!” he exulted. He met her at the movies in the morning; he drove out to her flat in the late afternoon or on evenings when he was believed to be at the Elks. He knew her financial affairs and advised her about them, while she lamented her feminine ignorance, and praised his masterfulness, and proved to know much more about bonds than he did. They had remembrances, and laughter over old times. Once they quarreled, and he raged that she was as “bossy” as his wife and far more whining when he was inattentive. But that passed safely. Their high hour was a tramp on a ringing December afternoon, through snow-drifted meadows down to the icy Chaloosa River. She was exotic in an astrachan cap and a short beaver coat; she slid on the ice and shouted, and he panted after her, rotund with laughter.... Myra Babbitt never slid on the ice. He was afraid that they would be seen together. In Zenith it is impossible to lunch with a neighbor’s wife without the fact being known, before nightfall, in every house in your circle. But Tanis was beautifully discreet. However appealingly she might turn to him when they were alone, she was gravely detached when they were abroad, and he hoped that she would be taken for a client. Orville Jones once saw them emerging from a movie theater, and Babbitt bumbled, “Let me make you ’quainted with Mrs. Judique. Now here’s a lady who knows the right broker to come to, Orvy!” Mr. Jones, though he was a man censorious of morals and of laundry machinery, seemed satisfied. His predominant fear—not from any especial fondness for her but from the habit of propriety—was that his wife would learn of the affair. He was certain that she knew nothing specific about Tanis, but he was also certain that she suspected something indefinite. For years she had been bored by anything more affectionate than a farewell kiss, yet she was hurt by any slackening in his irritable periodic interest, and now he had no interest; rather, a revulsion. He was completely faithful—to Tanis. He was distressed by the sight of his wife’s slack plumpness, by her puffs and billows of flesh, by the tattered petticoat which she was always meaning and always forgetting to throw away. But he was aware that she, so long attuned to him, caught all his repulsions. He elaborately, heavily, jocularly tried to check them. He couldn’t. They had a tolerable Christmas. Kenneth Escott was there, admittedly engaged to Verona. Mrs. Babbitt was tearful and called Kenneth her new son. Babbitt was worried about Ted, because he had ceased complaining of the State University and become suspiciously acquiescent. He wondered what the boy was planning, and was too shy to ask. Himself, Babbitt slipped away on Christmas afternoon to take his present, a silver cigarette-box, to Tanis. When he returned Mrs. Babbitt asked, much too innocently, “Did you go out for a little fresh air?”

“Yes, just lil drive,” he mumbled. After New Year’s his wife proposed, “I heard from my sister to-day, George. She isn’t well. I think perhaps I ought to go stay with her for a few weeks.” Now, Mrs. Babbitt was not accustomed to leave home during the winter except on violently demanding occasions, and only the summer before, she had been gone for weeks. Nor was Babbitt one of the detachable husbands who take separations casually. He liked to have her there; she looked after his clothes; she knew how his steak ought to be cooked; and her clucking made him feel secure. But he could not drum up even a dutiful “Oh, she doesn’t really need you, does she?” While he tried to look regretful, while he felt that his wife was watching him, he was filled with exultant visions of Tanis.

“Do you think I’d better go?” she said sharply.

“You’ve got to decide, honey; I can’t.” She turned away, sighing, and his forehead was damp. Till she went, four days later, she was curiously still, he cumbrously affectionate. Her train left at noon. As he saw it grow small beyond the train-shed he longed to hurry to Tanis.

“No, by golly, I won’t do that!” he vowed. “I won’t go near her for a week!” But he was at her flat at four. He who had once controlled or seemed to control his life in a progress unimpassioned but diligent and sane was for that fortnight borne on a current of desire and very bad whisky and all the complications of new acquaintances, those furious new intimates who demand so much more attention than old friends. Each morning he gloomily recognized his idiocies of the evening before. With his head throbbing, his tongue and lips stinging from cigarettes, he incredulously counted the number of drinks he had taken, and groaned, “I got to quit!” He had ceased saying, “I will quit!” for however resolute he might be at dawn, he could not, for a single evening, check his drift. He had met Tanis’s friends; he had, with the ardent haste of the Midnight People, who drink and dance and rattle and are ever afraid to be silent, been adopted as a member of her group, which they called “The Bunch.” He first met them after a day when he had worked particularly hard and when he hoped to be quiet with Tanis and slowly sip her admiration. From down the hall he could hear shrieks and the grind of a phonograph. As Tanis opened the door he saw fantastic figures dancing in a haze of cigarette smoke. The tables and chairs were against the wall.

“Oh, isn’t this dandy!” she gabbled at him. “Carrie Nork had the loveliest idea. She decided it was time for a party, and she ’phoned the Bunch and told ’em to gather round.... George, this is Carrie.”

“Carrie” was, in the less desirable aspects of both, at once matronly and spinsterish. She was perhaps forty; her hair was an unconvincing ash-blond; and if her chest was flat, her hips were ponderous. She greeted Babbitt with a giggling “Welcome to our little midst! Tanis says you’re a real sport.” He was apparently expected to dance, to be boyish and gay with Carrie, and he did his unforgiving best. He towed her about the room, bumping into other couples, into the radiator, into chair-legs cunningly ambushed. As he danced he surveyed the rest of the Bunch: A thin young woman who looked capable, conceited, and sarcastic. Another woman whom he could never quite remember. Three overdressed and slightly effeminate young men—soda-fountain clerks, or at least born for that profession. A man of his own age, immovable, self-satisfied, resentful of Babbitt’s presence. When he had finished his dutiful dance Tanis took him aside and begged, “Dear, wouldn’t you like to do something for me? I’m all out of booze, and the Bunch want to celebrate. Couldn’t you just skip down to Healey Hanson’s and get some?”

“Sure,” he said, trying not to sound sullen.

“I’ll tell you: I’ll get Minnie Sonntag to drive down with you.” Tanis was pointing to the thin, sarcastic young woman. Miss Sonntag greeted him with an astringent “How d’you do, Mr. Babbitt. Tanis tells me you’re a very prominent man, and I’m honored by being allowed to drive with you. Of course I’m not accustomed to associating with society people like you, so I don’t know how to act in such exalted circles!” Thus Miss Sonntag talked all the way down to Healey Hanson’s. To her jibes he wanted to reply “Oh, go to the devil!” but he never quite nerved himself to that reasonable comment. He was resenting the existence of the whole Bunch. He had heard Tanis speak of “darling Carrie” and “Min Sonntag—she’s so clever—you’ll adore her,” but they had never been real to him. He had pictured Tanis as living in a rose-tinted vacuum, waiting for him, free of all the complications of a Floral Heights. When they returned he had to endure the patronage of the young soda-clerks. They were as damply friendly as Miss Sonntag was dryly hostile. They called him “Old Georgie” and shouted, “Come on now, sport; shake a leg” ... boys in belted coats, pimply boys, as young as Ted and as flabby as chorus-men, but powerful to dance and to mind the phonograph and smoke cigarettes and patronize Tanis. He tried to be one of them; he cried “Good work, Pete!” but his voice creaked. Tanis apparently enjoyed the companionship of the dancing darlings; she bridled to their bland flirtation and casually kissed them at the end of each dance. Babbitt hated her, for the moment. He saw her as middle-aged. He studied the wrinkles in the softness of her throat, the slack flesh beneath her chin. The taut muscles of her youth were loose and drooping. Between dances she sat in the largest chair, waving her cigarette, summoning her callow admirers to come and talk to her. (“She thinks she’s a blooming queen!” growled Babbitt.) She chanted to Miss Sonntag, “Isn’t my little studio sweet?” (“Studio, rats! It’s a plain old-maid-and-chow-dog flat! Oh, God, I wish I was home! I wonder if I can’t make a getaway now?”) His vision grew blurred, however, as he applied himself to Healey Hanson’s raw but vigorous whisky. He blended with the Bunch. He began to rejoice that Carrie Nork and Pete, the most nearly intelligent of the nimble youths, seemed to like him; and it was enormously important to win over the surly older man, who proved to be a railway clerk named Fulton Bemis. The conversation of the Bunch was exclamatory, high-colored, full of references to people whom Babbitt did not know. Apparently they thought very comfortably of themselves. They were the Bunch, wise and beautiful and amusing; they were Bohemians and urbanites, accustomed to all the luxuries of Zenith: dance-halls, movie-theaters, and roadhouses; and in a cynical superiority to people who were “slow” or “tightwad” they cackled: “Oh, Pete, did I tell you what that dub of a cashier said when I came in late yesterday? Oh, it was per-fect-ly priceless!”

“Oh, but wasn’t T. D. stewed! Say, he was simply ossified! What did Gladys say to him?”

“Think of the nerve of Bob Bickerstaff trying to get us to come to his house! Say, the nerve of him! Can you beat it for nerve? Some nerve I call it!”

“Did you notice how Dotty was dancing? Gee, wasn’t she the limit!” Babbitt was to be heard sonorously agreeing with the once-hated Miss Minnie Sonntag that persons who let a night go by without dancing to jazz music were crabs, pikers, and poor fish; and he roared “You bet!” when Mrs. Carrie Nork gurgled, “Don’t you love to sit on the floor? It’s so Bohemian!” He began to think extremely well of the Bunch. When he mentioned his friends Sir Gerald Doak, Lord Wycombe, William Washington Eathorne, and Chum Frink, he was proud of their condescending interest. He got so thoroughly into the jocund spirit that he didn’t much mind seeing Tanis drooping against the shoulder of the youngest and milkiest of the young men, and he himself desired to hold Carrie Nork’s pulpy hand, and dropped it only because Tanis looked angry. When he went home, at two, he was fully a member of the Bunch, and all the week thereafter he was bound by the exceedingly straitened conventions, the exceedingly wearing demands, of their life of pleasure and freedom. He had to go to their parties; he was involved in the agitation when everybody telephoned to everybody else that she hadn’t meant what she’d said when she’d said that, and anyway, why was Pete going around saying she’d said it? Never was a Family more insistent on learning one another’s movements than were the Bunch. All of them volubly knew, or indignantly desired to know, where all the others had been every minute of the week. Babbitt found himself explaining to Carrie or Fulton Bemis just what he had been doing that he should not have joined them till ten o’clock, and apologizing for having gone to dinner with a business acquaintance. Every member of the Bunch was expected to telephone to every other member at least once a week. “Why haven’t you called me up?” Babbitt was asked accusingly, not only by Tanis and Carrie but presently by new ancient friends, Jennie and Capitolina and Toots. If for a moment he had seen Tanis as withering and sentimental, he lost that impression at Carrie Nork’s dance. Mrs. Nork had a large house and a small husband. To her party came all of the Bunch, perhaps thirty-five of them when they were completely mobilized. Babbitt, under the name of “Old Georgie,” was now a pioneer of the Bunch, since each month it changed half its membership and he who could recall the prehistoric days of a fortnight ago, before Mrs. Absolom, the food-demonstrator, had gone to Indianapolis, and Mac had “got sore at” Minnie, was a venerable leader and able to condescend to new Petes and Minnies and Gladyses. At Carrie’s, Tanis did not have to work at being hostess. She was dignified and sure, a clear fine figure in the black chiffon frock he had always loved; and in the wider spaces of that ugly house Babbitt was able to sit quietly with her. He repented of his first revulsion, mooned at her feet, andhappily drove her home. Next day he bought a violent yellow tie, to make himself young for her. He knew, a little sadly, that he could not make himself beautiful; he beheld himself as heavy, hinting of fatness, but he danced, he dressed, he chattered, to be as young as she was... as young as she seemed to be. As all converts, whether to a religion, love, or gardening, find as by magic that though hitherto these hobbies have not seemed to exist, now the whole world is filled with their fury, so, once he was converted to dissipation, Babbitt discovered agreeable opportunities for it everywhere. He had a new view of his sporting neighbor, Sam Doppelbrau. The Doppelbraus were respectable people, industrious people, prosperous people, whose ideal of happiness was an eternal cabaret. Their life was dominated by suburban bacchanalia of alcohol, nicotine, gasoline, and kisses. They and their set worked capably all the week, and all week looked forward to Saturday night, when they would, as they expressed it, “throw a party;” and the thrown party grew noisier and noisier up to Sunday dawn, and usually included an extremely rapid motor expedition to nowhere in particular. One evening when Tanis was at the theater, Babbitt found himself being lively with the Doppelbraus, pledging friendship with men whom he had for years privily denounced to Mrs. Babbitt as a “rotten bunch of tin-horns that I wouldn’t go out with, not if they were the last people on earth.” That evening he had sulkily come home and poked about in front of the house, chipping off the walk the ice-clots, like fossil footprints, made by the steps of passers-by during the recent snow. Howard Littlefield came up snuffling.

“Still a widower, George?”

“Yump. Cold again to-night.”

“What do you hear from the wife?”

“She’s feeling fine, but her sister is still pretty sick.”

“Say, better come in and have dinner with us to-night, George.”

“Oh—oh, thanks. Have to go out.” Suddenly he could not endure Littlefield’s recitals of the more interesting statistics about totally uninteresting problems. He scraped at the walk and grunted. Sam Doppelbrau appeared.

“Evenin’, Babbitt. Working hard?”

“Yuh, lil exercise.”

“Cold enough for you to-night?”

“Well, just about.”

“Still a widower?”

“Uh-huh.”

The 4:17 from Chicago was, as the Tamarack *Morning Advocate* had long pointed out with civic distress, invariably late. It was eleven minutes late on the Tuesday afternoon when Harlan Pettibone stood on the platform of the Union Station waiting for his cousin Lucius. He passed those eleven minutes in a state of alternate pride and dread, a state natural to a man who has not seen a blood relation in twenty-two years and who is not certain whether he will be ashamed of the relation or the relation will be ashamed of him.

Harlan was forty-seven. He was the president, general manager, and, as he liked to tell the Good Fellows' Luncheon Club, "chief bottle-washer and head janitor" of the Pettibone Tire & Accessory Company, Inc., which occupied a corner of Grand and Fourteenth and displayed in its window a revolving pyramid of inner tubes that was considered by some of the more advanced citizens of Tamarack to be a genuine work of art. He was a member of the Elks, the Chamber of Commerce, the Second Methodist Church (though he went chiefly at Easter, and then because Mrs. Pettibone had a new hat), and the Tamarack Country Club, to which he had been elected after only four years of waiting. He believed in Prosperity, the Protective Tariff, the Ten Commandments in a general way, and the eventual triumph of the balloon tire over the high-pressure tire. He was a little stout, a little bald, and a good deal pink. He had on that afternoon a gray suit, a gray felt hat, a gray-and-lavender tie, and an expression of deliberate heartiness. He had been rehearsing it in the car.

Lucius Hackett, son of Harlan's mother's sister Hattie, had gone East in 1904. He had gone, people in Pelham Center said, to be an Artist. Nobody in Pelham Center had ever known an Artist, and they spoke of the calling with the mixture of awe and contempt they reserved for the Catholic religion and the State of California. In the twenty-two years since, Harlan had received from him precisely six letters, two of them asking for loans (which Harlan had sent, and which had been repaid, to his slight disappointment, since it spoiled a good story), and one picture postcard of the Woolworth Building with the message: "Saw this today and thought of you. L." Harlan had never quite decided whether that was a compliment.

And now Lucius was coming through Tamarack on his way to Denver, "on a matter of business," he had written, and would stop over for a night if it wasn't too much trouble.

"Trouble!" Harlan had roared to his wife across the breakfast table. "Why, it'll be a pleasure! Old Lute! Why, Ione, we were like brothers, regular Damon and—and what's-his-name. Say, I'll show him a town that'll make him sit up! I guess they think out there in New York that we're still a bunch of hayseeds, trading eggs for calico. Well, I'll show him!"

"I hope he isn't one of those Bolshevik kind," said Ione. "I read where a lot of those artists are."

"Bolshevik nothing! Lute was the best catcher Pelham Center ever had."

The train came in with that air of exhausted importance which trains assume at junctions. Porters swung down; a drummer with two sample-cases descended and looked about as if he expected a brass band; a large woman in a fur piece was received by three daughters, all of whom looked exactly like her and all of whom kissed her in order of age. And then, from the rear Pullman, came a tall, stooped man in a brown tweed suit that was baggy at the knees and expensive at the shoulders. He wore no hat. His hair, which Harlan remembered as a wheat-colored thatch, was a thin, grizzled mat. He carried a leather bag of the sort that has been to Europe and wants you to know it.

Harlan's prepared heartiness came out a little too loud. "Well, well, WELL! If it isn't the old prodigal himself! Lute, you old son of a gun!"

"Hello, Harl," said Lucius, and shook hands. His hand was thin and dry. His smile was quick, a little tired, and Harlan could not tell whether it was amused or merely polite. "You haven't changed a bit."

Now, this was obviously untrue, and both men knew it, and both men were grateful for it.

"Neither have you, Lute! Not a day! Here, give me that grip. No, sir, I insist! You're company!"

He led the way to the curb, where waited a sedan of a make advertised as "The Car of Quiet Distinction," maroon, with nickel trimmings and a radiator ornament in the form of a winged goddess who appeared to be in some discomfort. Harlan opened the door with a flourish that was meant to seem careless.

"Nice little bus," he said. "Not much, but she gets me there. Six cylinders. Four-wheel brakes. Course, I could've had the eight, but I says to myself, 'Harlan, what's the sense of throwing money away for show?'"

"Very handsome," said Lucius. "I don't own a car myself. In New York one doesn't, you know."

Harlan was not sure whether this was a confession of poverty or a boast of superiority, and he brooded over it for six blocks.

---

He drove the long way, by Grand Avenue and the new Federal Building and the Soldiers' and Sailors' Memorial Fountain, which had not been turned on since the previous July because of a difficulty about the plumbing that was the subject of three investigations by the City Council. He pointed out the Hotel Tamarack ("fourteen stories and every room with bath, and I mean bath, not one of these shower-in-the-closet affairs"), the plant of the Wolverine Gasket Corporation ("biggest gasket works west of Toledo"), and the site where the new Masonic Temple was going to be just as soon as they got the rest of the money pledged. He spoke as a host, a guide, and a stockholder in all creation.

"Twenty-two years ago," he said, "this was nothing but a burg. Hundred and eighteen thousand now. Hundred and eighteen thousand! And that's not counting the suburbs. Census fellows had it at ninety-four, but you can't go by those Washington boys; they never get out of their swivel chairs. Lute, I tell you, this town is going places. It's got pep. It's got punch. It's got the kind of folks that don't just sit around and wait for the train; they get out and lay the track!"

He had used this sentence at the Good Fellows' annual banquet and it had been well received.

"It's very impressive," said Lucius, looking out the window at a row of houses which were identical except for the color of their porch swings. "It reminds me of—" He seemed to search. "It reminds me of nothing whatever I've ever seen. That's a compliment, Harl."

"Well, I should hope so!"

There followed one of those pauses which occur between relatives who have exhausted the weather and the train schedule and have not yet dared the past. Harlan cleared his throat. Lucius lit a cigarette, a foreign cigarette, oval, with a gold tip, and the smell of it filled the Car of Quiet Distinction with something exotic and faintly reproachful.

"Remember the old swimming hole?" said Harlan suddenly. "Down at Kessler's Bend?"

Lucius's face changed. For a moment the tired smile went out of it, and what came in was something younger and less guarded.

"Remember it! Harl, I've dreamed about it. In Paris, once, I dreamed I was diving off that sycamore root and the water was full of—what were they—crawdads, and old Kessler's bull was standing on the bank—"

"That bull!" Harlan pounded the steering wheel. "Remember the day he chased Wilbur Stang clean up the windmill?"

"And Wilbur stayed up there till supper!"

"And his pa had to come with a pitchfork!"

They laughed together, really laughed, the dry and the hearty voices blending, and for half a block the twenty-two years were nothing at all. Then Harlan, who could never leave a good thing alone, said, "Wilbur's done pretty well, too. He's got the Ford agency over in Pelham Center now. Doing eighty thousand a year gross, I hear."

And Lucius said, "Ah," and looked out the window again.

---

The Pettibone residence stood on Hillcrest Drive in the Sherwood Heights addition, which had been platted in 1919 by the Sherwood Realty Company with the announced intention of "bringing the Charm of Old England to the Heart of the Middle West." It brought this charm by means of half-timbering, done in stained pine nailed to stucco, and by means of street names like Coventry Lane and Canterbury Way, which the residents pronounced in ways that would have puzzled the Archbishop. The Pettibone house was a Tudor bungalow with a two-car garage, a sun parlor, a breakfast nook, a built-in ironing board, a vacuum-cleaning system with outlets in every room, an electric refrigerator that made its own ice in little cubes (Harlan never tired of demonstrating the cubes), and a radio set in a mahogany cabinet that could, on clear nights, get Pittsburgh.

Ione Pettibone met them at the door. She was a plump, anxious, kindly woman who had spent the afternoon rearranging the living room three times and had finally restored it to its original condition. She wore her second-best georgette and an expression of preparedness for Bolshevism.

"So this is Lucius! Harlan's told me so much about you!"

This was true only in the sense that Harlan had told her the same four stories many times.

"Mrs. Pettibone," said Lucius, and bowed over her hand. He actually bowed. Ione was so flustered that she said, "Oh, my!" and then, to cover it, "Won't you come in and sit down and make yourself to home?"

There was also Gwendolyn, sixteen, who had been instructed to be nice to her cousin and who was nice in the way of sixteen, which is to say she looked at him as though he were an exhibit at the Field Museum and then went upstairs to telephone her friend Marjorie Huckins that he was "kind of foreign-looking and terribly distinguished and, Marge, honestly, he doesn't even wear a hat!"

Harlan conducted the tour. He showed Lucius the sun parlor, and the breakfast nook, and the built-in ironing board, which he let down and put up again twice. He showed him the vacuum outlets. He showed him the ice cubes. He took one out with his own fingers and held it up to the light as a jeweler holds a diamond.

"Makes 'em right there in the tray. No iceman tracking up the kitchen. No drip pan. Just set the dial and forget it. Electricity, Lute. Science! I tell you, the average American home today has got more comfort in it than the palace of any king in history. Louis the Fourteenth never had a thing like that!"

"No," said Lucius, regarding the cube with grave attention, "I don't believe he did. He had to make do with Versailles."

Harlan suspected for an instant that he was being kidded, but Lucius's face was perfectly solemn, and Harlan decided that this was the way artists talked, and put the cube back.

---

Dinner was roast chicken, mashed potatoes with a well of gravy in the middle, creamed peas, Parker House rolls, cranberry jelly molded in the shape of a fluted castle, and a salad composed of a slice of canned pineapple, a dab of mayonnaise, a maraschino cherry, and a curl of cream cheese, arranged on a lettuce leaf in a manner that Ione had found in the *Ladies' Home Companion* and considered the summit of civilization. For dessert there was devil's food cake. Lucius praised everything, and ate little, and Ione decided he must be dyspeptic and resolved to send him away with a box of her own bicarbonate.

It was at dinner that the inquiry began. Harlan conducted it with the delicacy of a county prosecutor.

"Well, Lute, so what are you doing with yourself these days? Still at the old paint pots?"

"Oh, a little. Not as much as I'd like. I do a good deal of illustration now. Magazine work. And I teach two afternoons a week at a school on Fourteenth Street."

"Teaching, huh? That's fine, that's fine. Steady. Good pay in that?"

"It keeps the wolf at a respectful distance."

"Ha! Wolf! That's good." Harlan buttered a roll with deliberation. "Magazine work. Which magazines? Any of the big ones? *Saturday Evening Post*?"

Lucius named two. Neither of them had ever been seen in Tamarack, except possibly in the reading room of the public library, where they were kept on a high shelf beside the *Atlantic Monthly* and the *Journal of the American Medical Association*.

"Hm," said Harlan. "Highbrow stuff, I guess."

"Rather."

"Well, there's room for everything." Harlan spoke with the magnanimity of a man who has just found out that his cousin is not getting rich. He felt suddenly warm toward Lucius, warm and generous and protective. "Course, you always did have the talent. "Married?" said Ione, who had been waiting for an opening.

---

It contained a leather chair, a smoking stand shaped like a butler holding a tray, a framed certificate of membership in the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks, a stuffed pike which Harlan had caught at Lake Minnetonka and which had been mounted by a taxidermist with a sense of drama, and a bookcase containing the *Book of Knowledge* in twenty volumes, *Pep Talks for Salesmen*, the collected works of a poet who wrote about mothers and sunsets for the newspaper syndicates, and a novel by a lady from Indiana which Ione had given him for Christmas in 1921 and which he intended some day to read.

Harlan unlocked a drawer of his desk and brought out, with a conspirator's air, a bottle.

"Real stuff, Lute. Canadian. Not that bathtub hooch. Got a fellow who brings it down from Detroit."

"You're a law-breaker, Harl."

"Aw, now." Harlan poured with a generous hand. "Prohibition's all right for the working man. Keeps him on the job. But a fellow in my position—well, a business man's got to entertain. Here's how!"

"Here's how."

They drank. Harlan lit a cigar. Lucius lit another of the oval cigarettes. The stuffed pike regarded them both with glassy disapproval.

The whisky did something the dinner had not. It loosened them. Harlan leaned back in the leather chair and put his feet up on a hassock, and Lucius took off his coat, which Harlan observed had a London tailor's label, and which Harlan would mention later at the club as though he had seen it on a duke.

"You know, Harl," said Lucius after the second glass, "I've thought about you a good deal. All these years."

"You have? Well, I'll be darned. I've thought about you, too, Lute."

"I mean it. When things were bad—and they've been bad, now and then, the way they are—I used to think, 'There's Harl, back in the Middle West, with a house and a wife and children and a business, and he knows what he wants, and he's got it.' I used to envy you like the devil."

Harlan was so astonished that he took his feet off the hassock.

"Envy me? Why, Lute, I was just thinking, all through dinner, how I envied *you*! Paris and London and New York and all those artist fellows and—why, I bet you've met all kinds of famous people!"

"One or two."

"There! You see? And here I am, selling inner tubes. Inner tubes! Why, Lute, sometimes I lie awake nights and I think, 'Harlan, is this all there is? Is a fellow just supposed to sell tires and go to Rotary—Good Fellows, I mean—and play golf Saturdays and go to bed and get up and sell more tires?' Sometimes I think if I could just once get on a boat and go to—to Naples, or someplace, and just sit in one of those little cafés and not have to think about the March inventory—"

He stopped, alarmed. He had never said this to anyone. He had never quite said it to himself. He looked at the whisky in his glass as though it had betrayed him.

Lucius was looking at him with an expression that was neither amused nor polite.

"It isn't much better in Naples, Harl. The cafés have flies. And you still think about the March inventory. It's only that yours is a different kind."

"Is that so?" Harlan was relieved, and disappointed, and he could not have said which more. "Well, I guess—I guess a fellow always thinks the grass is greener."

"It's a very old observation."

"Yes, sir. Very true."

And then, because they had come so near to something and both were frightened by it, they retreated at once into the past, where it was safe, and the evening became a tournament of Remember.

Remember Uncle Ezra's barn and the hayloft where they smoked corn silk and Lute was sick? Remember the Fourth of July when Harl set fire to the Methodist privy with a cannon cracker? Remember Grandma Pettibone's molasses cookies, and the way she kept them in a stone crock on the top shelf, and the time they built a ladder out of a chair and a cheese box? Remember Alma Kittredge, with the yellow braids, whom they had both loved in the seventh grade, and who had married a druggist in Council Bluffs and had, Harlan heard, seven children and a goiter?

"Alma!" said Lucius softly. "I painted her once, from memory. In Brittany. Sold it to a Dutchman for two hundred francs."

"You don't say! Alma Kittredge hanging in Holland! Wait'll I tell the folks back home!"

By midnight they were sitting side by side on the floor, which Harlan had not sat on since 1912, singing "In the Good Old Summertime" in two keys, and Ione came down in her wrapper and said, "Harlan Pettibone, you'll wake the neighbors!" and Harlan said, "Let 'em wake! It isn't every day a man gets his own flesh and blood back!" and Ione, who had been prepared for Bolshevism, went back upstairs relieved to find only drunkenness, which she understood.

---

In the morning they were stiff with each other again.

Breakfast was grapefruit, oatmeal, bacon, eggs, toast, and coffee from an electric percolator that Harlan demonstrated. Lucius drank only the coffee. Harlan, who had a headache, talked about the Rotarians—the Good Fellows—and the new golf course, and the prospects for the fall tire market, and the danger of the radicals in the state legislature, with a vehemence that seemed to say, "Whatever I said last night, I didn't mean it." And Lucius, whose eyes were pouched, spoke of a gallery on Fifty-Seventh Street and an exhibition in the spring and a critic named something with a hyphen, and his voice seemed to say, "Whatever I said last night, I didn't mean it either."

Harlan drove him to the station. They spoke of the weather, which was fine, and of the 9:40 to Denver, which was reported to be on time, though Harlan said darkly that he'd believe it when he saw it.

On the platform they shook hands.

"Well, Lute. Don't be such a stranger."

"I won't, Harl. You must come to New York. I'll show you the town."

"I'll do that. I'll sure do that." Both knew he would not.

Lucius hesitated. For an instant it seemed that he was about to say something else, something real, and Harlan's chest tightened in expectation. But the conductor bawled "Bo-o-oard!" and Lucius only said, "Give my love to Ione. And—keep those ice cubes coming," and swung up into the car with his bag that had been to Europe.

Harlan watched the train until it was a smudge beyond the freight sheds. He felt, for a moment, unaccountably lonely, as though something had been taken away that he had not known he possessed. He stood there with his hands in his pockets and thought about Kessler's Bend, and the sycamore root, and how cold the water had been, and how it had seemed, at eleven, that a fellow could do anything at all.

Then he looked at his watch, which was a seventeen-jewel Hamilton, and remembered that the man from the Goodrich people was coming at ten-thirty.

---

Here is an excerpt of Sinclair Lewis's writing, to show you their style:

The assurance of Tanis Judique’s friendship fortified Babbitt’s self-approval. At the Athletic Club he became experimental. Though Vergil Gunch was silent, the others at the Roughnecks’ Table came to accept Babbitt as having, for no visible reason, “turned crank.” They argued windily with him, and he was cocky, and enjoyed the spectacle of his interesting martyrdom. He even praised Seneca Doane. Professor Pumphrey said that was carrying a joke too far; but Babbitt argued, “No! Fact! I tell you he’s got one of the keenest intellects in the country. Why, Lord Wycombe said that—” “Oh, who the hell is Lord Wycombe? What you always lugging him in for? You been touting him for the last six weeks!” protested Orville Jones.

“George ordered him from Sears-Roebuck. You can get those English high-muckamucks by mail for two bucks apiece,” suggested Sidney Finkelstein.

“That’s all right now! Lord Wycombe, he’s one of the biggest intellects in English political life. As I was saying: Of course I’m conservative myself, but I appreciate a guy like Senny Doane because—” Vergil Gunch interrupted harshly, “I wonder if you are so conservative? I find I can manage to run my own business without any skunks and reds like Doane in it!” The grimness of Gunch’s voice, the hardness of his jaw, disconcerted Babbitt, but he recovered and went on till they looked bored, then irritated, then as doubtful as Gunch. He thought of Tanis always. With a stir he remembered her every aspect. His arms yearned for her. “I’ve found her! I’ve dreamed of her all these years and now I’ve found her!” he exulted. He met her at the movies in the morning; he drove out to her flat in the late afternoon or on evenings when he was believed to be at the Elks. He knew her financial affairs and advised her about them, while she lamented her feminine ignorance, and praised his masterfulness, and proved to know much more about bonds than he did. They had remembrances, and laughter over old times. Once they quarreled, and he raged that she was as “bossy” as his wife and far more whining when he was inattentive. But that passed safely. Their high hour was a tramp on a ringing December afternoon, through snow-drifted meadows down to the icy Chaloosa River. She was exotic in an astrachan cap and a short beaver coat; she slid on the ice and shouted, and he panted after her, rotund with laughter.... Myra Babbitt never slid on the ice. He was afraid that they would be seen together. In Zenith it is impossible to lunch with a neighbor’s wife without the fact being known, before nightfall, in every house in your circle. But Tanis was beautifully discreet. However appealingly she might turn to him when they were alone, she was gravely detached when they were abroad, and he hoped that she would be taken for a client. Orville Jones once saw them emerging from a movie theater, and Babbitt bumbled, “Let me make you ’quainted with Mrs. Judique. Now here’s a lady who knows the right broker to come to, Orvy!” Mr. Jones, though he was a man censorious of morals and of laundry machinery, seemed satisfied. His predominant fear—not from any especial fondness for her but from the habit of propriety—was that his wife would learn of the affair. He was certain that she knew nothing specific about Tanis, but he was also certain that she suspected something indefinite. For years she had been bored by anything more affectionate than a farewell kiss, yet she was hurt by any slackening in his irritable periodic interest, and now he had no interest; rather, a revulsion. He was completely faithful—to Tanis. He was distressed by the sight of his wife’s slack plumpness, by her puffs and billows of flesh, by the tattered petticoat which she was always meaning and always forgetting to throw away. But he was aware that she, so long attuned to him, caught all his repulsions. He elaborately, heavily, jocularly tried to check them. He couldn’t. They had a tolerable Christmas. Kenneth Escott was there, admittedly engaged to Verona. Mrs. Babbitt was tearful and called Kenneth her new son. Babbitt was worried about Ted, because he had ceased complaining of the State University and become suspiciously acquiescent. He wondered what the boy was planning, and was too shy to ask. Himself, Babbitt slipped away on Christmas afternoon to take his present, a silver cigarette-box, to Tanis. When he returned Mrs. Babbitt asked, much too innocently, “Did you go out for a little fresh air?”

“Yes, just lil drive,” he mumbled. After New Year’s his wife proposed, “I heard from my sister to-day, George. She isn’t well. I think perhaps I ought to go stay with her for a few weeks.” Now, Mrs. Babbitt was not accustomed to leave home during the winter except on violently demanding occasions, and only the summer before, she had been gone for weeks. Nor was Babbitt one of the detachable husbands who take separations casually. He liked to have her there; she looked after his clothes; she knew how his steak ought to be cooked; and her clucking made him feel secure. But he could not drum up even a dutiful “Oh, she doesn’t really need you, does she?” While he tried to look regretful, while he felt that his wife was watching him, he was filled with exultant visions of Tanis.

“Do you think I’d better go?” she said sharply.

“You’ve got to decide, honey; I can’t.” She turned away, sighing, and his forehead was damp. Till she went, four days later, she was curiously still, he cumbrously affectionate. Her train left at noon. As he saw it grow small beyond the train-shed he longed to hurry to Tanis.

“No, by golly, I won’t do that!” he vowed. “I won’t go near her for a week!” But he was at her flat at four. He who had once controlled or seemed to control his life in a progress unimpassioned but diligent and sane was for that fortnight borne on a current of desire and very bad whisky and all the complications of new acquaintances, those furious new intimates who demand so much more attention than old friends. Each morning he gloomily recognized his idiocies of the evening before. With his head throbbing, his tongue and lips stinging from cigarettes, he incredulously counted the number of drinks he had taken, and groaned, “I got to quit!” He had ceased saying, “I will quit!” for however resolute he might be at dawn, he could not, for a single evening, check his drift. He had met Tanis’s friends; he had, with the ardent haste of the Midnight People, who drink and dance and rattle and are ever afraid to be silent, been adopted as a member of her group, which they called “The Bunch.” He first met them after a day when he had worked particularly hard and when he hoped to be quiet with Tanis and slowly sip her admiration. From down the hall he could hear shrieks and the grind of a phonograph. As Tanis opened the door he saw fantastic figures dancing in a haze of cigarette smoke. The tables and chairs were against the wall.

“Oh, isn’t this dandy!” she gabbled at him. “Carrie Nork had the loveliest idea. She decided it was time for a party, and she ’phoned the Bunch and told ’em to gather round.... George, this is Carrie.”

“Carrie” was, in the less desirable aspects of both, at once matronly and spinsterish. She was perhaps forty; her hair was an unconvincing ash-blond; and if her chest was flat, her hips were ponderous. She greeted Babbitt with a giggling “Welcome to our little midst! Tanis says you’re a real sport.” He was apparently expected to dance, to be boyish and gay with Carrie, and he did his unforgiving best. He towed her about the room, bumping into other couples, into the radiator, into chair-legs cunningly ambushed. As he danced he surveyed the rest of the Bunch: A thin young woman who looked capable, conceited, and sarcastic. Another woman whom he could never quite remember. Three overdressed and slightly effeminate young men—soda-fountain clerks, or at least born for that profession. A man of his own age, immovable, self-satisfied, resentful of Babbitt’s presence. When he had finished his dutiful dance Tanis took him aside and begged, “Dear, wouldn’t you like to do something for me? I’m all out of booze, and the Bunch want to celebrate. Couldn’t you just skip down to Healey Hanson’s and get some?”

“Sure,” he said, trying not to sound sullen.

“I’ll tell you: I’ll get Minnie Sonntag to drive down with you.” Tanis was pointing to the thin, sarcastic young woman. Miss Sonntag greeted him with an astringent “How d’you do, Mr. Babbitt. Tanis tells me you’re a very prominent man, and I’m honored by being allowed to drive with you. Of course I’m not accustomed to associating with society people like you, so I don’t know how to act in such exalted circles!” Thus Miss Sonntag talked all the way down to Healey Hanson’s. To her jibes he wanted to reply “Oh, go to the devil!” but he never quite nerved himself to that reasonable comment. He was resenting the existence of the whole Bunch. He had heard Tanis speak of “darling Carrie” and “Min Sonntag—she’s so clever—you’ll adore her,” but they had never been real to him. He had pictured Tanis as living in a rose-tinted vacuum, waiting for him, free of all the complications of a Floral Heights. When they returned he had to endure the patronage of the young soda-clerks. They were as damply friendly as Miss Sonntag was dryly hostile. They called him “Old Georgie” and shouted, “Come on now, sport; shake a leg” ... boys in belted coats, pimply boys, as young as Ted and as flabby as chorus-men, but powerful to dance and to mind the phonograph and smoke cigarettes and patronize Tanis. He tried to be one of them; he cried “Good work, Pete!” but his voice creaked. Tanis apparently enjoyed the companionship of the dancing darlings; she bridled to their bland flirtation and casually kissed them at the end of each dance. Babbitt hated her, for the moment. He saw her as middle-aged. He studied the wrinkles in the softness of her throat, the slack flesh beneath her chin. The taut muscles of her youth were loose and drooping. Between dances she sat in the largest chair, waving her cigarette, summoning her callow admirers to come and talk to her. (“She thinks she’s a blooming queen!” growled Babbitt.) She chanted to Miss Sonntag, “Isn’t my little studio sweet?” (“Studio, rats! It’s a plain old-maid-and-chow-dog flat! Oh, God, I wish I was home! I wonder if I can’t make a getaway now?”) His vision grew blurred, however, as he applied himself to Healey Hanson’s raw but vigorous whisky. He blended with the Bunch. He began to rejoice that Carrie Nork and Pete, the most nearly intelligent of the nimble youths, seemed to like him; and it was enormously important to win over the surly older man, who proved to be a railway clerk named Fulton Bemis. The conversation of the Bunch was exclamatory, high-colored, full of references to people whom Babbitt did not know. Apparently they thought very comfortably of themselves. They were the Bunch, wise and beautiful and amusing; they were Bohemians and urbanites, accustomed to all the luxuries of Zenith: dance-halls, movie-theaters, and roadhouses; and in a cynical superiority to people who were “slow” or “tightwad” they cackled: “Oh, Pete, did I tell you what that dub of a cashier said when I came in late yesterday? Oh, it was per-fect-ly priceless!”

“Oh, but wasn’t T. D. stewed! Say, he was simply ossified! What did Gladys say to him?”

“Think of the nerve of Bob Bickerstaff trying to get us to come to his house! Say, the nerve of him! Can you beat it for nerve? Some nerve I call it!”

“Did you notice how Dotty was dancing? Gee, wasn’t she the limit!” Babbitt was to be heard sonorously agreeing with the once-hated Miss Minnie Sonntag that persons who let a night go by without dancing to jazz music were crabs, pikers, and poor fish; and he roared “You bet!” when Mrs. Carrie Nork gurgled, “Don’t you love to sit on the floor? It’s so Bohemian!” He began to think extremely well of the Bunch. When he mentioned his friends Sir Gerald Doak, Lord Wycombe, William Washington Eathorne, and Chum Frink, he was proud of their condescending interest. He got so thoroughly into the jocund spirit that he didn’t much mind seeing Tanis drooping against the shoulder of the youngest and milkiest of the young men, and he himself desired to hold Carrie Nork’s pulpy hand, and dropped it only because Tanis looked angry. When he went home, at two, he was fully a member of the Bunch, and all the week thereafter he was bound by the exceedingly straitened conventions, the exceedingly wearing demands, of their life of pleasure and freedom. He had to go to their parties; he was involved in the agitation when everybody telephoned to everybody else that she hadn’t meant what she’d said when she’d said that, and anyway, why was Pete going around saying she’d said it? Never was a Family more insistent on learning one another’s movements than were the Bunch. All of them volubly knew, or indignantly desired to know, where all the others had been every minute of the week. Babbitt found himself explaining to Carrie or Fulton Bemis just what he had been doing that he should not have joined them till ten o’clock, and apologizing for having gone to dinner with a business acquaintance. Every member of the Bunch was expected to telephone to every other member at least once a week. “Why haven’t you called me up?” Babbitt was asked accusingly, not only by Tanis and Carrie but presently by new ancient friends, Jennie and Capitolina and Toots. If for a moment he had seen Tanis as withering and sentimental, he lost that impression at Carrie Nork’s dance. Mrs. Nork had a large house and a small husband. To her party came all of the Bunch, perhaps thirty-five of them when they were completely mobilized. Babbitt, under the name of “Old Georgie,” was now a pioneer of the Bunch, since each month it changed half its membership and he who could recall the prehistoric days of a fortnight ago, before Mrs. Absolom, the food-demonstrator, had gone to Indianapolis, and Mac had “got sore at” Minnie, was a venerable leader and able to condescend to new Petes and Minnies and Gladyses. At Carrie’s, Tanis did not have to work at being hostess. She was dignified and sure, a clear fine figure in the black chiffon frock he had always loved; and in the wider spaces of that ugly house Babbitt was able to sit quietly with her. He repented of his first revulsion, mooned at her feet, andhappily drove her home. Next day he bought a violent yellow tie, to make himself young for her. He knew, a little sadly, that he could not make himself beautiful; he beheld himself as heavy, hinting of fatness, but he danced, he dressed, he chattered, to be as young as she was... as young as she seemed to be. As all converts, whether to a religion, love, or gardening, find as by magic that though hitherto these hobbies have not seemed to exist, now the whole world is filled with their fury, so, once he was converted to dissipation, Babbitt discovered agreeable opportunities for it everywhere. He had a new view of his sporting neighbor, Sam Doppelbrau. The Doppelbraus were respectable people, industrious people, prosperous people, whose ideal of happiness was an eternal cabaret. Their life was dominated by suburban bacchanalia of alcohol, nicotine, gasoline, and kisses. They and their set worked capably all the week, and all week looked forward to Saturday night, when they would, as they expressed it, “throw a party;” and the thrown party grew noisier and noisier up to Sunday dawn, and usually included an extremely rapid motor expedition to nowhere in particular. One evening when Tanis was at the theater, Babbitt found himself being lively with the Doppelbraus, pledging friendship with men whom he had for years privily denounced to Mrs. Babbitt as a “rotten bunch of tin-horns that I wouldn’t go out with, not if they were the last people on earth.” That evening he had sulkily come home and poked about in front of the house, chipping off the walk the ice-clots, like fossil footprints, made by the steps of passers-by during the recent snow. Howard Littlefield came up snuffling.

“Still a widower, George?”

“Yump. Cold again to-night.”

“What do you hear from the wife?”

“She’s feeling fine, but her sister is still pretty sick.”

“Say, better come in and have dinner with us to-night, George.”

“Oh—oh, thanks. Have to go out.” Suddenly he could not endure Littlefield’s recitals of the more interesting statistics about totally uninteresting problems. He scraped at the walk and grunted. Sam Doppelbrau appeared.

“Evenin’, Babbitt. Working hard?”

“Yuh, lil exercise.”

“Cold enough for you to-night?”

“Well, just about.”

“Still a widower?”

“Uh-huh.”

“Oh, isn’t this dandy!” she gabbled at him. “Carrie Nork had the loveliest idea. She decided it was time for a party, and she ’phoned the Bunch and told ’em to gather round.... George, this is Carrie.”

“Carrie” was, in the less desirable aspects of both, at once matronly and spinsterish. She was perhaps forty; her hair was an unconvincing ash-blond; and if her chest was flat, her hips were ponderous. She greeted Babbitt with a giggling “Welcome to our little midst! Tanis says you’re a real sport.” He was apparently expected to dance, to be boyish and gay with Carrie, and he did his unforgiving best. He towed her about the room, bumping into other couples, into the radiator, into chair-legs cunningly ambushed. As he danced he surveyed the rest of the Bunch: A thin young woman who looked capable, conceited, and sarcastic. Another woman whom he could never quite remember. Three overdressed and slightly effeminate young men—soda-fountain clerks, or at least born for that profession. A man of his own age, immovable, self-satisfied, resentful of Babbitt’s presence. When he had finished his dutiful dance Tanis took him aside and begged, “Dear, wouldn’t you like to do something for me? I’m all out of booze, and the Bunch want to celebrate. Couldn’t you just skip down to Healey Hanson’s and get some?”

“Sure,” he said, trying not to sound sullen.

“I’ll tell you: I’ll get Minnie Sonntag to drive down with you.” Tanis was pointing to the thin, sarcastic young woman. Miss Sonntag greeted him with an astringent “How d’you do, Mr. Babbitt. Tanis tells me you’re a very prominent man, and I’m honored by being allowed to drive with you. Of course I’m not accustomed to associating with society people like you, so I don’t know how to act in such exalted circles!” Thus Miss Sonntag talked all the way down to Healey Hanson’s. To her jibes he wanted to reply “Oh, go to the devil!” but he never quite nerved himself to that reasonable comment. He was resenting the existence of the whole Bunch. He had heard Tanis speak of “darling Carrie” and “Min Sonntag—she’s so clever—you’ll adore her,” but they had never been real to him. He had pictured Tanis as living in a rose-tinted vacuum, waiting for him, free of all the complications of a Floral Heights. When they returned he had to endure the patronage of the young soda-clerks. They were as damply friendly as Miss Sonntag was dryly hostile. They called him “Old Georgie” and shouted, “Come on now, sport; shake a leg” ... boys in belted coats, pimply boys, as young as Ted and as flabby as chorus-men, but powerful to dance and to mind the phonograph and smoke cigarettes and patronize Tanis. He tried to be one of them; he cried “Good work, Pete!” but his voice creaked. Tanis apparently enjoyed the companionship of the dancing darlings; she bridled to their bland flirtation and casually kissed them at the end of each dance. Babbitt hated her, for the moment. He saw her as middle-aged. He studied the wrinkles in the softness of her throat, the slack flesh beneath her chin. The taut muscles of her youth were loose and drooping. Between dances she sat in the largest chair, waving her cigarette, summoning her callow admirers to come and talk to her. (“She thinks she’s a blooming queen!” growled Babbitt.) She chanted to Miss Sonntag, “Isn’t my little studio sweet?” (“Studio, rats! It’s a plain old-maid-and-chow-dog flat! Oh, God, I wish I was home! I wonder if I can’t make a getaway now?”) His vision grew blurred, however, as he applied himself to Healey Hanson’s raw but vigorous whisky. He blended with the Bunch. He began to rejoice that Carrie Nork and Pete, the most nearly intelligent of the nimble youths, seemed to like him; and it was enormously important to win over the surly older man, who proved to be a railway clerk named Fulton Bemis. The conversation of the Bunch was exclamatory, high-colored, full of references to people whom Babbitt did not know. Apparently they thought very comfortably of themselves. They were the Bunch, wise and beautiful and amusing; they were Bohemians and urbanites, accustomed to all the luxuries of Zenith: dance-halls, movie-theaters, and roadhouses; and in a cynical superiority to people who were “slow” or “tightwad” they cackled: “Oh, Pete, did I tell you what that dub of a cashier said when I came in late yesterday? Oh, it was per-fect-ly priceless!”

“Oh, but wasn’t T. D. stewed! Say, he was simply ossified! What did Gladys say to him?”

“Think of the nerve of Bob Bickerstaff trying to get us to come to his house! Say, the nerve of him! Can you beat it for nerve? Some nerve I call it!”

“Did you notice how Dotty was dancing? Gee, wasn’t she the limit!” Babbitt was to be heard sonorously agreeing with the once-hated Miss Minnie Sonntag that persons who let a night go by without dancing to jazz music were crabs, pikers, and poor fish; and he roared “You bet!” when Mrs. Carrie Nork gurgled, “Don’t you love to sit on the floor? It’s so Bohemian!” He began to think extremely well of the Bunch. When he mentioned his friends Sir Gerald Doak, Lord Wycombe, William Washington Eathorne, and Chum Frink, he was proud of their condescending interest. He got so thoroughly into the jocund spirit that he didn’t much mind seeing Tanis drooping against the shoulder of the youngest and milkiest of the young men, and he himself desired to hold Carrie Nork’s pulpy hand, and dropped it only because Tanis looked angry. When he went home, at two, he was fully a member of the Bunch, and all the week thereafter he was bound by the exceedingly straitened conventions, the exceedingly wearing demands, of their life of pleasure and freedom. He had to go to their parties; he was involved in the agitation when everybody telephoned to everybody else that she hadn’t meant what she’d said when she’d said that, and anyway, why was Pete going around saying she’d said it? Never was a Family more insistent on learning one another’s movements than were the Bunch. All of them volubly knew, or indignantly desired to know, where all the others had been every minute of the week. Babbitt found himself explaining to Carrie or Fulton Bemis just what he had been doing that he should not have joined them till ten o’clock, and apologizing for having gone to dinner with a business acquaintance. Every member of the Bunch was expected to telephone to every other member at least once a week. “Why haven’t you called me up?” Babbitt was asked accusingly, not only by Tanis and Carrie but presently by new ancient friends, Jennie and Capitolina and Toots. If for a moment he had seen Tanis as withering and sentimental, he lost that impression at Carrie Nork’s dance. Mrs. Nork had a large house and a small husband. To her party came all of the Bunch, perhaps thirty-five of them when they were completely mobilized. Babbitt, under the name of “Old Georgie,” was now a pioneer of the Bunch, since each month it changed half its membership and he who could recall the prehistoric days of a fortnight ago, before Mrs. Absolom, the food-demonstrator, had gone to Indianapolis, and Mac had “got sore at” Minnie, was a venerable leader and able to condescend to new Petes and Minnies and Gladyses. At Carrie’s, Tanis did not have to work at being hostess. She was dignified and sure, a clear fine figure in the black chiffon frock he had always loved; and in the wider spaces of that ugly house Babbitt was able to sit quietly with her. He repented of his first revulsion, mooned at her feet, andhappily drove her home. Next day he bought a violent yellow tie, to make himself young for her. He knew, a little sadly, that he could not make himself beautiful; he beheld himself as heavy, hinting of fatness, but he danced, he dressed, he chattered, to be as young as she was... as young as she seemed to be. As all converts, whether to a religion, love, or gardening, find as by magic that though hitherto these hobbies have not seemed to exist, now the whole world is filled with their fury, so, once he was converted to dissipation, Babbitt discovered agreeable opportunities for it everywhere. He had a new view of his sporting neighbor, Sam Doppelbrau. The Doppelbraus were respectable people, industrious people, prosperous people, whose ideal of happiness was an eternal cabaret. Their life was dominated by suburban bacchanalia of alcohol, nicotine, gasoline, and kisses. They and their set worked capably all the week, and all week looked forward to Saturday night, when they would, as they expressed it, “throw a party;” and the thrown party grew noisier and noisier up to Sunday dawn, and usually included an extremely rapid motor expedition to nowhere in particular. One evening when Tanis was at the theater, Babbitt found himself being lively with the Doppelbraus, pledging friendship with men whom he had for years privily denounced to Mrs. Babbitt as a “rotten bunch of tin-horns that I wouldn’t go out with, not if they were the last people on earth.” That evening he had sulkily come home and poked about in front of the house, chipping off the walk the ice-clots, like fossil footprints, made by the steps of passers-by during the recent snow. Howard Littlefield came up snuffling.

“Still a widower, George?”

“Yump. Cold again to-night.”

“What do you hear from the wife?”

“She’s feeling fine, but her sister is still pretty sick.”

“Say, better come in and have dinner with us to-night, George.”

“Oh—oh, thanks. Have to go out.” Suddenly he could not endure Littlefield’s recitals of the more interesting statistics about totally uninteresting problems. He scraped at the walk and grunted. Sam Doppelbrau appeared.

“Evenin’, Babbitt. Working hard?”

“Yuh, lil exercise.”

“Cold enough for you to-night?”

“Well, just about.”

“Still a widower?”

“Uh-huh.”
