response:
It was in the late spring of a year when wages in the yards and shops of the West Side of Chicago were none too good, and when men who had been earning eleven and twelve dollars a week were glad enough to be earning nine, that the incident here set down took place in the small frame cottage of Thomas Wenzel, car-repairer, in Throop Street. It was not a large incident, as the world reckons such things. No newspaper would have troubled itself with it, and no neighbor, unless it were Mrs. Schaub, who kept the little candy and notion store at the corner, and who had a sharp ear for the doings of her customers, would have known anything about it at all. Yet in its way it was as illustrative of the forces which play upon all human beings, the great and the small, the wise and the unwise, as any battle or bankruptcy or scandal of which the papers make so much, and for that reason, if for no other, it may be worth the telling.

Thomas Wenzel was at this time a man of thirty-eight, stocky, rather heavy of shoulder, with a short sandy beard and a pair of pale blue eyes that had in them something of the patient, wondering look of an ox that has been long in harness. He had come over from Hesse as a boy of fifteen, had worked first on a farm near Belleville, then in a brickyard at Joliet, and finally, by dint of a slow and dogged industry which was the only gift life had seen fit to bestow upon him, had arrived at his present position in the shops of the railway, where he earned, when there was work, a dollar and seventy-five cents a day. Out of this he paid nine dollars a month for the cottage, which consisted of four small rooms and a lean-to kitchen, all of them heated in winter by a single soft-coal stove; he fed and clothed a wife and three children; he contributed a quarter each Sunday to the little Lutheran church in Racine Avenue; and he laid by, when he could, which was not often, a dollar or two toward that dim and ever-receding day when he should own a house of his own and be beholden to no landlord. It was a narrow life, a grinding life, and he knew it, though he would have been at a loss to say so in words. What he felt rather than thought was that the world was a hard place, full of temptations and pitfalls, of men who drank and gambled and came to nothing, of women who painted their faces and went to the bad, and that the only safety for a poor man lay in honesty, in thrift, and in the fear of God. These three things he held to as a drowning man might hold to a spar, and with something of the same desperation.

His wife, Hannah, was of a softer mould. She was a thin, pale, fair-haired woman, a little bent already from the washtub and the cookstove, who had been born in Milwaukee of German parents and who had in her, for all her drudgery, a certain wistful fondness for pretty things which she had long since given up any hope of possessing. She liked a bit of ribbon, a picture in a magazine, the sight of the fine carriages that went by on Ashland Avenue of a Sunday afternoon. She did not argue with her husband, for she had learned long ago that argument with him was useless, but she softened, where she could, the hard edges of his rule, and the children, quite naturally, turned to her rather than to him when they were in trouble.

Of the three children, it is the second, Albert, a boy of seven, with whom we are concerned. He was a slight, dark-eyed, eager little fellow, more like his mother than his father, and possessed of a temperament which was, in that household, a decided misfortune. For he was sensitive, imaginative, easily excited by color and sound and the movement of things, and drawn, as a moth is drawn to a lamp, by whatever glittered or shone. A brass band going by on the street would hold him rooted to the curb until it had passed out of hearing. The gilded sign of a saloon, the red and green bottles in the window of the drug store at the corner of Twelfth Street, the bright tin toys that hung in festoons in the doorway of the Jew's shop on Halsted, were to him so many visions of a world more wonderful than any he knew. And above all, and most dangerous of all, there were the glass jars in the window of Mrs. Schaub's store, filled with licorice whips and horehound drops and striped peppermint sticks and those round, hard, many-colored balls which the children called jawbreakers, and which could be had, two for a penny, by anyone who possessed a penny.

Albert did not possess a penny. He had never, in so far as he could remember, possessed one for longer than it took to walk from the place where it had been given him to Mrs. Schaub's counter. His father did not believe in giving money to children. It made them wasteful, he said; it taught them to want things; and wanting things was the beginning of all evil. And so the boy would stand before that window, his nose pressed flat against the glass, his eyes going from jar to jar, and dream. What he dreamed it would be difficult to say. Not of the candy merely, though that was a part of it. Rather of a kind of richness, a fullness and brightness of living, which the candy somehow stood for, and which was so entirely absent from the bare little rooms in Throop Street.

Now it so happened that on a certain Thursday in May, Hannah Wenzel, having been paid a dollar by a neighbor for a day's washing, had put the money, in the form of four silver dimes and a number of nickels and pennies, into a small black purse which she kept in the top drawer of the bureau in the front room. And it further happened that Albert, coming in from the street that afternoon while his mother was out in the yard hanging up clothes and his older sister was minding the baby in the kitchen, saw the drawer standing a little open, and the purse within it. What passed through his mind at that moment no one, least of all himself, could have told. It was not a reasoned thing. There was no weighing of right and wrong, no deliberate choice of evil. There was only the purse, and the memory of the jars, and a sudden, overwhelming impulse, as chemic and as blind as the impulse which turns a plant toward the sun. He opened the purse, took out a nickel, closed it again, and was gone from the house before he had fairly realized what he had done.

At Mrs. Schaub's he bought ten jawbreakers, a licorice whip, and a stick of peppermint, and he ate the greater part of them sitting on the curb behind the coal yard, where no one could see him. They were very good. And yet, even as he ate them, something had begun to stir in him which spoiled their sweetness, a vague, uneasy heaviness, a sense of having stepped outside some invisible line, which grew rather than lessened as the afternoon wore on. By the time he came home to supper he had two jawbreakers left, hidden in the pocket of his knee-pants, and a face so guilty that his mother, had she not been tired and preoccupied, must have noticed it at once.

It was not his mother, however, but his father who discovered the theft. Thomas Wenzel had a habit, which his wife found irksome but did not oppose, of going over the household money each evening after supper, counting it, and entering the sum in a small, greasy account book in which he kept a record of every cent that came into or went out of the house. On this particular evening, sitting at the kitchen table under the smoky lamp, with his spectacles on his nose and his stubby fingers moving slowly among the coins, he found that there were ninety-five cents in the purse instead of a dollar.

"Hannah," he said, looking up, "how much did Mrs. Kranz pay you?"

"A dollar," said his wife from the sink. "Why?"

"Did you spend some?"

"No. I put it right in the drawer."

He counted it again, slowly, his lips moving. It was still ninety-five cents. And then, as he sat there frowning, his eye fell upon Albert, who was sitting on the low stool by the stove, very still, with his hands between his knees, and something in the boy's attitude, in the stiffness of his small back and the way he would not look up, told the man everything.

"Albert," he said. "Come here."

The boy came. He came slowly, dragging his feet a little, and stood before his father with his eyes on the floor.

"Did you take a nickel out of your mother's purse?"

There was a silence. In that silence many things might have happened. Had the boy been of a bolder or a more calculating disposition, he might have lied, and very possibly been believed, for the evidence against him was nothing more than a look. But he was neither bold nor calculating. He was only frightened, and ashamed, and possessed by that terrible inability to dissemble which is the mark of so many sensitive natures. His lip began to tremble.

"Yes," he whispered.

Thomas Wenzel put down his spectacles. It is necessary, if one is to judge him fairly, to understand what that admission meant to him. To the outsider, the affluent, comfortable observer who has never had to count his pennies, it may seem a small thing indeed, a nickel, a little candy, a childish lapse such as all children are guilty of at one time or another. But to Thomas Wenzel it was not small. It was the very thing he had feared and fought against all his life, appearing suddenly in his own house, in his own child. He had seen men go down. He had seen, in the brickyard at Joliet, a young fellow of his own age who had begun by pilfering small sums from the paymaster's box and had ended, five years later, in the penitentiary across the road. He had seen families in this very street broken up and scattered because the father drank, or stole, or could not keep a job. The world, as he saw it, was a vast and pitiless machine which would grind to powder anyone who stepped out of the narrow path of rectitude, and his son had just stepped out of it. That the step was a small one made no difference. All great falls began with small steps. Was it not so written? And who was he, a poor ignorant workingman, to know where this one might lead?

So it was that something more than anger rose in him at that moment, something compounded of fear, and of shame, and of a dim, half-conscious bitterness against the life which had made him what he was, and which now seemed bent upon taking even his children from him. His face darkened. His heavy hands, lying on the table, closed slowly into fists.

"What did you do with it?"

"I bought candy," said the boy, and began to cry.

"Candy!" The word seemed to strike the man like a blow. "Candy! Your mother stands over a washtub all day, all day, for a dollar, and you steal from her for candy! Do you know what a nickel is? Do you know what it buys? It buys bread. It buys a quart of milk for your little sister. And you throw it away on candy, like a, like a" he searched for a word strong enough to express his feeling, and found none, "like a thief!"

"Thomas," said his wife from the sink, in a low voice. "He's only little."

"Little!" He turned on her. "So he is little. And when he is big? When he is big, what then? He takes from the till where he works. He takes from his boss. And then they put him in jail, and then what do you say? He was only little?" He turned back to the child. "Look at me."

The boy looked up. His face was wet, his dark eyes swimming, his mouth drawn down into that square, quivering shape which a child's mouth takes when grief has passed beyond all control. It was a pitiful sight, and perhaps somewhere in the father's heart it was felt as such. But the man was caught now in the current of his own emotion, and it carried him on.

"Do you know what God does to thieves? Do you know what the Bible says? 'Thou shalt not steal.' It is one of the commandments. You know the commandments. Pastor Mueller teaches you. And you break it. In your own house you break it, from your own mother." He shook his head slowly, heavily, as if the weight of the thing were almost more than he could bear. "I work all my life. All my life I am honest. Never once do I take a penny that is not mine. Never once. And now my own boy."

He stopped. There was a silence in the little kitchen, broken only by the boy's sobbing and the ticking of the cheap nickel clock on the shelf above the stove. The older girl, Lena, had come to the doorway with the baby in her arms and stood there staring, round-eyed. Hannah Wenzel had turned from the sink and was wiping her hands slowly on her apron, her thin face drawn and anxious.

"Have you any left?" said the father at length.

The boy put his hand into his pocket and drew out the two jawbreakers, one red and one green, a little sticky now from the warmth of his body. He held them out on his palm. Thomas Wenzel looked at them for a moment, and then he took them, rose, opened the door of the stove, and threw them into the fire. Then he came back and sat down.

"Tomorrow," he said, "you go to Mrs. Schaub and you tell her what you did. You tell her you stole the money she has in her drawer. And on Saturday you carry coal for Mr. Brandt, and what he pays you, you give to your mother. Every cent. And tonight you go to bed with no supper tomorrow either, only bread. And you get down on your knees and ask God to forgive you, because I do not know if He will."

Whether he should also have whipped the boy, as his own father in Hesse would certainly have whipped him, was a question that crossed his mind and was put aside. He did not quite know why he put it aside. Perhaps it was the look on his wife's face. Perhaps it was something in the child himself, some quality of fragility and helplessness which made the thought of striking him seem, even to this rigid and unimaginative man, a thing not to be done. At any rate he did not do it, and the boy, still sobbing, was sent off to the little back bedroom which he shared with his sister, and the door was closed upon him.

What the child felt, lying there in the dark on the hard straw mattress, with the sounds of the household coming faintly to him through the thin board wall, it would take a wiser pen than this to set down fully. There was shame in it, certainly, a deep and burning shame, and fear of God, whom he pictured, after the manner of Pastor Mueller's sermons, as a vast and bearded and very angry old man seated somewhere above the clouds, keeping a book not unlike his father's account book in which every sin was entered. There was misery at his father's anger, and a dread of the morrow and of Mrs. Schaub's sharp eyes. But there was something else too, something which he could not have named and which his father would not have understood, a kind of dull, bewildered resentment, not against his father exactly, nor against God, but against the whole order of things which set the bright jars in the window and then forbade him to have what was in them. Why should there be such things, if one could not have them? Why should Mrs. Schaub's window be so beautiful, and his own house so bare? He did not know. No one had ever told him. And lying there, with his face in the thin pillow and the taste of peppermint still faintly in his mouth, he felt for the first time, dimly and without words, that vast and insoluble disproportion between desire and possession which is perhaps the oldest and most universal of all human griefs.

In the kitchen, meanwhile, Thomas Wenzel sat for a long time at the table without moving. He had put away the account book and the purse, and his wife had finished the dishes and gone in to put the baby down, and still he sat there, his heavy hands lying loosely before him, his eyes on the lamp. The anger had gone out of him now, and what was left was a kind of weary heaviness, an aching sense of something wrong which he could neither define nor mend. He had done his duty. He was sure of that. A father must punish wrongdoing; otherwise the child grows up wicked. And yet he could not rid himself of the memory of the boy's face, and of the two jawbreakers lying on that small, sticky palm, and of the way the child had looked at him, not defiantly, but with a kind of terrible, uncomprehending appeal, as if asking for something which his father did not know how to give.

After a while he got up and went to the door of the back bedroom and stood listening. The sobbing had stopped. He opened the door softly and looked in. In the faint light from the kitchen he could see the boy lying on his side, asleep, one arm flung up over his head, his cheeks still streaked with dried tears. He looked very small. Thomas Wenzel stood there for some minutes, his hand on the latch, his heavy face working in a way that no one had ever seen it work. Then he closed the door again and went back to the table and sat down.

"Hannah," he said, when his wife came out again, "maybe Saturday, if he carries the coal, I give him a penny for himself."

His wife looked at him, and something softened in her tired face. But she said nothing, for she knew him, and knew that he would very likely not do it, or that if he did, he would give it in such a manner as to rob it of half its sweetness. And in this she was right. For Thomas Wenzel was what life had made him, as Albert was what life was making him, and neither of them could have been otherwise. The forces which had shaped the one, the poverty, the fear, the narrow creed, the long years of grinding toil, were even now at work upon the other, and would go on working, silently and inexorably, long after this small evening in Throop Street had been forgotten by everyone save, perhaps, the boy himself. Such is the way of things. We punish in our children the very hungers which the world has planted in them, and which it has refused, in ourselves, to satisfy; and we call it righteousness, and lie awake, not knowing why we are sad.

Here is an excerpt of Theodore Dreiser's writing, to show you their style:

But in the interim, in connection with his relations with Roberta no least reference to Sondra, although, even when near her in the factory or her room, he could not keep his thoughts from wandering away to where Sondra in her imaginary high social world might be. The while Roberta, at moments only sensing a drift and remoteness in his thought and attitude which had nothing to do with her, was wondering what it was that of late was beginning to occupy him so completely. And he, in his turn, when she was not looking was thinking—supposing?—supposing—(since she had troubled to recall herself to him), that he could interest a girl like Sondra in him? What then of Roberta? What? And in the face of this intimate relation that had now been established between them? (Goodness! The deuce!) And that he did care for her (yes, he did), although now—basking in the direct rays of this newer luminary—he could scarcely see Roberta any longer, so strong were the actinic rays of this other. Was he all wrong? Was it evil to be like this? His mother would say so! And his father too—and perhaps everybody who thought right about life—Sondra Finchley, maybe—the Griffiths—all. And yet! And yet! It was snowing the first light snow of the year as Clyde, arrayed in a new collapsible silk hat and white silk muffler, both suggested by a friendly haberdasher—Orrin Short, with whom recently he had come in contact here—and a new silk umbrella wherewith to protect himself from the snow, made his way toward the very interesting, if not so very imposing residence of the Trumbulls on Wykeagy Avenue. It was quaint, low and rambling, and the lights beaming from within upon the many drawn blinds gave it a Christmas-card effect. And before it, even at the prompt hour at which he arrived, were ranged a half dozen handsome cars of various builds and colors. The sight of them, sprinkled on tops, running boards and fenders with the fresh, flaky snow, gave him a keen sense of a deficiency that was not likely soon to be remedied in his case—the want of ample means wherewith to equip himself with such a necessity as that. And inside as he approached the door he could hear voices, laughter and conversation commingled. A tall, thin servant relieved him of his hat, coat and umbrella and he found himself face to face with Jill Trumbull, who apparently was on the look-out for him—a smooth, curly-haired blonde girl, not too thrillingly pretty, but brisk and smart, in white satin with arms and shoulders bare and rhinestones banded around her forehead.

"No trouble to tell who you are," she said gayly, approaching and giving Clyde her hand. "I'm Jill Trumbull. Miss Finchley hasn't come yet. But I can do the honors just as well, I guess. Come right in where the rest of us are." She led the way into a series of connecting rooms that seemed to join each other at right angles, adding as she went, "You do look an awful lot like Gil Griffiths, don't you?"

"Do I?" smiled Clyde simply and courageously and very much flattered by the comparison. The ceilings were low. Pretty lamps behind painted shades hugged dark walls. Open fires in two connecting rooms cast a rosy glow upon cushioned and comfortable furniture. There were pictures, books, objects of art.

"Here, Tracy, you do the announcing, will you?" she called. "My brother, Tracy Trumbull, Mr. Griffiths. Mr. Clyde Griffiths, everybody," she added, surveying the company in general which in turn fixed varying eyes upon him, while Tracy Trumbull took him by the hand. Clyde, suffering from a sense of being studied, nevertheless achieved a warm smile. At the same time he realized that for the moment at least conversation had stopped. "Don't all stop talking on my account," he ventured, with a smile, which caused most of those present to conceive of him as at his ease and resourceful. At the same time Tracy added: "I'm not going to do any man-to-man introduction stuff. We'll stand right here and point 'em out. That's my sister, Gertrude, over there talking to Scott Nicholson." Clyde noted that a small, dark girl dressed in pink with a pretty and yet saucy and piquant face, nodded to him. And beside her a very de rigueur youth of fine physique and pink complexion nodded jerkily. "Howja do." And a few feet from them near a deep window stood a tall and yet graceful girl of dark and by no means ravishing features talking to a broad-shouldered and deep-chested youth of less than her height, who were proclaimed to be Arabella Stark and Frank Harriet. "They're arguing over a recent Cornell-Syracuse foot-ball game ... Burchard Taylor and Miss Phant of Utica," he went on almost too swiftly for Clyde to assemble any mental notes. "Perley Haynes and Miss Vanda Steele ... well, I guess that's all as yet. Oh, no, here come Grant and Nina Temple." Clyde paused and gazed as a tall and somewhat dandified-looking youth, sharp of face and with murky gray eyes, steered a trim, young, plump girl in fawn gray and with a light chestnut braid of hair laid carefully above her forehead, into the middle of the room.

"Hello, Jill. Hello, Vanda. Hello, Wynette." In the midst of these greetings on his part, Clyde was presented to these two, neither of whom seemed to pay much attention to him. "Didn't think we'd make it," went on young Cranston speaking to all at once. "Nina didn't want to come, but I promised Bertine and Jill or I wouldn't have, either. We were up at the Bagley's. Guess who's up there, Scott. Van Peterson and Rhoda Hull. They're just over for the day."

"You don't say," called Scott Nicholson, a determined and self-centered looking individual. Clyde was arrested by the very definite sense of social security and ease that seemed to reside in everybody. "Why didn't you bring 'em along? I'd like to see Rhoda again and Van, too."

"Couldn't. They have to go back early, they say. They may stop in later for a minute. Gee, isn't dinner served yet? I expected to sit right down."

"These lawyers! Don't you know they don't eat often?" commented Frank Harriet, who was a short, but broad-chested and smiling youth, very agreeable, very good-looking and with even, white teeth. Clyde liked him.

"Well, whether they do or not, we do, or out I go. Did you hear who is being touted for stroke next year over at Cornell?" This college chatter relating to Cornell and shared by Harriet, Cranston and others, Clyde could not understand. He had scarcely heard of the various colleges with which this group was all too familiar. At the same time he was wise enough to sense the defect and steer clear of any questions or conversations which might relate to them. However, because of this, he at once felt out of it. These people were better informed than he was—had been to colleges. Perhaps he had better claim that he had been to some school. In Kansas City he had heard of the State University of Kansas—not so very far from there. Also the University of Missouri. And in Chicago of the University of Chicago. Could he say that he had been to one of those—that Kansas one, for a little while, anyway? On the instant he proposed to claim it, if asked, and then look up afterwards what, if anything, he was supposed to know about it—what, for instance, he might have studied. He had heard of mathematics somewhere. Why not that? But these people, as he could see, were too much interested in themselves to pay much attention to him now. He might be a Griffiths and important to some outside, but here not so much—a matter of course, as it were. And because Tracy Trumbull for the moment had turned to say something to Wynette Phant, he felt quite alone, beached and helpless and with no one to talk to. But just then the small, dark girl, Gertrude, came over to him.

"The crowd's a little late in getting together. It always is. If we said eight, they'd come at eight-thirty or nine. Isn't that always the way?"

"It certainly is," replied Clyde gratefully, endeavoring to appear as brisk and as much at ease as possible.

"I'm Gertrude Trumbull," she repeated. "The sister of the good-looking Jill," a cynical and yet amused smile played about her mouth and eyes. "You nodded to me, but you don't know me. Just the same we've been hearing a lot about you." She teased in an attempt to trouble Clyde a little, if possible. "A mysterious Griffiths here in Lycurgus whom no one seems to have met. I saw you once in Central Avenue, though. You were going into Rich's candy store. You didn't know that, though. Do you like candy?"

"Oh, yes, I like candy. Why?" asked Clyde on the instant feeling teased and disturbed, since the girl for whom he was buying the candy was Roberta. At the same time he could not help feeling slightly more at ease with this girl than with some others, for although cynical and not so attractive, her manner was genial and she now spelled escape from isolation and hence diffidence.

"You're probably just saying that," she laughed, a bantering look in her eyes. "More likely you were buying it for some girl. You have a girl, haven't you?"

"Why—" Clyde paused for the fraction of a second because as she asked this Roberta came into his mind and the query, "Had any one ever seen him with Roberta?" flitted through his brain. Also thinking at the same time, what a bold, teasing, intelligent girl this was, different from any that thus far he had known. Yet quite without more pause he added: "No, I haven't. What makes you ask that?" As he said this there came to him the thought of what Roberta would think if she could hear him. "But what a question," he continued a little nervously now. "You like to tease, don't you?"

"Who, me? Oh, no. I wouldn't do anything like that. But I'm sure you have just the same. I like to ask questions sometimes, just to see what people will say when they don't want you to know what they really think." She beamed into Clyde's eyes amusedly and defiantly. "But I know you have a girl just the same. All good-looking fellows have."

"Oh, am I good-looking?" he beamed nervously, amused and yet pleased. "Who said so?"

"As though you didn't know. Well, different people. I for one. And Sondra Finchley thinks you're good-looking, too. She's only interested in men who are. So does my sister Jill, for that matter. And she only likes men who are good-looking. I'm different because I'm not so good-looking myself." She blinked cynically and teasingly into his eyes, which caused him to feel oddly out of place, not able to cope with such a girl at all, at the same time very much flattered and amused. "But don't you think you're better looking than your cousin," she went on sharply and even commandingly. "Some people think you are." Although a little staggered and yet flattered by this question which propounded what he might have liked to believe, and although intrigued by this girl's interest in him, still Clyde would not have dreamed of venturing any such assertion even though he had believed it. Too vividly it brought the aggressive and determined and even at times revengeful-looking features of Gilbert before him, who, stirred by such a report as this, would not hesitate to pay him out.

It was a little after eight o'clock of a raw November evening when Harvey Lusk, a clerk of some twelve years' standing in the shipping department of the Ohio Wholesale Hardware Company, let himself into the three-room flat on Bancroft Street, Toledo, which for the past six years he and his wife, Ida, had occupied together. And at once, even before he had hung his derby and his worn brown overcoat on the hook behind the door, he sensed that something was wrong. For the lamp in the little front room, ordinarily turned low and left burning for him upon the center table, was turned high, too high, so that the chimney was smudged with a faint ring of soot. And beside it, under the yellow glare, lay an envelope, long and buff-colored, of the kind that the Mutual Savings & Loan sent out once in each quarter, and which he, by a ruse that had served him well enough for a time, had arranged to have directed to him at the office rather than here. How, then, had it come? And opened? He stood quite still, his hand still upon the knob of the door, and felt the blood go out of his face and then come back with an uncomfortable rush to his ears.

For it must be explained that Harvey Lusk, a man of forty-one, of medium height, rather heavy-shouldered and soft of build, with thinning sandy hair and pale, uncertain blue eyes that gave him at times an air of mild apology, had been, for upwards of a year now, engaged in a secret enterprise of which his wife knew nothing. Some fourteen months before, through the agency of one Ed Hollister, a traveling man for a varnish concern whom he had come to know at the office, he had been drawn into the purchase of certain lots in a proposed suburb to be called Maumee Heights, lying several miles to the south and west of the city along a projected car line. The car line, as Hollister had represented it, was a certainty. The lots, so Hollister said, would treble in value inside of two years. And Harvey, who had been watching for twelve years the slow, almost imperceptible accretion of their savings at the rate of four and a half per cent (eleven hundred and forty dollars, the whole fruit of his and Ida's skimping and self-denial, intended, as both of them had long said, for a little house of their own), had been seized with a fever which he could not now very well account for even to himself. To be something more than a clerk! To walk into the office some day with a check for three or four thousand dollars in his pocket, and say to old Tuttle, the manager, that he was through! To buy Ida a sealskin coat such as Mrs. Rennick, the doctor's wife across the way, wore to church! These were the visions, cheap and gaudy as a chromo, and yet compelling as all such visions are to the starved, which had led him by degrees to draw out first two hundred, then three hundred and fifty, and at last nearly the whole of the account. And the car line had not come. And Hollister had gone to Indianapolis. And the lots—well, the lots were there still, a stretch of wet, stubbled pasture with a few weathered stakes in it, and a sign, now half blown down, which read MAUMEE HEIGHTS—THE COMING SUBURB.

He hung up his coat now very slowly, as though by delaying he might somehow alter what was before him. Then he turned. And there in the doorway of the little kitchen, drying her hands upon a gingham apron, stood Ida.

She was a woman of thirty-eight, small, rather thin, with a sallow, careful face which in her girlhood in Defiance had been called pretty, and which even now, when she was pleased, had a kind of pinched sweetness about it. But she was not pleased now. Her lips were drawn together into a thin line, and her eyes, which were brown and small and very steady, were fixed upon him with an expression which he had seen in them only once or twice before in all their married life—a look not so much of anger as of a cold, settled, appraising contempt, as though she were seeing him for the first time and did not like what she saw.

"Well," she said, "you're late."

"Yes, I—we had a car of stoves come in at five. Tuttle wanted it checked tonight." This was true, as it happened, and yet as he said it he was conscious that it sounded like a lie, and that she would take it for one.

"Supper's on the back of the stove. It's been there since six." She did not move from the doorway.

"I'm not very hungry." He went toward the table, not to the envelope, but around it, as one might skirt a hole in the floor, and sat down heavily in the Morris chair by the window. Outside, the arc light at the corner swung a little in the wind, sending a pale, shifting radiance across the wet pavement and the bare, dripping branches of the one maple that stood before the house. A street car went by, clanging, its windows full of tired faces. He looked at it rather than at her.

"Aren't you going to ask me what that is?" she said at last.

"What what is?"

"Harvey Lusk, don't you dare." Her voice did not rise, and that was the worst of it. Had she screamed, had she wept, he would have known better what to do. "Don't you dare sit there and act as though you didn't see it. Mr. Fenwick brought it. He came here himself, this afternoon, about three. He said they'd been sending things to you at the office and you hadn't answered, and he thought—he thought maybe there was some mistake, because he knew it was a joint account and I'd always been the one to come in and sign. Twelve years I've made over my dresses and turned your collars and cuffs and bought soup bones instead of meat and walked instead of taking the car, and didn't go home to see my own mother when she was sick last winter because it was three dollars and forty cents for the round trip, and you said—you said yourself—we ought to put it by. "It wasn't all the time," he said weakly. "It was only this last year."

"Only this last year! Oh, well, then!"

He winced. And then, because there was no help for it and because, besides, a kind of desperate need to justify himself had begun to stir in him, he told her—haltingly, with many pauses and much rubbing of his forehead with the back of his hand—about Hollister, and the Heights, and the car line that was to have come, and how it was a sure thing, everybody said so, men in the office who knew more about such things than he did, and how in two years, or three at the most, they would have had three times as much, four times maybe, and then she could have had her house—not a little box of a place like the Rennicks', but something on Collingwood Avenue, maybe, with a porch all round it. And as he talked, the vision came back to him a little, so that his voice took on, almost against his will, something of the old eagerness, and he leaned forward in the chair. But she only stood and looked at him, and the eagerness died.

"And where is it now, this car line?"

"Well, they—the company—they decided to run it out Monroe Street instead. For the present. But that's not to say they won't—"

"And Mr. Hollister?"

"He's gone to Indianapolis. He's got a new territory." He did not look up.

"And the lots? What are they worth? Today? If you went out and tried to sell them?"

He was silent. She knew. He knew she knew. There was no market for them at all, or at best perhaps forty or fifty dollars apiece to some farmer who might want the pasture back. He had found that out a month ago from a real estate man on Summit Street, who had laughed at him—not unkindly, but laughed all the same.

"So that's it," she said quietly. "That's what it comes to."

And now she sat down, not in the rocker across from him, but on the straight cane-bottomed chair by the table, very upright, with her hands folded in her lap upon the apron, and stared not at him but at the lamp. The clock on the shelf over the gas grate, a cheap nickel affair which they had bought at Lamson's the first year they were married, ticked loudly. Somewhere below, in the flat of the Ruhlmans, a child was crying fretfully and a woman's voice was hushing it. And Harvey, looking at his wife's profile in the hard yellow light, the little lines about her mouth and at the corners of her eyes, the gray that had begun to come into her hair just above the temple, and which he had never before particularly noticed, was seized with a kind of horror. Not at what he had lost—that he had lived with for weeks—but at what he saw now, as in a flash, of the whole of their life together. The narrow rooms. The soup bones. The made-over dresses. The years running on and on like this, just like this, with nothing at the end of them. And he had tried—God knows, after his fashion he had tried—to break out of it. And now this. Was it not cruel, the way life used a man? Was he so much worse than other men, than Hollister, say, who was in Indianapolis with a new territory and no doubt laughing? Or the street railway people, who could move a car line from one street to another with a stroke of a pen and never know or care what happened to the little people who had staked everything on its coming? He did not know. He was not a thinker. But he felt, dimly, as such men do, that he was caught in something larger than himself, some vast, indifferent, grinding machine of chance and greed, and that he had been ground.

"Ida," he said at last, huskily, "I'm sorry. I'm—I don't know what to say. I thought—I honestly thought—"

"You thought." She turned toward him now, and the contempt was back, but mingled with something else, something tired and almost pitying, which was worse. "You never thought, Harvey. That's just it. You never once in your life thought. You just wanted. Like a child at a candy counter. You saw that sealskin coat on Myra Rennick, I suppose, and you thought—" She laughed again. "Oh, I know. Don't tell me. I've seen you look at their automobile when it comes round the corner. I've seen you look at those men that come out of the Secor Hotel with cigars. You think I don't see things? I see everything. I've been seeing for twelve years."

"Well, and what if I did?" he flared, stung at last into a feeble defiance. "What if I did look? Is a man to go on all his life checking stoves in a freight shed at seventy dollars a month and never even look? Is that what you want? Is that all you want? Well, I don't. I didn't. I wanted something better for both of us. Is that a crime?"

"Something better," she repeated slowly, as though tasting the words. "Something better. And so you took the only thing we had—the only thing, Harvey—and you threw it into a mud field out past the city limits on the word of a varnish drummer you'd known six weeks. And never said a word to me. Not one word. That's what I can't—" and here her voice broke at last, and she put one hand up quickly to her mouth, "—that's what I can't get past. Not the money. I could stand the money. We've been poor before. But that you'd sit across from me at this table, night after night, all those months, and eat what I'd cooked and talk about the weather and the Ruhlmans' baby and what Tuttle said, and all the time—all the time—"

She could not finish. She bent forward a little in the chair, her thin shoulders shaking, though she made almost no sound. And Harvey, watching her, was torn by such a welter of emotions as he had seldom known—remorse, and pity, and a desire to go to her, and at the same time a strange, sullen reluctance that held him in the chair, because he feared that if he went she would push him away, and that he could not bear. Also—and this was the ugliest thing, and he knew it even as he felt it—a small, mean voice in him was saying: There, now. She'll cry it out. And then it'll be over, and things will go on. They always do.

But would they? He looked at her and was not sure.

"Ida," he said again, and got up, and went over to her, and stood beside her chair, awkwardly, his hand hovering above her shoulder. "Ida, listen. I'll make it up. I swear I will. I'll speak to Tuttle about that place in the order department. Baines is leaving the first of the year—everybody knows it. That's ninety a month. And I'll—I'll get a little something on the side. Bookkeeping, maybe, nights. There's men do that. In two years—three, maybe—we'll have it back. Every cent. I'll never touch it again. I'll never do anything again without asking you first. Never. I promise you."

She did not answer for a long time. Then she sat up, and wiped her eyes with the corner of the apron, quite deliberately, and looked up at him. And what he saw in her face then he was to remember for many a year afterward—not forgiveness, exactly, nor yet its opposite, but a kind of final, weary knowledge, as though she had just added up a long column of figures and found the sum to be what she had always, in some secret place, feared it would be.

"Two years," she said. "Three years. I'll be forty-one, Harvey. And you'll be forty-four. And Baines's place will go to young Kessler, because Tuttle likes him, and you know it. And you'll come home some night and tell me about some other man you've met, with some other sure thing." She shook her head slowly. "No. Don't. I don't want to hear any more promises tonight. I've heard enough. I'm tired."

"But you'll—you're not going to—" He did not know how to say it. Leave? Go back to Defiance, to her mother and her married sister and their pitying, knowing glances? It had never once occurred to him, in all these months of dread, that she might do that. And now, looking at her, it occurred to him with a force that turned him cold.

"I don't know what I'm going to do," she said. "I'm going to wash up the supper things. That's what I'm going to do. And then I'm going to bed." She rose, and smoothed the apron, and picked up the buff-colored envelope from the table, and looked at it a moment, and then, very carefully, as one might put away a thing of value, slipped it into the pocket of her apron. "You'd better eat something. It's pork and potatoes. It'll be dried out by now, but it's all there is."

And she went back into the kitchen. And presently he heard the clatter of the pump at the sink, and the scrape of the pans, and the small, ordinary, domestic sounds that he had heard every night for twelve years and had never once listened to before.

He stood where she had left him, in the middle of the little front room, under the too-bright lamp with its smudged chimney, his hands hanging at his sides. Outside, the wind had risen, and the arc light swung wider, and a few flakes of wet snow, the first of the year, drifted slantwise past the window and melted on the glass. A car went by. Then another. And Harvey Lusk, clerk, aged forty-one, owner of four lots in the coming suburb of Maumee Heights, stood and listened to his wife washing the dishes, and wondered, in his dim, groping, helpless way, what it was that a man was supposed to do with his life, and why it was that everything he had ever reached for had turned, at the very touch of his hand, to mud and ashes. Was it his fault? Was it anybody's? He could not tell. He only knew that something had happened tonight which could not be undone—that a door somewhere had closed, softly, without any slamming, and that he was on the wrong side of it.

After a while he went and turned the lamp down to where it ought to be.

But in the interim, in connection with his relations with Roberta no least reference to Sondra, although, even when near her in the factory or her room, he could not keep his thoughts from wandering away to where Sondra in her imaginary high social world might be. The while Roberta, at moments only sensing a drift and remoteness in his thought and attitude which had nothing to do with her, was wondering what it was that of late was beginning to occupy him so completely. And he, in his turn, when she was not looking was thinking—supposing?—supposing—(since she had troubled to recall herself to him), that he could interest a girl like Sondra in him? What then of Roberta? What? And in the face of this intimate relation that had now been established between them? (Goodness! The deuce!) And that he did care for her (yes, he did), although now—basking in the direct rays of this newer luminary—he could scarcely see Roberta any longer, so strong were the actinic rays of this other. Was he all wrong? Was it evil to be like this? His mother would say so! And his father too—and perhaps everybody who thought right about life—Sondra Finchley, maybe—the Griffiths—all. And yet! And yet! It was snowing the first light snow of the year as Clyde, arrayed in a new collapsible silk hat and white silk muffler, both suggested by a friendly haberdasher—Orrin Short, with whom recently he had come in contact here—and a new silk umbrella wherewith to protect himself from the snow, made his way toward the very interesting, if not so very imposing residence of the Trumbulls on Wykeagy Avenue. It was quaint, low and rambling, and the lights beaming from within upon the many drawn blinds gave it a Christmas-card effect. And before it, even at the prompt hour at which he arrived, were ranged a half dozen handsome cars of various builds and colors. The sight of them, sprinkled on tops, running boards and fenders with the fresh, flaky snow, gave him a keen sense of a deficiency that was not likely soon to be remedied in his case—the want of ample means wherewith to equip himself with such a necessity as that. And inside as he approached the door he could hear voices, laughter and conversation commingled. A tall, thin servant relieved him of his hat, coat and umbrella and he found himself face to face with Jill Trumbull, who apparently was on the look-out for him—a smooth, curly-haired blonde girl, not too thrillingly pretty, but brisk and smart, in white satin with arms and shoulders bare and rhinestones banded around her forehead.

"No trouble to tell who you are," she said gayly, approaching and giving Clyde her hand. "I'm Jill Trumbull. Miss Finchley hasn't come yet. But I can do the honors just as well, I guess. Come right in where the rest of us are." She led the way into a series of connecting rooms that seemed to join each other at right angles, adding as she went, "You do look an awful lot like Gil Griffiths, don't you?"

"Do I?" smiled Clyde simply and courageously and very much flattered by the comparison. The ceilings were low. Pretty lamps behind painted shades hugged dark walls. Open fires in two connecting rooms cast a rosy glow upon cushioned and comfortable furniture. There were pictures, books, objects of art.

"Here, Tracy, you do the announcing, will you?" she called. "My brother, Tracy Trumbull, Mr. Griffiths. Mr. Clyde Griffiths, everybody," she added, surveying the company in general which in turn fixed varying eyes upon him, while Tracy Trumbull took him by the hand. Clyde, suffering from a sense of being studied, nevertheless achieved a warm smile. At the same time he realized that for the moment at least conversation had stopped. "Don't all stop talking on my account," he ventured, with a smile, which caused most of those present to conceive of him as at his ease and resourceful. At the same time Tracy added: "I'm not going to do any man-to-man introduction stuff. We'll stand right here and point 'em out. That's my sister, Gertrude, over there talking to Scott Nicholson." Clyde noted that a small, dark girl dressed in pink with a pretty and yet saucy and piquant face, nodded to him. And beside her a very de rigueur youth of fine physique and pink complexion nodded jerkily. "Howja do." And a few feet from them near a deep window stood a tall and yet graceful girl of dark and by no means ravishing features talking to a broad-shouldered and deep-chested youth of less than her height, who were proclaimed to be Arabella Stark and Frank Harriet. "They're arguing over a recent Cornell-Syracuse foot-ball game ... Burchard Taylor and Miss Phant of Utica," he went on almost too swiftly for Clyde to assemble any mental notes. "Perley Haynes and Miss Vanda Steele ... well, I guess that's all as yet. Oh, no, here come Grant and Nina Temple." Clyde paused and gazed as a tall and somewhat dandified-looking youth, sharp of face and with murky gray eyes, steered a trim, young, plump girl in fawn gray and with a light chestnut braid of hair laid carefully above her forehead, into the middle of the room.

"Hello, Jill. Hello, Vanda. Hello, Wynette." In the midst of these greetings on his part, Clyde was presented to these two, neither of whom seemed to pay much attention to him. "Didn't think we'd make it," went on young Cranston speaking to all at once. "Nina didn't want to come, but I promised Bertine and Jill or I wouldn't have, either. We were up at the Bagley's. Guess who's up there, Scott. Van Peterson and Rhoda Hull. They're just over for the day."

"You don't say," called Scott Nicholson, a determined and self-centered looking individual. Clyde was arrested by the very definite sense of social security and ease that seemed to reside in everybody. "Why didn't you bring 'em along? I'd like to see Rhoda again and Van, too."

"Couldn't. They have to go back early, they say. They may stop in later for a minute. Gee, isn't dinner served yet? I expected to sit right down."

"These lawyers! Don't you know they don't eat often?" commented Frank Harriet, who was a short, but broad-chested and smiling youth, very agreeable, very good-looking and with even, white teeth. Clyde liked him.

"Well, whether they do or not, we do, or out I go. Did you hear who is being touted for stroke next year over at Cornell?" This college chatter relating to Cornell and shared by Harriet, Cranston and others, Clyde could not understand. He had scarcely heard of the various colleges with which this group was all too familiar. At the same time he was wise enough to sense the defect and steer clear of any questions or conversations which might relate to them. However, because of this, he at once felt out of it. These people were better informed than he was—had been to colleges. Perhaps he had better claim that he had been to some school. In Kansas City he had heard of the State University of Kansas—not so very far from there. Also the University of Missouri. And in Chicago of the University of Chicago. Could he say that he had been to one of those—that Kansas one, for a little while, anyway? On the instant he proposed to claim it, if asked, and then look up afterwards what, if anything, he was supposed to know about it—what, for instance, he might have studied. He had heard of mathematics somewhere. Why not that? But these people, as he could see, were too much interested in themselves to pay much attention to him now. He might be a Griffiths and important to some outside, but here not so much—a matter of course, as it were. And because Tracy Trumbull for the moment had turned to say something to Wynette Phant, he felt quite alone, beached and helpless and with no one to talk to. But just then the small, dark girl, Gertrude, came over to him.

"The crowd's a little late in getting together. It always is. If we said eight, they'd come at eight-thirty or nine. Isn't that always the way?"

"It certainly is," replied Clyde gratefully, endeavoring to appear as brisk and as much at ease as possible.

"I'm Gertrude Trumbull," she repeated. "The sister of the good-looking Jill," a cynical and yet amused smile played about her mouth and eyes. "You nodded to me, but you don't know me. Just the same we've been hearing a lot about you." She teased in an attempt to trouble Clyde a little, if possible. "A mysterious Griffiths here in Lycurgus whom no one seems to have met. I saw you once in Central Avenue, though. You were going into Rich's candy store. You didn't know that, though. Do you like candy?"

"Oh, yes, I like candy. Why?" asked Clyde on the instant feeling teased and disturbed, since the girl for whom he was buying the candy was Roberta. At the same time he could not help feeling slightly more at ease with this girl than with some others, for although cynical and not so attractive, her manner was genial and she now spelled escape from isolation and hence diffidence.

"You're probably just saying that," she laughed, a bantering look in her eyes. "More likely you were buying it for some girl. You have a girl, haven't you?"

"Why—" Clyde paused for the fraction of a second because as she asked this Roberta came into his mind and the query, "Had any one ever seen him with Roberta?" flitted through his brain. Also thinking at the same time, what a bold, teasing, intelligent girl this was, different from any that thus far he had known. Yet quite without more pause he added: "No, I haven't. What makes you ask that?" As he said this there came to him the thought of what Roberta would think if she could hear him. "But what a question," he continued a little nervously now. "You like to tease, don't you?"

"Who, me? Oh, no. I wouldn't do anything like that. But I'm sure you have just the same. I like to ask questions sometimes, just to see what people will say when they don't want you to know what they really think." She beamed into Clyde's eyes amusedly and defiantly. "But I know you have a girl just the same. All good-looking fellows have."

"Oh, am I good-looking?" he beamed nervously, amused and yet pleased. "Who said so?"

"As though you didn't know. Well, different people. I for one. And Sondra Finchley thinks you're good-looking, too. She's only interested in men who are. So does my sister Jill, for that matter. And she only likes men who are good-looking. I'm different because I'm not so good-looking myself." She blinked cynically and teasingly into his eyes, which caused him to feel oddly out of place, not able to cope with such a girl at all, at the same time very much flattered and amused. "But don't you think you're better looking than your cousin," she went on sharply and even commandingly. "Some people think you are." Although a little staggered and yet flattered by this question which propounded what he might have liked to believe, and although intrigued by this girl's interest in him, still Clyde would not have dreamed of venturing any such assertion even though he had believed it. Too vividly it brought the aggressive and determined and even at times revengeful-looking features of Gilbert before him, who, stirred by such a report as this, would not hesitate to pay him out.

"Why I don't think anything of the kind," he laughed. "Honest, I don't. Of course I don't."

"Oh, well, then maybe you don't, but you are just the same. But that won't help you much either, unless you have money—that is, if you want to run with people who have." She looked up at him and added quite blandly. "People like money even more than they do looks." What a sharp girl this was, he thought, and what a hard, cold statement. It cut him not a little, even though she had not intended that it should. But just then Sondra herself entered with some youth whom Clyde did not know—a tall, gangling, but very smartly-dressed individual. And after them, along with others, Bertine and Stuart Finchley.

"Here she is now," added Gertrude a little spitefully, for she resented the fact that Sondra was so much better-looking than either she or her sister, and that she had expressed an interest in Clyde. "She'll be looking to see if you notice how pretty she looks, so don't disappoint her." The impact of this remark, a reflection of the exact truth, was not necessary to cause Clyde to gaze attentively, and even eagerly. For apart from her local position and means and taste in dress and manners, Sondra was of the exact order and spirit that most intrigued him—a somewhat refined (and because of means and position showered upon her) less savage, although scarcely less self-centered, Hortense Briggs. She was, in her small, intense way, a seeking Aphrodite, eager to prove to any who were sufficiently attractive the destroying power of her charm, while at the same time retaining her own personality and individuality free of any entangling alliance or compromise. However, for varying reasons which she could not quite explain to herself, Clyde appealed to her. He might not be anything socially or financially, but he was interesting to her. Hence she was now keen, first to see if he were present, next to be sure that he gained no hint that she had seen him first, and lastly to act as grandly as possible for his benefit—a Hortensian procedure and type of thought that was exactly the thing best calculated to impress him. He gazed and there she was—tripping here and there in a filmy chiffon dance frock, shaded from palest yellow to deepest orange, which most enhanced her dark eyes and hair. And having exchanged a dozen or more "Oh, Hellos," and references with one and another to this, that and the other local event, she at last condescended to evince awareness of his proximity.

"Oh, here you are. You decided to come after all. I wasn't sure whether you would think it worth while. You've been introduced to everybody, of course?" She looked around as much as to say, that if he had not been she would proceed to serve him in this way. The others, not so very much impressed by Clyde, were still not a little interested by the fact that she seemed so interested in him.

"Yes, I met nearly everybody, I think."

"Except Freddie Sells. He came in with me just now. Here you are, Freddie," she called to a tall and slender youth, smooth of cheek and obviously becurled as to hair, who now came over and in his closely-fitting dress coat looked down on Clyde about as a spring rooster might look down on a sparrow.

"This is Clyde Griffiths, I was telling you about, Fred," she began briskly. "Doesn't he look a lot like Gilbert?"

"Why, you do at that," exclaimed this amiable person, who seemed to be slightly troubled with weak eyes since he bent close. "I hear you're a cousin of Gil's. I know him well. We went through Princeton together. I used to be over here before I joined the General Electric over at Schenectady. But I'm around a good bit yet. You're connected with the factory, I suppose."

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, who, before a youth of obviously so much more training and schooling than he possessed, felt not a little reduced. He began to fear that this individual would try to talk to him about things which he could not understand, things concerning which, having had no consecutive training of any kind, he had never been technically informed.

"In charge of some department, I suppose?"

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, cautiously and nervously.

"You know," went on Mr. Sells, briskly and interestingly, being of a commercial as well as technical turn, "I've always wondered just what, outside of money, there is to the collar business. Gil and I used to argue about that when we were down at college. He used to try to tell me that there was some social importance to making and distributing collars, giving polish and manner to people who wouldn't otherwise have them, if it weren't for cheap collars. I think he musta read that in a book somewhere. I always laughed at him." Clyde was about to attempt an answer, although already beyond his depth in regard to this. "Social importance." Just what did he mean by that—some deep, scientific information that he had acquired at college. He was saved a non-committal or totally uninformed answer by Sondra who, without thought or knowledge of the difficulty which was then and there before him, exclaimed: "Oh, no arguments, Freddie. That's not interesting. Besides I want him to meet my brother and Bertine. You remember Miss Cranston. She was with me at your uncle's last spring." Clyde turned, while Fred made the best of the rebuff by merely looking at Sondra, whom he admired so very much.

"Yes, of course," Clyde began, for he had been studying these two along with others. To him, apart from Sondra, Bertine seemed exceedingly attractive, though quite beyond his understanding also. Being involved, insincere and sly, she merely evoked in him a troubled sense of ineffectiveness, and hence uncertainty, in so far as her particular world was concerned—no more.

"Oh, how do you do? It's nice to see you again," she drawled, the while her greenish-gray eyes went over him in a smiling and yet indifferent and quizzical way. She thought him attractive, but not nearly as shrewd and hard as she would have preferred him to be. "You've been terribly busy with your work, I suppose. But now that you've come out once, I suppose we'll see more of you here and there."

"Well, I hope so," he replied, showing his even teeth. Her eyes seemed to be saying that she did not believe what she was saying and that he did not either, but that it was necessary, possibly amusing, to say something of the sort. And a related, though somewhat modified, version of this same type of treatment was accorded him by Stuart, Sondra's brother.

And a few feet from them near a deep window stood a tall and yet graceful girl of dark and by no means ravishing features talking to a broad-shouldered and deep-chested youth of less than her height, who were proclaimed to be Arabella Stark and Frank Harriet. "They're arguing over a recent Cornell-Syracuse foot-ball game ... Burchard Taylor and Miss Phant of Utica," he went on almost too swiftly for Clyde to assemble any mental notes. "Perley Haynes and Miss Vanda Steele ... well, I guess that's all as yet. Oh, no, here come Grant and Nina Temple." Clyde paused and gazed as a tall and somewhat dandified-looking youth, sharp of face and with murky gray eyes, steered a trim, young, plump girl in fawn gray and with a light chestnut braid of hair laid carefully above her forehead, into the middle of the room.

"Hello, Jill. Hello, Vanda. Hello, Wynette." In the midst of these greetings on his part, Clyde was presented to these two, neither of whom seemed to pay much attention to him. "Didn't think we'd make it," went on young Cranston speaking to all at once. "Nina didn't want to come, but I promised Bertine and Jill or I wouldn't have, either. We were up at the Bagley's. Guess who's up there, Scott. Van Peterson and Rhoda Hull. They're just over for the day."

"You don't say," called Scott Nicholson, a determined and self-centered looking individual. Clyde was arrested by the very definite sense of social security and ease that seemed to reside in everybody. "Why didn't you bring 'em along? I'd like to see Rhoda again and Van, too."

"Couldn't. They have to go back early, they say. They may stop in later for a minute. Gee, isn't dinner served yet? I expected to sit right down."

"These lawyers! Don't you know they don't eat often?" commented Frank Harriet, who was a short, but broad-chested and smiling youth, very agreeable, very good-looking and with even, white teeth. Clyde liked him.

"Well, whether they do or not, we do, or out I go. Did you hear who is being touted for stroke next year over at Cornell?" This college chatter relating to Cornell and shared by Harriet, Cranston and others, Clyde could not understand. He had scarcely heard of the various colleges with which this group was all too familiar. At the same time he was wise enough to sense the defect and steer clear of any questions or conversations which might relate to them. However, because of this, he at once felt out of it. These people were better informed than he was—had been to colleges. Perhaps he had better claim that he had been to some school. In Kansas City he had heard of the State University of Kansas—not so very far from there. Also the University of Missouri. And in Chicago of the University of Chicago. Could he say that he had been to one of those—that Kansas one, for a little while, anyway? On the instant he proposed to claim it, if asked, and then look up afterwards what, if anything, he was supposed to know about it—what, for instance, he might have studied. He had heard of mathematics somewhere. Why not that? But these people, as he could see, were too much interested in themselves to pay much attention to him now. He might be a Griffiths and important to some outside, but here not so much—a matter of course, as it were. And because Tracy Trumbull for the moment had turned to say something to Wynette Phant, he felt quite alone, beached and helpless and with no one to talk to. But just then the small, dark girl, Gertrude, came over to him.

"The crowd's a little late in getting together. It always is. If we said eight, they'd come at eight-thirty or nine. Isn't that always the way?"

"It certainly is," replied Clyde gratefully, endeavoring to appear as brisk and as much at ease as possible.

"I'm Gertrude Trumbull," she repeated. "The sister of the good-looking Jill," a cynical and yet amused smile played about her mouth and eyes. "You nodded to me, but you don't know me. Just the same we've been hearing a lot about you." She teased in an attempt to trouble Clyde a little, if possible. "A mysterious Griffiths here in Lycurgus whom no one seems to have met. I saw you once in Central Avenue, though. You were going into Rich's candy store. You didn't know that, though. Do you like candy?"

"Oh, yes, I like candy. Why?" asked Clyde on the instant feeling teased and disturbed, since the girl for whom he was buying the candy was Roberta. At the same time he could not help feeling slightly more at ease with this girl than with some others, for although cynical and not so attractive, her manner was genial and she now spelled escape from isolation and hence diffidence.

"You're probably just saying that," she laughed, a bantering look in her eyes. "More likely you were buying it for some girl. You have a girl, haven't you?"

"Why—" Clyde paused for the fraction of a second because as she asked this Roberta came into his mind and the query, "Had any one ever seen him with Roberta?" flitted through his brain. Also thinking at the same time, what a bold, teasing, intelligent girl this was, different from any that thus far he had known. Yet quite without more pause he added: "No, I haven't. What makes you ask that?" As he said this there came to him the thought of what Roberta would think if she could hear him. "But what a question," he continued a little nervously now. "You like to tease, don't you?"

"Who, me? Oh, no. I wouldn't do anything like that. But I'm sure you have just the same. I like to ask questions sometimes, just to see what people will say when they don't want you to know what they really think." She beamed into Clyde's eyes amusedly and defiantly. "But I know you have a girl just the same. All good-looking fellows have."

"Oh, am I good-looking?" he beamed nervously, amused and yet pleased. "Who said so?"

"As though you didn't know. Well, different people. I for one. And Sondra Finchley thinks you're good-looking, too. She's only interested in men who are. So does my sister Jill, for that matter. And she only likes men who are good-looking. I'm different because I'm not so good-looking myself." She blinked cynically and teasingly into his eyes, which caused him to feel oddly out of place, not able to cope with such a girl at all, at the same time very much flattered and amused. "But don't you think you're better looking than your cousin," she went on sharply and even commandingly. "Some people think you are." Although a little staggered and yet flattered by this question which propounded what he might have liked to believe, and although intrigued by this girl's interest in him, still Clyde would not have dreamed of venturing any such assertion even though he had believed it. Too vividly it brought the aggressive and determined and even at times revengeful-looking features of Gilbert before him, who, stirred by such a report as this, would not hesitate to pay him out.

"Why I don't think anything of the kind," he laughed. "Honest, I don't. Of course I don't."

"Oh, well, then maybe you don't, but you are just the same. But that won't help you much either, unless you have money—that is, if you want to run with people who have." She looked up at him and added quite blandly. "People like money even more than they do looks." What a sharp girl this was, he thought, and what a hard, cold statement. It cut him not a little, even though she had not intended that it should. But just then Sondra herself entered with some youth whom Clyde did not know—a tall, gangling, but very smartly-dressed individual. And after them, along with others, Bertine and Stuart Finchley.

"Here she is now," added Gertrude a little spitefully, for she resented the fact that Sondra was so much better-looking than either she or her sister, and that she had expressed an interest in Clyde. "She'll be looking to see if you notice how pretty she looks, so don't disappoint her." The impact of this remark, a reflection of the exact truth, was not necessary to cause Clyde to gaze attentively, and even eagerly. For apart from her local position and means and taste in dress and manners, Sondra was of the exact order and spirit that most intrigued him—a somewhat refined (and because of means and position showered upon her) less savage, although scarcely less self-centered, Hortense Briggs. She was, in her small, intense way, a seeking Aphrodite, eager to prove to any who were sufficiently attractive the destroying power of her charm, while at the same time retaining her own personality and individuality free of any entangling alliance or compromise. However, for varying reasons which she could not quite explain to herself, Clyde appealed to her. He might not be anything socially or financially, but he was interesting to her. Hence she was now keen, first to see if he were present, next to be sure that he gained no hint that she had seen him first, and lastly to act as grandly as possible for his benefit—a Hortensian procedure and type of thought that was exactly the thing best calculated to impress him. He gazed and there she was—tripping here and there in a filmy chiffon dance frock, shaded from palest yellow to deepest orange, which most enhanced her dark eyes and hair. And having exchanged a dozen or more "Oh, Hellos," and references with one and another to this, that and the other local event, she at last condescended to evince awareness of his proximity.

"Oh, here you are. You decided to come after all. I wasn't sure whether you would think it worth while. You've been introduced to everybody, of course?" She looked around as much as to say, that if he had not been she would proceed to serve him in this way. The others, not so very much impressed by Clyde, were still not a little interested by the fact that she seemed so interested in him.

"Yes, I met nearly everybody, I think."

"Except Freddie Sells. He came in with me just now. Here you are, Freddie," she called to a tall and slender youth, smooth of cheek and obviously becurled as to hair, who now came over and in his closely-fitting dress coat looked down on Clyde about as a spring rooster might look down on a sparrow.

"This is Clyde Griffiths, I was telling you about, Fred," she began briskly. "Doesn't he look a lot like Gilbert?"

"Why, you do at that," exclaimed this amiable person, who seemed to be slightly troubled with weak eyes since he bent close. "I hear you're a cousin of Gil's. I know him well. We went through Princeton together. I used to be over here before I joined the General Electric over at Schenectady. But I'm around a good bit yet. You're connected with the factory, I suppose."

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, who, before a youth of obviously so much more training and schooling than he possessed, felt not a little reduced. He began to fear that this individual would try to talk to him about things which he could not understand, things concerning which, having had no consecutive training of any kind, he had never been technically informed.

"In charge of some department, I suppose?"

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, cautiously and nervously.

"You know," went on Mr. Sells, briskly and interestingly, being of a commercial as well as technical turn, "I've always wondered just what, outside of money, there is to the collar business. Gil and I used to argue about that when we were down at college. He used to try to tell me that there was some social importance to making and distributing collars, giving polish and manner to people who wouldn't otherwise have them, if it weren't for cheap collars. I think he musta read that in a book somewhere. I always laughed at him." Clyde was about to attempt an answer, although already beyond his depth in regard to this. "Social importance." Just what did he mean by that—some deep, scientific information that he had acquired at college. He was saved a non-committal or totally uninformed answer by Sondra who, without thought or knowledge of the difficulty which was then and there before him, exclaimed: "Oh, no arguments, Freddie. That's not interesting. Besides I want him to meet my brother and Bertine. You remember Miss Cranston. She was with me at your uncle's last spring." Clyde turned, while Fred made the best of the rebuff by merely looking at Sondra, whom he admired so very much.

"Yes, of course," Clyde began, for he had been studying these two along with others. To him, apart from Sondra, Bertine seemed exceedingly attractive, though quite beyond his understanding also. Being involved, insincere and sly, she merely evoked in him a troubled sense of ineffectiveness, and hence uncertainty, in so far as her particular world was concerned—no more.

"Oh, how do you do? It's nice to see you again," she drawled, the while her greenish-gray eyes went over him in a smiling and yet indifferent and quizzical way. She thought him attractive, but not nearly as shrewd and hard as she would have preferred him to be. "You've been terribly busy with your work, I suppose. But now that you've come out once, I suppose we'll see more of you here and there."

"Well, I hope so," he replied, showing his even teeth. Her eyes seemed to be saying that she did not believe what she was saying and that he did not either, but that it was necessary, possibly amusing, to say something of the sort. And a related, though somewhat modified, version of this same type of treatment was accorded him by Stuart, Sondra's brother.
