It was raining, a thin, cold, insistent rain of late October, when Elmer Strader, having walked the six blocks from the elevated station in his one good overcoat (a brown herringbone, purchased two winters before at a sale at Rothschild's and now just slightly gone at the cuffs), made his way along Michigan Avenue toward the Hotel Grantham, where his cousin Walter, of whom he had not had so much as a line in eleven years, was stopping. The lamps along the boulevard, blurred and haloed by the wet, cast long wavering streaks of yellow upon the pavement, and the taxicabs and private cars, their tops glistening, drew up and departed before the great bronze-and-glass entrance with a kind of steady, purring importance which impressed him even before he had come near enough to see the doorman, a large man in a maroon coat and gold braid who seemed to Elmer to look upon everyone approaching on foot with a faint and practiced doubt. And Elmer, conscious of his wet shoes and of the fact that he had come on foot, felt this doubt, or imagined that he did, and was not a little troubled by it.

For what, after all, was he? A clerk, a sort of under-head in the order department of Bassett, Lowe & Company, wholesale hardware, at thirty-two dollars a week, with a wife, Lottie, and a little girl of four, and a flat of five rooms on the second floor of a frame building on Wrightwood Avenue, where the gas jets hissed and the radiators knocked in winter and the street cars clanged past the front windows at all hours. Not much, as he himself was well aware. And Walter? Well, that was just it. He did not know exactly what Walter was, except that the letter, a short, brisk note on heavy cream-colored paper with the name of a Minneapolis land and investment company engraved across the top, had said that he would be in Chicago for three days on business and would like nothing better than to "look up old Elmer and talk over the old times," and that he could be found at the Grantham. And the Grantham, as Elmer knew, was not a place where men of thirty-two dollars a week were likely to be found, either stopping or dining.

Inside, the warmth and the light and the soft murmur of voices struck him all at once. There was a great lobby with marble columns veined in green and gold, and deep leather chairs, and palms in brass tubs, and a long desk behind which young men in black coats moved with a quiet, efficient air. And everywhere were people—men in well-cut coats and gray spats, smoking cigars and talking in low, assured tones; women in furs and small, close hats, with that air of being entirely at home in such surroundings which Elmer had always noted and always envied in people of means. He stood a moment, uncertain whether to inquire at the desk or to wait, and was just deciding that he had better inquire, when a voice, loud and hearty and yet with some quality in it that he recognized on the instant, called out:

"Well, by George! If it isn't Elm! Elm Strader, as I live!"

And there, crossing the lobby toward him with his hand already out, was Walter—a Walter heavier by thirty pounds than the lank, freckled, sandy-haired youth who had left Sullivan County, Indiana, a dozen years before, with a straw suitcase and a ticket to St. Paul; a Walter in a double-breasted suit of dark blue with a faint chalk stripe, a pearl stickpin, a gold watch chain across a waistcoat that had begun to round itself comfortably, and with a face which, though it was still the same face in its general outline, had acquired a ruddy, well-fed, self-satisfied look, a kind of glow, that Elmer had seen often enough on the faces of the buyers and traveling men who came into the office at Bassett, Lowe's, but never before upon anyone so near to him.

"Walt," he said, and smiled, and took the hand, which gripped his own with an almost painful heartiness. "Well, Walt. You look—you look fine. I'd hardly have known you."

"Hardly have known me! Ha! Well, I guess the years do something to a fellow, don't they? Put a little meat on him, anyhow." Walter laughed and patted his waistcoat. "But you—you don't look a day older, Elm. Not a day. A little thinner, maybe. Here, let me get that coat off of you. You're wet through. Didn't you take a cab?"

"Why, no," said Elmer, flushing a little, though he could not have said exactly why. "It's only a step from the L."

"Only a step! In this weather! Well, never mind. Come on in. I've got a table. I told 'em to hold it for us. They know me here now—I always stop here when I'm in town." And with this he took Elmer's arm and steered him, with that easy, proprietary air which Elmer could not help noting, past the columns and the palms and through a wide doorway into a dining room which seemed to Elmer the most splendid he had ever been in—a long, high room with crystal chandeliers and walls paneled in some pale, polished wood, and white tables set with silver and glass that gleamed in the soft light, and waiters gliding here and there, and at one end, behind a screen of ferns, a small orchestra of five or six pieces playing something light and lilting which he did not recognize.

They were shown to a table near a window, where the rain streamed down the dark glass and the lights of the boulevard showed through in long, dissolving smears. And Walter, having ordered for both of them without much consultation—oysters and a clear soup and a planked whitefish, which, he said, was the thing to have here, and coffee afterward—leaned back in his chair and surveyed his cousin with a broad, comfortable, and yet faintly appraising smile.

"Well, Elm," he said, "it's been a long time. A long, long time. Eleven years, isn't it? Twelve, almost. I was thinking about it on the train coming down. I said to myself, I wonder if old Elm remembers the time we swiped the watermelons out of old man Pfeiffer's patch and he set the dog on us?"

"I remember," said Elmer, and laughed, for he did remember, and the memory, coming upon him there in that glittering room, brought with it a sudden and curiously poignant vision—the hot, dusty road between the cornfields, the dull green of the melon vines in the August twilight, the barking of the dog, and the two of them, barefoot and breathless, running and stumbling down the ditch toward the creek, and lying afterward on the bank in the dark, eating the warm, sweet melon with their hands and laughing until they were sick. How free they had been then! How equal! There had been no difference between them at all in those days—none, at any rate, that either of them could have seen. Walter's father had had the eighty acres next to Elmer's father's sixty, and both of them were poor and both mortgaged, and both families went to the same little white Lutheran church on the Carlisle road, and wore the same kind of clothes, and ate the same kind of food. And now—now look!

"And the time," Walter went on, warming to it, "that you fell through the ice on Busseron Creek and I had to pull you out with a fence rail? Your ma liked to have skinned you alive."

"She did, too," said Elmer.

"How is she, by the way? Is she still living?"

"No," said Elmer quietly. "She died three years ago this past spring. Pa went the year before."

"Well, now, that's too bad. I'm sorry to hear it, Elm. I am, honestly. I hadn't heard. You lose track of things, somehow, moving around the way I have." He shook his head and was silent for a moment, though Elmer could not help feeling that the silence was more a matter of form than of feeling—a kind of decent pause, such as one observes, before the talk goes on to other things. "And the farm?"

"Sold," said Elmer. "There wasn't much left after the mortgage was paid off. I got a little over four hundred dollars out of it, all told."

"Four hundred dollars," repeated Walter, and pursed his lips, and Elmer saw in his eyes a flicker of something—was it pity? was it a sort of amused contempt?—which made him wish on the instant that he had not mentioned the sum at all. For to Walter, plainly, four hundred dollars was nothing, a trifle, the price, perhaps, of a good suit of clothes and a week at a hotel like this. Whereas to him it had been—well, it had been the money which had bought the furniture for the flat on Wrightwood Avenue, and paid the doctor when little Edna was born, and there had been nothing left of it after that. Nothing at all.

The oysters came, cold and glistening on beds of cracked ice, and Walter attacked them with gusto, talking the while. He was in land, he explained—farm lands in the Red River Valley and up into Saskatchewan, and lately town lots too, in some of the new places along the railroad lines that were opening up. It was a great country up there, a wonderful country, and growing all the time. A man with a little nerve and a little capital, and the knack of handling people, could make more money in a year than he could make in ten anywhere else. He himself—and here he lowered his voice slightly, though with an air of not caring much who heard—had cleared better than eighteen thousand dollars the past year, and expected to do better this year. He had a house in Minneapolis, on Lowry Hill, with a lawn and a garage and a car, a Pierce-Arrow; and a wife, Florence, whose father was a director in one of the big milling companies there; and two boys, eight and six, who were going to go to a private school, and later to Yale, if he had anything to say about it.

"Yale," he repeated, and nodded with satisfaction, as though the very word were a kind of guarantee. "That's what counts nowadays, Elm. Connections. Knowing the right people. It isn't what you know, it's who you know. I found that out pretty quick when I went up there."

And Elmer, listening, eating his oysters slowly and carefully (for he was not quite sure that he was eating them correctly, and kept glancing at Walter to see how it was done), felt within himself a strange commingling of emotions—admiration, certainly, and a kind of wonder, and pride, too, in a way, that a cousin of his, a Strader, out of the same dusty Indiana fields, should have come to this; and yet underneath all this, gnawing and insistent, a dull, heavy sense of his own failure, of his own smallness, of the meagerness and narrowness of the life that he himself had made. For what had he done? What had he to show? Eleven years—and here he was, at thirty-four, a clerk at thirty-two dollars a week, with no prospects, or none worth speaking of, beyond a possible raise of three dollars at the first of the year, if old Mr. Lowe remembered and was in a good humor. And he had worked—God knew he had worked! Ten hours a day, and Saturdays until three, and never late, and never sick, and always careful and exact and conscientious. And yet—and yet! Where had it got him? What was the difference, after all, between himself and Walter? Was it that Walter was smarter? He did not think so. In school, at the little brick schoolhouse at the crossroads, he had always been ahead of Walter, always. Was it luck, then? Or nerve? Or something else—some quality, some force, some chemic difference in the blood which made one man reach out and seize and hold, while another merely waited and hoped and worked and was passed over? He did not know. He could not have said. He only knew that it was so, and that it hurt.

"And you, Elm?" Walter was saying now, having finished his oysters and dabbed at his mouth with the heavy white napkin. "What've you been doing with yourself all this time? Married, you said in your letter?"

"Yes," said Elmer. "Married six years now. Lottie—her name was Lottie Brandt. Her folks are from over around Elgin. And we've got a little girl, Edna. She's four."

"Well, that's fine. That's fine. A little girl, eh? I always wanted a girl, myself. And what line are you in?"

"Hardware," said Elmer. "Wholesale. Bassett, Lowe & Company, on Lake Street. I'm in the order department."

"Bassett, Lowe," Walter repeated, frowning slightly, as though trying to place it. "Sure, I've heard of 'em. Good, solid house, I guess. In charge of the department, are you?"

And here Elmer hesitated—for the fraction of a second only, but long enough to feel the temptation sharply. For it would be so easy to say yes, or to say something which would let Walter think so—"I've got charge of a section of it," or "I'm next to the head." Who would ever know? Walter would go back to Minneapolis on Thursday and very likely never come to Chicago again, or, if he did, never look him up. And it would be pleasant—oh, it would be very pleasant—to have Walter think a little better of him, to see that faint, appraising look in his cousin's eyes give way to something more like respect. And yet something in him, some stubborn, plodding honesty which had been bred into him, perhaps, by his mother and the little Lutheran church on the Carlisle road, would not let him.

"No," he said slowly. "Not in charge. I'm sort of assistant to the man that is. I keep the order books and check the shipments and that sort of thing."

"I see," said Walter. And that was all. But there was a little silence after it, and in that silence Elmer felt, as plainly as though it had been spoken, the measuring and the weighing and the final placing of himself in his cousin's mind—not unkindly, perhaps, but definitely, finally, as one places a thing on a shelf where it belongs. And he looked out of the window at the rain, which was coming down harder now, and at the lights of the cars sliding past in the wet, and felt, for a moment, very tired.

The whitefish came, brown and steaming on its oaken plank, with a border of piped potato and little heaps of peas and carrots around it; and the orchestra behind the ferns began to play a waltz, slow and sentimental and somehow sad, and at a table across the room a woman in a gown of pale green silk laughed, a high, clear, careless laugh that rose above the murmur of voices and the clink of silver; and Walter, having helped himself liberally, began to talk again—of Minneapolis, of the Athletic Club to which he belonged, of a trip that he and Florence were planning to California in the spring, of a man named Hollister, a banker, who had taken a great liking to him and was going to put him in the way of something really big next year. And Elmer listened and nodded and said "Is that so?" and "Well, that's fine, Walt," at the proper intervals, and ate his whitefish, which was very good, better than anything he had eaten in a long time, though somehow he could not quite taste it.

It was only when the coffee had come, and Walter had lighted a long, dark cigar from a leather case and offered another to Elmer (who took it, though he seldom smoked cigars, and then only five-cent ones), that his cousin leaned forward across the table, his elbows on the white cloth, and looked at him with an expression which was different from any that he had worn thus far—more serious, and more searching, and with something in it, too, of that old Walter of the cornfields and the creek.

"Look here, Elm," he said. "I don't want you to take this wrong, now. But thirty-two a week—you can't get anywhere on that. Not with a wife and a kid. You know that as well as I do."

"I get along," said Elmer, a little stiffly.

"Sure you get along. But getting along isn't living. Not the way a man ought to live." He drew on his cigar and blew the smoke out slowly toward the chandelier. "Now, I'll tell you what. I could use a man up there. A man I could trust—somebody who's careful and honest and knows how to keep books and isn't going to try to put anything over on me. I've had two fellows in the office the last year and neither one of 'em was worth the powder to blow him up. I could start you at—well, say forty-five a week, and more later if things go the way I think they will. It isn't the city, of course. Not like Chicago. But it's a good town, and growing, and there's room for a man to get ahead. What do you say?"

And Elmer, sitting there with the unlighted cigar in his fingers and the warm, rich air of the dining room about him and the waltz still playing behind the ferns, felt something rise in him—something warm and swelling and almost painful, a kind of hope, which he had not felt in years. Forty-five a week! And more later! And a chance—a real chance, at last—to get out of the rut, out of the order books and the shipping slips and the dingy office on Lake Street with its one window looking out upon a brick wall. To give Lottie the things she ought to have, and Edna. A house, maybe, some day, with a lawn. And yet—at the same time, and quite as strongly, there rose in him something else, something he could not have put into words: a reluctance, a sort of shrinking, a dim and troubled sense that to go up there, to Minneapolis, to work for Walter, to be Walter's man, his clerk, his poor relation, beholden to him, nodding to him, watching his moods, would be in some way to acknowledge once and for all that Walter was the better man and he the lesser—that the thing which had been decided in that little silence a while ago was decided forever. Was that pride? Was it foolishness? Lottie would say it was foolishness. Lottie would say, "Why, Elmer, what on earth is there to think over?" And perhaps she would be right. Perhaps she would.

"Why, I—that's mighty good of you, Walt," he said at last, slowly. "Mighty good. I'd have to talk it over with Lottie, of course."

"Sure, sure. Talk it over. Take your time. I'm here till Thursday." Walter leaned back again, expansive, pleased with himself, the old ruddy glow upon his face once more. "Only don't take too long. Opportunities don't wait around for a fellow, Elm. That's one thing I've learned."

And afterward, when they had said good night under the great bronze marquee, and Walter had pressed upon him a dollar for a cab ("No, no, I insist—you're not going to walk in this, not after a dinner like that"), which Elmer had taken, flushing, and then had not used, but had put away in his vest pocket and walked to the elevated after all—afterward, riding north in the swaying, half-empty car, with the rain beating against the windows and the lights of the West Side flats flickering past, he sat and stared at his own pale reflection in the dark glass and thought and thought. Forty-five a week. Lowry Hill. A Pierce-Arrow. Yale. And old man Pfeiffer's dog, barking in the August dusk, and the two of them running, running, side by side, equal and free, down the long ditch toward the creek. Where had it gone, all that? These people were better informed than he was—had been to colleges. Perhaps he had better claim that he had been to some school. In Kansas City he had heard of the State University of Kansas—not so very far from there. Also the University of Missouri. And in Chicago of the University of Chicago. "But I know you have a girl just the same. All good-looking fellows have."

"Oh, am I good-looking?" he beamed nervously, amused and yet pleased. "Who said so?"

"As though you didn't know. Well, different people. I for one. And Sondra Finchley thinks you're good-looking, too. She's only interested in men who are. So does my sister Jill, for that matter. She blinked cynically and teasingly into his eyes, which caused him to feel oddly out of place, not able to cope with such a girl at all, at the same time very much flattered and amused. "But don't you think you're better looking than your cousin," she went on sharply and even commandingly. "Some people think you are." Too vividly it brought the aggressive and determined and even at times revengeful-looking features of Gilbert before him, who, stirred by such a report as this, would not hesitate to pay him out.

"Why I don't think anything of the kind," he laughed. "Honest, I don't. Of course I don't."

"Oh, well, then maybe you don't, but you are just the same. But that won't help you much either, unless you have money—that is, if you want to run with people who have." She looked up at him and added quite blandly. "People like money even more than they do looks." What a sharp girl this was, he thought, and what a hard, cold statement. But just then Sondra herself entered with some youth whom Clyde did not know—a tall, gangling, but very smartly-dressed individual. And after them, along with others, Bertine and Stuart Finchley.

"Here she is now," added Gertrude a little spitefully, for she resented the fact that Sondra was so much better-looking than either she or her sister, and that she had expressed an interest in Clyde. "She'll be looking to see if you notice how pretty she looks, so don't disappoint her." She was, in her small, intense way, a seeking Aphrodite, eager to prove to any who were sufficiently attractive the destroying power of her charm, while at the same time retaining her own personality and individuality free of any entangling alliance or compromise. However, for varying reasons which she could not quite explain to herself, Clyde appealed to her. He might not be anything socially or financially, but he was interesting to her. Hence she was now keen, first to see if he were present, next to be sure that he gained no hint that she had seen him first, and lastly to act as grandly as possible for his benefit—a Hortensian procedure and type of thought that was exactly the thing best calculated to impress him. He gazed and there she was—tripping here and there in a filmy chiffon dance frock, shaded from palest yellow to deepest orange, which most enhanced her dark eyes and hair. "Oh, here you are. You decided to come after all. I wasn't sure whether you would think it worth while. You've been introduced to everybody, of course?" She looked around as much as to say, that if he had not been she would proceed to serve him in this way. The others, not so very much impressed by Clyde, were still not a little interested by the fact that she seemed so interested in him.

"Yes, I met nearly everybody, I think."

"Except Freddie Sells. He came in with me just now. Here you are, Freddie," she called to a tall and slender youth, smooth of cheek and obviously becurled as to hair, who now came over and in his closely-fitting dress coat looked down on Clyde about as a spring rooster might look down on a sparrow.

"This is Clyde Griffiths, I was telling you about, Fred," she began briskly. "Doesn't he look a lot like Gilbert?"

"Why, you do at that," exclaimed this amiable person, who seemed to be slightly troubled with weak eyes since he bent close. "I hear you're a cousin of Gil's. I know him well. "Yes, I am," said Clyde, who, before a youth of obviously so much more training and schooling than he possessed, felt not a little reduced. He began to fear that this individual would try to talk to him about things which he could not understand, things concerning which, having had no consecutive training of any kind, he had never been technically informed.

"In charge of some department, I suppose?"

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, cautiously and nervously.

"You know," went on Mr. Sells, briskly and interestingly, being of a commercial as well as technical turn, "I've always wondered just what, outside of money, there is to the collar business. Gil and I used to argue about that when we were down at college. He used to try to tell me that there was some social importance to making and distributing collars, giving polish and manner to people who wouldn't otherwise have them, if it weren't for cheap collars. I think he musta read that in a book somewhere. I always laughed at him." Clyde was about to attempt an answer, although already beyond his depth in regard to this. "Social importance." Just what did he mean by that—some deep, scientific information that he had acquired at college. He was saved a non-committal or totally uninformed answer by Sondra who, without thought or knowledge of the difficulty which was then and there before him, exclaimed: "Oh, no arguments, Freddie. That's not interesting. Besides I want him to meet my brother and Bertine. You remember Miss Cranston. She was with me at your uncle's last spring." Clyde turned, while Fred made the best of the rebuff by merely looking at Sondra, whom he admired so very much.

"Yes, of course," Clyde began, for he had been studying these two along with others. To him, apart from Sondra, Bertine seemed exceedingly attractive, though quite beyond his understanding also. Being involved, insincere and sly, she merely evoked in him a troubled sense of ineffectiveness, and hence uncertainty, in so far as her particular world was concerned—no more.

"Oh, how do you do? It's nice to see you again," she drawled, the while her greenish-gray eyes went over him in a smiling and yet indifferent and quizzical way. She thought him attractive, but not nearly as shrewd and hard as she would have preferred him to be. "You've been terribly busy with your work, I suppose. "Well, I hope so," he replied, showing his even teeth. And a related, though somewhat modified, version of this same type of treatment was accorded him by Stuart, Sondra's brother.

The others, not so very much impressed by Clyde, were still not a little interested by the fact that she seemed so interested in him.

"Yes, I met nearly everybody, I think."

"Except Freddie Sells. He came in with me just now. Here you are, Freddie," she called to a tall and slender youth, smooth of cheek and obviously becurled as to hair, who now came over and in his closely-fitting dress coat looked down on Clyde about as a spring rooster might look down on a sparrow.

"This is Clyde Griffiths, I was telling you about, Fred," she began briskly. "Doesn't he look a lot like Gilbert?"

"Why, you do at that," exclaimed this amiable person, who seemed to be slightly troubled with weak eyes since he bent close. "I hear you're a cousin of Gil's. I know him well. We went through Princeton together. I used to be over here before I joined the General Electric over at Schenectady. But I'm around a good bit yet. You're connected with the factory, I suppose."

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, who, before a youth of obviously so much more training and schooling than he possessed, felt not a little reduced. He began to fear that this individual would try to talk to him about things which he could not understand, things concerning which, having had no consecutive training of any kind, he had never been technically informed.

"In charge of some department, I suppose?"

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, cautiously and nervously.

"You know," went on Mr. Sells, briskly and interestingly, being of a commercial as well as technical turn, "I've always wondered just what, outside of money, there is to the collar business. Gil and I used to argue about that when we were down at college. He used to try to tell me that there was some social importance to making and distributing collars, giving polish and manner to people who wouldn't otherwise have them, if it weren't for cheap collars. I think he musta read that in a book somewhere. I always laughed at him." Clyde was about to attempt an answer, although already beyond his depth in regard to this. "Social importance." Just what did he mean by that—some deep, scientific information that he had acquired at college. He was saved a non-committal or totally uninformed answer by Sondra who, without thought or knowledge of the difficulty which was then and there before him, exclaimed: "Oh, no arguments, Freddie. That's not interesting. Besides I want him to meet my brother and Bertine. You remember Miss Cranston. She was with me at your uncle's last spring." Clyde turned, while Fred made the best of the rebuff by merely looking at Sondra, whom he admired so very much.

"Yes, of course," Clyde began, for he had been studying these two along with others. To him, apart from Sondra, Bertine seemed exceedingly attractive, though quite beyond his understanding also. Being involved, insincere and sly, she merely evoked in him a troubled sense of ineffectiveness, and hence uncertainty, in so far as her particular world was concerned—no more.

"Oh, how do you do? It's nice to see you again," she drawled, the while her greenish-gray eyes went over him in a smiling and yet indifferent and quizzical way. She thought him attractive, but not nearly as shrewd and hard as she would have preferred him to be. "You've been terribly busy with your work, I suppose. But now that you've come out once, I suppose we'll see more of you here and there."

"Well, I hope so," he replied, showing his even teeth. Her eyes seemed to be saying that she did not believe what she was saying and that he did not either, but that it was necessary, possibly amusing, to say something of the sort. And a related, though somewhat modified, version of this same type of treatment was accorded him by Stuart, Sondra's brother.

response:
It was in that portion of the city which lay below the railroad yards and along the flats of the river, where the streets were unpaved for the most part and the houses, small, frame and of one pattern, stood shoulder to shoulder like so many weary workmen waiting for a car, that Henry Ostrander lived with his wife Minna and their two children, Della, eleven, and Willard, who was not yet eight. The house was a poor thing at best, four rooms and a lean-to kitchen, with a stove that smoked when the wind came from the east and a front step that had been patched more than once with boards of a different color. Yet inside, owing to the industry of Minna, who was a stout, practical and not unkindly German woman, and who had been raised in a home far poorer than this, there was an air of order and even of comfort, as these things went. There was a rag carpet, a sewing machine with a fern upon it, a horsehair sofa that had come from her mother's house in Fort Wayne, and on the wall a colored lithograph of a stag at bay among snowy pines, which Henry had won years before at a church raffle and which he still regarded, without quite knowing why, as a thing of some distinction.

On this particular evening in November, a raw, gray day with a fine sleet driving in from the river and the gas lamps along Kessler Street burning yellow and indistinct in the murk, Henry came home later than usual and in no very agreeable frame of mind. He was a checker in the shipping room of Haverly and Sons, wholesale grocers, a position he had held for nine years now at a wage which had advanced in that time from twelve to sixteen dollars a week, and which, so far as he could see, was not likely to advance further. And on this very afternoon young Mr. Pruett, a nephew of old Mr. Haverly, who had come into the business only the spring before from some college in the East and who knew no more about the shipping of goods than a cat (or so Henry thought), had stood over him in the presence of the other men and called him to account for a case of canned peaches that had gone to the wrong customer. It was not Henry's error. It was the error of a boy named Mulcahy, who had chalked the wrong number upon the crate. But Henry had not said so. Somehow, before this smooth, well-dressed youth, with his gray spats and his gold watch chain and his air of one who had never had to stand for anything in his life, Henry had found himself saying, "Yes, sir," and "I'll see to it, sir," and "It won't happen again, Mr. Pruett," the while a hot, choking sense of injustice rose in his throat and would not go down. And the other men had looked at him, or so he imagined, with a kind of pitying contempt, as much as to say, "There's Ostrander. Nine years, and he takes it from a kid like that." What else could he have done, though? There were Minna and the children, and the rent of eleven dollars a month, and the coal, and the doctor's bill from Della's sickness in the spring which was not yet paid. A man in his position could not talk back. He could not afford to have opinions, or a temper, or pride. That was a thing for people like Pruett, who had money behind them.

So, plodding home through the sleet with his collar turned up and his dinner pail swinging at his side, he had nursed this grievance, turning it over and over, until by the time he reached his own door it had grown into a kind of general resentment against life itself, against the city and the company and the weather and his own luck. He was not a bad man. Quite the contrary. He was, in the main, a sober, plodding, conscientious soul, not overly bright, not imaginative, who had been raised by a stern and religious father on a farm near Kendallville and who believed, without ever having examined the matter very closely, that the world was governed by certain fixed rules of right and wrong, and that those who kept them would in time be rewarded and those who broke them would be punished. Only of late, and in moments such as this one, a troubling doubt had begun to creep in upon him. Was it so? Was it really so? For here was he, who had kept the rules, and there was Pruett, who had kept none that Henry knew of and had needed none, and which of them was the better off? Yet he put the thought away from him. It was not a thing to think about.

Inside, the kitchen was warm and smelled of fried potatoes and boiled cabbage, and Minna, her sleeves rolled to the elbow and her face red from the stove, looked up and said, "You're late, Henry. Sit down. It's all ready." Della was setting the table, a thin, pale, serious child with her hair in two tight braids, and Willard was on the floor by the woodbox playing with something which, as his father entered, he thrust quickly into the pocket of his knee-pants.

Henry noticed the movement but said nothing at the time. He was tired. He washed his hands and face at the basin by the door, dried them on the roller towel, and sat down heavily at the head of the table. Minna said a short grace in German, as was her custom, and they ate for a while in silence, broken only by the clink of forks and the hiss of the sleet against the window. But presently, as if by some impulse of curiosity or perhaps because his father's mood oppressed him and he wished to escape from it into something pleasanter, Willard drew the object from his pocket under the edge of the table and began to turn it over in his fingers. It was a whistle—a small, bright, celluloid whistle in the shape of a bird, painted red and yellow and blue, with a little brass ring at the tail by which it might be hung on a string. And in the lamplight it shone with a gay, cheap, enticing brilliance which, to the child at least, was more beautiful than anything in the house.

"What's that you've got there?" asked Henry, laying down his fork.

Willard started and closed his hand over it. "Nothin'," he said.

"Don't tell me nothing. I saw it. Let's see it."

Slowly, and with a look first at his mother and then at his sister, as though one or the other might save him, the boy opened his hand. Henry took the whistle and examined it. It was new. There was not a mark upon it. He knew—for he had seen such things in the window of Bauer's notion store on Michigan Street, among the tops and marbles and candy hearts and cheap tin horns—that it had cost a dime. Perhaps fifteen cents.

"Where'd you get this?"

"I—I found it."

"Found it? Where?"

"Down by—down by the school. In the gutter."

Henry looked at it again. It was perfectly clean. And there had been sleet and mud in every gutter in the city since noon. He looked at Minna, and she, divining at the same instant what he was thinking, rose without a word and went to the shelf above the stove, where, behind the coffee mill, she kept a small tin box with a hinged lid, once a container for Huyler's cocoa, in which she put away the coins she saved from her market money against the coal man's monthly call. She opened it, counted, and turned around with a troubled face.

"There was a dollar and forty cents," she said in a low voice. "Now there's a dollar thirty."

There was a silence in the kitchen then, a heavy, dreadful silence, in which the ticking of the clock on the shelf and the hiss of the sleet and the faint bubbling of the kettle seemed suddenly very loud. Della had stopped eating and sat staring at her plate. Willard's face had gone first red and then white, and his lower lip had begun to tremble, though he did not cry—not yet. And Henry, looking at him, felt rising within him a feeling so complex, so commingled of anger and shame and fear and something else which he could not name, that for a moment he could not speak at all.

A thief! His son! And a liar besides! It was the thing of all things which his own father had most despised and most severely punished. He could remember yet—how vividly!—a day when he himself was perhaps nine and had taken two apples from a neighbor's tree, and his father had taken him out to the woodshed and whipped him with a harness strap until he could not sit down, saying all the while in his slow, heavy, Biblical way, "Thou shalt not steal. Thou shalt not steal." And he had never stolen again—never so much as a pin. That was how a boy was made honest. That was how a boy learned. And yet—and yet—even as he thought this, there came to him, unbidden, the memory of Pruett's smooth face that afternoon, and of the case of peaches, and of his own humiliation, and the thought, confused and only half-formed, that he was angrier now than he had any right to be, and that it was not altogether the dime, nor altogether the lie, which made him so.

"Come here," he said.

The boy did not move.

"Come here, I said!"

Willard slid down from his chair and came around the end of the table and stood before his father, his hands at his sides, his eyes fixed on the floor. He was a small, thin child, with light hair that fell over his forehead and large, gray, rather dreamy eyes—his mother's eyes—and a sensitive mouth that was always, as Minna said, "wanting something." For he was not like Della, who was serious and obedient and never asked for anything. He was forever stopping before shop windows on his way home from school, gazing at the bright things within—the painted soldiers, the toy engines, the bags of colored candy, the gilt-framed pictures, the sleds with their red runners—and coming home late, and being scolded for it, and doing it again. Something in these things drew him, as a moth is drawn to a flame, with a force he did not understand and could not resist. And it was so with the whistle. For a week he had passed Bauer's window and seen it there, hanging on a card among others like it, red and yellow and blue, and he had thought of it in school and at night in bed, and had wanted it as he had wanted nothing else in his short life. And this morning, alone in the kitchen while his mother was in the yard hanging out a wash, he had seen the cocoa box upon the shelf, and climbed upon a chair, and—well, he had not thought very much about it at all. It had seemed so easy. There were so many dimes in the box, and only one whistle in the world.

"Did you take that money out of your mother's box?" demanded Henry.

The boy said nothing.

"Answer me! Did you?"

"Yes, sir," whispered Willard, so low that he could scarcely be heard.

"And you went and bought this—this thing—with it?"

"Yes, sir."

"And then you sat there and lied to me about it! Found it in the gutter! Do you know what you are? Do you know what they call people who do things like that? A thief, that's what! And a liar! Do you know where thieves and liars end up? In jail, that's where! In the penitentiary over at Michigan City, with stripes on their backs and chains on their legs! Is that what you want? Is it?"

His voice had risen until it filled the little kitchen, and Willard, terrified now beyond all endurance, began at last to cry—not loudly, but in a low, choking, hopeless way, with his shoulders shaking and the tears running down his face. And Minna, who could bear a great deal but not this, came forward a step and put her hand on her husband's arm.

"Henry," she said. "Henry. He's only a little boy. He didn't know—"

"Didn't know! Didn't know it was wrong to steal? Didn't know it was wrong to lie? He knows, all right. He knew enough to hide it when I come in. You leave this to me, Minna. If I let it go now, where'll it stop? It'll be a quarter next time, and then a dollar, and then—" He did not finish. He did not quite know what came after that. But he had a vague, terrible picture of a long road leading downward, of saloons and poolrooms and police stations and newspapers, and of himself as an old man reading of his son's disgrace. "My father would've took the strap to me," he said. "And I'd have deserved it, too."

"Henry, please."

He looked at her, and then at the boy, and for a moment the two forces within him—the old, hard, inherited conviction that punishment was the only teacher, and some newer, softer, more uncertain feeling which he could not have put a name to—struggled together. It was not only Minna's pleading face. It was the boy himself, so small, so thin, so utterly helpless before him, as he, Henry, had been helpless that afternoon before Pruett. Was this what it came to, then? The big ones over the little ones, all down the line? Pruett over him, and he over this child? He did not think it in just these words. He was not a man who thought in words at all, very much. But something of the sort passed through him, like a cold draft through a warm room, and left him uneasy and confused.

And yet the thing had been done. It could not be let go. A boy who stole must be shown, must be made to feel. That much, at least, he was sure of. Or was he? Was he sure of anything any more?

"Hold out your hand," he said.

Willard, sobbing, held out his right hand, palm up, and Henry, with his own broad, calloused palm, struck it twice—sharply, so that the sound cracked in the little room like a breaking stick. The boy cried out and drew his hand back and held it against his chest, and Della, at the table, put her face in her hands. And Henry, the instant the blows had fallen, felt not satisfaction, as he had expected, nor righteousness, nor even the dull relief of a duty done, but a sudden, sickening shame which went through him from head to foot and left him almost weak.

"Now go to bed," he said roughly, to cover it. "No more supper. And tomorrow after school you take this thing back to Bauer's and tell him what you done and ask him for the dime back. And if he won't give it, you'll work it out somehow. You hear me?"

"Y-yes, sir."

"And don't you ever—ever—let me catch you at a thing like this again. Now go on."

The boy went, stumbling, through the door into the little bedroom off the kitchen which he shared with his sister, and they heard the creak of the bed as he threw himself upon it, and then his muffled crying, which went on for a long time and then slowly died away into silence.

For a while after that no one in the kitchen said anything. Minna cleared the table, her face set and averted, and Della helped her, and Henry sat by the stove with his elbows on his knees and the bright little whistle in his hand, turning it over and over. A cheap, foolish, gaudy thing. Ten cents' worth of painted celluloid. And yet, looking at it, he seemed to see, as in a kind of half-vision, the whole of his son's longing—the shop windows, the bright displays, the endless parade of things which other people had and which the Ostranders could not have and never would. Wasn't that what the world was, after all? One great window, full of bright things behind glass, and most people standing outside in the sleet, looking in? And was it so strange, then, that a child, not yet eight, not yet hardened to the way things were, should once put out his hand and take? He himself had wanted things, too, as a boy—a pair of skates, a jackknife, a red sweater such as the doctor's son wore. He had not taken them. His father would have killed him. But he had wanted them none the less, and that wanting had never quite died, had only gone underground, as it were, and become something else—a dull ache, a resentment, a sense of being cheated by he knew not whom.

"You was too hard on him, Henry," said Minna at last, quietly, wiping her hands on her apron.

"Maybe," he said. And then, after a pause, "I don't know. I don't know what's right any more, Minna. I swear I don't. You try to raise them decent. You try to teach them. And then—" He made a vague gesture with the hand that held the whistle, a gesture which took in the kitchen, the smoking stove, the sleet at the window, the whole poor, narrow, struggling circumstance of their lives. "What's the use of it? What's he going to have? What've I got?"

Minna did not answer. She had no answer. She came and stood beside him for a moment and put her hand upon his shoulder, and they remained so, the two of them, in the warm, dim kitchen, while the clock ticked and the kettle bubbled and the sleet drove on and on against the glass.

And in the little bedroom, Willard lay with his face to the wall, his hand still smarting, his eyes swollen and hot. He had stopped crying now. He was thinking—in so far as a child of seven can be said to think—of many things at once, confusedly. Of his father's face, red and terrible, which he had never seen so before. Of the penitentiary at Michigan City, with its stripes and chains, which he pictured as a vast, dark building like the roundhouse by the yards. Of Mr. Bauer, a fat, bald man with spectacles, to whom tomorrow he must go and say what he had done—a prospect so dreadful that he could scarcely bear to think of it. He was sorry. Yes, he was sorry. He would never do it again—never. And yet, beneath all this, beneath the fear and the shame and the smarting of his hand, there persisted in him, stubbornly and quite against his will, the image of the whistle itself—red and yellow and blue, shining in the lamplight—and the memory of the moment, earlier in the day, when he had first blown it in the alley behind Bauer's and heard its thin, sweet, piercing note go up among the wet roofs and chimneys like the cry of some strange, bright bird from another world than this. And he could not, try as he might, make himself feel that this had been wicked. It had been so beautiful.

So he lay, and the gas lamp in the street outside cast a pale, wavering square of light upon the ceiling, and the sleet ticked at the window, and presently, worn out, he slept. But the thing remained in him, as such things do—a small, bright splinter of desire, lodged deep and never wholly to be drawn out—and his father's blows, and his father's shame, and his mother's silence, and the gray, wet street, and the shop window with its painted toys, all became a part of him, mingling and combining in that obscure, chemic way in which the substance of a nature is formed, and in which, for good or ill, the man that is to be is shaped out of the child that is.
