In the town of Lattimer, Ohio, there lived a man named Hal Brodie who kept the feed and seed store on the corner of Main and Duane Streets, across from the hotel. He was a thick slow-moving man of thirty-eight with heavy shoulders and small grey eyes, and in the town he was thought to be a good fellow. In the evening men came into the store and sat on the sacks of bran and talked of the price of clover seed and of the doings of the county fair, and Hal sat behind the counter on a high stool and listened and laughed. He did not talk much himself. When he laughed his shoulders shook and he put his hand over his mouth like a boy laughing in church. "Hal's all right," the men said. "You can't get a rise out of Hal." They did not know that in the night when he lay beside his wife in the house on Elm Street he sometimes lay awake for hours staring at the ceiling and that thoughts went through his mind that would have made them stare at him and wonder.

Hal's wife was named Mary and she had been a school teacher before she married him. She was a small dark woman with a sharp chin and quick hands and she had come to Lattimer from a town in Indiana to teach in the grammar school. For three years she had taught there and had boarded at the house of the Methodist minister, and then one summer evening Hal Brodie had walked home with her from a strawberry festival on the church lawn and after that he walked home with her many times. He did not know how it had happened that they were married. It seemed to him that one day they were walking under the maple trees on Elm Street and that on the next day she was in his house and he was coming home to her at noon to eat his dinner. They had been married eleven years and there were no children.

On an evening in October Hal did not come home to supper. He had closed the store at six as was his custom and had stood for a moment on the sidewalk before the door. The sun had gone down and over the roofs of the stores across the street the sky was red. A farmer's wagon went past, the wheels rattling on the hard road, and a boy sat on the tail of the wagon swinging his legs. Hal did not know why he did not go home. He walked along Main Street past the hotel and past the bank and the hardware store and turned into the Trunion Pike that went out of town past the cemetery and the fair grounds. He walked a long time. When he came to the bridge over Wine Creek, two miles from town, he stopped and leaned on the railing and looked down at the water. It was dark by that time and he could not see the water but he heard it running over the stones. He stood there a long time and then turned and walked back to town.

When Hal came into the kitchen of his house it was after nine o'clock. Mary sat by the table under the lamp with her hands in her lap. The supper dishes were on the table, and his plate with the food on it. The food had grown cold and a skin had formed over the gravy. Mary did not get up when he came in. She looked at him and then she looked at the plate. Hal stood by the door with his hat in his hand. He felt like a boy who has been caught stealing apples and at the same time he felt something else, something hard and stubborn that rose up in him and made him want to laugh. He did not laugh. He hung his hat on the nail by the door and sat down at the table across from his wife.

"Well," Mary said, "you might as well eat it. It's there." Her voice was thin and quiet. Hal looked at the plate and took up his fork and then put it down again. "I'm not hungry," he said. "I went for a walk." Mary laughed. It was not a pleasant laugh. "A walk," she said. "Three hours you walked. I suppose you walked to Cleveland and back." She got up and began to take the dishes from the table and to put them into the pan on the stove. Her back was toward him and he looked at her back, at the narrow shoulders and the knot of dark hair at the back of her head. He thought of the first time he had walked home with her from the strawberry festival and how she had talked all the way of a book she was reading, a book about a man who went to live in the woods alone, and how he had not understood what she was saying and had been ashamed. "She knows a lot," he had thought then. "She's been to the normal school. She can talk." He had been proud that she would walk with him.

Now as he sat by the table he wanted to tell her about the walk. He wanted to tell her about the bridge and the sound of the water running over the stones in the darkness. He did not know why he wanted to tell her. It seemed to him that something had happened to him out there on the bridge, that something had come into his mind that had never been there before, and that if he could only say it to her everything would be different between them. He opened his mouth to speak and then closed it again. The words would not come. He sat looking at the lamp and the moths that flew about the chimney of the lamp, and Mary rattled the dishes in the pan.

"I'll tell you what it is," Mary said suddenly. She turned around from the stove and her face was white and her lips trembled. "I'll tell you what it is. You're tired of me. That's what it is. Eleven years and you're tired of me. Well, I'm tired too. I'm tired of sitting here in this kitchen every night and waiting for you to come home and then when you do come home you sit there like a post and don't say anything. You talk to the men down at the store. I've heard you. Mrs. Wilmot told me she heard you laughing clear across the street. You laugh with them. You never laugh here."

Hal looked at his wife. A strange thing happened in him. He had expected to be angry and he was not angry. He felt only a great tiredness and under the tiredness something that was almost tenderness. He wanted to get up and go to her and put his big hand on her shoulder. He did not do it. "I don't laugh with them," he said slowly. "I just sit there. They talk and I sit there. That's all it is."

Mary came and sat down again at the table. She put her elbows on the table and her chin in her hands and looked at him. Her eyes were bright and hard. "Then what is it?" she asked. "What did you go out walking on the pike for? Who did you see out there?" Hal shook his head. "I didn't see anybody," he said. "I went out to the Wine Creek bridge and stood there. I don't know why I went. I just went."

It is a strange thing about the people of small towns that they live side by side for years and do not know each other. In Lattimer there was a man named Joe Ransom who had been married for thirty years and who one day got up from the dinner table and walked out of his house and was never seen again. His wife sat for a week by the front window watching the street. Afterward she went to live with her sister in Sandusky. When the people of the town talked of Joe Ransom they shook their heads and said he must have gone crazy. Nobody thought that perhaps he had been crazy for thirty years and had only kept it hidden, or that perhaps he had been sane all that time and had at last grown tired of hiding his sanity. Hal Brodie had known Joe Ransom. He had sold him oats for his horse. As he sat in the kitchen with his wife looking at him across the table he thought of Joe Ransom and of how Joe had stood in the store one day with a sack of oats on his shoulder and had looked out of the window at the street and had said, "Hal, did you ever think a man could just walk off?" Hal had laughed. He remembered now that he had laughed and that Joe had looked at him with a queer look and had gone out of the store without saying anything more.

"You're thinking about something," Mary said. "I can see it in your face. You've been thinking about something for a long time. I'm not a fool. I know when a man's thinking." She leaned toward him across the table and her voice grew softer. "Hal," she said, "what is it? Tell me what it is. Is it some woman? Because if it is some woman I'd rather know it. I'd rather know than sit here and wonder."

Hal laughed then. He could not help it. The laugh came up out of him and he put his hand over his mouth as he did in the store. Mary's face grew red and she got up quickly from the table. "Oh, you can laugh," she cried. "You can laugh. That's what you can do." She went to the window and stood looking out into the darkness with her back to him. Her shoulders shook and Hal knew that she was crying. He took his hand away from his mouth and sat looking at her. He was ashamed. "There isn't any woman," he said. "There isn't anybody. I don't know any woman but you."

Mary did not turn around. "Then it's worse," she said in a low voice. "If there was a woman I'd understand. I'd know what to do. I'd hate her and I'd know what to do. But if there isn't anybody—" She stopped and Hal heard her breath catch in her throat. "If there isn't anybody then it's just me. It's just that you're sick of me."

Hal got up from his chair. He went across the kitchen and stood behind his wife. He was a big man and he stood over her like a tree. He wanted to touch her and his hands hung at his sides. "I'll tell you," he said and his voice was husky. "I'll try to tell you. I don't know as I can." He stopped and swallowed. "Out there on the bridge," he said, "I got to thinking. I got to thinking about when I was a boy. There was a time when I was a boy, maybe sixteen, when I thought I'd go somewhere. I don't know where. I used to lie in the hay mow at father's place out on the Medina road and think about it. I thought I'd go west maybe, or to the city. I thought I'd be something. I don't know what. Then father died and there was the store and I just stayed. I've stayed ever since. I didn't think about it. Tonight on the bridge I heard the water running and it came back to me like it was yesterday. I thought, 'Why, I'm thirty-eight years old. Why, I'm thirty-eight.'"

Mary turned around slowly and looked up at him. Her face was wet with tears and in the light of the lamp her face looked old. Hal had never noticed before that there were lines about her mouth. He looked at the lines and something hurt in his breast. "You wanted to go away," she said. "That's it. You wanted to go away and you married me instead." Hal shook his head. "No," he said, "it isn't that. You don't understand. It isn't anything to do with you."

"Everything you do has to do with me," she said fiercely. "Don't you know that? I'm your wife. You can't think anything that hasn't got to do with me." She pushed past him and went back to the table and sat down. She put her face in her hands. "Do you think I didn't want things?" she said through her fingers. "Do you think I came here from Indiana to teach in a school because I wanted to teach in a school? I wanted things too. I read books. I used to think—" She took her hands away from her face and laughed a short bitter laugh. "I used to think I would write books. Imagine that. Me. I used to sit up nights in Mrs. Ellsworth's front room at the minister's house and write things on paper. Then you came walking home with me from the festival and you were so big and quiet and I thought, 'There is a man who is strong. There is a man who doesn't talk foolishness like the others.' I thought you had things in you. I thought you were thinking things all the time. And you were thinking about clover seed."

Hal stood in the middle of the kitchen floor. He did not know what to say. A great confusion came over him. He had not known that his wife had written things on paper. He had never thought of her as wanting anything. It seemed to him that she had always been there in the house, getting the meals and sweeping the floors and sitting in the evening by the lamp reading the Cleveland paper, and that she had been satisfied. He looked at her now as though she were a stranger. "I didn't know that," he said stupidly. "I didn't know you wrote things."

"No," Mary said, "you didn't know. You never asked. In eleven years you never once asked me what I was thinking." She got up and went to the stove and lifted the lid and looked at the fire, and put the lid back. Her hands moved quickly and aimlessly. "I burned them," she said. "The papers. The first winter we were married I burned them in that stove. One night when you were down at the store. I sat here and put them in one at a time and watched them burn. I thought, 'I'm married now. I've got a husband. I don't need them.'"

The two people stood in the kitchen and looked at each other. Outside a dog barked and somewhere down the street a door slammed. The clock on the shelf over the sink ticked loudly. Hal thought that he had never heard the clock tick so loudly. It seemed to him that it was counting something, counting the years, eleven years, thirty-eight years. He wanted to go to his wife and take her in his arms and he wanted at the same time to go out of the house and walk again on the pike in the darkness. The two wants fought in him and he stood still, his big hands opening and closing at his sides.

"Well," Mary said at last, "what are we going to do?" Her voice was flat and tired. Hal looked at the floor. "I don't know," he said. "I don't know as there's anything to do." Mary nodded her head slowly. "No," she said, "I don't suppose there is. You'll go down to the store in the morning and I'll get the breakfast and that's all there is. That's all there's ever going to be." She began to wipe the table with a cloth, rubbing hard at a spot where the gravy had spilled. "You'd better go to bed," she said. "It's late."

Hal did not go to bed. He went to the door and took his hat from the nail. Mary looked up quickly. "Where are you going?" she asked, and her voice was sharp with fear. "I'm just going out to the barn," he said. "I want to see to the horse." There was no need to see to the horse. He had fed and watered the horse at noon and had told the boy who worked for him to bed it down at five. They both knew there was no need. Mary stood with the cloth in her hand and looked at him. "Hal," she said, and then she said nothing more. He stood in the doorway with the darkness behind him and waited for her to speak and she did not speak. After a while he went out and closed the door.

In the barn Hal stood in the darkness beside the horse. He could hear it moving in the stall and smell the warm smell of it and of the hay. He put out his hand and laid it on the horse's neck. The horse turned its head and pushed its nose against his shoulder. Hal stood there a long time. He thought of his wife sitting at night in the minister's front room writing things on paper, and of the papers burning one at a time in the kitchen stove. He thought of himself lying in the hay mow on his father's farm when he was sixteen. It seemed to him that the boy in the hay mow and the young woman in the minister's front room had been two people who might have understood each other, and that they had both died somewhere along the road and that he and Mary were what was left of them. "We're like a couple of empty sacks," he thought, and the thought seemed to him a true one and he said it aloud in the darkness of the barn. "Empty sacks," he said. The horse stamped its foot.

When he went back to the house the lamp was still burning in the kitchen. He looked through the window and saw Mary sitting at the table where he had left her. She had a pencil in her hand and a piece of brown wrapping paper before her on the table, and she sat with the pencil held over the paper and did not write. Hal stood outside the window in the darkness and watched her. He wanted to go in and sit down beside her and ask her what she was going to write. He thought that if he went in now and asked her that one thing, everything might come right. He stood a long time with his hand on the window sill. Then the lamp went out and he heard her feet going up the stairs, and he stood alone in the yard under the bare branches of the apple tree and looked at the dark house.

One Sunday afternoon three boys sat on a log on the side of the hill that looked down into Coal Creek. From where they sat they could see the workers of the night shift idling in the sun on Main Street. From the coke ovens a thin line of smoke rose into the sky. A freight train heavily loaded crept round the hill at the end of the valley. It was spring and over even that hive of black industry hung a faint promise of beauty. The boys talked of the life of people in their town and as they talked thought each of himself. Although he had not been out of the valley and had grown strong and big there, Beaut McGregor knew something of the outside world. It isn't a time when men are shut off from their fellows. Newspapers and magazines have done their work too well. They reached even into the miner's cabin and the merchants along Main Street of Coal Creek stood before their stores in the afternoon and talked of the doings of the world. Beaut McGregor knew that life in his town was exceptional, that not everywhere did men toil all day black and grimy underground, that not all women were pale bloodless and bent. As he went about delivering bread he whistled a song. “Take me back to Broadway,” he sang after the soubrette in a show that had once come to Coal Creek. Now as he sat on the hillside he talked earnestly while he gesticulated with his hands. “I hate this town,” he said. “The men here think they are confoundedly funny. They don't care for anything but making foolish jokes and getting drunk. I want to go away.” His voice rose and hatred flamed up in him. “You wait,” he boasted. “I'll make men stop being fools. I'll make children of them. I'll——” Pausing he looked at his two companions. Beaut poked the ground with a stick. The boy sitting beside him laughed. He was a short well—dressed black—haired boy with rings on his fingers who worked in the town poolroom, racking the pool balls. “I'd like to go where there are women with blood in them,” he said. Three women came up the hill toward them, a tall pale brown-haired woman of twenty-seven and two fairer young girls. The black-haired boy straightened his tie and began thinking of a conversation he would start when the women reached him. Beaut and the other boy, a fat fellow, the son of a grocer, looked down the hill to the town over the heads of the newcomers and continued in their minds the thoughts that had made the conversation.

“Hello girls, come and sit here,” shouted the black-haired boy, laughing and looking boldly into the eyes of the tall pale woman. They stopped and the tall woman began stepping over the fallen logs, coming to them. The two young girls followed, laughing. They sat down on the log beside the boys, the tall pale woman at the end beside red-haired McGregor. An embarrassed silence fell over the party. Both Beaut and the fat boy were disconcerted by this turn to their afternoon's outing and wondered how it would turn out. The pale woman began to talk in a low tone. “I want to get away from here,” she said, “I wish I could hear birds sing and see green things grow.” Beaut McGregor had an idea. “You come with me,” he said. He got up and climbed over the logs and the pale woman followed. The fat boy shouted at them, relieving his own embarrassment by trying to embarrass them. “Where're you going—you two?” he shouted. Beaut said nothing. He stepped over the logs to the road and began climbing the hill. The tall woman walked beside him and held her skirts out of the deep dust of the road. Even on this her Sunday gown there was a faint black mark along the seams—the mark of Coal Creek. As McGregor walked his embarrassment left him. He thought it fine that he should be thus alone with a woman. When she had tired from the climb he sat with her on a log beside the road and talked of the black-haired boy. “He has your ring on his finger,” he said, looking at her and laughing. She held her hand pressed tightly against her side and closed her eyes. “The climbing hurts me,” she said. Tenderness took hold of Beaut. When they went on again he walked behind her, his hand upon her back pushing her up the hill. The desire to tease her about the black-haired boy had passed and he wished he had said nothing about the ring. He remembered the story the black-haired boy had told him of his conquest of the woman. “More than likely a mess of lies,” he thought. Over the crest of the hill they stopped and rested, leaning against a worn rail fence by the woods. Below them in a wagon a party of men went down the hill. The men sat upon boards laid across the box of a wagon and sang a song. One of them stood in the seat beside the driver and waved a bottle. He seemed to be making a speech. The others shouted and clapped their hands. The sounds came faint and sharp up the hill. In the woods beside the fence rank grass grew. Hawks floated in the sky over the valley below. A squirrel running along the fence stopped and chattered at them. McGregor thought he had never had so delightful a companion. He got a feeling of complete, good fellowship and friendliness with this woman. Without knowing how the thing had been done he felt a certain pride in it. “Don't mind what I said about the ring,” he urged, “I was only trying to tease you.” The woman beside McGregor was the daughter of an undertaker who lived upstairs over his shop near the bakery. He had seen her in the evening standing in the stairway by the shop door. After the story told him by the black-haired boy he had been embarrassed about her. When he passed her standing in the stairway he went hurriedly along and looked into the gutter. They went down the hill and sat on the log upon the hillside. A clump of elders had grown about the log since his visits there with Cracked McGregor so that the place was closed and shaded like a room. The woman took off her hat and laid it beside her on the log. A faint colour mounted to her pale cheeks and a flash of anger gleamed in her eyes. “He probably lied to you about me,” she said, “I didn't give him that ring to wear. When Hal Steadman came back to Union Ridge after eleven years in Chicago he got off the afternoon train and stood on the station platform with his grip in his hand and did not know where to go. He had written to no one. It had come into his head on a Tuesday, sitting at his desk in the office on Monroe Street where he wrote the words that went under pictures of stoves and harness and patent medicines, that he would go home, and on Thursday he had gone. Now that he was there he felt foolish. The station agent, a man named Pruitt who had been old when Hal was a boy and was not much older now, looked at him through the little window and did not know him. Hal was glad of that. He set the grip down and lit a cigar and looked along the tracks to where the town began.

It was October. The maples along Walnut Street had turned and the leaves lay in the gutters and boys were burning them in little piles so that a blue smoke hung in the air. A wagon loaded with sugar beets went past toward the factory at the edge of town, the driver asleep on the seat with the lines wound about his wrist. Hal watched the wagon. He thought of himself as a man of the city who had come back to look at the place he had escaped from, and the thought pleased him, but beneath it there was something else that did not please him. He could not have said what it was. He picked up the grip and walked up Walnut Street toward the square.

His cousin Ed Wentling had a harness shop on the north side of the square, between the bank and Heffner's saloon. Hal had known that. His mother had written it to him in one of the letters she sent every month before she died, letters he had read hurriedly at his desk and thrown into the basket. "Ed has bought out old Miller's harness business and is doing well," she had written. "He married the Clark girl, Mabel, the one with the bad eye. They have two children." Hal had thought nothing of it at the time. Now as he crossed the square he looked for the shop and found it, a narrow place with a wooden horse in the window wearing a set of new harness, the brass on the hames shining in the afternoon sun.

Ed was inside, sitting on a low bench with a collar across his knees, sewing. He was a big man with thick shoulders and a heavy brown mustache and he wore a leather apron. When the door opened and the little bell over it rang he looked up and then went on sewing for a moment as though he had seen nothing. Then he put the collar down very carefully on the bench beside him and stood up.

"Well, I'll be darned," he said. "Well, I'll be darned. Hal."

They shook hands. Ed's hand was hard and dry and smelled of leather and neatsfoot oil, and Hal's hand in it felt small and soft. He was ashamed of his hand. He took it away and put it in his pocket. The two men stood looking at each other. Neither of them knew what to say. It is a thing that happens often between men who have been boys together and have gone different ways. They want to go back to the old ease and they cannot find the road. Each of them looks at the other and sees a stranger wearing the face of someone he once knew, and is a little afraid.

"You got fat," Ed said finally and laughed. It was true. Hal had grown heavy about the middle in the city. He laughed too, too loudly, and slapped his stomach.

"City living," he said. "We eat too much and don't do anything."

Ed went to the back of the shop and took off his apron and hung it on a nail. He called through a door to a boy who was cutting straps in the back room. "You mind things, Willie," he said. "I'm going out a while. This is my cousin from Chicago."

---

They walked out along the Turner pike toward the old quarry. Neither of them had suggested it. They went that way as though their feet remembered something their heads had forgotten. When they were boys they had gone there on summer afternoons to swim in the green water that filled the bottom of the quarry, and had lain on the warm stones afterward and talked of what they would do when they were men. Hal remembered that now and wondered if Ed remembered it. He looked at his cousin walking beside him, a little ahead, his big shoulders swinging, and could not tell.

The pike ran between fields where the corn had been cut and stood in shocks. Crows rose from the fields as they passed and settled again behind them. A farmer named Ebinger, whom Ed knew, drove past in a buggy and raised his whip in greeting, and Ed raised his hand. "Ebinger's got a new team," he said. "I made the harness. Brass mountings." He said it with pride and then seemed ashamed of having said it and was silent.

Hal began to talk. He talked of Chicago, of the tall buildings and the lake and the crowds on State Street at noon, of the theatres and the restaurants where men he knew ate oysters brought in ice from the east. He talked of his work. He told how he had written the words for an advertisement for a patent liniment and how the words had been printed in a thousand newspapers so that men and women all over the country read them. "You've probably read them yourself," he said. "'For the Aching Back of the Toiling Man.' That's mine." He laughed. He was boasting and he knew it and could not stop. Something in him wanted Ed to be impressed, to look at him with the look a boy gives a man who has done great things. At the same time something else in him was sick at what he was saying. The words came out of his mouth and he heard them and they sounded thin and foolish in the open country with the crows flying and the smell of the fields.

Ed listened. He walked along with his head down, looking at the dust of the road. Once he said, "Is that so," and once he said, "Well, I'll be darned." When Hal had finished he walked a long way without saying anything. Then he said, "I read that about the liniment. Mabel bought a bottle of it. It didn't do any good."

Hal stopped in the road and stared at his cousin. Then he began to laugh, and this time the laughter was real. It shook him so that he had to put his hand on Ed's shoulder. Ed laughed too. They stood in the road laughing like two boys, and for a moment the strangeness between them went away.

"No," Hal said, wiping his eyes, "I don't suppose it did. I don't suppose it ever did anybody any good."

---

The quarry had not changed. The stones went down in great steps to the water, and the water was green and still and there were yellow leaves floating on it. Someone had built a little wooden platform at the edge for diving, but it was old now and half the boards were gone. The two men climbed down to the ledge where they had lain as boys and sat on the stones. The stones were warm. The sun was going down over the woods on the far side and the light came slanting across the water.

Ed took out a pipe and filled it and lit it. Hal threw his cigar into the water and watched it float. He thought of how many cigars he had smoked in Chicago, sitting at his desk, sitting in restaurants, sitting in his room on Ohio Street at night alone. He had smoked them, he thought, the way a man walks up and down in a room when he is waiting for something.

"Remember when Tom Hardesty nearly drowned here?" Ed said.

Hal remembered. Tom Hardesty had dived from the high ledge and struck his head and Ed had gone in after him and brought him out. Hal had stood on the stones and shouted. He had not gone in. He remembered that now with a sharp shame he had not felt in years. He looked at Ed's big hands holding the pipe and thought of those hands, a boy's hands then, gripping Tom Hardesty by the hair.

"Tom's dead," Ed said. "Died in the Philippines. Fever."

"I didn't know that."

"No," Ed said. "I don't suppose you would."

There was no reproach in it. Ed said it simply, as a man states a fact about the weather. But Hal felt the reproach anyway. He felt that he had gone away and that while he was gone life had gone on in Union Ridge, people had married and had children and died of fevers in far places, and he had known nothing about it and had not cared. He had thought that life was in the city. He had thought that in Union Ridge nothing happened, that people only grew old and stupid there like cattle in a pasture. Now he sat on the stone beside his cousin and was not sure.

"How's Mabel?" he asked.

"All right," Ed said. "She's all right." He sucked at his pipe. "She's a good woman. She keeps the house nice. The children are fine children. The boy is seven and he can already braid a quirt. I showed him how." He stopped. "She's a good woman," he said again.

Hal waited. He felt that his cousin wanted to say something and was struggling with it, the way he himself had struggled, sitting before a blank sheet of paper in the office, for the words to sell a thing. But Ed's struggle was different. It was a struggle to get something out of himself that had been in him a long time and had grown there like a stone in the flesh.

"You know," Ed said, "I was going to go too."

"Go where?"

"Away. Chicago. Anywhere." Ed got up and walked to the edge of the ledge and stood looking down at the water. His back was to Hal. "After you went," he said, "I thought about it all the time. I used to lie awake at night thinking about it. I had it all planned. I was going to work in the packing houses until I learned something, and then I don't know what. Something. I didn't know what. I just wanted to get out where things were going on." He turned around. His face was red. "I had forty dollars saved," he said. "I kept it in a baking powder can under the floor of the barn."

"What happened?"

Ed shrugged his big shoulders. "Pa got sick," he said. "Then there was Mabel. I don't know. Things happened. I don't know how it was. One day I went out to the barn and took up the board and took the money out of the can and paid it on the harness shop. I didn't think about it much. I just did it." He sat down again on the stone. "Then I didn't lie awake any more," he said. "I slept fine after that."

Hal did not know what to say. He looked at his cousin's face and saw there something he had not expected to see, a kind of bewilderment, the look of a man who has walked a long way down a road and has turned around and cannot see where he started from. He wanted to put his hand on Ed's arm. He wanted to say, "It's nothing there, Ed. It's nothing. You didn't miss anything." But he could not say it, because he did not know if it was true. He had believed for eleven years that it was not true. He had believed that he had escaped and that Ed had been caught. Now, sitting in the quarry, he did not know what he believed.

---

The sun went down behind the woods and the water in the quarry turned dark. A chill came into the air. Ed knocked out his pipe against the stone and put it in his pocket.

"What made you come back?" he asked.

Hal thought about it. He wanted to give a true answer. It seemed to him suddenly important to give his cousin a true answer, as though he owed him that for the forty dollars in the baking powder can, for Tom Hardesty, for everything.

"I don't know," he said. "I was sitting at my desk. I had to write something about a cream separator. I'd written about a hundred cream separators. And I thought, I don't know what a cream separator is. I've never seen one. I've never touched one. I write that it is the best cream separator in the world and I don't know anything about it. One Sunday afternoon three boys sat on a log on the side of the hill that looked down into Coal Creek. From where they sat they could see the workers of the night shift idling in the sun on Main Street. From the coke ovens a thin line of smoke rose into the sky. A freight train heavily loaded crept round the hill at the end of the valley. It was spring and over even that hive of black industry hung a faint promise of beauty. The boys talked of the life of people in their town and as they talked thought each of himself. Although he had not been out of the valley and had grown strong and big there, Beaut McGregor knew something of the outside world. It isn't a time when men are shut off from their fellows. Newspapers and magazines have done their work too well. They reached even into the miner's cabin and the merchants along Main Street of Coal Creek stood before their stores in the afternoon and talked of the doings of the world. Beaut McGregor knew that life in his town was exceptional, that not everywhere did men toil all day black and grimy underground, that not all women were pale bloodless and bent. As he went about delivering bread he whistled a song. “Take me back to Broadway,” he sang after the soubrette in a show that had once come to Coal Creek. Now as he sat on the hillside he talked earnestly while he gesticulated with his hands. “I hate this town,” he said. “The men here think they are confoundedly funny. They don't care for anything but making foolish jokes and getting drunk. I want to go away.” His voice rose and hatred flamed up in him. “You wait,” he boasted. “I'll make men stop being fools. I'll make children of them. I'll——” Pausing he looked at his two companions. Beaut poked the ground with a stick. The boy sitting beside him laughed. He was a short well—dressed black—haired boy with rings on his fingers who worked in the town poolroom, racking the pool balls. “I'd like to go where there are women with blood in them,” he said. Three women came up the hill toward them, a tall pale brown-haired woman of twenty-seven and two fairer young girls. The black-haired boy straightened his tie and began thinking of a conversation he would start when the women reached him. Beaut and the other boy, a fat fellow, the son of a grocer, looked down the hill to the town over the heads of the newcomers and continued in their minds the thoughts that had made the conversation.

“Hello girls, come and sit here,” shouted the black-haired boy, laughing and looking boldly into the eyes of the tall pale woman. They stopped and the tall woman began stepping over the fallen logs, coming to them. The two young girls followed, laughing. They sat down on the log beside the boys, the tall pale woman at the end beside red-haired McGregor. An embarrassed silence fell over the party. Both Beaut and the fat boy were disconcerted by this turn to their afternoon's outing and wondered how it would turn out. The pale woman began to talk in a low tone. “I want to get away from here,” she said, “I wish I could hear birds sing and see green things grow.” Beaut McGregor had an idea. “You come with me,” he said. He got up and climbed over the logs and the pale woman followed. The fat boy shouted at them, relieving his own embarrassment by trying to embarrass them. “Where're you going—you two?” he shouted. Beaut said nothing. He stepped over the logs to the road and began climbing the hill. The tall woman walked beside him and held her skirts out of the deep dust of the road. Even on this her Sunday gown there was a faint black mark along the seams—the mark of Coal Creek. As McGregor walked his embarrassment left him. He thought it fine that he should be thus alone with a woman. When she had tired from the climb he sat with her on a log beside the road and talked of the black-haired boy. “He has your ring on his finger,” he said, looking at her and laughing. She held her hand pressed tightly against her side and closed her eyes. “The climbing hurts me,” she said. Tenderness took hold of Beaut. When they went on again he walked behind her, his hand upon her back pushing her up the hill. The desire to tease her about the black-haired boy had passed and he wished he had said nothing about the ring. He remembered the story the black-haired boy had told him of his conquest of the woman. “More than likely a mess of lies,” he thought. Over the crest of the hill they stopped and rested, leaning against a worn rail fence by the woods. Below them in a wagon a party of men went down the hill. The men sat upon boards laid across the box of a wagon and sang a song. One of them stood in the seat beside the driver and waved a bottle. He seemed to be making a speech. The others shouted and clapped their hands. The sounds came faint and sharp up the hill. In the woods beside the fence rank grass grew. Hawks floated in the sky over the valley below. A squirrel running along the fence stopped and chattered at them. McGregor thought he had never had so delightful a companion. He got a feeling of complete, good fellowship and friendliness with this woman. Without knowing how the thing had been done he felt a certain pride in it. “Don't mind what I said about the ring,” he urged, “I was only trying to tease you.” The woman beside McGregor was the daughter of an undertaker who lived upstairs over his shop near the bakery. He had seen her in the evening standing in the stairway by the shop door. After the story told him by the black-haired boy he had been embarrassed about her. When he passed her standing in the stairway he went hurriedly along and looked into the gutter. They went down the hill and sat on the log upon the hillside. A clump of elders had grown about the log since his visits there with Cracked McGregor so that the place was closed and shaded like a room. The woman took off her hat and laid it beside her on the log. A faint colour mounted to her pale cheeks and a flash of anger gleamed in her eyes. “He probably lied to you about me,” she said, “I didn't give him that ring to wear. I don't know why I gave it to him. He wanted it. He asked me for it time and again. He said he wanted to show it to his mother. And now he has shown it to you and I suppose told lies about me.” Beaut was annoyed and wished he had not mentioned the ring. He felt that an unnecessary fuss was being made about it. He did not believe that the black-haired boy had lied but he did not think it mattered. He began talking of his father, boasting of him. His hatred of the town blazed up. “They thought they knew him down there,” he said, “they laughed at him and called him 'Cracked.' They thought his running into the mine just a crazy notion like a horse that runs into a burning stable. He was the best man in town. He was braver than any of them. He went in there and died when he had almost enough money saved to buy a farm over here.” He pointed down the valley. Beaut began to tell her of the visits to the hillside with his father and described the effect of the scene on himself when he was a child. “I thought it was paradise,” he said. She put her hand on his arm and seemed to be soothing him like a careful groom quieting an excitable horse. “Don't mind them,” she said, “you will go away after a time and make a place for yourself out in the world.” He wondered how she knew. A profound respect for her came over him. “She is keen to guess that,” he thought. He began to talk of himself, boasting and throwing out his chest. “I'd like to have the chance to show what I can do,” he declared. A thought that had been in his mind on the winter day when Uncle Charlie Wheeler put the name of Beaut upon him came back and he walked up and down before the woman making grotesque motions with his hands as Cracked McGregor had walked up and down before him.

“I'll tell you what,” he began and his voice was harsh. He had forgotten the presence of the woman and half forgotten what had been in his mind. He sputtered and glared over his shoulder up the hillside as he struggled for words. “Oh to Hell with men!” he burst forth. “They are cattle, stupid cattle.” A fire blazed up in his eyes and a confident ring came into his voice. “I'd like to get them together, all of them,” he said, “I'd like to make them——” Words failed him and again he sat down on the log beside the woman. “Well I'd like to lead them to an old mine shaft and push them in,” he concluded resentfully.

On the eminence Beaut and the tall woman sat and looked down into the valley. “I wonder why we don't go there, mother and I,” he said. “When I see it I'm filled with the notion. I think I want to be a farmer and work in the fields. Instead of that mother and I sit and plan of the city. I'm going to be a lawyer. That's all we talk about. Then I come up here and it seems as though this is the place for me.” The tall woman laughed. “I can see you coming home at night from the fields,” she said. “It might be to that white house there with the windmill, You would be a big man and would have dust in your red hair and perhaps a red beard growing on your chin. And a woman with a baby in her arms would come out of the kitchen door to stand leaning on the fence waiting for you. When you came up she would put her arm around your neck and kiss you on the lips. The beard would tickle her cheek. You should have a beard when you grow older. Your mouth is so big.” A strange new feeling shot through Beaut. He wondered why she had said that and wanted to take hold of her hand and kiss her then and there. He got up and looked at the sun going down behind the hill far away at the other end of the valley. “We'd better be getting along back,” he said. The woman remained seated on the log. “Sit down,” she said, “I'll tell you something—something it's good for you to hear. You're so big and red you tempt a girl to bother you. First though you tell me why you go along the street looking into the gutter when I stand in the stairway in the evening.” Beaut sat down again upon the log, and thought of what the black-haired boy had told him of her. “Then it was true—what he said about you?” he asked.

“No! No!” she cried, jumping up in her turn and beginning to pin on her hat. “Let's be going.” Beaut sat stolidly on the log. “What's the use bothering each other,” he said. “Let's sit here until the sun goes down. We can get home before dark.” They sat down and she began talking, boasting of herself as he had boasted of his father.

“I'm too old for that boy,” she said; “I'm older than you by a good many years. I know what boys talk about and what they say about women. I do pretty well. I don't have any one to talk to except father and he sits all evening reading a paper and going to sleep in his chair. If I let boys come and sit with me in the evening or stand talking with me in the stairway it is because I'm lonesome. There isn't a man in town I'd marry—not one.” The speech sounded discordant and harsh to Beaut. He wished his father were there rubbing his hands together and muttering rather than this pale woman who stirred him up and then talked harshly like the women at the back doors in Coal Creek. He thought again as he had thought before that he preferred the black-faced miners drunk and silent to their pale talking wives. On an impulse he told her that, saying it crudely so that it hurt. Their companionship was spoiled. They got up and began to climb the hill, going toward home. Again she put her hand to her side and again he wished to put his hand at her back and push her up the hill. Instead he walked beside her in silence, again hating the town. Halfway down the hill the tall woman stopped by the road-side. Darkness was coming on and the glow of the coke ovens lighted the sky. “One living up here and never going down there might think it rather grand and big,” he said. Again the hatred came. “They might think the men who live down there knew something instead of being just a lot of cattle.” A smile came into the face of the tall woman and a gentler look stole into her eyes. “We get at one another,” she said, “we can't let one another alone. I wish we hadn't quarrelled. We might be friends if we tried. You have got something in you. You attract women. I've heard others say that. Your father was that way. Most of the women here would rather have been the wife of Cracked McGregor ugly as he was than to have stayed with their own husbands. I heard my mother say that to father when they lay quarrelling in bed at night and I lay listening.” The boy was overcome with the thought of a woman talking to him so frankly. He looked at her and said what was in his mind. “I don't like the women,” he said, “but I liked you, seeing you standing in the stairway and thinking you had been doing as you pleased. I thought maybe you amounted to something. I don't know why you should be bothered by what I think. I don't know why any woman should be bothered by what any man thinks. I should think you would go right on doing what you want to do like mother and me about my being a lawyer.” He sat on a log beside the road near where he had met her and watched her go down the hill. “I'm quite a fellow to have talked to her all afternoon like that,” he thought and pride in his growing manhood crept over him.
