Gaffney's Court lay at the bottom of a canyon of brick, and the sun reached it only at noon, and then grudgingly, as a miser drops a coin into a beggar's hat. The tenements leaned toward each other as if they wished to exchange confidences of a disreputable sort. From window to window stretched lines of washing, shirts and petticoats and grey stockings, that hung motionless in the dead air like the banners of an army that had been defeated long ago and had forgotten to take them down. Below, in the mud and the litter of the court, small children waged war.

Willie Delahunt was six years old, and on this afternoon he was a general. He had in his possession a tin trumpet of a fierce scarlet color, with a gilt mouthpiece and a tassel of green worsted that swung from it like a scalp. He had obtained it at noon from a pushcart on the avenue, where an old man with a beard like dirty cotton had sold it to him for five cents. The five cents had come from a cracked teapot that stood on the shelf above the stove at home. Willie did not dwell upon this fact. A conqueror is not obliged to remember the sources of his treasury.

He marched up and down the length of the court with his chest thrust out and his small legs lifting high. At intervals he raised the trumpet to his lips and blew a blast that rang against the brick walls and came back to him multiplied, so that it seemed a regiment was blowing. The other children ceased their own wars and gazed at him. Their faces were filled with a vast envy. A little girl with a dirty bandage about her head followed after him at a respectful distance, as camp-followers trail behind a victorious column.

A boy from the next court, a person of seven years and of reputation, came and stood squarely in Willie's path. He had a cap pulled low over one eye, and he regarded the trumpet with scorn.

"Aw, dat ain' nottin'," he said. "Me uncle's got a horn what's as big as a stove-pipe. He plays it in a band. Dat t'ing ain' nottin'."

Willie halted. He was momentarily appalled. Then a great wrath came upon him. He lifted the trumpet and blew into the face of the boy from the next court a blast of such savage quality that the latter fell back two paces. The spectators shrieked with joy. The boy from the next court made a feint of fighting, but his heart was not in it. He retreated toward the alley, uttering threats concerning the future which nobody heeded. Willie paraded on. He was conscious that he had become a great figure in the world.

From a window on the third floor of the opposite building, Mrs. Feeney watched these things. Mrs. Feeney was a woman who knew the affairs of Gaffney's Court as a priest knows the sins of his parish, but without the obligation of silence. She had seen Willie at the pushcart. She had seen, two days previously, Mrs. Delahunt counting coins into the cracked teapot with the care of a woman who counts the beads of a rosary. Mrs. Feeney put these facts together with the satisfaction of a philosopher who has discovered a law of the universe. She went down one flight of stairs and up another, and across the hall, and knocked upon the Delahunt door.

Mrs. Delahunt was ironing. She was a washerwoman, and the room was filled with steam that rose from the tubs and clung to the walls and dripped from the ceiling in slow, warm drops. Her arms were bared to the elbow and were as red as things that have been boiled. Her hair had escaped from its knot and hung in damp strings about her face. She held the flatiron aloft as she opened the door, as if she half-expected an enemy.

The two women conferred. Mrs. Feeney spoke in a low voice, with many shakings of the head and many pious glances toward the ceiling. Mrs. Delahunt listened. Her face grew slowly crimson, beginning at the neck and mounting upward, like a thermometer in a fire. When Mrs. Feeney had finished she went away with the air of one who has done a painful duty toward the community, and as she went down the stairs she hummed a little.

Mrs. Delahunt crossed to the shelf and took down the teapot. She shook it. Then she poured the contents into her palm and counted them with a forefinger that trembled. She counted them twice. She set the teapot back upon the shelf with an elaborate gentleness that was more terrible than violence. Then she went to the window and put out her head.

"Willie!"

The voice fell into the court like a stone into a pool. The children scattered to the edges. Willie, in the midst of a triumphal blast, lowered his trumpet. He looked up at the window and saw his mother's face, red and enormous, framed by the hanging washing. He knew at once that the heavens had fallen. He did not know why, but he perceived that it was so. A child possesses an instinct for the coming of doom as a dog possesses an instinct for the coming of a storm.

"You come up here," said the mother. "You come up here dis minute, or I'll come down an' skin yeh alive in front of deh hull court."

Willie stood still. He looked about him for allies, but the children had fled. The little girl with the bandage had disappeared entirely. The court, which a moment before had been filled with his admirers, was now a desert. He discovered, as greater generals have discovered, that glory has no rear-guard.

He did not move fast enough. His mother came down. She descended the stairs with a sound like falling furniture, and burst out into the court, and seized him by the arm with a grip that he felt to the bone. She hauled him up the stairs. He was obliged to take each step in a kind of leap, his feet scarcely touching, so that he went upward in a series of bounds like a small animal being dragged to the slaughter. He still clutched the trumpet. It was the last of his empire, and he held it.

In the kitchen she flung him toward the middle of the floor. He stood there among the tubs in the steam, which wavered about him and made him seem a small ghost. She closed the door and stood against it with her arms folded across her vast bosom.

"Now, den," she said.

Willie looked at the floor. The boards were worn into hollows, and in one of the hollows there was a little pool of soapy water in which the light from the window shone. He gazed into it as if it were a deep well into which he might presently be able to escape.

"Look at me when I'm talkin' teh yeh!"

He looked at her. Her face was a red cloud.

"Where'd yeh git dat t'ing?"

Willie was silent. He held the trumpet behind his back, as if by putting it out of his own sight he might put it out of hers.

"I ast yeh where'd yeh git it!"

"Off deh man," said Willie.

"Off deh man! Off deh man, he says! An' where'd yeh git deh money teh give deh man? Answer me dat! Where'd yeh git deh money?"

Willie said nothing. His mother's eyes went to the shelf, and his own followed them, against his will. There sat the teapot. It had a crack running down its side like a scar, and a chip out of its spout. It looked, now, extraordinarily guilty, as if it had been an accomplice.

"Out of me teapot," said the mother, in a voice that was suddenly low and dreadful. "Out of me own teapot dat I puts deh rent in. Out of deh money I slaves over deh tubs fer, day in an' day out, wid me hands like raw meat. Look at dese hands!" She thrust them toward him. He looked at them. They were indeed red and swollen, and the knuckles were cracked. He had seen them every day of his life and they had never before seemed remarkable.

"Look at 'em! Dat's what I gits fer bringin' yeh up. Dat's what I gits. I washes deh dirty shirts of every bum in deh ward so's yeh kin have a roof over yer head, an' den yeh goes an' robs me. Robs me! Yer own mudder! Me own son robs me!"

The words struck Willie with peculiar force. He had not known that he robbed. He had known only that there was money in the teapot and a trumpet on the pushcart, and that the one might be converted into the other by a process as simple and wonderful as the turning of water into steam. The idea that this was robbery came upon him as a revelation. He looked at the trumpet in his hand with a new and fearful respect, as if it had suddenly become a pistol.

The mother, perceiving that her words had effect, grew eloquent. She had in her a fund of oratory which the occasions of her life did not often call forth, and now it rushed out of her like water from a burst main. She described to him, at length, the hardships of her existence. She told him of the landlord, who was a bloodsucker, and of the grocer, who was a thief, and of the people for whom she washed, who were too proud to know their own dirt. She told him that she had brought him into the world in suffering, and that he was bringing her out of it in sorrow. She told him that she had never in her life taken a cent that was not her own. She raised her eyes to the steaming ceiling and called upon the saints to witness that this was so. The saints, it appeared, were not at home.

"I never," she cried. "Never in me life! Not a red cent! An' yeh do dis teh me!"

Then she painted for him his future. It was a picture done in the darkest colors. She saw him growing up a thief, a loafer on the corners, a frequenter of saloons. She saw him in the Tombs. She saw him in a striped suit upon the Island. She saw him at last, with a terrible relish of detail, standing upon a scaffold with a rope about his neck, and herself, an old woman with white hair, weeping at the foot of it.

"An' deh people'll say, 'Dere's his poor mudder, what done everyt'ing fer him, an' look at him now!' Dat's what dey'll say! An' it'll be deh death of me! Yeh'll kill me, Willie Delahunt! Yeh'll put me in me grave!"

She began to weep. The tears ran down her red face and mingled with the steam. Willie regarded her with a stony fascination. He had a dim conception of the scaffold. He had seen a picture of one, once, in a newspaper that had wrapped a fish. He tried to imagine himself standing upon it with the trumpet, and he found, to his shame, that the picture was not altogether displeasing. There was a certain grandeur in it. He would blow the trumpet, and the crowd would be silent.

His mother saw something of this in his face. She ceased weeping instantly.

"Wipe dat look off yer mug!" she screamed. "Gimme dat t'ing!"

She lunged for the trumpet. Willie, with the instinct of all property-holders, retreated. He backed against a washtub and could retreat no further. She wrenched the trumpet from his fingers. The green tassel came away in his hand, and he stood holding it, a small pathetic relic of his lost dominion.

At this moment there came a knock at the door.

The mother stood still with the trumpet raised. The knock came again, a dry, thin, regular knock, the knock of a man who knocks for a living. Her face underwent a swift and remarkable change. The fury went out of it as the color goes out of a coal that is plucked from the fire. She thrust the trumpet into the pocket of her apron, smoothed her hair with both hands, and assumed an expression of meek suffering, like that of a martyr in a cheap print.

"Not a word outa you," she hissed at Willie. Then she opened the door.

A thin man stood in the hall. He wore a derby hat that was too large for him and a coat that was too small, and he carried under his arm a ledger bound in black. His face had the color and the expression of the ledger. He was the agent of the landlord. He did not say good afternoon. He said, "Rent."

"Oh, Mister Haskins," said the mother, in a voice that Willie had never heard before. It was soft, and it trembled, and it seemed to come from a long distance, from a sickbed. "Oh, Mister Haskins, I was jes' goin' teh come down an' see yeh. I ain' got it. Not today. So help me Gawd, I ain' got a cent in deh house."

Willie looked at the teapot on the shelf.

"Dey ain' paid me," continued the mother, with a fine sorrow. "Deh people I washes fer. Dey ain' paid me in two weeks. An' me wid dis child teh feed, an' me man out of work, an'—" Her voice broke very prettily. She lifted a corner of the apron to her eyes. The trumpet clanked faintly in the pocket.

The agent of the landlord regarded her with eyes in which there was no more pity than there is in the eyes of a fish upon a slab. He had heard this speech, in various forms, upon every floor of every house in Gaffney's Court. He had heard it in Irish and in German and in Italian. He knew its every cadence. He opened his ledger and made a mark in it.

"Saturday," he said. "Saturday, or out you go."

"Saturday, Mister Haskins. Sure, sure. Saturday. Gawd bless yeh."

He went away. The mother closed the door. She stood with her back against it for a moment and breathed deeply. Then the martyr vanished from her face and the red cloud returned.

Willie had been watching this performance with his mouth open. A great question was forming in his mind. It was a question of such size and difficulty that he could not by any means get it into words. It had to do with the teapot, and with the saints who were not at home, and with the voice from the sickbed. He looked at his mother with a kind of awe, as one regards a magician who has done a trick before one's eyes.

"Mudder," he said, "dere's money in deh—"

The mother crossed the room in two strides and struck him upon the side of the head. He sat down suddenly upon the wet floor.

"An' a liar, too!" she cried. "A t'ief an' a liar! Where d'yeh learn it? Not from me, yeh didn't! Not in dis house! Talkin' back teh yer mudder after what yeh done! Gawd knows what yeh'll be! Gawd knows!"

Willie crawled under the table. It was a fortress which he had held many times before, against many sieges. From beneath its edge he looked out at the world, which consisted of his mother's skirts and the legs of the tubs and the little pool of soapy water shining in its hollow. His ear rang. He did not cry. He was occupied with the great question, which now seemed larger than ever, and which he perceived he would never be permitted to ask.

The mother took the trumpet from her apron pocket and looked at it. For a moment it seemed that she would destroy it. She raised it as if to dash it upon the floor. Then she paused, and turned it over in her red hands, and examined the gilt of the mouthpiece with a certain shrewdness. She was calculating whether the old man with the cotton beard could be brought to take it back. At length she put it upon the shelf, beside the teapot, where the two of them sat together like prisoners awaiting the same sentence.

She returned to her ironing. The flatiron came down upon the board with blows that shook the table above Willie's head. At each blow she muttered. The mutterings were fragments of her oration, repeated without order, as the last thunder of a storm rolls about the sky after the lightning has gone.

"Me own teapot. Robs his own mudder. Never a cent in me life. Deh gallows. Gawd knows."

At dusk the father came home. He was a truck-driver, a large man with shoulders like the hindquarters of his own horses, and he came up the stairs with a heavy, deliberate tread, as of a man who is carrying something precious and fears to spill it. He was carrying, in fact, a tin pail of beer. He set it upon the table, over Willie's head, and the boy heard the slosh of it, and smelled it.

The mother told him everything. She told it at length and with improvements. In her account the five cents had grown somewhat, and Willie's insolence had become a thing of monstrous dimensions, and the boy from the next court had been nearly murdered with the trumpet. The father listened, nodding gravely, his large face filled with the solemnity of a judge who hears a case of grave importance and who is also thirsty.

When she had finished he stooped and looked under the table.

"C'm 'ere," he said.

Willie came out. He stood before his father. The man looked down upon him from an enormous height.

"Did yeh do it?"

Willie nodded.

The father struck him, not hard, with the flat of his great hand, in the manner of a man who performs a ceremony of the church. Then he delivered judgment.

"Never take what ain' yours," he said, impressively. "Never. Dat's deh way teh git along in dis world. When I was a kid like you, if I'd 'a' took a cent off me ol' man, he'd 'a' broke me in two. In two! An' dat's why I'm what I am today. See? Dat's why."

He looked about him, at the steam and the tubs and the cracked walls, as if the room were a proof of his argument. Then he sat down and drew the pail toward him and drank deeply.

The mother watched him drink. Her eyes went from the pail to the shelf and back again. A new and darker red came into her face.

"An' where'd you git deh price of dat?" she demanded.

The father lowered the pail. He wiped his moustache with the back of his hand. "Never mind where I got it."

"Never mind, is it? Never mind! An' Haskins at deh door dis very day, an' me lyin' teh him like a—"

She stopped. She glanced at Willie. Willie was looking at her with the great question in his eyes.

"Git teh bed," she said to him. "Git outa me sight."

He went into the little dark room beyond the kitchen, where he slept upon a pallet in the corner. Behind him, through the thin partition, the voices of his parents rose. They rose and swelled and clashed together like the cymbals of a band. He heard the word "beer," and the word "rent," and the word "teapot," and several words which he knew he must not say. A chair fell over. A door slammed. Somebody upstairs pounded upon the floor and was cursed, and pounded no more.

Willie lay upon his back in the darkness and held in his fist the green tassel, which no one had thought to take from him. It was all that remained. He fingered it. The worsted was soft. He thought of the court that afternoon, of the children's faces filled with envy, of the boy from the next court falling back two paces before the blast. It seemed to him that it had all happened a long while ago, to some other person, a person of importance.

Presently the voices in the kitchen subsided. There came the sound of the pail being set down for the last time, empty, and a great creaking as his father lay down upon the bed, and then a long rasping snore, regular and sonorous, like the respiration of some vast and contented beast.

Willie got up. He crept to the doorway of the kitchen. The lamp had been turned low, and the room was filled with a dim yellow light and with the smell of soap and beer. His mother sat at the table with her head upon her arms. She was not asleep. Her shoulders moved a little. He could not tell whether she was weeping or only breathing heavily, and he did not go nearer to find out.

In the fall the season was over at the hotel and the boats were pulled up on the shore of the lake and turned over so the rain would not collect in them. There were only a few guests left. The waiter brought the drinks out to the terrace and set them on the iron table and went back inside, and the man and the woman sat and looked at the lake. It was grey and flat and there was no wind on it. Across the water the mountains went up steeply and there was new snow on the tops of them, and below the snow the trees were dark, and below the trees there were the vineyards and the brown fields and the road that ran along the far shore. A cart was moving on the road. It was too far to hear it.

"It's cold," the woman said.

"Do you want to go in?"

"No. I like it out here. I like the cold now."

"We can have the drinks inside if you want."

"I said I like it."

"All right."

He picked up his glass and drank from it. It was vermouth with a piece of lemon peel in it and it was very cold and he could taste the lemon.

"How is yours?" he said.

"It's fine."

"They make them well here."

"They make everything well here," she said. "That's the thing about this country. Everything is made very well and it's all very clean."

"You liked it when we came."

"I like it now. I didn't say I didn't like it."

They sat and looked at the lake. A man came down from the hotel carrying two oars on his shoulder and went down to the shore and laid the oars under one of the boats and went back up the path. He did not look at them. When he had gone into the hotel the woman took a cigarette out of the case on the table and the man struck a match and held it for her and she put her hand around his hand to keep the match steady, although there was no wind.

"Thank you," she said.

"Are you warm enough?"

"Please stop asking me if I'm warm."

"I'm sorry."

"You don't have to be sorry. Just stop asking."

He put his hand in his coat pocket and his fingers touched the paper there and he took his hand out again and put it on the table.

"I thought tomorrow we might take the boat out if it's clear," he said. "The man said the fishing is good at the end of the lake where the river comes in. He said this time of year they come up into the shallow water."

"You don't want to go fishing."

"Sure I do."

"You don't want to go fishing tomorrow," she said. "You want to talk about something and you are talking about fishing instead."

"I like to fish."

"I know you like to fish."

"Well, then."

"Well, then," she said. "Well, then. All right. We'll go fishing."

The waiter came out and asked if they wanted anything more and the man said yes, two more of the same, and the waiter took the empty glasses and went inside. It was getting darker now over the mountains and the snow on the tops was white and very clear against the sky, and lower down it was already dark in the trees.

"When did it come?" the woman said.

"When did what come?"

"Please don't."

He looked at her. She was looking out at the lake and the smoke from the cigarette went straight up and then flattened out over the table.

"This morning," he said. "While you were sleeping."

"I wasn't sleeping. I heard the boy come up the stairs. I heard you go to the door."

"I didn't know you were awake."

"I was awake. I lay there and I heard you open it and I heard you stand there a long time. You stood there a long time reading it. It must have been a long one."

"It wasn't long."

"Then you read it many times."

"I read it a few times."

"And then you put it in your coat and you came back and you got into the bed and you lay there and you didn't say anything. And I lay there. And we both lay there and we were very quiet and very polite with each other."

"I thought you were asleep."

"You knew I wasn't asleep."

He did not say anything. The waiter came out with the two glasses and set them down and took the money from the table and made the change from his pocket and put it on the saucer and thanked them and went inside again. The man moved the saucer with the change on it to the side of the table.

"Is it from Morrison?" she said.

"Yes."

"I knew it would be from Morrison. Nobody else knows where we are."

"I wrote him where we'd be."

"I know you did. I didn't say it was wrong. I only said nobody else knows."

"He has to know where to send things."

"He has to know where to send things," she said. "Yes. Of course he does."

The man drank from the new glass. It was as cold as the first one and it tasted the same and he held it in his mouth for a moment before he swallowed it.

"Do you want to read it?" he said.

"No."

"You can read it."

"I don't want to read it. I know what it says. I can tell you what it says without reading it. It says they need someone down there and it says you know the country and you know the people and you speak the language. It says it won't be long. It says the money is good. Does it say the money is good?"

"It says something about the money."

"And it says it won't be long."

"He doesn't know how long. Nobody knows how long."

"But it says it."

"Yes," he said. "It says it."

She put the cigarette out in the ashtray, pressing it down carefully until there was no more smoke, and then she sat back in the iron chair and put her hands in the pockets of her coat.

"Well," she said. "You'll go."

"I didn't say I'd go."

"You'll go. You've already gone. You went this morning standing at the door. You've been gone all day. You were gone at lunch. I sat and ate lunch with you and you were gone. I could see you down there already. I could see you thinking about what to take and what roads they'll have closed and who will still be in the hotel and who won't. You were gone at lunch and you were gone when we walked up the hill to the church and you were gone just now when you were telling me about the fishing."

"That isn't true."

"Isn't it?"

"I was thinking about it. I didn't say I wasn't thinking about it."

"You're always thinking about it. Even when there aren't any telegrams you're thinking about it. I wake up in the night and you're lying there with your eyes open and I know what you're thinking about."

"I don't sleep well. I've never slept well."

"You slept well in the summer," she said. "You slept fine in the summer. You slept like a child."

He did not answer that. Out on the lake a small steamer was coming down from the north end with its lights on. It was the last boat of the day and it would stop at the landing below the hotel and then go on across to the other shore. They watched it come. The lights were yellow and they made long lines on the water and the sound of the engine came to them now across the water, very faint and steady.

"There used to be more boats," he said.

"When?"

"In the summer. There were three a day in the summer."

"There's one now."

"Yes. Now there's one."

"It's enough," she said. "It's enough for the people who are left."

The steamer came in to the landing and they could hear a man calling out and the sound of a rope thrown onto the boards. No one got off. A woman with a basket got on and the man on the landing threw the rope back and the steamer backed away from the landing and turned and went out across the lake toward the other shore. They watched it until the lights were small.

"You could come," he said.

"Don't."

"I mean it. You could come as far as the border. There's a town there. It's a good town. There's a hotel there and you could stay at the hotel and I could come up when there was nothing doing. It would only be a few hours by car."

"And I would sit in the hotel."

"You could walk. There's good walking. There's a river."

"And I would sit in the hotel and walk by the river and wait for you to come up when there was nothing doing. And every night I would go down and ask the man at the desk if there was a message. And when there was a message I would be afraid to open it and when there wasn't a message I would be afraid there wasn't one."

"It wouldn't be like that."

"How would it be?"

He did not say anything.

"I did that," she said. "I did that once. You remember. I did that for four months in that town with the yellow walls, with the nuns next door. You remember the nuns. Every morning the bells. I learned all the bells. I learned which bells meant which thing. I could tell you the time of day from the bells and I could tell you the day of the week from the bells. I did that for four months and you came up five times."

"Six."

"Five. The sixth time was when they sent you up because of your leg and that doesn't count."

"It counts."

"It doesn't count," she said. "You came up five times and the sixth time they sent you."

"All right. Five."

"I'm not angry," she said. "I want you to know that I'm not angry. I'm only telling you how it was."

"I know how it was."

"You don't know how it was. You know how it was for you. You don't know how it was in that town."

The man finished the drink. He turned the glass in his fingers and looked at the piece of lemon peel in the bottom of it.

"I could tell him no," he said.

"Yes. You could."

"I could wire him tomorrow from the village and tell him no. I could tell him I'm through with it. I could tell him to get somebody else. There are plenty of others. There are young ones who would give anything to go."

"There are."

"So I could tell him."

"You could tell him," she said. "And then what?"

"And then we'd stay."

"Here?"

"Here or somewhere. Anywhere you like. We could go down to the coast for the winter. We could take the place we looked at, with the fig tree. You liked that place."

"I liked that place."

"So we'd do that."

"And you'd sit under the fig tree."

"I'd work. I'd write the book."

"You'd sit under the fig tree," she said, "and every morning you'd walk down to the village and buy the papers, all the papers, the French ones and the English ones and the ones from home that come a week late, and you'd bring them back and you'd read them all, every word, at the table under the fig tree. And you'd read about it. And you'd read about the men down there, the ones you know. And you'd read about the ones who were killed. And you'd sit there under the fig tree and you'd be very kind to me. You'd be kinder than you have ever been. And I would watch you being kind to me and I would know."

"Know what?"

"Know that I had done it. That it was me that kept you there."

"You wouldn't have done anything. I'd have decided."

"That's what you'd say," she said. "That's what you'd say every day. And it would be true. And it wouldn't matter."

It was nearly dark now. The lights had come on in the hotel behind them and the light came out through the windows onto the terrace and onto the table and the glasses. Across the lake there were lights in the villages along the shore, very small, and above them the mountains were black and the snow on the tops was grey now and you could hardly see where the snow stopped and the sky began.

"I don't know what you want me to do," he said.

"I don't want you to do anything."

"You must want something."

"I want it to be the summer," she said. "That's what I want. I want it to be July and I want us to be swimming off the rocks below the road. Do you remember? The water was so cold you couldn't breathe when you went in, and then after you could breathe, and it was fine. And afterward we'd lie on the rocks and the rocks were warm, and you'd fall asleep. You fell asleep every afternoon. I'd lie there and watch you sleep. I want that. Can you give me that?"

"No."

"No," she said. "So I don't want anything."

"Meg."

"I'm all right. Truly. I'm fine."

"You're not fine."

"I'm as fine as I'm going to be. That's fine enough."

He reached across the table and put his hand on her arm, on the sleeve of her coat. She did not move her arm away and she did not move it toward him. She let it lie there under his hand.

"It would only be until the spring," he said. "That's what he thinks. Until the spring at the latest. Everybody says it can't go past the spring."

"Everybody said that last year."

"This year it's different."

"How is it different?"

"It just is. You can feel it. It's coming to the end now. Everybody knows it."

"Then why do they need you?"

He took his hand from her arm.

"Because it's coming to the end," he said. "Because somebody ought to be there at the end. Somebody ought to see it who saw the rest of it."

"And it has to be you."

"It doesn't have to be me."

"But you want it to be you."

"Yes," he said. "I want it to be me."

She looked at him then for the first time in a long while. Her face was very calm in the light from the window and he could not tell anything from it.

"Thank you," she said.

"For what?"

"For saying it. For not saying it was the money or that Morrison needed you or that there was no one else. Thank you for saying it was because you wanted to."

"It's the truth."

"I know it's the truth. That's why I'm thanking you."

They sat there. Down at the shore there was a sound of water moving against the stones, very small, and then it stopped. Then it started again. A wind was coming down from the mountains. They could feel it on their faces, cold and smelling of the snow.

"It's going to rain," he said.

"Yes."

"The fishing will be no good if it rains."

"No," she said. "It won't be any good."

"Maybe it will clear by noon."

"Maybe."

"We could go in the afternoon."

"We could."

The waiter came to the door of the hotel and stood there and looked out at them. He did not come out. He had his napkin over his arm and he stood in the lighted doorway and waited, and after a while the man raised his hand and the waiter nodded and went back inside.

"We'd better eat," the man said. "They want to close the dining room early. There's only the four of us and the English couple."

"The English couple are leaving tomorrow."

"Are they?"

"She told me this morning. On the stairs. They're going home. She said it's too dull here now that everyone has gone. She said she couldn't bear the quiet."

"I like the quiet."

"I know you do," she said. "So do I. I've always liked it."

She stood up and buttoned her coat to the top. He stood up too and put some coins on the saucer with the change for the waiter, and then he stood there by the table with his hands in his pockets and felt the paper with his fingers.

"When would you leave?" she said.

"I don't know. I'd have to wire him first."

"But when?"

"Thursday," he said. "Maybe Thursday. There's a train Thursday from the city that makes the connection."

"Thursday's fine," she said. "Thursday will give us time to go fishing."

"Meg."

"No. I mean it. I want to go fishing. I want to go out in the boat to where the river comes in and I want you to show me where they come up in the shallow water. I want to catch one. I've never caught one here. All summer and I never caught one."

"You'll catch one."

"Will I?"

"Sure. If it clears. They're easy this time of year. They come right up."

"Then I'll catch one," she said. "And we'll bring it back and they'll cook it for us here, and we'll eat it, and it will be very good. It will be the best one we ever had."

"It will be good."

"It will be the best one."

The rain started then. It came across the lake from the far shore and they could hear it on the water before it reached them, a long hissing sound coming closer, and then it was on the terrace and on the iron table and in the empty glasses. She stood there in it a moment with her face turned up, and then she turned and went in through the lighted door, and he followed her.

The train came in at four o'clock and Walt was waiting on the platform. He was standing by the baggage truck with his hat pushed back and his hands in the pockets of his canvas coat. He was bigger than Tom remembered. He had been big before, but now he was big the way a man gets who works outside all year, thick in the neck and the shoulders, and his face was brown and lined at the corners of the eyes.

Tom stepped down with his bag. The conductor handed down the rod case after him.

"Hello, Walt," he said.

"Hello, Tommy."

They shook hands. Walt's hand was hard and dry. He took the bag and Tom kept the rod case, and they walked out past the station house to where the truck was parked in the shade of a cottonwood. The truck was old and green and there was a dog in the back of it. The dog stood up and wagged and watched them.

"That's not Duke," Tom said.

"Duke's dead. That's his pup. That's Sam."

"Hello, Sam."

The dog put his head down and Tom rubbed behind his ears. Walt put the bag in the back and they got in. The cab smelled of oil and tobacco and old hay. Walt started the truck and they drove out of town on the gravel road with the dust coming up behind them.

"You look thin," Walt said.

"I've been sick."

"Ellen said you'd been sick. Your mother wrote her."

"It wasn't anything. It's all right now."

"Good," Walt said.

They drove along the road. The wheat was up on both sides and it was green and moving in the wind. Beyond the wheat were the hills, and beyond the hills the mountains, and there was still snow on the mountains. Tom looked at the snow. It had been a long time since he had seen it.

"The wheat looks good," he said.

"It's all right. We had rain in May. We'll see."

"Is it all yours now?"

"The north half and the bottom land. I sold the section by the Hansen place. I had to."

"I didn't know that."

"No," Walt said. "There wasn't any way you'd know it."

They did not say anything for a while. The truck went over the bridge at the creek and Tom looked down and saw the water. It was high and fast and the color of tea. Walt saw him look.

"It'll clear in a week," Walt said. "It's still running off the snow. But there's a pool below the old dam that's fishing. I was down there Sunday."

"Any good?"

"I got four. Nothing big. But they were fat."

"I brought the rod."

"I saw you did."

---

The house was the same. It was white and square with the porch on two sides and the big elm in the yard, and the windmill behind it was turning slowly in the wind. Ellen came out on the porch when the truck stopped. She was drying her hands on her apron. She came down the steps and Tom got out and she put her arms around him and held him.

"Look at you," she said. "Look how thin you are."

"Walt already told me."

"Well, it's true. Come in. Come in and wash. Supper's nearly ready."

He went into the house. It smelled of bread and coffee and the oilcloth on the kitchen table. There were two children in the kitchen, a boy and a girl, and they looked at him and did not say anything.

"This is your cousin Tom," Ellen said. "Say hello."

"Hello," the boy said. The girl said nothing. She was very small.

"The last time I saw you," Tom said to the boy, "you were in a basket."

The boy looked at him. He did not believe it.

Tom washed at the sink and they ate supper. There was fried chicken and new potatoes and bread and butter and a dish of pickled beets, and there was coffee and afterward there was pie. Tom ate a great deal. He had not been hungry for a long time and now he was hungry and the food was good. Ellen watched him eat and was pleased.

"You'll stay a while," she said.

"A week. Maybe a little longer."

"You'll stay as long as you want."

"Thank you, Ellen."

Walt did not say anything. He ate his pie and drank his coffee and then he pushed his chair back.

"I've got to look at the heifer," he said. "You want to come?"

"All right."

---

They went out to the barn. It was getting dark now and the air was cool. The swallows were going in and out of the high door of the barn. Inside it was dark and smelled of manure and straw and the heifer was in the box stall at the end. She was lying down and she turned her head and looked at them.

Walt went in and squatted beside her and put his hand on her flank. He stayed there a long time.

"Tonight?" Tom said.

"Maybe. Maybe tomorrow. It's her first."

"You want me to stay out with you?"

"No. I'll come out and look at her at midnight. There's nothing to do yet."

He came out of the stall and latched it. They stood in the door of the barn and looked out at the yard. The kitchen window was yellow with the lamp and they could see Ellen moving in it.

Walt took a bottle out from behind a feed bin. It was a pint bottle and it was half full. He uncorked it and handed it to Tom.

"Ellen doesn't care," he said. "But I keep it out here anyway."

Tom drank. It was rough whiskey and it burned going down and then it was warm. He handed the bottle back. Walt drank and put the cork back in and held the bottle in his hand.

"She looks well," Tom said. "Ellen."

"She's fine."

"And the kids."

"They're fine. The boy's going to be smart. Smarter than me."

"That's not hard."

"No," Walt said. "It isn't."

He uncorked the bottle again and handed it over. Tom drank and gave it back.

"I got your letter," Walt said. "About your father's watch."

"I wanted you to have it."

"I know you did. I didn't write back."

"That's all right."

"No, it isn't. I meant to write back. I sat down to do it twice."

"It's all right, Walt."

Walt looked at the bottle. Then he drank from it.

"I wear it Sundays," he said. "It still keeps good time."

"He always kept it wound."

"I keep it wound too."

They stood there. It was dark now and the stars were out over the windmill. The windmill had stopped turning. There was no wind at all.

"We'll fish in the morning," Walt said. "Early. Before it gets hot."

"I'd like that."

"I'll get you up."

---

Walt got him up before it was light. He knocked on the door and Tom woke and did not know where he was. Then he heard the rooster and knew. He got up and dressed in the dark and went down to the kitchen. Walt had the stove going and there was coffee and he was frying eggs.

"How's the heifer?"

"She had it at three. A bull calf. They're both fine."

"You didn't wake me."

"There wasn't any need to."

They ate the eggs with bread and drank the coffee. Then they went out to the truck. Walt had put the rods in the back and a can of worms and a canvas bag with sandwiches in it, and the bottle. The dog got in the back. It was getting light in the east now and it was cold, and they drove with the windows up.

They drove out along the creek road and then turned off on a track that went down through the pasture. Walt stopped the truck by a gate and they got out and went through the gate and walked down toward the creek. The grass was wet and soon their trousers were wet to the knee. The dog went ahead of them through the grass and they could see where he had gone by the dark line he left in it.

The old dam was made of logs and rocks and most of it had washed out. The water came through the break in it and dropped into a long pool. The pool was deep and green at the head and the water was clearer here than at the bridge. At the tail of the pool there was a riffle and then the creek went on around a bend under the willows.

Tom put his rod together. His hands were cold and he was slow with it. He tied on a hook and put on a worm and then he walked up to the head of the pool and dropped the worm in where the water came over the logs. He let it go down with the current. He could feel it bumping along the bottom. Then it stopped and he felt the line go tight and he struck and the rod bent and the fish was on.

It was not a big fish but it fought well. It went down deep and then came up and jumped, and he saw it in the air, bright and spotted, and then it was down again. He kept the rod up and let it run and then brought it in. Walt came with the net and netted it for him.

"That's a good fish," Walt said.

"It's a nice fish."

He killed it and put it in the creel on the wet grass. Then he baited again. Walt had gone down to the tail of the pool and was fishing the riffle. Tom watched him. Walt fished the way he did everything, carefully and without hurry, and Tom saw him take a fish and then another. The sun was coming up over the hills and it was on the water now and it was warm on Tom's back.

They fished until the sun was high. Tom caught five and Walt caught seven. Then they sat on the grass under a cottonwood above the pool and ate the sandwiches. The sandwiches were cold meat and mustard and bread and they were very good. Walt took the bottle out of the bag and went down to the creek and filled a tin cup with water and came back. He poured whiskey in the cup with the water and handed it to Tom.

"That's the way to drink it," he said. "With creek water."

Tom drank and gave it back. The water was cold and the whiskey was warm in it. Walt drank and filled the cup again.

"This is fine," Tom said. "This is a fine place."

"It's the best place on the creek. Dad used to bring us here. You remember."

"I remember."

"You caught that big one. The summer you were twelve."

"You netted it and it got off."

"It didn't get off. You never brought it in close enough. I couldn't reach it."

"It got off in the net."

"That's not the way it happened."

"That's the way I remember it."

Walt laughed. "All right," he said. "That's the way it happened."

They drank. A kingfisher came down the creek and went past them, low over the water, and they heard it chattering after it was gone around the bend. The dog was lying in the shade with his head on his paws and he was asleep.

"How was it over there?" Walt said.

"It was all right."

"Ellen said you were in the hospital a long time."

"A while."

"Was it bad?"

"It was bad for a while. Then it was better."

"What was it?"

"It was a fever. Then it was something in the blood. They didn't know what it was for a while. Then they found out."

"But you're all right now."

"I'm all right now."

Walt looked at the creek. "I thought about going," he said. "When it started. I thought about it a lot."

"You had the place."

"I had the place and I had Ellen and the boy. And Dad was sick then. I didn't know how sick."

"You did right."

"I don't know if I did right. I didn't go. That's all."

"You did right, Walt."

Walt poured more whiskey in the cup and went down and put water in it and came back. He sat down and drank and handed it over. Tom drank. The whiskey was making him feel good and easy and he lay back on the grass and looked up through the leaves of the cottonwood. The leaves were moving a little now. There was a little wind coming up the creek.

"I should have come back," Tom said. "When he died."

Walt did not say anything.

"I got the cable. I couldn't get out. There wasn't any ship for three weeks. Then I was sick."

"I know it."

"I wanted to come."

"I know you did," Walt said. "It doesn't matter."

"It matters."

"It doesn't matter now. It was a long time ago. There wasn't anything you could have done."

"I could have been here."

"Yes," Walt said. "You could have been here."

They lay there. Tom looked up at the leaves. He did not want to look at Walt. He heard Walt drink and then he heard him put the cup down on the grass.

"He asked for you," Walt said. "At the end. He thought you were coming. He thought you were in the next room."

Tom did not say anything.

"I told him you were. I told him you were out in the kitchen with Ellen. He was all right after that. He went to sleep."

"Thank you."

"There wasn't anything else to tell him."

"I know. Thank you, Walt."

"Don't thank me."

The wind was moving the leaves and the light came down through them and moved on the grass. Tom shut his eyes. He could hear the creek going over the logs of the old dam. It made a steady sound. He lay and listened to it and after a while he opened his eyes and sat up.

"He was good to me," he said. "After my father."

"He liked you better than me."

"That's not true."

"It's true. You were quick. You read books. He used to say you were going to be something."

"I'm not anything."

"You're something. You went over there. You saw all that."

"It isn't anything to see. It's just a lot of places."

"It's more than I've seen."

"You've got this," Tom said. "You've got the place and Ellen and the kids. You've got the creek."

"I've got the mortgage on the place."

"You've still got it."

"Yes," Walt said. "I've still got it."

He picked up the cup and looked at it and then he threw the rest of the water and whiskey out onto the grass. He put the cup in the bag and corked the bottle and put it in too.

"We'll have some tonight," he said. "After supper. There's more in the barn."

"That's good."

"Let's fish down around the bend. There's a hole under the willows. Dad never fished it. He said it was too hard to get to. But there's fish in it."

"All right."

They got up. The dog woke and stood and stretched and looked at them. They picked up the rods and the creel and walked down along the creek. The grass was dry now and the sun was hot. At the bend the willows grew thick and they had to go down into the water to get past them. The water was cold on Tom's legs through his trousers. It was so cold it hurt and then it did not hurt.

Under the willows the water was deep and dark and it went slowly. There was a log in it. Walt pointed at the log.

"Under there," he said. "You go first."

"No, you go."

"Go on. You're the company."

Tom baited the hook. He swung the worm out and let it drop above the log and the current took it down and under. He waited. He did not feel anything. He let it go a little farther and then he felt something and he struck. The fish was heavy. It did not jump. It went down and back under the log and he could not hold it and the line went slack.

"Gone," he said.

"Was it big?"

"It was big."

"Bigger than the one when you were twelve?"

"Bigger."

"Well," Walt said. "You never could bring them in close enough."

Tom looked at him. Walt was not smiling, but his eyes were. Tom began to laugh. He stood in the cold water and laughed and Walt laughed too, and the dog stood on the bank and barked at them because he did not know what it was about.

"Let's go home," Walt said. "We've got enough fish. Ellen will fry them."

"All right."

They waded out of the water and climbed up the bank and walked back through the pasture to the truck. The sun was high and it was hot now and their trousers dried as they walked. At the gate Tom stopped and looked back. He could see the willows and the cottonwood and a piece of the pool shining through the trees. He could not see the dam.

"We'll come back tomorrow," Walt said.

"Yes."

"And the day after. Every day you're here, if you want."

"I want to."

"All right then," Walt said.

He opened the gate and they went through and he shut it behind them and put the wire loop over the post. The dog jumped in the back of the truck. They put the rods in and the creel and the bag. Then they got in the cab and Walt started the truck and they drove back up the track toward the road. The wheat was on both sides and it was moving in the wind and there was still snow on the mountains.

prompt:
Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Ernest Hemingway, depicting the following scene: A parent reprimanding a young child.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.

In the afternoon the wind came up out of the northwest. The man stopped splitting wood and stood and looked at the lake. It had been flat all morning, and now it was dark where the wind touched it, and you could see the wind moving across the water toward the point. The birches along the shore turned the pale undersides of their leaves up. He set the axe in the block and wiped his hands on his trousers and walked down through the long grass to the dock.

The boat was gone.

He stood on the dock and looked for it. The boards were gray and warm under his feet, and the water slapped against the pilings. He looked first toward the big rock where the boy was allowed to go, and the boat was not there. He looked toward the point, and then out toward the island, and then he saw it. It was very small and far out, past where the bottom dropped away. It was not moving the way a boat moves when someone is rowing it. It was turning slowly, sideways to the wind. He could see the boy sitting in the stern, and he could see one oar.

He did not shout. It was too far to shout, and the wind was wrong for it.

The canoe was on the rack under the cedars. He lifted it down and turned it over and carried it to the water and put it in. He went back for the paddle, and then he went back again for the coil of line that hung on the nail by the woodshed door. He knelt in the canoe a little behind the center and pushed off from the dock with the paddle and turned the bow out toward the island.

Inside the cove the water was not bad. When he came out past the point the wind took the bow and pushed it around, and he had to paddle hard on the one side to bring it back. The waves were short and steep and the color of slate, and the tops of them were beginning to break white. Spray came over the bow and wet his shirt. It was cold. The lake was always cold out past the drop, even in August. He knew that, and he did not think about it. He paddled and kept his eyes on the boat.

He paddled for a long time. His shoulders began to burn, and then they stopped burning and only ached, and then he did not notice them. He counted the strokes for a while and then stopped counting. The boat got larger. Once he lost it behind a wave and felt something go tight in his stomach, and then the canoe rose and he saw it again, closer now, still turning. The boy was sitting very still. He was holding the gunwales with both hands.

When he was close he eased off and let the canoe come up alongside. The boat was pitching, and he was careful not to let the two hulls knock. The boy looked at him. The boy's face was white, and there were marks on it where he had been crying, but he was not crying now.

"Where's the other oar?" the man said.

"It went over."

"Where?"

The boy pointed. Far off toward the north shore there was something small and yellow on the water, and then it was gone, and then it was there again.

"All right," the man said. "Hand me the painter. The rope at the front. Don't stand up. Crawl."

The boy crawled forward along the bottom of the boat with the water sloshing around his knees and found the painter and held it out. The man took it and tied it to the thwart behind him with two half hitches and pulled them tight.

"Now get back in the stern and sit down in the bottom. Not on the seat. In the bottom."

"What about the oar?"

"Leave the oar in the boat."

"I mean the other one."

"Sit down," the man said.

The boy sat down in the bottom of the boat.

Going back was harder. The wind was behind them, and that should have been easier, but the boat was heavy and yawed on the line, and the waves came up under the stern of the canoe and tried to turn it. He had to watch each one. He had to feel each one before it came. He did not look back at the boy, because he could not look back and keep the canoe straight, and he did not speak because there was nothing to say that needed saying out there. He paddled. The line went tight and slack and tight again. When they came around the point into the cove the water lay down all at once, and the noise of the wind went up into the tops of the cedars, and he could hear his own breathing.

He ran the canoe up on the sand beside the dock and got out into the shallow water and pulled the boat in by the painter until it grounded. The boy started to climb out.

"Stay there," the man said.

He pulled the canoe higher on the sand and turned it over. He coiled the line. He pulled the boat up and untied the painter and took the one oar out and laid it on the dock. He tipped the boat on its side and let the water run out of it, and set it down again. Then he sat down on the end of the dock with his feet hanging over the water. His shirt was wet through, and the wind was cold on it. His hands were shaking a little, and he put them between his knees.

"Come here," he said.

The boy got out of the boat and came up onto the dock. He stood a little way off.

"Sit down."

"Are you going to whip me?"

"I don't know yet," the man said. "Sit down."

The boy sat down on the dock. He sat with his legs crossed under him, not hanging over the water, and he looked at the boards.

"Who said you could take the boat?"

"Nobody."

"Did I say you could take the boat?"

"No, sir."

"What did I tell you about the boat?"

"You said I could take it to the big rock."

"That's right. And what else?"

"You said I had to ask first."

"Did you ask?"

"You were splitting wood."

"Did you ask?"

"No," the boy said.

"Where were you when I found you?"

The boy did not answer.

"Where were you?"

"Past the rock."

"How far past it?"

The boy picked at a splinter in the board with his fingernail. He did not answer.

"How far past it?"

"A long way."

"That's right," the man said. "A long way."

They sat there. Out on the lake the whitecaps were running all the way across now, and the island looked dark and close the way it did before rain. A gull came over low and turned and went back out.

"Look at me," the man said.

The boy looked at him.

"Why did you go out there?"

"I don't know."

"Yes, you do."

"I wanted to see the loons."

"There are loons in the cove. You can see loons from the porch."

"Not the young ones. The young ones are by the island."

"That's not why."

The boy looked down again. "I wanted to fish," he said. "Where you fish. Off the island where the bottom comes up. Where you got the big one."

The man did not say anything for a while.

"I brought the worms," the boy said. "They're in the can. They went in the water when the oar went."

"How did the oar go?"

"I was trying to turn around. When the wind came. It was in the lock and then it wasn't."

"You tried to reach for it."

"Yes."

"Did you stand up?"

The boy didn't answer.

"Did you stand up in the boat?"

"A little."

The man looked out at the water. He was quiet for a long time, and the boy watched him and then stopped watching him.

"Do you know how deep it is out there?" the man said.

"No."

"Neither do I. Nobody knows. They tried to sound it once with a line and the line wasn't long enough." He said it flatly, the way he would say what time it was. "It's cold down there. It's cold even now, at the end of the summer. You put your hand in it out there and it hurts your hand."

"I can swim."

"You can swim to the rock."

"I can swim farther than the rock."

"You can swim to the rock in the cove on a flat day in July with me standing on the dock. You can't swim in that." He moved his chin toward the lake. "Nobody can swim very long in that. Not grown men. Not strong ones."

The boy was quiet.

"If you had gone over out there," the man said, "I would not have found you. Do you understand that? I would have come out in the canoe and there would have been the boat and nobody in it. I would have looked and looked and there would have been nothing to find."

The boy began to cry. He did not make much noise. His face went tight and red, and the tears came, and he wiped at them with the back of his wrist.

"Don't cry," the man said.

The boy kept crying.

"All right," the man said. "Cry if you want to."

He waited. The wind moved the tops of the cedars, and down along the shore a loose board on the boathouse knocked and knocked. After a while the boy stopped crying and sat with his shoulders going up and down, and then they stopped going up and down.

"You're not to take the boat again this summer," the man said.

The boy looked up quickly.

"Not to the rock. Not anywhere."

"The whole summer?"

"The whole summer."

"But there's three weeks."

"That's right. There's three weeks."

"That's not fair."

"No," the man said. "It isn't fair. It's what it is."

"You didn't say that before. You didn't say if I went past the rock I couldn't have it."

"I didn't think I had to say it."

"You should have said it."

"Maybe I should have," the man said. "I'm saying it now."

The boy looked at the boat lying on its side on the sand. The water had run out of it and the bottom was dark and wet.

"Are you still going to whip me?"

The man looked at his hands. They had stopped shaking. He opened them and closed them.

"No," he said.

"Why not?"

"Because I don't want to."

"You whipped me when I broke the window."

"That was different."

"How?"

"It was a window," the man said. "Go on up to the house and get out of those wet things. Put on your dry trousers and the wool shirt. Then come back down and help me put the canoe away."

The boy got up. He stood for a moment as though he were going to say something, and then he did not say it, and he turned and went up the path through the grass toward the house. The man watched him go. He was very thin, and his wet shirt stuck to his back, and he walked carefully, the way you walk when you are trying not to run.

When the boy was in the house the man sat on the dock for a while longer. He looked out toward the north shore for the oar, but he could not see it now. It was too far, or the waves were too high, or it had gone in among the rocks. It was a good oar. He had shaped it himself two winters ago out of a piece of ash, and it had taken him a long time to get the blade right. It did not matter.

He had been on bad water before. There had been a river once, a long time ago, and a night on it, and men in it who had not come out. He had not thought about that river in a long time and he did not want to think about it now. He sat and looked at the lake and did not think about it. The wind was dropping. You could see it dropping. The whitecaps did not run so far now before they broke, and over toward the west the clouds had come apart and there was light behind them.

The boy came back down in his dry clothes, and they carried the canoe up together and put it on the rack. The boy took the stern end, and it was too heavy for him, and he did not say anything about it. The man took the paddle and the line up to the woodshed and hung them on their nails. Then he went in and made supper.

He fried potatoes in the iron pan with onions and some bacon fat, and when they were brown he broke four eggs into the pan beside them. He cut bread. He poured milk for the boy and opened a bottle of beer for himself and set the bottle on the table by his plate. They ate at the table by the window, where they could see the lake. Neither of them said much. The boy ate everything on his plate, and the man gave him the other egg, and he ate that too.

"Are you going to tell Mother?" the boy said.

"Yes."

"Do you have to?"

"Yes."

"When she comes Saturday?"

"When she comes Saturday."

The boy pushed a piece of bread around the plate in the yellow of the egg.

"She'll be sore."

"She'll be scared," the man said. "It's the same thing, mostly."

"Were you scared?"

The man drank from the bottle and set it down.

"Eat your bread," he said.

After supper the boy dried the dishes while the man washed them. Then the boy read for a while by the lamp in a book about a dog in the Klondike, and then he went to bed. The man went in after a time to put out the lamp. The boy was lying on his back with the blanket pulled up to his chin, and his eyes were open.

"Are you still sore at me?" the boy said.

"No."

"Honest?"

"Honest."

"I'm sorry about the oar."

"It's only an oar."

"You said it was a good oar."

"It was a good oar," the man said. "Go to sleep."

"Can we look for it tomorrow?"

"Maybe. If it's flat."

"In the canoe?"

"In the canoe."

"Can I paddle?"

"Go to sleep," the man said.

He put out the lamp and went out onto the porch. It was dark now, and the wind was gone. The lake was flat and black, and there was a moon coming up behind the island, and the moon made a road on the water all the way to the dock. A loon called out there somewhere, and then another one answered it from farther off. It was very quiet. He could hear the water moving a little against the pilings.

He sat down in the chair and lit a cigarette and smoked it. He looked out at the lake where the boat had been. It was hard to believe now that it had been the way it was. It looked like a lake you could walk on. It always looked that way at night, and it was never true.

The trout were in the bottom of the creel on a bed of ferns and he walked up from the river with the rod in one hand and the creel strap cutting into his shoulder. It was a cold morning and the mist had not burned off the beeches yet. The grass in the meadow was wet and his boots were wet through and he could feel the cold in his toes. Four good trout. He had lost a fifth one under the bank where the water was dark and deep, and he had sat on a log afterward and smoked a cigarette and not minded very much. It was a fine river. It was the best river he knew.

The inn was a low stone house with a slate roof and a wooden balcony across the front. Ellen was sitting on the balcony in a heavy sweater with her legs drawn up under her on the chair. She had a letter in her lap. He saw the letter before he saw her face.

"Hello," he called up.

"Hello, Jack."

"I got four. Do you want to see them?"

"Bring them up."

He went in through the kitchen. The woman of the house was at the stove and he showed her the trout and she took them out of the ferns one at a time and held them up and said they were very good, very beautiful, and that she would cook them for the lunch. He gave her the creel and went out and washed his hands at the pump in the yard. The water was cold enough to hurt. Then he went up the stairs and out onto the balcony.

"They were too good to bring up," he said. "She has them. She's going to fry them in ham fat."

"That's nice."

He sat down on the other chair and stretched out his legs. The wet boots steamed a little where the sun came through onto them.

"When did that come?"

"The boy brought it up from the village. About an hour ago."

"Is it from Paris?"

"It's from Martin. In Madrid. It's for you, darling. I opened it. I'm sorry. I thought it might be about the money."

"That's all right."

She held it out to him and he took it and did not read it. He folded it once and put it in the pocket of his shirt.

"Aren't you going to read it?"

"I'll read it after lunch."

"I read it," she said. "You might as well know I read it."

"All right."

"He says the paper wants you back. He says they've had three men there and none of them is any good and the paper wants you. He says you can name it. That's what he says. You can name it."

"Martin always says that."

"Does he?"

"He says that about everything."

She looked out at the meadow and the river and the beeches beyond the river where the mist was starting to lift. There were cows in the meadow now. They had not been there when he came up.

"Would you like a drink?" he said.

"It's eleven o'clock."

"I know what time it is. Would you like one?"

"All right."

He went down and got a bottle of the white wine from the cold room behind the kitchen and two glasses and brought them back up. He poured the wine and it was very cold and pale and the outside of the glasses clouded. He gave her one.

"It's good," she said.

"It's the best thing they have."

"It's the only thing they have."

"It's still the best."

She smiled at that and he thought it was going to be all right. They drank the wine and watched the cows. One of the cows walked down into the river and stood in the shallow water at the tail of the pool, drinking.

"She's in my pool," he said.

"Is that your pool?"

"That's where I lost the big one."

"Poor Jack."

"He was a fine fish. He went under the bank and it was over."

"Do you think about him?"

"Some."

"You'll think about him in Madrid," she said.

He did not say anything. He drank the wine and poured more into his glass and held the bottle toward her and she shook her head.

"You haven't said you're going to Madrid," she said.

"No."

"But you're going."

"I haven't read the letter."

"Please don't do that."

"Do what?"

"You know what. You read it in my face when you came up the meadow. I saw you read it. You don't have to read it twice."

"I'll read it after lunch," he said. "We'll talk about it after lunch. We'll have the trout and some of the ham and the cheese and then we'll talk about it. All right?"

"It isn't going to be different after lunch."

"It might be."

"No," she said. "It won't be. Nothing is ever different after lunch."

They had lunch in the dining room downstairs where it was dark and cool and there was a long table with a white oilcloth on it and only the two of them at the end. The other guests had gone in September. The woman brought the trout on a long platter, brown and crisp, with the strips of ham laid across them, and there was bread and the cold wine and a bowl of salad with oil on it. He boned a trout for her. He did it carefully, opening it along the back and lifting the bone out whole with the head still on it, and laid the two pieces of white meat on her plate.

"You do that beautifully," she said.

"There's nothing to it."

"You do everything beautifully when you want to."

He boned his own trout and ate it. It was very good. The skin was crisp and the meat was sweet and tasted of the river. He ate a second one and a piece of the ham and some bread. She ate slowly and did not finish.

"Don't you like it?"

"I like it very much. I'm not hungry."

"You ought to eat."

"I know I ought to eat."

The woman came and took the platter away and brought a plate of the hard white sheep's cheese and some quince paste. He cut a piece of cheese and a piece of quince and ate them together. Ellen lit a cigarette.

"Well," she said.

"Well."

"Read it now."

He took the letter out of his shirt pocket and unfolded it and read it. It was a short letter. Martin wrote the way he talked. It said what she had said it said and then at the end it said that the shelling was bad in the mornings along the Gran Vía and that the hotel had lost its windows on the north side but that the food was better than it had been in the spring. It said that they would hold. Martin always said they would hold. He folded the letter and put it back in his pocket.

"It's what you said."

"I know it's what I said."

"They want me for three months."

"It doesn't say three months."

"Three months is what it would be."

"It was three months last time," she said. "Then it was six. Then it was the whole winter and you came back in March and you couldn't sleep unless the light was on in the hall."

"That was a long time ago."

"It was a year ago."

"It seems like a long time."

"It doesn't to me."

He cut another piece of the cheese but did not eat it. He sat with it on the end of the knife.

"Listen," he said. "We've had a good time here."

"We've had a lovely time."

"We've had a fine time. It's been the best time we've had."

"Yes."

"Well, it was going to finish anyway. It's October. The river closes the end of the month. We were always going to go back."

"We were going to go back to Paris."

"You can go back to Paris."

She put the cigarette down in the saucer and looked at him. She had gray eyes and when she was angry they did not change at all. That was what he had noticed first about her, a long time ago, in a café in Montparnasse. Her eyes had not changed at all when the man at the next table had said the thing he had said, and she had stood up and walked out and he had followed her.

"I can go back to Paris," she said.

"I didn't mean it like that."

"How did you mean it?"

"I meant you'd be all right there. You'd have the flat and you have friends there and you could work. You said you wanted to work this winter."

"I said I wanted to work this winter with you there."

"I'd write."

"You'd write," she said. "You'd write every week the first month and then you'd write when somebody was going out and could carry it. And then you wouldn't write because there wouldn't be anything you could put in a letter. I know how it goes, Jack. I've done it once."

"It wouldn't be like that."

"It would be exactly like that."

He ate the piece of cheese. He did not taste it. He drank some of the wine.

"What do you want me to do?" he said.

"I don't want you to do anything."

"You want me to write Martin and tell him no."

"I didn't say that."

"You didn't have to say it."

"No," she said. "I suppose I didn't."

The woman came in from the kitchen and asked if they wanted coffee and he said yes, please, and she went away again. They did not say anything until the coffee came. It was in a tin pot and it was very strong and she had put a glass of the clear marc beside each cup without being asked. He drank the marc first. It went down hot and he felt it in his chest.

"You could come," he said.

"To Madrid?"

"Plenty of people's wives are there."

"I'm not plenty of people's wife."

"No. You're mine."

"Am I?" she said. "That's very nice. Am I really?"

"Don't."

"I'm sorry."

"I mean it. You could come. They'd give you papers. You could stay at the hotel. Some of the women work. They do things for the hospitals."

"And I'd sit in the hotel in the mornings and listen to the shells come down on the Gran Vía and wait to see if you came back for lunch."

"It's not like that."

"Isn't it?"

"Not exactly."

"What is it exactly?"

He did not answer her. He did not know how to answer her. It was like that and it was not like that and there was no way to say it to someone who had not been there and he did not want her to be there, and she knew he did not want her to be there, and that was why she had asked.

"You don't want me to come," she said.

"I want you to be safe."

"That isn't what I asked."

"It's the answer."

"It's an answer," she said. "It's a very good answer. You always have very good answers."

She stood up and went to the window. The window looked out on the yard where the pump was and beyond the yard on the road that went down to the village. There was a cart on the road with a load of bracken on it and a boy walking beside the ox. She watched it.

"Do you know what I thought this morning?" she said. "When you went down to the river. I watched you go down. You had the rod over your shoulder and you were walking very fast the way you do and you didn't look back. And I thought, he's happy. He's really happy. He's happier than I've ever seen him. And I sat there on the balcony and I was happy too because you were. I was so happy, Jack. And then the boy came up the road with the letter."

"I'm sorry."

"It isn't your fault."

"It isn't anybody's fault."

"No. It's never anybody's fault. That's the trouble with it."

He got up and went over to the window and stood behind her. He put his hands on her shoulders. She did not move away and she did not lean back against him. She stood there and he stood there with his hands on her shoulders and they watched the cart go down the road until it went around the bend by the chestnut trees and was gone.

"I have to go," he said.

"I know you do."

"It isn't the paper. It isn't Martin."

"I know what it is."

"It's that I said I would. Last winter. I said I'd come back. There are people there."

"There are always people there."

"These are people I know."

"I know they are," she said. "I know them too. I liked them. I liked them very much. I liked Paco and I liked the little one from the brigade, the one who played the guitar so badly. What was his name?"

"Esteban."

"Esteban. Is he still there?"

"No."

"I'm sorry."

"It was in February. At the river."

"You didn't tell me."

"No."

"Why didn't you tell me?"

"I don't know. There wasn't any good time."

She turned around then and looked at him and he saw that her eyes were wet but that they had not changed at all.

"That's why I don't want you to go," she said. "That's all. That's the whole thing. There won't be any good time to tell me. There'll just be a telegram from Martin and it will say what they always say, and I'll be in the flat in Paris and I'll read it standing up in the hall. I've thought about it. I've thought about it so many times. I know exactly where I'll be standing."

"Don't think about it."

"How do you not think about it?"

"You just don't."

"Is that what you do?"

"Yes."

"And does it work?"

"Sometimes."

"Sometimes," she said. "That's very fine. Sometimes."

He took his hands off her shoulders. He went back to the table and poured himself another marc and drank it. He did not want it but he drank it. Outside the sun had gone behind a cloud and the yard was gray now and the light in the dining room was gray.

"I'll stay till the end of the month," he said. "I'll write Martin that I'll come the first of November. We'll have the rest of the month here."

"That's two weeks."

"Two weeks is a good long time."

"Is it?"

"It can be."

"And we'll fish," she said. "And we'll eat the trout and drink the wine and walk up to the pass in the afternoons and come back and make love and have dinner, and every day it will be one day less, and we'll both be counting and neither of us will say it."

"We don't have to count."

"Darling, I'm counting already."

He looked at her. She was standing against the window with the gray light behind her and he could not see her face very well.

"What do you want?" he said. "Tell me what you want and I'll do it if I can."

"You won't do it."

"Tell me."

"I want you to write Martin and say no. I want you to say that you're through. I want us to go back to Paris and have the winter and not have anybody's war in it. I want you to sleep with the light off. That's what I want." She stopped. "There. Now I've said it. Now you know."

"All right."

"Will you do it?"

He did not say anything for a long time. The woman was moving around in the kitchen and he could hear the pans and the water running.

"No," he said.

"No," she said. "I didn't think you would."

"I'm sorry, Ellen."

"Don't be sorry. Please don't be sorry. I can't stand it if you're sorry."

"All right. I'm not sorry."

"Thank you."

She came away from the window and picked up her cigarettes from the table and put them in the pocket of her sweater.

"I think I'll go up for a while," she said. "I'm tired. I didn't sleep very well."

"Do you want me to come up?"

"No. Stay down. Go and fish if you want to. The light will be good again later. You said it was good in the evening."

"It's best in the evening."

"Then go in the evening."

"Maybe I will."

"You'll catch the big one."

"Maybe."

"I hope you do," she said. "I really do. I hope you catch him."

She went out and he heard her on the stairs and then on the floor above, crossing the room, and then the springs of the bed. Then it was quiet. He sat at the table and finished the coffee. It was cold. He took the letter out of his pocket and read it again and put it back. Then he went out into the yard.

It had started to rain a little. It was a fine rain and it came straight down because there was no wind. He stood by the pump and looked at the road going down toward the village and the chestnut trees at the bend. The rain would put the fish down for a while and then it would bring them up again. It was a good rain for fishing. It would be very good in the evening. He went into the shed and took the rod down from the pegs and sat on an upturned box in the doorway and began to check the line, running it slowly through his fingers, feeling for the places where it had frayed on the rocks. He found one place and cut it out and tied the line again. He tied it carefully. It was a good knot and it would hold. Then he sat with the rod across his knees and listened to the rain on the slates of the roof and did not think about anything at all.
