The train from Lincoln was an hour late, and Ingrid Haugen had been sitting in the spring wagon at the end of the platform since half-past three. She had brought her mending with her, but she had not taken it out of the basket. She sat with her hands folded in her lap and looked down the track, where the two rails ran together and were lost in the yellow stubble. It was the last week of September. The wheat had all been threshed and hauled, and the corn stood brown and rustling in the fields on either side of the town, waiting to be husked. Over everything lay that still, gold light which comes in the autumn on the high prairie, when the wind has dropped and the dust has settled, and the whole country seems to be resting after a long labor.

The station agent came out twice to tell her there was no news. He was a young man from Omaha who had not been long in the town, and he did not know who Mrs. Haugen was waiting for. Everyone else in the place knew. Her husband had told it at the blacksmith's, and the blacksmith had told it at the post office. Ingrid's cousin, Nils Lindahl, who had gone away to the West when he was a boy of fourteen, was coming back to visit after twenty-two years, and he was said to have done very well for himself in Seattle.

Ingrid did not think much about whether he had done well. She was thinking of a thin, freckled boy in a cap too large for him, who had stood on the platform of this same station, when it was nothing but a shed and a water-tank, and had waved to her until the train carried him out of sight. She had been twelve then. She had cried all the way home in the wagon, and her mother had let her cry, because her mother had been crying too. Nils's father was her mother's only brother, and after the boy's mother died there had been nothing to keep them on the Divide. Uncle Gustaf had sold his claim for less than he had paid in filing fees, and had gone off to the mines in Colorado, taking his son with him. For a few years letters had come at Christmas; then they came less often, and then Uncle Gustaf was killed in a cave-in at Leadville, and after that there was only a card now and then, in a hand Ingrid did not know, to say that Nils was well and working in a lumber camp, or on a boat, or in a store.

When the train came at last, it came very suddenly, as trains do on the prairie, where one can see the smoke for half an hour and still be surprised when the engine rolls in. Ingrid got down from the wagon and stood by the wheel. Only three people got off. One was the Methodist preacher's wife, coming back from her sister's; one was a drummer with two sample cases; and the third was a tall man in a grey overcoat, who stood for a moment looking about him as if he were not sure he had come to the right place. He had a short brown beard and wore gold spectacles. Ingrid would not have known him. But when he took off his hat and she saw his forehead, and the way the hair grew back from it in a point, she knew him at once, for it was her mother's forehead, and her grandfather's in the picture that hung in the parlor.

"Nils," she said, and went toward him.

He looked at her for a moment without speaking, and then he laughed, and took both her hands in his. "Ingrid! I would have walked right past you. I was looking for a little girl with braids."

"I was looking for a little boy," she said, "and here is a gentleman with spectacles."

They stood there holding hands and laughing a little foolishly, while the station agent wheeled the trunk down the platform. It was a fine leather trunk with brass corners, and the agent handled it carefully. Then Nils helped his cousin into the wagon and climbed up beside her, and Ingrid took the lines and turned the horses toward the north road.

She saw that he was looking for things which were no longer there, and she let him look. Where he remembered open prairie, with the red grass running in waves before the wind, there were now fenced fields, and windmills, and white farmhouses with groves of cottonwood and box-elder planted about them. The road, which had been a wagon trail winding wherever the ground was hardest, now ran straight north along the section line, with a ditch on either side.

"It's there still, but it's mostly dry, except in the spring. They have cut out the plum bushes to make more corn land. But there are some left down by our place. I'll show you."

He was quiet again. Presently he said, "I suppose I thought it would all wait for me. That's foolish, isn't it? A man goes away and lives his own life, and he thinks the place he came from will stand still, like a picture in a frame."

"Nothing stands still out here," said Ingrid. "The land won't let it."

She said this simply, as she said most things, and he turned and looked at her. She was a large woman now, broad in the shoulders, with a brown, weathered face and strong hands that held the lines easily. Her hair, which had been yellow as straw, had gone darker, and there was grey in it at the temples. But her eyes were the same, a clear, light blue, and they still had that look of steady attention, as if she were always measuring something and finding it about what she had expected. He remembered that look. When they were children, it had been Ingrid who decided how far they could walk from the house without being missed, and Ingrid who knew which cow would kick and which would stand quiet for milking. She had been a sensible child, and she had grown into a sensible woman. He found that he was very glad of it.

The Haugen farm lay four miles north of town, on a rise of ground that looked out over the river valley. Ingrid's husband had come from Norway as a young man and had worked for her father before he married her. He was a quiet, slow-moving person who had never been to school beyond the third reader, but he understood land and cattle, and in the twenty years of their marriage he had added three quarter-sections to the original homestead and had paid for every acre. The house was a square, two-story frame house, painted white, with green shutters and a long porch across the front. There was an orchard behind it, and a row of tall cottonwoods along the drive which Ingrid's father had planted the year Nils went away.

"I remember when those were sticks," Nils said, as they drove under them. "Your father set them out with a spade, and you and I carried water to them from the well. We thought they would never grow."

"Father didn't think so either. He used to say he was planting them for his grandchildren. Now his grandchildren climb them, and fall out of them, and break their arms."

Four of the grandchildren were waiting on the porch. They had been washed and combed and told to behave, and they stood in a row according to size, staring at the stranger with the round, solemn eyes of children who seldom see anyone they do not know. The oldest was a tall boy of seventeen, who had already gone out to help his father with the stock and had come back in a clean shirt to be polite. The youngest was a little girl of six, with white hair and a pink calico dress, who hid behind her brother when Nils got down from the wagon and would not come out until he had given her a paper of peppermints from his overcoat pocket.

Lars Haugen came up from the barn, wiping his hands on a sack. He shook hands with Nils gravely and said he was welcome. That was about all Lars said that evening, but he said it as if he meant it, and Nils, who had lived among many kinds of men, understood that this one was not unfriendly but merely saving his words for when they would be needed.

Supper was a serious matter in the Haugen house, and Ingrid had been preparing for it since the day before. There was fried chicken and mashed potatoes, and sweet corn from the late patch, and new bread, and three kinds of preserves, and cucumber pickles, and a dish of wild plums stewed with sugar. There was a custard pie and a chocolate cake. Nils ate as if he had not eaten in a week. He told Ingrid that he had not tasted such bread since he was a boy, and that in Seattle he boarded in a house where the landlady bought her bread from a bakery and her pies from a man with a cart. Ingrid was shocked, though she tried not to show it. She could not imagine a woman who would buy pies from a man with a cart. She thought it must be a hard, lonely sort of place, Seattle, in spite of all the money people said was made there.

After supper the children were sent to bed, protesting, and Lars went out to see to a heifer that was about to calve. Ingrid and her cousin took two chairs out onto the porch. The night had come down cool and clear. Away to the west the last of the light lay along the edge of the land in a thin band of green, and above it the evening star hung low and very bright. The windmill creaked now and then when a little wind came up from the river, and down in the pasture a horse was cropping the grass. They could hear it tearing the stems, it was so still.

"Now tell me," said Ingrid. "Tell me everything. Your letters never said anything. 'I am well and working in a store.' What sort of store? Where? Did you have enough to eat? Were you warm in winter?"

Nils laughed. "Some winters I was warm and some I wasn't. I'll tell you, but it's a long story, and most of it isn't very interesting."

He told her, all the same, and she listened without interrupting. He told her about the mining camp in Colorado, where he had carried water and run errands for the men when he was too young to go underground, and about the morning the shaft fell in and they brought his father up dead. He had been sixteen then, and alone. He had worked his way north to Oregon with a railroad gang, and had spent two winters in the lumber camps, where the snow lay ten feet deep among the big trees and the men played cards by lantern light every night until they quarreled. He had gone to sea for a year on a ship that carried lumber to San Francisco, and he had been seasick the whole year. Then he had found work in a hardware store in Seattle, sweeping out and unpacking crates, and the owner, an old Scotchman with no family, had taken a liking to him and taught him the business. When the old man died, he had left the store to Nils. That was nine years ago. Now Nils had two stores, and a share in a third, and a house on a hill above the water.

"And a wife?" asked Ingrid. "You never wrote about a wife."

"No," he said. "There isn't any wife."

She waited, but he did not say anything more, and she did not ask. She had learned, in twenty years of living among silent people, that some questions are better left to answer themselves.

"It's a beautiful place," he went on after a while. "Seattle, I mean. The mountains come right down to the water, and in the morning, when the fog lifts, you can see them across the Sound, all white with snow. And the trees! You have never seen trees like that, Ingrid. Some of them were growing before Columbus. A man feels small among them. I used to think, when I first went there, that I would never want to see flat country again."

"And now?"

He looked out at the dark fields for a long time before he answered. "Now I don't know. When the train came out of the hills this morning, and I saw the prairie again, with the sun coming up over it, I felt something here." He touched his breast. "I felt as if I had been holding my breath for twenty years, and I could let it out at last. Isn't that strange? I was only a boy when I left. I didn't think I remembered much."

"You remember more than you think," said Ingrid. "Do you remember the winter of the big blizzard? The one where Father was caught in town?"

"I remember. We were alone in the sod house, your mother and mine and the two of us. My mother was already sick then."

"She was. And the snow drifted over the door, and we couldn't get out to the stable, and Mother was afraid the cow would die. And you dug a tunnel through the drift with the fire shovel. You worked all day. Your hands bled."

"I had forgotten that," he said slowly. "I had forgotten my hands bled. But I remember coming into the stable at last, and the cow turning her head to look at me, and the warm smell of her. I thought she was the most beautiful thing in the world."

"Mother never forgot it," Ingrid said. "She used to tell about it to the children. 'Your cousin Nils saved our cow,' she would say. They thought you must be some kind of giant."

He laughed, but she saw that he was moved. He took off his spectacles and wiped them carefully with his handkerchief, a thing she remembered he had always done, even as a boy, with his sleeve, when he did not want anyone to see his face.

"Is she buried here?" he asked. "Your mother?"

"In the Norwegian churchyard, on the hill east of town. Father beside her. And your mother is there too, Nils. Father had a stone put up for her, after you went away. He thought you would want it."

"I didn't know that." He was quiet for a moment. "I've never seen her grave. We left so soon afterward. I would like to go there tomorrow, if it isn't too much trouble."

"I'll take you in the morning. We can take some of the asters from the garden. She was fond of them. I remember she had a little row of them by the door of your house, and she carried water to them from the creek in the dry summer, when there was hardly enough to drink."

Nils put his spectacles back on. "You remember a great deal, Ingrid."

"Someone had to," she said. "When you live in one place all your life, you get to be a sort of storehouse. Everyone else goes away, or dies, and you are left with the things they knew. Sometimes I think I am the only one left who remembers what this country looked like before the fences. The children don't believe me when I tell them. They think the corn was always here."

There was no complaint in her voice. She said it as she might have said that the rain had been late that year, or that the hens were laying well. But Nils, looking at her strong profile against the lamplight from the window, thought that he had never before understood what it meant to stay. He had always believed that he was the one who had gone through hardships, and that those who stayed behind had had the easier time of it. Now he saw that it was not so. He had only carried his life from place to place, and when one place grew hard he had left it for another. Ingrid had taken all her hardships in one place. She had watched the dry years burn up the crops, and the hail beat them down, and the grasshoppers eat them; she had buried her parents here, and two of her children, for there had been two more, she told him later, who had died of diphtheria in one week; and she had stayed. The land had taken from her what it wanted, and she had given it, and in return it had given her this house, and these fields, and the children asleep upstairs. It seemed to him a hard bargain, and a fair one.

"Are you happy, Ingrid?" he asked suddenly. It was not a question people asked on the Divide, and he felt foolish as soon as he had said it.

She did not seem to think it foolish. She considered it seriously, with her hands folded in her lap, as she had considered his face at the station.

"I don't know that I ever thought about it," she said at last. "I have had a great deal to do. But I think I am. I have a good husband, and the children are healthy, and the land is paid for. When I look out of my kitchen window in the morning and see the wheat coming up green, or the corn tasseling in July, I feel that it has all come out right, somehow. That everything we went through was for something." She turned to him. "And you, Nils? You have done well. Everyone says so. Are you happy?"

He smiled a little. "I have done well. I have a good business and a house with a view, and I belong to a club where men sit in leather chairs and read the newspapers. But I think I have been homesick for twenty years, Ingrid, and I didn't know it until this morning."

She reached over and laid her hand on his arm, a large, rough hand, brown from the sun. She did not say anything. There was nothing that needed saying.

Out in the pasture the horse had stopped cropping and was standing still, a dark shape against the sky. Lars came up from the barn with a lantern swinging in his hand, and the light went bobbing along the path, throwing long shadows across the yard. He stopped at the foot of the porch steps and said that the heifer had a fine bull calf, and that it was standing already. Then he said good night and went in.

The cousins sat on a while longer. The stars had come out thick and close over the prairie, so many of them that the sky looked crowded, and the Milky Way stretched from one edge of the land to the other like a road that someone had traveled long ago and left behind. Nils looked up at it and thought that in Seattle he never saw the stars like this; there was always fog, or the lights of the city, or the mountains standing in the way. Here there was nothing between a man and the sky. He had been afraid of that, when he was a boy. Now it seemed to him a kind of freedom.

"I'll stay a week, if you'll have me," he said.

"Stay as long as you like," said Ingrid. "There is always room. Your father's chair is in the parlor; Father brought it over when he sold the place, and we have kept it. You can sit in it."

She got up and took her chair inside, and he heard her moving about in the kitchen, setting the bread to rise for the morning. He did not go in at once. He sat alone on the porch, listening to the windmill and the faint rustling of the corn, and thinking of a sod house with asters by the door, and a cow turning her head in the warm dark of a stable, and a boy with bleeding hands who had believed, for one whole day, that he could save everyone he loved.

Here is an excerpt of Willa Cather's writing, to show you their style:

Bergson had spent his first five years on the Divide getting into debt, and the last six getting out. He had paid off his mortgages and had ended pretty much where he began, with the land. He owned exactly six hundred and forty acres of what stretched outside his door; his own original homestead and timber claim, making three hundred and twenty acres, and the half-section adjoining, the homestead of a younger brother who had given up the fight, gone back to Chicago to work in a fancy bakery and distinguish himself in a Swedish athletic club. So far John had not attempted to cultivate the second half-section, but used it for pasture land, and one of his sons rode herd there in open weather. John Bergson had the Old-World belief that land, in itself, is desirable. But this land was an enigma. It was like a horse that no one knows how to break to harness, that runs wild and kicks things to pieces. He had an idea that no one understood how to farm it properly, and this he often discussed with Alexandra. Their neighbors, certainly, knew even less about farming than he did. Many of them had never worked on a farm until they took up their homesteads. They had been handwerkers at home; tailors, locksmiths, joiners, cigar-makers, etc. Bergson himself had worked in a shipyard. For weeks, John Bergson had been thinking about these things. His bed stood in the sitting-room, next to the kitchen. Through the day, while the baking and washing and ironing were going on, the father lay and looked up at the roof beams that he himself had hewn, or out at the cattle in the corral. He counted the cattle over and over. It diverted him to speculate as to how much weight each of the steers would probably put on by spring. He often called his daughter in to talk to her about this. Before Alexandra was twelve years old she had begun to be a help to him, and as she grew older he had come to depend more and more upon her resourcefulness and good judgment. His boys were willing enough to work, but when he talked with them they usually irritated him. It was Alexandra who read the papers and followed the markets, and who learned by the mistakes of their neighbors. It was Alexandra who could always tell about what it had cost to fatten each steer, and who could guess the weight of a hog before it went on the scales closer than John Bergson himself. Lou and Oscar were industrious, but he could never teach them to use their heads about their work. Alexandra, her father often said to himself, was like her grandfather; which was his way of saying that she was intelligent. John Bergson’s father had been a shipbuilder, a man of considerable force and of some fortune. Late in life he married a second time, a Stockholm woman of questionable character, much younger than he, who goaded him into every sort of extravagance. On the shipbuilder’s part, this marriage was an infatuation, the despairing folly of a powerful man who cannot bear to grow old. In a few years his unprincipled wife warped the probity of a lifetime. He speculated, lost his own fortune and funds entrusted to him by poor seafaring men, and died disgraced, leaving his children nothing. But when all was said, he had come up from the sea himself, had built up a proud little business with no capital but his own skill and foresight, and had proved himself a man. In his daughter, John Bergson recognized the strength of will, and the simple direct way of thinking things out, that had characterized his father in his better days. He would much rather, of course, have seen this likeness in one of his sons, but it was not a question of choice. As he lay there day after day he had to accept the situation as it was, and to be thankful that there was one among his children to whom he could entrust the future of his family and the possibilities of his hard-won land. The winter twilight was fading. The sick man heard his wife strike a match in the kitchen, and the light of a lamp glimmered through the cracks of the door. It seemed like a light shining far away. He turned painfully in his bed and looked at his white hands, with all the work gone out of them. He was ready to give up, he felt. He did not know how it had come about, but he was quite willing to go deep under his fields and rest, where the plow could not find him. He was tired of making mistakes. He was content to leave the tangle to other hands; he thought of his Alexandra’s strong ones.

“Dotter,” he called feebly, “dotter!” He heard her quick step and saw her tall figure appear in the doorway, with the light of the lamp behind her. He felt her youth and strength, how easily she moved and stooped and lifted. But he would not have had it again if he could, not he! He knew the end too well to wish to begin again. He knew where it all went to, what it all became. His daughter came and lifted him up on his pillows. She called him by an old Swedish name that she used to call him when she was little and took his dinner to him in the shipyard.

“Tell the boys to come here, daughter. I want to speak to them.”

“They are feeding the horses, father. They have just come back from the Blue. Shall I call them?” He sighed. “No, no. Wait until they come in. Alexandra, you will have to do the best you can for your brothers. Everything will come on you.”

“I will do all I can, father.”

“Don’t let them get discouraged and go off like Uncle Otto. I want them to keep the land.”

“We will, father. We will never lose the land.” There was a sound of heavy feet in the kitchen. Alexandra went to the door and beckoned to her brothers, two strapping boys of seventeen and nineteen. They came in and stood at the foot of the bed. Their father looked at them searchingly, though it was too dark to see their faces; they were just the same boys, he told himself, he had not been mistaken in them. The square head and heavy shoulders belonged to Oscar, the elder. The younger boy was quicker, but vacillating.

“Boys,” said the father wearily, “I want you to keep the land together and to be guided by your sister. I have talked to her since I have been sick, and she knows all my wishes. I want no quarrels among my children, and so long as there is one house there must be one head. Alexandra is the oldest, and she knows my wishes. She will do the best she can. If she makes mistakes, she will not make so many as I have made. When you marry, and want a house of your own, the land will be divided fairly, according to the courts. But for the next few years you will have it hard, and you must all keep together. Alexandra will manage the best she can.” Oscar, who was usually the last to speak, replied because he was the older, “Yes, father. It would be so anyway, without your speaking. We will all work the place together.”

“And you will be guided by your sister, boys, and be good brothers to her, and good sons to your mother? That is good. And Alexandra must not work in the fields any more. There is no necessity now. Hire a man when you need help. She can make much more with her eggs and butter than the wages of a man. It was one of my mistakes that I did not find that out sooner. Try to break a little more land every year; sod corn is good for fodder. Keep turning the land, and always put up more hay than you need. Don’t grudge your mother a little time for plowing her garden and setting out fruit trees, even if it comes in a busy season. She has been a good mother to you, and she has always missed the old country.” When they went back to the kitchen the boys sat down silently at the table. Throughout the meal they looked down at their plates and did not lift their red eyes. They did not eat much, although they had been working in the cold all day, and there was a rabbit stewed in gravy for supper, and prune pies. John Bergson had married beneath him, but he had married a good housewife. Mrs. Bergson was a fair-skinned, corpulent woman, heavy and placid like her son, Oscar, but there was something comfortable about her; perhaps it was her own love of comfort. For eleven years she had worthily striven to maintain some semblance of household order amid conditions that made order very difficult. Habit was very strong with Mrs. Bergson, and her unremitting efforts to repeat the routine of her old life among new surroundings had done a great deal to keep the family from disintegrating morally and getting careless in their ways. The Bergsons had a log house, for instance, only because Mrs. Bergson would not live in a sod house. She missed the fish diet of her own country, and twice every summer she sent the boys to the river, twenty miles to the southward, to fish for channel cat. When the children were little she used to load them all into the wagon, the baby in its crib, and go fishing herself. Alexandra often said that if her mother were cast upon a desert island, she would thank God for her deliverance, make a garden, and find something to preserve. Preserving was almost a mania with Mrs. Bergson. Stout as she was, she roamed the scrubby banks of Norway Creek looking for fox grapes and goose plums, like a wild creature in search of prey. She made a yellow jam of the insipid ground-cherries that grew on the prairie, flavoring it with lemon peel; and she made a sticky dark conserve of garden tomatoes. She had experimented even with the rank buffalo-pea, and she could not see a fine bronze cluster of them without shaking her head and murmuring, “What a pity!” When there was nothing more to preserve, she began to pickle. The amount of sugar she used in these processes was sometimes a serious drain upon the family resources. She was a good mother, but she was glad when her children were old enough not to be in her way in the kitchen. She had never quite forgiven John Bergson for bringing her to the end of the earth; but, now that she was there, she wanted to be let alone to reconstruct her old life in so far as that was possible. She could still take some comfort in the world if she had bacon in the cave, glass jars on the shelves, and sheets in the press. She disapproved of all her neighbors because of their slovenly housekeeping, and the women thought her very proud. Once when Mrs. Bergson, on her way to Norway Creek, stopped to see old Mrs. Lee, the old woman hid in the haymow “for fear Mis’ Bergson would catch her barefoot.”

One Sunday afternoon in July, six months after John Bergson’s death, Carl was sitting in the doorway of the Linstrum kitchen, dreaming over an illustrated paper, when he heard the rattle of a wagon along the hill road. Looking up he recognized the Bergsons’ team, with two seats in the wagon, which meant they were off for a pleasure excursion. Oscar and Lou, on the front seat, wore their cloth hats and coats, never worn except on Sundays, and Emil, on the second seat with Alexandra, sat proudly in his new trousers, made from a pair of his father’s, and a pink-striped shirt, with a wide ruffled collar. Oscar stopped the horses and waved to Carl, who caught up his hat and ran through the melon patch to join them.

“Want to go with us?” Lou called. “We’re going to Crazy Ivar’s to buy a hammock.”

“Sure.” Carl ran up panting, and clambering over the wheel sat down beside Emil. “I’ve always wanted to see Ivar’s pond. They say it’s the biggest in all the country. Aren’t you afraid to go to Ivar’s in that new shirt, Emil? He might want it and take it right off your back.” Emil grinned. “I’d be awful scared to go,” he admitted, “if you big boys weren’t along to take care of me. Did you ever hear him howl, Carl? People say sometimes he runs about the country howling at night because he is afraid the Lord will destroy him. Mother thinks he must have done something awful wicked.” Lou looked back and winked at Carl. “What would you do, Emil, if you was out on the prairie by yourself and seen him coming?” Emil stared. “Maybe I could hide in a badger-hole,” he suggested doubtfully.

“But suppose there wasn’t any badger-hole,” Lou persisted. “Would you run?”

“No, I’d be too scared to run,” Emil admitted mournfully, twisting his fingers. “I guess I’d sit right down on the ground and say my prayers.” The big boys laughed, and Oscar brandished his whip over the broad backs of the horses.

“He wouldn’t hurt you, Emil,” said Carl persuasively. “He came to doctor our mare when she ate green corn and swelled up most as big as the water-tank. He petted her just like you do your cats. I couldn’t understand much he said, for he don’t talk any English, but he kept patting her and groaning as if he had the pain himself, and saying, ‘There now, sister, that’s easier, that’s better!’” Lou and Oscar laughed, and Emil giggled delightedly and looked up at his sister.

“I don’t think he knows anything at all about doctoring,” said Oscar scornfully. “They say when horses have distemper he takes the medicine himself, and then prays over the horses.” Alexandra spoke up. “That’s what the Crows said, but he cured their horses, all the same. Some days his mind is cloudy, like. But if you can get him on a clear day, you can learn a great deal from him. He understands animals. Didn’t I see him take the horn off the Berquist’s cow when she had torn it loose and went crazy? She was tearing all over the place, knocking herself against things. And at last she ran out on the roof of the old dugout and her legs went through and there she stuck, bellowing. Ivar came running with his white bag, and the moment he got to her she was quiet and let him saw her horn off and daub the place with tar.”

She called him by an old Swedish name that she used to call him when she was little and took his dinner to him in the shipyard.

“Tell the boys to come here, daughter. I want to speak to them.”

“They are feeding the horses, father. They have just come back from the Blue. Shall I call them?” He sighed. “No, no. Wait until they come in. Alexandra, you will have to do the best you can for your brothers. Everything will come on you.”

“I will do all I can, father.”

“Don’t let them get discouraged and go off like Uncle Otto. I want them to keep the land.”

“We will, father. We will never lose the land.” There was a sound of heavy feet in the kitchen. Alexandra went to the door and beckoned to her brothers, two strapping boys of seventeen and nineteen. They came in and stood at the foot of the bed. Their father looked at them searchingly, though it was too dark to see their faces; they were just the same boys, he told himself, he had not been mistaken in them. The square head and heavy shoulders belonged to Oscar, the elder. The younger boy was quicker, but vacillating.

“Boys,” said the father wearily, “I want you to keep the land together and to be guided by your sister. I have talked to her since I have been sick, and she knows all my wishes. I want no quarrels among my children, and so long as there is one house there must be one head. Alexandra is the oldest, and she knows my wishes. She will do the best she can. If she makes mistakes, she will not make so many as I have made. When you marry, and want a house of your own, the land will be divided fairly, according to the courts. But for the next few years you will have it hard, and you must all keep together. Alexandra will manage the best she can.” Oscar, who was usually the last to speak, replied because he was the older, “Yes, father. It would be so anyway, without your speaking. We will all work the place together.”

“And you will be guided by your sister, boys, and be good brothers to her, and good sons to your mother? That is good. And Alexandra must not work in the fields any more. There is no necessity now. Hire a man when you need help. She can make much more with her eggs and butter than the wages of a man. It was one of my mistakes that I did not find that out sooner. Try to break a little more land every year; sod corn is good for fodder. Keep turning the land, and always put up more hay than you need. Don’t grudge your mother a little time for plowing her garden and setting out fruit trees, even if it comes in a busy season. She has been a good mother to you, and she has always missed the old country.” When they went back to the kitchen the boys sat down silently at the table. Throughout the meal they looked down at their plates and did not lift their red eyes. They did not eat much, although they had been working in the cold all day, and there was a rabbit stewed in gravy for supper, and prune pies. John Bergson had married beneath him, but he had married a good housewife. Mrs. Bergson was a fair-skinned, corpulent woman, heavy and placid like her son, Oscar, but there was something comfortable about her; perhaps it was her own love of comfort. For eleven years she had worthily striven to maintain some semblance of household order amid conditions that made order very difficult. Habit was very strong with Mrs. Bergson, and her unremitting efforts to repeat the routine of her old life among new surroundings had done a great deal to keep the family from disintegrating morally and getting careless in their ways. The Bergsons had a log house, for instance, only because Mrs. Bergson would not live in a sod house. She missed the fish diet of her own country, and twice every summer she sent the boys to the river, twenty miles to the southward, to fish for channel cat. When the children were little she used to load them all into the wagon, the baby in its crib, and go fishing herself. Alexandra often said that if her mother were cast upon a desert island, she would thank God for her deliverance, make a garden, and find something to preserve. Preserving was almost a mania with Mrs. Bergson. Stout as she was, she roamed the scrubby banks of Norway Creek looking for fox grapes and goose plums, like a wild creature in search of prey. She made a yellow jam of the insipid ground-cherries that grew on the prairie, flavoring it with lemon peel; and she made a sticky dark conserve of garden tomatoes. She had experimented even with the rank buffalo-pea, and she could not see a fine bronze cluster of them without shaking her head and murmuring, “What a pity!” When there was nothing more to preserve, she began to pickle. The amount of sugar she used in these processes was sometimes a serious drain upon the family resources. She was a good mother, but she was glad when her children were old enough not to be in her way in the kitchen. She had never quite forgiven John Bergson for bringing her to the end of the earth; but, now that she was there, she wanted to be let alone to reconstruct her old life in so far as that was possible. She could still take some comfort in the world if she had bacon in the cave, glass jars on the shelves, and sheets in the press. She disapproved of all her neighbors because of their slovenly housekeeping, and the women thought her very proud. Once when Mrs. Bergson, on her way to Norway Creek, stopped to see old Mrs. Lee, the old woman hid in the haymow “for fear Mis’ Bergson would catch her barefoot.”

One Sunday afternoon in July, six months after John Bergson’s death, Carl was sitting in the doorway of the Linstrum kitchen, dreaming over an illustrated paper, when he heard the rattle of a wagon along the hill road. Looking up he recognized the Bergsons’ team, with two seats in the wagon, which meant they were off for a pleasure excursion. Oscar and Lou, on the front seat, wore their cloth hats and coats, never worn except on Sundays, and Emil, on the second seat with Alexandra, sat proudly in his new trousers, made from a pair of his father’s, and a pink-striped shirt, with a wide ruffled collar. Oscar stopped the horses and waved to Carl, who caught up his hat and ran through the melon patch to join them.

“Want to go with us?” Lou called. “We’re going to Crazy Ivar’s to buy a hammock.”

“Sure.” Carl ran up panting, and clambering over the wheel sat down beside Emil. “I’ve always wanted to see Ivar’s pond. They say it’s the biggest in all the country. Aren’t you afraid to go to Ivar’s in that new shirt, Emil? He might want it and take it right off your back.” Emil grinned. “I’d be awful scared to go,” he admitted, “if you big boys weren’t along to take care of me. Did you ever hear him howl, Carl? People say sometimes he runs about the country howling at night because he is afraid the Lord will destroy him. Mother thinks he must have done something awful wicked.” Lou looked back and winked at Carl. “What would you do, Emil, if you was out on the prairie by yourself and seen him coming?” Emil stared. “Maybe I could hide in a badger-hole,” he suggested doubtfully.

“But suppose there wasn’t any badger-hole,” Lou persisted. “Would you run?”

“No, I’d be too scared to run,” Emil admitted mournfully, twisting his fingers. “I guess I’d sit right down on the ground and say my prayers.” The big boys laughed, and Oscar brandished his whip over the broad backs of the horses.

“He wouldn’t hurt you, Emil,” said Carl persuasively. “He came to doctor our mare when she ate green corn and swelled up most as big as the water-tank. He petted her just like you do your cats. I couldn’t understand much he said, for he don’t talk any English, but he kept patting her and groaning as if he had the pain himself, and saying, ‘There now, sister, that’s easier, that’s better!’” Lou and Oscar laughed, and Emil giggled delightedly and looked up at his sister.

“I don’t think he knows anything at all about doctoring,” said Oscar scornfully. “They say when horses have distemper he takes the medicine himself, and then prays over the horses.” Alexandra spoke up. “That’s what the Crows said, but he cured their horses, all the same. Some days his mind is cloudy, like. But if you can get him on a clear day, you can learn a great deal from him. He understands animals. Didn’t I see him take the horn off the Berquist’s cow when she had torn it loose and went crazy? She was tearing all over the place, knocking herself against things. And at last she ran out on the roof of the old dugout and her legs went through and there she stuck, bellowing. Ivar came running with his white bag, and the moment he got to her she was quiet and let him saw her horn off and daub the place with tar.”

response:
The Kolars had come to the high prairie north of the Little Blue in the spring of the dry year, when the grass was short and the creeks had shrunk back into their beds like frightened animals. Joe Kolar had been a cabinet-maker in a town near Pilsen, and he had brought with him a chest of fine tools, which he kept oiled and wrapped in flannel and seldom used, for there was little call on the prairie for dovetailed drawers or carved bed-posts. What the country wanted was sod broken and wells dug, and these things he learned to do slowly and rather badly, with the patience of a man who had once been good at something else. His wife learned faster. Anna Kolar had grown up on a farm in the old country, the daughter of a tenant who rented his fields from a count and paid in rye and geese, and she knew from her childhood what it meant to work land that did not belong to you. Now the land was theirs, or would be when the papers were proved up, and she worked it as if every acre were a child that might be taken from her.

There were four children living. Two had died in the first winter, of a fever that went through the settlement, and were buried on the rise behind the house, under a wooden cross that Joe had made with his good tools and painted white. The eldest girl, Bozena, was fifteen and already as tall as her mother, and almost as capable. Then there were the twins, Mary and Rose, who were eleven, and who did everything together, even quarreling. The youngest was Franta, who was eight, and who had been born in the sod house before the frame one was built. He was a thin, brown, quick boy, with his father's narrow hands and his mother's light eyes, and because he was the only son and the youngest, the girls had made a great deal of him. Bozena especially had carried him about when he was little, and still let him have the best of everything, the heel of the loaf and the wishbone of the chicken. Mrs. Kolar saw this and did not altogether like it. She had an idea that boys who are spoiled by their sisters grow up expecting the whole world to be their sisters, and she knew that the world was nothing of the kind.

A mile to the east, where the land dipped toward a draw full of plum thickets and box-elders, old Mrs. Rehor lived alone in a dugout. She had come out with a husband and three grown sons, years before the Kolars, when there was nothing on the prairie but buffalo grass and the wind. The husband had died of a rupture, lifting a wagon out of a slough. Two of the sons had gone to Omaha to work in the packing-houses and had stopped writing; the third had been killed by lightning while he was mowing, and the old woman had found him herself, lying in the windrow with his hat beside him and his scythe still shining. After that something went out of her. She stayed on in the dugout because she did not know where else to go, and she raised geese, which she sold in town at Christmas, and she kept a few hens and a garden of poppies and cabbages. She talked to herself as she worked, and to her geese, in a high, cracked voice, and she walked with one shoulder lower than the other, because of a hip that had never mended properly after a fall on the ice. The children of the neighborhood were afraid of her, and, like most children who are afraid, they made fun of her when they could do it from a safe distance.

It was late in August, and the heat lay over the country like a weight. The corn stood high and dark in the fields, and the leaves rattled when the wind went through them, a dry, papery sound that Mrs. Kolar did not like to hear, for it meant they needed rain. All the morning she had been putting up wild plums, which the girls had gathered in the draw the day before. The kitchen was full of steam and the sour, sweet smell of the fruit, and the jars stood in rows on the table, red and gold, with the light coming through them. She liked to see them there. They were something saved out of the summer, something the winter could not take from her.

She was skimming the kettle when she heard the gate. She looked out and saw old Mrs. Rehor coming up the path, very slowly, with her shoulder down and her shawl over her head in spite of the heat. She carried something in her apron, holding the corners together with both hands as a woman carries eggs. Mrs. Kolar set the skimmer down and wiped her hands and went out on the step. She was surprised, for the old woman seldom came to anyone's house; she had a kind of pride about it.

"Good day, neighbor," Mrs. Kolar said in Bohemian. "Come in out of the sun. I have coffee on the stove."

Mrs. Rehor did not come in. She stood at the foot of the step and looked up, and Mrs. Kolar saw that her face was working, and that her eyes, which were very pale and watery, were full of tears. Then the old woman opened her apron. In it lay a young goose, half grown, its grey feathers just turning white. Its neck hung down limply over the edge of the cloth, and there was a smear of blood on its head, near the eye.

"Your boy," the old woman said. "Your little boy. With a clod of dirt. I saw him from the garden. Three of them he threw, and the third one—" She stopped and shook her head, and the tears ran down into the wrinkles at the sides of her mouth. "He called me a name, too. I heard it. An ugly name. I did not think it of your house, Mrs. Kolar."

Mrs. Kolar felt the blood come up into her face. She had not been ashamed in that way since she was a girl, and the feeling was so strong that for a moment she could not speak at all. She looked at the dead goose, and at the old woman's hands, which were knotted and brown as roots, and shaking.

"Come in," she said at last. "Please. Sit down in the kitchen. I will see to this."

But Mrs. Rehor would not come in. She folded her apron over the goose again and turned around and went back down the path, her shoulder dipping at every step, and out of the gate, and along the road toward the draw. Mrs. Kolar watched her until she was only a dark spot against the yellow stubble. Then she went into the kitchen and pushed the plum kettle to the back of the stove, and stood for a little while with her hand on the table, thinking.

She did not call Franta at once. She was a woman who believed that anger was a poor counselor, and she knew that if she called him then, she would take the strap to him, and that would be the end of it. A whipping was soon over. Joe whipped the children sometimes, when they had been careless with the stock or had left a gate open, and it did them no harm; but she did not think this was a thing to be settled with a strap. When she had finished skimming the last kettle and had set the jars to cool, she went out to the barn. Bozena was in the yard, hanging out dish-towels, and her mother asked her where the boy was.

"He's in the haymow, I think, mother. He came home a while ago and went straight up there. He didn't want any bread and butter." Bozena looked at her mother's face and her own grew anxious. "Has he done something?"

"Go in and watch the stove," Mrs. Kolar said. "Don't let the girls touch the jars."

The barn was dim and hot and smelled of horses and dust. She went to the foot of the ladder and called up, "Franta! Come down here."

There was a long silence, and then a rustling in the hay, and presently his bare feet appeared on the top rung, and then his legs, and then all of him, coming down very slowly, with hay in his hair and on his shirt. He stood at the bottom of the ladder and did not look at her. He looked at a knot in the floor-boards, and dug at it with his big toe.

"Look at me," his mother said.

He looked up. His face was dirty and streaked, as if he had been crying in the hay, but his eyes had a stubborn shine in them that she knew well; it was her own look, and she had seen it often enough in the glass.

"Where were you this afternoon?"

"Down in the draw," he said. "Hunting plums."

"Did you find any?"

"No'm. The girls picked them all yesterday."

"Did you go past Mrs. Rehor's place?"

He dug at the knot again. "I guess I went past it. A little ways off."

"Franta." She waited until he raised his eyes again. "Mrs. Rehor has been here. She brought one of her geese with her, a young one. It was dead. She says you killed it with a clod. Did you?"

His chin began to tremble, but he held it hard. "I didn't go to kill it," he said. "I didn't go to, mother. I was only throwing at them to see them run. They look so funny when they run, all stretching their necks out. I didn't think I could hit one. And then it fell down and kicked, and she came out of the garden hollering, and I ran home."

"And before she came out of the garden, what did you say to her?"

He did not answer. The stubbornness had gone out of his eyes now, and they were frightened.

"She says you called her a name. What was it?"

"It's what the Votava boys call her," he said in a low voice. "I didn't make it up. Everybody calls her that."

"I did not ask you what everybody calls her. I asked you what you called her."

He told her, so faintly she could hardly hear. It was a word the boys used for a witch, a crooked old creature in the fairy stories who ate children. Mrs. Kolar stood still for a moment. Then she sat down on an upturned feed-box near the door, where the light came in, and drew him over in front of her by his shoulders, and held him there. His shoulders were thin and hot under her hands, and she could feel him trembling.

"Now you listen to me," she said, "because I am only going to tell you this once, and you will remember it all your life. When I was a little girl, younger than you are, my father worked land for the count, the way I have told you. We had nothing. We had a room and a stove and a bed, and a goose or two that we raised and fattened, and then we gave them up to the count's steward at Martinmas, because that was the rent. One year my mother had raised a goose of her own, a little extra one, that the steward did not know about. She was going to sell it and buy me shoes for the winter. I had never had shoes of my own; I wore my brother's old ones, stuffed with straw. And one day the count's boys came riding by the cottage, two fine boys in velvet jackets, and they saw the goose in the yard and they set their dogs on it, for fun, to see it run. And it ran, and the dogs caught it, and the boys laughed and rode away. My mother went out and picked it up. I remember how she stood there holding it. She did not cry. But that winter I went without shoes again, and my feet were frozen, and I have the marks still."

Franta was looking at her now, and his mouth had come open a little.

"Those boys did not go to kill anything either," his mother said. "They only wanted to see it run. They did not think. Rich people's children never have to think, because somebody else always pays. But we are not rich people, Franta, and we do not have that excuse. We know what a goose is worth. We know what it is to be poor and to have one thing taken away. That old woman down in the draw has had everything taken away from her, everything God gave her, her husband and her sons, one after another. And now she has her geese, and she talks to them because there is nobody else to talk to. And my son, my own son, comes along and kills one of them for sport and calls her a witch to her face. When she stood at our gate and showed it to me, I would rather have had you dead and buried up there on the hill with your little brothers than to hear it."

She had not meant to say that last thing, and she saw it go into him like a knife. He began to cry, not loudly, but with his whole body, the way a child cries when he has been badly frightened and is at last ashamed. She let him cry. She did not take him on her lap, though her arms wanted to; she held him by the shoulders and waited, looking past him through the barn door at the yard, where the chickens were scratching in the dust and the windmill turned slowly in the hot wind.

When he was quieter, she said, "How much money do you have in your box? The gopher money?"

He wiped his nose on his sleeve. "Forty cents," he said. "And a Canada penny."

All that summer he had been trapping gophers in the pasture and taking the tails to the county clerk, who paid a bounty on them, and he had been saving the money for a jackknife with two blades and a corkscrew, which he had seen in the window of the hardware store in town. He talked about that knife at supper, and in bed, and the girls teased him about it.

"Go and get it," his mother said. "All of it, the penny too. And then you will take the basket from the kitchen, and Bozena will put a dozen eggs in it, and two jars of the plums, and you will carry it to Mrs. Rehor, and you will give her the money for her goose. And you will tell her that you are sorry, in Bohemian, the way she can understand. And you will not run away when she talks to you, whatever she says. You will stand there and take it, like a man."

He looked at her with a kind of terror. "Alone, mother? Can't Bozena come with me?"

"Alone," said Mrs. Kolar. "Bozena did not throw any clods."

He went into the house without a word. She heard the girls' voices rise, curious and alarmed, and Bozena's voice hushing them. Presently he came out again with the basket on his arm and the money tied in a corner of his handkerchief, and walked across the yard and out of the gate without looking back. Bozena came and stood beside her mother in the doorway of the barn, wiping her hands on her apron.

"He's so little, mother," she said. "It's a long way, in this heat."

"It is a mile," said Mrs. Kolar. "He walked it this afternoon well enough, to throw clods at geese."

They stood and watched him go down the road. He grew smaller and smaller against the great spread of the stubble-fields, a little bent figure with the basket dragging at one arm, until he was hardly more than a moving speck. The country was so big, and he was so small in it. Mrs. Kolar thought how the land swallowed everything, men and horses and houses, and how all the work of a lifetime looked, from a little distance, like nothing at all, like a scratch on the face of the earth. It was a hard country for anyone to be alone in, and for an old woman who had lost everything it must be hardest of all. She had not thought much about Mrs. Rehor before. She had been too busy with her own children and her own fields and her own troubles, and she reproached herself for it now. It was not only Franta who had been careless.

She went back to the kitchen and finished her work. She set the jars on the shelf in the cellar, and washed the kettles, and put the bread to rise for the next day. The sun went down red and swollen behind the cornfield, and the long shadows came across the yard and up the side of the barn, and a coolness began to rise out of the ground, the first in many days. Joe came in from the far field and washed at the bench by the door, and she told him what had happened. He listened with his head bent, rubbing the towel slowly over his arms.

"You should have let me take the strap to him," he said. "He would have been done with it by now."

"He will be done with it soon enough," she said. "But he will not forget it."

It was nearly dark when Franta came home. They were sitting at supper, and the lamp was lit, and the girls kept looking toward the window. Then the gate clicked, and he came in, and set the empty basket down by the door. His face was pale and solemn, and there were crumbs on his chin. He stood just inside the doorway and did not come to the table.

"Well?" said his father.

"I told her," said Franta. "I said it the way mother said. She didn't holler at me. She cried some, and then she made me come into her house and sit down, and she gave me coffee with a lot of milk in it, and kolache with poppy seed. She has pictures on her wall. There's one of a soldier, and she says it's her boy that got killed. She wouldn't take the money at first, but I made her." He hesitated, and then his voice broke a little. "She says I can come and help her with the geese when she takes them to town at Christmas, if you'll let me, and she'll pay me. She says she's too old to drive them alone."

Nobody said anything for a moment. The twins looked at each other across the table, and Bozena bent her head over her plate. Mrs. Kolar got up and went to the stove and filled a bowl with soup, and set it at his place.

"Sit down and eat," she said. "Wash your hands first. You have been in the hay all day, and you are dirty as a little pig."

He washed at the basin and came and sat down beside her, and ate his soup in silence. Once, while the others were talking, she put her hand on the back of his neck and left it there for a little while, as if she were feeling whether he had a fever. He did not look up, but she felt him lean ever so slightly against her hand. Outside, the wind had gone down, and the cornfields were still, and over the draw to the east, where the old woman's dugout lay hidden among the plum bushes, a single star had come out, very large and bright, and hung there low above the edge of the world.
