Mr. Lucius Hollister arrived at the Union Station forty minutes before the eastern train was due, which was precisely thirty-five minutes earlier than he had told his wife he would arrive, and fully half an hour earlier than any reasonable man would think necessary. He was aware of this himself, and he explained it, to a baggageman who had not inquired, by remarking that "you never could tell about those eastern trains"; though in truth the eastern train had come in upon its schedule every afternoon for eleven years, and Mr. Hollister could have told about it very accurately if he had cared to. He was a stout man of forty-six, with a stout gold watch-chain stretched across a stout waistcoat. He had been to the barber's at noon, which he did not do upon weekdays, and his son Herbert, who accompanied him, had been to the barber's under protest at one, and still bore upon his neck the faint powdery evidences of the outrage.

Herbert was fifteen, and of that age at which a boy suffers acutely from the public appearance of his parents. He kept a distance of four or five feet from his father on the platform, so that strangers might suppose them unconnected, and he looked at the locomotives with an air of hardened worldliness, as one who had seen a great many locomotives in his time and found them, upon the whole, overrated. Nevertheless, he was in a state of considerable inward excitement, for the person whose arrival they awaited was his father's cousin, Fenwick Hollister, and around the name of Cousin Fen there had gathered, in Herbert's mind, a mist of legend not unlike that which surrounds the name of Robin Hood.

It was known in the family (it was known, indeed, to most of the older residents of the town, who still mentioned it when the conversation flagged) that Fen Hollister, at the age of nineteen, had borrowed the fire department's best team from the engine-house on Pratt Street, without consulting the fire department, and had driven it four times around the Court House square at midnight, standing up, with a young lady beside him who was never identified; that he had subsequently fought a professional pugilist at the County Fair for a purse of five dollars, and won it; that he had been engaged to three girls in a single winter, one of them twice; and that, upon the death of his father, he had sold out his share of the old Hollister grocery business to his cousin Lucius, and had gone East "to make a big thing of it," leaving behind him a debt at the livery stable which he had afterward paid by mail, with a letter so humorous that the liveryman had it framed. He had not been home since. That was twenty-two years ago. He had written perhaps once a year—breezy, brief letters on the stationery of hotels in New York, Philadelphia, Chicago, and places further off, with mentions of "a deal I have on" and "some people I am seeing"—and from these Herbert had built a figure of dazzling vagueness, a sort of composite of a railway magnate and a soldier of fortune, wearing a silk hat.

"Pa," said Herbert, edging two feet nearer, for the platform was momentarily deserted and there was no one to see, "what's he do, anyway? Cousin Fen. What's his business?"

"Well, sir," said Mr. Hollister, "it's hard to say, exactly. He's been in a good many things. Promoting, mostly, I guess. Fen always was a promoter. Why, when we were boys he promoted a circus in our barn, and charged admission, and the only animal in it was our cow, and he billed her as the 'Sacred White Buffalo of the Sioux,' and got eleven cents out of the Kittredge boys before their mother found out." Mr. Hollister laughed so heartily at this recollection that he was obliged to wipe his eyes; and Herbert, perceiving a stranger approaching, withdrew instantly to his former distance.

There is a peculiar anxiety which attends the meeting of kinsmen long separated, and Mr. Hollister, as the train time drew near, became subject to it. He found himself buttoning his coat and then unbuttoning it again, upon the theory that a buttoned coat made a stout man look stouter, and an unbuttoned one made him look careless; and he could not decide which was worse. For the truth is that Lucius Hollister, who had stayed at home and minded the business, and enlarged it until "Hollister Wholesale Groceries" was painted across the whole side of a five-story building near the freight yards, and who was a director of a bank and a deacon of a church and had been mentioned, though not seriously, for the City Council—Lucius Hollister had, all those twenty-two years, felt himself in some obscure way a dull dog beside his cousin Fen. He would never have admitted this to anyone, and had scarcely admitted it to himself; but it was there, and it rose up in him now like a schoolboy's dread of a recitation.

The train came in with a great deal of hissing and clanging, and an important Pullman porter got down and set a little step upon the platform, and people began to emerge. Mr. Hollister searched the faces eagerly. A young woman with a canary in a cage came first; then two drummers with sample cases; then a very old lady assisted by the porter; then a lean, grey gentleman in a somewhat narrow-brimmed hat and an overcoat with a velvet collar, carrying a single valise of the kind that has been a good valise once. This gentleman paused upon the step and surveyed the station with an expression of amused tolerance, as if he had been asked to pass judgment upon it and was inclined to be lenient. Then his eye fell upon Mr. Hollister, and he raised his hand in a broad gesture that seemed to include the station, the train, the town, and the afternoon.

"Lucius!" he cried. "Lucius, by all that's holy! Don't tell me! I'd have known you in the dark—in a coal mine—at the bottom of the sea!"

"Fen!" said Mr. Hollister; and the two cousins advanced upon each other and shook hands with a violence which caused the old lady to look back at them in alarm. They shook hands for a long time, neither of them able to think how to stop; and then Mr. Hollister, with an inspiration, clapped his cousin upon the shoulder, and Fen clapped him upon the shoulder, and that brought it to a conclusion.

"Well, well, well!" said Mr. Hollister.

"Well, sir!" said Fen. "Well, sir, well, sir!"

"Well, well!" said Mr. Hollister again; and there seemed nothing to add to this, for a moment, so he turned and beckoned. "Herbert! Come here. This is my boy, Fen. This is Herbert."

Herbert came forward, scarlet, and gave his hand. He had been examining his legendary kinsman with the frank and terrible eye of youth, and he had already observed several things: that the velvet collar was worn shiny at the back; that the narrow-brimmed hat was not a silk hat; and that the gentleman's shoes, though highly polished, had been half-soled. But Cousin Fen, gripping his hand, looked down at him with an eye so bright and a smile so knowing that Herbert's observations became, for the moment, of no account.

"So this is the heir," said Fen. "This is the young man that's going to inherit the Hollister groceries and run the whole state. Well, sir, I'm glad to know you. I hear you're quite a rounder."

"Sir?" said Herbert.

"I say I hear you're quite a rounder. Stay out late. Break hearts. Your father wrote me." Fen winked tremendously; and Herbert, who had never been out later than half-past ten in his life, and whose father had certainly written nothing of the sort, felt a warm and grateful glow suffuse him. He perceived that here was a man who understood.

They went out to the automobile, which Mr. Hollister had bought only that spring, and of which he was so proud that he had been unable to sleep the first night he owned it. He watched his cousin from the corner of his eye as they approached it, and was rewarded; for Fen stopped short upon the pavement and whistled.

"Lucius! Is that yours?"

"Oh, it's just a little runabout kind of thing," said Mr. Hollister carelessly. "Five-passenger. Forty horse-power. They tell me it'll do fifty miles an hour, but I never tried it." He said this in a tone of indifference so elaborate that Herbert, climbing into the tonneau, was obliged to look the other way.

"Well, sir, you've come up in the world," said Fen, settling himself in the front seat with his valise between his feet; and then, as if he feared he had conceded too much, he added: "Of course, in New York you hardly notice 'em any more. Fifth Avenue's just one solid stream. A man gets so he doesn't see 'em."

"I suppose so," said Mr. Hollister, a little dashed.

They drove up from the station through streets which the returning cousin had last seen as a boy, and the experience was evidently a strange one to him. He kept turning his head this way and that, and making exclamations, and asking "Where's this?" and "What's that?" in a voice which had lost some of its breeziness. For the town had done what all the Midland towns were doing in those years: it had grown, and it had not grown handsomely. Where there had been elms there were telegraph poles; where there had been big brick houses with cupolas and iron deer upon the lawns, there were boarding-houses with placards in the windows, or new apartment buildings of yellow brick with names like "The Alhambra" and "The Ivanhoe"; and over all of it hung the soft-coal smoke, so that the October sun came through like a lamp behind a dirty shade.

"Why, where's the Mayberry place?" Fen demanded. "Used to be right along here—big place with the conservatory?"

"That's it," said Mr. Hollister, pointing to a building in which, upon the ground floor, there was a plumbing supply company, and upon the upper floors a business college.

"That?" said Fen. He was silent for a block. "Why, I used to go to dances there," he said, in a lower voice. "Old Mrs. Mayberry used to have the floors waxed so you couldn't stand up on 'em. Dora Mayberry and I—" He did not finish, and Mr. Hollister did not ask him to.

"Dora married a man from Cincinnati," Mr. Hollister said, after a while. "She's a grandmother."

"A grandmother!" Fen exclaimed; and then, recovering himself with an effort that was visible to Herbert in the back seat, he laughed loudly. "Well, sir, so would I be, I suppose, if I'd settled down like the rest of you. That's what this town does to a man. Settles him. I always said it would, and I guess I was right. You can't do anything big in a place like this, Lucius. You've got to get out where things are moving."

"I guess that's so," said Mr. Hollister humbly; and he drove on in silence, thinking of the five-story building near the freight yards, and wondering why it seemed so small all of a sudden.

Mrs. Hollister was waiting for them in the front hall, in her second-best silk, which was the one she liked best. She had been, as a girl, Miss Nettie Arbogast, and it was a fact known to every elderly gossip in town, though Herbert had never heard of it, that Fen Hollister had been one of her suitors in the winter before he went away; indeed, it was believed by some that she was the young lady who had ridden behind the fire department's horses, though she had always denied it with a firmness which convinced nobody. She had chosen Lucius, the steady one; and the wise ladies of that day had said that she had chosen sensibly, and that a girl could not marry a fire-team. She was a plump, pleasant woman now, with a great deal of good sense and a habit of seeing through her husband which he had never suspected; and she gave her hand to Fen with a composure that was perfect, except that her cheeks were rather pink.

"Well, Fenwick," she said. "You haven't changed a bit."

"Nettie!" cried Fen. "Nettie Arbogast!" And he kissed her upon the cheek, which was the privilege of cousinship, though, strictly speaking, she was not his cousin. "Why, you're younger than you were! Lucius, what have you been doing to her? She looks like a girl of twenty!"

"Nonsense," said Mrs. Hollister; but she looked pleased, and patted her hair.

At dinner Cousin Fen was magnificent. He told stories of New York, of Saratoga, of a winter in San Francisco and a summer in Denver; of a mine in Colorado that had been on the point of making him a millionaire, and would have done so, but for the treachery of a partner whose name he declined to mention, being a gentleman; of a theatrical enterprise that had been on the point of making him a millionaire, and would have done so, but for the stupidity of the public; of a patent fly-trap, a street railway in Texas, and a hotel in Florida, all of which had been on the point of making him a millionaire. He told these things with such dash, and such generous gestures, and such fine contempt for the misfortunes that had attended them, that Herbert forgot his dinner, and sat with his mouth open and his fork suspended; and even Mr. Hollister, who could add a column of figures faster than any man in the wholesale district, did not once think to inquire what had been the actual financial outcome of any of these enterprises. Only Mrs. Hollister, listening with her pleasant smile, observed that Cousin Fen ate as if he had not had a good dinner in some time, and accepted a third helping of chicken with an alacrity which his anecdotes did not explain.

"And what are you in now, Fenwick?" she asked him gently, when the ice cream came.

"Now?" said Fen. He laid down his spoon. "Well, Nettie, I'm just looking around. Just looking around. I've got two or three things on the string. Big things. I thought I'd run out and see the old place while I'm making up my mind." He took up his spoon again. "Of course," he added, with a laugh, "I don't suppose there's anything in this town for a man like me."

"I don't suppose there is," said Mrs. Hollister, still gently; and she looked across the table at her husband, who did not see her.

After dinner the two cousins went out to sit upon the front porch, for the evening was warm with that last warmth of October which seems, in the Midland country, to be a kind of farewell. Herbert, who had been told that it was time for him to do his lessons, did not do them; he went up to his room, which was directly over the porch, and sat upon the floor beside the open window, in the darkness, with his chin upon the sill. He did not consider this eavesdropping. He considered it research.

For some time the cousins smoked in silence. Mr. Hollister had brought out a box of his best cigars, which he kept for the visits of the bank president, and Fen had taken three, putting two of them in his waistcoat pocket with the remark that he would "try 'em later." Down the street an arc-light sputtered and hissed; somewhere a mother was calling a boy named Willie, and Willie was declining to hear her; a street car went by on the next block with a long dwindling whine. Herbert, at the window above, began to fear that nothing more was going to happen.

"Lucius," said Fen at last, and his voice was different. It was lower, and had lost its flourish. "Lucius, that's a fine boy you've got."

"Oh, Herbert's all right," said Mr. Hollister. "He's at a kind of a funny age."

"He's a fine boy," Fen repeated. "And that's a fine wife. And that's a fine house, and a fine automobile, and I guess it's a fine business, too, from what I saw of the sign. You've done well, Lucius. You've done mighty well."

"Oh, I don't know," said Mr. Hollister uncomfortably. "I just kept on with what father left. Anybody could have done it. It's not like—well, it's not like what you've done, Fen. Getting around. Seeing things. I've never been further east than Pittsburgh in my life, except the once we went to Niagara Falls. Sometimes I've thought—" He paused, and the cigar glowed and faded in the darkness. "Sometimes I've thought I'd missed a good deal, Fen. Sitting here. I used to read your letters and think, 'There's Fen, out in the world, doing things, and here I am, figuring the price of canned tomatoes.' I guess I always kind of envied you, if you want to know the truth."

There was a long silence upon the porch. Above, at the window, Herbert held his breath.

"You envied me," said Fen slowly. "You envied me!" And then, to Herbert's consternation, his cousin began to laugh—not the loud laugh of the dinner table, but a queer, low, shaking laugh, that went on for some time and did not sound altogether like laughter. "Lucius," he said, when he could speak, "do you know what I've got in that valise? Two shirts and a razor. Do you know what I'm in, now? I'm not in anything. I've been selling a kind of encyclopædia, on commission, in the small towns of Pennsylvania, and the company went bankrupt last month, and owes me sixty dollars I'll never see. That's what I'm in. That's the big thing I've got on the string."

"Fen!"

"That's right. And the mine was a hole in the ground, and the theatrical company stranded in Ogden, Utah, and I walked a good part of the way to Salt Lake. And the fly-trap didn't catch flies. I've been thinking about this house, Lucius—about this porch—on and off for twenty-two years. When things were bad, I used to think, 'Well, there's Lucius, sitting on his porch, safe and solid, with Nettie inside, and nobody can touch him.' Envied me!" He laughed again, more quietly. "I guess I'm the one that did the envying."

Mr. Hollister did not answer for a while. When he did, it was in a voice which Herbert had never heard him use, and which made the boy feel suddenly that his father was a stranger, and a rather fine one.

"Fen," he said, "there's a place down at the store. I've been needing a man to go out on the road and handle the new accounts in the southern part of the state—a man that can talk to people and make them like him. I never could do it myself. It's not a big thing. But it's a salary, and there's a room upstairs here that nobody uses—"

"Now, Lucius, I didn't come out here to—"

"I know you didn't," said Mr. Hollister. "That's why I'm asking."

What Cousin Fen replied, Herbert never knew; for at that moment a firm hand descended upon his shoulder from behind, and he found his mother standing over him in the darkness. She did not scold him. She merely drew him away from the window, and closed it, and stood for a moment looking down through the glass at the two glowing points of the cigars upon the porch below.

"Mamma," Herbert whispered, in a kind of grief, "he isn't anything! He hasn't got anything! He just—he just sold books!"

"I know it," said Mrs. Hollister. "I knew it at the station, from the way your father described him on the telephone. I knew it twenty-three years ago, if it comes to that." She smiled a little, in the dark. "But he drove those horses four times around the square, Herbert, and nobody else in this town ever did. You go do your lessons."

Herbert went; but he did not do his lessons. He sat at his desk for a long time, with his geometry open before him, considering the strange case of a man who had nothing, and was glorious, and of another who had everything, and envied him; and he arrived at no conclusion whatever, which, considering his age, was perhaps the soundest conclusion available. The next morning, at breakfast, Cousin Fen was magnificent again, and told a story about a duel in New Orleans that had certainly never happened; and Herbert, who now knew better, listened to every word of it with his mouth open, and believed it all.

content:
Here are three excerpts of Booth Tarkington's writing, to show you their style:

Excerpt 1: The ineligible young men of the town (they were all ineligible) were unable to content themselves with the view that had so charmed Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster: they spent their time struggling to keep Miss Amberson’s face turned toward them. She turned it most often, observers said, toward two: one excelling in the general struggle by his sparkle, and the other by that winning if not winsome old trait, persistence. The sparkling gentleman “led germans” with her, and sent sonnets to her with his bouquets—sonnets lacking neither music nor wit. He was generous, poor, well-dressed, and his amazing persuasiveness was one reason why he was always in debt. No one doubted that he would be able to persuade Isabel, but he unfortunately joined too merry a party one night, and, during a moonlight serenade upon the lawn before the Amberson Mansion, was easily identified from the windows as the person who stepped through the bass viol and had to be assisted to a waiting carriage. One of Miss Amberson’s brothers was among the serenaders, and, when the party had dispersed, remained propped against the front door in a state of helpless liveliness; the Major going down in a dressing-gown and slippers to bring him in, and scolding mildly, while imperfectly concealing strong impulses to laughter. Miss Amberson also laughed at this brother, the next day, but for the suitor it was a different matter: she refused to see him when he called to apologize. “You seem to care a great deal about bass viols!” he wrote her. “I promise never to break another.” She made no response to the note, unless it was an answer, two weeks later, when her engagement was announced. She took the persistent one, Wilbur Minafer, no breaker of bass viols or of hearts, no serenader at all. A few people, who always foresaw everything, claimed that they were not surprised, because though Wilbur Minafer “might not be an Apollo, as it were,” he was “a steady young business man, and a good church-goer,” and Isabel Amberson was “pretty sensible—for such a showy girl.” But the engagement astounded the young people, and most of their fathers and mothers, too; and as a topic it supplanted literature at the next meeting of the “Women’s Tennyson Club.”

“Wilbur Minafer!” a member cried, her inflection seeming to imply that Wilbur’s crime was explained by his surname. “Wilbur Minafer! It’s the queerest thing I ever heard! To think of her taking Wilbur Minafer, just because a man any woman would like a thousand times better was a little wild one night at a serenade!”

“No,” said Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “It isn’t that. It isn’t even because she’s afraid he’d be a dissipated husband and she wants to be safe. It isn’t because she’s religious or hates wildness; it isn’t even because she hates wildness in him.”

“Well, but look how she’s thrown him over for it.”

“No, that wasn’t her reason,” said the wise Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “If men only knew it—and it’s a good thing they don’t—a woman doesn’t really care much about whether a man’s wild or not, if it doesn’t affect herself, and Isabel Amberson doesn’t care a thing!”

“Mrs. Foster!”

“No, she doesn’t. What she minds is his making a clown of himself in her front yard! It made her think he didn’t care much about her. Your son has caused a painful distress in my household. He made an unprovoked attack upon a little nephew of mine who is visiting in my household, insulted him by calling him vicious names and falsehoods, stating that ladies of his family were in jail. He then tried to make his pony kick him, and when the child, who is only eleven years old, while your son is much older and stronger, endeavoured to avoid his indignities and withdraw quietly, he pursued him into the enclosure of my property and brutally assaulted him. When I appeared upon this scene he deliberately called insulting words to me, concluding with profanity, such as “go to hell,” which was heard not only by myself but by my wife and the lady who lives next door. Georgie had muttered various interruptions, and as she concluded the reading he said: “He’s an ole liar!”

“Georgie, you mustn’t say ‘liar.’ Isn’t this letter the truth?”

“Well,” said Georgie, “how old am I?”

“Ten.”

“Well, look how he says I’m older than a boy eleven years old.”

“That’s true,” said Isabel. “He does. But isn’t some of it true, Georgie?” Georgie felt himself to be in a difficulty here, and he was silent.

“Georgie, did you say what he says you did?”

“Which one?”

“Did you tell him to—to—Did you say, ‘Go to hell?’” Georgie looked worried for a moment longer; then he brightened. “Listen here, mamma; grandpa wouldn’t wipe his shoe on that ole story-teller, would he?”

“Georgie, you mustn’t—” “I mean: none of the Ambersons wouldn’t have anything to do with him, would they? He doesn’t even know you, does he, mamma?”

“That hasn’t anything to do with it.”

“Yes, it has! I mean: none of the Amberson family go to see him, and they never have him come in their house; they wouldn’t ask him to, and they prob’ly wouldn’t even let him.”

“That isn’t what we’re talking about.”

“I bet,” said Georgie emphatically, “I bet if he wanted to see any of ’em, he’d haf to go around to the side door!”

“No, dear, they—” “Yes, they would, mamma! So what does it matter if I did say somep’m’ to him he didn’t like? That kind o’ people, I don’t see why you can’t say anything you want to, to ’em!”

“No, Georgie. And you haven’t answered me whether you said that dreadful thing he says you did.”

“Well—” said Georgie. “Anyway, he said somep’m’ to me that made me mad.” And upon this point he offered no further details; he would not explain to his mother that what had made him “mad” was Mr. Smith’s hasty condemnation of herself: “Your mother ought to be ashamed,” and, “A woman that lets a bad boy like you—” Georgie did not even consider excusing himself by quoting these insolences. Isabel stroked his head. “They were terrible words for you to use, dear. From his letter he doesn’t seem a very tactful person, but—” “He’s just riffraff,” said Georgie.

“You mustn’t say so,” his mother gently agreed “Where did you learn those bad words he speaks of? Where did you hear any one use them?”

“Well, I’ve heard ’em several places. I guess Uncle George Amberson was the first I ever heard say ’em. Uncle George Amberson said ’em to papa once. Papa didn’t like it, but Uncle George was just laughin’ at papa, an’ then he said ’em while he was laughin’.”

“That was wrong of him,” she said, but almost instinctively he detected the lack of conviction in her tone. It was Isabel’s great failing that whatever an Amberson did seemed right to her, especially if the Amberson was either her brother George, or her son George. She knew that she should be more severe with the latter now, but severity with him was beyond her power; and the Reverend Malloch Smith had succeeded only in rousing her resentment against himself. Georgie’s symmetrical face—altogether an Amberson face—had looked never more beautiful to her. It always looked unusually beautiful when she tried to be severe with him. “You must promise me,” she said feebly, “never to use those bad words again.”

“I promise not to,” he said promptly—and he whispered an immediate codicil under his breath: “Unless I get mad at somebody!” This satisfied a code according to which, in his own sincere belief, he never told lies.

“That’s a good boy,” she said, and he ran out to the yard, his punishment over. Some admiring friends were gathered there; they had heard of his adventure, knew of the note, and were waiting to see what was going to “happen” to him. They hoped for an account of things, and also that he would allow them to “take turns” riding his pony to the end of the alley and back. They were really his henchmen: Georgie was a lord among boys. In fact, he was a personage among certain sorts of grown people, and was often fawned upon; the alley negroes delighted in him, chuckled over him, flattered him slavishly. For that matter, he often heard well-dressed people speaking of him admiringly: a group of ladies once gathered about him on the pavement where he was spinning a top. “I know this is Georgie!” one exclaimed, and turned to the others with the impressiveness of a showman. “Major Amberson’s only grandchild!” The others said, “It is?” and made clicking sounds with their mouths; two of them loudly whispering, “So handsome!” Georgie, annoyed because they kept standing upon the circle he had chalked for his top, looked at them coldly and offered a suggestion: “Oh, go hire a hall!” As an Amberson, he was already a public character, and the story of his adventure in the Reverend Malloch Smith’s front yard became a town topic. Many people glanced at him with great distaste, thereafter, when they chanced to encounter him, which meant nothing to Georgie, because he innocently believed most grown people to be necessarily cross-looking as a normal phenomenon resulting from the adult state; and he failed to comprehend that the distasteful glances had any personal bearing upon himself. If he had perceived such a bearing, he would have been affected only so far, probably, as to mutter, “Riffraff!” Possibly he would have shouted it; and, certainly, most people believed a story that went round the town just after Mrs. Amberson’s funeral, when Georgie was eleven. Georgie was reported to have differed with the undertaker about the seating of the family; his indignant voice had become audible: “Well, who is the most important person at my own grandmother’s funeral?” And later he had projected his head from the window of the foremost mourners’ carriage, as the undertaker happened to pass.

She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. “Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

“Oh, I like him well enough,” George returned, with a short laugh, as he sat down and began to unlace his shoes. “I like him well enough—in his place.”

“No, dear,” she said hurriedly. “I’ve had a feeling from the very first that you didn’t really like him—that you really never liked him. Sometimes you’ve seemed to be friendly with him, and you’d laugh with him over something in a jolly, companionable way, and I’d think I was wrong, and that you really did like him, after all; but to-night I’m sure my other feeling was the right one: you don’t like him. I can’t understand it, dear; I don’t see what can be the matter.”

“Nothing’s the matter.” This easy declaration naturally failed to carry great weight, and Isabel went on, in her troubled voice, “It seems so queer, especially when you feel as you do about his daughter.” At this, George stopped unlacing his shoes abruptly, and sat up. “How do I feel about his daughter?” he demanded.

“Well, it’s seemed—as if—as if—” Isabel began timidly. “It did seem—At least, you haven’t looked at any other girl, ever since they came here and—and certainly you’ve seemed very much interested in her. Certainly you’ve been very great friends?”

“Well, what of that?”

“It’s only that I’m like your grandfather: I can’t see how you could be so much interested in a girl and—and not feel very pleasantly toward her father.”

“Well, I’ll tell you something,” George said slowly; and a frown of concentration could be seen upon his brow, as from a profound effort at self-examination. “I haven’t ever thought much on that particular point, but I admit there may be a little something in what you say. The truth is, I don’t believe I’ve ever thought of the two together, exactly—at least, not until lately. I’ve always thought of Lucy just as Lucy, and of Morgan just as Morgan. I’ve always thought of her as a person herself, not as anybody’s daughter. I don’t see what’s very extraordinary about that. You’ve probably got plenty of friends, for instance, that don’t care much about your son—” “No, indeed!” she protested quickly. “And if I knew anybody who felt like that, I wouldn’t—” “Never mind,” he interrupted. “I’ll try to explain a little more. If I have a friend, I don’t see that it’s incumbent upon me to like that friend’s relatives. If I didn’t like them, and pretended to, I’d be a hypocrite. If that friend likes me and wants to stay my friend he’ll have to stand my not liking his relatives, or else he can quit. I decline to be a hypocrite about it; that’s all. Now, suppose I have certain ideas or ideals which I have chosen for the regulation of my own conduct in life. Suppose some friend of mine has a relative with ideals directly the opposite of mine, and my friend believes more in the relative’s ideals than in mine: Do you think I ought to give up my own just to please a person who’s taken up ideals that I really despise?”

“No, dear; of course people can’t give up their ideals; but I don’t see what this has to do with dear little Lucy and—” “I didn’t say it had anything to do with them,” he interrupted. “I was merely putting a case to show how a person would be justified in being a friend of one member of a family, and feeling anything but friendly toward another. I don’t say, though, that I feel unfriendly to Mr. Morgan. I don’t say that I feel friendly to him, and I don’t say that I feel unfriendly; but if you really think that I was rude to him to-night—” “Just thoughtless, dear. You didn’t see that what you said to-night—” “Well, I’ll not say anything of that sort again where he can hear it. There, isn’t that enough?” This question, delivered with large indulgence, met with no response; for Isabel, still searching his face with her troubled and perplexed gaze, seemed not to have heard it. On that account, George repeated it, and rising, went to her and patted her reassuringly upon the shoulder. “There, old lady, you needn’t fear my tactlessness will worry you again. I can’t quite promise to like people I don’t care about one way or another, but you can be sure I’ll be careful, after this, not to let them see it. It’s all right, and you’d better toddle along to bed, because I want to undress.”

“But, George,” she said earnestly, “you would like him, if you’d just let yourself. You say you don’t dislike him. Why don’t you like him? I can’t understand at all. What is it that you don’t—” “There, there!” he said. “It’s all right, and you toddle along.”

“But, George, dear—” “Now, now! I really do want to get into bed. Good-night, old lady.”

“Good-night, dear. But—” “Let’s not talk of it any more,” he said. “It’s all right, and nothing in the world to worry about. So good-night, old lady. I’ll be polite enough to him, never fear—if we happen to be thrown together. So good-night!”

“But, George, dear—” “I’m going to bed, old lady; so good-night.” Thus the interview closed perforce. She kissed him again before going slowly to her own room, her perplexity evidently not dispersed; but the subject was not renewed between them the next day or subsequently. Nor did Fanny make any allusion to the cryptic approbation she had bestowed upon her nephew after the Major’s “not very successful little dinner”; though she annoyed George by looking at him oftener and longer than he cared to be looked at by an aunt. He could not glance her way, it seemed, without finding her red-rimmed eyes fixed upon him eagerly, with an alert and hopeful calculation in them which he declared would send a nervous man into fits. For thus, one day, he broke out, in protest: “It would!” he repeated vehemently. “Given time it would—straight into fits! What do you find the matter with me? Is my tie always slipping up behind? Can’t you look at something else? My Lord! We’d better buy a cat for you to stare at, Aunt Fanny! A cat could stand it, maybe. What in the name of goodness do you expect to see?” But Fanny laughed good-naturedly, and was not offended. “It’s more as if I expected you to see something, isn’t it?” she said quietly, still laughing.

“Now, what do you mean by that?”

“Never mind!”

“All right, I don’t. But for heaven’s sake stare at somebody else awhile. Try it on the house-maid!”

“Well, well,” Fanny said indulgently, and then chose to be more obscure in her meaning than ever, for she adopted a tone of deep sympathy for her final remark, as she left him: “I don’t wonder you’re nervous these days, poor boy!” And George indignantly supposed that she referred to the ordeal of Lucy’s continued absence. During this period he successfully avoided contact with Lucy’s father, though Eugene came frequently to the house, and spent several evenings with Isabel and Fanny; and sometimes persuaded them and the Major to go for an afternoon’s motoring. He did not, however, come again to the Major’s Sunday evening dinner, even when George Amberson returned. Sunday evening was the time, he explained, for going over the week’s work with his factory managers. When Lucy came home the autumn was far enough advanced to smell of burning leaves, and for the annual editorials, in the papers, on the purple haze, the golden branches, the ruddy fruit, and the pleasure of long tramps in the brown forest. George had not heard of her arrival, and he met her, on the afternoon following that event, at the Sharons’, where he had gone in the secret hope that he might hear something about her. Janie Sharon had just begun to tell him that she heard Lucy was expected home soon, after having “a perfectly gorgeous time”—information which George received with no responsive enthusiasm—when Lucy came demurely in, a proper little autumn figure in green and brown. Her cheeks were flushed, and her dark eyes were bright indeed; evidences, as George supposed, of the excitement incidental to the perfectly gorgeous time just concluded; though Janie and Mary Sharon both thought they were the effect of Lucy’s having seen George’s runabout in front of the house as she came in. George took on colour, himself, as, he rose and nodded indifferently; and the hot suffusion to which he became subject extended its area to include his neck and ears. Nothing could have made him much more indignant than his consciousness of these symptoms of the icy indifference which it was his purpose not only to show but to feel. She kissed her cousins, gave George her hand, said “How d’you do,” and took a chair beside Janie with a composure which augmented George’s indignation.

“How d’you do,” he said. “I trust that ah—I trust—I do trust—” He stopped, for it seemed to him that the word “trust” sounded idiotic. Then, to cover his awkwardness, he coughed, and even to his own rosy ears his cough was ostentatiously a false one. Whereupon, seeking to be plausible, he coughed again, and instantly hated himself: the sound he made was an atrocity. Meanwhile, Lucy sat silent, and the two Sharon girls leaned forward, staring at him with strained eyes, their lips tightly compressed; and both were but too easily diagnosed as subject to an agitation which threatened their self-control. He began again.

“I er—I hope you have had a—a pleasant time. I er—I hope you are well. I hope you are extremely—I hope extremely—extremely—” And again he stopped in the midst of his floundering, not knowing how to progress beyond “extremely,” and unable to understand why the infernal word kept getting into his mouth.

“I beg your pardon?” Lucy said. George was never more furious; he felt that he was “making a spectacle of himself”; and no young gentleman in the world was more loath than George Amberson Minafer to look a figure of fun. And while he stood there, undeniably such a figure, with Janie and Mary Sharon threatening to burst at any moment, if laughter were longer denied them, Lucy sat looking at him with her eyebrows delicately lifted in casual, polite inquiry. Her own complete composure was what most galled him.

“Nothing of the slightest importance!” he managed to say. “I was just leaving. Good afternoon!” And with long strides he reached the door and hastened through the hall; but before he closed the front door he heard from Janie and Mary Sharon the outburst of wild, irrepressible emotion which his performance had inspired. He drove home in a tumultuous mood, and almost ran down two ladies who were engaged in absorbing conversation at a crossing. They were his Aunt Fanny and the stout Mrs. Johnson; a jerk of the reins at the last instant saved them by a few inches; but their conversation was so interesting that they were unaware of their danger, and did not notice the runabout, nor how close it came to them. George was so furious with himself and with the girl whose unexpected coming into a room could make him look such a fool, that it might have soothed him a little if he had actually run over the two absorbed ladies without injuring them beyond repair. At least, he said to himself that he wished he had; it might have taken his mind off of himself for a few minutes. For, in truth, to be ridiculous (and know it) was one of several things that George was unable to endure. He was savage. He drove into the Major’s stable too fast, the sagacious Pendennis saving himself from going through a partition by a swerve which splintered a shaft of the runabout and almost threw the driver to the floor. George swore, and then swore again at the fat old darkey, Tom, for giggling at his swearing.

“Hoopee!” said old Tom. “Mus’ been some white lady use Mist’ Jawge mighty bad! White lady say, ‘No, suh, I ain’ go’n out ridin’ ’ith Mist’ Jawge no mo’!’ Mist’ Jawge drive in. ‘Dam de dam worl’! Dam de dam hoss! Dam de dam nigga’! Dam de dam dam!’ Hoopee!”

“That’ll do!” George said sternly.

“Yessuh!” George strode from the stable, crossed the Major’s back yard, then passed behind the new houses, on his way home. These structures were now approaching completion, but still in a state of rawness hideous to George—though, for that matter, they were never to be anything except hideous to him. Behind them, stray planks, bricks, refuse of plaster and lath, shingles, straw, empty barrels, strips of twisted tin and broken tiles were strewn everywhere over the dried and pitted gray mud where once the suave lawn had lain like a green lake around those stately islands, the two Amberson houses. And George’s state of mind was not improved by his present view of this repulsive area, nor by his sensations when he kicked an uptilted shingle only to discover that what uptilted it was a brickbat on the other side of it. After that, the whole world seemed to be one solid conspiracy of malevolence. In this temper he emerged from behind the house nearest to his own, and, glancing toward the street, saw his mother standing with Eugene Morgan upon the cement path that led to the front gate. She was bareheaded, and Eugene held his hat and stick in his hand; evidently he had been calling upon her, and she had come from the house with him, continuing their conversation and delaying their parting. They had paused in their slow walk from the front door to the gate, yet still stood side by side, their shoulders almost touching, as though neither Isabel nor Eugene quite realized that their feet had ceased to bear them forward; and they were not looking at each other, but at some indefinite point before them, as people do who consider together thoughtfully and in harmony. The conversation was evidently serious; his head was bent, and Isabel’s lifted left hand rested against her cheek; but all the significances of their thoughtful attitude denoted companionableness and a shared understanding. Yet, a stranger, passing, would not have thought them married: somewhere about Eugene, not quite to be located, there was a romantic gravity; and Isabel, tall and graceful, with high colour and absorbed eyes, was visibly no wife walking down to the gate with her husband. George stared at them. A hot dislike struck him at the sight of Eugene; and a vague revulsion, like a strange, unpleasant taste in his mouth, came over him as he looked at his mother: her manner was eloquent of so much thought about her companion and of such reliance upon him. And the picture the two thus made was a vivid one indeed, to George, whose angry eyes, for some reason, fixed themselves most intently upon Isabel’s lifted hand, upon the white ruffle at her wrist, bordering the graceful black sleeve, and upon the little indentations in her cheek where the tips of her fingers rested. She should not have worn white at her wrist, or at the throat either, George felt; and then, strangely, his resentment concentrated upon those tiny indentations at the tips of her fingers—actual changes, however slight and fleeting, in his mother’s face, made because of Mr. Eugene Morgan. For the moment, it seemed to George that Morgan might have claimed the ownership of a face that changed for him. It was as if he owned Isabel. The two began to walk on toward the gate, where they stopped again, turning to face each other, and Isabel’s glance, passing Eugene, fell upon George. Instantly she smiled and waved her hand to him; while Eugene turned and nodded; but George, standing as in some rigid trance, and staring straight at them, gave these signals of greeting no sign of recognition whatever. Upon this, Isabel called to him, waving her hand again.

“Georgie!” she called, laughing. “Wake up, dear! Georgie, hello!” George turned away as if he had neither seen nor heard, and stalked into the house by the side door.

Excerpt 3: We debate sometimes what is to be the future of this nation when we think that in a few years public affairs may be in the hands of the fin-de-siècle gilded youths we see about us during the Christmas holidays. Such foppery, such luxury, such insolence, was surely never practised by the scented, overbearing patricians of the Palatine, even in Rome’s most decadent epoch. In all the wild orgy of wastefulness and luxury with which the nineteenth century reaches its close, the gilded youth has been surely the worst symptom. As for her insinuation, pencilled upon the border, he supposed she meant to joke—a supposition which neither surprised him nor altered his lifelong opinion of her wit. He read her letter with more interest:
... The dinner your mother gave for the Morgans was a lovely affair. It was last Monday evening, just ten days after you left. It was peculiarly appropriate that your mother should give this dinner, because her brother George, your uncle, was Mr. Morgan’s most intimate friend before he left here a number of years ago, and it was a pleasant occasion for the formal announcement of some news which you heard from Lucy Morgan before you returned to college. At least she told me she had told you the night before you left that her father had decided to return here to live. It was appropriate that your mother, herself an old friend, should assemble a representative selection of Mr. Morgan’s old friends around him at such a time. He was in great spirits and most entertaining. As your time was so charmingly taken up during your visit home with a younger member of his family, you probably overlooked opportunities of hearing him talk, and do not know what an interesting man he can be. He will soon begin to build his factory here for the manufacture of automobiles, which he says is a term he prefers to “horseless carriages.” Your Uncle George told me he would like to invest in this factory, as George thinks there is a future for automobiles; perhaps not for general use, but as an interesting novelty, which people with sufficient means would like to own for their amusement and the sake of variety. However, he said Mr. Morgan laughingly declined his offer, as Mr. M. was fully able to finance this venture, though not starting in a very large way. Your uncle said other people are manufacturing automobiles in different parts of the country with success. Your father is not very well, though he is not actually ill, and the doctor tells him he ought not to be so much at his office, as the long years of application indoors with no exercise are beginning to affect him unfavourably, but I believe your father would die if he had to give up his work, which is all that has ever interested him outside of his family. I never could understand it. Mr. Morgan took your mother and me with Lucy to see Modjeska in “Twelfth Night” yesterday evening, and Lucy said she thought the Duke looked rather like you, only much more democratic in his manner. I suppose you will think I have written a great deal about the Morgans in this letter, but thought you would be interested because of your interest in a younger member of his family. Hoping that you are finding college still as attractive as ever, Affectionately, Aunt Fanny. George read one sentence in this letter several times. Then he dropped the missive in his wastebasket to join the clipping, and strolled down the corridor of his dormitory to borrow a copy of “Twelfth Night.” Having secured one, he returned to his study and refreshed his memory of the play—but received no enlightenment that enabled him to comprehend Lucy’s strange remark. However, he found himself impelled in the direction of correspondence, and presently wrote a letter—not a reply to his Aunt Fanny. Dear Lucy: No doubt you will be surprised at hearing from me so soon again, especially as this makes two in answer to the one received from you since getting back to the old place. I hear you have been making comments about me at the theatre, that some actor was more democratic in his manners than I am, which I do not understand. You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. Well, here I sit smoking my faithful briar pipe, indulging in the fragrance of my tobacco as I look out on the campus from my many-paned window, and things are different with me from the way they were way back in Freshman year. I can see now how boyish in many ways I was then. I believe what has changed me as much as anything was my visit home at the time I met you. So I sit here with my faithful briar and dream the old dreams over as it were, dreaming of the waltzes we waltzed together and of that last night before we parted, and you told me the good news you were going to live there, and I would find my friend waiting for me, when I get home next summer. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. I am not capable of friendship except for the very few, and, looking back over my life, I remember there were times when I doubted if I could feel a great friendship for anybody—especially girls. I do not take a great interest in many people, as you know, for I find most of them shallow. Here in the old place I do not believe in being hail-fellow-well-met with every Tom, Dick, and Harry just because he happens to be a classmate, any more than I do at home, where I have always been careful who I was seen with, largely on account of the family, but also because my disposition ever since my boyhood has been to encourage real intimacy from but the few. What are you reading now? I have finished both “Henry Esmond” and “The Virginians.” I like Thackeray because he is not trashy, and because he writes principally of nice people. My theory of literature is an author who does not indulge in trashiness—writes about people you could introduce into your own home. I agree with my Uncle Sydney, as I once heard him say he did not care to read a book or go to a play about people he would not care to meet at his own dinner table. I believe we should live by certain standards and ideals, as you know from my telling you my theory of life. Well, a letter is no place for deep discussions, so I will not go into the subject. From several letters from my mother, and one from Aunt Fanny, I hear you are seeing a good deal of the family since I left. I hope sometimes you think of the member who is absent. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. It is the only girl’s photograph I ever took the trouble to have framed, though, as I told you frankly, I have had any number of other girls’ photographs, yet all were only passing fancies, and oftentimes I have questioned in years past if I was capable of much friendship toward the feminine sex, which I usually found shallow until our own friendship began. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. I will have to rise and fill it, then once more in the fragrance of My Lady Nicotine, I will sit and dream the old dreams over, and think, too, of the true friend at home awaiting my return in June for the summer vacation. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. Lucy and her father were living at the Amberson Hotel, while Morgan got his small machine-shops built in a western outskirt of the town; and George grumbled about the shabbiness and the old-fashioned look of the hotel, though it was “still the best in the place, of course.” He remonstrated with his grandfather, declaring that the whole Amberson Estate would be getting “run-down and out-at-heel, if things weren’t taken in hand pretty soon.” He urged the general need of rebuilding, renovating, varnishing, and lawsuits. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

Mr. Harlan Pettibone was a man of fixed habits and an unfixed temper, and of the two it was the habits that his household relied upon. He came home from his office in the Second National Bank building at a quarter before six. He hung his hat upon the third peg of the walnut rack in the hall, never the second, which belonged to the umbrella. He kissed his wife upon the left temple, inquired whether the evening paper had come, and was told that it had. He then went into the library, sat in the leather chair that had taken his shape so faithfully over twelve years that it seemed to resent visitors, and read the paper until Delia rang the bell for supper. In all this he had the deep satisfaction of a man who believes he governs his own life, and the world was kind enough, as a rule, not to contradict him.

Upon a certain Thursday in the late spring, however, the world contradicted him at the very threshold. His wife did not wait to be kissed upon the temple; she met him in the vestibule, closed the inner door behind her with the air of one shutting a prisoner away from his rescuers, and said in a low voice:

"Harlan, before you go in, you must hear about Roscoe."

Mr. Pettibone held his hat in mid-air, the third peg forgotten. "What's he done now?"

"I want you to promise first that you won't be too severe with him."

This was not encouraging. Long experience had taught Mr. Pettibone that his wife asked him not to be too severe only when the case was one in which she would have been severe herself, if she could have managed it. Mrs. Pettibone's severity, like a lady's revolver, was something she owned but had never been able to fire.

"I'll promise nothing of the kind," he said. "What is it?"

"Well, you know Mrs. Corliss's dog?"

"I know it," Mr. Pettibone admitted gloomily. Everybody on Meridian Street knew it. It was a white bull-terrier of great age and settled melancholy, named Prince Albert, and it slept upon the Corliss front steps in a manner that suggested it had been placed there by an undertaker.

"It's blue," said Mrs. Pettibone.

"It's what?"

"Blue. All over. Roscoe and the Tinker boy and that little Heffelfinger got it into our stable this afternoon and put it in the wash-tub with a whole bottle of Delia's bluing, and then they kept it there and charged the children in the neighbourhood to come and look at it. They called it 'The Sacred Blue Hound of India.' Roscoe painted a sign. It's on the stable door now. Mrs. Corliss has been here twice. The second time she cried."

Mr. Pettibone's face underwent a change that his wife watched anxiously, for she had never been sure, in eleven years of married life, whether this particular change preceded wrath or laughter; and indeed it was possible that Mr. Pettibone himself did not know. There was an interval, during which a muscle in his cheek moved and was sternly mastered.

"Charged them?" he said. "Charged them what?"

"Pins, mostly. And some marbles. And a cent from the Willoughby child, and an agate. And—Harlan, this is the worst of it—when Mrs. Corliss came over the first time and asked him what he meant by it, he told her—" Mrs. Pettibone lowered her voice still further, as though Mrs. Corliss might be crouching in the shrubbery. "He told her she ought to be glad, because you'd said yourself that Prince Albert was the dullest-looking dog in the state, and now at least he'd be interesting."

"I never said any such thing!"

"You said it at supper on Sunday. 'Dullest-looking dog in the whole commonwealth' were the words. Roscoe was right there."

Mr. Pettibone was silent. It is one of the profounder sorrows of parenthood that the child, who will not remember for five minutes where he left his cap, retains with the fidelity of a court stenographer every incautious word let fall at the dinner table; and he will produce these words, not at home where they might be safely discussed, but in the presence of precisely the person they concern. Mr. Pettibone felt himself, for the moment, more the defendant than the judge, and the sensation did not soften him toward his son. On the contrary, it hardened him. A man will forgive a great deal in a child before he will forgive being quoted.

"Where is he?"

"Upstairs in his room. I sent him there as soon as Mrs. Corliss left. He's been very quiet."

"I should hope so," said Mr. Pettibone, and hung up his hat, upon the second peg, with the umbrella.

He did not go upstairs at once. He went into the library and sat in the leather chair and held the evening paper before him for perhaps ten minutes without reading a word of it; for he was composing what he intended to say. Mr. Pettibone had a great belief in the efficacy of a well-ordered speech. He had been, in his youth, a member of the Philo-Rhetorian Society at Wabash, and he still thought of most of the difficulties of life as things that could be met by the proper arrangement of three points and a peroration. His points, upon this occasion, were to be: first, the wickedness of tormenting dumb animals; second, the dishonesty of taking pins and marbles from smaller children upon a false pretense; and third, the grave disrespect of repeating to a neighbour words spoken in the privacy of one's own home. He was a little uneasy about the third point, which seemed to him to lead somewhere he did not wish to go; but he decided that if he spoke of it firmly enough it would not lead anywhere at all.

Having thus prepared himself, he folded the paper, rose, and went to the foot of the stairs.

"Roscoe!"

There was no answer, though there was a sound overhead that might have been made by a boy of nine getting quickly off a window-sill.

"Roscoe! Come down here to the library. I want to speak to you."

The door of the room above opened, very slowly, as doors do when they are opened by people who have a strong preference for remaining behind them; and Master Roscoe Pettibone descended the stairs. He descended them one at a time, with a hand upon the rail, and his eyes fixed upon each step as though it were new to him and might not bear his weight. He was a small, compact boy with a round head of cropped yellow hair, freckles distributed over him with great liberality, and that expression of limpid, heavenly innocence which nature, in her unfathomable humour, bestows most generously upon those boys who least deserve it. His mother had once been told by a visiting cousin that he looked like a cherub by Correggio, and she had believed it ever since, in the face of evidence that would have convinced a jury.

He arrived at the bottom step, and paused there, as at a frontier.

"In here," said his father, and led the way.

Mr. Pettibone resumed the leather chair, which gave him an advantage of position, and Roscoe stood upon the hearth-rug before him, with his hands behind his back. There was blue upon them, to the wrists, and a long streak of blue upon one cheek, and his stockings, which had been tan in the morning, were now of an indeterminate shade not found in nature. Mrs. Pettibone had followed them as far as the doorway, where she stood with one hand at her throat, in the attitude of a woman who has delivered someone to the authorities and immediately regretted it.

"Well, sir," said Mr. Pettibone.

Roscoe said nothing. He had learned, by the age of nine, that "Well, sir" was not a question, and that to treat it as one was only to hasten matters.

"I have been hearing," said Mr. Pettibone, "some very remarkable things about you."

"Yes, sir."

"Very remarkable and very disgraceful things."

Roscoe's gaze travelled slowly from his father's face to the clock on the mantel, as though he wished to fix the hour of the proceedings for future reference, and then returned.

"Do you know what you've done?"

"Yes, sir," said Roscoe. Then, upon reflection, he added cautiously, "Well—which?"

Mr. Pettibone was momentarily disconcerted by the implication that the list was a long one, and that his son was not sure how much of it had come to light. He chose to ignore it, and proceeded to his first point.

"You took a poor, harmless old dog," he said, "a dog that never did you any harm in its life, and you dragged it into our stable, and you—"

"We didn't drag him."

"What?"

"We didn't haf to drag him," Roscoe explained earnestly. "He came. Willie Tinker had a piece of liver. He came right along. He liked it."

"He liked having bluing poured all over him, I suppose!"

"Well, he didn't mind it any," said Roscoe. "He just stood there. He never even wiggled. Prince Albert never does wiggle, papa. He's too old to wiggle. Mr. Heffelfinger's hired man says he's been dead three years and nobody's told him."

This was so exactly the sort of remark that Mr. Pettibone might have made himself, at the Thursday Club, that he was obliged to pause and look severely at the fire-irons. When he looked back at his son his face was stern again, and he passed hastily on to his second point.

"And then," he said, "you charged other children to come and look at this poor animal. You took their pins and their marbles—you took a cent from little Effie Willoughby, who can't be more than five years old—and you told them it was a—what was it?"

"The Sacred Blue Hound of India," said Roscoe, not without a certain quiet pride.

"And it was not a sacred blue hound of India! It was Mrs. Corliss's dog! You knew perfectly well it was Mrs. Corliss's dog! That was obtaining money under false pretenses, sir! Do you know what they do to grown men who do that?"

Roscoe's eyes widened with a lively interest that was not altogether what his father had intended. "What do they do?"

"They put them in jail!"

"For how long?"

"For years!" said Mr. Pettibone, with feeling. "For years and years!"

Roscoe considered this, and his brow cleared. "Well, but anyway Effie Willoughby knew it was Prince Albert. Everybody knew it. Effie said, 'Why, that's ole Prince Albert!' the minute she came in, and she paid her cent just the same. She said she'd rather see him blue than white any day. She said it was worth it."

"That has nothing to do with it."

"Well, but papa, if everybody knew it was Prince Albert, then it wasn't any false pretenses, was it? It was only a show. Like the Wild Man of Borneo at the County Fair, that Mr. Heffelfinger's hired man says is a colored fellow from Terre Haute. Everybody knows that, too, and they all pay a dime."

It is a curious thing that a man who can conduct himself with perfect competence before a board of directors, and who has more than once silenced the president of a rival bank in open meeting, may find himself wholly at a loss before a child of nine standing upon a hearth-rug in blue stockings. Mr. Pettibone was aware that his second point had somehow been taken from him and was lying in fragments upon the rug; and he was aware, too, of a faint sound from the doorway that he preferred to believe was his wife clearing her throat. He did not look toward it. He gathered himself, and advanced upon his third point with the determination of a general who has lost two redoubts and means at any cost to hold the citadel.

"Roscoe," he said, in his deepest voice, "when Mrs. Corliss came to ask you what you meant by this conduct, what did you say to her?"

For the first time, the cherub by Correggio looked uneasy. His glance went to the doorway, found no ally there, and came reluctantly back.

"I don't remember exactly."

"Then I will remind you. You told her that I had said her dog was—that I had made a certain remark about her dog."

"Well, you did, papa."

"That is not the point!"

"You said it Sunday," Roscoe insisted, with the doggedness of a witness who perceives that the truth is his only friend. "You said, 'That Corliss dog is the dullest-looking dog in the whole commonwealth,' and mamma said, 'Harlan, the child,' and you said, 'Well, it is,' and then you had some more chicken."

There was a silence in the library. Mr. Pettibone, who had not expected to hear himself reproduced with such terrible accuracy, even to the chicken, sat very still. The doorway was silent too.

"What I say at my own table," he said at last, rather slowly, "is said in private, to my own family. It is not intended to be carried to the neighbours. A gentleman does not repeat what he hears in his own home. He does not go out and tell people things that will hurt their feelings. Mrs. Corliss is an old lady, Roscoe. She is a widow. That dog is all she has. She cried, Roscoe. She sat in our parlour and cried. Do you understand that? You made an old lady cry."

He had not prepared this; it came of itself, and it was better than anything he had prepared. Roscoe's lower lip, which had been firm throughout the cross-examination upon pins and marbles, now showed signs of instability. He looked at the rug, and at his blue hands, and swallowed.

"I didn't mean to make her cry."

"What did you mean, then?"

"I meant—" Roscoe struggled. It was evident that he was trying to recover, for his father's benefit, the precise logic that had seemed so luminous at three o'clock in the afternoon, and that it was not coming back to him in its original shape. "I meant she oughtn't to be so mad, because he wasn't hurt any, and he was a whole lot more interesting blue, and you said yourself he was dull, so I thought—I thought she'd be kind of glad, if she knew you thought so, too. Because now he isn't. Now everybody looks at him. Before, nobody ever looked at him at all."

Mr. Pettibone opened his mouth and closed it again. He was conscious that somewhere in this answer there lay a principle—a perverse, upside-down principle, but a principle nevertheless—and that a boy who could find it at nine would very likely end either in the legislature or in the penitentiary, and that it was the duty of a father to steer him firmly toward the former. He took refuge in authority, which is the last resort of a man who has run out of arguments, and the first resort of a man who never had any.

"That will do," he said. "I have heard enough. You have behaved very badly indeed, and you are going to be punished. In the first place, every pin and every marble and every cent you took from those children is going back to them to-morrow morning, and you are going to take them yourself."

"Yes, sir," said Roscoe, in a small voice; then, with sudden anxiety, "The agate, too?"

"Certainly the agate, too!"

"But papa, Sammy Heffelfinger only gave me that agate because he owed it to me anyway, from last week, and he—"

"The agate goes back."

Roscoe was silent, though the silence was eloquent of a deep sense of injustice in the matter of the agate.

"In the second place," his father went on, "you are going over to Mrs. Corliss's house to-morrow, and you are going to tell her you are sorry, and you are going to help wash that dog until he is white again."

"It won't come out," Roscoe said simply. "We tried. Willie Tinker said it would come out, but it won't. Delia says it'll have to wear off."

Mr. Pettibone had a sudden, distinct vision of Prince Albert reclining upon the Corliss steps through the remainder of the season, an enduring azure monument visible from the car-line, and of the remarks that would be made concerning it by the Thursday Club, and by the president of the rival bank, who lived three doors down. The muscle in his cheek moved again, and this time it was only with an effort that resembled pain that he compelled it to be still.

"Then you will help wash him every day until it does wear off," he said. "And in the third place, you will go up to your room now, and you will have your supper there—bread and milk—and you will not come down again to-night. Do you understand?"

"Yes, sir."

"And I want you to think, Roscoe. I want you to think about Mrs. Corliss, and about how you would feel if somebody did such a thing to a dog of yours."

"I haven't got a dog," said Roscoe, in a tone that suggested this was a grievance of long standing and that his father had at last stumbled upon the root of the whole matter.

"Go upstairs!"

Roscoe went. He went more briskly than he had come down, as one whose ordeal is over and whose sentence, though harsh, is at least known; and his mother, as he passed her in the doorway, put out a hand and touched the blue streak upon his cheek, and then, recollecting herself, withdrew it and looked stern. Roscoe, who understood perfectly well the value of that touch, did not presume upon it. He mounted the stairs, and they heard his door close.

Mrs. Pettibone came into the library, and Mr. Pettibone, without looking at her, unfolded the evening paper and held it before him.

"Harlan," she said, "you were very fine with him. At the end, about Mrs. Corliss crying. I think he really felt it."

"I hope so," said Mr. Pettibone, from behind the paper.

"Only—you won't say things like that at the table any more, will you? About the neighbours?"

"I don't intend to discuss it."

"Of course, dear." She lingered a moment. "Harlan—the dog really is very blue. I saw it from the side window. It's the bluest thing I ever saw in my life. It's bluer than the sky."

The paper trembled slightly.

"I'll go and see about the bread and milk," said Mrs. Pettibone hastily, and went out.

Mr. Pettibone remained alone in the library. He read, or appeared to read, the same column three times; it concerned the tariff, and he could not afterward have said which side of it he had been on. Presently, with the air of a man performing an act of purely civic duty, he rose and walked to the side window, which commanded, across the lilac hedge, a partial view of the Corliss front steps. The light of the long spring evening still lay over Meridian Street, and in that light, upon the top step, unmoving and serene and incomparably blue, lay Prince Albert. A small group of children had gathered upon the sidewalk before him, keeping a respectful distance and gazing upward in silence, as pilgrims gaze upon a shrine; and Mr. Pettibone observed that one of them, a very small girl in a sunbonnet, was attempting to pass something between the palings of the Corliss fence, and that the something glinted like a pin.

He stood there for some time. Then he went back to the leather chair, and those in the kitchen, Delia afterward reported, heard a sound from the library that she could not account for, unless the master had swallowed something the wrong way; for it went on a good while, and stopped, and then began again worse than before.

Upstairs, Master Roscoe Pettibone, eating his bread and milk upon the window-sill, heard it too, and was much puzzled by it. But he was a philosopher in his way, and after a little consideration he concluded that it was probably something about the bank, and that it was none of his business; and he returned to the more pressing question of how, if the agate must go back to Sammy Heffelfinger, it might be got back again from Sammy Heffelfinger by Saturday.
