It was nearly six o'clock when little Wladek came home, and his mother had been watching for him from the window for more than an hour. The window looked out upon an alley, and beyond the alley upon a board fence plastered with circus bills, and beyond the fence upon the long black wall of the rolling mill, from whose stacks there poured, day and night, a smoke so thick that the sun had to fight its way through it like a swimmer through a flood. There was not much to see from that window; but Agnieszka Mrozek had stood at it so long that she knew every crack in the fence and every tatter of the circus bills, and she could have told you how many times in that hour the switch engine had gone puffing by with its string of ore cars, and how many times the whistle had blown at the gate. She had gone down to the street twice, with her shawl over her head, and had stood at the corner and peered both ways; and each time she had come back up the three flights of stairs, holding her side, for she was seven months gone with her fifth child, and the stairs were very steep.

She had sent the boy at four o'clock to Kowalski's on the avenue, with a quarter of a dollar tied up in the corner of a handkerchief. He was to buy a loaf of bread, which was five cents, and a pound of lard, which was twelve, and with what was left he was to get soup bones from the butcher next door. It was a simple errand, and he had done it many times before; he was a bright boy, and he could count up to a hundred in English and in Polish both, and he knew the price of everything in Kowalski's store as well as his mother did. But the quarter of a dollar was the last money in the house. That was a thing which Wladek did not know, and which it would not have occurred to his mother to tell him. One does not tell a child of seven that the rolling mill has been shut down for six weeks for "repairs," and that the father goes out every morning at five to stand in the crowd at the gate of the Harvester works, and comes back every night at dark without having been let in. One does not explain to a child that there are four dollars owing at Kowalski's already, and that the agent has been twice about the rent, and that the last time he had looked about the room at the bed and the stove and the trunk from the old country in a way that had made Agnieszka's heart stand still. These are the affairs of grown persons, and children have no part in them—or so the grown persons believe, until the day comes when the children find out.

It was the shoes which Agnieszka heard first; Wladek wore a pair of shoes which had belonged to a boy in the next building, and which were three sizes too big for him, so that he went clumping up the stairs like a cart horse. She ran to the door and flung it open; and there he stood upon the landing, breathless and rosy-cheeked from the cold, with the loaf of bread under one arm and the package of lard under the other—and with his mouth all smeared about with red, and his two fists clutched tight upon something which he held behind his back.

"Where have you been?" cried his mother. "Do you know what time it is? Where are the bones?"

The boy did not answer, but came in slowly, and laid the bread and the lard upon the table. His mother seized him by the shoulder and turned him about. "What have you got there? Show me!"

He brought his hands around, very reluctantly; and in one of them there was a tin whistle, painted red and blue, with a little bird on the end of it, and in the other there was a stick of candy, striped like a barber's pole, which he had already sucked down to a point. Agnieszka stared at these objects as if they had been two live snakes. It took her a moment to comprehend what they meant; and when she did, the color went out of her face, and she sat down suddenly in a chair.

"Jezus Maria!" she whispered. "The money! What did you do with the money?"

Wladek began to tremble. He had known all the way home that he had done something wrong; he had stood for a long time on the corner of the avenue, feeling of the two pennies and the nickel that were left in the handkerchief, and trying to make up his mind to go back. But he had not known how wrong it was; he had thought that perhaps he would be scolded, and that would be all. Now he saw his mother's face, and he did not understand it, and that frightened him more than any scolding.

"I bought—" he stammered. "There was a store—there was a window—"

There was indeed a store, and there was indeed a window; and if the reader will take the trouble to walk along the avenue he will find it still, a narrow little shop between a saloon and an undertaker's, kept by a Greek with a cast in one eye. It is a place which has been arranged with a great deal of cunning, for it lies directly upon the path which the children of the district must take to the school and to the church and to the grocery; and in its window, which is the only clean window in the block, there is spread out such a display as is calculated to work upon the soul of a child as the sight of a saloon works upon the soul of a drunkard. There are candies of every color in the rainbow, and several which the rainbow has never thought of: red and green and yellow and purple, in sticks and in balls and in the shapes of animals and fishes; there are licorice whips and chocolate mice and little hearts with mottoes printed upon them. There are tin trumpets and tin whistles and jumping jacks and rubber balls, and paper masks with grinning faces, and pistols that shoot caps. And over it all there hangs a great placard, with a picture of a fat and happy little boy in a velvet suit, who holds up a stick of candy and smiles at you, and underneath him the words, in letters a foot high, "EVERY BOY LIKES BUSTER'S!"

Now it does not matter to the man who made that placard, nor to the man who made the candy, nor to the man with the cast in his eye who sells it, that the little boys who pass that window have never seen a velvet suit in their lives, and that most of them have never had enough to eat in their lives either. It does not matter that the candy is made of glucose and coal-tar dyes and a little flour, and that it costs perhaps a tenth of a cent to make, and that the whistle is made of tin scraps from a canning factory and will be broken in three days. All that matters is that the little boys shall stop and stare, and that every now and then one of them shall have a penny in his pocket. There are a great many little boys in the district behind the rolling mills—some thirty thousand of them, according to the census—and if each one of them can be made to spend only a penny a week, it comes to fifteen thousand dollars in the course of a year; and that is a sum which will keep a candy manufacturer in a very fine house upon the Lake Shore Drive, with a velvet suit for each of his own little boys, and a governess to see that they do not eat too many sweets and spoil their digestions.

Wladek had stood before that window for a long time—he did not know how long. He had not meant to go in; he had gone into the butcher's first, and found a crowd there, and had come out again to wait until it should thin. And then the little boy in the velvet suit had smiled at him, and the whistle with the bird on the end of it had seemed to call to him; and there had come over him all at once a feeling such as he could not have put into words, a hunger that was not in his stomach but somewhere farther in. He had never owned a toy in his life that had not been somebody else's first; and here was a whistle that nobody had ever blown, painted fresh and shining, and it cost only ten cents. He had told himself that he would ask the price, and no more; and then, somehow, the handkerchief was untied, and the Greek had taken the dime and given him the whistle, and had thrown in a stick of candy for a penny more—because he was such a fine boy, the Greek had said. So there had been only two cents left for the soup bones; and the butcher had laughed at him, and given him nothing.

All of this came out at last, in broken pieces, between sobs; and his mother listened to it, sitting motionless in her chair, with her hands lying in her lap. When he had finished, she said nothing for a while. Then she got up slowly, and went to the nail behind the stove, and took down the strap.

It was a leather strap, about two feet long and two inches wide, which had once been part of a harness; Wladek's father had brought it from the old country, and it had hung on a nail in every place where they had lived, as a sort of household god. It was not often taken down. Agnieszka was not a harsh woman; she had been a merry girl once, in the village of Brzeziny, where she had danced at the harvest festivals with a wreath of cornflowers in her hair, and the young men had come from three villages around to see her. She loved her children with the fierce and anxious love of the poor, which is a different thing from the love of the rich, as different as a wolf is from a lapdog. But there are times when love itself becomes a terror, when it sees the danger so plainly that it can think of nothing but to strike; and this was one of those times.

"Come here," she said.

The boy shrank back against the wall. "Mamo!" he wailed. "I didn't mean—I'll take it back—I'll take the whistle back to the man!"

"You will take nothing back," said his mother. "Do you think he will give you the money? Do you think anybody in this country gives anybody back their money? Come here, I say!"

He came, because there was nothing else for him to do; there is no place to hide in a room twelve feet square, which holds a stove and a table and two beds and a trunk, and in which four children and two grown persons sleep. The other children had gathered in the corner—little Hela, who was five, and the twins, who were three, and who did not understand what was happening, but who began to cry because Hela was crying. Agnieszka took her son by the arm and bent him over her knee, and lifted the strap.

"Ty lobuzie!" she cried, and brought it down. "You good-for-nothing! You thief! Do you know what you have done? Do you know?" And at each question the strap came down again.

But the reader must not think that she was beating him for the whistle, or for the stick of candy, or even for the soup bones. She did not know what she was beating him for—she only knew that she must beat something. All the misery of the past six weeks rose up in her and came down with that strap: the nights she had lain awake listening to her husband's breathing, and knowing by the sound of it that he was not asleep either; the mornings she had divided the bread into six pieces and then into seven, so that there would be a little for the noon; the face of the rent agent, and the voice of Kowalski when she had asked him for credit the last time, and the way the women at the pump had looked at her when she said that her man would surely be taken on next week. She was beating the mill that had shut down, and the Harvester works that would not open their gates, and the agent and the grocer and the man with the cast in his eye, and the man who had painted the little boy in the velvet suit. She was beating the whole vast and pitiless city, which had lured them across the ocean with its promises and was now squeezing them slowly to death; and since she could not reach any of these things, she beat the only thing within her reach, which was the body of her own child.

"Do you know," she cried, "that your father has had nothing to eat since morning? Do you know there is no more money—none—not a penny? What are we to eat tomorrow? Your whistle? Will you blow your whistle for the agent when he comes to put us in the street? Will you give your candy to the twins when they cry for bread?"

The boy did not answer; he could not have answered if he had tried, for he was screaming so that the people in the next room began to pound upon the wall. He did not understand the words; he understood only that the world, which had seemed to him a fairly safe and comfortable place, in spite of cold and hunger, had turned all at once into a place of horror, where his own mother had become a stranger with a white face and blazing eyes. Many years afterward, when he was a grown man working in the mill himself, Wladek would remember that moment; he would remember the smell of the stove, and the sound of the twins wailing in the corner, and the red-and-blue whistle lying on the floor where it had fallen, with the little tin bird broken off its end. It was the first lesson he had ever had in political economy, and it was a lesson he never forgot—though it was many years more before he learned to read it rightly.

It did not last long—perhaps a minute, perhaps two. Then quite suddenly the strap fell from Agnieszka's hand, and she pushed the boy off her knee, and put both hands over her face, and began to sob. They were not the sobs of a woman who weeps easily; they came up from somewhere deep inside her, harsh and dreadful, shaking her whole body, so that the boy, who had crawled away under the table, stopped his own crying to stare at her in terror. He had never seen his mother cry before, not even when the baby died the winter before last; and it seemed to him somehow far worse than the strap.

"O Matko Boska," she moaned, rocking herself to and fro. "Mother of God, what will become of us? What will become of us?"

There is a picture which the comfortable classes have of the poor, and which they put into their novels and their Sunday sermons: the picture of the honest workingman's home, humble but clean, where the mother sits by the hearth with her knitting and the children say their prayers at her knee, and the father comes home in the evening to his pipe and his slippers. The comfortable classes like this picture very much; they hang it up in their minds, as it were, and look at it whenever they feel uneasy about the wages they are paying. And if they were to come upon such a scene as this in the Mrozek tenement—the woman with her apron over her head, the child cowering under the table, the strap upon the floor—they would turn away with a shudder and say that these foreigners were a brutal and degraded lot, who did not know how to raise their children; and they would go home and write a check to the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, and feel that they had done their duty. It would not occur to them that the strap had been put into Agnieszka Mrozek's hand by the same men who had shut down the mill to keep up the price of steel rails; and that the blows which fell upon little Wladek had been struck, in the last analysis, by persons who would never in their lives set foot in that alley, and who were at that very hour sitting down to dinners of seven courses in houses upon the Lake Shore Drive.

After a while the sobbing grew quieter; and then Agnieszka lifted her head and looked about her, at the frightened children, and at the bread and the lard upon the table, and at the broken whistle upon the floor. She got up heavily and went over to the table, and got down upon her knees—which was not an easy thing for her to do—and looked under it, where Wladek lay curled up against the wall with his face hidden in his arms.

"Wladziu," she said. "Come out, little one."

He did not move; and so she reached in and took hold of him, gently this time, and drew him out, and gathered him up into her lap, there upon the floor. He was stiff at first, and would not look at her; but she held him close and rocked him, and smoothed his hair, which was yellow like her own had been once, and murmured to him in Polish, the old words that she had learned from her own mother in Brzeziny—words about little birds in the forest, and the Christ child in the manger, and the good God who watches over children while they sleep. And little by little the boy's body loosened, and he turned his face against her breast and began to cry again—but quietly now, as a child cries when the worst is over.

"I'll never do it again, Mamo," he whispered. "Never, never. I'll go and work. I'll sell papers like Stefek Nowak. I'll get the money back."

"Hush," said his mother. "Hush, now. You are too little to work."

But even as she said it she was thinking—for she could not help thinking—that Stefek Nowak was only eight, and brought home thirty cents on a good day; and that there was a glass works over on the river that took boys of ten, if their parents would swear that they were fourteen; and that in three years Wladek would be ten. She put the thought away from her with a shudder; but it came back, as such thoughts always do, and she knew that it would come back again and again, until one day it would not have to come back any more, because it would have become a fact. That is the way such things happen in the district behind the rolling mills. Nobody decides them; nobody wishes them; they simply come, as the smoke comes down from the stacks and settles upon everything, and nobody can say just when it was that the window turned black.

So they sat there upon the floor in the gathering dusk, the mother and the child, while the twins crept up and clung to her skirts and little Hela brought the broken whistle and laid it in her brother's hand. Outside the switch engine went puffing by again, and the circus bills fluttered upon the fence, and the long black wall of the mill stood silent and dark, as it had stood for six weeks now; and upon the avenue, a few blocks away, the window of the little shop between the saloon and the undertaker's was all lit up with gas, so that the candies glowed like jewels, and the little boy in the velvet suit smiled down upon the passing children and told them, in letters a foot high, that every boy liked Buster's.

It was nearly nine o'clock when the father came up the stairs. He came slowly, as he always did now, and he stood for a moment in the doorway, looking at the bread and the lard upon the table, and at his wife's red eyes, and at the strap upon the floor. He asked no questions; he was a man of few words at any time, and these six weeks had taken most of the words out of him. He hung up his cap, and sat down at the table, and cut the loaf into seven pieces, very carefully, with his big knife; and when he came to Wladek's piece he hesitated a moment, and then cut it a little bigger than the rest, and handed it to the boy without a word.

Lyman J. Tuttle came home at six-fourteen, which was one minute earlier than usual, and he came home whistling. He whistled "Smile, Smile, Smile," and then, because the first had gone so well, he whistled it again, with a trill at the end which he believed to be the trill of a professional. He was president of the Tuttle Household Appliance Company, sole agent in Sioux Bend for the Glo-Rite Electric Washer, the Purity Vacuum Sweeper, and the Kold-Kist Ice Box with the Patented Seepless Drain, and he was forty-six years old, and that afternoon he had been elected chairman of the Greater Sioux Bend Week Committee of the Forward Club.

He put his car, a 1922 Comet Six sedan with nickel-plated bumpers and a motometer on the radiator cap, into the garage, which was of the same tapestry brick as the house and which had cost him eleven hundred and forty dollars, not counting the cement drive. He stood for a moment in the drive and looked at his house. It was a good house. Everyone said so. It was a Dutch Colonial with green shutters that could not be shut, a sun-parlor with wicker furniture which no one sat in, and a front door with a brass knocker in the shape of a lion's head which no one knocked, since there was also an electric bell. On the lawn there was a concrete birdbath, and in the birdbath there was a sparrow, and Lyman regarded the sparrow with approval, as a fellow citizen who knew a good residential district when he saw one.

"Some little old shack," he said aloud, and went in.

His wife Hazel was in the living-room. She was not, as a wife should be at six-fourteen, in the kitchen supervising the hired girl, nor upstairs changing into her blue foulard, nor on the telephone talking to Mrs. Doc Haverstraw about the Thursday Bridge Club. She was sitting in the overstuffed davenport, beneath the hand-colored photograph of the Grand Canyon, with her hands folded in her lap, and she was looking at nothing. Lyman did not observe this. He was a man who observed sales charts, weather which might affect the sale of electric fans, and the faces of competitors at Forward Club luncheons; but he had been married for twenty-two years, and he had not looked at his wife with real attention since approximately the Taft administration.

"Well, well, well!" he boomed. "Guess who's the new big noise around this burg! Go on, guess!"

"I'm sure I couldn't, Lyman."

"Old Lyme Tuttle, that's who! Chairman of Greater Sioux Bend Week! Unanimous! Well, practically unanimous. Ed Sorensen voted for Charley Pruitt, but that's just because Charley sold him his furnace. Old Ed, he's a good scout, but he hasn't got any more vision than a—than a bedbug. And say, listen here. Here's the big news. Senator Bloodgood is coming down for the Wednesday banquet, and the committee figured, well, the chairman ought to put him up, and so I said, why, sure, the Senator'll stay with us, and Hazel'll give a little dinner Tuesday night, nothing fancy, just the Haverstraws and the Pruitts and maybe the Reverend and Mrs. Gilchrist, and—what's the matter? Don't you feel good?"

For Hazel had not risen. She had not cried, "Why, Lyman, isn't that splendid!" which was the speech that had been composed for her, in his mind, all the way home from the Hotel Majestic.

"Sit down a minute, Lyman," she said. "I've got something to tell you."

He sat down, warily, on the edge of the Morris chair. He had a quick vision of disasters: the boy, Delbert, had been fired out of the State University for drinking; the girl, Marjorie, had eloped with that pimply young cub from the bond house; the furnace had blown up; Hazel had been to see Doc Haverstraw about that pain in her side and Doc had found—

"It's nothing bad," said Hazel. "At least I don't think it's bad. I've rented the store on Fremont Street. The little one between the shoe repair and the Greek's. I signed the lease this afternoon. I'm going to open a book shop."

Lyman Tuttle looked at her. He looked at the Grand Canyon above her head, as though the Grand Canyon might explain. He looked at the radio cabinet, a Melodia Super-Five, which had brought in Pittsburgh on a clear night, and at the phonograph, and at the bronze lady holding up a lamp with a silk shade, and at the set of Kipling in maroon limp-leather which had been given to him by the Glo-Rite Company as a prize for exceeding his quota in 1921. None of them explained anything.

"You've what?"

"I've rented a store. For a book shop. And a circulating library, two cents a day. I'm going to call it the Hearthside Book Nook. Or maybe not. I haven't decided on the name."

"Now, look here, Hazel. Now, just a minute. You mean to sit there and tell me you went downtown and signed a lease, a legal lease, without so much as asking—without even consulting—"

"I knew what you'd say."

"Well, by golly, I should think you would know what I'd say! What any man would say! I never heard of such a thing! Where's the money coming from? You think I'm made of money? You think a man in the appliance game with the Kold-Kist people raising the dealer's price on him six per cent can just go and throw away—"

"It's Aunt Lottie's money," said Hazel.

That checked him. He had forgotten Aunt Lottie's money. Aunt Lottie, of Red Wing, had died the previous winter and left Hazel three thousand two hundred dollars in Liberty Bonds and a set of hand-painted china depicting the cathedrals of Europe. The china was in the dining-room. The bonds were in the safety deposit box at the Farmers' and Merchants' National, and Lyman had always thought of them, vaguely and comfortably, as his own, as part of the general Tuttle prosperity, like the garage and the motometer and the brass knocker; for it is a principle of American domestic economy that what is the wife's is the husband's, and what is the husband's is his own business.

"Well, Aunt Lottie's money, then. All the more reason. That's—that's capital, that's what that is. You don't go throwing capital into some fool proposition like a—a book shop. My gosh, Hazel, who reads books in Sioux Bend? I ask you. Name me one person."

"I do."

"Oh, well, you."

He said it kindly. He said it with the tolerance of a man who indulges his wife in her small eccentricities, as other men indulge their wives in canaries or the Christian Science. It was true that Hazel read books. She took out three a week from the Carnegie Library, and sometimes she bought one, and once, at dinner with the Pruitts, she had mentioned a novel which had been banned in Boston, and there had been a silence, and Lyman had had to tell the story about the Swede and the mule to make things go again.

"Yes, me," said Hazel, and her voice was not loud, but it was not the voice he knew. "And Mrs. Gilchrist, she reads. And the girls at the high school, the teachers. And there's the young people. And there's lots of women, Lyman, women in this town that sit home all afternoon with the housework done by ten o'clock and nothing on earth to do but play bridge and talk about each other, and they'd read if there was anything to read besides what's in the drugstore rack, and they'd come in and talk about it—"

"Talk!" said Lyman. "That's what I'm afraid of! Talk! Have you thought for one minute what people are going to say? About me? Lyme Tuttle's wife keeping store! Why, they'll say I can't support my own family! They'll say the business is on the rocks! Charley Pruitt'll have it all over the Forward Club by Thursday noon—'Heard about poor old Lyme? Wife had to go to work.' My gosh! The week I get elected chairman! The very week! And Senator Bloodgood coming!"

He stood up. He walked to the window and looked out at the birdbath. The sparrow had gone. He walked back. He took a cigar from his vest pocket, a Corona del Plaza at fifteen cents straight, and bit off the end, and did not light it.

"Lyman," said Hazel, "I'm not going to work. Not the way you mean. I'm going to have a book shop."

"It's the same thing."

"It isn't the same thing. Mrs. Fenstermacher runs the hat shop, and her husband's the cashier at the bank, and nobody says he can't support her."

"Mrs. Fenstermacher," said Lyman with dignity, "is a widow in everything but name, and everybody knows it, and you know it, and anyway that's millinery. That's different. That's a woman's line. Hats. Women understand hats. But books—why, a book store, that's—" He searched for the word; he was not a man accustomed to examining the foundations of his own opinions, any more than he would have examined the foundations of the Farmers' and Merchants' National Bank before depositing his money there. "That's highbrow," he said at last. "People'll think you're getting stuck-up. They'll think you think you're better than they are."

There was a pause, and in the pause the kitchen door swung, and Tillie, the hired girl, put her head in and said, "Supper's on, Mrs. Tuttle," and withdrew, having received the impression that there was trouble, which she would communicate that evening to the Pruitts' hired girl, who would communicate it to Mrs. Pruitt, so that Lyman's fears concerning the Forward Club on Thursday noon were, as it happened, entirely justified, though not for the reason he supposed.

They went in to supper. There was pot roast with brown gravy, and mashed potatoes, and creamed carrots, and a bowl of piccalilli, and bread-and-butter, and lemon meringue pie. The table was mahogany veneer, and the chairs were mahogany veneer, and the sideboard held a silver-plated coffee service which they had received as a wedding present from the Lodge and had used twice. Lyman ate heavily and with resentment. He felt that he was being deprived not only of his rightful triumph but of his digestion as well, and he chewed each mouthful as though it were an argument.

"I suppose," he said, after a time, "you've thought about the lease. What kind of lease is it? What's the rent?"

"Thirty-five a month. One year."

"Thirty-five! For that hole? Hazel, you've been stung. Who owns it? Old man Kratzer? He saw you coming. Thirty-five! I could have got it for you for twenty-eight, twenty-eight-fifty at the outside, if you'd let me handle it. That's what comes of a woman trying to do business. You don't know the first thing about it."

"If I'd let you handle it," said Hazel, "you wouldn't have got it for me at all."

He could not answer that, because it was true, and he did not like her for saying it.

"And what about the house?" he said. "Who's going to run the house? Who's going to see to Tillie? Who's going to be here when I come home? And the Bridge Club, and the Eastern Star, and the Ladies' Aid—you just going to drop all that? And this dinner. Tuesday. For the Senator. You're going to give that dinner, aren't you? You're not going to be down in some store selling—selling poetry—when the Senator comes?"

"I'll give your dinner, Lyman."

"Well. Well, that's something, anyway."

But it did not feel like something. It felt, obscurely, like a concession granted to him, and Lyman Tuttle was not used to having concessions granted to him by his wife. He was used to granting them. He granted her the household allowance on the first of each month, with a little speech about economy. He granted her a new spring coat every second year. He granted her permission to have the Bridge Club in the house, and permission to put up the new curtains in the sun-parlor, and permission to go to Minneapolis to see the Follies with her sister, provided she was back by Thursday. He had always considered himself a generous husband, broad-minded, a regular modern husband, not one of those old-fashioned tyrants you read about, and he felt, eating his lemon meringue pie, that his generosity was being thrown back in his face.

"I don't get it," he said, and there was genuine bewilderment in it now, and a little pain. "I just don't get it, Hazel. What do you want? Haven't you got everything? Haven't I always given you everything? Look at this house. Look at that car. Look at the furniture. You got the best electric washer in the state of Minnesota, I don't care where you go. There isn't a woman in Sioux Bend has got any more than you have. What do you want to go and do a thing like this for?"

Hazel put down her fork. She looked at him across the mahogany veneer, and for a moment he saw her, really saw her, the way he had not seen her in years: a woman of forty-four with gray coming in above her ears, and a mouth that had gotten thinner, and eyes that were the same eyes he remembered from a Methodist strawberry social in 1899, gray-blue and serious and, he now realized with alarm, not entirely friendly.

"Lyman," she said, "do you know what I did today? Before I went down to see Mr. Kratzer?"

"How should I know what you did?"

"I got up. I had breakfast with you. You read me the part in the paper about the new viaduct. Then you went to the store. Then I told Tillie about the meat order. Then I dusted the living-room, though Tillie had dusted it yesterday. Then I sat down and looked at the Grand Canyon. Then I telephoned Lou Haverstraw, and she told me about Mrs. Pruitt's new permanent wave, and I told her about the sale at Bjornstad's. Then it was eleven o'clock. Then I went upstairs and lay down. Then it was lunch. And I thought—I thought, I'm forty-four years old. And Delbert's gone, and Marjorie'll be gone in a year, and I'm going to do this, this very same thing, every day, until I die. And then they'll say at the Ladies' Aid, 'She was a fine woman, Hazel Tuttle, she kept a lovely home.' And that'll be all. That'll be the whole of it."

"Well, what's wrong with that?" said Lyman. "My gosh, that's what every woman—that's a fine thing to have said about you. I'd be proud. A lovely home. What's wrong with a lovely home?"

"Nothing's wrong with it," said Hazel. "Nothing at all. Only it isn't enough."

And there it was, the thing that could not be answered, the thing that had no column in the ledger and no line in the Glo-Rite sales manual. Lyman Tuttle knew how to answer an objection about price, or about the reliability of the wringer mechanism, or about whether a family of four really needed the Kold-Kist Model Twelve or could make do with the Model Eight. He had been to the Glo-Rite Dealers' Convention in Chicago, three times, and had heard Dr. J. Harold Speers, the Business Psychologist, lecture on Overcoming Customer Resistance, and he had taken notes in a small leather book which he still carried. But he did not know how to answer "It isn't enough." Nobody had ever told him that a thing could fail to be enough when it was, by every reasonable standard, the best on the market.

He tried, nevertheless.

"Now, look here, Hazel. Let's be sensible about this. Let's look at this thing like two grown-up people. I'll tell you what I'll do. You want something to do, fine. That's fine. I'm for it. Hundred per cent. Now, there's the Women's Auxiliary of the Forward Club. They're putting on a pageant for Greater Sioux Bend Week, 'The Spirit of Progress,' and they need somebody to head up the costumes, and I could speak to Mrs. Pruitt—"

"No, Lyman."

"Or the Red Cross. Or the Library Board! There you are! You like books! I could get you on the Library Board, easy, I know Judge Lindquist, and you could pick out the books, and it'd be a real honor, and nobody'd say a word—"

"No."

"Well, then, I don't know what you want!" He brought his fist down on the table, not hard, but hard enough to rattle the piccalilli. "I'm trying to meet you halfway! I'm doing my darnedest! I come home with the biggest news a man in this town could have, chairman of the whole works, Senator Bloodgood coming to stay in this house, in our house, Hazel, and I can't even tell it. I can't even get it out. And you sit there and spring this on me. On this night, of all nights. I'd think you'd at least have the—the consideration—"

He stopped, because he saw that she was smiling, a small, tired, curious smile, and he could not tell whether she was laughing at him.

"Congratulations on the chairmanship, Lyman," she said. "I mean it. I know how much you wanted it."

"Well," he said, somewhat mollified. "Well, it's a big thing. It's a big thing for the business, too. Gets your name around."

"And I'll give your dinner Tuesday. I'll get a ham, and Tillie can do the scalloped potatoes, and we'll have the Haverstraws and the Pruitts and the Gilchrists. And I'll wear my blue foulard. And when the Senator asks me what I do, I'll tell him I run the Hearthside Book Nook on Fremont Street."

"You wouldn't."

"I would, Lyman. I'd be proud to."

He looked at her a long time. Then he took out the Corona del Plaza again and lighted it, with hands that were not quite steady, and puffed, and looked at the coffee service from the Lodge.

"I suppose," he said at last, heavily, "I suppose if you're bound and determined. I suppose a fellow can't stop you. It's your money. Aunt Lottie's money. I suppose you got a legal right."

"Yes," said Hazel. "I suppose I have."

"Only don't come crying to me when it goes bust. That's all I ask. Don't come crying to me in six months when you've lost every cent and old Kratzer's after you for the rent. Because I warned you. I want that understood. I warned you."

"It's understood, Lyman."

He went out to the sun-parlor after supper, to the wicker furniture in which no one sat, and sat in it, and read the Sioux Bend Evening Clarion, the editorial page and the sporting page and the advertisement which the Tuttle Household Appliance Company ran every Tuesday, "Let Glo-Rite Make Monday a Holiday!" He read it twice. It was a good advertisement; he had written it himself. Then he sat with the paper in his lap and thought about what he would say to Charley Pruitt.

He would say—he worked it out carefully, the way he worked out a sales talk—he would say, "Well, sir, the Missus has gone and got herself a little hobby. Bound to do it. You know how women are. Wants to run a little book shop. I said, sure, go ahead, Hazel, have your fun, I can afford it." And he would laugh, and Charley would laugh, and it would be all right. It would be, in fact, rather a good thing: a broad-minded man, Lyman Tuttle, a modern man, lets his wife have her little hobby. He could afford it. That was the point. That was the whole point.

By ten o'clock he had very nearly convinced himself that the book shop had been his own idea.

At ten-thirty he wound the clock on the mantel, and locked the front door, and looked in on the furnace, and went upstairs. Hazel was already in bed, in the twin bed nearer the window, with the light off. He undressed in the bathroom, and brushed his teeth with Dento-Glo, and came out in his pajamas, which were striped in lavender, and got into his own bed.

"Hazel?"

"Yes, Lyman."

"I was thinking. About that name. 'Hearthside Book Nook.' That's not bad. That's got a homey ring. But you want something with more pep to it. Something that'll catch the eye. How about 'Tuttle's Better Books'? Then folks'd know right off it was connected with—well, with the family. Kind of a tie-in. Good for both businesses."

There was a long silence from the other bed.

"I'll think about it, Lyman."

"You do that. Night, Hazel."

"Good night."

He was asleep in four minutes, and dreamed that he was introducing Senator Bloodgood to an audience of eleven hundred, and that the Senator, at the end of his speech, turned to him and said, before them all, "And to the man who made this possible, our distinguished chairman—" and that the applause went on and on, like the sound of a Glo-Rite washer on the rinse cycle.

But Hazel lay awake. She lay awake a long time, listening to her husband breathe and to the Great Northern freight going through at midnight, its whistle sounding long and lonely across the flat dark fields beyond the edge of town, toward Minneapolis and Chicago and places farther still, places she had read about and would never see. The train from Chicago was nineteen minutes late, and Walter Ebbing, who sold the Thermo-King Automatic Furnace ("Heat That Thinks for Itself") to the more progressive householders of Vandalia Springs, spent the nineteen minutes walking up and down the platform of the Union Station with the air of a man who personally owned the railroad and was disappointed in it.

He was forty-four. He was a large, pink, scrubbed man, with the scrubbed look of a boy who has been made to wash behind the ears for a party, and he wore a gray suit from Feldheimer & Sons ("Clothes for the Man Who Gets There"), a pearl stickpin in the shape of a horseshoe, and the button of the Benevolent and Protective Order of Moose. Every few minutes he took out his watch, a seventeen-jewel Hamilton presented to him by the Thermo-King Corporation for Outstanding Sales Achievement in the Upper Mississippi District, looked at it with irritation, and then, because it was a very fine watch, looked at it again with pleasure.

He was waiting for his cousin Lester Pruitt, whom he had not seen in twenty-two years.

They had been boys together on adjoining farms outside Kettle Creek, where their mothers were sisters and their fathers were not on speaking terms, owing to a dispute about a line fence which neither could remember the origin of and both could defend with Scripture. They had fished together, stolen melons together, been licked together in the woodshed of Grandfather Haskell, and had together made a solemn vow, at the age of fourteen, beside a dead muskrat, that they would never, never settle down in any town smaller than Minneapolis. Then Lester had gone East to study art, which was considered in Kettle Creek to be a kind of illness, like consumption, only less respectable. And Walter had gone to Vandalia Springs to clerk in a hardware store, which was considered to be the beginning of a career.

The careers had gone their ways. Walter had married Myrtle Bloomquist, the daughter of the man who owned the hardware store; had two children, a bungalow on Fernwood Terrace, a Buick sedan, and a seat on the Program Committee of the Rotary Club. Lester had, so far as Walter could tell from his infrequent letters, gone to New York and then to Paris, and then to New York again, and had been in something called a Salon, and had illustrated books, and had once been mentioned in the Saturday Evening Post, though only in an advertisement.

The train came in. It came in with the snorting self-importance of all trains entering all Midwestern cities, as though it were bringing news of great events from the capitals of the world, though it was actually bringing a drummer in notions, two Lutheran ministers returning from a synod, a lady with a canary, and Lester Pruitt.

Walter would not have known him. He had expected, he did not know why, a slender youth in a flowing tie, with a beret, perhaps, and a sensitive mouth. He saw a thin, stooped, graying man of forty-five in a brown suit that had been good once and was now merely tolerable, with a cane, a cigarette, and a face that seemed to have been folded up and put away in a drawer and taken out again without being pressed.

"Les!" roared Walter. "Lester, you old son of a gun! Well, I'll be a hammered tinker! Well, well, well!"

He pounded his cousin on the back. Lester, who had not been pounded on the back since 1904, coughed and smiled and said, "Hello, Walt. You've gotten—you've gotten prosperous."

"Well, I don't know about that, I don't know about that," said Walter, who did know about it, and who had hoped that it would be noticed. "Can't complain. Mustn't complain. Here, give me that grip. No, no, I insist. Car's right outside. Wait'll you see the old burg, Les. You won't know it. Why, when you left here—well, you never were here, you were back home in Kettle Creek, but when you left, why, Vandalia Springs wasn't anything but a jerkwater whistle-stop with a couple of grain elevators and a saloon. Population eighteen thousand. Know what it is now?"

"I'm afraid I don't."

"Ninety-four thousand, six hundred and twelve. That's by the 1920 census. We figure we'll crowd a hundred and twenty-five by 'thirty. Fastest-growing city of its size between Chicago and the Rockies, bar none. That's a fact. I've seen the figures."

---

The Buick was a dark-blue sedan with nickel trimmings, and it had, Walter explained as he drove, a self-starter, a gasoline gauge on the dash, balloon tires, a cigar lighter, and a rear window with a little curtain that could be pulled down, though he did not know why anyone would want to pull it down. He drove his cousin up Commercial Avenue, past the Second National Bank (eleven stories, the tallest building in the state outside the Twin Cities), past the Orpheum Theatre, past the new Elks Temple with its granite elk, past Hamberger's Department Store, the Mid-Continent Life Insurance Building, the Bon Ton Lunch, the Vandalia Springs Daily Clarion, and a vacant lot on which a sign announced that THIS SITE WILL SOON BE THE HOME OF THE VANDALIA SPRINGS ATHLETIC CLUB—WATCH US GROW!

"Watch us grow," Walter repeated with satisfaction. "That's our slogan. I was on the committee that picked it. We had it narrowed down to that and 'The Springs Spring Ahead,' but some of the boys thought that one was kind of highbrow. Too much like a pun."

"I think you chose wisely," said Lester.

Walter glanced at him sharply, for there had been something in the voice—some dryness, some little curl at the end of it—that he did not quite like. But Lester was gazing out at the Elks Temple with an expression of gentle and apparently sincere interest, and Walter concluded that he had imagined it. Lester had always been a quiet kid. Artistic. Probably he had been brooding about something artistic.

"Now that," said Walter, slowing the car, "is the new Carnegie Library. Cost a hundred and sixty thousand dollars. Got eleven thousand books in it. And over there's the Methodist church. I'm a Presbyterian myself, but you've got to hand it to the Methodists, they put up a dandy building. Organ come all the way from Philadelphia. Say, do you still—I mean, are you a churchgoing man, Les?"

"Not especially."

"Well, I don't know as I'd hold that against a fellow. Lot of fine men aren't. Still, it's good for business. A man's got to belong."

---

The bungalow on Fernwood Terrace was exactly like the bungalows on either side of it, except that it was painted cream instead of gray-green, and had a pergola, which was considered in Fernwood Terrace to be very artistic and slightly daring. It had a living room with a fumed-oak davenport, a Victrola, a reading lamp with a shade of beaded silk, a set of the Book of Knowledge in a glass-fronted case, a framed reproduction of a painting of a stag at sunset, and a radio set, with a loudspeaker shaped like a morning-glory, on which Walter had once received, at two in the morning, a station in Havana.

"Havana, Cuba," he told his cousin. "Clear as a bell. Some fellow talking Spanish. Couldn't understand a word, of course, but think of it! Havana! Right here in my own living room!"

Myrtle Ebbing came in from the kitchen, wiping her hands on her apron and then hastily taking off the apron, as though she had been caught in some indecency. She was a plump, anxious, kind woman who had been pretty at twenty and was still pretty in the dim light of the reading lamp. She shook hands with Lester and said she had heard so much about him and she certainly hoped he liked pot roast, because that was what they were having, and she certainly hoped it wasn't too plain for him after all those fancy foreign places.

"I've eaten a great many meals in Paris," said Lester, "that I'd trade gladly for a good pot roast."

Myrtle flushed with pleasure, and Walter, who had been watching his cousin with the suspicion of a man who has been sold a bad lot of carburetors, relaxed again.

The children were produced. There was Harold, who was sixteen and had a pompadour and a ukulele and a passionate conviction that his parents were the most old-fashioned people in the United States. And there was Dorothy, who was twelve and stared at Lester with frank fascination, because she had been told he was an Artist, and she had expected him to have a mustache that curled up at the ends.

"Do you paint ladies without any clothes on?" she asked.

"Dorothy!" cried her mother.

"Sometimes," said Lester gravely. "But mostly I paint fruit. Fruit is less trouble. It doesn't want to be paid, and it doesn't talk."

Dorothy considered this, decided it was a joke, and laughed. Harold looked at his uncle (for so he had been instructed to call him, though the relation was more remote) with sudden respect. A man who painted ladies without any clothes on, and could say so in front of Mother, was a man of some consequence.

---

At dinner Walter talked. He talked about the Thermo-King Automatic Furnace, which had a thermostat that regulated itself, so that a man did not have to go down cellar in his nightshirt at three o'clock on a January morning and shake down the clinkers, which was, he observed, a real step forward in civilization, a bigger step forward, if you wanted his opinion, than any number of these Bolshevik notions they were always talking about in Europe. He talked about the Rotary Club and the fine bunch of fellows in it, live wires, men who did things. He talked about the Volstead Act, which he supported on principle and violated in practice, and about the price of lots in the new Glenwood Heights addition, and about the Republican party, and about a fellow named Swanson who had cheated him on a deal in 1919 and whom he had nevertheless forgiven, since you couldn't hold a grudge in business.

Lester listened. He listened with his head a little on one side, the way he had listened as a boy to the whippoorwills at dusk, and he ate Myrtle's pot roast with every appearance of enjoyment, and now and then he said "Really?" or "I see," or "That's remarkable," and Walter, warmed by the pot roast and by the sound of his own voice, decided that his cousin was a pretty good scout after all, even if he was a little quiet, and that maybe all those years among foreigners had not ruined him entirely.

It was only toward the end of the meal, over Myrtle's lemon meringue pie, that Walter thought to ask, "Well, Les, and what about you? How's the painting game? Making a good thing out of it?"

There was a pause, and in the pause the clock on the mantel, a Seth Thomas with Westminster chimes, struck the half hour.

"It goes along," said Lester.

"Sell many pictures?"

"Some."

"What do they bring? Ballpark figure. A good picture, I mean. Say a big one. Oil."

"It depends," said Lester. "Sometimes several hundred dollars. Sometimes nothing at all."

"Nothing at all! Well, I'll be darned. How do you figure overhead in a line like that?"

Lester smiled. It was a curious smile, and Walter could not read it, and the not reading it made him obscurely uneasy, as he was uneasy in the presence of the Episcopal rector, and the president of the Second National, and the one Negro physician in Vandalia Springs, who had attended Harvard.

"I don't figure it," said Lester. "That's probably my trouble."

---

After dinner, while Myrtle washed up and refused all help with the cheerful martyrdom of the American housewife, and Harold went off to a dance at the Masonic Hall in a raccoon coat that his father had bought him against his better judgment, and Dorothy was sent protesting to bed, the two cousins sat on the front porch in the dark.

It was a fine night in early October. The elms along Fernwood Terrace were turning, and the smell of burning leaves came up from the gutters, where the householders had raked them in neat, smoldering piles, and somewhere down the block a radio was playing "Valencia," and somewhere farther off a dog was barking with the steady, unhurried conviction of a dog that has nothing else to do. Walter lit a cigar, a Flor de Melba, and offered one to his cousin, who declined and lit one of his own cigarettes instead, from a flat silver case that had a crest on it and that Walter suspected, with a small thrill, had once belonged to a duke.

For a while neither of them said anything. Then Walter, with the air of a man taking a plunge into cold water, said, "Les, I want to ask you something. Man to man."

"Go ahead."

"You remember that time out by Pickerel Slough? With the dead muskrat? When we swore we'd never settle down in a hick town?"

Lester laughed softly in the dark. "I'd forgotten that. Yes. Yes, I remember."

"Well." Walter cleared his throat. "Well, I just wanted to say. I guess you figure I broke that. Settling down here, and all. I guess you figure Vandalia Springs is just a—just a hick town. Like Kettle Creek, only bigger."

"Walt, I didn't—"

"No, now, hold on. Let me say my say. I know how you fellows talk back East. I read the magazines. I know what they say about towns like this. Boosters. Babbling about population and lots and so on. And I'll tell you something, Les, sometimes I lie awake nights and I think, maybe they're right. Maybe I am just a—" He waved the cigar helplessly. "A furnace salesman. Selling furnaces to fellows who'd be just as warm with the old kind. Going to Rotary and singing songs and slapping backs. And I think, there's old Les, over in Paris, France, painting pictures and drinking wine with counts and baronesses and I don't know what all, living the way a man ought to live, free, and here's me, forty-four years old and I've never even been to New York City. Not once. I had a chance in 'twenty-two, the convention was there, but Dorothy had the measles."

He stopped, appalled at himself. He had not meant to say any of this. He had not, so far as he knew, ever thought any of it, not in so many words. It had simply come out of him, the way a cough comes out of a man who did not know he had a cold.

Lester was quiet for so long that Walter began to be afraid he had offended him. Then his cousin said, very low, "Walt, do you know where I live in New York?"

"Why, no. Some studio, I suppose. Greenwich Village, isn't it?"

"I live in one room on West Fourteenth Street. Over a delicatessen. It smells of pickled herring from six in the morning until midnight. The radiator works two days in five. I share a bathroom with a Polish tailor and a man who plays the trombone in a dance hall and comes home at four. I haven't sold a picture in fourteen months. I make my living, such as it is, drawing ladies' corsets for the Sunday supplement of a newspaper. Very lifelike corsets. I'm considered rather good at them."

"Corsets," said Walter faintly.

"And the counts and baronesses—well, there was one baroness. She was from Cleveland. She'd married a Hungarian who turned out to be a waiter. She borrowed three hundred francs from me and I never saw her again." Lester drew on his cigarette, and in the brief glow of it Walter saw his face, and it was a face that Walter would remember a long time, though he could never afterward have said why. "I came out here, Walt, because the man I work for told me to take two weeks off without pay, because business was slow. And I had nowhere else to go. And I thought—I thought I'd like to see somebody who knew me before."

The radio down the block had stopped playing "Valencia" and begun, after a burst of static, to broadcast a lecture on the cultivation of soybeans.

"And I'll tell you something else," said Lester. "I've been sitting at your table tonight and looking at your wife and your kids and your car and your—your radio set, and listening to you talk about your furnaces, and I've been thinking that you're the one who got it right. You've got a place. You belong somewhere. People know your name when you walk down the street."

"Well, sure they know my name. I'm on the Program Committee."

"I've never been on a Program Committee in my life."

Walter considered this. It seemed to him a fact of enormous and terrible significance, like learning that a man had never been baptized.

"Les," he said at last, "I tell you what. You stay here. Stay a while. As long as you want. Myrtle won't mind, she likes you, I can tell. And look here, I've been thinking. We need a fellow to do the art work on the Thermo-King ads in the Clarion. Right now we just use the cuts the company sends out, and they're no good, they show a furnace in a cellar in Massachusetts or someplace, with a fellow in a smoking jacket, and nobody out here wears a smoking jacket. What we need is a local touch. A fellow who knows the people. And you could do portraits, too. Why, old Judge Kittredge has been wanting his portrait done for the courthouse for years. And there's the Rotary—we could get you in the Rotary, easy. They've got a classification open for Fine Arts. Nobody's ever filled it."

He turned to his cousin eagerly, his pink face shining in the light from the parlor window, and for a moment Lester Pruitt looked at him with an expression of the most profound and tender horror.

Then he laughed. He laughed until he coughed, and Walter, after a moment's bewilderment, laughed too, without knowing why, slapping his knee, and the two of them sat there on the porch of the cream-colored bungalow on Fernwood Terrace, two middle-aged men laughing in the dark like boys beside Pickerel Slough, while the smoke of the burning leaves drifted past them and the soybean lecture droned on.

"I'll think about it, Walt," said Lester, wiping his eyes. "I'll honestly think about it."

"You do that. You do that. No hurry. Sleep on it."

---

Later, in the twin bed beside Myrtle's (they had gone over to twin beds in 1923, on the advice of an article in the Ladies' Home Journal, and Walter had never been sure whether he liked it), Walter lay awake and stared at the ceiling, on which the streetlight threw the shadow of an elm branch.

"Myrtle," he said. "You awake?"

"Mm."

"Les is all right. Isn't he? Kind of a sad bird, but all right."

"He's very nice, Walter. Very refined."

"I offered him a job. Doing the ads."

"That was sweet of you."

"He won't take it, I guess." Walter was silent a moment. "Myrtle, you ever think we ought to go to New York? Just for a trip. See the shows. Go up the Woolworth Building."

"Why, Walter Ebbing. Whatever for?"

He did not know whatever for. He lay there and tried to think of a reason, and he could not think of one, except that he had seen his cousin's face for a moment in the glow of a cigarette, and that face had been lonelier than any face he had ever seen, and yet he had envied it. He had envied it terribly. He could not have said what he envied.

"Oh, nothing," he said. "Just a notion."

And presently, because he had a breakfast meeting of the Furnace Dealers' Association at seven-thirty, and because he was to speak on "Thermostatic Control: The Coming Thing," and because a man had to keep up, had to be on his toes, had to belong, he turned over and went to sleep, and dreamed that he was standing at the top of the Woolworth Building, selling furnaces to a crowd of Hungarian waiters, all of whom wore smoking jackets, and none of whom could understand a word he said.

The house of Mr. Lowell T. Pettibone, on Crestmere Drive in the Ridgewood Park section of the city of Monarch, was in every respect what a house ought to be in the year when Monarch passed the two-hundred-and-fifty-thousand mark and the Chamber of Commerce paid for a banner across Grand Avenue to say so. It was of tapestry brick, with a sun-parlor at one end and a sleeping-porch above, and it had a breakfast nook which Mrs. Pettibone had seen in a magazine and which nobody had ever eaten breakfast in. It had a radio cabinet of genuine walnut veneer, a player-piano with forty-one rolls, a vacuum cleaner that sounded like an aeroplane, and in the living room a fireplace in which no fire had been built since the evening of the Pettibones' housewarming, when the damper had been closed and the guests had been smoked out onto the lawn, laughing heartily and saying it was a great joke on Lowell.

It was a house of standardized comfort, and Mr. Pettibone was its standardized master. He was forty-three, a little thick at the belt, a little thin at the crown, and he sold real estate. He did not call it selling real estate. He called it Building Monarch, and at the weekly luncheon of the Monarch Go-Ahead Club he had once said, to considerable applause, that the realtor was the true pioneer of the twentieth century, blazing trails not with the axe but with the plat-map.

On this particular Thursday in October he came home at six-ten, which was eleven minutes later than usual, because he had stopped at the Velox Motor Company to look at the new Velox Eight Sport Sedan, which he did not intend to buy and which he had been looking at for three weeks. He came up the cement walk whistling "Smile, Darn Ya, Smile" and feeling a good deal like a Captain of Industry, for that afternoon he had disposed of the last two lots in the Willowbrook Addition, down by the river flats, to a man named Gus Brunnemeyer, who ran a bakery on the South Side and who wished to rise in the world.

There had been a small matter, in the selling of those lots, of the river. In April the river had a habit of coming up over the flats and remaining there, sullen and brown, until about the middle of May. Mr. Pettibone had not mentioned this to Gus Brunnemeyer. Mr. Brunnemeyer had not asked. Mr. Pettibone had, indeed, spoken a good deal about the Wonderful Opportunity of the South Extension and the New Boulevard which the city council was Practically Certain to put through, and Mr. Brunnemeyer had signed, and Mr. Pettibone had shaken his hand with real warmth and called him Gus, and had felt that he was a fine, simple, honest sort of fellow, the backbone of the country.

So Lowell Pettibone came home whistling.

He hung his hat on the hall-tree, he flung his topcoat over the newel-post because his wife always told him not to, and he called out, "Hello, everybody! The old man's home! Where's the bunch?"

His wife came out of the kitchen. Mrs. Pettibone, whose name was Myrtle and who had been the prettiest girl in the Junior Class at Monarch Central High School, was now plump and anxious and given to sighing. She wore an apron over her blue foulard, and her face had the expression which Mr. Pettibone had learned, through sixteen years of matrimony, to associate with Trouble About the Children.

"Lowell," she said, "you've got to speak to Buddy."

"Huh? What's he done now?"

"He's taken money. Out of your bureau. Out of the little china pig on your bureau."

Mr. Pettibone stood still. His whistle died on his lips. He said, "Taken money? Buddy has?"

"Fifty cents. Two quarters. Mrs. Kneedler telephoned me—she said she saw him at the Rexall store treating the Kneedler twins and that Hoffmeier boy to ice-cream sodas, and buying jawbreakers and licorice whips and one of those little tin cricket things that go *click*, and she said she thought I'd want to know, and of course, oh, of course she would have to be the one that saw it, you know how she is, she'll have it all over the Wednesday Afternoon Bridge Club by next week, and I went up and looked in the pig and it was all gone except a nickel and three pennies, and I asked him and he just stood there and wouldn't say anything, and Lowell, I just don't know what to *do* with that child, he's only seven, and when I think of—"

"All right, all right, all right! Now don't get all worked up. I'll handle it. Where is he?"

"He's up in his room. I sent him up there. He's been crying."

"Well, he darn well ought to be crying," said Mr. Pettibone, and was surprised to hear that his voice had become loud and heavy, the voice of a Father, the voice he had heard his own father use, back in Turnbull Falls, on the occasion when Lowell had shot out the window of the Lutheran church with an air-rifle.

He went into the living room and sat down in his own chair, the big mohair chair with the smoking-stand beside it, and he lit a cigar, and he considered.

It was, he felt, a serious matter. It was the most serious matter that had come up in the family since Junie, who was now fourteen, had been discovered using lipstick. A thief! His own son! The son for whom he had already taken out an endowment policy that would mature at the age of twenty-one and send the boy to the State University, where he would join a good fraternity and make Contacts! There rose in Mr. Pettibone's mind, unbidden, a picture of Buddy at thirty-five, unshaven, in a striped suit, being led into the county jail by Sheriff Haupt, who belonged to the Go-Ahead Club and would be extremely embarrassed. He shook his head to clear it.

The question was: should he lick him?

Mr. Pettibone's own father had believed in licking. Old Amos Pettibone had kept a razor-strop hanging behind the kitchen door, and he had applied it to Lowell's person, by Lowell's later reckoning, something over two hundred times between the ages of five and fourteen, and Lowell had turned out all right. He frequently said so. "I got licked plenty when I was a kid, and it never hurt me any," he would say at the Go-Ahead luncheons, "and these modern parents that let their kids run hog-wild—well, I'm not saying anything, but you look at the jails." And the other Go-Aheaders would nod and say "You said it, Lowell," and "That's the stuff."

But Mrs. Pettibone took a magazine called *The Modern Parent*, and she had left it, open, on the smoking-stand on several occasions, and Mr. Pettibone had read in it, while waiting for dinner, an article by a Professor of Child Psychology at a large Eastern university, who said that corporal punishment produced Inhibitions and Complexes, and that the wise parent would instead Reason with the child, appealing to his Better Nature and Sense of Fair Play. Mr. Pettibone had snorted at the article. He had said that these college professors had never met a payroll. But he had read it twice, and it had remained with him, for he had a profound respect for anything that was printed and that came from the East.

Moreover, he did not, in fact, much like the idea of licking Buddy. Buddy was small for his age, and freckled, and had a way of looking up at you, with his mouth a little open, as though you were the greatest man in the world, which Mr. Pettibone had come to depend upon more than he knew.

He decided he would have a Talk with him. A real man-to-man talk. He would make it clear to the boy, in terms the boy could understand, the importance of Honesty in the modern world. He had, he reflected with satisfaction, a certain gift for that sort of thing. It was he who had given the talk on "Service Before Self" at the Go-Ahead Club's Ladies' Night, and the president of the Monarch Savings and Trust had come up afterward and said, "Lowell, that was a corker."

He knocked the ash off his cigar, rose, pulled down his vest, and called up the stairs, "Buddy! Come down here. I want to see you in the library."

The library was a small room off the living room which contained a desk at which Mr. Pettibone never wrote anything, a leather couch, a framed photograph of the Monarch Go-Ahead Club at the District Convention in Sioux City, and a glass-fronted bookcase holding a set of Dickens in maroon morocco, a set of the World's Great Orations, an Encyclopedia of Business Correspondence, and four novels about the Canadian Northwest. Mr. Pettibone had read two of the novels about the Canadian Northwest.

Buddy came down the stairs one step at a time, holding onto the banister as though it were the rail of a ship in a storm. He was in his blue sailor suit, which was wrinkled, and there were damp tracks down both his cheeks, and he had a licorice stain on his collar, which was evidence. He came into the library and stood by the door, and he did not look up at his father as though his father were the greatest man in the world. He looked at the rug.

"Shut the door, son," said Mr. Pettibone, in the voice.

Buddy shut the door.

Mr. Pettibone sat down at the desk, swiveled the chair around, folded his hands over his stomach, and looked at his son for a long moment in silence, which was a technique he employed with prospects who were hesitating over a down-payment.

"Well, Buddy," he said at last, "I guess you know what I want to talk to you about."

Buddy said nothing.

"Your mother tells me that you took some money out of Daddy's pig. Is that right?"

Buddy said, to the rug, "Yes, sir."

"How much?"

"Two quarters."

"Fifty cents. Fifty cents!" Mr. Pettibone shook his head slowly. "Now, Buddy, I want you to understand something. I'm not mad at you. Daddy's not mad. But Daddy is—well, Daddy is mighty disappointed. Mighty disappointed. You know what it's called, son, when you take money that doesn't belong to you?"

Buddy's lower lip began to move independently of the rest of his face. "Stealing," he said.

"That's right. That's exactly right. Stealing. And you know what happens to people who steal?"

"They go to jail."

"They go to jail," Mr. Pettibone agreed, gravely. He felt that the interview was going very well. The professor in *The Modern Parent* would have had nothing to complain of. "But that's not the main thing, Buddy. That's not the worst of it. The worst of it is, nobody can *trust* 'em. Now, you take a fellow in business. You take your Daddy. What do you suppose is the most important thing a man in business has got? More important than money? More important than a fine house and a big car and all?"

Buddy considered. He was, his teachers at the Ridgewood Park Grammar School said, a thoughtful child. "A Velox Eight?" he offered.

"No! No, no. I said more important than a car. It's his *word*, Buddy. His word. A man's word is his bond. You ever hear that? A man's word is his bond. That means when a man in business says a thing, folks know it's so. They know they can depend on him. You take your Daddy. When your Daddy tells a fellow something, that fellow knows Lowell Pettibone is telling him the straight goods. That's why folks come to Daddy when they want to buy a lot or a house. That's why we can have this nice house and you can have a nice room and a bicycle next summer, maybe, if you're a good boy. Because folks trust Daddy. You see?"

Buddy looked up from the rug for the first time. There was something in his face which Mr. Pettibone took for dawning comprehension.

"Is that a man's word," said Buddy, "what you said on the telephone?"

"Huh? What telephone?"

"On Sunday. When you were telephoning Mr. Brunny—Mr. Brunnymire. In the hall. You said those lots were high and dry as a church steeple. And then you hung up and you said to Mama, 'If that Dutchman ever sees 'em in April he'll think he bought a duck pond,' and Mama said 'Hush, Lowell, the children,' and you laughed."

There was a pause in the library. Outside, on Crestmere Drive, a Velox Six went by with its cut-out open, and somewhere down the block the Kneedlers' radio was playing a saxophone selection from the Hotel Belvidere in Chicago.

Mr. Pettibone uncrossed his legs and crossed them the other way.

"Now, see here, Buddy," he said. "That's—that's a different thing entirely. That's business. You're too young to understand about business. When you're older you'll understand. A fellow in business has got to—well, he's got to present his proposition in the best light. That's just salesmanship. Everybody does it. Mr. Brunnemeyer, he's a grown man, he's got eyes in his head, he could've asked anybody. Why, the Lord knows Gus Brunnemeyer has sold plenty of day-old bread for fresh in his time, I'll bet a dollar on that. That's just the way things are done. It's not the same as—as going into somebody's pig and—"

"But it was *your* pig," said Buddy.

"What's that got to do with it?"

"Mr. Brunnymire's money was *his* money," Buddy explained, patiently, as to a slow pupil, "and you took it, and you got it. And your money was your money, and I took it, and I got it. And I gave Albert and Elmer Kneedler a soda, and Fritzie Hoffmeier a soda, so it wasn't even all for me. You said at Sunday school picnic we should *share*."

"I never said any such thing at the Sunday school picnic. That was Reverend Gossage said that."

"You said 'Amen,'" said Buddy.

Mr. Pettibone got up from the desk chair. He was aware that his face had become red and that something had gone wrong with the interview, as sometimes in the middle of a sale a prospect would suddenly ask about the sewer assessments. He walked to the window and looked out at Crestmere Drive, at the row of tapestry-brick bungalows and Dutch Colonials with their identical lawns and their identical porch-swings and their identical concrete birdbaths, and he felt, for a moment, a vague and terrible loneliness, as though there were nobody in all that row of houses to whom he could explain anything.

Then he rallied. He was a Go-Aheader. He had been in tight corners before.

"Buddy," he said, turning, "you listen to me. I don't want to hear any more back-talk. There's a whole lot of difference between what grown folks do in business and what a little boy does in his Daddy's bureau, and someday you'll see it, and when you do you'll thank me. Grown men have got—well, they've got obligations. They've got families to support. They've got to keep up with things. Now, the point is, you took money that wasn't yours, without asking, and you lied about it—"

"I didn't lie. I didn't say anything."

"Well, you—you *concealed* it. That's the same as lying. And I'm not going to have it. I'm not going to have a boy of mine growing up to be a—a crook. You hear me? Now, I'm going to tell you what's going to happen. You're going to go without your dessert tonight, and there's chocolate layer cake, too. And you're not going to the Bijou on Saturday afternoon, Hoot Gibson or no Hoot Gibson. And you're going to pay that fifty cents back out of your allowance, a nickel a week, for ten weeks. And you're going to go over to Mrs. Kneedler's tomorrow and tell her you're sorry."

"What for? I didn't take *her* money."

"Because she—because she saw you. Never mind why! Because I say so, that's why! Now you go on upstairs and think about what you've done, and I don't want to hear another peep out of you tonight."

Buddy looked at his father for a long moment. Then his face crumpled, and the tears came again, but silently, which was worse than if he had howled; and he turned and opened the door and went out, and Mr. Pettibone heard him going up the stairs, one step at a time.

Mr. Pettibone sat down on the leather couch. His cigar had gone out. He relit it, and it tasted like burnt rope, and he put it down.

"Well, I gave it to him straight," he said aloud, to the photograph of the Go-Ahead Club at Sioux City. "Somebody's got to teach him. Can't let a kid get away with a thing like that." The Go-Aheaders, in their rows, with their badges and their paper hats, smiled back at him and said nothing.

At dinner, which was pot roast with brown gravy and mashed potatoes and creamed onions and Waldorf salad and the chocolate layer cake, Mrs. Pettibone said, "Well? What did you do?" and Mr. Pettibone said, "I handled it," with such finality that she did not ask again; and Junie, who was fourteen and knew everything, said, "I bet he licked him," and Mr. Pettibone said, "I did not lick him, and you mind your own business, young lady," and Junie said, "Well, *goodness*," and tossed her bobbed head. Mr. Pettibone ate two helpings of pot roast, but only one of cake, and he did not enjoy it. Twice during the meal he began to say something about Gus Brunnemeyer and the lots in Willowbrook, which he had been looking forward all afternoon to telling, and twice he stopped.

After dinner he read the evening *Monarch Advocate-Times*: an editorial on the menace of radicalism in the colleges, a column of humorous verse about golf, the market report, and an advertisement for the Willowbrook Addition, Monarch's Coming Residential Paradise, Where Your Dollar Grows While You Sleep, which he had written himself and of which he had been proud. He found that he was reading the advertisement for the third time.

At ten o'clock he went upstairs. He paused outside Buddy's door. He did not mean to go in. He went in.

Buddy was asleep, curled up on his side, with one fist under his chin and the tin cricket clutched in the other. His face, in the light from the hall, looked smaller than it did in the daytime, and younger, and there were still marks on it where the tears had dried. On the chair beside the bed his sailor suit was folded with a terrible, conscientious neatness, as though he had been trying to make up for something.

Mr. Pettibone stood there for some time. He wanted to say something, but there was nobody awake to say it to, and he was not sure what it was. He had a confused notion that it would have something to do with April, and the river, and a fat, trusting baker with flour in the creases of his knuckles who had called him Mr. Pettibone all through the signing and had thanked him at the end. He thought, perhaps, that he might call Gus Brunnemeyer in the morning. He might say—well, he might say that the boulevard was not quite so certain after all. That there was some question about drainage. That if Gus wanted to reconsider—

He bent down and very gently took the tin cricket out of his son's hand and put it on the bureau. Then he picked it up again and put it back on the pillow, near the small fist, where it could be found in the morning.

He went out to the sleeping-porch, where the October air was sharp and smelled of burning leaves, and he lay for a long while looking up at the screen, and he thought about being an honest man, and about Turnbull Falls, and the razor-strop, and his own father, who had once sold a blind horse to a Swede and laughed about it at supper for a week; and he did not sleep until nearly midnight.

In the morning it was raining. The coffee was strong, and the toast came up out of the electric toaster at precisely the right moment, and Buddy came down to breakfast and said "Good morning, Daddy," in a small voice, and Mr. Pettibone said "Good morning, old-timer," and rumpled his hair, and everything was all right. He drove downtown in the rain, behind the beat of the windshield wiper, and by the time he had passed the new Second National Bank building, with its eighteen stories of glazed terra cotta, the night's confusion had grown faint and slightly ridiculous, like a dream about falling. Gus Brunnemeyer was a grown man. Everybody did it. That was business.

He did not telephone Gus Brunnemeyer.

At the Go-Ahead luncheon that noon, in the Gold Room of the Hotel Thornbury, between the cream of tomato soup and the chicken à la king, he told the story to the table, and he told it well.

"So the kid looks me right in the eye," he said, "and he says, 'But Dad, Mr. Brunnemeyer's money was *his* money, and you got it!' Seven years old!

Here is an excerpt of Sinclair Lewis's writing, to show you their style:

The assurance of Tanis Judique’s friendship fortified Babbitt’s self-approval. At the Athletic Club he became experimental. Though Vergil Gunch was silent, the others at the Roughnecks’ Table came to accept Babbitt as having, for no visible reason, “turned crank.” They argued windily with him, and he was cocky, and enjoyed the spectacle of his interesting martyrdom. He even praised Seneca Doane. Professor Pumphrey said that was carrying a joke too far; but Babbitt argued, “No! Fact! I tell you he’s got one of the keenest intellects in the country.
