Mr. Harvey J. Wetherbee, of the Wetherbee Hot-Air Furnace and Sanitary Heating Company, had come home on that Thursday in October expecting the reward of a man who has sold three furnaces before noon. He meant to have his pork chops, read the editorial in the *Evening Clarion* on the menace of the Non-Partisan League, and then perhaps, if Lulu was agreeable and the radiator in the sun-parlor quit its knocking, run the car down to the Bijou to see the new William S. Hart. He had worked up, on the drive home through Sylvan Knolls, a fine contented glow, the glow of a man who is a member of the Live Wires' Luncheon Club, the Elks, and the First Methodist, and who has paid on his house all but four thousand dollars.

He found instead his wife standing in the front hall, in the manner of a sentry who has been posted against the Hun.

"Harvey, I want you to go right up-stairs and speak to Chester."

"Huh? Why? What's he done? Gosh, can't a man get his coat off before—"

"He's taken fifty cents out of my purse. Out of my black purse, the one I keep on the hall-tree. And bought candy with it, and one of those horrid cap-pistols, and when I asked him, he lied to me. He looked me right square in the face and lied. Now I've done all I can do. It's for his father to handle."

Mr. Wetherbee hung up his coat with a deliberation which he hoped was paternal and grave. He had, in his eight years as a father, attended chiefly to the profitable and decorative aspects of the profession: the buying of tricycles, the exhibition of Chester's report-card to men at the Live Wires, the anecdote (told at least forty times) of how Chester at the age of three had called the minister "Mister Preacher-Man." The punitive department he had left, on the whole, to Lulu, who was home all day and had, he considered, more of a knack for it. But he understood that this was a Crisis. He felt it in his stomach, a cold and important feeling, such as he experienced when the bank called him in about his note.

"Well, now," he said. "Well, now. I'll attend to it. Yes, sir, I'll certainly attend to it. You leave this to me."

"I hope you will attend to it. And don't you go and get soft with him the way you always do, and end up taking him out for an ice-cream soda."

"Who? Me? Soft? Say, when did I ever—"

"Last spring. The time with the Kramer boy's wagon."

"Well, that was different. That was a— That wasn't the same thing at all. Now, you just let me handle this. I know a thing or two about boys, I guess. I was a boy once myself, wasn't I?"

Mrs. Wetherbee did not commit herself on this question. She went into the kitchen, and Mr. Wetherbee heard her say to Hilda, the maid, in the bright voice which women use for maids and which is intended to be overheard by husbands, "Well, Mr. Wetherbee is going to talk to Chester."

He did not go up-stairs at once. He went, rather, into the room which he called his den, a small chamber off the living-room furnished with a Mission rocker, a cabinet of cigars, a photograph of the Live Wires at their 1919 Outing (Mr. Wetherbee was second from the left in the third row, wearing a paper hat), a set of the Little Masterpieces of Literature in limp leather which had come with a subscription to the *American Home Monthly*, and a pennant from the State University, which Mr. Wetherbee had attended for one year and a half. Here he stood, rubbing his chin, and he felt the need of a Method.

He was a man who believed in Methods. He had a Method for selling furnaces (you began by asking the prospect whether he loved his kiddies, and then you spoke of drafts), a Method for remembering names (you associated Mr. Herzog with a hare's dog), a Method for keeping fit (deep breathing at the open window, done twice that year). It came to him that among the magazines on the stand beside the davenport there was a booklet which Lulu had sent for, called *Firm Hands and Fond Hearts: Practical Talks to the Twentieth-Century Father*, by Dr. Orrin P. Gage, A.M., Ph.D., Lecturer in Child Psychology at the Chautauqua Normal Institute. He found it under a seed catalogue. He sat in the Mission rocker and opened it, with the respect a man feels for a book written by somebody with three degrees and a middle initial.

"The modern father," Dr. Gage observed, "must be at once the comrade and the judge of his little man. Let him never chastise in anger. Let him first ascertain the Motive. Let him appeal to the child's natural instinct for Fair Play, which is the very bedrock of American institutions. A quiet talk, man to man, will often accomplish more than a hundred spankings."

"That's the stuff," said Mr. Wetherbee. "That's the dope. Man to man. That's what I always say."

He read on a little, but the next chapter dealt with the Adolescent Period and certain Dangers on which Dr. Gage became so delicate as to be unintelligible, and Mr. Wetherbee, flushing slightly, closed the book. He stood up. He threw out his chest, as he did when he rose to report for the Membership Committee at the Live Wires. He went up the stairs, slowly, each tread creaking under his hundred and ninety pounds, and with each creak he felt more like a judge and less like a man who wanted his pork chops.

Chester's room was at the end of the hall, a small room papered with a design of ducks in blue bonnets, which Mrs. Wetherbee had selected when Chester was an infant and which Chester now loathed with the whole strength of his seven years. The boy was sitting on the edge of his bed. He was a thin child, all knees and ears and freckles, with a cowlick which no application of water could subdue, and he was looking at the floor with that profound and suspicious interest in carpets which is displayed by children, defendants, and men who have been asked to make a speech.

On the bureau, where it had evidently been placed in exile by Mrs. Wetherbee, lay the cap-pistol. It was a magnificent object, nickel-plated, with a pearl (or what is called pearl) handle and the words TEXAS RANGER stamped upon the barrel. Beside it were two rolls of red caps and the wrapper of a Hershey bar.

Mr. Wetherbee shut the door behind him. He did not know quite where to stand. He tried the window, but that put the light behind him and he could not see the boy's face, which Dr. Gage had said was important. He tried the foot of the bed, but there was nothing to do with his hands. Finally he lowered himself into the small white chair before Chester's small white desk, and it was much too small, so that his knees came up and he resembled a large and worried grasshopper.

"Well, Chester," he began.

Chester said nothing.

"Well, Chester, I guess you know what I'm here for."

Chester nodded to the carpet.

"Your mother tells me—" Mr. Wetherbee cleared his throat, and it was a Rotund Throat-Clearing, the kind with which he opened the monthly meeting of the Sylvan Knolls Improvement Association. "Your mother tells me you took fifty cents out of her purse. Now I want you to tell me, man to man, is that so or isn't it so?"

There was a pause of such length that Mr. Wetherbee could hear, from the kitchen below, the spit of the pork chops in the pan, and he was enraged by it, as though the pork chops were mocking him.

"I just borrowed it," said Chester.

"Borrowed it! Borrowed it! Did you ask anybody?"

"No, sir."

"Then you didn't borrow it! When you take something without asking, that isn't borrowing! I'll tell you what that is! That's—" He stopped. The word *stealing* had arrived in his mouth with an ugliness which startled him; it was not a word one used about a boy who had been, only last June, a Lamb in the Sunday-School pageant. "That's—well, it's taking, that's what it is. And then on top of that, you told your mother a fib about it! You went and told her you didn't."

"I was scared."

"Scared! Well, now, that's no excuse! Do you think I go around telling fibs every time I'm scared? Do you think if a fellow down at the office, if a prospect asks me a question, and I get scared he won't buy, I go and tell him a fib? No, sir! You can't do business that way! Honesty is— Why, honesty is the whole foundation of American business, and the fellow that doesn't understand that is going to get left at the post every time! Why, do you know what the Live Wires have got printed up right over the speakers' table at the Hotel Pemberton? 'Square Dealing Is Our Middle Name.' That's what it says. In gold letters. And there isn't a man in that club that doesn't live up to it."

He was pleased with this. It had the right ring. He had very nearly said it, a month before, in a talk to the Junior Chamber on "Pep and Principle," and it had gone over big. He saw that Chester was looking at him now, not at the carpet, and he felt the warm flush of the orator who has got his audience.

"Now, I'm not going to lick you," he went on, more mildly. "Your granddad would have licked me, and licked me good. Out behind the woodshed, back in Bellport, with a strap. Why, one time—" He was suddenly diverted by a pleasant memory. "One time I swiped a watermelon out of old man Tewksbury's patch, and your granddad found out, and say, I couldn't sit down for a week! Cracky! But that was the old-fashioned way. We've got more modern ideas now. We believe in reasoning with a boy. Appealing to his sense of fair play."

"Did you eat it?" said Chester.

"Huh? Eat what?"

"The watermelon."

"Why—sure—that is— That isn't the point! The point is, I got licked for it, and I learned my lesson. That's the point." Mr. Wetherbee perceived that he had, in some manner which he could not trace, lost ground. He shifted on the little chair, which creaked like a hen-house door. "Now, what I want to know, son, is what made you do it. What was your—your Motive?"

Chester considered this word, which was new to him. He studied it as he would have studied a beetle. "I wanted the pistol," he said, at last, simply.

"Well, why didn't you ask for it? Why didn't you come to me and say, 'Dad, I'd like a cap-pistol'? Haven't I always been square with you? Didn't I buy you that Flexible Flyer last Christmas, and the baseball mitt, and that—that Erector set, that cost me eleven dollars, and you never even put it together but once?"

"You said I couldn't have a pistol. You said they were dangerous. You said Mama said."

This was true. Mr. Wetherbee recalled, with a sort of humiliation, that he had said precisely that, three weeks before, at breakfast, while reading the sporting page, in order to get out of a discussion. He had not believed it. He had owned, at the age of seven, an air-rifle, a slingshot, and a Barlow knife with which he had very nearly removed the thumb of Ollie Swenson. But a man had to back up his wife. That was one of the fundamentals. He set his jaw, the jaw which, as Mrs. Wetherbee had once said in the days of their courtship, was "just like a Western hero's," and which had since grown a companion beneath it.

"Well, then! There you are! You knew you weren't supposed to have it, and you went right ahead and got it anyway, and with your mother's money! Now isn't that a fine thing! Isn't that a fine way to treat your mother, that works her fingers to the bone for you!"

He thought of Lulu's fingers, which were plump and had two diamond rings and a sapphire on them, and which had not been to the bone in several years, as Hilda did the heavy work. But it was a thing one said. His own father had said it. All fathers said it. It had about it the solid comfort of a tradition, like the Fourth of July and putting the storm windows up.

Chester's lower lip began to tremble. Mr. Wetherbee saw it, and something in his chest moved uneasily, but he remembered his wife's warning about being soft, and he remembered Dr. Gage, who had said nothing about lips, and he pressed on.

"Now, you're going to give that pistol back. You're going to take it right back to—where'd you get it?"

"Schoenfeldt's."

"Schoenfeldt's! That little Dutch notion-store over on Baxter Avenue? Why, I wouldn't trade with that fellow if he was the last— Well, never mind that. You're going to take it back and get the money and give it to your mother, and you're going to tell her you're sorry. And then, by golly— By gosh— Then you're going to stay in your room every afternoon this week, and no picture-show Saturday, either. That's what's going to happen. You understand me?"

"Schoenfeldt won't take it back," said Chester. "I shot off half a roll."

Mr. Wetherbee had not thought of this. He looked at the pistol on the bureau as though it had been put there by a business rival. It came to him that the price of a cap-pistol was a matter of perhaps thirty-five cents, and that the candy had accounted for the remaining fifteen, and that he was proposing to send his only son, at dusk, through the dangerous traffic of Baxter Avenue, to beg a refund from a man he despised, on a nickel-plated object which had been fired. It also came to him, with a little stab of real-estate shrewdness, that it was a pretty good pistol for thirty-five cents.

"Well— Well, then, you'll pay it back out of your allowance. Ten cents a week, for five weeks. And no candy money for five weeks, either. That's fair, isn't it? Isn't that fair and square?"

Chester said it was fair. He said it with the hopelessness of a man agreeing to the terms of a mortgage.

There was a silence. Mr. Wetherbee felt that the talk had been, on the whole, a success; he had been firm, he had been reasonable, he had not lost his temper, he had appealed to fair play. He was preparing to rise from the little white chair, and was already composing, for the benefit of Lulu, a modest account of how he had "talked to the kid like a Dutch uncle and got the whole thing straightened out," when Chester asked the question.

"Dad, did you ever tell a fib?"

"Me? Why, certainly not! That is— Well, of course, everybody makes a mistake once in a while. When I was a kid, maybe. But a grown man, a business man, he's got to be on the level. He can't afford not to be."

"You told Mr. Gilchrist on the 'phone you were in a meeting. Last Sunday. And you were just reading the funnies."

Mr. Wetherbee opened his mouth and shut it again.

He was not, by any reasonable standard, a dishonest man. He had never stolen anything since the watermelon. He paid his taxes, or nearly all of them, and he had been known to give back excess change to a street-car conductor. But he was suddenly and uncomfortably aware of the day which lay behind him. He recalled that he had told Mrs. Ellsworth Dodd that very morning that the new Wetherbee Sunbeam Pipeless Furnace would "cut her coal bill clean in half," which was not precisely what the factory claimed, and which the factory, indeed, had specifically asked its agents not to say. He recalled that he had told old Mr. Haskins, who wanted a furnace for his daughter's house, that there were "only three left at this price," when there were in the warehouse forty-one. He recalled that he had told the Live Wires at luncheon that he had shot an eighty-eight at the Maple Hills Country Club, and that he had in fact shot ninety-six, with one mulligan. These were not lies. They were—well, they were business. They were salesmanship. They were the sort of thing that every live-wire, up-and-coming, forward-looking man did as a matter of course, and that nobody but a crank or a Socialist or a college professor would call lying. Yet they rose up in the duck-papered room and stood about him like the Bunch at a party where one does not know anyone.

"Now that—" he said heavily. "That's different. That was— When you're grown up, there's a lot of things— When a fellow calls you up on a Sunday— You'll understand when you're older. That's a different kind of thing altogether. That's what you call a—a convention. A social convention. It isn't the same as taking money out of your mother's purse."

"Oh," said Chester.

He did not seem convinced. He looked at his father with an expression of the most terrible fairness, the fairness of Dr. Gage, the fairness of the gold letters at the Hotel Pemberton, and Mr. Wetherbee, under that gaze, felt himself grow hot about the collar.

"Now, don't you go getting smart with me, young man!" he said, more loudly than he had meant. "Don't you go turning this thing around! I'm not the one that's in trouble here! You are! You understand that? You're the one that took the money!"

"Yes, sir."

"All right then."

"Yes, sir."

The lip was trembling again, and this time there was a tear, a single and enormous tear, which rolled down past the freckles and dropped upon the knickerbockers. Mr. Wetherbee looked at it with dismay. It was, for some reason, far worse than the question about Mr. Gilchrist. He remembered Bellport, and the woodshed, and the strap; and he remembered that what had hurt was not the strap but the way his father had not spoken to him for two days afterward, but had passed him at the supper table as though he were a chair. He remembered that he had resolved, at seven, lying on a corn-husk mattress with his face in the pillow, that when he had a boy of his own he would never do like that. He had forgotten the resolve for thirty-five years. It came back to him now, entire, with the very smell of the corn-husks.

"Aw, now," he said. "Aw, now, Chet. Now, don't you go to bawling. Big boy like you."

"I'm n-not bawling."

"No, sure you're not. Sure you're not. Say, look here." He hitched the little chair forward with a horrible scraping and put a large pink hand on the boy's knee. "Look here, old man. I'm not mad at you. Not really mad. It's only— You got to learn, see? A fellow's got to learn these things while he's young. That's all. Your old dad's only trying to help you out. You know that, don't you?"

"Yes, sir."

"Sure you do. Sure you do."

He sat there a moment longer, patting the knee, and from below there came Lulu's voice, high and accusing: "Harvey! Supper's on the table, and the chops are getting cold!"

He rose, with relief and with a great crackling of his joints. At the door he paused and looked back. Chester was still sitting on the edge of the bed, but he was now looking, not at the carpet, but at the cap-pistol on the bureau.

"Five weeks," said Mr. Wetherbee. "Ten cents a week. Don't forget."

"No, sir."

"And you stay up here till you're called." He hesitated. He felt about in his vest pocket, where he kept his loose change and the little gold pencil the Live Wires had given him for securing seventeen new members in one year. He drew out his hand, looked at what was in it, and put it back again, guiltily, as though Lulu had been standing in the hall. "Well," he said. "Well. That's all."

He went down-stairs. Mrs. Wetherbee was at the head of the table, and the pork chops were, as she had prophesied, getting cold.

"Well?" she said.

"Well, I talked to him." He unfolded his napkin with a flourish. "Talked to him man to man. Got right down to the bottom of the whole business. He's going to pay it back, out of his allowance. Ten cents a week. I tell you, Lulu, the trouble with most parents is they don't reason with a kid. They just whale him and let it go at that. You got to appeal to his sense of fair play. That's the modern idea. That's what this Dr. Gage says, and I guess he knows, with all those letters after his name."

"Did you take the pistol away?"

"Huh? The— Why, I—" He reached for the applesauce. "Well, there wasn't any sense in taking it back. It's been shot. Half a roll. Schoenfeldt wouldn't take it. That Dutchman wouldn't give you back a cent if you were dying. So I figured—"

"So you let him keep it."

It was a Sunday afternoon at the end of August, and the fog had come in early. All the morning the sun had lain hot and yellow upon the roofs of Tehama Street, upon the tarred gravel and the leaning chimney-pots, upon the little sheds where the cabinet-makers kept their lumber; but toward three o'clock the wind had begun to blow from the ocean, steadily, monotonously, and with it had come the fog, rolling in over the hills of the Presidio, pouring down into the hollows of the city, smothering the whole vast reach of the town in a gray, damp, impenetrable blanket. From somewhere far off, beyond the wharves, beyond the black hulls of the colliers and the coasting schooners, a fog-horn had commenced to bellow, at long, regular intervals, a hoarse, prolonged lowing, like that of some enormous animal lost in the mist.

In the front room of the second-floor flat over Schreiber's bakery Minna Gorst sat at the window with her sewing in her lap. She was not sewing. The needle, threaded with black cotton, was stuck into the hem of the skirt she had been making over, and her hands, small and red and very clean, lay folded on top of it. She was watching the street. Every now and then she drew her breath quickly, and her lips, which were thin and set close together, moved a little, as though she were counting.

The room was small and very neat. There was a rag carpet upon the floor, and a lounge covered with green rep, and a what-not in the corner upon which stood a china shepherdess, a conch shell, and a photograph of Minna's mother in a frame of plush and gilt. Upon the wall over the lounge hung a steel engraving of the Battle of Gettysburg, and between the windows a canary in a brass cage hopped from perch to perch, and from perch to perch again, uttering at times a thin, querulous chirp. The room smelled of bread. All day long, and all the night through, the warm, heavy, yeasty smell of Schreiber's ovens came up through the floor and through the cracks of the door, so that the very curtains were saturated with it, and Minna had long since ceased to notice it at all.

At a little after four she heard her husband's step upon the stairs.

She knew it at once, for it was like no other step in the house. It was the tread of a big man, a heavy man, deliberate and ponderous, the boards of the staircase complaining under each footfall. Minna did not move. She only sat a little straighter in her chair, and her hands closed upon the skirt in her lap, gathering the cloth into a little wad.

The door opened and Christian Gorst came in.

He was a stevedore on the Mission Street wharf, and he had the build of his calling. He was enormous. His shoulders filled the doorway; his neck was thick and red and corded like the neck of a draught-ox; his hands, hanging at his sides, were huge, hard, knotted, the fingers blunt, the nails broken, the backs of them covered with a coarse, reddish hair. His face was large and flat and slow, the jaw salient, massive, the jaw of the carnivora; and his eyes, small and pale blue, set close under a heavy ridge of brow, had in them the dull, patient, uncomprehending look of an animal that has been worked hard and fed well. He had been drinking a little. Not much. Christian was never drunk. But there was a flush upon his cheek-bones, and he brought with him into the room, through the smell of the bread, a faint, sour odour of beer.

He hung his hat upon the nail behind the door, and stood for a moment looking at his wife. Then he said:

"Well, Minna."

"Well," she answered, without turning her head.

He crossed the room, the floor trembling a little under his weight, and sat down upon the lounge, which creaked. He spread his knees apart and put his hands upon them, and for a long time he said nothing at all. The canary hopped from perch to perch. Far off, beyond the wharves, the fog-horn lowed, and was silent, and lowed again.

"I seen Otto Riemer," said Christian at last.

Minna's lips tightened. "Yes?"

"I seen him down to Kessler's place. We had a glass of beer. Him and me, we got to talking."

"I know what you got to talking."

"Well, then," said Christian heavily, "if you know, why don't you say so? What's the use of all this, then? Say, Minna, look here. You know it's a good thing. You know it is. Riemer's got the lease on the corner at Fourth and Bryant, and the fixtures, and the license is paid up till the first of the year. All he wants is somebody to come in with him, half and half. Three hundred and fifty dollars, he says. That's all. Three hundred and fifty, and I'm a partner. I'm a saloon-keeper, and no more humping sacks of cement off the Oregon boats for six bits a day. Think of that, Minna. Think of it."

"I've thought of it," said Minna.

"Well, then?"

She did not answer. She turned a little in her chair, so that her back was more nearly toward him, and she began to smooth out the wad of cloth in her lap, slowly, carefully, pressing the wrinkles flat with the palms of her hands.

Christian watched her. A slow, dull red began to mount from his collar into his face.

"You got the money," he said.

"It's my money."

"I didn't say it wasn't. I said you got it."

"It's my money," repeated Minna. "I made it. I made every cent of it. I made it sewing for Mrs. Hochmuth and for the Lindquist girls and for that woman on Folsom Street that never paid on time. I made it doing over hats. I made it out of the housekeeping. I made it out of what I didn't eat, and what I didn't wear, and the car fare I didn't spend when I walked to the market and back again. Four years I been making it. It's mine."

She spoke without heat, in a low, even voice, almost in a monotone, and as she spoke her hands went on smoothing the cloth in her lap, round and round, flat and flat.

It was true. In the four years of her marriage Minna Gorst had saved three hundred and eighty-two dollars and forty cents. She knew the sum to the penny. She could have told it at any hour of the day or night, waking or sleeping. It was in gold and silver, in a stout baking-powder tin with a tight lid, and the tin was hidden in the bottom of her trunk in the bedroom, under her wedding dress and her mother's Bible and a bundle of letters tied with a shoe-string. Every Saturday night, when Christian was asleep, she took it out and counted it, piece by piece, by the light of a candle, arranging the gold in little yellow stacks upon the counterpane, and the silver in little white stacks beside it, and touching each one, and counting again. And each Saturday night there was a little more. Twenty cents, fifty cents, a dollar, sometimes two dollars. Once, the week she had made the wedding dress for the Lindquist girl, it had been seven dollars and a half, and she had lain awake the whole night through, trembling, almost sick with happiness, hearing the clink of the coins in her ears long after she had put out the candle.

The money. The money in the baking-powder tin. It had become a part of her. It had grown into her life as a root grows into the crevices of a rock. It was hers—hers—hers.

"I ain't saying it ain't yours," said Christian. "Ain't we married? What's yours is mine, and what's mine is yours, ain't it? Ain't I give you my wages every Saturday, all but what I keep for beer and tobacco? Don't I? Huh? Don't I?"

"You give me your wages to keep the house."

"Well, and you kept back out of it. That's half my money, then, that's in there. More'n half."

Minna turned around in her chair. Her face had gone white, and two little spots of colour burned upon her cheek-bones.

"You don't touch that money," she said. "You hear me, Christian? Not one cent of it. You don't touch it."

"Ah, now, Minna—"

"You don't touch it. It's mine. You'll put it into Otto Riemer's saloon, and Otto Riemer'll drink it up, and you'll help him, and in six months there won't be no saloon and no money and nothing. I know Otto Riemer. I know the kind of him. And I know you."

"What do you know about me?" said Christian. His voice had dropped. He leaned forward upon the lounge, his huge hands gripping his knees.

"I know you'll drink it up."

"I never was drunk in my life."

"You'll drink it up. A glass here and a glass there. You'll stand treat for the boys off the wharf. You'll give credit. You'll be a big man for 'em. And then it'll be gone, and you'll go back to humping cement, and I won't have nothing. Nothing. Four years. Four years, and nothing."

She was breathing quickly. Her hands were clenched upon the skirt. The canary, frightened by her voice, had stopped hopping and clung to the side of its cage, its little head turning sharply from side to side.

Christian sat for a long moment without speaking. The red had spread over all his face now, up to the roots of his coarse yellow hair, and the veins stood out upon his forehead. He was not quick. Ideas came to him slowly, heavily, one at a time, and he turned each one over and over in his mind before he let it go. And now, slowly, laboriously, an idea was coming to him. He had asked his wife for something, and she had refused it. He had asked her for money, and she had said no. And she had said that he would drink it up. Him. Christian Gorst. She had said that.

He got up from the lounge.

He stood for a moment in the middle of the room, his arms hanging, his head thrust a little forward, his small eyes fixed upon her. Minna watched him. She did not move from her chair, but her face had grown whiter still, and her lips had begun to tremble.

"Where is it?" said Christian.

"I won't tell you."

"Where is it? It's in the bedroom. It's in your trunk. I know where it is."

"You won't touch it."

He took a step toward her, and the floor shook. Then another. Minna rose to her feet, letting the skirt fall to the carpet, and backed against the window. Through the glass behind her the fog drifted, gray and thick, so that the houses across the street were no more than shadows, and the gas-lamp at the corner, already lit, made only a dim yellow blur in the mist.

"Christian," she said. "Christian."

He stopped. He was quite close to her now, looming over her, enormous, so that she had to tip back her head to see his face. She was afraid of him. For the first time in four years she was afraid of him. She had seen him angry before—angry at the wharf boss, angry at the landlord, angry once at a Portuguese who had jostled him in a car—but never at her, never like this. And something in his face, something in the thrust of the heavy jaw and the narrowing of the little eyes, something brutal, something primitive, something that seemed to come up out of the very depths of him, frightened her as she had never been frightened before.

It was the animal in the man. It was the brute that lies hidden, coiled and asleep, in the depths of every human creature, under the thin crust of habit and decency and law; the brute that is the inheritance of a thousand generations of savage forbears; the brute that in most men sleeps on undisturbed through all their lives, but that in some, at a word, at a look, at the touch of a woman's refusal, stirs and wakes and stretches, and shows its teeth.

Christian put out his hand and took her by the wrist.

He did not twist it. He did not hurt her. He only held it, his huge fingers closing round it completely, so that her small red hand hung helpless from his grip like a thing caught in a trap. But he held it hard, and she could feel the enormous strength of him, the strength that lifted the cement sacks off the Oregon boats, the strength that could have snapped the bones of her wrist like a dry stick, if he had chosen.

"Let me go," she said.

"You give me that money."

"Let me go, Christian."

"You give it to me. You hear? I'm your husband. You give it to me."

"No."

He shook her. Once, not very hard. Her head jerked back against the window-sash, and the glass rattled in its frame. The canary uttered a sharp little cry and fluttered wildly against the bars of its cage.

"No," said Minna again. Her voice was hardly more than a whisper, but it did not shake now. "No. You can kill me if you want. You can break my arm. But you don't get it. It's mine."

They stood there, face to face, the great hulking man and the little thin-lipped woman, in the narrow front room that smelled of bread, and neither one of them moved. Outside the fog drifted past the window. Down below, in the bakery, someone was rattling the iron doors of the ovens, and the sound came up to them, faint and far away, through the floor. And away off beyond the wharves, beyond the black hulls of the colliers and the schooners, the fog-horn lowed, long, hoarse, prolonged, like the voice of some great beast lost in the mist and calling.

Christian looked down at her. His breath came heavily through his nose, and his little eyes were fixed upon her face. He saw her lips, pressed close and white; he saw the two spots of colour on her cheeks; he saw her eyes, which did not drop before his own, but stared back at him, hard, unwinking, full of a kind of fierce, small, desperate obstinacy, like the eyes of a little animal that has been cornered and will bite.

And slowly, very slowly, he let go of her wrist.

He did not know why. He could not have told. Perhaps it was something in her eyes. Perhaps it was only that he was slow, that the brute in him had waked too late, and found itself, upon waking, confused, bewildered, uncertain what to do. He let her go, and stood back from her a step, and looked at his own hand as though it belonged to someone else.

"Ah, what's the use," he muttered. "What's the use."

Minna did not answer. She stood against the window, rubbing her wrist with her other hand. There was a red mark upon it where his fingers had been, and already it was beginning to turn dark.

Christian turned away from her. He went across the room to the door and took his hat down from the nail behind it, and stood for a moment turning it round and round in his hands.

"I'm going down to Kessler's," he said, without looking at her.

"Go on, then."

"I'm going to tell Riemer it's off."

"Tell him, then."

He put on his hat. He stood a moment longer with his hand on the knob of the door, his great back toward her, his head bowed a little, as though he were thinking, as though some other idea, slow and heavy and confused, were coming to him and he were waiting for it. But it did not come. He opened the door and went out, and closed it behind him, not loudly, and she heard his step going down the stairs—the heavy, deliberate, ponderous step, the boards complaining under each footfall—down and down and down, until the street door banged, and the sound of it died away.

Minna stood motionless by the window for a long time.

Then she crossed the room, stooping on the way to pick up the skirt that had fallen to the carpet, and folding it carefully, and laying it across the back of her chair. She went into the bedroom. It was nearly dark in there, for the one window gave upon the air-shaft, and the fog had made the shaft dim and gray as twilight. She did not light the lamp. She knelt down before the trunk and raised the lid, and felt beneath the wedding dress, beneath her mother's Bible and the bundle of letters tied with a shoe-string, until her fingers closed upon the baking-powder tin.

She took it out and held it in her lap, there on the floor in the half-darkness, and pried off the lid with her thumb-nails. She did not need to count it. She knew to the penny how much was there. But she put her hand into the tin, and let the coins run through her fingers, gold and silver, cold and heavy and smooth, and listened to the little clinking sound they made as they fell. And she felt, as she sat there, a thrill go through her, a strange, keen, almost sensual pleasure, so sharp that it was almost pain. It was all there. Every piece of it. He had not touched it. He had not touched one cent.

Hers. Hers. All hers.

She sat for a long time on the floor of the darkening room, with the tin in her lap, letting the money run through her fingers. Her wrist ached, and once or twice she lifted it and looked at the dark marks upon it, in a puzzled, absent way, as though she did not quite remember how they had come there. Then she put her hand back into the tin. From below came the warm, heavy smell of the bread, and the faint rattle of the oven doors. In the front room the canary, quieted at last, hopped from perch to perch, and from perch to perch again. And far away, beyond the wharves, beyond the colliers and the schooners and the black, cold water of the bay, the fog-horn lowed, and was silent, and lowed again, hoarse, prolonged, unceasing, like the voice of some vast, blind, patient brute, groping its way through the mist toward a thing that it could not see.

It was a little after four o'clock on a Saturday afternoon in the latter part of October when Ambrose Tull, bookkeeper's assistant in the commission house of Gaylord & Wenck, Front Street, came down to the ferry slip at the foot of Market Street to meet his cousin, whom he had not seen in eleven years.

He had been there since half-past three. He had left the office early, by special permission of the head bookkeeper, a dry, yellowish man who had given his consent without lifting his eyes from the ledger. Ambrose had hurried down Front Street in a fever of anticipation, threading his way among the drays and trucks, the hand-carts heaped with crates of onions, the enormous wagons of the produce merchants backed against the sidewalks, and had arrived breathless, his collar wilted, a little cough catching at his throat. Now he stood by one of the iron pillars of the waiting-room, his hat pushed back from his forehead, watching the gates.

The place was thronged. The air was thick with the odours of the bay, of tar, of oakum, of wet planking, and with the smell of the crowd itself, of sweat and of cheap tobacco and of oranges. Newsboys shrilled the evening editions. A peanut-roaster in a corner shrieked continually upon a single exasperating note. Every now and then the floor trembled as a ferry-boat ground against the piles of the slip, and there came a vast clanking of chains and a rumbling of the gangway let down, and then the crowd poured through the gates in a solid mass, a torrent of men and women, hurrying, jostling, crowding one another, their feet making a prodigious shuffling noise upon the boards.

Ambrose was a small man, narrow in the shoulders, with a thin, peaked face and pale eyes, eyes that blinked continually as though the light of day were too much for them. His mustache was sparse and of no particular colour. He wore a suit of black, shiny at the elbows, and on the second finger of his right hand, where the pen rested, was a small ink stain, ineradicable, a mark that no scrubbing removed, so that it had come to be a part of the hand itself. He was thirty-four years old. For eleven years he had sat upon a high stool in the counting-room of Gaylord & Wenck, adding columns of figures relating to hay, barley, potatoes, and wheat, wheat above all, the wheat of the great valleys, which he had never seen growing.

The four-thirty boat came in. The gates opened. The crowd surged forward, and Ambrose, standing on his toes, craned his neck, searching the faces.

All at once he saw him. There was no mistaking him. He towered above the crowd by half a head. He came through the gate like an ox through a flock of sheep, the people falling back from him on either side, and he bore upon his shoulder a carpet-bag that in his grasp seemed no larger than a lunch-pail.

"Ezra!" cried Ambrose. "Ezra! Here! This way!"

The giant turned his head slowly, looking about him, and caught sight of the little bookkeeper waving his hat. A slow grin overspread his face.

"Well, I'll be durned," he said. "Ambrose. Well, I'll be durned."

He came up, dropped the carpet-bag, and put out his hand. It was an enormous hand, red and hairy, hard as a wooden mallet, the knuckles cracked and seamed with dirt that was not dirt but the very soil of the valley ground into the skin. Ambrose's hand disappeared in it. The grip was terrible. Ambrose winced, and laughed to cover his wincing.

"Ezra, I'd have known you anywhere. Anywhere. You haven't changed a particle. Not a particle. Only bigger, I guess."

"I guess I've filled out some," said Ezra.

He had filled out. At twenty-two he had been a raw-boned, gangling youth, all wrists and shanks. Now at thirty-three he was colossal. His shoulders were immense, his neck a column of brick-red muscle that ran down without a break into the vast barrel of his chest. His face was burned almost black by the sun, the skin about his eyes crinkled into a myriad of fine white lines from much squinting across the glare of open country. His hair was yellow, coarse as rope. He wore a suit of brown cheviot, new, bought evidently for the journey, which strained across his back and was too short in the sleeves, and a celluloid collar, and a necktie of brilliant green. He smelled of the train, of coal-smoke and of the dust of the San Joaquin.

"And you," he said, looking down at his cousin. "Why, you ain't hardly growed at all, Ambrose."

"Oh, I keep about the same," said Ambrose, and coughed.

They stood a moment looking at each other, not knowing what to say, smiling foolishly. Then Ambrose caught up the carpet-bag, or tried to, staggered under its weight, and Ezra took it from him gently, as one takes a burden from a child, and swung it to his shoulder again.

"Let's get something to eat," said Ambrose. "I know a place. You must be about starved."

"I could eat some," Ezra admitted.

They went up Market Street together, the little bookkeeper trotting to keep pace with the long, heavy, deliberate stride of the rancher. The street was in the full roar of its Saturday traffic. The cable-cars went clanging by, their grip-men leaning upon the levers; the cables hummed in their slots; there was a never-ending thunder of iron-shod wheels upon the cobbles. The sidewalks were packed. Clerks released from their offices, shop-girls with their arms linked, sailors, Chinamen, messenger boys, women with market baskets, all pushed and elbowed one another in a dense, hurrying, interminable procession. Ezra looked about him with a slow, unwinking stare, like an animal brought suddenly into strange surroundings. He said nothing. Once, when a cable-car shot past within a yard of him, he started violently and put out his free hand as though to fend it off.

"You get used to it," said Ambrose, with a little air of pride.

"I guess you do," said Ezra.

The place Ambrose knew was a German restaurant on Kearny Street, two steps down from the sidewalk, called the Schweizerhalle. It was low-ceilinged and warm, the walls hung with chromos of Swiss lakes and of the Kaiser, and it was full of the smell of sauerkraut, of frying onions, of hot grease, and of beer. There was a long bar at one side, and behind it a fat proprietor in a white apron, polishing glasses. Ambrose came here every Sunday of his life. He was known. The proprietor nodded to him.

They took a table in a corner. Ezra lowered himself upon a bentwood chair, which creaked alarmingly beneath him, and planted his enormous elbows upon the oil-cloth. Ambrose ordered. He ordered lavishly, recklessly, with the prodigality of the poor man playing host: a pot roast with potato pancakes, red cabbage, pickled herring, a dish of sausages, rye bread with caraway seeds, a great wedge of cheese, and two schooners of steam beer. When the food came Ezra ate as he had done everything else, slowly, enormously, steadily, bending his face down over his plate, shovelling in the cabbage with his knife, crushing the bread in his huge fist, his jaws working with the regularity of a machine. Ambrose picked at his herring and watched him, delighted.

"Well," he said at length, "and how's everybody? How's Aunt Sarah?"

Ezra put down his knife.

"Why, didn't you hear? Mother died. Two years ago come February."

Ambrose was dismayed.

"No! I never heard. Nobody ever wrote me. Ezra, I never heard a word."

"Well," said Ezra, "she died. It was her heart. She was out feeding the chickens, and she just set down on the step, and that was all." He took up his knife again. "She used to speak of you. She used to say, 'Ambrose was always the bright one.'"

Ambrose was silent. He saw the little farm in Placer County, the unpainted house, the woodpile, the lean hens scratching in the dooryard, and his aunt, a gaunt, flat-chested woman in a sunbonnet, calling them in to supper across the stubble. He had lived there four years after his own mother died. He had forgotten so much of it. It all came back to him now, abruptly, in the smell of the cabbage and the beer.

"And the old place?" he said.

"Sold. Sold it to a Portugee from Auburn. I didn't want it. It wasn't no good, that place. Never was. Rocks and chaparral." Ezra spoke with the contempt of the valley farmer for the foothills. "I got eleven hundred acres now down on the Kings River. In wheat. All in wheat."

"Eleven hundred acres!"

"Leased," explained Ezra. "Leased, mostly. Three hundred is mine, clear. The rest I lease off the Tolliver estate." He drank half his schooner at a single draught and wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. "I got married," he added.

"Married! Ezra!"

"Four years ago. Her name's Minnie. Minnie Haas. Her folks are Dutch, from over Hanford way. We got two kids. Boys, both of 'em." He fumbled in an inside pocket and brought out a tintype, which he passed across the table with a certain awkward pride. It showed a broad, fair woman with heavy braids wound about her head, seated rigidly, a baby in her lap, and beside her, scowling at the camera, a fat child in a dress.

"That's Elkanah," said Ezra, pointing with his enormous forefinger. "We named him after Grandpa."

Ambrose looked at the picture a long time. Then he handed it back.

"Grandpa," he repeated. "Elkanah. I'd almost forgot."

"You remember Grandpa?"

"I remember him," said Ambrose.

He remembered him well enough. Old Elkanah Doane, who had come out from Maine in '50 and had dug for gold on the American River and had found a little, and had drunk it, and had dug for more. He remembered him sitting on the porch of the Placer County house in the long summer afternoons, an old man with a tangled white beard stained yellow about the mouth, his eyes red and swimming, and the brown jug always beside his chair. He remembered how the old man would fall into terrible, sudden rages, roaring and smashing things, and how Aunt Sarah would take the two boys out to the barn and keep them there until it was over. There was a bad strain in the Doanes. Everybody in the county said so. The old man's father had been the same, and his brother, back in Maine, had died in the street in a snowdrift, drunk.

Ambrose's hand went out to his schooner. It was empty. He signalled the waiter.

"Another," he said. "Ezra, you'll have another?"

"I guess one's my limit," said Ezra. He was watching his cousin. "I don't hardly touch it, generally. Minnie don't like it."

"Oh, well, one more," said Ambrose. "Just one. It isn't every day."

The beer came. Ambrose drank. A little colour came into his thin cheeks. He began to talk, to talk rapidly, volubly, as he had not talked in years. He told Ezra about the city, about his place at Gaylord & Wenck's, about the head bookkeeper, Mr. Pfluger, who had been there thirty years and who would retire some day, and then, perhaps, then there would be a chance; about his boarding-house on Pine Street, and his landlady, Mrs. Hatch, who was a widow and very respectable and who gave him an egg for breakfast on Sundays; about the band concerts in Golden Gate Park and the Chutes and the Cliff House and the seals on the rocks. He made it all sound very fine. He spoke of the great firms of Front Street with a sort of reverence, of the tremendous transactions, of cargoes of wheat sold in a morning to Liverpool, of the fortunes made and lost.

"Why, Ezra," he said, "I bet you some of your own wheat has gone through our books. I bet you I've written it down myself, Kings River wheat, so many centals at so much. Think of that. Me sitting up there on my stool writing down your wheat."

Ezra considered this gravely.

"I sell to Bodkin, at Hanford," he said.

"Well, but Bodkin sells to somebody, and they sell to us. It all comes through Front Street in the end. It all comes through here." Ambrose struck the table with his small fist. "That's the city for you. Everything comes through here."

He coughed, a dry, hacking little cough that bent him over the table. Ezra watched him, his heavy brows drawn together.

"That's a bad cough you got, Ambrose."

"Oh, that? That's nothing. It's the fog. Everybody has it. You get it in the winter and it goes away in the summer."

"It's October," said Ezra.

"Well, it's a little early this year," said Ambrose, and laughed.

He ordered a third schooner. Ezra said nothing, but he watched the little bookkeeper's hand as it went out to the glass, the thin, white, nervous hand with the ink stain on the second finger.

It was dark when they came out of the Schweizerhalle. The street lamps were lit. Ambrose, who was a little unsteady, proposed that they should walk; he wanted Ezra to see the city at night. They went up Kearny Street and climbed by long flights of wooden steps and by steep, crooked lanes, between rows of shabby frame houses, where Italian women sat upon the doorsteps and goats were tethered in the little yards, until they came out upon the summit of Telegraph Hill.

Below them the city spread out on every side, a vast, glittering confusion of lights, row upon row, tier upon tier, climbing the hills and plunging into the hollows, pricking out the lines of the streets, clustering thick about the water-front, thinning away toward the dark spaces of the west. From below there rose a dull, unceasing murmur, the voice of the city, made up of a thousand thousand sounds, the rumble of wheels, the hum of the cables, the shouts, the whistles, the footsteps, blended together into a single prolonged note, deep and sombre as the sound of the sea. Beyond the water-front the bay lay black and wide, and the lights of the ferry-boats moved slowly across it, and the riding-lights of the ships at anchor swayed gently, and far off on the other side were the lights of Oakland, faint and small.

"There," said Ambrose, flinging out his arm. "There's the city. What do you think of that?"

Ezra looked a long time without speaking. The wind came in from the Golden Gate, cold and wet, smelling of salt. It flattened his coat against his huge body. He put his hands in his pockets.

"It's big," he said at last.

"Big! I guess it's big."

"It's big," Ezra repeated slowly, "but it ain't as big as the valley."

Ambrose laughed.

"Oh, come now, Ezra."

"No," said Ezra. He spoke deliberately, searching for his words, his heavy brows knitted. "You don't know, Ambrose. You never seen it. You get up on the windmill platform of a morning in May, and you look off, and there ain't nothing but wheat. Nothing but wheat. Clear to the mountains. Clear to the Coast Range one way, and clear to the Sierra the other, and the wind going over it, and it all moving, like that bay down there, only green, and then yellow, and you can't see no end to it. It goes on and on. It don't care about nothing. It don't care if you're there or not. You can die, and it'll keep right on growing. That's big. This here," he jerked his head toward the city, "this is just a lot of folks."

Ambrose did not answer. He stood shivering a little in his thin black coat. The wind was very cold.

"Ambrose," said Ezra suddenly. "Why don't you come down to the ranch?"

"What? Me?"

"Sure. Come down. I could use a man to keep the books. Bodkin skins me every year, and I don't know enough figures to catch him at it. Minnie'd be glad. There's a room. You could get out in the sun some. Get shut of that cough."

Ambrose was taken aback. For a moment he could not speak. He saw it all as Ezra spoke: the great sun, the dry wind, the room under the eaves, the broad, fair woman with the braids, the children. And then he saw the high stool in the counting-room, and Mr. Pfluger bending over the ledger, and the Schweizerhalle on Sunday afternoons, and the band in the park, and the long, lighted streets. The city had him. It had had him for eleven years. He belonged to it as the ink stain belonged to his finger.

"Why, Ezra," he said, "I couldn't. I couldn't do that. Mr. Pfluger's going to retire. Next year maybe. Or the year after. And then there'll be a chance for me. I've been there eleven years. I couldn't throw that away. Why, a man has got to look to his future."

"Well," said Ezra. "Well. Suit yourself."

"But I'm obliged to you. I'm awfully obliged to you, Ezra. It was mighty decent of you to ask."

"That's all right," said Ezra.

They stood a while longer. Below them a steamer at the water-front let off a long, hoarse blast, and the sound rolled out over the bay and died away. Then Ezra took out a great silver watch, as thick as a biscuit, and held it close to his eyes.

"I got to go," he said. "The train leaves Oakland at nine-forty."

"So soon? Why, you just got here. I thought you'd stay over. I thought you'd stay over Sunday."

"Can't. We're plowing Monday. I only come up to see the lawyer about the Tolliver lease. I seen him this morning." He hesitated. "And to see you, some."

They went down the hill together in silence. At the foot of Market Street the ferry building blazed with light. The waiting-room was emptier now; a few belated passengers sat about upon the benches, and the peanut-roaster in the corner still shrieked upon its one note. Ezra set down the carpet-bag, opened it, and rummaged among its contents. He brought out a glass jar wrapped in newspaper.

"Minnie sent you this," he said. "It's quince. She put it up herself. She said you'd likely be living on boarding-house truck."

Ambrose took the jar in both hands. He turned it over. Through the glass the preserves glowed amber in the light. Something rose in his throat. He could not speak. He coughed instead, and the cough shook him, and he stood bent over the jar, coughing, while Ezra looked down at him with his heavy, troubled face.

The gong sounded for the boat. The gates swung open.

"Well," said Ezra. He put out his hand. Again the little hand disappeared in that tremendous grip. "Well, so long, Ambrose."

"So long, Ezra. Give my best to Minnie. Tell her I'm awfully obliged. Tell her, tell her I'll come down some time. In the summer, maybe."

"Sure," said Ezra. "In the summer."

He swung the carpet-bag to his shoulder and went through the gate, stooping a little under the lintel, a huge, slow, lumbering figure, and the crowd closed in behind him, and he was gone.

Ambrose stood a moment longer by the iron pillar. Then he put the jar of quince under his arm and went out into the street.

The fog had come in. It had come in from the ocean in the last hour, as it came every night, rolling over the hills and down through the streets, swallowing the lights one by one. Market Street was a long, dim tunnel of grey, through which the lamps glowed as yellow blurs and the cable-cars loomed up suddenly and vanished again, their gongs sounding muffled and far away. The pavements were wet. The air was raw and penetrating; it got into the lungs. The voice of the city came through the fog, dulled, unceasing, indifferent, the deep monotone of a multitude that knew nothing of him and cared nothing.

It was a Saturday, toward six o'clock in the evening, and Anders Hallgren was coming home from his work. All the week long he had been hauling for the Pacific Coast Lumber and Mill Company, driving a great four-horse truck between the wharves at the foot of Third Street and the yards out beyond Brannan, and now the week was finished, his wages were in his pocket, and he was going home to his supper. He walked heavily, with the slow, lurching gait of a man who has stood all day upon the swaying seat of a dray. His boots were enormous. His hands, thrust into the pockets of his canvas coat, were enormous. He was a huge, blond Swede, six feet two in his socks, with a red, square face, a straw-colored mustache that hung down over his mouth, and a jaw like the jaw of one of his own horses: massive, angular, grinding slowly upon a quid of tobacco. His mind was slow and his temper was slow, but when it came it came like the bursting of a dam, and the men at the lumber yards had learned to let him be.

He lived on Tehama Street, between Fourth and Fifth, in the second flat of a narrow wooden house that had once been painted yellow. The street was full of the noise of Saturday evening. Children swarmed upon the sidewalks, shrieking, quarrelling, playing at hop-scotch and leap-frog. A German band was playing in front of a corner saloon, the cornet bellowing, the trombone groaning out its long, rasping notes. There was a smell of frying onions in the air, the smell of coal smoke, of stale beer, of horses, of the tide flats along the bay. A Chinese vegetable peddler went by with his baskets swinging from the pole across his shoulders. Over all, the fog was coming in from the ocean, gray and cold, blotting out the tops of the houses, and the electric lights along Fourth Street were already beginning to show, each with its little halo of mist.

Hallgren climbed the outside stairs. They creaked under his weight. He was thinking of his supper. He was thinking of the pork chops and the boiled potatoes and the coffee that would be waiting for him, and of the pipe he would smoke afterward in the bay window, in his stocking feet, with his coat off, while Lottie washed the dishes and the cuckoo clock that he had brought with him from Göteborg fourteen years before ticked upon the wall. It was his week's end. It was the one hour of the week that he looked forward to. He was content. His content was the content of the ox that has been unyoked and turned into the stall.

But at the head of the stairs his wife met him, and at once he saw that something was wrong.

Lottie Hallgren was a little woman, thin and nervous, with a sharp nose and pale eyes, and hair the color of dead grass, twisted up into a tight knot at the back of her head. She was wiping her hands upon her apron, over and over again, though they were quite dry. She had been crying.

"Oh, Anders," she said, "oh, Anders, I'm glad you've come. I didn't know what to do. I didn't know what to do."

"What is it?" he said. "Hey? What's the matter, then?"

"It's Nils. Oh, it's Nils again. He's hurt the Fennessy girl. He's hurt her bad. He hit her with a rock, a great big rock as big as your fist, and her head was all bleeding, and Mrs. Fennessy came up here and screamed at me. Oh, she screamed at me something terrible, Anders, right out on the landing where everybody could hear. She said she'd have the police. She said she'd have him took up and put in the Reform School. She said he was a little devil, and that he'd end on the gallows. Oh, I didn't know what to do. I didn't know what to do."

Hallgren stood still in the doorway, his hat on his head, his hands still in his pockets. He did not understand at first. His mind moved slowly, like one of his own loaded trucks starting up a grade, and it was some time before it was fairly under way. Then little by little he understood. Nils had hurt somebody. Nils had struck a little girl with a rock. There had been blood. There had been a scene, a scandal, a screaming woman on the landing. The police had been spoken of.

"Where is he?" he said.

"He's in the back room. He's hiding under the bed. He's been there ever since. I couldn't get him out. Oh, Anders, don't be too hard on him. He's only a baby. He didn't know. He didn't mean it."

Hallgren took his hands out of his pockets.

"Get supper," he said.

He went down the narrow, dark entry toward the back room. The floor shook under him. The dishes rattled upon the shelf in the kitchen. Lottie, standing by the stove, the frying pan in her hand, listened to his steps, her lips parted, her pale eyes very wide.

The back room was small and close, and smelled of soap and of damp plaster. It had one window that gave upon the back yards, upon a wilderness of clothes-lines and board fences and tin cans and ash barrels, and beyond, upon the blank wall of a cigar factory. The light was failing. In one corner was the bed, a great iron bed painted white, with brass knobs at the corners, and a patchwork quilt; and under the bed, far back against the wall, in the dust and the darkness, crouched a little boy.

"Come out," said Hallgren.

There was no answer.

"Come out. You hear me? Come out of there."

Nothing stirred. Only, from under the bed, there came a sound of breathing, short and quick, like the breathing of some small animal that has been run to earth.

Hallgren stooped, and putting one enormous hand beneath the bed, took hold of whatever he could find. It was an ankle. He pulled, and the boy came out, sliding over the floor upon his stomach, clutching at the legs of the bed, at the edge of the rag carpet, at the floor itself, kicking, struggling, silent. His father set him upon his feet in the middle of the room and stood looking down at him.

Nils Hallgren was seven years old. He was large for his age, broad in the shoulders, solid in the legs, with a round head covered with tow-colored hair that stood up in a tuft at the crown. His face was smeared with dust and with the dried marks of tears. His blouse was torn at the neck. He did not cry now. He stood with his feet planted wide apart, his hands clenched at his sides, his head lowered, looking up at his father from under his eyebrows. And his jaw was set. That was what one noticed first and last about him: his jaw, square and heavy, too heavy for a child's face, thrust forward, the lower lip pushed out, the teeth shut tight.

"Did you hit the Fennessy girl with a rock?" said Hallgren.

The boy said nothing.

"You hear me? Did you do it? Hey? Answer me when I talk to you."

"Yes," said Nils.

"What for?"

The boy was silent a moment, then, all at once, the words came out of him in a rush, thick and choked:

"She took my top. She took my new top what Uncle Sven gave me, and she wouldn't give it back, and she laughed at me. She laughed. And she said I talked like a Swede. And I told her to give it back, and she wouldn't, and she held it up high so I couldn't reach, and laughed, and all the other kids laughed. And so I hit her. I hit her with a rock. And I'm glad. I'm glad I hit her. I'd do it again."

"Ha!" said Hallgren.

He felt the blood come up into his face. He felt it beat in his neck, in his temples, behind his eyes. It was not so much what the boy had done; it was the defiance of him, the stubbornness, the little set jaw thrust up at him, the fists clenched, the voice that said, "I'd do it again." This was his son. This was his own boy, and he stood there and talked back to him, to him, Anders Hallgren, who had been driving four horses all day long through the mud and the dray-traffic of Townsend Street, who had come home tired and wanted his supper and his pipe, and who must stand here in the dusk and be defied by a child that did not come up to his belt.

"You'd do it again, would you?" he said. His voice was rising. "You'd do it again? You hit a little girl with a rock, so the blood come, and her mother come up here and yell at your mother, and say the police come, and you'd do it again? By God, I show you. I show you something."

He looked about him. Upon a nail behind the door there hung a strap, an old leather strap that had once been part of a set of harness, black and supple and cracked with use. He took it down. The boy's eyes followed it. They grew suddenly very wide. But he did not move, and his jaw did not relax.

Then a strange thing happened to Anders Hallgren.

He had the strap in his hand, and he had taken a step toward the boy, and his arm was lifted; and all at once he was no longer in the back room on Tehama Street. He was in a low, dark kitchen in a farmhouse in Småland, with a peat fire smoldering on the hearth and snow lying deep outside, and he was seven years old himself; and over him there stood a man, a great, gaunt, silent man with a beard, his father, Olaf Hallgren, and in his father's hand there was a strap. He remembered it all, suddenly, with an extraordinary vividness, as one remembers things in dreams. He remembered the smell of the peat smoke and of wet wool. He remembered the sound of the strap. He remembered how his father's face had looked, not angry, but quite still and white, and his eyes, how they had gone small and bright and fixed, like the eyes of a dog that has caught the scent of blood. And he remembered that his father had not been able to stop. That was the thing he remembered best of all. His father had begun, and then he had not been able to stop. Something had got hold of him, something that was not Olaf Hallgren at all, but older than he, deeper, a thing that had come up out of some black pit inside him and taken possession of him, so that he struck, and struck, and struck, long after the boy had ceased to cry, until the mother had come running in from the barn and flung herself between them. And afterward, the father had gone out of the house without a word and had not come back until the next day. And Anders had lain on the straw in the loft for a week, and had not been able to sit down.

And his father's father, they said, had been the same. A great man in his parish, a hard man, a man who drank and fought and, in a rage once, had killed a horse with an axe. It was in the blood. It came down from father to son, the vicious taint, the evil heritage, like a dark stream running underground, never seen, never heard, but always there; flowing on beneath the surface of things, beneath the decent, sober, hard-working life of honest men, waiting, waiting, ready at any moment to burst up into the daylight. It was the brute in them. It was the beast.

Anders Hallgren stood still in the middle of the room with the strap in his hand, and he felt it stirring in him now. He felt it plainly. It was like a hot, thick liquid rising slowly in his throat. He felt his fingers tighten upon the strap. He felt a kind of tingling in his arm, an itching, an eagerness, a desire to strike and to go on striking. His breath came short. His eyes, he knew, were growing small. And there before him stood the boy, the little stubborn boy with the square jaw, looking up at him, waiting.

The jaw. It was his own jaw. It was Olaf Hallgren's jaw. Hallgren saw it suddenly, and he saw it with a kind of terror. It was the same, it was the very same; the heavy, protruding, salient jaw, the jaw of the carnivora, the jaw that the Hallgrens had carried with them out of Småland, generation after generation, as they carried their blond hair and their great hands and their slow, terrible tempers. The boy had it. It was in him already. He was seven years old, and already he had hit a girl with a rock so that the blood came, and was glad. Already it was rising in him, the dark stream, the foul heritage. And here was he, the father, with the strap in his hand, ready to beat it into him, to beat it in deeper, as it had been beaten into himself in the kitchen in Småland thirty years ago.

"Ah," said Hallgren, aloud. "Ah, no. No."

He dropped the strap. It fell upon the floor between them, and lay there in a black coil like a dead snake.

The boy stared at it, and then at his father. He did not understand. His lower lip began to tremble. All at once, now that the blow was not coming, he began to cry, not as a child cries, loudly, but silently, his face working, the big tears running down through the dust on his cheeks. He did not unclench his fists.

Hallgren sat down upon the edge of the iron bed. It creaked and sagged beneath him. He was breathing hard, as though he had been lifting heavy timbers. He took off his hat and turned it round and round between his knees, looking at it. For a long time he did not say anything. Out in the kitchen they could hear the pork chops sizzling in the pan, and the clatter of dishes, and Lottie moving about. From the street there came the sound of the German band, and of the children shrieking, and of a car-bell on Fourth Street, clang, clang, clang. In the front room the cuckoo clock struck the half-hour, and the little wooden bird came out of its door and said "Cuckoo" once, and went back again.

"Come here," said Hallgren at last.

The boy came slowly, dragging his feet, and stood in front of him. Hallgren put one huge hand upon his shoulder. The hand covered it entirely, and part of his arm besides.

"Listen," he said. "You listen to me now. I don't lick you. Not this time. But you listen to what I say. You understand me?"

The boy nodded, sniffling.

"You got a bad temper. Hey? You know that. You got a bad temper, like I got, like your grandfather got. It's in you. It's in all of us Hallgrens. Something gets hold of you, and you don't know what you do. You get mad, and you see red, and you hit. You hit with a rock. Bimeby when you get big you hit with something else, maybe, a knife, maybe a club, and then you kill somebody. Then they hang you. That's what Mrs. Fennessy say, and by God she's right. You understand that?"

He shook the boy a little, not roughly, but heavily, as he might have shaken a sack to settle the grain in it.

"She took my top," said Nils, in a whisper.

"Sure she took your top. And she laugh at you. And she say you talk like a Swede. All right. You *are* a Swede. I'm a Swede. That's nothing. You don't hit girls with a rock for that. You don't hit nobody with a rock for that. Listen. When I was a little feller like you, my father licked me. He licked me so I couldn't sit down for a week. He licked me because I was mad, and he was mad, too, and so he licked me. And it don't do no good. It make me madder. It make me worse. I fight every boy in the parish after that. And when I come over here I fight on the boats, and I fight on the docks, and once I near kill a man in a saloon on Pacific Street. Ya, I near kill him. I don't tell your mother that. I'm telling you. And I don't want you should be like that. You hear? I don't want you should be like me."

He had never said so much at one time in his life. The words came hard. He was not used to them. He stumbled over them and repeated himself, and his great red face grew redder; but he kept on, doggedly, the way he drove his horses up the hill on Second Street with a load of redwood behind them, a step at a time.

"When you feel it come, that mad feeling, you know what you do? You put your hands in your pockets. Like this. See? You put them in your pockets and you hold on tight, and you count, one, two, three, four, all the way up to twenty. And you don't take them out. Not till it go away. And it go away. Bimeby it always go away. You hear me?"

"Yes," said Nils.

"You promise me that?"

"Yes."

"All right."

Hallgren got up. He picked the strap off the floor, looked at it a moment, and then, instead of hanging it upon the nail behind the door, he opened the window and flung it out into the back yard among the ash barrels and the tin cans. Then he put on his hat.

"Now," he said, "you come along with me."

The boy hung back. "Where we going?"

"We go down to the Fennessys'. You tell Mrs. Fennessy you're sorry. You tell the little girl you're sorry. Then we see."

In his office at San Francisco, seated before a massive desk of polished redwood, very ornate, Lyman Derrick sat dictating letters to his typewriter, on a certain morning early in the spring of the year. The subdued monotone of his voice proceeded evenly from sentence to sentence, regular, precise, businesslike.

“I have the honour to acknowledge herewith your favour of the 14th instant, and in reply would state——” “Please find enclosed draft upon New Orleans to be applied as per our understanding——” “In answer to your favour No. 1107, referring to the case of the City and County of San Francisco against Excelsior Warehouse & Storage Co., I would say——” His voice continued, expressionless, measured, distinct. While he spoke, he swung slowly back and forth in his leather swivel chair, his elbows resting on the arms, his pop eyes fixed vaguely upon the calendar on the opposite wall, winking at intervals when he paused, searching for a word.

“That's all for the present,” he said at length. Without reply, the typewriter rose and withdrew, thrusting her pencil into the coil of her hair, closing the door behind her, softly, discreetly. When she had gone, Lyman rose, stretching himself putting up three fingers to hide his yawn. To further loosen his muscles, he took a couple of turns the length of he room, noting with satisfaction its fine appointments, the padded red carpet, the dull olive green tint of the walls, the few choice engravings—portraits of Marshall, Taney, Field, and a coloured lithograph—excellently done—of the Grand Canyon of the Colorado—the deep-seated leather chairs, the large and crowded bookcase (topped with a bust of James Lick, and a huge greenish globe), the waste basket of woven coloured grass, made by Navajo Indians, the massive silver inkstand on the desk, the elaborate filing cabinet, complete in every particular, and the shelves of tin boxes, padlocked, impressive, grave, bearing the names of clients, cases and estates. He was between thirty-one and thirty-five years of age. Unlike Harran, he resembled his mother, but he was much darker than Annie Derrick and his eyes were much fuller, the eyeball protruding, giving him a pop-eyed, foreign expression, quite unusual and unexpected. His hair was black, and he wore a small, tight, pointed mustache, which he was in the habit of pushing delicately upward from the corners of his lips with the ball of his thumb, the little finger extended. As often as he made this gesture, he prefaced it with a little twisting gesture of the forearm in order to bring his cuff into view, and, in fact, this movement by itself was habitual. He was dressed carefully, his trousers creased, a pink rose in his lapel. His shoes were of patent leather, his cutaway coat was of very rough black cheviot, his double-breasted waistcoat of tan covered cloth with buttons of smoked pearl. An Ascot scarf—a great puff of heavy black silk—was at his neck, the knot transfixed by a tiny golden pin set off with an opal and four small diamonds. At one end of the room were two great windows of plate glass, and pausing at length before one of these, Lyman selected a cigarette from his curved box of oxydized silver, lit it and stood looking down and out, willing to be idle for a moment, amused and interested in the view. His office was on the tenth floor of the EXCHANGE BUILDING, a beautiful, tower-like affair of white stone, that stood on the corner of Market Street near its intersection with Kearney, the most imposing office building of the city. Below him the city swarmed tumultuous through its grooves, the cable-cars starting and stopping with a gay jangling of bells and a strident whirring of jostled glass windows. Drays and carts clattered over the cobbles, and an incessant shuffling of thousands of feet rose from the pavement. Around Lotta's fountain the baskets of the flower sellers, crammed with chrysanthemums, violets, pinks, roses, lilies, hyacinths, set a brisk note of colour in the grey of the street. But to Lyman's notion the general impression of this centre of the city's life was not one of strenuous business activity. It was a continuous interest in small things, a people ever willing to be amused at trifles, refusing to consider serious matters—good-natured, allowing themselves to be imposed upon, taking life easily—generous, companionable, enthusiastic; living, as it were, from day to day, in a place where the luxuries of life were had without effort; in a city that offered to consideration the restlessness of a New York, without its earnestness; the serenity of a Naples, without its languor; the romance of a Seville, without its picturesqueness. “The man from the lithograph company, sir,” announced the boy.

“Well, what does he want?” demanded Lyman, adding, however, upon the instant: “Show him in.” A young man entered, carrying a great bundle, which he deposited on a chair, with a gasp of relief, exclaiming, all out of breath: “From the Standard Lithograph Company.”

“What is?”

“Don't know,” replied the other. “Maps, I guess.”

“I don't want any maps. Who sent them? I guess you're mistaken.” Lyman tore the cover from the top of the package, drawing out one of a great many huge sheets of white paper, folded eight times. Suddenly, he uttered an exclamation: “Ah, I see. They ARE maps. But these should not have come here. They are to go to the regular office for distribution.” He wrote a new direction on the label of the package: “Take them to that address,” he went on. “I'll keep this one here. The others go to that address. It was a commissioner's official railway map of the State of California, completed to March 30th of that year. Upon it the different railways of the State were accurately plotted in various colours, blue, green, yellow. However, the blue, the yellow, and the green were but brief traceries, very short, isolated, unimportant. At a little distance these could hardly be seen. The whole map was gridironed by a vast, complicated network of red lines marked P. and S. W. R. R. These centralised at San Francisco and thence ramified and spread north, east, and south, to every quarter of the State. From Coles, in the topmost corner of the map, to Yuma in the lowest, from Reno on one side to San Francisco on the other, ran the plexus of red, a veritable system of blood circulation, complicated, dividing, and reuniting, branching, splitting, extending, throwing out feelers, off-shoots, tap roots, feeders—diminutive little blood suckers that shot out from the main jugular and went twisting up into some remote county, laying hold upon some forgotten village or town, involving it in one of a myriad branching coils, one of a hundred tentacles, drawing it, as it were, toward that centre from which all this system sprang. It was as though the State had been sucked white and colourless, and against this pallid background the red arteries of the monster stood out, swollen with life-blood, reaching out to infinity, gorged to bursting; an excrescence, a gigantic parasite fattening upon the life-blood of an entire commonwealth.
