It was in that part of the West Side of Chicago which lies between Halsted Street and the river, and which in the year 1894 was given over almost entirely to the small frame cottages and two-story flats of those who labored for a wage, that Mrs. Clara Hulme, the wife of a motorman on the Blue Island Avenue line, kept house for her husband and her two children upon an income which, at its very best, came to no more than fourteen dollars and a half a week. Out of this, eleven dollars a month went for the rent of the upper floor of a gray clapboard building on Laflin Street, a place of four small rooms, two of which looked out upon a yard of cinders and a leaning fence, and two upon the street, where the wagons of the coal dealers and the ice men passed and repassed throughout the day. The remainder had to be stretched, as such sums are always stretched in such homes, over the coal and the kerosene, the meat and the flour, the shoes which wore out so rapidly upon the children's feet, and that small margin, never more than a few dimes, which Mrs. Hulme liked to set by against the illness or the lay-off that she felt, in the dim, anxious way of her kind, was always waiting for them somewhere in the future.

She was not a woman of any great force or understanding. Born on a farm near Urbana, Ohio, the fourth daughter of a Methodist harness-maker who had failed at farming, she had brought to the city, at nineteen, little more than a certain prim prettiness, now fading, and a set of moral notions which she had never examined and would never have dreamed of examining, since they seemed to her as fixed and as necessary as the rising of the sun. One did not lie. One did not steal. One did not take the name of the Lord in vain, nor play cards on Sunday, nor drink, nor permit one's children to grow up "wild," which last was a word that covered, in her mind, a vast and shadowy region of sin, idleness, and ultimate destruction, of the kind she had seen pictured in the tracts that were handed about at camp-meetings in her girlhood. That these notions were themselves the product of conditions, of a narrow agricultural life in which a stolen hen or an unpaid debt might mean actual want to a neighbor, never occurred to her. They were simply right, and their opposites were simply wrong, and there was an end of it.

Her husband, Asa Hulme, was a large, slow, good-natured man of thirty-four, who had come up from the country somewhat as she had and who, having found employment with the street railway, had held it for nine years without either advancement or complaint. He left the house at half-past five in the morning and returned at seven at night, gray with fatigue, smelling of the oil and the electric dust of his car, and wanting nothing so much as his supper and his pipe. The management of the children he left entirely to her, as did nearly all men of his station, regarding it as a thing outside his province, like the washing or the mending of socks.

Of these children there were two: a girl, Nettie, not yet three, and a boy, Willard, who was in his seventh year and attended the primary grade of the Throop Street school. He was a thin, quick, light-haired child, with his mother's narrow face and something else besides, an eagerness, a responsiveness to color and sound and movement, which she did not possess and did not understand. The street fascinated him. The wagons with their great dappled horses, the hurdy-gurdy man who came on Saturdays, the gaudy posters of the circus pasted upon the fences along Twelfth Street, the windows of the little shops in which were displayed things of a brightness and a desirability that seemed to him beyond anything in the world: all these drew him as a light draws a moth, and he would stand before them, his hands in the pockets of his patched knee-breeches, for long minutes together, lost in a kind of dream. And it is just here that we must pause, for in this matter of desire, of the pull which things exert upon the untutored mind, lies the whole secret of what follows.

For what, after all, is a child but a small bundle of wants, set down in a world which it did not make and whose rules it cannot possibly comprehend? It sees, it desires, it reaches out. That the thing it reaches for belongs to another, that it has been paid for with labor and is guarded by law and custom and the whole elaborate apparatus of property, is a fact as remote from its understanding as the movement of the planets. The notion of mine and thine is not born in us; it is laid upon us, layer by layer, by those who have themselves had it laid upon them, and very often at no small cost of tears.

Now, upon the shelf above the kitchen stove, behind the coffee-mill and a china figure of a shepherdess which had been a wedding present from her sister in Dayton, Mrs. Hulme kept a small tin canister, painted blue and bearing upon its side the faded legend "Arbuckle's," in which she placed, from week to week, such coins as she could spare toward the rent. It was a kind of shrine with her, this canister. She counted its contents on Saturday nights, after Asa had brought home his envelope, and again on Tuesdays, out of a mere nervous habit, and the sight of the small heap of silver and copper upon the oilcloth gave her a feeling of security which nothing else in her life afforded. On this particular Tuesday in early May, then, having put Nettie down for her nap and finished the ironing, she took the canister down, as was her custom, emptied it upon the table, and counted. There should have been, as she well knew, three dollars and eighty-five cents. There were three dollars and sixty.

She counted again, slowly, sliding the coins one by one across the oilcloth with her forefinger, her lips moving. Three dollars and sixty. A quarter was gone.

It is difficult to convey to those who have never known actual want the effect which so small a discovery may produce upon a mind such as hers. A quarter was not, in itself, a great deal of money, even to the Hulmes. It was a pound and a half of round steak, or a peck of potatoes, or a pair of the cheap cotton stockings which Nettie was forever wearing through at the knees. But it was not the quarter alone. It was the sense of violation, of a breach in the frail wall which she had built between her family and the abyss. If a quarter could vanish from the canister, then anything could vanish, and the whole careful structure of her economy, upon which she had spent so many anxious hours, seemed suddenly to tremble. She sat very still, her hands upon the table, and a cold feeling went over her.

Her first thought, naturally enough, was of the woman downstairs, a Mrs. Kubelik, the wife of a cooper, who sometimes came up to borrow a cup of sugar or an iron. But Mrs. Kubelik had not been up in more than a week. Her second thought was of Asa, and this she put away at once, for Asa never touched the canister and would not, she knew, have taken anything without telling her. And then, slowly, unwillingly, as one approaches a thing one does not wish to see, her mind came round to Willard.

She remembered now, as people do remember such things once suspicion has given them a direction, that on Saturday afternoon he had been alone in the kitchen for some little time while she was in the front room with Nettie, who had been fretful with a tooth. She remembered that he had gone out afterward without being told, and had come back nearly an hour later with a flushed face and an air of excitement which she had attributed at the time to some game in the street. And she remembered, too, that on Sunday morning, in brushing his other jacket for Sunday school, she had found in the pocket a small sticky fragment of something black, which she had taken for a bit of tar and had thrown into the stove without a second thought. Licorice. It had been licorice.

She got up and went into the small back bedroom which the boy shared with his sister, and there, in the drawer of the rickety washstand where he kept the few poor treasures of his childhood, a broken top, a picture card from a package of cigarettes which he had found in the gutter, a piece of colored glass, she discovered a tin whistle, painted red and gold, such as were sold at Madden's notion store on Twelfth Street for ten cents, and three marbles of a kind she had never seen before, glassy, with twists of brilliant color inside them, which she judged, rightly, to have cost a penny apiece.

She stood looking at these things for a long time. They were cheap and bright and useless, and to her eye, trained in a hard school of utility, there was something almost wicked in their very brightness. She thought of her father, who had once whipped her brother Lon with a harness strap until he could not stand because he had taken a pocketknife from a peddler's cart, and she thought of Lon himself, who had gone to Cincinnati at seventeen and of whom nothing good had ever been heard since. It was in her mind, in a confused and frightened way, that this was how such things began. A quarter today, and tomorrow, what? She saw, as in a kind of vision, the long downward road of the tracts, the saloon, the jail, the gallows even, and her son, her Willard, going down it.

It was a little after three when the boy came in from school, banging the door at the foot of the stairs and coming up two steps at a time, as he always did, his slate and his primer strapped together and swinging from one hand. He was humming something, a scrap of a tune he had heard from the hurdy-gurdy, and his face, in the dim light of the stairway, was cheerful and unsuspecting. His mother was waiting for him in the kitchen. She had put the whistle and the marbles upon the table, beside the open canister, and she stood behind them with her hands folded in front of her apron, her face pale and set.

"Willard," she said, "come here."

He stopped in the doorway. His eyes went to the table, and to the whistle and the marbles there, and in an instant the whole of his small being underwent a change. The color drained from his cheeks and then came back in a rush; his mouth, which had been open in the shape of the tune, closed; and he looked up at her with that peculiar expression, at once guilty and wary and pleading, which is common to all creatures, human and otherwise, who feel themselves caught.

"Come here, I said."

He came, slowly, and stood before her, the strap of his books hanging from his fingers.

"Where did you get these things?"

He did not answer at once. One could see, if one were watching closely, the swift and desperate working of a small mind seeking an avenue of escape. "A boy gave 'em to me," he said at last.

"What boy?"

"A boy. At school. Eddie Ryan."

"Willard Hulme, you look at me." She bent toward him, and her voice, which was ordinarily rather thin and complaining, took on a hard, high note which he had heard only once or twice before in his life. "There was a quarter in that box on Saturday that isn't there now. Did you take it?"

"No'm."

"Don't you lie to me. Don't you dare stand there and lie to me. You took it. You took it out of that box when I was in with your sister, and you went down to Madden's and spent it on this trash. Didn't you?"

The boy's lip began to tremble. He looked at the whistle, red and gold upon the oilcloth, and at the marbles, which only on Saturday had seemed to him the most beautiful objects in the whole world, and which now lay there like evidence in a court. He had not, in any true sense, thought of what he was doing when he took the coin. He had seen it, bright among the others, in a moment when he had climbed upon a chair to look at the china shepherdess, and the window of Madden's, with its glittering tray of marbles and its row of painted whistles, had risen up before him with a force he could not withstand. There had been no reasoning about it, no weighing of right and wrong. There had been only the want, and the coin, and the opportunity, and the thing had been done almost before he knew it. Afterward, it is true, there had been a small, cold uneasiness, which had made him hide the things in his drawer instead of showing them to his mother; but the joy of possession had been stronger, and the uneasiness had faded with each hour that passed without discovery. Now it came back upon him all at once, magnified a hundredfold by the look in her face.

"Yes'm," he whispered.

"You took it."

"Yes'm."

"And you lied to me about it. You stood right there and told me a boy gave them to you." She straightened up, and her hands, which had been folded, came apart and fell to her sides. "Do you know what that money was for? Do you know? That was the rent money. That was what keeps a roof over your head. Your father works from before daylight till after dark for that money, out in the rain and the cold, and you go and take it and throw it away on candy and whistles and marbles. Do you know what you are? You're a thief. That's what they call people who take what isn't theirs. Thieves. And they put them in jail."

At this word the boy burst into tears. He did not know, any more than she did, the full meaning of what she was saying; but the word "jail," with its dark associations of policemen and the patrol wagon that he had sometimes seen clanging along Halsted Street, struck into him like a blow. He dropped his books and stood there, his face screwed up and wet, his thin shoulders heaving, crying in that helpless, open-mouthed way of very young children.

And here it must be said that his mother, at this moment, was by no means unmoved. There was within her, beneath the hard surface of the conventions she had been taught, a great deal of the natural tenderness of a woman for her child, and the sight of his tears went to her heart. She wanted, almost, to take him up in her arms. But she did not. For there rose up in her, stronger than her tenderness, the voice of her own upbringing, the voice of her father and of the preacher at the Urbana camp-meeting and of all the generations of stern, narrow, fearful people from whom she was descended, telling her that this was the moment, that if she were weak now she would be responsible for whatever came after, that to spare the rod was to spoil the child. It is one of the strange ironies of our moral life that the very love we bear toward those in our charge is so often made the instrument of their pain, and that we strike them most hardly precisely because we fear for them most. She was afraid for him; and fear, in natures such as hers, has only one outlet.

"Stop that crying," she said. "Stop it this minute. Crying won't help you now. You should have thought of that before." She went to the nail behind the pantry door, where hung a narrow leather strap which Asa had brought home from the car barns and which had hitherto served chiefly as a threat. "Come here."

He backed away from her toward the window, still sobbing. "I won't do it again, Ma. I won't. I won't never do it again."

"Come here, I said."

He came, because there was nothing else to do, because the habit of obedience was stronger in him even than his terror; and she took him by one thin arm and turned him about and struck him three times across the backs of his legs, below the knee-breeches, where the skin was bare above his stockings. They were not, as such punishments went in that day and in that neighborhood, particularly severe blows. Mrs. Kubelik downstairs beat her boys with a stove-lifter, and the Irish family across the street were heard to raise the very roof on Saturday nights. But to Willard, who had been struck only rarely and never with the strap, they seemed the end of the world. He screamed at each one, and when she let go of his arm he fell down upon the floor beside the stove and lay there with his face against the boards, crying as though his heart would break. In the front room Nettie woke and began to wail in sympathy.

Mrs. Hulme hung the strap back upon its nail. Her hands were shaking. She stood for a moment looking down at her son, and then she said, in a voice that was not quite steady, "Now you get up and go in your room and stay there till your father comes home. And you get down on your knees and ask God to forgive you, because I don't know as He will." And she went in to quiet the baby.

The rest of that afternoon passed in a kind of gray, heavy silence. The boy lay upon his bed in the back room, sobbing at first and then only catching his breath at long intervals, and finally staring dully at the ceiling, where a water-stain in the plaster made a shape like the map of some unknown country. He did not pray. He did not, in fact, think very clearly about anything. There was in him only a vast, confused sense of having been cast out, of being somehow different from what he had been that morning, of having become, in his mother's eyes and perhaps in the eyes of God, something dark and shameful, a thief. The word went round and round in his mind. It is in such hours, perhaps, more than in any formal instruction, that the moral nature of a child is shaped, and it is shaped not so much by reason as by pain and fear, by the memory of a face turned hard against him and of a voice that had changed. Whether it is shaped for good or ill is a question which those who administer such lessons seldom pause to ask.

As for his mother, she went about the work of getting supper with a tight, preoccupied air, peeling potatoes, slicing bread, setting the table with the heavy white plates, and stopping now and again to stare out of the window at the cinder yard, where a gray cat was picking its way along the top of the fence. She was not satisfied. She had done, as she conceived it, her duty, and yet the doing of it had left her not relieved but strangely heavy and sick at heart. She thought of the marbles, with their twists of color, and of the boy's face when he had first seen them upon the table, and it came to her, dimly and without words, that he had wanted them very badly, in a way that she herself had perhaps once wanted things, ribbons, a hat with a feather, a pair of kid gloves in the window of a store in Springfield, which she had never had and had long since ceased to think about. But this thought was too vague and too disturbing to be followed out, and she put it away, as she put away all such thoughts, and went on slicing the bread.

At a little after seven Asa came heavily up the stairs, hung his cap and his coat upon the hook by the door, and sat down at the table with a long sigh of weariness. She told him, as she set the potatoes and the fried salt pork before him, what had happened. He listened, chewing slowly, his large red hands upon either side of his plate.

"Didn't think we'd make it," went on young Cranston speaking to all at once. "Nina didn't want to come, but I promised Bertine and Jill or I wouldn't have, either. We were up at the Bagley's. "Oh, here you are. You decided to come after all. I wasn't sure whether you would think it worth while. You've been introduced to everybody, of course?" She looked around as much as to say, that if he had not been she would proceed to serve him in this way. The others, not so very much impressed by Clyde, were still not a little interested by the fact that she seemed so interested in him.

"Yes, I met nearly everybody, I think."

"Except Freddie Sells. He came in with me just now. Here you are, Freddie," she called to a tall and slender youth, smooth of cheek and obviously becurled as to hair, who now came over and in his closely-fitting dress coat looked down on Clyde about as a spring rooster might look down on a sparrow.

"This is Clyde Griffiths, I was telling you about, Fred," she began briskly. "Doesn't he look a lot like Gilbert?"

"Why, you do at that," exclaimed this amiable person, who seemed to be slightly troubled with weak eyes since he bent close. "I hear you're a cousin of Gil's. I know him well. We went through Princeton together. I used to be over here before I joined the General Electric over at Schenectady. But I'm around a good bit yet. You're connected with the factory, I suppose."

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, who, before a youth of obviously so much more training and schooling than he possessed, felt not a little reduced. He began to fear that this individual would try to talk to him about things which he could not understand, things concerning which, having had no consecutive training of any kind, he had never been technically informed.

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, cautiously and nervously.

"You know," went on Mr. Sells, briskly and interestingly, being of a commercial as well as technical turn, "I've always wondered just what, outside of money, there is to the collar business. Gil and I used to argue about that when we were down at college. He used to try to tell me that there was some social importance to making and distributing collars, giving polish and manner to people who wouldn't otherwise have them, if it weren't for cheap collars. I think he musta read that in a book somewhere. I always laughed at him." Clyde was about to attempt an answer, although already beyond his depth in regard to this. "Social importance." Just what did he mean by that—some deep, scientific information that he had acquired at college. He was saved a non-committal or totally uninformed answer by Sondra who, without thought or knowledge of the difficulty which was then and there before him, exclaimed: "Oh, no arguments, Freddie. Clyde turned, while Fred made the best of the rebuff by merely looking at Sondra, whom he admired so very much.

"Yes, of course," Clyde began, for he had been studying these two along with others. To him, apart from Sondra, Bertine seemed exceedingly attractive, though quite beyond his understanding also. Being involved, insincere and sly, she merely evoked in him a troubled sense of ineffectiveness, and hence uncertainty, in so far as her particular world was concerned—no more.

"Oh, how do you do? It's nice to see you again," she drawled, the while her greenish-gray eyes went over him in a smiling and yet indifferent and quizzical way. "Well, I hope so," he replied, showing his even teeth. For apart from her local position and means and taste in dress and manners, Sondra was of the exact order and spirit that most intrigued him—a somewhat refined (and because of means and position showered upon her) less savage, although scarcely less self-centered, Hortense Briggs. She was, in her small, intense way, a seeking Aphrodite, eager to prove to any who were sufficiently attractive the destroying power of her charm, while at the same time retaining her own personality and individuality free of any entangling alliance or compromise. However, for varying reasons which she could not quite explain to herself, Clyde appealed to her. He might not be anything socially or financially, but he was interesting to her. Hence she was now keen, first to see if he were present, next to be sure that he gained no hint that she had seen him first, and lastly to act as grandly as possible for his benefit—a Hortensian procedure and type of thought that was exactly the thing best calculated to impress him. He gazed and there she was—tripping here and there in a filmy chiffon dance frock, shaded from palest yellow to deepest orange, which most enhanced her dark eyes and hair. And having exchanged a dozen or more "Oh, Hellos," and references with one and another to this, that and the other local event, she at last condescended to evince awareness of his proximity.

"Oh, here you are. You decided to come after all. I wasn't sure whether you would think it worth while. You've been introduced to everybody, of course?" She looked around as much as to say, that if he had not been she would proceed to serve him in this way. The others, not so very much impressed by Clyde, were still not a little interested by the fact that she seemed so interested in him.

"Yes, I met nearly everybody, I think."

"Except Freddie Sells. He came in with me just now. Here you are, Freddie," she called to a tall and slender youth, smooth of cheek and obviously becurled as to hair, who now came over and in his closely-fitting dress coat looked down on Clyde about as a spring rooster might look down on a sparrow.

"This is Clyde Griffiths, I was telling you about, Fred," she began briskly. "Doesn't he look a lot like Gilbert?"

"Why, you do at that," exclaimed this amiable person, who seemed to be slightly troubled with weak eyes since he bent close. "I hear you're a cousin of Gil's. I know him well. We went through Princeton together. I used to be over here before I joined the General Electric over at Schenectady. But I'm around a good bit yet. You're connected with the factory, I suppose."

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, who, before a youth of obviously so much more training and schooling than he possessed, felt not a little reduced. He began to fear that this individual would try to talk to him about things which he could not understand, things concerning which, having had no consecutive training of any kind, he had never been technically informed.

"In charge of some department, I suppose?"

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, cautiously and nervously.

"You know," went on Mr. Sells, briskly and interestingly, being of a commercial as well as technical turn, "I've always wondered just what, outside of money, there is to the collar business. Gil and I used to argue about that when we were down at college. He used to try to tell me that there was some social importance to making and distributing collars, giving polish and manner to people who wouldn't otherwise have them, if it weren't for cheap collars. I think he musta read that in a book somewhere. I always laughed at him." Clyde was about to attempt an answer, although already beyond his depth in regard to this. "Social importance." Just what did he mean by that—some deep, scientific information that he had acquired at college. He was saved a non-committal or totally uninformed answer by Sondra who, without thought or knowledge of the difficulty which was then and there before him, exclaimed: "Oh, no arguments, Freddie. That's not interesting. Besides I want him to meet my brother and Bertine. You remember Miss Cranston. She was with me at your uncle's last spring." Clyde turned, while Fred made the best of the rebuff by merely looking at Sondra, whom he admired so very much.

"Yes, of course," Clyde began, for he had been studying these two along with others. To him, apart from Sondra, Bertine seemed exceedingly attractive, though quite beyond his understanding also. Being involved, insincere and sly, she merely evoked in him a troubled sense of ineffectiveness, and hence uncertainty, in so far as her particular world was concerned—no more.

"Oh, how do you do? It's nice to see you again," she drawled, the while her greenish-gray eyes went over him in a smiling and yet indifferent and quizzical way. She thought him attractive, but not nearly as shrewd and hard as she would have preferred him to be. "You've been terribly busy with your work, I suppose. But now that you've come out once, I suppose we'll see more of you here and there."

"Well, I hope so," he replied, showing his even teeth. Her eyes seemed to be saying that she did not believe what she was saying and that he did not either, but that it was necessary, possibly amusing, to say something of the sort. And a related, though somewhat modified, version of this same type of treatment was accorded him by Stuart, Sondra's brother.

It was nearly eleven o'clock of a raw March evening when Lewis Harnack, having climbed the three flights of the narrow and none too clean stairway of the building on West Ohio Street in which he and his wife, Ada, occupied a flat of four small rooms at nineteen dollars the month, let himself in with his key and found her not asleep, as he had hoped and half calculated she would be, but sitting up in the little front room beside the table with the green-shaded lamp upon it, a basket of mending at her elbow, and before her, laid out flat and smoothed as though it were a document of the gravest consequence (as indeed, for them, it was), a slip of buff-colored paper which he recognized on the instant. It was the receipt from the Calumet Realty and Development Company, signed by one J. Whitney Barge, Agent, for the sum of four hundred and twenty dollars, being payment in full upon two lots, numbers seventeen and eighteen, in a subdivision known as Lakeview Heights, near Gary, Indiana. And at the sight of it, lying there under the lamp, a sinking, chilling sensation, not unlike that of one who has stepped from a curb in the dark and found it deeper than he supposed, went through him. For he had put that paper away, and carefully, he thought, in the inside pocket of his old gray coat, which hung in the closet behind his other clothes, and which he had not worn since the fall.

"Well, you're up late," he began, as easily as he could, removing his derby and hanging it on the hook beside the door, the while his mind raced this way and that, in search of some ground upon which he might stand. "I thought you'd be in bed long ago. Hamel kept us till after nine on the inventory, and then I stopped in at Kerner's for a sandwich with Fritz Hollis, him and me being—"

"Lewis," she said, not looking up at once, but keeping her eyes fixed upon the paper, "what is this?"

She was a woman of twenty-nine, not plain and yet not pretty either, with a broad, pale, rather heavy face, good brown hair which she wore drawn back plainly, and gray eyes that were capable, at times, of a kind of dumb, persistent intensity which he had come of late to dread more than any outburst of temper. For Ada, as he well knew, was not one to scream or throw things, as some women did—as his own mother, for instance, had done in the old days in Racine. Rather she would sit and look, and say a thing over and over, quietly, until it seemed that the very walls must give back the sound of it. And she was looking now—had raised her eyes from the paper and fixed them upon him with that same slow and terrible steadiness.

"That?" he said, coming forward and pretending to peer at it, as though he were not perfectly sure. "Oh, that. Why, that's—I was going to tell you about that, Ada. Honest, I was. Only I wanted to wait until it was all fixed up right, so's I could show you the whole thing at once. That's a piece of property."

"A piece of property," she repeated. "Four hundred and twenty dollars. Where did you get four hundred and twenty dollars, Lewis?"

And now he could not answer, for the simple reason that she knew—must know—as well as he, where he had got it. There was only one place from which he could have got it, and that was the savings account at the Prairie State Bank on Milwaukee Avenue, which stood in both their names, and into which, for nearly five years now, by dint of the most pinching and contriving economy on her part (and not a little on his, as he would have insisted), they had put by, a dollar and two dollars and sometimes five at a time, the sum of four hundred and sixty-eight dollars and some cents. It had been intended—or so at least Ada had always intended—for a little house of their own somewhere, out Irving Park way perhaps, or in Maywood, where there were trees and lawns and where one need not climb three flights of stairs smelling of cabbage and coal oil to reach one's bed. Or, if not that, then against a time of sickness, or the loss of his place at Hamel and Strauss, which, as she had often pointed out, was not so very secure, since he was only a shipping clerk at sixteen dollars a week and there were plenty who would be glad to take it at fourteen.

"Why, out of the bank, of course," he said at last, with an attempt at bluffness which deceived neither of them. "Where else? But listen, Ada, you don't understand. It's not like it was spent. It's invested. It's the same as having it in the bank, only better. A whole lot better. You'll see."

"I went to the bank this afternoon," she said, in that same level tone, as though he had not spoken. "I went to put in the three dollars I saved out of the grocery money this month. And the man looked at the book and he went away and came back and said, 'Mrs. Harnack, there's only forty-eight dollars and some cents here. Didn't you know that?' And I said no, I didn't know that, there must be some mistake. And he said there wasn't any mistake, that you had come in on the eleventh of February and drawn out four hundred and twenty dollars. And then I came home and looked." She laid her hand flat upon the paper. "And I found this."

"You went through my things," he said, seizing, as weak men will, upon the one point at which he might appear the injured party.

"Yes, I went through your things."

There was a silence then, during which the clock on the shelf, a cheap nickel one for which they had paid a dollar and a quarter at the Fair, ticked loudly, and somewhere below them in the building a child set up a thin, complaining wail and was hushed. Lewis Harnack stood by the table, his overcoat still on, and looked down at his wife, and she looked up at him, and between them lay the buff-colored paper with its neat, engraved border and the signature of J. Whitney Barge, Agent.

Now it should be explained that Lewis Harnack was not, at bottom, a bad or even a particularly selfish man, but merely one of those innumerable and essentially unfortunate individuals in whom the desire for more—more of ease, more of show, more of the bright, warm, comfortable things which they see others possess—is not balanced by any corresponding capacity, either of intellect or of will, for achieving them. He was thirty-two, of medium height, with a soft, rather full, pleasant face, a small brown mustache which he kept carefully trimmed, and a manner which, in the presence of those above him, was eager and ingratiating, and in the presence of those beneath him, or whom he fancied beneath him, a little lofty and condescending. He liked good clothes, and could not afford them. He liked to stand at the bar in Kerner's or at the cigar counter of the Briggs House and talk with men who wore diamond pins and spoke familiarly of deals and options and turns in wheat. And he had come, in the last year or two, to feel a kind of slow, gnawing resentment—not against Ada exactly, and yet in some way connected with her—at the meagerness and fixity of his lot. Sixteen dollars a week! And at thirty-two! While here and there about him, in this vast, roaring, money-mad city, men no brighter than he—he was sure of it—were rising, rising, riding in carriages, building houses on the North Shore, having their names in the papers. And how? By taking chances. By seeing an opportunity and seizing it. By not being afraid. That was the secret, as J. Whitney Barge himself had explained to him so convincingly over a glass of beer and a free lunch in the back room of a saloon on Clark Street, where they had first fallen into talk. Gary! Did he realize what was going to happen at Gary? The Steel Trust was pouring millions into it. Millions! There would be a city there of a hundred thousand inside of ten years. And land that could be had today for two hundred dollars a lot would be worth two thousand—five thousand, maybe—and the man who had the foresight and the nerve to get in now, at the bottom—

"It's going to be worth ten times what I paid for it," he said now, with a sudden access of eagerness, pulling out a chair and sitting down across from her, his overcoat still on. "Ten times, Ada. Maybe more. You don't know about Gary. Nobody around here knows about it hardly yet. That's why the price is so low. But the Steel people are building the biggest mills in the world over there—it was in the Tribune, you can look it up yourself—and all those men that work in the mills have got to live somewhere, haven't they? And they'll want lots to build on. And here we'll be, with two of 'em, right there. Barge says—"

"Who is Barge?"

"Why, Barge is the agent. J. Whitney Barge. He's a fine fellow. He's been in real estate for fifteen years. He's made a lot of money for people. He showed me letters from them—"

"Have you seen the lots, Lewis?"

He hesitated, and the hesitation was itself an answer. "Well, no, not exactly. Not yet. But I've seen the map. He's got a big map in his office in the Monadnock Building—you ought to see it, Ada, all laid out, streets and everything, and a park, and a place for a school. And he's going to take a party of us out on the cars some Sunday, soon as the weather lets up, and show us the whole thing. He said so."

She said nothing to this, only continued to look at him, and in her look—he could feel it rather than see it—was something worse than anger, a kind of weary, heavy, comprehending contempt, as of one who, having long suspected a thing, now has it confirmed and finds no satisfaction in the confirmation. And it stung him—how it stung him! For was he a child, to be looked at like that? Was he not a man, and the head of this house, and entitled to do with his own money—for after all, was it not his money, earned by his labor, week after week, year after year, at that dingy shipping desk at Hamel and Strauss?—as he saw fit?

"Well, you needn't look at me like that," he burst out at last. "Anybody'd think I'd gone and stolen something. It was half mine anyhow, wasn't it? More than half, if you come right down to it. Who earned it?"

"Who saved it?" she said.

And there it was—the whole of their difference, as it were, in four words. For it was true, and he knew it to be true, that but for her it would never have been saved at all. It was she who had made over her old dresses, year after year, and gone without the new hat she wanted, and walked to the market on Halsted Street to save a nickel on carfare and three cents on a pound of butter. It was she who had refused to go to the theater, except once in a great while, and then to the gallery, and who had said no to the new carpet, and no to the phonograph that he had wanted so much, and no, no, no, to one thing after another, until he had come, at moments, almost to hate the sound of the word on her lips. And yet that was the very thing! That was the very reason why he had done it, if she only knew—had done it, partly at least, to show her, to prove to her once and for all that there was another way of getting on in the world than this endless, grinding, penny-pinching saving, which, as he saw it, got one nowhere at all. Five years, and four hundred and sixty-eight dollars! At that rate, when would they ever have a house? When they were sixty? And by then what good would it be?

"Oh, I know you saved it," he said, with a kind of sullen, half-apologetic irritation. "I'm not saying you didn't. But what's the good of saving if you just let it lie there and draw two per cent? That's what I want to know. That's no way to get ahead. Nobody ever got ahead that way. You've got to take a chance sometimes. Look at Fritz Hollis' brother-in-law. He bought into that laundry on Division Street with three hundred dollars, and now look at him."

"And look at Mr. Prager," she said quietly, "downstairs."

He was silent at that, for Prager, a little bald German cabinetmaker on the first floor, had put all that he had, some eleven hundred dollars, into the stock of a gold mine in Colorado two years before, and had never seen a cent of it again, and now went about with a strange, dazed, inward look, as though he were still trying to understand what had happened to him. And Ada had known Mrs. Prager, and had heard the whole of it, sitting in that woman's kitchen while she cried.

"That's different," he said at last, not very convincingly. "That was mining stock. Anybody knows you can't trust mining stock. This is land. Land's different. Land's always there. You can't lose land."

"Can't you, Lewis?"

He got up then, abruptly, and took off his overcoat at last and threw it across the back of the cheap plush rocker by the window, and walked to the window and stood looking out, his hands thrust deep into his trouser pockets. Below him, Ohio Street lay dark and wet under a thin, cold drizzle, the arc light at the corner of Halsted making a blurred, violet-white globe in the mist, and beyond it the great black bulk of the warehouses and the gas tanks, and farther still, low on the horizon, the dull red glow of the city reflected upon the clouds. Somewhere a street car ground and clanged its way along. And all the vast, indifferent, teeming life of the place, which he had come to as a youth of nineteen from Racine with such high hopes—what had it given him? This! These four rooms, and the shipping desk, and the sixteen dollars, and a wife who sat and looked at him as though he were a fool.

And was he a fool? The question came to him, there at the window, unbidden and unwelcome. Supposing—supposing Barge were not what he seemed? Supposing there were no streets, no park, no school—only a stretch of sand and scrub oak and marsh, such as he had seen once from the train window, going to Michigan City? Supposing—but no! He would not think of that. Barge had an office in the Monadnock Building. A man did not have an office in the Monadnock Building and go about swindling people. It was not possible. The thing was sound. It must be sound. For if it were not—

Behind him he heard Ada stir, and the faint rustle of the paper as she folded it.

"I'm going to go over there," she said. "Tomorrow. To this Barge."

He turned. "You'll do nothing of the kind!"

"I'm going to go over there and ask him to give it back."

"Give it back! Why, you're crazy, Ada. He can't give it back. It's a sale. It's all signed and recorded and everything. You'd only make a fool of yourself—and of me. What would he think of me, having my wife come down there whining and crying for the money back, like I didn't know my own mind? Do you want to make me a laughingstock?"

"I don't care what he thinks of you," she said, and for the first time her voice trembled a little, not with tears, as he at first thought, but with a kind of suppressed passion which he had rarely heard in her. "I don't care what anybody thinks. Five years, Lewis. Five years I've been putting that by. I've gone without—you don't know what I've gone without. You don't know the half of it. And you go and give it away to a man you met in a saloon—"

"It wasn't a saloon! It was—"

"—to a man you met in a saloon, and never told me, never said one word to me, and hid the paper in your old coat like—like a thief. That's what hurts, Lewis. Not the money so much. That you hid it."

And this, being the exact truth, struck home as nothing else had. For he had hidden it—had gone about for nearly a month now with the knowledge of it lying in him like a stone, unable to bring himself to speak of it, putting it off from day to day, telling himself that he would wait until he had seen the lots, until he could come home some evening with a letter from Barge, perhaps, offering him twice what he had paid, and lay it before her triumphantly and say, "There! What do you think of that? And you wanted to leave it in the bank at two per cent!" That had been the dream. And now instead—this.

"I was going to tell you," he said again, but weakly now, and without conviction.

"When?"

He did not answer. He could not. And she, seeing that he could not, sat a moment longer, very still, her large, work-roughened hands lying folded upon the paper in her lap, and then she got up and went slowly into the little bedroom beyond, and he heard her sit down upon the bed, and then nothing more.

And he, left alone in the front room with the green-shaded lamp and the ticking clock and the basket of mending, stood a long while at the window, looking out at the wet street and the violet arc light and the red glow upon the sky, and turning it over and over in his mind. Was he wrong? Had he been a fool? Barge had seemed so sure, so easy, so prosperous, with his gray waistcoat and his gold watch chain and his large, confident, friendly way of laying a hand on one's shoulder. And all those men he had read about, who had risen from nothing—had they not taken chances too? Had their wives not wept and reproached them? And then afterward, when the money came—what then? Then it was all forgotten, and they were called shrewd and far-seeing, and lived on the Lake Shore Drive. It was only the ones who failed who were called fools. And he would not fail. He would not. Gary was going to be a great city. It had said so in the Tribune.

And yet! And yet! Supposing—

From the bedroom came no sound at all, not even of weeping, and somehow that was worse than any weeping could have been. He thought of going in to her, of sitting down beside her on the bed and putting his arm about her and saying—what? That he was sorry? But he was not sorry—or not entirely. That it would all come out right? But he did not know that it would. And so he did not go, but stood there, a figure of indecision and half-defiance and half-shame, the while the clock ticked on and the rain fell and the great city outside, careless of him and of her and of J. Whitney Barge and of all the little hoards and hopes of all the millions like them, went roaring on its way into the night.

Here is an excerpt of Theodore Dreiser's writing, to show you their style:

But in the interim, in connection with his relations with Roberta no least reference to Sondra, although, even when near her in the factory or her room, he could not keep his thoughts from wandering away to where Sondra in her imaginary high social world might be. The while Roberta, at moments only sensing a drift and remoteness in his thought and attitude which had nothing to do with her, was wondering what it was that of late was beginning to occupy him so completely. And he, in his turn, when she was not looking was thinking—supposing?—supposing—(since she had troubled to recall herself to him), that he could interest a girl like Sondra in him? What then of Roberta? What? And in the face of this intimate relation that had now been established between them? (Goodness! The deuce!) And that he did care for her (yes, he did), although now—basking in the direct rays of this newer luminary—he could scarcely see Roberta any longer, so strong were the actinic rays of this other. Was he all wrong? Was it evil to be like this? His mother would say so! And his father too—and perhaps everybody who thought right about life—Sondra Finchley, maybe—the Griffiths—all. And yet! And yet! It was snowing the first light snow of the year as Clyde, arrayed in a new collapsible silk hat and white silk muffler, both suggested by a friendly haberdasher—Orrin Short, with whom recently he had come in contact here—and a new silk umbrella wherewith to protect himself from the snow, made his way toward the very interesting, if not so very imposing residence of the Trumbulls on Wykeagy Avenue. It was quaint, low and rambling, and the lights beaming from within upon the many drawn blinds gave it a Christmas-card effect. And before it, even at the prompt hour at which he arrived, were ranged a half dozen handsome cars of various builds and colors. The sight of them, sprinkled on tops, running boards and fenders with the fresh, flaky snow, gave him a keen sense of a deficiency that was not likely soon to be remedied in his case—the want of ample means wherewith to equip himself with such a necessity as that. And inside as he approached the door he could hear voices, laughter and conversation commingled. A tall, thin servant relieved him of his hat, coat and umbrella and he found himself face to face with Jill Trumbull, who apparently was on the look-out for him—a smooth, curly-haired blonde girl, not too thrillingly pretty, but brisk and smart, in white satin with arms and shoulders bare and rhinestones banded around her forehead.

"No trouble to tell who you are," she said gayly, approaching and giving Clyde her hand. "I'm Jill Trumbull. Miss Finchley hasn't come yet. But I can do the honors just as well, I guess. Come right in where the rest of us are." She led the way into a series of connecting rooms that seemed to join each other at right angles, adding as she went, "You do look an awful lot like Gil Griffiths, don't you?"

"Do I?" smiled Clyde simply and courageously and very much flattered by the comparison. The ceilings were low. Pretty lamps behind painted shades hugged dark walls. Open fires in two connecting rooms cast a rosy glow upon cushioned and comfortable furniture. There were pictures, books, objects of art.

"Here, Tracy, you do the announcing, will you?" she called. "My brother, Tracy Trumbull, Mr. Griffiths. Mr. Clyde Griffiths, everybody," she added, surveying the company in general which in turn fixed varying eyes upon him, while Tracy Trumbull took him by the hand. Clyde, suffering from a sense of being studied, nevertheless achieved a warm smile. At the same time he realized that for the moment at least conversation had stopped. "Don't all stop talking on my account," he ventured, with a smile, which caused most of those present to conceive of him as at his ease and resourceful. At the same time Tracy added: "I'm not going to do any man-to-man introduction stuff. We'll stand right here and point 'em out. That's my sister, Gertrude, over there talking to Scott Nicholson." Clyde noted that a small, dark girl dressed in pink with a pretty and yet saucy and piquant face, nodded to him. And beside her a very de rigueur youth of fine physique and pink complexion nodded jerkily. "Howja do." And a few feet from them near a deep window stood a tall and yet graceful girl of dark and by no means ravishing features talking to a broad-shouldered and deep-chested youth of less than her height, who were proclaimed to be Arabella Stark and Frank Harriet. "They're arguing over a recent Cornell-Syracuse foot-ball game ... Burchard Taylor and Miss Phant of Utica," he went on almost too swiftly for Clyde to assemble any mental notes. "Perley Haynes and Miss Vanda Steele ... well, I guess that's all as yet. Oh, no, here come Grant and Nina Temple." Clyde paused and gazed as a tall and somewhat dandified-looking youth, sharp of face and with murky gray eyes, steered a trim, young, plump girl in fawn gray and with a light chestnut braid of hair laid carefully above her forehead, into the middle of the room.

"Hello, Jill. Hello, Vanda. Hello, Wynette." In the midst of these greetings on his part, Clyde was presented to these two, neither of whom seemed to pay much attention to him. "Didn't think we'd make it," went on young Cranston speaking to all at once. "Nina didn't want to come, but I promised Bertine and Jill or I wouldn't have, either. We were up at the Bagley's. Guess who's up there, Scott. Van Peterson and Rhoda Hull. They're just over for the day."

"You don't say," called Scott Nicholson, a determined and self-centered looking individual. Clyde was arrested by the very definite sense of social security and ease that seemed to reside in everybody. "Why didn't you bring 'em along? I'd like to see Rhoda again and Van, too."

"Couldn't. They have to go back early, they say. They may stop in later for a minute. Gee, isn't dinner served yet? I expected to sit right down."

"These lawyers! Don't you know they don't eat often?" commented Frank Harriet, who was a short, but broad-chested and smiling youth, very agreeable, very good-looking and with even, white teeth. Clyde liked him.

"Well, whether they do or not, we do, or out I go. Did you hear who is being touted for stroke next year over at Cornell?" This college chatter relating to Cornell and shared by Harriet, Cranston and others, Clyde could not understand. He had scarcely heard of the various colleges with which this group was all too familiar. At the same time he was wise enough to sense the defect and steer clear of any questions or conversations which might relate to them. However, because of this, he at once felt out of it. These people were better informed than he was—had been to colleges. Perhaps he had better claim that he had been to some school. In Kansas City he had heard of the State University of Kansas—not so very far from there. Also the University of Missouri. And in Chicago of the University of Chicago. Could he say that he had been to one of those—that Kansas one, for a little while, anyway? On the instant he proposed to claim it, if asked, and then look up afterwards what, if anything, he was supposed to know about it—what, for instance, he might have studied. He had heard of mathematics somewhere. Why not that? But these people, as he could see, were too much interested in themselves to pay much attention to him now. He might be a Griffiths and important to some outside, but here not so much—a matter of course, as it were. And because Tracy Trumbull for the moment had turned to say something to Wynette Phant, he felt quite alone, beached and helpless and with no one to talk to. But just then the small, dark girl, Gertrude, came over to him.

"The crowd's a little late in getting together. It always is. If we said eight, they'd come at eight-thirty or nine. Isn't that always the way?"

"It certainly is," replied Clyde gratefully, endeavoring to appear as brisk and as much at ease as possible.

"I'm Gertrude Trumbull," she repeated. "The sister of the good-looking Jill," a cynical and yet amused smile played about her mouth and eyes. "You nodded to me, but you don't know me. Just the same we've been hearing a lot about you." She teased in an attempt to trouble Clyde a little, if possible. "A mysterious Griffiths here in Lycurgus whom no one seems to have met. I saw you once in Central Avenue, though. You were going into Rich's candy store. You didn't know that, though. Do you like candy?"

It was on a raw evening in late November, with the wind coming in off the lake in long, cold, searching gusts that rattled the signboards along Cottage Grove Avenue and sent bits of paper and dust whirling about the feet of the homeward-bound, that Walter Pruett, having brushed his one good suit and blacked his shoes twice over and examined himself in the small, wavy mirror of his hall bedroom on Indiana Street with no little dissatisfaction, set out to call upon his cousin Della, whom he had not seen in eleven years. Eleven years! And in that time what had not happened to her, and what, as he could not help reflecting, had not happened to him! For she, as he had learned only a fortnight before through a letter from his mother in Pelham, was now Mrs. Harvey Kinsolving, the wife of a building contractor of some means, and lived (so his mother had written, with an underscoring that conveyed more than any words) on Drexel Boulevard. Whereas he—well, he was a bookkeeper's assistant in the office of the Lake Shore Coal & Coke Company at fourteen dollars a week, and had been for nearly three years, and with no very definite prospect, as he was compelled to admit when he was honest with himself, of being anything much better.

And yet, as he rode southward in the clanging, overheated car, his hands thrust deep into the pockets of an overcoat which had seen two winters too many, he could not keep his mind from going back to the old days in Pelham, when Della Pruett, the daughter of his father's younger brother, had been a thin, freckled, rather tomboyish girl with two long brown braids, who had climbed the Weller apple trees with him and fished for sunfish in Turkey Creek and once (he remembered it now with a sudden warmth) had cried bitterly when he had been whipped by old Professor Haines for a prank that was more hers than his. They had been very close then—as close, almost, as brother and sister. And when her family had moved away to Indianapolis, and later, after her father's death, she had come to Chicago to work in a millinery establishment, he had written to her once or twice, and she to him. But then the letters had stopped, as such letters do, and life, with its endless and impersonal shuffling, had carried them each along their separate ways.

But Drexel Boulevard! The very name, to one who had walked along it on Sunday afternoons and gazed at the great stone and brick houses set back behind their lawns and iron fences, with their bay windows and porte-cocheres and the carriages drawn up before them, held a magic which was not easily to be dispelled. How had she come to that? What chance, what luck, what quality in her had fitted her for such a change? And would she, now that she was a part of all that, care to see him at all? He had written her a note, a stiff and labored thing that had cost him an entire evening, and she had answered promptly enough—a little lavender-scented card in a large, sloping hand: "Dear Walter—of course! Come Thursday at eight. I'm so anxious to see you. Della." Yet even so, he was not sure. People said such things. And she would see at once (he was certain of it) the shine on the elbows of his coat, the frayed edge of his cuff, which he had trimmed with scissors and turned under as best he could.

The house, when at last he found it, after walking two blocks in the wrong direction and being compelled to inquire of a policeman, proved to be a large, square, gray stone affair with a round tower at one corner capped by a pointed slate roof, and with lights glowing warmly behind lace curtains on both floors. A lamp of wrought iron burned at the head of the steps. Walter paused at the foot of these and looked up, conscious of a sinking in the region of his stomach which was not entirely the result of the cold. Here was something—solid, substantial, secure. Here was what money did. And he thought, with a twinge of bitterness which he could not quite suppress, of his own narrow room with its single gas jet and its cracked washbowl and the smell of cabbage that ascended every evening from the kitchen of Mrs. Dorgan below.

He rang. A fire of cannel coal burned brightly in a grate of polished brass. The carpet beneath his feet was thick and soft. He stood very straight, his hands at his sides, and then, deciding that this looked foolish, clasped them behind his back, and then, thinking that this too was not quite right, let them fall again.

And then she came—down the broad staircase, which he could see through the archway, and into the room with a soft rustle of silk, and he scarcely knew her. For this was not the thin, freckled girl of Turkey Creek at all, but a full-figured woman of twenty-eight or nine, handsome in a rather showy way, with her brown hair, now darker than he remembered it, piled high in a pompadour and held by a comb of tortoise shell set with brilliants, and wearing a gown of dove-gray silk with a bodice of cream lace and a high collar, and at her throat a brooch of pearls. Her face had filled out, and the freckles had gone (or had been banished by some art which he did not understand), and yet about the eyes—those same quick, gray-green, half-mocking eyes—there was something which went straight back to the old days and brought them before him with a rush.

"Walter! Walter Pruett! Well, for goodness' sake!" She came toward him with both hands extended, and he took them awkwardly, not knowing whether he was expected to kiss her cheek, as he might have once, or merely to shake hands, as one did with a lady. In his uncertainty he did neither, but stood holding her hands and smiling, a little foolishly, he feared. "Why, you've grown so tall! And a mustache! I'd never have known you on the street—never in this world. Sit down, sit down. Here, by the fire. You must be frozen. Isn't it a perfectly awful night?"

"It is pretty cold," he admitted, seating himself gingerly on the edge of one of the gilt chairs, which seemed to him much too frail for any real use, and wondering whether he ought to have said something about the house first, or about her looks. "But it's not so bad once you get moving. You—you look fine, Della. I mean—you look awful well."

"Do I?" She laughed, pleased, and sank into a deep chair opposite him with a little sigh of comfort, arranging her skirts about her. "Well, I'm getting fat, if you want to know the truth. Harvey says I'm not, but I am. That's what comes of not doing anything. You remember how skinny I used to be? Bean-pole, you used to call me. Bean-pole Della."

"Did I?" he said, and flushed, for he did remember it. "I guess I was a pretty mean kid."

"Oh, no, you weren't. You were the nicest boy in Pelham, and you know it. Don't you remember the time old Haines licked you for putting the garter snake in his desk drawer, and it was really me that put it there? I never forgot that. I cried all night." She laughed again, a warm, throaty laugh that filled the room, and Walter laughed too, feeling for the first time a little of his stiffness go out of him. For whatever else had changed, it was plain that she had not wholly forgotten, and that she was, in some fashion at least, glad to see him.

And then for a time, as is the way with those who have shared a childhood and then been long parted, they talked eagerly and almost at random—of Pelham, and of who had married whom, and of old Mrs. Weller's death, and of the Methodist church that had burned and been rebuilt, and of Hank Shiveley, who had gone to the Klondike and come back with nothing but a frozen foot. And of his mother, and her mother, who had died four years since in Indianapolis (and here Della's face clouded a little and she looked into the fire), and of the creek, which, so he told her, had been dammed up now for a mill and was not what it had been at all. And all the while Walter, even as he talked, was studying her—the rings upon her fingers, three of them, one with a diamond as large as a pea, the soft white hands that had once been brown and scratched with briars, the way she held her head, the faint air of assurance and of being accustomed to service which hung about her like a perfume. How had it come about? What had she done? Was it merely luck—the luck of a pretty face in the right place at the right moment? Or was there something in her, some shrewdness or force, which he himself lacked? For he had always thought himself, in the old days, the quicker of the two.

"But tell me about you, Walter," she said at last, turning to him with renewed interest. "What are you doing here in Chicago? Aunt Mattie wrote that you were with some big company."

And now he was confronted with the very thing which, all the way down in the car, he had dreaded. For what was he to say? That he sat on a high stool in a dingy office on South Water Street, adding columns of figures relating to tons of anthracite and bituminous, under the eye of a sour old Scotchman named McPhail who had been there thirty years and expected to be there thirty more? That he had been passed over twice for a raise? That his whole capital, after three years in the city, came to forty-one dollars in the Hibernian Savings Bank? It was not to be thought of—not here, in this room, with the bronze youth and the onyx pedestal and the diamond the size of a pea. And so, with a readiness which surprised even himself, he heard himself saying:

"Oh, I'm with the Lake Shore Coal and Coke people. In the accounting end. It's a pretty big concern—they do a lot of business with the railroads. I'm—well, I'm in line for something better pretty soon, I think. They've been talking about it." And then, feeling that this was perhaps not sufficient, and being carried along by the very momentum of the lie: "I'm kind of looking around, too. A fellow I know has been after me to go in with him on something—a real estate proposition out in Englewood."

"Why, Walter, that's fine!" she exclaimed, and seemed so genuinely pleased that he felt at once a fresh pang. "I always knew you'd get on. You were always so smart in school. Harvey says there's no end of money in real estate out there, if a person only knows how to go about it."

"That's what they say," he agreed, though he knew nothing whatever about it and was already wishing he had held his tongue. For supposing she should mention it to her husband, and supposing her husband should ask him about it? What then? And he looked down at his shoes, which in the light of the fire showed a crack across the left toe that no blacking could hide, and drew that foot back under the chair.

But just then there was the sound of the front door opening and closing, a heavy step in the hall, and a voice—a large, comfortable, somewhat husky voice—calling: "Del? Where are you, Del?" And Della, with a quick, half-nervous movement of her hand to her hair, rose and said: "In here, Harvey. Walter's here. My cousin, you know, from Pelham." And into the room came a man of perhaps forty-five, broad and heavy and red-faced, with a close-cropped grayish mustache and small, shrewd, pale-blue eyes, wearing a suit of good gray worsted that stretched a little across his middle, and a heavy gold watch chain with an elk's tooth charm depending from it. He had about him that air of large, easy, self-satisfied solidity which Walter had often observed in successful men in the Loop—men who rode in cabs and lunched at the Union League and spoke of thousands as he spoke of dimes.

"Well, well, so this is the cousin," said Mr. Kinsolving, extending a thick, warm hand and gripping Walter's with a force that made him wince. "Glad to know you, young fellow. Del's been talking about you all week. Sit down, sit down. Don't let me break anything up." He lowered himself into the largest chair in the room with a grunt and drew a cigar from his waistcoat pocket, bit off the end and lit it, his small eyes moving over Walter the while in a manner which, though not unfriendly, seemed to Walter to take in everything—the suit, the cuffs, the collar, the very crack in the shoe. "From down in Indiana, eh? I was through there once. Flat country. Good farming, though. What line you in?"

"Coal," said Walter, and then, because it seemed too bald, "the Lake Shore Coal and Coke Company. In the office."

"Lake Shore? That's old Tilden's outfit. I buy from 'em sometimes for the boilers on my jobs. Pretty close-fisted crowd, I hear. Old Tilden'd skin a flea for its hide." He laughed, a short, rumbling laugh, and blew a cloud of smoke toward the ceiling. "Don't pay their help much either, from what I hear."

Walter flushed and said nothing, and Della, catching perhaps something of his discomfiture, put in quickly: "Walter's thinking of going into real estate, Harvey. Out in Englewood. With a friend of his."

"That so?" Mr. Kinsolving turned his pale eyes upon Walter with a new and somewhat sharper interest. "Who with? I know most of the fellows operating out there."

"Oh—it's just a young fellow," Walter stammered. "Nobody you'd know, I guess. It isn't settled yet. It's just—talk, mostly."

"Well, that's mostly what it is," observed Mr. Kinsolving, not unkindly, and, as it seemed to Walter, with a kind of amused knowledge that cut deeper than any rebuke. "Talk. I've seen a lot of young fellows talk themselves into that game and out of their shirts. You want to watch your step. You hang on to your job, young man, till you've got something real. That's my advice." And having delivered himself of this, he turned to his wife and began to speak of a man named Dolan who had failed to deliver a load of brick to a job on Michigan Avenue, and of what he intended to do to Dolan on the morrow, while Walter sat silent, turning his hat in his hands (for he had taken it from the hall stand in anticipation of leaving and then, finding no graceful moment, had been compelled to hold it), and feeling himself smaller and more out of place with every passing minute.

And yet, as he watched them, he became aware of something else—something which he could not at first have named. For Della, as her husband talked, had grown quieter. She sat listening with an expression of polite attention, nodding now and again and saying "Yes, Harvey," and "I should think so," but her eyes, he noticed, wandered more than once to the fire, and once to the window, where the wind was flinging sleet against the panes, and there was in her face a kind of patient, set look which he did not remember from the old days and which did not, somehow, fit with the silks and the diamonds and the bronze youth on his pedestal. Was she happy? It had not occurred to him to wonder. He had supposed, as one does, that with all this—the house, the maid, the rings—she must be. And yet—

Presently Mr. Kinsolving, having finished both his cigar and his account of Dolan, rose heavily and announced that he had some figures to go over in his den and would leave them to their visiting. "Come again, young fellow," he said, again crushing Walter's hand. "Del gets lonesome, I guess, with me out all day. Don't you, Del?" And he patted her shoulder with a large, careless hand and went out, and they heard his step going up the stairs and a door closing somewhere above.

For a moment neither of them spoke. The fire crackled. The sleet ticked against the glass. Then Della, with a little laugh that was not quite the laugh of before, said: "Harvey's awfully good to me, Walter. You mustn't mind the way he talks. He's like that with everybody."

"Oh, I don't mind," said Walter quickly. "He's right, I guess. About the real estate, I mean." And then, moved by something in her face, and by the warmth of the fire, and by the old memories which their talk had stirred, he added, almost before he knew it: "There isn't any real estate, Della. Not really. I just said that. I'm just a clerk down there. Fourteen a week." And he looked at her, half defiantly, half in shame, waiting.

But she did not laugh, or look at him with pity, as he had feared. Instead she gazed at him for a long moment with those gray-green eyes, and then she said, very softly: "Oh, Walter. You didn't have to tell me that. I knew." And then, after a pause: "I was making six dollars a week at Madame Furlong's when I met Harvey. Trimming hats. Six dollars. And living in one room on Wabash Avenue with a girl from Kankakee who stole my stockings. You don't know what that's like for a girl. Or maybe you do." She turned the large diamond on her finger round and round. "I was so tired, Walter. I was so tired of it all."

He did not know what to say. He sat looking at her, and at the room, and at the fire, and for the first time it came to him, dimly and confusedly, that there might be more than one way of paying for things, and that not all of the prices were written on the tags. And yet—and yet! How he envied her, just the same! How gladly, if he could, he would have traded his narrow room and his high stool and his forty-one dollars for all this, whatever it cost! Was that wrong? Was it base? His mother would have said so, no doubt. But his mother had never sat on a stool on South Water Street for three years, adding up other men's coal.

It was after ten when he left, Della going with him to the door herself and pressing his hand and making him promise to come again—to come for Sunday dinner, soon—and he went down the steps into the whirling sleet and turned up his collar and stood a moment looking back at the lighted windows, at the round tower with its pointed slate roof, at the iron lamp. Then he walked toward the car line, his hands deep in his pockets, his head bent against the wind, thinking—of her, of Kinsolving and his cigar and his elk's tooth, of the diamond turning round and round on her finger, and of himself, and of what, in this great, hard, glittering city, a man without money might ever hope to be.
