The house of Mrs. Lettie Cranshaw stood upon one of those broad and comfortable avenues of Walnut Hills which, in the early nineties, had come to represent for the city of Cincinnati all that was solid, prosperous, and assured. It was of red brick, three stories in height, with a slate roof, a deep veranda supported by turned white pillars, and a lawn which descended in a gentle slope to an iron fence. Here and there along the street stood other houses of a like character, some more pretentious, some less, but all bearing that air of quiet self-satisfaction which money, long held and comfortably spent, lends to the dwellings of men. To one coming up from the lower city, from the smoke and clatter of the river front and the mean tenements of the bottoms, the change was as from one world to another, and it was with this feeling, half of awe and half of a vague resentment which she did not trouble to analyse, that Agnes Moody stepped down from the cable car at the corner and looked about her for the number she had written upon a slip of paper.

She was a woman of thirty-four, rather tall, thin of face, with brown hair drawn back plainly from a forehead which had once been considered handsome. Her dress was of black serge, made over from one she had worn two winters before, and her hat, a small affair with a single grey feather, had been purchased for a dollar and forty cents at a shop in Vevay, Indiana, where she had lived until a month before. She had been a widow for something over a year. Her husband, a clerk in a hardware store, had died of a fever contracted, as it was said, from the bad water of the river towns, leaving her a small insurance of four hundred dollars and a debt to the undertaker which consumed nearly a third of it. The remainder she had husbanded with what care she could, but it had dwindled, as such sums will, under the steady pressure of rent and food and the hundred small necessities which the poor cannot escape. Now she had come to the city to find work, and, having found it after a fashion, at eight dollars a week in the office of a wholesale drug concern on Pearl Street, she had resolved at last to call upon her cousin.

It had cost her something to make this resolution. She and Lettie had been girls together upon their grandfather's farm near Madison, had slept in the same bed under the slanting roof of the upper room, had gone berrying and to the county fair, and had confided to each other those first fancies concerning young men which girls of fifteen hold so dear. That was nearly twenty years ago. Since then their fortunes had diverged as widely as the paths of two streams which, rising in the same meadow, flow the one into a broad river and the other into a marsh. Lettie had married well—a young man named Cranshaw, then a salesman for a furniture house, now one of its partners. Agnes had married Henry Moody. There had been letters at first, then fewer, then only a card at Christmas, and at last, for some five or six years, nothing at all. It was not that either had willed this silence. It had simply come about, as such things do, through the slow, insensible action of circumstance, which separates people more surely than any quarrel.

She found the number and paused before the gate. A boy was raking leaves upon the lawn of the next house, and she fancied that he looked at her curiously. There was a carriage standing at the curb a little farther on, with a coachman in a dark green coat sitting upon the box. She felt, as she lifted the latch, that she did not belong here, that anyone seeing her must know at a glance what she was and whence she had come, and she was half minded to turn back. Then she thought of the long ride down again, of her room in the boarding house on Ninth Street, of the evening which must be got through somehow, and she went up the walk and rang the bell.

The door was opened by a maid in a white cap and apron, a stout, red-cheeked girl of the kind which the German families of the city supplied in such numbers to the households of the well-to-do.

"Is Mrs. Cranshaw at home?" asked Agnes.

"Who shall I say, please?"

"Tell her it's her cousin—Agnes. Agnes Moody. She'll know."

The maid showed her into a front parlour and went away. Agnes sat down upon the edge of a plush chair and looked about her. It was a large room, heavily furnished after the manner of the time, with a carpet of red and gold, lace curtains at the windows, a black marble mantel upon which stood a gilt clock under a glass bell, and on the walls several oil paintings in deep frames—a landscape with cattle, a ship at sea, and a portrait of an elderly man whom she took to be some relative of Cranshaw's. There was a piano in one corner, with music open upon it, and upon a small table a great lamp with a painted globe. Everything was rich, everything was heavy, everything spoke of an ease of living which she had never known and now never expected to know. She could not help comparing it with the three rooms in Vevay where she had kept house for seven years, with their rag carpets and their cheap walnut set purchased upon the instalment plan, and the comparison gave her a dull ache which she could not have put into words.

It must not be supposed that Agnes was of an envious disposition, or that she had come to this house with any thought of gain. She had not. Her nature was rather simple and good, given to small kindnesses and unused to scheming. But the human heart is not proof against the evidence of the senses, and there is nothing which so instantly and so cruelly measures the difference between two lives as the furniture of a room. She had been, in her own town, a respectable woman, a little above the average of her neighbours in taste and bearing. Here she was nothing—a poor relation, an applicant, one who must be received with that particular graciousness which is reserved for those who can confer no benefit in return.

Presently there was a rustle upon the stair, and Lettie came in. She was a plump woman now, fuller of figure than Agnes remembered, with a round, pleasant face, a high colour, and hair done in the latest fashion, with a fringe over the forehead. She wore a house gown of dark blue silk, trimmed with lace at the throat and wrists, and upon one hand were two rings which caught the light from the window. For a moment the two women looked at each other, and in that moment each took in the other completely—the one seeing prosperity, the other seeing its opposite.

"Why, Agnes!" exclaimed Lettie, coming forward with both hands extended. "Of all people! I never was so surprised. Whatever brought you to Cincinnati?"

"I'm living here now," said Agnes, rising and allowing herself to be kissed upon the cheek. "I've been here nearly a month."

"A month! And you never came to see me before this? Sit down, sit down. Why, I can't get over it. Let me look at you." She held her off at arm's length and surveyed her with frank interest. "You're thinner, Agnes. You've grown thin."

"I suppose I have," said Agnes, smiling a little. "I've had a good deal to think about."

"Yes, I heard about Henry," said Lettie, her face taking on that expression of sympathy which is so readily assumed and so honestly felt in the first instant. "Aunt Sarah wrote me. I meant to write you, Agnes, I truly did, but we were going to Atlantic City just then, and one thing and another—you know how it is. I was so sorry."

"Thank you," said Agnes simply.

They sat down, Lettie upon a sofa and Agnes again upon the plush chair, and for a little while the conversation ran upon those matters which are always first to be disposed of between relatives long parted—the health of this one and that, who had married, who had died, who had moved away to Kansas. Aunt Sarah was still living at Madison, though she was crippled with rheumatism. Uncle Will had sold the farm and gone to live with his son in Indianapolis. The old house had been torn down, Lettie had heard, and a new one built in its place.

"Torn down!" said Agnes, with real regret. "I didn't know that."

"Oh, yes. Two years ago. Charlie and I drove over there once when we were visiting at Madison. You wouldn't know the place. They've cut down the orchard, and the spring house is gone."

"The spring house," repeated Agnes. A picture rose before her of a low stone building, cool and dim within, with crocks of milk and butter standing in the running water, and two girls in calico dresses sitting upon the step, their bare feet in the wet grass. "Do you remember how we used to hide in there when Grandpa wanted us to pick up potatoes?"

Lettie laughed heartily. "Don't I! And the time you fell in the trough and spoiled your new dress, and Grandma whipped you. My, but you cried!"

"You cried, too," said Agnes.

"Did I? I suppose I did. I always cried when you did."

For a few minutes they were girls again, and the room and its furnishings were forgotten. They spoke of the old Methodist church at the crossroads, of the camp meetings in the summer, of a young man named Ed Pierce who had walked home with first one and then the other of them, and who, as Lettie now related, had become a dentist in Louisville and grown very fat. There was a warmth in this which neither had anticipated, a renewal of something which both had supposed lost. Yet it could not last. The past is a country to which we may make brief excursions, but we cannot live there, and the present has a way of reasserting itself with a harshness proportionate to the pleasure of the escape.

It was Lettie who first returned to it.

"And what are you doing here, Agnes?" she asked, settling back among the cushions. "Are you staying with someone?"

"No. I have a room on Ninth Street. I'm working."

"Working!" Lettie's face showed a faint surprise, as though the idea of a relative of hers being employed for wages were a novel and not altogether agreeable one. "Where?"

"At Hollister and Bane's, the drug house. I keep books for them—or help to. I learned a little bookkeeping from Henry, and they were willing to take me on."

"Well, now," said Lettie, thoughtfully. "Do they pay you well?"

"Eight dollars," said Agnes. She said it plainly, without apology, but she felt the colour come into her face as she did so.

"Eight dollars a week," repeated Lettie, and there was in her voice the tone of one who hears of some curious condition of life in a far country. She had not, in fifteen years, had occasion to consider what eight dollars a week would buy. Her husband gave her thirty for the house alone, and she frequently complained that it did not go far enough. "Can you live on that?"

"Oh, yes. My room is two and a half, and I get my meals for three. It does very well."

"But your clothes, and everything?"

"I had some things," said Agnes. "I make them do."

Lettie looked at her cousin's dress, at the made-over serge and the small hat with its single feather, and for the first time the full meaning of the matter came home to her. She was not an unkind woman. She had a good heart, as such hearts are measured, and was given to charities of the more visible sort—to the Orphan Asylum fair and the Christmas baskets of her church. But she had lived so long in comfort that comfort had become, for her, the natural condition of mankind, and poverty a thing which happened to other people, chiefly to the improvident and the unlucky. That it should happen to one who had slept beside her under the eaves of her grandfather's house was a thing which disturbed her obscurely, as though it were a reflection upon herself.

"Agnes," she said, after a moment, "why didn't you write to me? Charlie might have done something. He knows ever so many people."

"I didn't like to," said Agnes.

"Didn't like to! Why, we're cousins."

"I know. But it's been so long, Lettie. I didn't know how you'd feel."

"How I'd feel!" Lettie's tone was one of injured affection, and yet beneath it there was something else—a faint relief that the question had not been put to her before, when it might have been less convenient. "You know I'd always be glad to see you. Always."

Agnes said nothing. She was thinking that in all the years since her marriage Lettie had never once asked her to come, though she must have known, through Aunt Sarah, how things went with her. She did not hold it against her cousin. It was only the way of the world, which she was beginning to understand. People who have much are not unkind to those who have little; they simply forget them. The prosperous live in a bright room, and the poor stand outside in the dark, and it is the nature of light that those within it cannot see beyond the windows.

The maid came in presently with tea upon a silver tray, and a plate of small cakes, and Lettie poured. Agnes took her cup and held it carefully, conscious of the thinness of the china and of her own hands, which were reddened at the knuckles from the cold water of her washbasin. Lettie's hands were white and soft, and she handled the pot with an ease which spoke of long habit.

"We have a girl and a woman who comes in to wash," Lettie observed, as though in answer to some question Agnes had not asked. "Charlie wanted me to have a cook as well, but I said no. I like to see to things myself. It's so hard to get good help."

"I suppose it is," said Agnes.

"You've no idea. The last girl we had stole a pair of my gloves and a silver spoon. Charlie wanted to have her arrested, but I said let her go. They're so ignorant, most of them."

Agnes sipped her tea and said nothing. She was thinking of the girls in the office at Hollister and Bane's, who wrapped packages and addressed labels for five dollars a week, and who sometimes, as she had heard them say among themselves, went without lunch to buy a ribbon. She did not think they were ignorant. She thought they were poor, which was a different thing, though she perceived that to Lettie the two words had come to mean very much the same.

They talked on. Lettie spoke of her children—a boy of twelve, who was at a military school in Kentucky, and a girl of nine, who was out just now at her music lesson. She spoke of their summer at Atlantic City, of the great hotels there and the board walk and the bathing, of a trip they had made the year before to New York, where they had stayed at the Fifth Avenue Hotel and seen a play by Mr. Daly. She spoke of these things not boastfully, but as one speaks of the ordinary furniture of one's existence, and it was this very naturalness which made them the more crushing to her listener. Agnes had never seen the ocean. She had never stayed in a hotel. The farthest she had travelled in her life was to Louisville, once, on an excursion boat, with Henry, in the second summer of their marriage.

"You ought to go East sometime, Agnes," said Lettie, with the generous thoughtlessness of the fortunate. "It would do you good."

"Perhaps I will," said Agnes, smiling faintly, "some day."

It was growing dusk now. The light at the windows had turned from grey to a deeper blue, and the maid came in and lighted the gas in the chandelier, which sprang up with a soft hiss and filled the room with a yellow glow. In this light the heavy furnishings took on a richer look, and the portrait of the elderly man upon the wall seemed to gaze down with an air of stern approval upon all that his descendants had accomplished. Agnes felt that she ought to go. She did not wish to stay until the husband should come in, nor to be asked to supper and so placed under an obligation she could not return. Yet she lingered, held by something she could not have named—a reluctance to go back into the cold and the dark, to the boarding house and its smells of cabbage and coal oil, to the narrow bed and the single gas jet and the long, quiet evening.

Before she could rise, however, the front door opened, and a man's step sounded in the hall.

"That's Charlie," said Lettie, brightening. "Now you'll see him. He's grown so stout, Agnes, you won't know him."

Mr. Cranshaw came in, rubbing his hands. He was a man of forty-five, broad and heavy, with a short brown beard and small, shrewd, good-natured eyes. He wore a suit of dark grey cloth, well cut, and a heavy watch-chain across his waistcoat, from which depended a Masonic charm. He had about him that air of genial authority which comes to men who have succeeded in trade and who feel that the world, on the whole, is a very sensible arrangement.

"Well, well," he said, when Lettie had explained. "Lettie's cousin, eh? I remember now. I've heard her speak of you often. Glad to know you, Mrs. Moody. Very glad." He shook her hand heartily and stood before the fire with his hands clasped behind him. "And you're living in town, you say?"

"Yes," said Agnes.

"She's working at Hollister and Bane's, Charlie," said Lettie. "Keeping books. For eight dollars a week."

"Hollister and Bane's," said Cranshaw, reflectively. "I know Bane. Know him well. Sharp man. Close, too." He looked at Agnes with a kind of practical sympathy, as a man might regard a good horse that had been badly placed. "Eight dollars isn't much. Isn't much at all for a woman that can keep books. I'll tell you what, Mrs. Moody. I'll speak to a man I know over at the Gibson House. They need somebody in the office there, I believe. Might be ten or twelve in it. I'll speak to him."

"That's very kind of you," said Agnes.

"Not at all. Not at all. Glad to do it." He was pleased with himself, as men are when they have discovered an opportunity for benevolence which costs them nothing but a word. "You come up to dinner some Sunday, and I'll let you know what he says. Won't she, Lettie?"

"Of course she will," said Lettie warmly. "You must, Agnes. Come next Sunday."

Agnes said that she would, and rose to go. They pressed her to stay to supper, but she would not, giving as her reason that her landlady expected her. This was not true, but it was the kind of untruth which pride invents for its protection. Lettie went with her to the door and kissed her again upon the cheek.

"Now don't you forget," she said. "Sunday. And Agnes—" she hesitated, and then, with a quick movement, pressed something into her cousin's hand—"get yourself something. A pair of gloves or something. Please. For old times."

Agnes looked down. It was a five-dollar gold piece. She felt the blood rush to her face, and for an instant she was on the point of giving it back. Then she thought of her shoes, which were worn through at the sole and which she had been stuffing with paper for a week, and of the coming winter, and of the eight dollars which never quite reached the end of the week. Her fingers closed upon the coin.

"Thank you, Lettie," she said, in a low voice.

"Don't thank me. Goodness! It's nothing." And Lettie, flushed and happy with the consciousness of having done a good thing, stood in the lighted doorway and waved as her cousin went down the walk.

The night had come on clear and cold. Above the roofs of the great houses the stars were out, and the street lamps made little pools of light along the pavement. From the windows on either side came the glow of gas and the sound, here and there, of a piano. Agnes walked slowly toward the corner where the car would pass, holding the gold piece tightly in her hand within her muff. She was not unhappy, exactly. Her cousin had been kind—kinder than she had expected. The husband had promised to speak for her. There would be a dinner on Sunday, with good food and a warm room. And yet there was in her heart a feeling which she could not shake off, a sense of having been weighed and measured and found wanting, of having come as an equal and gone away as a dependent. She did not blame Lettie. She did not blame anyone. It was simply the way things were.

What she did not understand, and could not have understood, was that the force which had divided them was neither virtue nor vice, neither merit nor its lack, but chance—the blind chance which had sent one young man to a furniture house and another to a hardware store in a dying river town, which had given to one a constitution proof against fever and to the other none. Lettie had done nothing to deserve her silk gown and her silver tea service, and Agnes nothing to merit her made-over serge. Yet the world, which is not given to such reflections, would judge them both by these things, and they themselves, in time, would come to judge each other so. That is the chief cruelty of fortune: not that it raises some and lowers others, but that it persuades both the raised and the lowered that the arrangement is just.

The car came clanking up the hill, its single lamp swinging, and she got on and sat in a corner and looked out at the passing houses. Below, as the car descended, the city spread out before her, a great dark mass pricked with innumerable lights, and beyond it the river, black and silent, flowing on toward Vevay and Madison and all the little towns where she had been young. She thought of the spring house, of the cool water running over the stones, of two girls sitting upon the step with their feet in the grass. Then the car swung around a corner, the river was lost to view, and she was among the tenements again, with their smells and their noises and their dim, crowded windows, and she got down at Ninth Street and went up to her room.

author: Theodore Dreiser
content:
Here are three excerpts of Theodore Dreiser's writing, to show you their style:

Excerpt 1: Once across the river and into the wholesale district, she glanced about her for some likely door at which to apply. As she contemplated the wide windows and imposing signs, she became conscious of being gazed upon and understood for what she was—a wage-seeker. She had never done this thing before, and lacked courage. To avoid a certain indefinable shame she felt at being caught spying about for a position, she quickened her steps and assumed an air of indifference supposedly common to one upon an errand. In this way she passed many manufacturing and wholesale houses without once glancing in. At last, after several blocks of walking, she felt that this would not do, and began to look about again, though without relaxing her pace. A little way on she saw a great door which, for some reason, attracted her attention. It was ornamented by a small brass sign, and seemed to be the entrance to a vast hive of six or seven floors. “Perhaps,” she thought, “they may want some one,” and crossed over to enter. When she came within a score of feet of the desired goal, she saw through the window a young man in a grey checked suit. That he had anything to do with the concern, she could not tell, but because he happened to be looking in her direction her weakening heart misgave her and she hurried by, too overcome with shame to enter. Over the way stood a great six-story structure, labelled Storm and King, which she viewed with rising hope. It was a wholesale dry goods concern and employed women. She could see them moving about now and then upon the upper floors. This place she decided to enter, no matter what. She crossed over and walked directly toward the entrance. As she did so, two men came out and paused in the door. A telegraph messenger in blue dashed past her and up the few steps that led to the entrance and disappeared. Several pedestrians out of the hurrying throng which filled the sidewalks passed about her as she paused, hesitating. She looked helplessly around, and then, seeing herself observed, retreated. It was too difficult a task. She could not go past them. So severe a defeat told sadly upon her nerves. Her feet carried her mechanically forward, every foot of her progress being a satisfactory portion of a flight which she gladly made. Block after block passed by. Upon streetlamps at the various corners she read names such as Madison, Monroe, La Salle, Clark, Dearborn, State, and still she went, her feet beginning to tire upon the broad stone flagging. She was pleased in part that the streets were bright and clean. The morning sun, shining down with steadily increasing warmth, made the shady side of the streets pleasantly cool. She looked at the blue sky overhead with more realisation of its charm than had ever come to her before. Her cowardice began to trouble her in a way. She turned back, resolving to hunt up Storm and King and enter. On the way, she encountered a great wholesale shoe company, through the broad plate windows of which she saw an enclosed executive department, hidden by frosted glass. Without this enclosure, but just within the street entrance, sat a grey-haired gentleman at a small table, with a large open ledger before him. She walked by this institution several times hesitating, but, finding herself unobserved, faltered past the screen door and stood humbly waiting.

“Well, young lady,” observed the old gentleman, looking at her somewhat kindly, “what is it you wish?”

“I am, that is, do you—I mean, do you need any help?” she stammered.

“Not just at present,” he answered smiling. “Not just at present. Come in some time next week. Occasionally we need some one.” She received the answer in silence and backed awkwardly out. The pleasant nature of her reception rather astonished her. She had expected that it would be more difficult, that something cold and harsh would be said—she knew not what. That she had not been put to shame and made to feel her unfortunate position, seemed remarkable. Somewhat encouraged, she ventured into another large structure. It was a clothing company, and more people were in evidence—well-dressed men of forty and more, surrounded by brass railings. An office boy approached her.

“Who is it you wish to see?” he asked.

“I want to see the manager,” she said. He ran away and spoke to one of a group of three men who were conferring together. One of these came towards her.

“Well?” he said coldly. The greeting drove all courage from her at once.

“Do you need any help?” she stammered.

“No,” he replied abruptly, and turned upon his heel. She went foolishly out, the office boy deferentially swinging the door for her, and gladly sank into the obscuring crowd. It was a severe setback to her recently pleased mental state. Now she walked quite aimlessly for a time, turning here and there, seeing one great company after another, but finding no courage to prosecute her single inquiry. High noon came, and with it hunger. She hunted out an unassuming restaurant and entered, but was disturbed to find that the prices were exorbitant for the size of her purse. A bowl of soup was all that she could afford, and, with this quickly eaten, she went out again. It restored her strength somewhat and made her moderately bold to pursue the search. In walking a few blocks to fix upon some probable place, she again encountered the firm of Storm and King, and this time managed to get in. Some gentlemen were conferring close at hand, but took no notice of her. She was left standing, gazing nervously upon the floor. When the limit of her distress had been nearly reached, she was beckoned to by a man at one of the many desks within the near-by railing.

“Who is it you wish to see?” he required.

“Why, any one, if you please,” she answered. “I am looking for something to do.”

“Oh, you want to see Mr. McManus,” he returned. “Sit down,” and he pointed to a chair against the neighbouring wall. He went on leisurely writing, until after a time a short, stout gentleman came in from the street.

“Mr. McManus,” called the man at the desk, “this young woman wants to see you.” The short gentleman turned about towards Carrie, and she arose and came forward.

“What can I do for you, miss?” he inquired, surveying her curiously.

“I want to know if I can get a position,” she inquired.

“As what?” he asked.

“Not as anything in particular,” she faltered.

“Have you ever had any experience in the wholesale dry goods business?” he questioned.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Are you a stenographer or typewriter?”

“No, sir.”

“Well, we haven’t anything here,” he said. “We employ only experienced help.” She began to step backward toward the door, when something about her plaintive face attracted him.

“Have you ever worked at anything before?” he inquired.

“No, sir,” she said.

“Well, now, it’s hardly possible that you would get anything to do in a wholesale house of this kind. Have you tried the department stores?” She acknowledged that she had not.

“Well, if I were you,” he said, looking at her rather genially, “I would try the department stores. They often need young women as clerks.”

“Thank you,” she said, her whole nature relieved by this spark of friendly interest.

“Yes,” he said, as she moved toward the door, “you try the department stores,” and off he went. At that time the department store was in its earliest form of successful operation, and there were not many. The first three in the United States, established about 1884, were in Chicago. Carrie was familiar with the names of several through the advertisements in the “Daily News,” and now proceeded to seek them. The words of Mr. McManus had somehow managed to restore her courage, which had fallen low, and she dared to hope that this new line would offer her something. Some time she spent in wandering up and down, thinking to encounter the buildings by chance, so readily is the mind, bent upon prosecuting a hard but needful errand, eased by that self-deception which the semblance of search, without the reality, gives. At last she inquired of a police officer, and was directed to proceed “two blocks up,” where she would find “The Fair.” The nature of these vast retail combinations, should they ever permanently disappear, will form an interesting chapter in the commercial history of our nation. Such a flowering out of a modest trade principle the world had never witnessed up to that time. They were along the line of the most effective retail organisation, with hundreds of stores coordinated into one and laid out upon the most imposing and economic basis. They were handsome, bustling, successful affairs, with a host of clerks and a swarm of patrons. Carrie passed along the busy aisles, much affected by the remarkable displays of trinkets, dress goods, stationery, and jewelry. Each separate counter was a show place of dazzling interest and attraction. She could not help feeling the claim of each trinket and valuable upon her personally, and yet she did not stop. There was nothing there which she could not have used—nothing which she did not long to own. The dainty slippers and stockings, the delicately frilled skirts and petticoats, the laces, ribbons, hair-combs, purses, all touched her with individual desire, and she felt keenly the fact that not any of these things were in the range of her purchase. She was a work-seeker, an outcast without employment, one whom the average employee could tell at a glance was poor and in need of a situation. It must not be thought that any one could have mistaken her for a nervous, sensitive, high-strung nature, cast unduly upon a cold, calculating, and unpoetic world. Such certainly she was not. But women are peculiarly sensitive to their adornment. Not only did Carrie feel the drag of desire for all which was new and pleasing in apparel for women, but she noticed too, with a touch at the heart, the fine ladies who elbowed and ignored her, brushing past in utter disregard of her presence, themselves eagerly enlisted in the materials which the store contained. Carrie was not familiar with the appearance of her more fortunate sisters of the city. Neither had she before known the nature and appearance of the shop girls with whom she now compared poorly. They were pretty in the main, some even handsome, with an air of independence and indifference which added, in the case of the more favoured, a certain piquancy. Their clothes were neat, in many instances fine, and wherever she encountered the eye of one it was only to recognise in it a keen analysis of her own position—her individual shortcomings of dress and that shadow of manner which she thought must hang about her and make clear to all who and what she was. A flame of envy lighted in her heart. She realised in a dim way how much the city held—wealth, fashion, ease—every adornment for women, and she longed for dress and beauty with a whole heart. On the second floor were the managerial offices, to which, after some inquiry, she was now directed. There she found other girls ahead of her, applicants like herself, but with more of that self-satisfied and independent air which experience of the city lends; girls who scrutinised her in a painful manner. After a wait of perhaps three-quarters of an hour, she was called in turn.

“Now,” said a sharp, quick-mannered Jew, who was sitting at a roll-top desk near the window, “have you ever worked in any other store?”

“No, sir,” said Carrie.

“Oh, you haven’t,” he said, eyeing her keenly.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Well, we prefer young women just now with some experience. I guess we can’t use you.” Carrie stood waiting a moment, hardly certain whether the interview had terminated.

“Don’t wait!” he exclaimed. “Remember we are very busy here.” Carrie began to move quickly to the door.

“Hold on,” he said, calling her back. “Give me your name and address. We want girls occasionally.” When she had gotten safely into the street, she could scarcely restrain the tears. It was not so much the particular rebuff which she had just experienced, but the whole abashing trend of the day. She was tired and nervous. She abandoned the thought of appealing to the other department stores and now wandered on, feeling a certain safety and relief in mingling with the crowd. In her indifferent wandering she turned into Jackson Street, not far from the river, and was keeping her way along the south side of that imposing thoroughfare, when a piece of wrapping paper, written on with marking ink and tacked up on the door, attracted her attention. It read, “Girls wanted—wrappers & stitchers.” She hesitated a moment, then entered. The firm of Speigelheim & Co., makers of boys’ caps, occupied one floor of the building, fifty feet in width and some eighty feet in depth. It was a place rather dingily lighted, the darkest portions having incandescent lights, filled with machines and work benches. At the latter laboured quite a company of girls and some men. The former were drabby-looking creatures, stained in face with oil and dust, clad in thin, shapeless, cotton dresses and shod with more or less worn shoes. Many of them had their sleeves rolled up, revealing bare arms, and in some cases, owing to the heat, their dresses were open at the neck. They were a fair type of nearly the lowest order of shop-girls—careless, slouchy, and more or less pale from confinement. They were not timid, however; were rich in curiosity, and strong in daring and slang. Carrie looked about her, very much disturbed and quite sure that she did not want to work here. Aside from making her uncomfortable by sidelong glances, no one paid her the least attention. She waited until the whole department was aware of her presence. Then some word was sent around, and a foreman, in an apron and shirt sleeves, the latter rolled up to his shoulders, approached.

“Do you want to see me?” he asked.

“Do you need any help?” said Carrie, already learning directness of address.

“Do you know how to stitch caps?” he returned.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Have you ever had any experience at this kind of work?” he inquired. She answered that she had not.

“Well,” said the foreman, scratching his ear meditatively, “we do need a stitcher. We like experienced help, though. We’ve hardly got time to break people in.” He paused and looked away out of the window. “We might, though, put you at finishing,” he concluded reflectively.

“How much do you pay a week?” ventured Carrie, emboldened by a certain softness in the man’s manner and his simplicity of address.

“Three and a half,” he answered.

“Oh,” she was about to exclaim, but checked herself and allowed her thoughts to die without expression.

“We’re not exactly in need of anybody,” he went on vaguely, looking her over as one would a package. “You can come on Monday morning, though,” he added, “and I’ll put you to work.”

“Thank you,” said Carrie weakly.

“If you come, bring an apron,” he added. He walked away and left her standing by the elevator, never so much as inquiring her name. While the appearance of the shop and the announcement of the price paid per week operated very much as a blow to Carrie’s fancy, the fact that work of any kind was offered after so rude a round of experience was gratifying. She could not begin to believe that she would take the place, modest as her aspirations were. She had been used to better than that. Her mere experience and the free out-of-door life of the country caused her nature to revolt at such confinement. Dirt had never been her share. Her sister’s flat was clean. This place was grimy and low, the girls were careless and hardened. They must be bad-minded and hearted, she imagined. Still, a place had been offered her. Surely Chicago was not so bad if she could find one place in one day. She might find another and better later. Her subsequent experiences were not of a reassuring nature, however. From all the more pleasing or imposing places she was turned away abruptly with the most chilling formality. In others where she applied only the experienced were required. She met with painful rebuffs, the most trying of which had been in a manufacturing cloak house, where she had gone to the fourth floor to inquire.

“No, no,” said the foreman, a rough, heavily built individual, who looked after a miserably lighted workshop, “we don’t want any one. Don’t come here.”

Excerpt 2: Passion in a man of Hurstwood’s nature takes a vigorous form. It is no musing, dreamy thing. There is none of the tendency to sing outside of my lady’s window—to languish and repine in the face of difficulties. In the night he was long getting to sleep because of too much thinking, and in the morning he was early awake, seizing with alacrity upon the same dear subject and pursuing it with vigour. He was out of sorts physically, as well as disordered mentally, for did he not delight in a new manner in his Carrie, and was not Drouet in the way? Never was man more harassed than he by the thoughts of his love being held by the elated, flush-mannered drummer. He would have given anything, it seemed to him, to have the complication ended—to have Carrie acquiesce to an arrangement which would dispose of Drouet effectually and forever. What to do. He dressed thinking. He moved about in the same chamber with his wife, unmindful of her presence. At breakfast he found himself without an appetite. The meat to which he helped himself remained on his plate untouched. His coffee grew cold, while he scanned the paper indifferently. Here and there he read a little thing, but remembered nothing. Jessica had not yet come down. His wife sat at one end of the table revolving thoughts of her own in silence. A new servant had been recently installed and had forgot the napkins. On this account the silence was irritably broken by a reproof.

“I’ve told you about this before, Maggie,” said Mrs. Hurstwood. “I’m not going to tell you again.” Hurstwood took a glance at his wife. She was frowning. Just now her manner irritated him excessively. Her next remark was addressed to him.

“Have you made up your mind, George, when you will take your vacation?” It was customary for them to discuss the regular summer outing at this season of the year.

“Not yet,” he said, “I’m very busy just now.”

“Well, you’ll want to make up your mind pretty soon, won’t you, if we’re going?” she returned.

“I guess we have a few days yet,” he said.

“Hmff,” she returned. “Don’t wait until the season’s over.” She stirred in aggravation as she said this.

“There you go again,” he observed. “One would think I never did anything, the way you begin.”

“Well, I want to know about it,” she reiterated.

“You’ve got a few days yet,” he insisted. “You’ll not want to start before the races are over.” He was irritated to think that this should come up when he wished to have his thoughts for other purposes.

“Well, we may. Jessica doesn’t want to stay until the end of the races.”

“What did you want with a season ticket, then?”

“Uh!” she said, using the sound as an exclamation of disgust, “I’ll not argue with you,” and therewith arose to leave the table.

“Say,” he said, rising, putting a note of determination in his voice which caused her to delay her departure, “what’s the matter with you of late? Can’t I talk with you any more?”

“Certainly, you can talk with me,” she replied, laying emphasis on the word.

“Well, you wouldn’t think so by the way you act. Now, you want to know when I’ll be ready—not for a month yet. Maybe not then.”

“We’ll go without you.”

“You will, eh?” he sneered.

“Yes, we will.” He was astonished at the woman’s determination, but it only irritated him the more.

“Well, we’ll see about that. It seems to me you’re trying to run things with a pretty high hand of late. You talk as though you settled my affairs for me. Well, you don’t. You don’t regulate anything that’s connected with me. If you want to go, go, but you won’t hurry me by any such talk as that.” He was thoroughly aroused now. His dark eyes snapped, and he crunched his paper as he laid it down. Mrs. Hurstwood said nothing more. He was just finishing when she turned on her heel and went out into the hall and upstairs. He paused for a moment, as if hesitating, then sat down and drank a little coffee, and thereafter arose and went for his hat and gloves upon the main floor. His wife had really not anticipated a row of this character. She had come down to the breakfast table feeling a little out of sorts with herself and revolving a scheme which she had in her mind. Jessica had called her attention to the fact that the races were not what they were supposed to be. The social opportunities were not what they had thought they would be this year. The beautiful girl found going every day a dull thing. There was an earlier exodus this year of people who were anybody to the watering places and Europe. In her own circle of acquaintances several young men in whom she was interested had gone to Waukesha. She began to feel that she would like to go too, and her mother agreed with her. Accordingly, Mrs. Hurstwood decided to broach the subject. She was thinking this over when she came down to the table, but for some reason the atmosphere was wrong. She was not sure, after it was all over, just how the trouble had begun. She was determined now, however, that her husband was a brute, and that, under no circumstances, would she let this go by unsettled. She would have more lady-like treatment or she would know why. For his part, the manager was loaded with the care of this new argument until he reached his office and started from there to meet Carrie. Then the other complications of love, desire, and opposition possessed him. His thoughts fled on before him upon eagles’ wings. He could hardly wait until he should meet Carrie face to face. What was the night, after all, without her—what the day? She must and should be his. For her part, Carrie had experienced a world of fancy and feeling since she had left him, the night before. She had listened to Drouet’s enthusiastic maunderings with much regard for that part which concerned herself, with very little for that which affected his own gain. She kept him at such lengths as she could, because her thoughts were with her own triumph. She felt Hurstwood’s passion as a delightful background to her own achievement, and she wondered what he would have to say. She was sorry for him, too, with that peculiar sorrow which finds something complimentary to itself in the misery of another. She was now experiencing the first shades of feeling of that subtle change which removes one out of the ranks of the suppliants into the lines of the dispensers of charity. She was, all in all, exceedingly happy. On the morrow, however, there was nothing in the papers concerning the event, and, in view of the flow of common, everyday things about, it now lost a shade of the glow of the previous evening. Drouet himself was not talking so much of as for her. He felt instinctively that, for some reason or other, he needed reconstruction in her regard.

“I think,” he said, as he spruced around their chambers the next morning, preparatory to going down town, “that I’ll straighten out that little deal of mine this month and then we’ll get married. I was talking with Mosher about that yesterday.”

“No, you won’t,” said Carrie, who was coming to feel a certain faint power to jest with the drummer.

“Yes, I will,” he exclaimed, more feelingly than usual, adding, with the tone of one who pleads, “Don’t you believe what I’ve told you?” Carrie laughed a little.

“Of course I do,” she answered. Drouet’s assurance now misgave him. Shallow as was his mental observation, there was that in the things which had happened which made his little power of analysis useless. Carrie was still with him, but not helpless and pleading. “Yes,” said Carrie. They walked on as if bound for some objective point, while Hurstwood drank in the radiance of her presence. The rustle of her pretty skirt was like music to him.

“Glad you liked them,” he answered, simply.

“No,” he said, in his sanest moments, “I can’t do it. I’ll get something else and save up.” This getting-something proposition complicated itself the moment he began to think of what it was he wanted to do. Manage a place? Into a place important enough to need such a manager he had not money enough to buy. Nevertheless, he started out. The mere getting up and down, if long continued, produced this result. The fact that people took him to be better off than he was, he well understood. It was so painfully clear to him that it retarded his search. Not that he wished to be less well-appearing, but that he was ashamed to belie his appearance by incongruous appeals. So he hesitated, wondering what to do. He thought of the hotels, but instantly he remembered that he had had no experience as a clerk, and, what was more important, no acquaintances or friends in that line to whom he could go. He did know some hotel owners in several cities, including New York, but they knew of his dealings with Fitzgerald and Moy. He could not apply to them. He thought of other lines suggested by large buildings or businesses which he knew of—wholesale groceries, hardware, insurance concerns, and the like—but he had had no experience. How to go about getting anything was a bitter thought. Would he have to go personally and ask; wait outside an office door, and, then, distinguished and affluent looking, announce that he was looking for something to do? He strained painfully at the thought. No, he could not do that. He really strolled about, thinking, and then, the weather being cold, stepped into a hotel. He knew hotels well enough to know that any decent individual was welcome to a chair in the lobby. This was in the Broadway Central, which was then one of the most important hotels in the city. Taking a chair here was a painful thing to him. To think he should come to this! He had heard loungers about hotels called chairwarmers. He had called them that himself in his day. But here he was, despite the possibility of meeting some one who knew him, shielding himself from cold and the weariness of the streets in a hotel lobby.

“I can’t do this way,” he said to himself. “There’s no use of my starting out mornings without first thinking up some place to go. I’ll think of some places and then look them up.” It occurred to him that the positions of bartenders were sometimes open, but he put this out of his mind. Bartender—he, the ex-manager! It grew awfully dull sitting in the hotel lobby, and so at four he went home. He tried to put on a business air as he went in, but it was a feeble imitation. The rocking chair in the dining-room was comfortable. He sank into it gladly, with several papers he had bought, and began to read. As she was going through the room to begin preparing dinner, Carrie said:
“The man was here for the rent to-day.”

“Oh, you haven’t,” he said, eyeing her keenly.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Do you want to see me?” he asked.

“Do you need any help?” said Carrie, already learning directness of address.

“Do you know how to stitch caps?” he returned.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Have you ever had any experience at this kind of work?” he inquired. She answered that she had not.

“Well,” said the foreman, scratching his ear meditatively, “we do need a stitcher. We like experienced help, though. We’ve hardly got time to break people in.” He paused and looked away out of the window. “We might, though, put you at finishing,” he concluded reflectively.

“How much do you pay a week?” ventured Carrie, emboldened by a certain softness in the man’s manner and his simplicity of address.

“Three and a half,” he answered.

“Oh,” she was about to exclaim, but checked herself and allowed her thoughts to die without expression.

“We’re not exactly in need of anybody,” he went on vaguely, looking her over as one would a package. “You can come on Monday morning, though,” he added, “and I’ll put you to work.”

“Thank you,” said Carrie weakly.

“If you come, bring an apron,” he added. He walked away and left her standing by the elevator, never so much as inquiring her name. She could not begin to believe that she would take the place, modest as her aspirations were. She had been used to better than that. Her mere experience and the free out-of-door life of the country caused her nature to revolt at such confinement. Dirt had never been her share. Her sister’s flat was clean. This place was grimy and low, the girls were careless and hardened. They must be bad-minded and hearted, she imagined. Still, a place had been offered her. Surely Chicago was not so bad if she could find one place in one day. She might find another and better later. Her subsequent experiences were not of a reassuring nature, however. She met with painful rebuffs, the most trying of which had been in a manufacturing cloak house, where she had gone to the fourth floor to inquire.

“No, no,” said the foreman, a rough, heavily built individual, who looked after a miserably lighted workshop, “we don’t want any one. Don’t come here.”

“Good-bye!” he said finally, and went out. This was the first strong result of the situation between them, but with the nearing of the last day of the business the gloom became almost a permanent thing. Hurstwood could not conceal his feelings about the matter. Carrie could not help wondering where she was drifting. It got so that they talked even less than usual, and yet it was not Hurstwood who felt any objection to Carrie. It was Carrie who shied away from him. This he noticed. It aroused an objection to her becoming indifferent to him. He made the possibility of friendly intercourse almost a giant task, and then noticed with discontent that Carrie added to it by her manner and made it more impossible. At last the final day came. When it actually arrived, Hurstwood, who had got his mind into such a state where a thunderclap and raging storm would have seemed highly appropriate, was rather relieved to find that it was a plain, ordinary day. The sun shone, the temperature was pleasant. He felt, as he came to the breakfast table, that it wasn’t so terrible, after all.

“Well,” he said to Carrie, “to-day’s my last day on earth.” Carrie smiled in answer to his humour. Hurstwood glanced over his paper rather gayly. He seemed to have lost a load.

“I’ll go down for a little while,” he said after breakfast, “and then I’ll look around. To-morrow I’ll spend the whole day looking about. I think I can get something, now this thing’s off my hands.” He went out smiling and visited the place. Shaughnessy was there. They had made all arrangements to share according to their interests. When, however, he had been there several hours, gone out three more, and returned, his elation had departed. As much as he had objected to the place, now that it was no longer to exist, he felt sorry. He wished that things were different. Shaughnessy was coolly businesslike.

“Well,” he said at five o’clock, “we might as well count the change and divide.” They did so. The fixtures had already been sold and the sum divided.

“Good-night,” said Hurstwood at the final moment, in a last effort to be genial.

“So long,” said Shaughnessy, scarcely deigning a notice. Thus the Warren Street arrangement was permanently concluded. Carrie had prepared a good dinner at the flat, but after his ride up, Hurstwood was in a solemn and reflective mood.

“Well?” said Carrie, inquisitively.

“I’m out of that,” he answered, taking off his coat. As she looked at him, she wondered what his financial state was now. They ate and talked a little.

“Will you have enough to buy in anywhere else?” asked Carrie.

“No,” he said. “I’ll have to get something else and save up.”

“It would be nice if you could get some place,” said Carrie, prompted by anxiety and hope.

“I guess I will,” he said reflectively. For some days thereafter he put on his overcoat regularly in the morning and sallied forth. On these ventures he first consoled himself with the thought that with the seven hundred dollars he had he could still make some advantageous arrangement. He thought about going to some brewery, which, as he knew, frequently controlled saloons which they leased, and get them to help him. Then he remembered that he would have to pay out several hundred any way for fixtures and that he would have nothing left for his monthly expenses. It was costing him nearly eighty dollars a month to live.

“No,” he said, in his sanest moments, “I can’t do it. I’ll get something else and save up.” This getting-something proposition complicated itself the moment he began to think of what it was he wanted to do. Manage a place? Where should he get such a position? The papers contained no requests for managers. Such positions, he knew well enough, were either secured by long years of service or were bought with a half or third interest. Into a place important enough to need such a manager he had not money enough to buy. Nevertheless, he started out. His clothes were very good and his appearance still excellent, but it involved the trouble of deluding. People, looking at him, imagined instantly that a man of his age, stout and well dressed, must be well off. He appeared a comfortable owner of something, a man from whom the common run of mortals could well expect gratuities. Being now forty-three years of age, and comfortably built, walking was not easy. He had not been used to exercise for many years. His legs tired, his shoulders ached, and his feet pained him at the close of the day, even when he took street cars in almost every direction. The mere getting up and down, if long continued, produced this result. The fact that people took him to be better off than he was, he well understood. It was so painfully clear to him that it retarded his search. Not that he wished to be less well-appearing, but that he was ashamed to belie his appearance by incongruous appeals. So he hesitated, wondering what to do. He thought of the hotels, but instantly he remembered that he had had no experience as a clerk, and, what was more important, no acquaintances or friends in that line to whom he could go. He did know some hotel owners in several cities, including New York, but they knew of his dealings with Fitzgerald and Moy. He could not apply to them. He thought of other lines suggested by large buildings or businesses which he knew of—wholesale groceries, hardware, insurance concerns, and the like—but he had had no experience. How to go about getting anything was a bitter thought. Would he have to go personally and ask; wait outside an office door, and, then, distinguished and affluent looking, announce that he was looking for something to do? He strained painfully at the thought. No, he could not do that. He really strolled about, thinking, and then, the weather being cold, stepped into a hotel. He knew hotels well enough to know that any decent individual was welcome to a chair in the lobby. This was in the Broadway Central, which was then one of the most important hotels in the city. Taking a chair here was a painful thing to him. To think he should come to this! He had heard loungers about hotels called chairwarmers. He had called them that himself in his day. But here he was, despite the possibility of meeting some one who knew him, shielding himself from cold and the weariness of the streets in a hotel lobby.

“I can’t do this way,” he said to himself. “There’s no use of my starting out mornings without first thinking up some place to go. I’ll think of some places and then look them up.” It occurred to him that the positions of bartenders were sometimes open, but he put this out of his mind. Bartender—he, the ex-manager! It grew awfully dull sitting in the hotel lobby, and so at four he went home. He tried to put on a business air as he went in, but it was a feeble imitation. The rocking chair in the dining-room was comfortable. He sank into it gladly, with several papers he had bought, and began to read. As she was going through the room to begin preparing dinner, Carrie said:
“The man was here for the rent to-day.”

The house of Martin Kessler stood in a row of six of its kind on Lincoln Street, not far from the place where that thoroughfare crosses Twelfth. It was a two-story frame affair, painted a dull drab which had once been grey, with a narrow porch in front and a small yard behind, in which a few stalks of hollyhock struggled against the soot that drifted down continually from the shops along the river. The rent was eleven dollars a month, a sum which Kessler paid promptly upon the first of each month and which he never once handed over without a certain grim satisfaction that he was able to do so. He was a pattern-maker at the Wells foundry, earning fourteen dollars a week, and he had been earning it for six years. It was his ambition, cherished in silence and spoken of only to his wife upon rare evenings, to own a house of his own somewhere farther out, perhaps in the neighbourhood of Humboldt Park, where the lots were still cheap and the air, as he had been told, was clean. Toward this end he saved. He saved as some men pray, regularly, without great joy, and with a feeling that the thing was right and that its neglect would bring a punishment not easily defined.

Men of Kessler's type are not uncommon in the working populations of our great cities. They are the product of a peasant ancestry transplanted, and they carry with them into the clangour of the factory and the street a set of notions concerning thrift, honesty, and the obedience of children which were well enough suited to the village and the field, but which the city, with its thousand lures and its endless display of desirable things, tends constantly to undermine. Kessler did not know this. He knew only that what he had been taught was right, and that his father had taught it to him with a strap. He was not a cruel man. He was, in the main, rather a kindly one, slow of speech, heavy of movement, and given to long silences in which he sat with his pipe upon the back step and looked at nothing. But he had fixed ideas, and when these were crossed he became hard, almost frighteningly so, with that hardness which comes not of malice but of a mind that has never been called upon to examine itself.

His son Willie was seven years of age at the time of which we write. He was a thin, light-haired boy with large grey eyes and a way of standing with one foot upon the other which his mother found endearing and his father found irritating. He went to the Garfield school, three blocks away, and upon his way there and back he passed a little shop kept by a man named Rubel, who sold candy, newspapers, tobacco, and a variety of small toys arranged in a window none too clean. It was this window which had become, for some weeks past, the centre of Willie's world. In it, among the marbles and the jackstraws and the paper masks, lay a top—a red-and-yellow top with a brass point, wound about with a white cord, and marked upon a slip of pasteboard, "10c." He had looked at it in the morning and looked at it again at noon, and upon the way home he had stood before it until the shopman, seeing him, had come to the door and asked him what he wanted. Willie had fled. He did not know what he wanted, except that he wanted the top, and that the wanting of it had become a thing which he carried about with him all day, as one carries an ache.

It must not be supposed that the boy had any clear notion of wrongdoing in what followed. A child's mind does not work upon such lines. Desire, in the young, is a simple and imperious thing, and the barriers which the adult world erects against it are understood only dimly, as so many inexplicable obstacles put there by persons who are larger and who do not see. Willie knew that his mother kept her purse in the drawer of the kitchen table, beneath the folded dish-towels. He had seen her take money from it a hundred times—for the milkman, for the iceman, for the boy who brought the evening paper. He knew that there was much money in it, as it seemed to him, and that ten cents was a very little part of much. On a Tuesday afternoon in October, when his mother had gone up to the second floor to look after the baby, who was ill with a cold, he opened the drawer, found the purse, and took from it a dime. His hand trembled as he did so, and he looked once over his shoulder at the stairway, but he did not stop. He closed the drawer softly and went out into the street.

The purchase of the top was accomplished with an ease which astonished him. Mr. Rubel took the dime without a word, reached into the window, and handed the thing over. Willie went off down the block clutching it, his heart beating with a strange mixture of triumph and dread. He did not dare to spin it in front of the house. He went instead around the corner into Thirteenth Street, where there was a stretch of board sidewalk before a vacant lot, and there, with the cord wound clumsily and his tongue between his teeth, he set it going. It spun beautifully. The red and yellow merged into a kind of orange blur, and the brass point hummed upon the boards. He spun it again and again. Two other boys came up and watched him, and one of them asked to try it, and Willie, with the air of a proprietor, allowed him. For the better part of an hour he was as happy as he had ever been in his life.

It was Mrs. Kessler who discovered the loss. She was a careful woman, careful by necessity rather than by nature, and she knew to the penny what her purse contained. When she went to it at five o'clock to pay the paper boy, she found it short. She counted it twice, standing by the window in the failing light, and then she stood a moment with her hand against her cheek, thinking. She did not want to believe what came into her mind. Willie had come in a little before and gone straight up to his room, which was unusual for him, and he had not asked, as he always did, what there was for supper. She went up the stairs slowly. The boy was sitting on the edge of his bed, and as she came in he thrust something hastily beneath the pillow.

"What have you got there, Willie?" she asked.

"Nothing," said the boy.

"Let me see it."

He did not move, and she went over and lifted the pillow. The top lay there, its cord trailing, a little dirty now from the sidewalk. She picked it up and turned it over in her hands.

"Where did you get this?"

The boy looked at the floor. His foot went up over the other foot. He said nothing.

"Did you take money out of my purse?"

Still he said nothing, but his face reddened slowly from the neck upward, and his lower lip began to tremble. Mrs. Kessler sat down on the bed beside him. Her first feeling was not anger but a kind of sick dismay, compounded of pity for the child and fear for what her husband would say. She knew Martin. She knew that a thing of this kind, which to her seemed sad and small, would seem to him enormous. She thought for a moment of saying nothing—of replacing the dime from the little store she kept separately for emergencies, and of letting the matter go. But she was an honest woman, and she was afraid, too, of what might come if the thing were hidden and afterward found out.

"You stay here," she said. "Your father will be home soon." And she went downstairs with the top in her apron pocket, feeling heavier than when she had come up.

Kessler came in at a quarter past six, as he always did. He took off his coat and hung it upon the nail behind the kitchen door, washed his hands and face at the sink, and sat down at the table. The kitchen was warm, and smelled of boiled cabbage and of the potatoes frying upon the stove. He was tired, as he always was at this hour, and he looked forward, as he always did, to his supper and his pipe. His wife set his plate before him without speaking. He noticed this, for she was ordinarily talkative at this hour, telling him the small news of the street and the house.

"Where's Willie?" he said.

"Upstairs."

"Is he sick, too?"

"No." She hesitated, standing by the stove with the fork in her hand. "Martin, I want to tell you something. I don't want you to be too hard."

He looked at her. "What is it?"

She took the top from her pocket and laid it on the oilcloth beside his plate. "He took ten cents out of my purse this afternoon and bought that."

Kessler looked at the top for a long moment without touching it. His face did not change greatly, but a certain stillness came into it, and his jaw set. He was not thinking of the dime. Ten cents was nothing—or rather, it was something, but it was not the thing. What he was thinking of, though he could not have put it into words, was a vague and terrible picture which the very word stealing called up in him: the jail on Michigan Avenue, the men he had seen led through the streets by policemen, the young loafers who stood about the saloon corners on Halsted Street at night and who, as everybody knew, would come to no good. He thought of his own father, a carter in a village near Hanover, who had whipped him once, when he was eight, for taking an apple from a neighbour's tree, and who had said to him then, in German, words which he had never forgotten: "A thief begins with an apple." It seemed to Kessler, sitting there in his own kitchen with the gas-light falling upon the cheap red-and-yellow toy, that he stood at the edge of some dark place, and that his son was already halfway into it.

"Bring him down," he said.

"Martin——"

"Bring him down."

She went up. Kessler sat motionless, his supper growing cold before him. He heard the creak of the stairs, and then the boy came in ahead of his mother, slowly, with his hands at his sides, and stopped by the door. He did not look at his father. He looked at the top lying upon the table, and his face, which had been pale, flushed again.

"Come here," said Kessler.

The boy came, step by step, and stood beside the table. He was so small, standing there, that his eyes were scarcely higher than the edge of the oilcloth. Kessler looked down at him. Something stirred in him which was not anger, but he put it aside.

"Did you take money from your mother's purse?"

The boy nodded, very slightly.

"Say it. Say yes or no."

"Yes," whispered Willie.

"How much?"

"Ten cents."

"What for?"

The boy's eyes went to the top. He did not answer. He did not know how to answer. How was he to explain the window, and the red and yellow, and the way the thing had seemed to call to him every morning and every noon? There were no words in him for it. He only stood, his foot creeping up over his other foot, his fingers twisting at the seam of his trousers.

"Stand up straight," said Kessler sharply. The foot came down.

"Do you know what you are?" he went on, his voice low and heavy. "You're a thief. That's what a person is that takes what isn't his. A thief. Do you know what they do with thieves?"

The boy shook his head. His eyes had filled now, and the tears stood in them without falling.

"They put them in jail. They lock them up. You've seen the patrol wagon go by on Twelfth Street. That's where thieves go. Do you want to go there?"

"No," said the boy, and now the tears fell.

"Martin," said Mrs. Kessler from the stove, "he's only seven."

"I know how old he is," said Kessler, without turning his head. "That's why I'm telling him now. Now's the time. Not when he's seventeen." He looked again at the boy. "Who works for that money? Tell me that. Who works for it?"

"You do," said Willie, through his sobs.

"I do. Ten hours a day, down there at Wells's, in the heat and the dirt. Six days a week. Do you think I like it? Do you think I go down there because I like it? I go so there's money for the rent, and for something to eat, and for shoes on your feet. And so some day we can get out of this place and have a house of our own. Every penny of it counts. Every penny. And you go and take it and throw it away on a thing like that." He struck the top with the back of his hand, and it rolled across the oilcloth and fell to the floor with a little clatter. The boy flinched as though he had been struck himself.

It is one of the curious facts of human nature that the passion of rebuke, once begun, tends to feed upon itself, and to carry the one who rebukes farther than he had intended to go. Kessler had meant to speak of the dime, and of honesty, and of the jail. But as he spoke he found other things rising in him—his own weariness, the heat of the foundry, the grinding sameness of the years, the house in Humboldt Park which seemed to recede a little further with each winter's coal bill—and these lent a bitterness to his words which had nothing to do with the child before him. He was, without knowing it, scolding the whole order of things which held him where he was, and the boy, who had merely wanted a top, received the full weight of it.

"I never had a top like that," he said. "Not once. When I was your age I was out in the fields picking stones for a farmer, at ten pfennigs a day. Ten pfennigs! And if I'd taken one of them that wasn't mine my father would have broke my back for me. And he'd have been right. You hear me? He'd have been right."

The boy was crying openly now, his shoulders shaking, his face screwed up and wet. He made no sound beyond a kind of catching in his throat. Mrs. Kessler, at the stove, had turned away and was pretending to look after the potatoes, though they were long since done. She could not bear to watch, and yet she could not bear to leave.

"Now you listen to me," said Kessler, lowering his voice somewhat, for the sight of the child's face had begun at last to reach him. "Tomorrow morning you're going to take that thing back to Rubel's. You're going to give it to him and tell him you bought it with money that wasn't yours. And you're going to ask him for the ten cents back, and if he gives it to you, you'll bring it straight here and put it in your mother's hand. And if he don't give it to you, then you'll go without your Sunday penny till it's paid. Ten weeks. Do you understand?"

The boy nodded. The thought of facing Mr. Rubel, of standing in that dim little shop and saying what he had done, filled him with a horror greater than anything his father had yet said. But he nodded.

"Say it."

"Yes, sir."

"And you'll never do a thing like that again."

"No, sir."

"Because if you do," said Kessler, and here he paused, for he had been about to say something about the strap, and something in him held back—"if you do, I don't know what I'll do. I don't know. Now go upstairs. You can go without supper tonight. Go on."

The boy went. They heard his feet upon the stairs, slow and uneven, and then the closing of his door. Mrs. Kessler stooped and picked up the top from the floor and put it on the shelf above the sink, beside the clock. She did not say anything. She brought the frying-pan and put some fresh potatoes upon her husband's plate, and he began to eat, slowly, without appetite.

"You were hard on him," she said at last.

"He needed it."

"Maybe. But he's only a little boy. He didn't know."

"He knew it wasn't his."

She did not answer this. There was nothing to answer. She sat down across from him and poured herself a cup of coffee and held it in both hands without drinking it. The baby, upstairs, had begun to cough, a thin, tight little cough which went on and on. Neither of them moved. Outside, a streetcar went by on Twelfth Street, its bell clanging, and the windows rattled faintly in their frames.

Kessler finished his supper and pushed back his chair. He took his pipe from his pocket and filled it, and then, instead of going out upon the back step, as was his custom, he sat on at the table, looking at the top upon the shelf. It was a cheap thing. Anybody could see it was a cheap thing. The paint was already chipped where it had struck the sidewalk. And yet he could see, too, in a dim way, how it might look to a child—how bright it was, how it would hum and blur. He thought of the window at Rubel's, which he had passed himself a thousand times without seeing, and of all the windows of the city, all the bright things set out in them, and of the people who went by them every day without the money to buy. He had never thought of such matters before. He did not think of them clearly now. They came to him only as a kind of discomfort, a vague unease which he could not name, and which he presently put aside as he had put aside so many things.

"Well," he said, rising, "it's done."

He went out upon the step and smoked his pipe in the dark. The air was chill, and the smoke from the foundries hung low over the roofs. Somewhere a dog was barking. He sat there a long time, longer than usual, and when he came in at last his wife had gone upstairs. He turned out the gas in the kitchen and followed her. At the door of the boy's room he stopped. It was quite dark within, and he could hear the child's breathing, slow and even now, with now and then a small catch in it, the aftermath of crying. He stood listening for some moments. Then, very quietly, he pushed the door open a little way and looked in. The boy lay on his side, one arm flung out over the coverlet, his face turned toward the wall. The light from the street lamp at the corner fell faintly across the bed.

Kessler did not go in. He stood in the doorway, a heavy, tired figure in his stocking feet, and what he felt he could not have said. It was not regret, exactly. He still believed he had done right. But there was mixed with this belief something softer and more troubling—a sense that the world into which his son had been born was larger and harder than the one he himself had known, and that it would take more than a dime returned and a supper missed to see the boy safely through it. He thought of the house in Humboldt Park, and it seemed to him, for the moment, very far away.

"By God," he said under his breath, not knowing just what he meant by it. Then he drew the door to, gently, and went on to bed.
