The rain, which had held off all through the Mortlakes' dinner, began again as the carriage turned into Fifth Avenue, and Kate Durand, leaning back in her corner, watched it streak the glass with long oblique threads that the street-lamps caught and lost again. Her husband sat beside her in the silence he generally kept after an evening out: a silence she had once taken for fatigue, later for indifference, and had lately learned to regard as a kind of tacit accounting, a summing-up of the hours just passed, in which she suspected that her own part was entered on the smaller side of the ledger. She had always admired his capacity for silence. It had seemed to her, in the first years of their marriage, the sign of a mind too well-furnished to need the noise of talk. She knew now that it was merely the sign of a mind that did not care to be overheard.

She had resolved, somewhere between the fish and the entrée, that she would speak to him that night; and the resolution had sustained her through the rest of the dinner, through the long half-hour in Mrs. Mortlake's drawing-room, where the ladies sat in a lustrous semicircle and discussed the new rector's wife, and even through the moment, ten minutes later, when the gentlemen came in and Philip, with his usual unhurried grace, crossed the room to the sofa where Mrs. Verrall sat alone. Kate had watched him go with the detached interest she might have given to a well-rehearsed scene in a play whose ending she already knew. It was not the crossing of the room that mattered; any man might cross a room to speak to a pretty woman sitting alone. It was the fact that Mrs. Verrall, as he approached, had not looked up.

The carriage drew up before their door, and Philip handed her out under the dripping awning with the same attentive courtesy he had shown her for eleven years. She had once thought that courtesy the finest thing about him; she still thought it very fine, as one admires the carving on a door one has ceased to expect will open.

In the hall the servants had left a lamp burning, and the fire in the small sitting-room behind the library had been made up for their return. It was the room Kate liked best in the house, partly because it was the smallest, and partly because it was the only one her mother-in-law had not furnished. Philip followed her in, as he usually did, to glance at the evening paper before going up; and she saw him take it from the table and unfold it, standing with his back to the fire, while she drew off her gloves slowly, finger by finger, as if the operation required all her attention.

"Mrs. Verrall looked extremely well tonight," she said.

He did not lower the paper at once. When he did, it was with a slight lift of the eyebrows that conveyed nothing more than a polite readiness to be interested in whatever she might choose to say.

"Did she? I don't know that I noticed particularly. The Mortlakes' lamps are so abominably shaded that one can never see anybody's face."

"Oh, one could see her face," Kate said. "And her wrists."

She laid the gloves on the table, side by side, and smoothed them with her hand. She had not meant to say it so soon; she had planned a longer approach, a series of small ascending steps, each one of which he might mount without perceiving that he was climbing. But the words had come of themselves, and having come, they hung in the warm air of the room with a kind of insolent distinctness, like a picture suddenly unveiled in a gallery where everyone had been talking of something else.

Philip folded the paper and laid it down. He did this deliberately, creasing it along its original folds, and Kate, watching his long fingers, reflected that she had never in her life seen him do anything in a hurry. Even his courtship had been conducted with a leisurely assurance that her family had taken for the confidence of an honourable man, and that she herself, at nineteen, had found more thrilling than any ardour.

"Her wrists?" he repeated pleasantly.

"She was wearing a very handsome bracelet. Sapphires, set very close, in a kind of chain. I noticed it because I had seen one like it before."

"Had you? Where?"

"In a description," said Kate. "On a bill from Ditmar's. It came here, in October, by mistake. Bassett put it with my letters instead of yours, and I opened it before I saw the name."

She had wondered, many times in the last six weeks, what his face would do when she told him; and now that she was watching it she was conscious of a faint, unreasonable disappointment, as if she had been promised a spectacle and cheated of it. His face did nothing at all. It remained the face she had always known: a little too long, a little too pale, with the fine dry lines about the eyes that the world called distinguished and that she had once traced with her finger in the dark. Only, after a moment, he turned and pushed a log farther back on the andirons with the toe of his shoe, so that she could no longer see his eyes.

"I'm sorry it should have come to you," he said. "That was careless of Ditmar's."

"It was careless of somebody."

He straightened himself and looked at her again; and now she perceived that something had altered after all, though it was not what she had expected. It was not guilt, nor anger, nor even embarrassment; it was a kind of watchful attention, the look of a man who has been playing a game he thought he understood and finds his opponent has introduced a new rule.

"I suppose," he said, "you have been keeping this for some time."

"Since the eleventh of October."

"That is a long while to keep anything."

"I have had a good deal of practice," said Kate.

The clock on the mantelpiece, a small gilt affair with a shepherdess leaning on a broken column, struck the half-hour with a thin, bright note. It had been a wedding present from one of Philip's aunts, and Kate had always disliked it; it seemed to her now to be commenting on the scene with a kind of tinkling irony, as though the shepherdess had witnessed a great many such conversations and found them all rather tiresome.

Philip sat down in the arm-chair on the other side of the hearth. He crossed his legs, and she noticed that he did not offer to light a cigarette, though his hand went once, by habit, toward the pocket where he kept his case.

"Well," he said, "I won't pretend I don't know what you mean. I've never cared for pretending with you, Kate. It has always seemed to me one of the advantages of our situation that we were both too intelligent for it."

She had a sudden sharp desire to laugh. It was so exactly like him to make a virtue of candour at the moment when candour had become the only course left open to him; and so exactly like him, too, to include her in the compliment, as if they were two partners in a well-conducted firm who had always understood each other's methods. She remembered how, in the early days, his habit of treating her as an intelligence had seemed to her the most delicate form of homage, a recognition that set her apart from the women whose husbands talked to them about the weather and their children's teeth. She saw now that it had been merely the most economical way of managing her.

"I didn't ask you to pretend," she said. "I haven't asked you anything."

"No. That's what puzzles me." He looked at her with what seemed genuine curiosity. "You might have spoken six weeks ago. You might have made a scene. Most women would. Instead you've waited until tonight, after we've dined in the same house with her and you've watched her wear the thing, and then you mention it as if you were telling me the carriage was late. I confess I should like to know why."

Kate considered him for a moment before answering. The fire had burned down, and in the reddened light the room seemed smaller and more intimate than usual, the familiar objects drawing closer round them like spectators at a private trial: the little rosewood writing-table where she paid the household bills, the shelf of French novels he had given her in the second year of their marriage and she had never finished, the photograph of their daughter in a silver frame, looking out with the grave unsmiling eyes of a child of nine who has been told to keep still.

"I waited," she said slowly, "because I wanted to be quite sure of what I meant to say. At first I didn't know. I thought of a great many things. I thought of going to my mother; I thought of going to your mother, which would have been worse. I even thought, for about a day, of going to Mrs. Verrall." She saw his lip move slightly at this, and went on with a certain grim satisfaction. "But all those things seemed to lead to the same place, and it wasn't a place I wanted to go. So I waited until I knew what I did want."

"And now you know?"

"Yes. I want to take Nora abroad for the winter. To Paris, and perhaps afterward to Rome. I should like to go by the twentieth of next month."

There was a pause, during which Philip looked at her with an expression she had never seen on his face before, and which it took her a moment to identify. It was respect: the reluctant, half-amused respect of a man who has been out-manoeuvred by someone he had not thought capable of manoeuvring at all.

"I see," he said. "That's all?"

"That's all."

"You don't wish me to give her up? To promise you anything?"

"What would be the use?" said Kate. "You would promise very gracefully, and I should have to believe you, and we should both know that I didn't. I'd rather not have the promise. It would only be one more thing in the house that neither of us looked at."

He got up and walked to the window, where the curtains were drawn against the rain, and stood there with his back to her, his hands in his pockets. She could hear the water running in the gutters of the street outside, and the far-off clatter of a cab going toward the Park.

"You realize," he said without turning, "that people will talk. A woman doesn't go off to Europe for a whole winter, alone with a child, in the middle of the season, without people asking why."

"People will say that Nora's chest is delicate, and that Dr. Ransome advised a change. Dr. Ransome did say something of the kind last spring; I have only to remind him of it. And people will say that it's very sad for you to be left alone, and that you bear it beautifully." She paused. "You will bear it beautifully, Philip. You always do."

He swung round at that, and for an instant she saw in his face a flash of something like anger: not the cold, contained displeasure she had known him to show to tradesmen and incompetent servants, but a quicker, warmer, more human emotion, as if her words had touched him in some place he had believed to be safely covered. It was gone almost as soon as she had seen it, and he came back to the fire and stood looking down at her with his usual composure.

"You've thought it all out very carefully," he said.

"I've had six weeks."

"And the expense? You know how things have been this year. The Southern Pacific business hit us harder than I let you know. A winter in Paris, with a governess and a maid, and the apartment, and the clothes you'll be expected to buy..." He spread his hands in a gesture of reasonable regret. "I don't say it's impossible. But it's a great deal of money, Kate."

She had been waiting for this; she had known, with the certainty that eleven years of marriage confer, that it would come at precisely this point, and in precisely this tone of patient and slightly wounded good sense. And yet, now that it had come, she found that her hands were trembling, and she folded them in her lap to keep him from seeing.

"I know exactly how much money it is," she said. "I have worked it out. It comes, as nearly as I can reckon, to a little less than the bill from Ditmar's."

The silence that followed was the longest of the evening. The shepherdess on the clock leaned upon her broken column; the fire settled with a soft crumbling sound; and somewhere in the upper part of the house a door closed, as one of the servants went to bed. Kate did not look at her husband. She looked at the photograph of her daughter, and thought, with a curious remoteness, of the day it had been taken, and of how Nora had cried afterward because the photographer had made her take off her coral beads.

When Philip spoke at last his voice had changed. It was lower, and had lost its edge of easy irony; and she understood that, for the first time in their life together, he was speaking to her without calculating the effect of his words.

"You're very hard, Kate."

"Am I?" She lifted her eyes to his. "I don't think I am. I think I've only stopped being soft. It isn't quite the same thing, though I daresay it looks the same from where you're standing."

"I never meant to hurt you."

"No," she agreed. "You never meant anything about me at all. That was what I minded, when I first understood it, more than the bracelet, more than her. I used to lie awake and think that if you had hated me, or been tired of me, or even been cruel to me, I should at least have been somebody you thought about. But I wasn't. I was simply the person who ordered the dinners and opened the wrong letters." She gave a little laugh that did not sound like her own. "I don't mean to reproach you. I daresay it's what most marriages come to. Only I found I didn't care to spend the winter watching it."

He was silent again; and she saw that he was looking at her as he might have looked at a stranger whom he had passed every day in the street and suddenly heard speak in a foreign language. It occurred to her, with a pang that was half triumph and half something sadder, that she had at last succeeded in making him think about her, and that it had taken a sapphire bracelet to do it.

"And when you come back?" he asked. "In the spring?"

"In the spring," said Kate, "we shall see. Perhaps I shall find that I've been foolish, and that it doesn't matter after all. Women get used to things; I've seen a great many of them do it, and they seem quite comfortable. Or perhaps I shall find that I like Rome." She rose and gathered up her gloves. "In any case, Nora will have had a winter abroad, and Dr. Ransome will be quite satisfied with her chest."

He did not move to stop her. He stood by the mantelpiece, one hand resting near the gilt clock, and she noticed, as she passed him, that the fine dry lines about his eyes had deepened, so that he looked for a moment older than his years, and oddly tired. She felt a sudden impulse, absurd and unbidden, to put her hand on his sleeve, as she would have done once without thinking; and the impulse frightened her more than anything that had happened that evening, so that she walked quickly to the door before it could overtake her.

"Kate."

She turned on the threshold. He had not moved from the fire.

"You'll want the letter of credit by the first, I suppose."

It was so entirely his manner, the quiet assumption of the practical detail, the graceful acceptance of a fact accomplished, that she understood he had already begun to arrange the matter in his mind, as he arranged everything: the sailing, the bankers, the version of events he would give at his club, the way he would look when people asked him how he managed without her. He would manage very well. He would dine out a great deal, and be thought charming and a little melancholy, and Mrs. Verrall would wear her bracelet at the opera; and it came to her, standing there with her hand on the door, that she had won exactly what she had asked for, and that it was precisely as much as he had always been willing to give.

"The fifteenth will do," she said, "if it's more convenient."

"Oh, the first," he answered. "I shouldn't like you to be put to any inconvenience."

She went out and closed the door behind her, and stood for a moment in the dim hall, listening to the rain. Above her the stairs mounted into darkness, and she remembered that she had not yet told Nora; and the thought of the child's face, grave and unsurprised, as if she, too, had long since learned that most things in that house were settled in small rooms after midnight, was harder to bear than all the rest. She put her hand on the banister and began to climb; and from the sitting-room behind her, faint and clear, the shepherdess struck the hour.

There had never been such a June in Eagle County. Usually it was a month of moods, with abrupt alternations of belated frost and mid-summer heat; this year, day followed day in a sequence of temperate beauty. Every morning a breeze blew steadily from the hills. Toward noon it built up great canopies of white cloud that threw a cool shadow over fields and woods; then before sunset the clouds dissolved again, and the western light rained its unobstructed brightness on the valley. On such an afternoon Charity Royall lay on a ridge above a sunlit hollow, her face pressed to the earth and the warm currents of the grass running through her. The train from New York was due at Westover at ten minutes past four, and by half-past three Miss Anna Brand had twice put on her bonnet and twice taken it off again. It was not that she doubted the hour; she had verified it the evening before in the time-table that hung beside the kitchen door, and again that morning in the newspaper. She had grown thin rather than stout, and that was something; her hair, though it had faded, had not greyed; and she had kept, as women who have lived much alone often keep, a certain stillness of feature which might pass, in a favourable light, for composure. But she knew that composure was the last thing Sophy had ever admired.

The house in which she waited was the one in which they had both been children. It stood at the upper end of the green, a square white house with a fanlight over the door and two elms before it, and it had passed to Anna on her mother's death, together with the furniture, the silver, a modest income, and the settled conviction of the village that Miss Brand would never marry. The conviction was by now so old that it had ceased to be a reproach and had become a kind of distinction; and Anna, who had at first resented it, had come in time to wear it as she wore her mother's cameo, as a thing belonging to her station. She had nursed her mother for eleven years, and her father for four before that; she had sat on the committee of the Library and the Ladies' Aid; she had read a great many books and travelled once to Boston and once to Quebec; and she had learned, as the years went by, to regard the narrowness of her life with the mixture of pride and resignation with which some people regard an inherited infirmity.

Sophy, meanwhile, had married. She had married, at nineteen, a man named Etherege, who had come up from New York for the shooting and had stayed on through a whole October because of her; and she had gone away with him to live first in Paris and then in Florence and then, as the letters grew rarer, in a succession of places whose names Anna had found on the map with a sense of being let, through a crack in a door, into a lighted and populous room. The letters had stopped altogether some fifteen years ago. There had been a line, after that, in a New York paper, announcing Mr. Etherege's death at San Remo; and Anna had written, and had received in reply a black-bordered card with three words on it in Sophy's sprawling hand. Then nothing, until the note of the week before, dated from a hotel in Fifth Avenue, which said that Sophy was "home for a little while" and wanted, "more than anything in the world," to see Westover again and the dear old house and Anna.

Anna had read the note many times, and each time it had seemed to her more like Sophy and less like anything she could account for. "More than anything in the world" was Sophy's; it was the phrase she had used at twelve about a pony and at seventeen about a ball; but the "little while," and the absence of any mention of plans, of friends, of the people she had been living among, struck a note that Anna did not recognise, and that troubled her, as an unfamiliar sound in a familiar house troubles one at night.

She walked to the station after all, though Hannah's nephew had offered to drive her, because she wanted the ten minutes of solitude on the road. It was a still afternoon at the end of October, with that suspended look which the New England country wears between the burning of the maples and the first snow. The fields were tawny; the stone walls ran grey and crooked over the low hills; and along the edge of the road the asters and goldenrod had gone to a brown fluff which caught the light like the down on a bird's breast. Far off, the river showed between the alders in long bright strips, and the smoke of a brush fire hung over the Dawson pasture without stirring. Anna had walked that road so many thousand times that she had ceased to see it; but today, because she was trying to imagine how it would look to Sophy, she saw it with a strange double vision, as if she were at once a stranger arriving and a ghost revisiting, and she was surprised to find that it was beautiful.

The train was late, and when it came there descended from it, besides two drummers and the Methodist minister's wife, a small woman in black who stood for a moment on the platform looking about her with a quick, bird-like turn of the head that Anna would have known among a thousand. The figure had thickened a little, and the face under the dotted veil had the indeterminate look of a picture seen through glass; but the gesture with which she lifted the veil, and the exclamation that accompanied it, carried Anna back across the years so abruptly that she felt the blood rush to her cheeks.

"Anna! Oh, my dear, you haven't changed in the least!"

It was so exactly what Anna had foreseen she would say, and so exactly what was not true, that the two women laughed together as they kissed; and the laugh, which might have been awkward, became instead a kind of bridge, over which they passed, still holding hands, to the little group of trunks and bags that the baggage-man was setting down beside them.

There was only one trunk, Anna noticed; and it was not new.

They walked back to the house, Sophy having declared that she would not be driven "for anything," and that she wanted to feel the road under her feet. She talked all the way, in the rapid, slightly breathless voice that Anna remembered, but with a foreign inflection in it now, a way of dropping her sentences at the end as if she expected the listener to supply the rest. She exclaimed at the elms, at the church spire, at the new brick front of the Savings Bank, at old Mr. Dawson's Jersey cow looking over the bars; she remembered names that Anna had forgotten, and confused others that Anna had supposed no one could forget. And all the while, beneath the bright surface of her talk, Anna was aware of something watchful and arrested, as though her cousin were listening for a sound that did not come.

"And you've stayed here all this time," Sophy said, when they had reached the gate and stood looking up at the fanlight. "All this time! I used to think of you, you know, at the oddest moments, at dinners and in hotel bedrooms, and wonder what you were doing at that very minute. I always pictured you sitting in the window over there with a book. Were you?"

"Very often, I suppose," Anna said, smiling. It occurred to her that she had been sitting in the window with a book on a great many evenings when Sophy was certainly not thinking of her; but she did not say so. She had a sudden vision of all those evenings stacked one upon another, like the leaves of a closed volume, and of Sophy turning them over with a light, curious finger.

Hannah had laid tea in the parlour, and the fire, which had been lit at three, had settled into a steady glow behind the brass fender. Sophy took off her bonnet and her gloves (Anna saw that the gloves had been carefully mended at the finger-tips) and sank into the wing-chair that had been Anna's mother's, stretching her small feet to the blaze.

"Aunt Lucy's chair," she said. "I always wanted to sit in it, and she never let me. Do you remember? She said it would spoil me for plain chairs. I suppose she was right." She laughed, and looked round the room. "Nothing has moved. The Copley engraving, and the shell-box, and the clock that stops at a quarter to three. Does it still stop at a quarter to three?"

"It hasn't gone at all since Mother died," Anna said. "I never had it seen to."

Sophy looked at her for a moment with an expression which Anna could not read. "No," she said slowly, "I don't suppose you would."

They talked, over the tea, of the family: of Uncle Ezra's death, and the scandal about the Hartford mortgage, and Cousin Mattie's marriage to the Baptist minister, and the twins who had gone west and done so surprisingly well in lumber. It was the kind of talk that serves between relations as a means at once of approach and of postponement; and Anna, who had dreaded the first hours, found herself grateful for the thick, familiar web of names into which she could weave her small contributions without fear of breaking a thread. But as the light faded from the windows, and Hannah came in to draw the curtains and light the lamp, she became aware that they had been speaking for more than an hour and that Sophy had said nothing whatever about herself.

It was this silence, more than the mended gloves or the solitary trunk, that told her what she had already half guessed; and the knowledge, when it came, brought with it a feeling she had not expected and was ashamed to recognise. It was not pity, though pity was part of it. It was something nearer to the sensation of a person who, having stood all her life outside a lighted house, is told at last that the rooms within were cold.

She had no intention of putting a question. It was one of the principles of her upbringing, and she had found it a serviceable one, that people who wished to be asked things would contrive to be asked them, and that people who did not had a right to their reserves. But Sophy, setting down her cup with a little clatter, forestalled her.

"You're wondering why I've come," she said. "You needn't pretend you're not, Anna; you always had the most transparent face in the county. Well, I'll tell you, and then it will be over. I've come because I had nowhere else to go."

Anna said nothing. The clock on the mantel, which did not go, gave out in the lamplight the faint gleam of its gilded hands.

"Oh, it isn't as bad as it sounds," Sophy went on, with a little shrug that was wholly un-American. "I have something. Enough to live on, in a small way, in some small place. But Walter left things in such a muddle—you never knew Walter, did you? No, of course not. He was the most charming man in Europe, and he hadn't the least idea what a dollar was. We lived for years on what he called expectations. And when the expectations came to nothing, and he died, I found that the people who had been our friends had really been his, and that the ones who had been mine had only been—well, the kind one has in hotels." She paused, and looked into the fire. "It's a curious thing, Anna, to find out at forty-three that one has been living in a house with no foundations. One doesn't notice, you see, as long as the music is playing."

"I'm very sorry," Anna said; and the inadequacy of the words seemed to her so great that she coloured as she spoke them.

But Sophy only smiled. "You needn't be. I had it all, you know—everything I wanted when I was nineteen and used to sit in that window-seat and cry because nothing ever happened in Westover. Things happened. I went to the opera in Vienna and was presented at Rome and danced with a Grand Duke at Cannes; and I would have died rather than miss any of it. Only, when it was over, I found I couldn't remember it very well. It was like a long dinner where all the courses are good and you can't recall a single dish afterward." She turned her head and looked at her cousin with a sudden directness. "Whereas I imagine you remember everything."

"There isn't so very much to remember," Anna said.

"Isn't there?" Sophy leaned forward, her chin on her hand, in the attitude which, at sixteen, had made her the despair of her governess and the admiration of the curate. "I wonder. Do you remember the summer at the Point, the year before I married? The summer the Lowndes boy was there?"

Anna felt the colour mount again to her forehead, and she was glad of the lamp-shade. She remembered the summer at the Point as one remembers a room in which a window was once opened upon a view and then closed for ever. She remembered the sound of the bathing-bell, and the smell of the bayberry on the dunes, and the evening on the porch of the old hotel when Harry Lowndes had sat beside her for an hour and talked to her of books, of a world of ideas she had only glimpsed through the windows of her father's library, while the others danced inside. She remembered how he had walked with her the next morning to the lighthouse; and how, that same evening, he had danced every dance with Sophy; and how, before the month was out, he had gone away to Colorado without a word to either of them, and had died there of a fever two years afterward. She had never spoken his name aloud since the day she read of his death; she had not supposed that anyone else remembered it.

"I remember him," she said.

"I thought you would." Sophy was silent for a moment, turning her wedding-ring about her finger. "I've wanted to tell you something about that summer for twenty years, and I've never had the courage, or perhaps the occasion. It seems foolish now. It can't matter to anyone. But I've found lately that the things that can't matter are the only ones I think about." She raised her eyes. "He meant to ask you to marry him, Anna."

The room was very still. Somewhere in the back of the house Hannah was rattling the stove-lid, and the sound came to Anna as though from a great distance, from the other side of a wide and silent water.

"He told me so himself," Sophy went on, in a low, rapid voice. "The night of the Hendersons' party, on the steps of the bath-house. He said you were the only girl he had ever met who understood what he was talking about, and that he was going to speak to Uncle Robert the next day. And I—" She broke off, and gave a little laugh that was not quite steady. "I was nineteen, and bored to death, and I had never had anyone look at me as he looked at you. It wasn't that I wanted him. I don't think I ever wanted him for a moment. I only wanted not to be the one who was passed over. So I made him dance with me, and I made him walk with me, and I let him think—I don't know what I let him think. I was very clever in those days, Anna; you never knew how clever. And by the time he understood that I had been amusing myself it was too late to go back to you with any self-respect, and he was too proud to try. So he went away." She drew a long breath. "There. I've said it. I suppose you hate me."

Anna did not answer at once. She was conscious, as she sat there with her hands folded in her lap, of a strange and almost physical sensation, as though the walls of the room, which she had known all her life, had softly withdrawn a little distance, and the furniture with them, leaving her in a space larger and emptier and at the same time more alive than any she had ever occupied. For twenty-two years she had believed that she had imagined it all: that the hour on the porch and the walk to the lighthouse had been a kindness, a young man's courtesy to a plain girl whom her prettier cousin had left alone; and she had built upon that belief, as one builds upon a rock, the whole quiet edifice of her renunciations. It had been, in its way, a consolation, for one cannot mourn what one never had. And now, in a single sentence, her cousin had taken the consolation from her and given her instead something infinitely more precious and infinitely more painful: the knowledge that her life had once stood at a turning, and had been turned.

"No," she said at last, and was surprised at the steadiness of her own voice. "I don't hate you, Sophy. I don't think I could."

"You ought to," said Sophy. "Anyone else would."

"Perhaps." Anna looked into the fire, where a log had broken and settled into a bed of rosy ash. "But you see, if you had not told me, I should never have known that it was true. I should have gone on thinking that I had made it all up. And that—" she hesitated, and then went on, with the deliberation of a person who is finding her way in the dark—"that would have been worse, I think. It is something, after all, to have been chosen, even if one was not taken."

Sophy stared at her; and then, with a sudden movement, she rose from the wing-chair and knelt on the hearth-rug beside her cousin and laid her head, as she had done in the nursery after a quarrel, against Anna's knee.

"Oh, Anna," she said, "you were always so much better than I. That was what I could never forgive."

They sat so for a long time, while the lamp hummed faintly on the table and the fire sank lower behind the fender. Anna's hand rested on her cousin's hair, which was thinner than it had been, and streaked, she now saw, with a grey that the dye had not quite concealed; and she felt, as she looked down at the bowed head, a tenderness so deep and so unlooked-for that it frightened her. It seemed to her that she had been waiting all her life for something to happen in that room, and that now, when it had happened, it was not at all what she had expected, and yet was the only thing that could have happened.

When Hannah came at last to announce supper, Sophy had gone back to the wing-chair and was talking, in her quick, bright, foreign voice, of a hotel in Lucerne where the waiters had all been Italian counts. Anna listened, and laughed in the right places, and helped her cousin up the stairs afterward to the spare room, where the fire had been lit and the bed turned down and a stone bottle put between the sheets. And when she had said good night, and had gone back alone to the parlour to put out the lamp, she stood for a while before the mantel, looking at the clock with its gilded hands fixed for ever at a quarter to three.

To-morrow, she thought, she would have it seen to. It was absurd to keep a clock that did not go. And then, with a smile that no one saw, she reflected that Sophy would very likely want to stay the winter, and that the spare room would need new curtains, and that it would be pleasant, after all, to have someone to read aloud to in the evenings; and she turned down the wick and went up through the dark house to bed.

Here is an excerpt of Edith Wharton's writing, to show you their style:

There had never been such a June in Eagle County. Usually it was a month of moods, with abrupt alternations of belated frost and mid-summer heat; this year, day followed day in a sequence of temperate beauty. Every morning a breeze blew steadily from the hills. Toward noon it built up great canopies of white cloud that threw a cool shadow over fields and woods; then before sunset the clouds dissolved again, and the western light rained its unobstructed brightness on the valley. On such an afternoon Charity Royall lay on a ridge above a sunlit hollow, her face pressed to the earth and the warm currents of the grass running through her. Directly in her line of vision a blackberry branch laid its frail white flowers and blue-green leaves against the sky. Just beyond, a tuft of sweet-fern uncurled between the beaded shoots of the grass, and a small yellow butterfly vibrated over them like a fleck of sunshine. This was all she saw; but she felt, above her and about her, the strong growth of the beeches clothing the ridge, the rounding of pale green cones on countless spruce-branches, the push of myriads of sweet-fern fronds in the cracks of the stony slope below the wood, and the crowding shoots of meadowsweet and yellow flags in the pasture beyond. All this bubbling of sap and slipping of sheaths and bursting of calyxes was carried to her on mingled currents of fragrance. Every leaf and bud and blade seemed to contribute its exhalation to the pervading sweetness in which the pungency of pine-sap prevailed over the spice of thyme and the subtle perfume of fern, and all were merged in a moist earth-smell that was like the breath of some huge sun-warmed animal. Charity had lain there a long time, passive and sun-warmed as the slope on which she lay, when there came between her eyes and the dancing butterfly the sight of a man's foot in a large worn boot covered with red mud.

“Oh, don't!” she exclaimed, raising herself on her elbow and stretching out a warning hand.

“Don't what?” a hoarse voice asked above her head.

“Don't stamp on those bramble flowers, you dolt!” she retorted, springing to her knees. The foot paused and then descended clumsily on the frail branch, and raising her eyes she saw above her the bewildered face of a slouching man with a thin sunburnt beard, and white arms showing through his ragged shirt.

“Don't you ever SEE anything, Liff Hyatt?” she assailed him, as he stood before her with the look of a man who has stirred up a wasp's nest. He grinned. “I seen you! That's what I come down for.”

“Down from where?” she questioned, stooping to gather up the petals his foot had scattered. He jerked his thumb toward the heights. “Been cutting down trees for Dan Targatt.” Charity sank back on her heels and looked at him musingly. She was not in the least afraid of poor Liff Hyatt, though he “came from the Mountain,” and some of the girls ran when they saw him. Among the more reasonable he passed for a harmless creature, a sort of link between the mountain and civilized folk, who occasionally came down and did a little wood cutting for a farmer when hands were short. Besides, she knew the Mountain people would never hurt her: Liff himself had told her so once when she was a little girl, and had met him one day at the edge of lawyer Royall's pasture. “They won't any of 'em touch you up there, f'ever you was to come up.... But I don't s'pose you will,” he had added philosophically, looking at her new shoes, and at the red ribbon that Mrs. Royall had tied in her hair. Charity had, in truth, never felt any desire to visit her birthplace. She did not care to have it known that she was of the Mountain, and was shy of being seen in talk with Liff Hyatt. But today she was not sorry to have him appear. A great many things had happened to her since the day when young Lucius Harney had entered the doors of the Hatchard Memorial, but none, perhaps, so unforeseen as the fact of her suddenly finding it a convenience to be on good terms with Liff Hyatt. She continued to look up curiously at his freckled weather-beaten face, with feverish hollows below the cheekbones and the pale yellow eyes of a harmless animal. “I wonder if he's related to me?” she thought, with a shiver of disdain.

“Is there any folks living in the brown house by the swamp, up under Porcupine?” she presently asked in an indifferent tone. Liff Hyatt, for a while, considered her with surprise; then he scratched his head and shifted his weight from one tattered sole to the other.

“There's always the same folks in the brown house,” he said with his vague grin.

“They're from up your way, ain't they?”

“Their name's the same as mine,” he rejoined uncertainly. Charity still held him with resolute eyes. “See here, I want to go there some day and take a gentleman with me that's boarding with us. He's up in these parts drawing pictures.” She did not offer to explain this statement. It was too far beyond Liff Hyatt's limitations for the attempt to be worth making. “He wants to see the brown house, and go all over it,” she pursued. Liff was still running his fingers perplexedly through his shock of straw-colored hair. “Is it a fellow from the city?” he asked.

“Yes. He draws pictures of things. He's down there now drawing the Bonner house.” She pointed to a chimney just visible over the dip of the pasture below the wood.

“The Bonner house?” Liff echoed incredulously.

“Yes. You won't understand—and it don't matter. All I say is: he's going to the Hyatts' in a day or two.” Liff looked more and more perplexed. “Bash is ugly sometimes in the afternoons.” She threw her head back, her eyes full on Hyatt's. “I'm coming too: you tell him.”

“They won't none of them trouble you, the Hyatts won't. What d'you want a take a stranger with you though?”

“I've told you, haven't I? You've got to tell Bash Hyatt.” He looked away at the blue mountains on the horizon; then his gaze dropped to the chimney-top below the pasture.

“He's down there now?”

“Yes.” He shifted his weight again, crossed his arms, and continued to survey the distant landscape. “Well, so long,” he said at last, inconclusively; and turning away he shambled up the hillside. From the ledge above her, he paused to call down: “I wouldn't go there a Sunday”; then he clambered on till the trees closed in on him. Presently, from high overhead, Charity heard the ring of his axe. She lay on the warm ridge, thinking of many things that the woodsman's appearance had stirred up in her. She knew nothing of her early life, and had never felt any curiosity about it: only a sullen reluctance to explore the corner of her memory where certain blurred images lingered. But all that had happened to her within the last few weeks had stirred her to the sleeping depths. She had become absorbingly interesting to herself, and everything that had to do with her past was illuminated by this sudden curiosity. She hated more than ever the fact of coming from the Mountain; but it was no longer indifferent to her. Everything that in any way affected her was alive and vivid: even the hateful things had grown interesting because they were a part of herself.

“I wonder if Liff Hyatt knows who my mother was?” she mused; and it filled her with a tremor of surprise to think that some woman who was once young and slight, with quick motions of the blood like hers, had carried her in her breast, and watched her sleeping. She had always thought of her mother as so long dead as to be no more than a nameless pinch of earth; but now it occurred to her that the once-young woman might be alive, and wrinkled and elf-locked like the woman she had sometimes seen in the door of the brown house that Lucius Harney wanted to draw. The thought brought him back to the central point in her mind, and she strayed away from the conjectures roused by Liff Hyatt's presence. Speculations concerning the past could not hold her long when the present was so rich, the future so rosy, and when Lucius Harney, a stone's throw away, was bending over his sketch-book, frowning, calculating, measuring, and then throwing his head back with the sudden smile that had shed its brightness over everything. She scrambled to her feet, but as she did so she saw him coming up the pasture and dropped down on the grass to wait. When he was drawing and measuring one of “his houses,” as she called them, she often strayed away by herself into the woods or up the hillside. It was partly from shyness that she did so: from a sense of inadequacy that came to her most painfully when her companion, absorbed in his job, forgot her ignorance and her inability to follow his least allusion, and plunged into a monologue on art and life. To avoid the awkwardness of listening with a blank face, and also to escape the surprised stare of the inhabitants of the houses before which he would abruptly pull up their horse and open his sketch-book, she slipped away to some spot from which, without being seen, she could watch him at work, or at least look down on the house he was drawing. She had not been displeased, at first, to have it known to North Dormer and the neighborhood that she was driving Miss Hatchard's cousin about the country in the buggy he had hired of lawyer Royall. She had always kept to herself, contemptuously aloof from village love-making, without exactly knowing whether her fierce pride was due to the sense of her tainted origin, or whether she was reserving herself for a more brilliant fate. Sometimes she envied the other girls their sentimental preoccupations, their long hours of inarticulate philandering with one of the few youths who still lingered in the village; but when she pictured herself curling her hair or putting a new ribbon on her hat for Ben Fry or one of the Sollas boys the fever dropped and she relapsed into indifference. Now she knew the meaning of her disdains and reluctances. She had learned what she was worth when Lucius Harney, looking at her for the first time, had lost the thread of his speech, and leaned reddening on the edge of her desk. But another kind of shyness had been born in her: a terror of exposing to vulgar perils the sacred treasure of her happiness. She was not sorry to have the neighbors suspect her of “going with” a young man from the city; but she did not want it known to all the countryside how many hours of the long June days she spent with him. What she most feared was that the inevitable comments should reach Mr. Royall. Charity was instinctively aware that few things concerning her escaped the eyes of the silent man under whose roof she lived; and in spite of the latitude which North Dormer accorded to courting couples she had always felt that, on the day when she showed too open a preference, Mr. Royall might, as she phrased it, make her “pay for it.” How, she did not know; and her fear was the greater because it was undefinable. If she had been accepting the attentions of one of the village youths she would have been less apprehensive: Mr. Royall could not prevent her marrying when she chose to. But everybody knew that “going with a city fellow” was a different and less straightforward affair: almost every village could show a victim of the perilous venture. And her dread of Mr. Royall's intervention gave a sharpened joy to the hours she spent with young Harney, and made her, at the same time, shy of being too generally seen with him. As he approached she rose to her knees, stretching her arms above her head with the indolent gesture that was her way of expressing a profound well-being.

“I'm going to take you to that house up under Porcupine,” she announced.

“What house? Oh, yes; that ramshackle place near the swamp, with the gipsy-looking people hanging about. It's curious that a house with traces of real architecture should have been built in such a place. But the people were a sulky-looking lot—do you suppose they'll let us in?”

“They'll do whatever I tell them,” she said with assurance. He threw himself down beside her. “Will they?” he rejoined with a smile. “Well, I should like to see what's left inside the house. And I should like to have a talk with the people. Who was it who was telling me the other day that they had come down from the Mountain?” Charity shot a sideward look at him. It was the first time he had spoken of the Mountain except as a feature of the landscape. What else did he know about it, and about her relation to it? Her heart began to beat with the fierce impulse of resistance which she instinctively opposed to every imagined slight.

“The Mountain? I ain't afraid of the Mountain!” Her tone of defiance seemed to escape him. He lay breast-down on the grass, breaking off sprigs of thyme and pressing them against his lips. Far off, above the folds of the nearer hills, the Mountain thrust itself up menacingly against a yellow sunset.

“I must go up there some day: I want to see it,” he continued. Her heart-beats slackened and she turned again to examine his profile. It was innocent of all unfriendly intention.

“What'd you want to go up the Mountain for?”

“Why, it must be rather a curious place. There's a queer colony up there, you know: sort of out-laws, a little independent kingdom. Of course you've heard them spoken of; but I'm told they have nothing to do with the people in the valleys—rather look down on them, in fact. I suppose they're rough customers; but they must have a good deal of character.” She did not quite know what he meant by having a good deal of character; but his tone was expressive of admiration, and deepened her dawning curiosity. It struck her now as strange that she knew so little about the Mountain. She had never asked, and no one had ever offered to enlighten her. North Dormer took the Mountain for granted, and implied its disparagement by an intonation rather than by explicit criticism.

“It's queer, you know,” he continued, “that, just over there, on top of that hill, there should be a handful of people who don't give a damn for anybody.” The words thrilled her. They seemed the clue to her own revolts and defiances, and she longed to have him tell her more.

“I don't know much about them. Have they always been there?”

“Nobody seems to know exactly how long. Down at Creston they told me that the first colonists are supposed to have been men who worked on the railway that was built forty or fifty years ago between Springfield and Nettleton. Some of them took to drink, or got into trouble with the police, and went off—disappeared into the woods. A year or two later there was a report that they were living up on the Mountain. Then I suppose others joined them—and children were born. Now they say there are over a hundred people up there. They seem to be quite outside the jurisdiction of the valleys. No school, no church—and no sheriff ever goes up to see what they're about. But don't people ever talk of them at North Dormer?”

“I don't know. They say they're bad.” He laughed. “Do they? We'll go and see, shall we?” She flushed at the suggestion, and turned her face to his. “You never heard, I suppose—I come from there. They brought me down when I was little.”

“You?” He raised himself on his elbow, looking at her with sudden interest. “You're from the Mountain? How curious! I suppose that's why you're so different....” Her happy blood bathed her to the forehead. He was praising her—and praising her because she came from the Mountain!

“Am I... different?” she triumphed, with affected wonder.

“Oh, awfully!” He picked up her hand and laid a kiss on the sunburnt knuckles.

“Come,” he said, “let's be off.” He stood up and shook the grass from his loose grey clothes. “What a good day! Where are you going to take me tomorrow?”

Usually it was a month of moods, with abrupt alternations of belated frost and mid-summer heat; this year, day followed day in a sequence of temperate beauty. Just beyond, a tuft of sweet-fern uncurled between the beaded shoots of the grass, and a small yellow butterfly vibrated over them like a fleck of sunshine. This was all she saw; but she felt, above her and about her, the strong growth of the beeches clothing the ridge, the rounding of pale green cones on countless spruce-branches, the push of myriads of sweet-fern fronds in the cracks of the stony slope below the wood, and the crowding shoots of meadowsweet and yellow flags in the pasture beyond. All this bubbling of sap and slipping of sheaths and bursting of calyxes was carried to her on mingled currents of fragrance. Every leaf and bud and blade seemed to contribute its exhalation to the pervading sweetness in which the pungency of pine-sap prevailed over the spice of thyme and the subtle perfume of fern, and all were merged in a moist earth-smell that was like the breath of some huge sun-warmed animal. “Oh, don't!” she exclaimed, raising herself on her elbow and stretching out a warning hand.

“Don't what?” a hoarse voice asked above her head.

“Don't stamp on those bramble flowers, you dolt!” she retorted, springing to her knees. The foot paused and then descended clumsily on the frail branch, and raising her eyes she saw above her the bewildered face of a slouching man with a thin sunburnt beard, and white arms showing through his ragged shirt.

“Down from where?” she questioned, stooping to gather up the petals his foot had scattered. He jerked his thumb toward the heights. “Been cutting down trees for Dan Targatt.” Charity sank back on her heels and looked at him musingly. She was not in the least afraid of poor Liff Hyatt, though he “came from the Mountain,” and some of the girls ran when they saw him. Among the more reasonable he passed for a harmless creature, a sort of link between the mountain and civilized folk, who occasionally came down and did a little wood cutting for a farmer when hands were short. Besides, she knew the Mountain people would never hurt her: Liff himself had told her so once when she was a little girl, and had met him one day at the edge of lawyer Royall's pasture. “They won't any of 'em touch you up there, f'ever you was to come up.... But I don't s'pose you will,” he had added philosophically, looking at her new shoes, and at the red ribbon that Mrs. Royall had tied in her hair. Charity had, in truth, never felt any desire to visit her birthplace. She did not care to have it known that she was of the Mountain, and was shy of being seen in talk with Liff Hyatt. “They'll do whatever I tell them,” she said with assurance. He threw himself down beside her. “Will they?” he rejoined with a smile. “Well, I should like to see what's left inside the house.
